records.title: Inside the shell of technique
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Inside the shell of technique

ROBERT CUSHMAN
interviews Ronald Pickup

AT 29, AND AFTER five years' service as the National Theatre's most consistently interesting young actor, Ronald Pickup is to play Oedipus--the Sophoclean one--at the National's new junior school, the Young Vic. He follows "Stomp," which is an indication of a catholic repertory if you like, though both, I suppose, could be described as a sort of atavistic. The presence as Jocasta of Hairy Annabel Leventon may strengthen the link as well as adding a final ingredient to the confusion of ages that must always surround this play. No wonder he had a complex.

National Theatre productions usually rehearse for about two months; Pickup has been at this one for only three and a half weeks, and a month ago he thought he was playing Creon. He is not an obvious choice for either role, and one pauses, in the middle of patting the Young Vic on the back for their enterprising casting, to reflect on how few obvious Pickup parts there are anyway. In a company in which most actors are known quantities, or quickly become so, he has remained remarkably open.

He has some definite, if paradoxical, advantages. His voice is conventionally pleasant, and his appearance, in his own words, "tall and thin and fairly angular." Everybody's idea of a sensitive young actor, in fact. Perhaps the closest he has come to being type-cast was when he took over from Edward Petherbridge (similar in shape, but sardonically individual in utterance) as Guildenstern in Tom Stoppard's long-running Shakespearean jollity. This part being by definition a "tabula rasa," the result should have been blank on blank and very boring. Actually, though, the part lost something in funniness, it gained in what he called "hopelessness." "You have a personality you draw on for every part; without it you're a shell of technical tricks."

Something unique

With Guildenstern one knew, finally, that there was something unique within the shell, even if its precise identity remained as mysterious as ever. Maybe he should play Kafka; certainly he could play Hamlet (Shakespeare's, not Stoppard's, which confusingly enough he has already done) but, then so could anybody, so we might not be much wiser.

Most of his career has been at the National or the Royal Court. "I've been spoiled; I've not known what it was to be out of work." He comes on as fairly equable, even when interviewed in a lunch-break three days away from Oedipus. One index is that he has stayed in the Waterloo Road while so many other bright young talents have moved on disconsolate. Of course he's had the breaks, but between them he has managed to play small parts without looking obtrusively unselfish.

"It is difficult, too, to think of any actor who could have brought such clarity to Rosalind in the all-male As You Like It." This was the only time I have ever been made to believe that Shakespeare's or anyone else's lines really could be made to speak for themselves. This, considering all the other possibilities inherent in the situation, was a triumph of tact.

The obverse of this, too infrequently seen at the National, is a great comic appetite for the mania of self-absorption. I remember him at the Court in a Jacobean farce capering with gleeful solemnity at one side of the stage while another man prepared to impregnate his wife. His lunatically malevolent Don John in Zeffirelli's "Much Ado About Nothing" was a wrong-headed conception carried out with magnificent abandon, a composite of every mad Mediterranean villain ever beheld.

Outrageous things

Another don, Armado in "Love's Labour's Lost" proved initially beyond him. "I started working too early from a physical picture of him," and the portrait which emerged was grave and a little thin. At Olivier's instigation, he added a Spanish accent and the performance flowered. Olivier "dared me to do outrageous things. There's nothing very subtle for example about 'Juno and the Paycock.' My character, Johnny Boyle, exists in a state of permanent paralytic fright. The temptation is to play it down. Olivier pushed me right over the cliff." And this kind of pushing I think he needs.

He received another kind of impetus from Peter Brook, who put him through "ten weeks of tortured work" in the Senecan "Oedipus," making him realise that "when you're totally committed to an idea it breeds relaxation and confidence." His was the account of Oedipus's blinding delivered with a staccato intensity behind which there echoed the crunch of technical barriers falling to the ground.

Now he has to enact the agony he depicted. The circumstances are different of course. Sophocles is a more compassionate dramatist than Seneca, and where Peter Brook scored the story as "a barbaric mass" Roland Joffe, the Young Vic's inordinately youthful director, is aiming for a more recognisable humanity.

The approach is reflected in the choice of translation, the tried, trusted and surprisingly homely W. B. Yeats version. "Homely" was my own diffident description; the new Oedipus briskly informed me that when he read it first he had found it "banal." He added though that further investigation had revealed it to be "urgent and immediate," and apt for this "short, sharp whirlwind of a play."

As for whether he's yet ready for Oedipus--well, when are you the right age for this "marvellous big child who has reached an extraordinary maturity without achieving self-knowledge? If I'm not going to dare now, I might as well pack up. The older you get, the harder it is to begin taking risks."

records.title: Brecht's man
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Brecht's man

Robert Cushman talks to producer William Gaskill

THERE MUST be those around the Royal Court who cannot quite believe that Brecht's "Man is Man" is actually being staged there. In fact, the present production might almost be regarded as the tenth anniversary celebration of an idea which has been in train since 1961. At that time, of course, the Royal Court's director was the late George Devine, and his principal colleague Tony Richardson. They were assisted by a clutch of young producers, prominent among them Devine's eventual successor, William Gaskill. "Man is Man" is his first Brecht show in some years; all the same, he ranks as the leading practitioner in the (English) field with productions--variously successful--of "The Caucasian Chalk Circle," "Baal," and "Mother Courage" to his credit.

"Man is Man" sets out to demonstrate that a man can be anything you make him. (You are society and you have a lot to answer for.) To survive, Galy Gay, the most pacific of civilians, is forced to take on the identity of Jeriah Jip, the most bloodthirsty of soldiers. Here at any rate is one part that cannot be type-cast. To prove the point: the Devine-Richardson idea was to mount the production as a vehicle for the mountainous Zero Mostel; Gaskill's lead is the infinitesimal Henry Woolf. There was a halfway point at which he envisaged Tony Hancock in the role, a scheme which, alas, went the way of all attempts to involve Hancock in the Higher Drama.

With all this intriguing casting in the air, the decade's delay seems almost inexplicable. High-flying ideas can, of course, be self-defeating and the task of tying down Zero Mostel to dates across the width of the Atlantic must have been a daunting one. Anyway, in the spring of 1962 he went, impenetrably, into a musical. "Only if it flops could he be available," wrote Eric Bentley to Devine. "The New Haven notices, for what comfort it may give you, are bad!" But the show was "A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum" and the New York notices were good.

Bentley's angle was the possibility of the Court using his translation (or one of his translations; he is a tireless reviser). And it was the translation problem which proved even more of an obstacle than the casting. For one thing it hindered the choice of a director, Richardson disliking the Bentley version (which Mostel approved) but unable to come up with a substitute.

Another factor was Stefan Brecht. Brecht's son, American-based, controls the English-speaking rights of his father's plays and he is inclined to hold rigid views about them. For "Man is Man" he stipulated a "Kiplingesque sophisticated music hall quality." One can see the point of the music hall bit, if only because the play contains songs and is constructed as a series of routines. As for Kipling, the action is presumed to take place in British India (though hardly in any era that an historian would recognise) and the association is obvious.

All the same, "Kiplingesque" is an easier word to throw round than to realise in a text; Devine and Gaskill (who by now was slated to direct) thought that Henry Livings might be the man to do it but since Stefan Brecht insisted on vetting a translation before actually agreeing to it, and since Livings was well past the stage of writing on spec, nothing came of it. John Arden, another bright idea, was too tied up with his own plays to undertake it, and in 1968 the most obvious choice of all--Charles Wood--found himself faced with the same unacceptable conditions as Livings.

Besides, Gaskill himself was far from sure that the translation could, or even should, be Kiplingesque.

Gaskill eventually came to think that even if Charles Wood were available "it would mean writing a new play and I am rather keen to do the play as written." Stefan Brecht's thoughts were still of Kipling. "There must," he declared a little puzzlingly, "be many talented young Irishmen around" who would leap at the assignment.

As far as is known no Irish versions arrived on Gaskill's desk but a straight translation by a virtually unknown young playwright named Steve Gooch did. It proved satisfactory to Gaskill, and even got past Stefan Brecht. Maybe he reckoned that 10 years was enough. Gaskill (who declared after his unsuccessful "Mother Courage" at the National Theatre that he would never tackle Brecht again without a first-rate translation ("I think he's too good an author to muck about")) has come to like the Gooch version very much.

"It's very speakable and he has a London ear which has stopped the actors from giving the peasant characters the usual Summerset treatment. English actors just don't look or sound like peasants anyway but they have a very strong 'Dad's Army' tradition of playing soldiers."

The mention of "Dad's Army" prompted a thought about the casting. Henry Woolf has a good deal of the stand-up comic in him and the other leads (Georgia Brown, Trevor Peacock, Roddy Maude-Roxby) are widely experienced in light entertainment. There was no schematic planning about this but, says Gaskill, "the play needs a strong, warm, earthy sort of actor." And he himself feels freer with it than he did with "Courage" since here he has no Berliner Ensemble production to provide a model.

The production might indeed mark a break-through for him. Allegiance to Brecht has given his previous work a dryness which has sometimes run to pedantry. He now wants to move into something rowdier. His notes to the actors have tended to boil down into the classic comedy injunctions to "keep it loud, fast, and funny." (One interesting maxim: "If you have a line like 'It's so dreary' sound cheerful about it.")

"Man is Man" is early Brecht and not strongly political, though the central image of a man brainwashed into another identity has as many reverberations as anyone could wish. "There's a very strange line: 'The difference between Yes and No is not great.' That bears looking at in the light of his later temporising heroes like Galileo and of his own life. The great Brechtian theme is survival. Survival whatever."

IN JULY 1926 Bertolt Brecht abandoned the play he was writing about the American wheat market. He discussed his reasons for doing so with his secretary who noted down a couple of sentences. They were: "Such matters aren't dramatic; and if one writes them up they aren't true any longer, and the drama ceases to be anything of the sort: and as soon as one sees that the modern world is no longer reconcilable with its drama then the drama can no longer be reconciled with the world..."

By "such matters," Brecht meant the way in which the market worked: the social structure; the machinery; the weather; the movement of history. Brecht is essentially a social writer. When he explores the nature of individuality (as in "Man is Man") it is in relation to the society to which the individual belongs.

Brecht's critics often shrug this off as "Marxism" but it is important to realise that his principal ideas were written in both plays and criticism (his "alienation theory" was first propounded in 1922) some years before he became a Marxist. In other words Brecht revealed the degree to which the thought of the twentieth century has been permeated without even realising it by Marxist social and historic ideas. He is a constant reminder that one should distinguish between Marxism and communism as between Christianity and any individual Church.

In the past 150 years Western civilisation has begun to study emotions, history, and social structures in a more systematic manner than before. No doubt there is a connection between the growth of these "scientific" studies and the decline of religious belief; that is not so relevant here as the fact that relatively new disciplines such as psychology, sociology, and economics have transformed the terms by which people define themselves.

Shakespeare's history plays, for example, actually succeed in dramatising a philosophy of history and are based on the best research work of their time. Their argument is that the overthrow of a however foolish legitimate order leads to universal discord. What is important is that the theatrical conventions of the day allowed Shakespeare to express these ideas without any strain on credibility. But the gardener's speech in "Richard II" is a classic example of intellectual ideas conveyed in a way that neither mocks the story nor challenges the suspension of disbelief.

Shakespeare could write plays like this, and through his minor characters suggest an entire social fabric, because his age regarded history as a book from which one could draw morals. The illustrations were the deeds, wicked or otherwise, of great men. The emphasis here is upon "deeds": history was a succession of incidents determined by will and character, and thus the very stuff of drama. Representations of decisive human actions are what Brecht means by "dramatic" in the discussion with his secretary.

Acting out a story is the thing, and when society believes that the most significant truths are displayed in the actions of one man the drama has its high moments, as in "Oedipus" and "Hamlet." The essence so far as the drama is concerned of the intellectual changes of the past 150 years is that we no longer believe that the significant truth about even one man can be told through his actions alone. We look not simply to willed action, but to a complexity of social, psychological, and historical facts of which the man himself may be entirely unaware.

Bernard Shaw was just as alive to this as Brecht but his solution was a trick. He wrote the play as though it was still the eighteenth century and put the intervening and vital information in the preface. Brecht knew that to be serious one must put the information in the play, and it is his grappling with this problem in both theory and practice that makes him so important. The whole "experimental" side of his work as a writer comes down to an attempt to pack in more information than the theatre had previously been able to carry.

The trappings of many Brecht plays, the placards, songs, bizarre locations, projections, films, and intoned narrations are all attempts to convey information: so really are the alienation effects and the theories about sport and the smokers' theatre. The idea here is not just to make the audience receptive to more information, but to persuade them to employ what they already have.

Consider for example, the BBC's "Henry VIII" series. Are we really to believe that the English Reformation and great shifts in political power, wealth, and economic organisation came about because a woman refused to be divorced? Or is the movement of history more complicated? Brecht's challenge would be (see his classic critique of the film of "Gunga Din") that if we conveniently forget what we know to enjoy a romantic diversion why should we not remember it again for a serious work of art?

To this attitude there is a vital qualification. For all his commitment to socialism and scientific appraisal Brecht was not a utopian. He believed in the survival of the human spirit but not that it is perfect or even very reliable. This is the source of his most characteristic ambiguities, like the end of both "Galileo" and "Man is Man." It is in the bitter sweet tone of his best work the flitting from emotion to emotion that he most effectively presents a new kind of information about life.

This is to say that he faces the problems of what is "dramatic" more squarely in his theory than in his actual writing: after all, he gave up the play about the wheat market. His best plays are traditional poetic images for the world his theories describe. They deal obliquely so that for all its dazzling newsreel analysis of a political upheaval the opening of "The Caucasian Chalk Circle" is still about a mythical central Asia and not the present age, just as "Man is Man" is about a never-never India. Yet what happens to Galy Gay in "Man is Man" is truly a nightmare.

It is true that for a Marxist Brecht is melancholy, and for a poet pedantic, and that sometimes he is very boring and makes his point too many times over. He is also a genius.

records.title: First cage your actors
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
First cage your actors

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

AS MUCH rubbish is talked about "ensemble" as about any other topic in the English theatre. It's something we all wanted for a very long time and we are now not quite sure whether or not we've actually got it. If we have, the feeling goes, then it's not all that it was cracked up to be.

Our biggest mistake, it becomes increasingly obvious, was in believing that the building of a company was principally a matter of time. It does seem to be true that if a sufficiently talented group of actors are caged up together for two or three years some interesting work will result in the brief period (a further year, not much more) before they begin to file their way through the bars. The Royal Shakespeare Company (founded 1960) reached its peak in 1962-3 and the National Theatre (founded 1963) reached its in 1965-6. But since those dates both organisations have zig-zagged and we have hardly known from one production to another whether we have a company or not. I am here concerned with the National currently going through one of its good patches. I'll get to "Coriolanus" later.

The critics have been sniffing a renaissance in the last two productions but misplacing the emphasis. Since "The Captain of Koepenick" has a larger cast than any previous National production it was pronounced an ensemble triumph. But nobody bothered to use that commendation for John Dexter's production of "A Woman Killed with Kindness" which, in its balance, sobriety, its exact sense of psychological and spatial relationships, was as worthy of it as anything in years. Dexter builds a whole world in this production and he builds it with every actor in the cast. The performances of the servants, many of them non-speaking, are jewel-like reminders of what permanent companies are supposed to be about. Hardly anybody seems to have noticed.

I enjoy watching the patterns created by a collection of actors in varying juxtaposition. I even enjoy revisiting productions and collecting performances denied for ever to the first-nighters.

The worst sort of situation for actors is when someone like, say, Patrick Garland cuts the ground from beneath the actors' feet by destroying the texture of a play like "Cyrano," not so much by deromanticising it as by neutering or eliminating the panoply of small parts handed to him by the author. It seems pretty pointless, too, to have a fine, watchful actor like Edward Woodward breeze into the company, play two enormous roles at present beyond his range, and leave without having the opportunity to consolidate anything.

Consolidation can often take place outside the company. It is obvious, for example, that Maggie Smith made a radical advance between leaving as Miss Julie and returning as Mrs Sullen and Hedda; and Anthony Hopkins the new Coriolanus, whom I sometimes think of as the Ruby Keeler of the company ("you're going off that stage as a spear-carrier and you're coming back a star") reached the heights in "A Woman Killed" with the minimum of warning.

What warning there was occurred in "The Architect and the Emperor" where his performance looks in retrospect like an impressive piece of muscle-flexing. Coriolanus should have completed the triptych and though a much less finished piece of acting than his Master Frankford it brings him within sight of full heroic stature, incorporating a sense of playfulness which suggests an ability to learn creatively from Olivier in an ambience where more or less unconscious imitation has become the norm. (And now that they possess, in Scofield, the other great figurehead of the actor's theatre the ramifications could be fascinating.) Hopkins's obvious technical faults (and Coriolanus is as demanding a role on this score as any in the canon) are only those of which Olivier himself was judged guilty at the same age. All the same, he is playing the part by default and at short notice and he can hardly be said to have been prepared for it.

Hopkins's progress offers perhaps the nearest parallel in the Waterloo Road to the process familiar in the RSC where the advancement of an Alan Howard can get to look like a military campaign. But development can be haphazard. Derek Jacobi, say, could hardly not have progressed in his eight years with the National. But it took him long enough to reach his summit in "The Idiot" and recognition was grudging enough when it came.

Maybe the new influx of resident directors (Dexter and Michael Blakemore to join Olivier and Frank Dunlop) will make future passages smoother. Although the actors seem to have few enough complaints about the constant stream of guest directors, each, in recent months, equipped with an interpreter, I cannot feel they have been well served in "Coriolanus." It's a far better production than "Cyrano" (and Hopkins's performance alone would keep it miles from disaster) but it suffers from the same disease. To cut a play to size means, almost invariably, to thin its human texture and to deny its supporting players their legitimate opportunities. Morale, I have been assured on all sides, has never been higher at the National. It should be used before it gets away again.

records.title: Cleotonic
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Cleotonic

MRS JOHN DANKWORTH talks to ROBERT CUSHMAN about her blossoming career

CLEO LAINE opened her act at the Ronnie Scott club this year with "On a Clear Day You Can See Forever," as overexposed a song as you could hope not to hear again. By the time the first chorus had been swung I could have written a letter of apology to Burton Lane, the fine and underrated composer who penned it. The song belongs in his collected works after all.

It is customary for singers to make the initial grab for their audience's attention with an up-tempo number. But Cleo perhaps needs it less than most since she customarily follows half a dozen sonorous complex instrumentals from whatever group her husband is currently fronting (this time it's the John Dankworth Tenfold--"because there are ten in the band and when the gig is over they fold"--R. Scott). I don't think many sleep while they are on, and I have long doubted the infallibility of the traditional opening belter. Even the great Peggy Lee failed to bring it off when she sang at the Albert Hall last year. So Miss Laine had a double set of my prejudices to overcome. But she made it. Hers was the clearest day ever embellished in the second chorus with additional lyrics that would, I suspected, have been as surprising to Alan Jay Lerner as they were to me.

Backstage between sets the lady confirmed my suspicions. "I ad-lib on the melody when working on a song. JD writes it down if he thinks it's any good, and adds lyrics to fit what I've sung."

"Clear Day" might reasonably be described as a modern standard. Traditionally, Cleo includes a number of the more ancient ones in her repertory as well, but they are no longer the staples they once were. She firmly states that "I still like the things I've always done," but also admits that "I may have drained them dry. I try when I sing standards to present them in a different light but there does come a moment when every song you sing starts to resemble every other song."

This is partly true of some of the oldies she does, but only partly. She gets exhilarating mileage out of a piece of vintage Cole Porter euphoria, "Ridin' High," and "I'm Gonna Sit Right Down and Write Myself a Letter" now belongs to her as inalienably as ever it did to Fats Waller. She and Dankworth have been trading opening phrases on this for as long as I remember, and the routine has now taken on an aspect of self-parody which actually augments its joyousness. On the other hand she finds little fresh to do for "I Could Write a Book." I think it might be better slower since it depends, like many of Lorenz Hart's lyrics, on self-mockery, and no vocalist can project this better than Cleo when she gives herself the breathing space. And though I hope there will always be some Gershwin in her performances she curiously fails to endow "But Not for Me" with its proper razor edge. But then I don't think I've heard anybody get it really right.

She started her career as a low contralto with a very sinewy range. She can now do upper register acrobatics that challenge Ella Fitzgerald's. Some of the credit goes to Dankworth who would take her arrangements progressively up half a tone without telling her, so that she had to sing higher to survive. "John hates to hear a run of songs in one key--of course it presupposes that you can sing in more than one." There is a danger, which she recognises, of doing vocal acrobatics for their own sake, but she now wants to sing as simply as she can: "I've done my soaring. The old devil still breaks out sometimes as in 'Clear Day' to delightful effect."

But she's more satisfying when she concentrates on delivering lyrics. Her current showpiece is Noel Coward's "Mad About the Boy." I've always thought it his best song, but I hardly knew the half of it. Cleo has restored the full text, sung in three voices--a sophisticate (giving the familiar words her most longing and languorous treatment), a schoolgirl ("I'm sure that Housman wrote the 'Shropshire Lad' about the boy") and a char. At another extreme, she stills the room with Joni Mitchell's "Both Sides Now." Everybody has sung this one but Cleo's control is consummate. She can half-talk a few lines and suddenly come down true and moving on a last note you hardly hoped to hear. And I treasure her frequent quizzical moods--a slightly aggrieved stressing "Why should I have spring fever" in "It Might as Well be Spring" and a sense of wonder carried through to an enraptured top note at the end of Michel Legrand's beautifully simple and dauntingly complex "What Are You Doing The Rest Of Your Life."

If you missed her at Ronnie Scott's you could try the Wavendon All Music Plan. Wavendon is the Dankworths' Buckinghamshire home, and home also of a festival (this year May 28-June 6) where advanced students can meet other musicians, in different spheres, talk, play each other's music, be taught by each other. Musicians should know a good deal more of other kinds of music--they can't afford to specialise.

She practises what she preaches--as everybody knows, she can now sing just about anything, including John Donne (actually, it may be just the Perry Como associations, but "Go and Catch a Falling Star" has always seemed to me like a natural song-lyric anyway. It now has a Dankworth setting). She also, from time to time, acts; last year she played Hedda Gabler at Canterbury "and I don't think I made a fool of myself." Later this year she turns to musicals as the mulatto Julie ("At least I'm ethnically right for the part") in a West End revival of "Showboat."

For her closer at Scott's she revived "It's a Pity to Say Goodnight," complete, as they say, with verse, and with a coda--"If you gotta go home, you gotta go home"--mischievously repeated as she gradually retreated from the mike and the stage. When she reached the final "Give me a good-night kiss" there could have been few in the audience who would have failed to oblige. By the end she had converted the room into a four-sided commune: herself, John Dankworth and company, Ronnie Scott, and the audience. I left feeling surpassingly happy.

records.title: Hands across the Channel
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Hands across the Channel

ROBERT CUSHMAN reviews a French 'Richard III' and a Shaw revival.

A pleasant nostalgia suffused the Aldwych Theatre last week. Richard III had returned, speaking French, but still looking remarkably English. The voice was the voice of the Comedie Francaise, taking part in the World Theatre Season, but the trappings, including the director, Terry Hands, were those of the Royal Shakespeare Company. It was a taking combination.

Against spare settings, apparently composed of steel and wire-wool, troops of soldiers marched, sinisterly dressed to blend in with the surroundings. Sometimes they stopped to plant banners in the stage. French actors do not seem to take too easily to this piece of elementary Shakespearean drill; some of the banners were seen to wobble.

Fun though it is to see these new dogs taught to play our old tricks, the evening had more to offer. For though Mr Hands has retained the characteristic look of a Stratford history production, he has altogether changed its emphasis. We have been trained to look at these plays as primarily political; their hero has been England. A French company must find another centre of interest and the Comedie has given the play back to its protagonist. Richard's himself again.

So is Terry Hands. His recent English work has been clotted and contorted; striving to turn drama into ritual, he has produced a kind of solemn puppetry. But his Richard is genuinely larger than life, a macabre game manoeuvred with fluency across the vast spaces of Farrah's open set. The moves are frequently electric. When the viciously squabbling nobles turn on old Queen Margaret, they converge and threaten to push her almost into the front stalls. Richard himself has a long, crab-like exit, walking backwards, up through an infinite depth of stage.

Doing the play in English, I imagine that Mr Hands would approach it with greater formality; it is one of Shakespeare's earliest, written in thumpingly regular iambics. Translation has actually loosened it up; 'quelle chance pour le roi du ciel' strikes me as an admirably economic exchange for 'The better for the king of heaven that hath him.'

When formality is essential, the French troupe are naturally poised to present it; their complement of weeping queens could hardly be bettered. Denise Gence is particularly fine as Margaret, a crazed relic of the Wars of the Roses, prostrating herself with painful humility before Jacques Charon's courtly Buckingham.

He, however, remains unflappable, thus eventually ensuring his own downfall. Robert Hirsch as Richard plays off him a good deal, making use of him, joshing him, envying his poise, finally hating him. M. Hirsch's Richard is not lacking in glamour. Facially he is a smiling fallen angel and his hypnotic wooing of the Lady Anne is quite credible, but resentment of his own deformity consumes him.

A searing sequence has been added to the play in which he tries desperately to straighten his back, having first compelled his followers to turn theirs. Then he embarks on his cajolery of the Lord Mayor. Cajolery is perhaps hardly the right word: Richard's real power resides in the armed thugs who surround him. But he enjoys assuming a mask of piety, switching rapidly in and out of character; he is truly a Player King.

Witty and dangerous though M. Hirsch's performance is, its brilliance is too lightweight to sustain this very long play through to the end, and the production's terms of reference do not encourage us to take any great interest in the usurper's downfall. Richmond is a cipher who doesn't even get to do his own killing; instead Richard is surrounded, overcome and dragged off by the ghosts of his former victims.

By this time he is wearing, rather puzzlingly, a horse's head. 'Mon royaume pour un cheval,' he has just proclaimed with great insistence, so perhaps some bizarre poetic justice is at work. Still, 30 disappointing minutes at the close seem a small price to pay for three of the most entertaining hours yet offered in a World Theatre Season.

Au revoir; and bless thee, Two Gentlemen of Verona, thou art Godspelled. Galt MacDermot's musical version of this frailer piece of early Shakespeare has arrived with a splash at the Phoenix after its huge success in New York. It shall be dealt with next week.

Shaw's Misalliance is currently being belted through twice nightly at the Mermaid. It doesn't exactly move like the wind, even so. In fact, it hardly moves at all. This is one of Shaw's most engaging plays, largely because it is so shameless about its author's characteristic weaknesses.

Shaw is popularly believed to have reduced drama to formless, rambling debate. Misalliance might have been written to substantiate this belief in lovingly documented detail. 'You are rather all over the shop with your ideas,' the central (or, anyway, the most voluble) character is informed by his son.

But the fact that they are father and son has some significance. The gulf between the generations is the play's theme, in so far as it has one. It is, at least, a constantly recurring topic, though, having acquired that information, there is little that either a director or an audience can do with it. It imposes no kind of shape on the piece.

The advantage of Shaw's open form, however, is the ease with which it can accommodate diversions, should inspiration suddenly descend. Misalliance survives by virtue of a self-contained miniature farce embedded in its second half, which commences when a frightened little man emerges from a portable Turkish bath to threaten an underwear tycoon with a revolver and the immortal words 'I am the son of Lucinda Titmus'.

This moment is not as hilarious at the Mermaid as, in all conscience, it should be; it is awkwardly staged and John Tordoff takes a few minutes to ease himself comfortably into the intruder's role. Once there, however, he proves a flawless operator and, as he proceeds to state the case of the underpaid overworked Edwardian clerk, the play attains that state of comic grace in which no turn of phrase or of events can lead anywhere but up. It ranks with the tea-party scene in Pygmalion among Shaw's funniest stretches of writing.

The other plum role, a Polish acrobat sworn to risk her life once a day for the family honour, is devoured with gusto by Caroline Blakiston. Bill Fraser proves himself again the prince of Shavian plutocrats, a natural intellectual weighed down by his unfortunate gift for making money. There are some other good performances, and a few deplorable ones.

John Antrobus's Captain Oates' Left Sock (Theatre Upstairs) is a sober and honest piece about group therapy. The director, Nicholas Wright, is to be congratulated on his casting, which is perhaps a perverse way of commending the exactness and control of the actors. In particular, Janet Webb, the buxom lady from the end of the Morecambe and Wise show, communicates a massive vulnerability. Good night, Janet, and we love you all.

records.title: Rock around the Bard
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Rock around the Bard

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE word is that the musical of Two Gentlemen of Verona (Phoenix) pays no attention to the themes of its original. This is unfair. The play is more narrowly concerned with love in its purest (which is to say its silliest) state than any other Shakespeare, and the musical has its own gloss on this. It comes at us loud, funky and often: "You can't love another without loving yourself."

That's almost good Shakespeare, though by the time he got to, say, Twelfth Night, he might have wanted to substitute "without knowing yourself." Self-love is what Malvolio was said to be sick of, and this show has caught the plague.

It suffers from the Godspell blight; it will do anything to be likeable. It is colourful and teeming with action: that much to its credit. But its idea of modernising Shakespeare is just to make the sex as explicit as possible. (Those poor, sonneteering Elizabethans with their Platonism and their Courtly Love, what did they know?)

So Silvia becomes a nymphomaniac. Proteus does not merely desert Julia; he gets her pregnant, though not without making provision for her future. He has at least ensured that she will get a laugh when, disguised as a boy, she reaches the line about women changing their shapes.

If it isn't sex, it's protest. There is, though it looks a little wan now, a Vietnam angle with the Duke of Milan conceived as (you should pardon the expression) a stylish President Nixon.

In New York, the show presumably had authentic American performers. By the time it got to the Phoenix, only two such natives were left in the cast. When B. J. Arnau and Samuel E. Wright combine on a number called "Night Letter," the whole house wakes up and realises, with a shock, that it is enjoying itself. Miss Arnau is, from her first entrance, a majestic Silvia; to her let us garlands bring. Mr Wright takes longer to establish himself but develops into a sweet comic Valentine with the lungs and the humour to tear a soul ballad properly apart.

Proteus (Ray C. Davis) displays similar verve when confronted by a calypso. He is a toothy performer, a quality which sorts well with calypsos, but not with much else. The supporting players must have looked at the script and run each for his peculiar brand of cover. We get a funny old Italian. We get a Scots wench with maxi-boobs, apt to break silence by saying, "We were just comparing you to a summer's day." (That's bringing Shakespeare to the people.) We get Benny Lee, attempting to impose Anglo-Jewish rhythms on Shakespeare's funniest stand-up comic. We get, at the curtain call, dozens of people I didn't remember seeing before.

Doing his own thing most furiously, but most forgivably, of all is Derek Griffiths, whose talent is to contort face, body and voice, gloriously and often simultaneously. One of nature's stars, he is condemned in his present role to be only (and this in a cast which includes a dog) an unrivalled scene stealer.

My view of the show has possibly been jaundiced by the blatant plugging it received on an appalling television documentary last Sunday. Throughout this, I noticed, the most celebrated member of the creative team--the composer, Galt MacDermot--kept very quiet.

Is there a real Mr MacDermot? His present score is fecund and ingratiatingly bouncy, but it has no character and very little body. It uses pastiche as a painless device for keeping the music coming and the party going. It implicitly obeys the two fashionable rules for rock musicals: the music forsakes rock as often as possible to parody other forms and the lyrics are painful.

There is matter in Tom Gallacher's Schellenbrack (King's Head) to touch any critic. One of our breed, name of Cope, momentously confesses to have changed his opinions. "Then how," comes the reply, "do I know you're Cope?"

That crusher falls from the lips of Schellenbrack himself, an historian with his own identity problem. He may be a Nobel Prizewinner and he may be mad. Mr Gallacher specialises in ambiguous portraits of genius and he has never before been so well served by his actor. The part requires a powerful physical impact to be filtered through a mercurial temperament and Wolfe Morris supplies both.

The King's Head is an Islington pub, but the play kept transporting me to the boozers round Broadcasting House. On its breath I smelled the liquorous intellectuality of the old Third Programme. Mr Gallacher's studies--written later, but produced earlier at this theatre--of an Ibsen-intoxicated actor and a Joyce-intoxicated Joyce had summoned similar associations. The current piece is a literary detective story--a favourite radio genre--but Mr Gallacher is no storyteller. Schellenbrack benefits from witty dialogue and some delectable insights, but he is a glittering portrait in search of a frame.

records.title: Gypsy triumphant
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Gypsy triumphant

Something remarkable is currently happening at the Piccadilly Theatre. That is not opinion, it's fact: on Wednesday night I witnessed a standing ovation accorded to Angela Lansbury by a second night audience.

The cheers were provoked, I think, by the show's closing 15 minutes. For most of its length Gypsy is a very good musical; at its close, it reaches greatness. We have watched Miss Lansbury as a selfish and bone-stupid theatrical mother, steam-rollering her two luckless young daughters through the death throes of vaudeville. Gradually, but not grudgingly, we have come to admire her resilience, and to sympathise with her bewilderment as both girls desert her.

One runs off to become a real actress; the other achieves fake stardom as the stripper Gypsy Rose Lee, and immediately sets about banishing her mother from her dressing-room and her life.

Suddenly it's Mama's turn. A light-studded platform has been shunted across the orchestra pit, annihilating the distance that generally separates a musical from its audience. She strides on to it to try her own hand as a performer. She falters, weighted down by memories of the past, and her failure is Miss Lansbury's acting and singing triumph. She stops the show. The effect is devastatingly direct and as moving as anything to be seen in London.

Robert Cushman

records.title: Noh to Vanbrugh
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Noh to Vanbrugh

THEATRE

Robert Cushman on a week of classic plays.

THERE has hardly been a play to be had this week much below the age of 300. It began, appropriately, with the Umewaka Noh Troupe, concluding their two-week season at the Aldwych.

I found them very restful, and less boring than many groups supposedly more accessible. It is heartening anyway, at a World Theatre Season, to meet with visitors so far outside our comprehension as to be beyond the reach even of simultaneous translation. Free of those crackling translations and their monotone messages, we could attend to the sound of the actors' stockinged feet upon the polished wooden floor, as much a part of the spectacle as the masks, the silken gowns, the chanting, and the guttural croakings that are the nearest these Japanese actors come to expressing recognisable emotion (though having once seen one of last week's plays in an English translation, I can testify that, divorced from its traditional presentation, Noh drama can be made to yield explicit emotional content).

While I doubt that the Umewaka troupe have taught our theatre much that it did not, in theory, know already about the strengths of formality and simplicity, it is pleasant to see the theories put so thoroughly into practice. It is pleasant, too, to have a demonstration of the basic principles of comic relief. Sandwiched between each pair of Noh dramas is a short farce; after half an hour of masked solemnity, the impact of a human face--emitting sounds that could only be human laughter--is almost physical.

Once there were modern-dress productions of Shakespeare. They were delightfully shocking, meticulously detailed (telephones always figured prominently) and only done occasionally, so as to jolt the audience out of their presumed complacency. They look, in photographs, extraordinarily dated. These days a new convention has taken hold. Pop has come among us, and, by introducing a style of clothing that is tied to no particular period, but thrives on joky anachronism, it has made casual, timeless Shakespeare a possibility. Two Gentlemen of Verona was cast in this mould, both at its most recent Stratford appearance and in the current rock version; so was As You Like It, first with an all-male cast at the National Theatre, and now in a new production at Stratford.

The style only obtrudes itself where, logically, it should be most useful. A unisex costume for Rosalind would seem to be the perfect solution to the problem of her male disguise. In her tight-fitting jacket and jeans, she could just as easily be a boy as a girl. She could, however, just as easily be a girl as a boy and I have never felt less inclination to suspend my disbelief.

Eileen Atkins has a wary, fine-drawn talent, and there is one corner of Rosalind--the mordant satirist of romantic attitudes--of which she takes complete possession. But the undertow of erotic abandon is barely there at all, and even the irony is muted. At moments, David Suchet's vigorous, confident Orlando (an understudy performance, calling for no indulgence whatever) was running rings round her and, in this play, that is the wrong way round for rings to be run.

Miss Atkins delivers the epilogue splendidly (with the houselights up as they should be), but the end of the play inevitably suffers at the moment from the ankle-injury which keeps her out of the final marriage-dance (as it nearly kept her out of the first night altogether). By this time, anyway, Buzz Goodbody's direction has run out of steam. She clearly recognises the importance of the marriage theme, but her methods of underlining it are tired. Grinning supers fling confetti into the house, and the audience gamely grins and wishes it would all go away.

These tactics spoil an agreeable lightweight production which has little to say on the play's main themes (court or country?--you choose), but makes good sense of individual scenes. The mod trappings are a great help to Brian Glover, puffing with professional pride as Charles the wrestler, and they work well, too, for Clement McCallin's icily capricious Duke Frederick. When we reach the forest, it is a great comfort to find it in the charge of Tony Church, a pipesmoking banished Duke, mercifully unembarrassed by his own pronouncement. Particularly telling is his rebuke to the cynically moralising Jaques: "For thou thyself hast been a libertine/As sensual as the brutish sting itself. . ."

Who would have guessed that Shakespeare had Malcolm Muggeridge's number so accurately?

In Richard Pasco's hands, Jaques becomes almost the central character of the play--paradoxically, really, since he spends most of his time prowling its periphery, peering at the action with beady distaste through rimless glasses. The mere sight of the amorous Touchstone and Audrey sends a visible shudder through him. I sympathised; they are played grossly enough for me to contribute a few winces myself.

For an even richer study of an Elizabethan malcontent, you go--reasonably enough--to The Malcontent; John Marston's play has now come from Nottingham to London's Bankside Globe Playhouse.

The experience is not without hazard, since neither playhouse nor play is innocent of chilly gaps in its structure. Shakespeare was almost unique among his contemporaries in knowing how to pace himself. In this piece, the work of an inchoate satirist whose quest for moral certainties finally took him into the Church, words and events tumble out, still knotted together and at breakneck speed.

Breakneck is the word. This is the conventional English idea of an Italian Renaissance Court, every man someone else's hired assassin, and yet--for once--every character ends up alive. The play is a comedy or, as Jonathan Miller has chosen to direct it, a satiric farce. His court is an assemblage of shadowy white-faced grotesques; setting and costumes suggest gorgeousness gone into decay. The treatment is sometimes too insistent; these dramatists were prone to sudden changes of gear, and Marston probably intended some of his twists of plot to be a good more than a giggle. The play, like many of its age, including the genuine revenge dramas of Webster and Tourneur, is apt to slide into parody with disconcerting speed; Mr Miller hardly ever lets it slide out. But he has accurately located the play's lunatic gusto and has, more surprisingly, done serious justice to its fits of morality.

Mr Miller's style is well suited to a cast generally stronger on enthusiasm than finesse. Hazel Hughes's old bawd is irreproachable, and there can be no reservations at all about Derek Godfrey. This malcontent is another banished duke, but one who has no intention of waiting for his supplanter to be converted by an old religious man (though he gets him to impersonate one). Mr Godfrey is always a witty, stylish actor; sometimes he lets loose a gleeful demon who, on this occasion, has one of his richest outings ever.

I would have welcomed his irruption during a leaden revival of Vanbrugh's The Provok'd Wife (Greenwich), which gets us as far as the 1690s. Next week I hope to venture into the twentieth century.

records.title: Two from the critics
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Two from the critics

Theatre

by Robert Cushman

I CLOSED last week with a promise to drag this column into the twentieth century. I was not rash enough to specify the 1970s, but I had hopes. They were pinned to two of my fellow reviewers with plays of their own about to appear. Broken reeds. In The Houseboy (Open Space), Irving Wardle offers sensitive transportation to the nineteen-fifties; in Sing of the Times (Vaudeville), Jeremy Kingston exhibits some of the typical humours of the sixties.

Mr Kingston's is the lighter play but the more serious offence, since it clearly suffers from delusions of contemporaneity. (This despite a pianist in the pit tinkling out the message that this is the dawning of the age of Aquarius: Hair arrived here in 1968 and it was already receding then.) Mr Wardle at least matches form to content, and period to both.

His play has the feel of autobiography, like most works about gauche, serious young men. John, 25 years old, recently down from Oxford, currently a music student, works as a scullion in a London hotel run by two middle-aged homosexuals. Their relationship is fraying ("two old hot-water bottles wrinkling up together"), and John, foreseeably, serves them as a battleground. For the first time he finds himself possessed of power; he begins, not altogether amiably, to grow up.

Mr Wardle easily makes us free of John's mind--too easily since the play works best when he remains a sounding-board for his patrons. John is most satisfying when most opaque; Philip Donaghy's silences are far more compelling than the glimpses we are clumsily offered of his inner life. When he quotes Shakespeare, at moments both frequent and inopportune, we can--unless I am being fanciful--observe a drama critic in the making; Mr Donaghy makes this eventual metamorphosis seem a very likely prospect. But the real interest resides with the rival queens. Mr Wardle has given them some neat dialogue and a ration of emotional depth; Nicholas Selby (who explodes) and Timothy West (a slow fuse burning beneath an ominously level surface) handle them efficiently.

The play's period flavour has one piquant aspect. No actual English play of the fifties ever managed to treat homosexuality so unflappably. The club theatres of the period (which would surely have been patronised by Mr Wardle's odd couple had he not drawn them as ballet-fanciers) were full of shrill, martyred approaches to the subject. The West End was as rife with plays whose authors, by way of obeisance to the Lord Chamberlain, disguised or discarded any homosexual relationships among their characters, and gravely impaired their credibility-rating as a result. One of the last playwrights from whom this homage was extracted (over a play called No Concern of Mine) was Mr Kingston. In his new piece he makes sacrifice to another of the theatre's antique deities, the god (surely not Eros, despite his convenient location) of West End sex comedy.

Before word spread of sexual revolution, this genre had a certain point. The author's ingenuity, and the audience's presumed censoriousness, combined to keep the bedroom door closed, and the heroine outside it. Now she is allowed in but, since nothing else in the play has changed, her emancipation seems remarkably incongruous. The artificial, asexual ambience is not to be transformed merely by allowing Kenneth More to make jokes about virgins. It appears, if you please, that he knew one once who worked for The Observer.

A lot of the jokes concern newspapers. So, in a way, does the plot, which presupposes--with more confidence than is strictly justified--a universal craze for all things astrological. Even The Times gets itself a stargazer, in the comfortably crumpled shape of Mr More. But since he only takes the job in order to influence the ladies in his life, both of them avid horoscope-heads, the comedy of gullibility dies at birth, and another evening is spent hovering round the bedchamber without so much as a maidenhead at stake. Sometimes people come in and tell us about the exciting things happening in the outside world, like in Greek tragedy.

The sad thing is that Mr Kingston does have some comic gift (he goes for the smart rattle where Mr Wardle is more your sombre ironist) and that he must have known, from his own critical experience, the kind of stereotype to which his idea was being reduced. Mr More, who has brought the art of passive comedy to a very high pitch, is a continual consolation. He is that treasurable phenomenon, the straight man who gets all the laughs. Not even Frankie Howerd is more adept at thinking of an entendre and then doubling it.

* * *

Strictly speaking, there are more laughs to be had at the Vaudeville than in Nuts (Theatre Workshop), but the latter has a cleaner smell. This show defies criticism. Songs and sketches by Joan Littlewood's regular troupe alternate with personal appearances by real East London journalists, whose speeches--whether attacking property developers or just hawking the Socialist Worker--are the best things in the evening, and the only occasions on which those delivering the material display any faith in it. As community theatre, this is totally honest. There is no attempt to pass propaganda off as drama, and none of the masturbatory quality of actors trying earnestly to act local.

But the ineptitude of most of the numbers passes belief. Some of the sketches might be salvageable, but there is no telling since few of the performers are bothering anyway. Well, at least they're relaxed. Kent Baker does Mae West to a nice turn ("Where's your Danny La Rue this noo") and Bill Wallis, a bearded roly-poly pudding of an actor, alone displays the anarchic offhandedness which presumably is the goal throughout.

* * *

At the Young Vic, an evening of Beckett Shorts (presumably to be worn with Tom Stoppard's Jumpers) is most noteworthy for a performance of Play which discovers a vein of humour missing from the original National Theatre production, and for the transformation of Krapp's Last Tape into a videocassette. How could he possibly have afforded the equipment?

* * *

Back to the Aldwych, to round off the World Theatre Season, come the Zulus in Umabatha. The dancing is the thing, to be relished without much reference to the Macbeth storyline, though the ceremonial does make you understand why a man might kill to become king. The original is closely followed, so don't bother to hire a translation receiver. I picked mine up to check out the hero's state of mind and found him wondering if that was an assegai he saw before him. As I suspected.

records.title: A Chekhovian powerhouse
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
IF THE author of The Wood Demon (Lyceum, Edinburgh) will just step along to my room, I shall explain to him how he may reassemble the elements of his immoderately exhilarating play into not just one masterpiece, as he might expect, but four. I shall do this (the author, one Chekhov, being safely dead) with the aid of an invaluable critical tool known as Hindsight.

In this Actors' Company production The Wood Demon, previously regarded only as a rough draft for Uncle Vanya, stands revealed as the great Chekhovian seed-bed. It foreshadows The Seagull in its alphabetical progression of broken hearts (A loves B who actually prefers C who is languishing for D); the luncheon party at which these emotional tangles are revealed to us looks like a trial run for the first act of Three Sisters. As for Dr Kruschov, the wood demon himself, his passion for forest preservation inaugurates the symbolic pattern that was to be completed with the laying of the first axe to that cherry orchard in which all Russia was prefigured.

But the play also looks backward, to the one-act farces on which Chekhov's playwriting skills were originally honed. The blustering soldier Theodore (who afterwards merged with the wood demon to produce Astrov, the hard-drinking medico-ecologist of Vanya) is a descendant of the tactless wooers of The Bear and The Proposal. There is nobody in the mature plays anything like as funny--or so I thought as I watched Robin Ellis, striking classical poses in bushy beard and blanket, and radically extending my view both of his range and of Chekhov's.

If the comedy in this play is more broadly conceived than in Vanya, the tragedy is more compressed, but also more direct. Where Uncle Vanya, at the climax of his desperation, tries unsuccessfully to shoot the Professor who has exploited him, his prototype here, Uncle George, tries successfully to shoot himself. Vanya spends the last act of his play in a hideous awareness of futility; George spends it in his grave, virtually forgotten by those who survived him. The play moves into a vein of romantic comedy; two elusive couples are hurriedly brought together at the final curtain. In David Giles's production these pairings are uproarious and slightly unreal, like Moliere's happy endings. Suddenly we remember that George is dead, and that the Professor's wife, Helen, who in this play makes a half-hearted attempt to escape her husband, has gone with docility back to her fate. Kruschov's diatribes (which included a generous measure of self-hatred) against the surrounding second-rateness ring ironically when we see him abruptly dismissed to happiness.

The irony is, of course, refined by our memories of the later play, which we can hardly expunge. They are actually encouraged by the quality of this production, the first Chekhov I have seen to approach the National Theatre Vanya of a decade ago. To watch the shooting scene in that production, or the reconciliation of Helen and Sonya, was like assisting at the realisation of a myth. In The Wood Demon the same episodes are played out almost word for word, but the diffuseness of the surrounding action prevents them from having a comparable effect.

However, if this dramatic powerhouse, which fuelled Chekhov for the rest of his career, has too much energy for its own immediate purposes, that is hardly a fault at which to repine--not, at any rate, with this cast. Tenniel Evans's hollering Uncle, Ian McKellen's mercurial forest-freak, and Robert Eddison's unreachable Professor constitute, with Mr Ellis's grandiloquent Cossack, as formidable a male quartet as I remember; John Woodvine, suave on the sidelines, comes in a good fifth. The girls are less impressive, but the sharp corners of action and dialogue (strongly emphasised in Ronald Hingley's translation) are negotiated with dashing adroitness. The craft of Mr Giles's direction is impeccable, but it is the performances that register.

Our National Theatre recently announced the engagement of half a dozen associate directors, with barely a word of who is to do the acting. The attitude this represents is now the theatrical norm; with this production, a year after their inception, the Actors' Company acquire the authority to supply a necessary corrective.

The other main Festival offering this week has been a version of Buchner's Woyzeck, offered matinees only in the Assembly Hall by the Young Lyceum Company, the junior branch of the Edinburgh Rep. Since Buchner himself died at 23, play and players might seem excellently matched, but Woyzeck is in spirit the oldest young play ever penned, and its ashen disillusion is beyond these actors' reach. As individuals, that is; when they function as anonymous members of a unit under the Romanian director, Radu Penciulescu, they can be numbingly impressive.

Early on, Mr Penciulescu has them lie down all over the stage, the field of the living dead. The only two actors left upright step among them, swapping images of gloom. As their conversation ends, drums sound: the prostrate cast beat an accelerating tattoo on the floor. For this effect, I felt I could forgive much; but as the afternoon ground on I began to repent of my charity. "Not so fast, Woyzeck," says the tyrant Captain at the start of the play, but he seems to have dictated the pacing throughout.

Buchner leads naturally (as he did historically) to early Brecht. Drums in the Night, poor B.B.'s second play, has been staged at the Traverse, whence it will shortly transfer to the Hampstead Theatre Club. I recommend it, though not without misgivings. Roland Rees's production seems imbued initially with the playful spirit which Brecht demanded but rarely obtains and which, if anything, intensifies his savagery. That savagery was still nihilistically indiscriminate when he wrote Drums; only when he revised it in East Berlin after the war did he point it in an approved political direction. But Brecht's second thoughts are not in the same league as Chekhov's. C. P. Taylor has adapted the play by following in the master's revisionist footsteps and then imprinting a few of his own, but thinking to sharpen the play's claws, he has actually pared them. There are residual ironies in the text which the relentlessly partisan production refuses to countenance; the acting meanwhile grows increasingly strident.

Dear old Uncle George attributed his downfall to his sense of irony; the contemporary theatre seems in little danger of succumbing to the same disease. Michael Almaz's Chicago Sunday School for Anarchists (Poole Theatre, lunchtime) is a possible exception; I assume Mr Almaz intends his schoolmistress with her dreams of dynamite (a left-wing Jean Brodie, or so it seems in Edinburgh) to share the responsibility for disaster with the fascist cop who opposes her.

The Poole and the Traverse are Edinburgh fixtures. The transient bulk of the Festival fringe is suffering this year from a bad attack of the Christopher Robins; everybody has gone down with Alice. Dodging all the plays by, from or about Lewis Carroll wound up with the Brontes. For the second time this year they failed to hold me past the interval, but Richard Crane's Thunder (Bradford University Drama Group), though fearfully overlong, has some good jokes and this time I forsook the sisterhood, if without regret, then also without malice.

records.title: Defeated by Congreve
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Defeated by Congreve

THEATRE

Robert Cushman on a revival of 'Way of the World.'

FIRST it is necessary to mop up after the Edinburgh Festival. During their two weeks at the Lyceum the Actors' Company followed 'The Wood Demon' with The Way of the World; both productions are now embarked on a provincial tour (for the next two weeks they are at the Arts Theatre, Cambridge). Having been elevated by Chekhov, the company were brought down a few bumps by Congreve. Such has been the way of this world for a good two and a half centuries.

David William's production can claim an honourable place in the doom-stretching line of good tries. That is not nothing; and for its first scene I had even higher hopes of it. The action has been advanced from the close of the seventeenth century to the beginning of the twentieth; in the cool spaciousness of a St James's club, the sparring of Fainall and Mirabell has a deliberate casualness which is both dangerous and appropriate. Robin Ellis's Fainall is a robust schemer and hypocrite; Edward Petherbridge's Mirabell is barely more likeable or trustworthy, but his fastidious pallor commands respect. In a battle of styles he could be the one to back; and since that is largely what the play consists of, this establishment of the combatants should yield valuable dividends.

They fail, however, to accrue. It is difficult for any director to keep the thread of a personal duel through the labyrinth of Congreve's plotting, and Mr William gets lost with his predecessors. The antagonists prove unequally balanced, and the choice of period unduly favourable to the villains. Fainall's Victorian mustachios seem to grow curlier by the minute, while he plays a series of vigorous duets with Paola Dionisotti's striking Mrs Marwood. These two characters, traditionally dismissed as mechanical creatures of intrigue, are emerging as the most convincing in the play. We are no longer scared or sceptical of melodrama, and their disregard of finer feelings works positively to their advantage.

For this play's finer feelings are notoriously difficult to convey, wrapped up as they are in the sad brilliance of its style. Passion, say the critics, underlies it all, but the passion of the schemers is far easier to realise than that of the lovers. Mirabell figures in both guises: Mr Petherbridge is a curiously detached actor and the distance which he so effectively maintains in his dealings with Fainall or the play's various fops is scarcely reduced in his courtship of Millamant. Caroline Blakiston (who enters pastoral-fashion, carrying a shepherd's crook like a large Bo-Peep) brings warmth and poise on with her, but little sense of erotic challenge: 'What would you give that you could help loving me?'--that line, with its combination of cruelty and tenderness, is the heart of the play; their ability to feel and inspire such emotions constitutes the true victory of Millamant and Mirabell over their adversaries. Neither Miss Blakiston's delivery of the line nor Mr Petherbridge's response to it has left any impression on me. (She, at least, is battling against historic odds; radio be thanked, even junior citizens now know how Edith Evans sounded in the part.)

Other complaints: the later settings look both fussy and cheap, and the same adjectives may serve for the playing of the fops (especially Witwoud), whose scenes can and do drag horribly. Help is to hand in a lively posse of servants, and in John Woodvine's Salopian intruder who, in what Arnold Bennett called the great cause of cheering us all up, does noble battle with a tiger-skin rug.

* * *

Stanley Eveling is one of the few current dramatists to whom one turns with a positive expectation of pleasure: his Union Jack (and Bonzo) (Traverse) was predictably the brightest new play of the Festival. For much of its length I felt some resentment at its apparent slightness; I laughed but nothing grabbed me. By the end, however, Mr Eveling had fashioned from his Boy Scout extravaganza a chilling image of alienated youth. Very alienated and very young: just a couple of pubescent schoolkids knifing their piggish elders and gleefully shouting their four-letter word for the day.

The seniors nearly justify such blithe contempt; the only honest soul among them is the scoutmaster, Union Jack himself, a hung-up adolescent of 40 or so, depicted by Richard Ireson with a caricaturist's unflinching conviction. You can almost smell his 'halitosis.' Katy Manning makes a dazzling addition to Mr Eveling's impressive gallery of nymphets (fantasies of juvenile seduction almost invariably furnish the most persuasive scenes of his plays) and Susan Carpenter draws a sharp, resonant picture of a district nurse who, to judge from the debauched angle at which her cigarette slouches from her lips, is clearly in training for matron of St Trinian's. Mike Ockrent's production makes exuberant use of the Traverse stage.

* * *

Returning to London, I can add little to other critics' findings on An Inspector Calls (Mermaid); like them I responded to J. B. Priestley's mastery of traditional stagecraft, agog to know what happened next or, since this inspector is concerned to elucidate the truth of past events, what happened last. I responded, too, to much of the acting in Bernard Miles's production: Philip Stone, his entry fittingly preceded by a cry of 'Give us some more light,' is so perfectly the police inspector, so unassuming and yet so authoritative with his bald head, his raincoat and his gentle disdain for plutocratic pastimes, like golf, that we will willingly accept him as a symbol of anything the author chooses (and, man, he chooses). The family he investigates is notably tough at the top--Campbell Singer as the cocksure industrialist and especially Elizabeth Tyrrell as his genteel armour-plated wife.

The family smugness proves impenetrable; so much so that a second inspector is required, and is on the way as the play ends. Gogol closed The Government Inspector on an identical note, but for him it was a comic climax and his instinct was surely correct. Mr Priestley has had to work hard to keep laughter out of this piece (despite some facile ironies of the kind associated with his 'time' plays), and this, coupled with the relentlessness of his reiterated if humane message, makes for a thinness in texture.

* * *

Finishing Touches (Apollo) is an American comedy about a menopausal marriage, whose central role has been Anglicised for Wendy Craig; she should have declined the compliment since her lines are still recognisably American and she is landed with all the wrong rhythms. The author, Jean Kerr, once wrote a book called Please Don't Eat the Daisies, about how it felt to be the wife of a theatre critic; since I might one day be married to the wife of a theatre critic this seemed to me amusing and useful information. After Finishing Touches, which is neither amusing nor useful, I no longer want to know. The author's husband, Walter Kerr of the New York Times, once wrote, 'Some plays are so bad you don't even feel like a drink afterwards.' Finishing Touches is a play for abstainers.

records.title: Wolf from Hungary
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Wolf from Hungary

I HAVE no wish to keep The Wolf from the door of any London theatre; indeed, the sooner this Oxford Playhouse production comes to town the brighter town will be. All the same, I have to present intending patrons with a stark choice: either you see the play or you read this review.

I cannot, I fear, discuss this play intelligibly without giving away its surprises. Its narrative twists are not the only pleasures it provides, but they are substantial--if that word may be permitted of a play which is largely concerned with manipulating levels of fantasy. In this connection the expertise of Ferenc Molnar, the Hungarian master of the boulevards who wrote this piece in 1914, prompts comparison with that of Jean Anouilh. I admire much of Anouilh's work, but despite his reputation for theatricality I have found no moment in his plays as arresting as the revelation at the end of Act II of The Wolf that the preceding scene has taken place inside the heroine's head. The information is craftily, economically conveyed. One is momentarily bewildered, then accepts it as a coup de theatre; only in the course of Act III does the psychological accuracy of this dream-sequence finally become apparent.

In the first act we have witnessed this heroine dining with her husband in a restaurant, and seen his jealousy aroused (not that it is ever exactly dormant) by the sight of one of her old admirers. After the interval we find the couple preparing to attend a diplomatic reception; and still embroiled. She unearths an old letter from her former swain in which he promises to return to her some day--as a soldier, a diplomat, an artist or a mere servant. We next meet her, duly arrived at the party, exposed and succumbing to the allurements of just such a quartet. Each appears in turn, and each exactly resembles her cast-off lover.

Here Molnar's manipulation of his audience is at its most magisterial. When the second suitor appears as the double of the first, we are bemused, and begin to hunt for realistic explanations. At the third appearance we think we see the dramatist's game and agree to play it with him. A similar stage of tacit connivance is reached in An Inspector Calls, but Molnar's strategy is more audacious than Mr Priestley's. There is a traditional understanding that running gags come in threes; when we are faced with the fourth mutation--the suitor as servant--we catch our breath. (We do; I heard us.) It is at this point that the dreamer awakes (and decides that it might be best after all not to go to the ball) and the release, though a theatrical shock, is as necessary for us as for her.

Frank Hauser's 17 years as director of the Playhouse (now sadly about to end) have never been notable for ensemble playing. His achievement has been to bring distinguished texts to the light, and to attract star players to their service. On this occasion the simultaneous (and well directed) presence of Judi Dench, Leo McKern and Edward Woodward renders the gaps below the top level fairly harmless.

Our theatre is not short of clever comediennes: Miss Dench is special because her brittleness is always an abstraction from a hard core of common-sense. She is thus able to combine the lady's languorous visions (happily flaunting her flunkey to the horror of Budapest society) with the practicality that can eventually send her lover on his way and out of town. She is, if you like, a classic bourgeois hypocrite, and the play could certainly be accused of coquetting with adultery while saving itself for marriage. The denouement on the surface could hardly be cosier; so why does the final curtain descend on the husband, alone and in tears?

The answer is supplied by Mr McKern, who plays the eternal cuckold in his own imagination, unable to credit his wife's fidelity in a world full of wenching hussars, seeking always to buy himself into her favour. He is a man of outward substance and inner vertigo. Finally confronted by his supposed rival he takes firm hold of the back of a chair and promptly loses his balance.

These are two consummate performances. When the wind is to Woodward the air is somewhat thinner; playing the lover in his various guises he is constrained to offer a string of what I can only call tours-de-farce. All are funny (a haughty impersonation of Mario Lanza brings the house down), but I still wait to see on stage the relaxed, compassionate, humorous actor who once shone out on television in an Evelyn Waugh trilogy.

* * *

The Actors' Company (currently at the Arts, Cambridge) offer at certain lunchtime and late-night showings a double bill of new plays. The first half did little to allay my suspicions, aroused by their Iris Murdoch premiere last year, of this company's susceptibility to the spuriously literary: Gabriel Josipovici's Flow intercuts five reminiscent monologues, a line at a time. Banality chopped up and counterpointed is still banal.

Edward Petherbridge's stage version of R. D. Laing's Knots is likewise fragmented, but here each segment makes a point. A wry, humorous and occasionally desperate image accumulates of the slippery delusions that clog up human relationships. Mr Petherbridge's brilliant production is a company showcase packed with surprises; we learn that he himself is a virtuoso mime, that Caroline Blakiston can play the organ, and that John Moreno can do almost anything.

* * *

There is more good company acting in And They Put Handcuffs on the Flowers (Open Space): Malcolm Storry, Anthony Milner and Ian McDiarmid hurl themselves with anthropoid abandon into Fernando Arrabal's demonstration that prison can be good sadomasochistic fun. The arresting title phrase is Garcia Lorca's; and due tribute is paid to his death at the hands of a Franco firing-squad. The play's intentions are of the best; Arrabal wrote it at the request of the Madrid prisoners whose incarceration he shared for 25 days in 1967, to tell the world of the conditions they endured. But, faced with the enticing prospect of actually writing about three men in a cell, this Peter Pan of the avant-garde goes all giggly. There are one or two passages of authentic horror, but there are many more (priest-baiting, excremental reveries and phallic frolics) which play like private jokes. Most unforgivable is the bonelessly reverential treatment accorded to the play's lone activist, who is most respectfully groomed for martyrdom. It seems that jail doesn't humiliate everyone after all; insulated from all the buffoonery he even gets to keep his clothes on. He represents the gesture to commitment of an apolitical talent, forcing itself to keep a straight face.

* * *

At least the production (by Arrabal himself) is physically and scenically striking. You look in vain for such attributes in The Cilla Black Show (Palladium), except in the performance of Philippe Genty & Co., invisible puppeteers who contrive a bewitching dance for a trio of emus, one of whom keeps burying his beak in the pink feather-duster that serves him for a body. Nobody else on stage evinces this becoming bashfulness. The star herself, as healthily winsome as ever, sings her older hits very well. Either that, or sixties nostalgia is on its way and I am its first victim.

records.title: Gay times for the CIA
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Wait till the Sun Shines, Nellie
records.body:
Gay times for the CIA

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on two very different products of the American theatre.

FOR their new experimental season at The Place, the Royal Shakespeare Company have abandoned the steeply banked arena seating that they adopted there two years ago. The actors now face the audience conventionally head-on; most directly they face the critics who, on first nights, are lined up in front in what must look from the stage like Murderers' Row.

This week a new American comedy called Section Nine came up before the bench which was seen, at various points in the evening, to shake with laughter. There were other points, though, at which it trembled with irritation.

Philip Magdalany has given us the latest specimen of doomsday comedy, a genre whose rules were firmly established some years ago by Dr Strangelove. An apocalyptic global threat is posited, generally with a severe time limit, and the action consists of frantic attempts to defuse it.
