records.title: Brave and bracing
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Brave and bracing

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a Harley Granville Barker revival.

ONE of the more disturbing features of the theatre this year has been the extent to which our two most highly subsidised theatres have been encouraged to play safe.

The National Theatre can hardly have been expected to fail with Ibsen, Shaw, Beckett and Pinter--standard authors, infallibly cast. But a national theatre should not only protect, but extend the national repertory, and though we may be within our rights to pronounce the attempted resurrection of Gilbert's 'Engaged' a failure, it is chilling to hear it declared that the attempt should never have been made.

To their credit, the National proceeded undeterred to honour another of the obscurer dead, a foreigner too. After a week of brooding over their 'Phaedra Britannica,' my admiration for the technical skill of translator, director and performers remains immense, though in altering Racine's mythology they have sacrificed more logic than they have gained.

I cannot begrudge the Aldwych their safe period earlier in the year, if only because the revival of Tom Stoppard's 'Travesties,' with John Wood picking his way unerringly through a minefield of jokes and Lenin (Harry Towb) accorded his proper status like the other characters among history's clowns, possesses twice the sparkle of the first attempt and three times the logic. ('If only Tom Stoppard had got it together,' I pontificated last Christmas, 'it would have been the play of the year.' I see now that he had, and it was.) But I respect the RSC the more for their new kamikaze tactics. True there are limits (David Mercer's 'Duck Song' last year was beyond them, even as it was beyond most of us), but Charles Wood's 'Jingo' was a thoroughly honourable flop, whatever it cost. Suppose we agree to stop using the economic situation as a critical sanction.

From all of which it follows that I wish to hear no puling objections to the latest offering at the Aldwych, where on Thursday we assisted at the second performance (not production, performance) of Granville Barker's The Marrying of Ann Leete, the first having taken place on a Sunday night in 1902. How pleasant to be in virtually at the birth of a major dramatist.

The play was actually written in 1899, and is set a hundred years previously; it is one dying era's tribute to another. No, tribute is not the word; and Barker and his characters are very careful of their words, very jealous of how much they may be permitted to convey. He was 21 when he composed it, and the play has the harshness of youth, though not (compared with some of our infant prodigies) either its hysteria or its priggishness. It is also extraordinarily brave.

Ann Leete is a politician's daughter. Her elder sister has been married off for her father's advantage, and she is about to be sent the same way. At first she acquiesces, somewhat frightened but resigned. Only she overhears too much of the family cynicism, the family scheming and--particularly in reference to her sister's marriage--the bitterness of the family failure. The same day as her match is made she breaks it off, and offers herself as the wife of the gardener, the new self-reliant man, named--with heavy but not unpleasant symbolism--Abud. At the play's end, Ann, removed from spacious gardens to her husband's narrow cottage, contemplates an unromantic future. 'I'll do my part . . . something will come of it.'

The play presages change, not only historical (and its characters live in submerged awareness of revolution across the Channel) but theatrical. To us it may recall Chekhov--but the play it most resembles, 'The Cherry Orchard,' it actually antedates. The dialogue can be cryptic and allusive beyond anything in Pinter. It requires attention (and, if possible, a preliminary squint at the text), but magnificently rewards it. Sometimes the words are used, in Jamesian fashion, to polish thought (and to convey a period style with no recourse to archaism), sometimes to conceal it; the characters play devious games. Barker's plays are oddly angled; they tell their stories with a teasing disregard for the obvious.

This one begins with a kissing-game, before dawn, and the images of kissing, of play, of light and darkness reverberate through it, in action as well as dialogue. The Leetes' intrigues are harshly, classically illuminated; the final scene, candle-lit, implies both completion and progression. David Jones's production seems to me a rarer achievement than his Gorki plays (and will, hopefully, inaugurate a similar Barker cycle); Gorki's are juicy plays; obvious gifts for actors. This needs to be played with passion, but within a strict, witty convention. Here, as in 'Phaedra Britannica,' those demands are met. Mr Jones finds the rhythms of the play, and shapes them into personal encounters.

The casting of Mia Farrow as Ann proves an inspiration. She is opposed to a collection of hard stylish actors; Paul Rogers, Richard Pasco, Estelle Kohler at her brittlest and best; only Mike Gwilym, as a brother half out of the family, makes some humane concessions. Among them all Miss Farrow, fiercely vulnerable, has to work out her own stance. Hers is, in no derogatory sense, a very painstaking performance; she learns, and grows, we watch and grow with her. 'I must study politics,' she says with her head on one side (her voice, too, it seems) and the impact on her consciousness is precisely charted. Not all of Barker's ideas come off the page; a Hogarthian rout of wedding-guests remains an intention rather than a fact. But the evening is fresh, vital, bracing, and all things pertaining to iced water.

* * *

Steven Berkoff has in the past directed the London Theatre Group, acted with it, adapted Kafka for it. He now puts it, himself included, through its paces in his first original work. Unfortunately East (King's Head) seems to have been written for little reason beyond that of furnishing the group with a text of Mr Berkoff's own; it is aimless, with a tyro's idea of shape. That is, it ends with the same lines as it has begun, in the apparent belief that there is something profound about a loop. (I would have said a circle, but 'East' is not so well rounded.)

The subject matter, loosely assembled, is life in the East End; vignettes have been selected in order to allow scope for maximum aggression which, when it slackens, necessarily entails maximum sentimentality. Much of the dialogue is pastiche blank verse, delivered in the clipped Shakespearean tones made familiar by Peter Sellers, Benny Hill and Laurence Olivier. Some of the prose bits, though, are good; notably a hard-pressed mum's dreamy monologue of escape, delivered in drag by Robert Longden.

Barry Stanton has some huffy, rosy-faced moments as Dad; his off-beat timing suggests that they may be improvised. And as a work-out for its actors the show, fluently staged, is reasonably enjoyable; enabling them to shine as motor-bikes, dodgem-cars (Mr Berkoff's arrival tending to the mechanistic) and even, sometimes, as people.

records.title: World of cads and tuxedos
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
World of cads
and tuxedos

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on
a revival of Noel
Coward's 'The Vortex.'

WANDERERS in an Art Deco wilderness, Florence Lancaster and her son Nicky appear on the stage of the Greenwich Theatre like late arrivals to last year's series of 'Family Romances.' You may remember that that season, under the direction of Jonathan Miller, consisted of 'Hamlet,' 'The Seagull' and 'Ghosts'; and at one time it was rumoured that Noel Coward's The Vortex would be of their company.

It is as well perhaps that the rumour proved false, and that we have had to wait till now to see Coward's play at Greenwich, under the direction of James Roose-Evans. Mr Miller, once he had started work on it, would surely have got irritated by its thinness, and this irritation would have communicated itself to us. Compared with Chekhov's and Ibsen's Hamlet-variations, never mind with the thing itself, Coward's play lacks body. It suffers, too, from a facile ending, curing mother and cadging son happy in each other's arms at the final curtain. Chekhov and Shakespeare placed their equivalent clinches in the middle of the action; by the end of the show such easy reconciliations have been left far behind. In Ibsen the embrace is saved for the finale, but it is a ghastly parody of a happy ending.

'The Vortex,' however, closes with Florence, who has had lovers, and Nicky, who has taken drugs, both promising never to do it again. We can believe them or not as we choose, I found it difficult to care either way. In this respect the play is partly the victim of history; or at least of that small tributary of history called fashion. Its true element is the twenties, the cocktail and tuxedo twenties: the Noel Coward twenties in short, by our lights the cutest period that ever was. Mr Roose-Evans has tried to woo us into the play by initially emphasising twenties charm (so that cloche-hatted Jennifer Hilary, as Florence's confidante, never sits on a chair when she can perch on its arm or drape herself against its back), and subsequently fading it out so that the last scene leaves us with unadorned timeless emotion.

Here he echoes his author, who fills out his first two acts with the bitchy humours of his heroine's entourage before turning relentlessly to business in the last. The result, however, in both writing and production is that manner, or just mannerism, outbalances matter. Having become attuned to a Coward comedy, though not one of his best, we are dashed to find mother and son upbraiding each other in a modern closet scene. (When they start rolling on the bed it's really too much.)

The turning-point has been a moment of sheer melodrama, well-made melodrama, but no more convincing for that. Florence discovers her current gigolo kissing Nicky's fiancee. 'What does this mean?' she asks rhetorically. 'You are an utter cad,' she states, even more rhetorically. The following year Coward himself parodied this kind of thing in 'Hay Fever' where the inveterate performer Judith Bliss ('Is this a game?' 'Yes, and a game that must be played to the finish') makes every blameless intrusion the occasion for a scene. Judith is a more truthful as well as a funnier version of Florence. Each one of them is a Bright Middle-aged Thing, a sad phenomenon, as 'The Vortex' keeps insisting, but not overwhelmingly tragic. Where Judith is an actress, Florence merely moves in a theatrical ambience. We are already within sight of Coward's typical snobbery towards non-thespians, treating them as bizarre objects to be sniffed at, patronised and touched with tongs.

The milieu is too shallow to be worth storming at or preaching over, but Coward does both in 'The Vortex.' He is fair enough to make his mouthpiece Nicky more than slightly suspect, though little of this emerges in the performance of Timothy Dalton, who seems undernourished but thoroughly healthy. Vivien Merchant, all of a flutter as Florence, speaking low, slow and breathy like an enervated Fenella Fielding, pays the same price as the play and production, livening the early scenes at the expense of the conclusion. The freshest acting comes from Gabrielle Drake, the fiancee who acts as foil to Nicky's grand filial passion.

* * *

Toby Robins, a leading Canadian actress over two decades, looks startlingly youthful as the recidivist heroine of The Ecstasy of Rita Joe. She is a better advertisement for Canadian theatre than George Ryga's play (at the fallible Hampstead Theatre Club), which treats of the dispossessed Indian in a manner stolid, documentary at best and leadenly fanciful otherwise. (Red man speak with ornamental tongue; often he trip over it.) It must have seemed more urgent in its own time (1967) as well as its own place. Technically it plods in a manner we have outgrown on both sides of the Atlantic; its avoidance of character confrontation strains both the patience and the nerves. Its original production probably owed much to the presence of genuine Indians. (One staging featured Chief Dan George, the indestructible ancient of 'Little Big Man.') At Hampstead it falls an easy victim to a miserably unauthentic production, which closes with blanketed white actors stomping hard, perhaps to ward off the evil spirits of embarrassment. They materialised nonetheless.

records.title: Laying the judge bare
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Laying the judge bare

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE title-figure of Howard Barker's Stripwell (Royal Court) is a man of variable disposition, and this seems to be one of the things his author has against him. Different people know him as different things: to his wife and son he is Graham, to his mistress Strip, a name to which her profession lends a certain displaced appropriateness. She is a go-go dancer, and you do not have to delve very far into contemporary mythology to discover what kind of elderly man would be hanging around her. Stripwell is a judge.

We catch him at it - the judging, I mean - at the very beginning of the play. He is about to hand out to a young tearaway what may be the toughest sentence imposed for misappropriating a motor-car since the celebrated case of Mr Toad. Asked for his comments before sentence is passed, the prisoner offers the following: "If you put me away, I'll escape and murder you."

Hearing this, Strip takes a recess, during which he consults his girlfriend (who arranges her touring dates to coincide with his) and returns to administer a term of 12 months. "Will that," he inquires nervously, "be all right?" The accused says that it won't and reiterates his threat. At the end of the play he returns to carry it out, his reappearance charged with just the right blend of necessity and surprise.

The play thus boasts a witty start and a powerful finish; only the in-between, which is of course the longest bit, goes wrong. Stripwell's nervous behaviour in court has shown him not to have the courage of his convictions; the rest of the play denies him even the convictions.

The promise from the dock impels him to examine his threatened life. He determines to introduce some truth and decision into it; to begin with he will leave his wife. Unfortunately his go-go girl sees him mainly as material for her autobiography and ditches him, in the interest of youth and her next chapter; Stripwell's own son, a prankish drug-trafficker who smuggles heroin in the private parts of female elephants, supplants his father. Stripwell is left bemoaning his fate: "She didn't want me because she'd fallen for somebody else."

There is no escaping the indebtedness of that line and of the whole situation to a hundred matinee-dramas. On what Mr Barker has given us we can feel sorry for Stripwell or bored with him or (as in my case) a bit of both, but no more serious response is possible; we have not the evidence.

Strip and his wife converse for ages without giving us any sense of what their marriage was like; Constance Cummings is left being stylish in a vacuum. The two young characters - conventional caricatures of cool - carry even less conviction in the writing and, though Patricia Quinn jerks a mean abdomen, hardly any in the acting.

All our sympathies go to the leading character which, with Michael Hordern playing him, was probably inevitable. He has all the best lines or at least (an attribute common to most of Mr Hordern's roles) he sounds as if he has. At first the character seems likely to become another Hordern eccentric, victimised but jovial. With superb resource he lays this familiar spectre, but in doing so makes a better case for hesitant liberalism than Mr Barker can have envisaged. His good intentions count for more than his backslidings and his isolation for more than either. With his extraordinary face (indestructibly lean, for all its pouches), he becomes a figure of pathos, if not of tragedy: a sardonic Don Quixote with, unfortunately, nothing to tilt against.

* * *

Earlier this year, Mr Barker's play Claw, at the Open Space drew apocalyptic conclusions from cartooned premises; the imbalance was plain, but, since the apocalypse was gripping and the cartoon fairly funny, forgivable. Moving up to the Royal Court he has tried for greater density, but only achieved sobriety, which is far less interesting. It has infected the production too: Chris Parr's handling of Claw was beautifully fluid. At the Court, given sets to play with, he lets the brief scenes trundle.

* * *

The kaleidoscopic method works much better in the studio confines of the Bush, where Stephen Poliakoff's City Sugar puts a supermarket, a bed-sit and a local radio station simultaneously on stage and leaves us to decide which is the most depressing. The play itself - though it enlarges on the pessimistic view of life in Leicester propounded by Mr Poliakoff's Hitting Town - is far from depressing. It pits a disc-jockey who has known more hopeful times against a salesgirl for whom there is only now: hard to say which cynicism is the more corroding. Both are to an extent their author's puppets, but they give Lynne Miller and John Shrapnel enough to go on.

Mr Shrapnel indeed is given, and returns, rather more. On one level he obviously enjoys the DJ bit (as his author has enjoyed writing it: it's a generation's fantasy). On another his round owlish glasses and curving moustache give him an air at once appalled and appalling; his depression at the girl's ignorance of the Beatles is very real. So is his relationship with his nudgingly ambitious sound engineer (admirably played by Leon Vitali), his butt on and off the air.

* * *

Thomas and the King confirms that, after all their play and movie exposure, Henry II and Becket have passed as securely into showbiz folklore as Robin Hood - whom I kept expecting them to meet. They wander on, thoughtless playboy and tight-lipped retainer, for all the world like Bertie and Jeeves in the last musical shipwreck at Her Majesty's; this show is similarly maladroit and also (unlike 'Jeeves') plain stupid.

records.title: Consumed by flames
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Aneurin Bevan: Struggles Against The Iron Heel
records.body:
Consumed by flames

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

J. A. WHITEHEAD'S Old Flames (New Vic Studio, Bristol) might be subtitled "Memories of a Catholic Boyhood."

At least, that at any rate is its main character - a youngish man called Edward who recalls that his first ever crisis was over the Pope. Later it transferred its affections to women but ultimately, to its author's discontent, on to other, consequent objects.

Most of its story has to do with sex. It is concerned, if I identify him correctly, with Edward himself who says that he uses it as cover for seduction, but he means it. And he thinks that by declaring it he in some way absolves himself from guilt and can continue as before. The same firmness underlies his refusal to his current girl to stop him when he goes too far. He half means it, but when she takes him literally and slashes his face he more than half resents it. This repression of an uneasy conscience upon a character too light to carry it is a subtle achievement, both in the writing and in the shifting heartlessness of Gary Bond's performance: a deep voyage into shallow waters.

The play actually takes place on a boat. Sally, Edward's new love, lives on one and she has invited him home. But she has also invited a selection of his current entanglements: two wives and, as aforesaid, a mother. The Pope, alas, fails to appear, but his influence is felt enough to deflect the new metaphorical overtones of the watery setting, but the dialogue and action reek of stillness.

At the simplest, there is Edward's mother, who has herself suffered a long and unsuitable marriage, pouring tight-lipped disapproval of her son for welshing on his first wretched alliance; his second of course turned out equally badly. Edward himself, giving thanks (typically half-baked and, as it turns out, rather premature) for the sexual revolution, toasts the assembled ladies with a magnificent unconscious pun: "We've been through the flames and we've survived." He has been through several flames and here they are, still burning, ready to lick him to death. He does not survive.

At the end of the first act, with everyone present, Edward lightly asks what's for supper. He is told, "you are," and he is. He is absent from the second act, which is largely devoted to a lively, not to say scabrous, discussion of his shortcomings and those of men in general. At length you fall to wondering what has become of him. He is not asleep, or in the lavatory, or even overboard. He has been killed, and the ladies, who appear to be consuming tomato juice and chunks of rhubarb (I was sitting quite far back), are in fact consuming his body and blood; the play concludes appropriately with a solemn parody of Communion.

Even the mother, who has sat in shocked silence through the younger women's more uninhibited exchanges, acknowledges firmly that Edward "had to be put down." This may strain credulity, but the play has been so formally constructed that the question hardly arises. But other questions do: is Edward, so finely exposed to us at the outset, anything worse than an ordinary man with common weaknesses?

But no sooner do you rebel against these women's unfairness to men than you remember that the author is a man; such rebellion is in fact a considerable compliment to him. Is this how women behave when alone together? I wouldn't know, would I. But the actresses seem convinced: in the case of Judy Cornwell and Susan Tracy, superb as the two wives, not just convinced, but possessed. Jane Asher is cool and bleached as the mistress of the revels who turns her houseboat into a Whitehead sepulchre; and Anne Dyson supplies one of her embittered elderly Northern women.

* * *

Miss Dyson is the only player in Jonathan Hale's production who strikes recognisably regional notes, and the disparity points to an ambiguity in the play. The characters at some points appear to be products of a specific background and culture (I assume Liverpudlian, though this is never made explicit); at others to stand for all contemporary men and women. Sexual exploitation may be general, but it does not always take the forms Mr Whitehead depicts. But in other respects his play is rewardingly impersonal; you might take it for the most fervent of propaganda for or against the women's movement. This means, not that it does not know its own mind, but that it has access into everybody's.

If Mr Whitehead writes well enough of women to convince one that he might be a woman, what of Charles Pierce, the American female impersonator at the Fortune? It would be interesting to hear his material - whose treatment of female sexuality is something more than innuendo and less than acknowledgment - actually delivered by a woman. Not, I think, since Mae West has there been a comedienne whose humour was primarily sexual; and she, of course, had censorship problems.

Mr Pierce does Miss West of course; he also offers a delectable Carol Channing addressing her choicest remarks to the Dress Circle with a smile and a curtsey; indeed with a smile that is almost a curtsey. He is most celebrated for his Bette Davis, most striking from behind, raunchily swinging her shoulders. His facial transformations are more remarkable than his vocal; even his account of Miss Davis is a bit approximate. He can do Tallulah Bankhead, but then (to use his own terms) couldn't everybody? There is something ventriloquial about his technique; he sets his creations bitching against one another, but you have to be a rabid film-nostalgia freak (simultaneously loving and resenting the idols) to get an enormous charge out of that. Now, if it were the real thing... But they are creations all the same, quite a few of the jokes are good, and Mr Pierce is quite free of the single-track hypocrisy of Danny La Rue whose humour consists in nudging you about how butch he really is.

* * *

Aneurin Bevan: Struggles Against The Iron Heel, seen last week at the Sherman, Cardiff, is now touring Wales; this week Aberystwyth. The first half is compilation-theatre at its worst; minced slogans which the actors must try hopelessly to convert into conversation. The author, David Illingworth, appears to be another of the breed, currently represented in London by Ian Taylor of Taramtara Taramtara, claiming to be dramatists at minimal expense. But in the second act he spreads himself a bit. Confining himself to two subjects - the birth of the NHS and the nuclear disarmament traumas of the fifties - he begins to build a play, and lets Colin McCormack as Bevan build a character. But the attitude to other figures is skittish, refusing to name them but banking on our knowing who they are.

* * *

The Haymarket, Leicester, has attempted Ibsen's last play When We Dead Awaken, an almost immovable monument which needs casting similar to or identical with the National's John Gabriel Borkman. Michael Meacham's production got the outlines of the play boldly right, but Andrew Cruickshank and Renee Asherson could not bring to life the hollow artist-Ibsen, his very self - nor the model he once betrayed (and condemned to a lifetime of posing on the halls). While they agonised, Heather Sears, in the more approachable role of the young wife intent on freedom, strode off with the play.

* * *

At Hampstead a group called Foco Novo has a free adaptation of Brecht's A Man's A Man, supplying it, among other things, with a happy ending, but failing to camouflage its elephantine (there's an in-joke for Brechtians) development.

records.title: Bond's prisoners of greed
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Bond's prisoners of greed

EDWARD BOND'S The Fool (Royal Court) begins with a mummers' play. A group of East Anglian villagers perform outside the local lord's door: very imposing as designed by William Dudley and apparently free-standing. The gentry applaud politely. It seems a reasonably happy, peaceful scene--the only such scene, it turns out, in the entire play.

The Napoleonic Wars have just ended, and we are in at the death of agricultural England. The parson, in attendance on the squire, preaches an impromptu sermon on the new industrial age. "An iron age," he calls it, and the ambiguous phrase gives promise of a complex evening. The parson talks of working for the common good, we sit back and wait for exploitation.

Two scenes on, the mummers have turned rioters. Once again they come up against the parson, this time to strip him, partly for the loot that adorns his body and partly so that they can cry "Under that he's same as us." When he is raked, though, they decide that this is not quite true. His skin, white and uncalloused, seems another mask it hides. "Where you stole that flesh, boy? Your flesh is stolen goods"; the obvious next step is to flay him. This is prevented, but the violent (and in context irresistible) logic of Mr Bond's writing makes it a real momentary possibility. Meanwhile the parson whimpers that he is a powerless old man; and that's true, too.

His attackers are arrested and condemned to death. Then their sentences are commuted to life imprisonment. This grisly mercy sets them laughing in thankful joy: a powerful device that survives its own awareness of how powerful it is.

While in prison they are visited by a friend. We have glimpsed him before, in the mummers' show. It now transpires--nearly half-way through the play--that he is a poet and also ("scribblin' come to summat") that he has found a publisher and is off to London. In fact he is the fool of the title: John Clare, whom the last scene will find in the madhouse.

Part of his folly seems at first to be lovesickness; he has become smitten with a maid at the squire's house. He misses the stripping of the parson having rushed off in search of her, but she returns in time not merely to witness it, but to make off with much of the booty: the others are too busy with the ritual of humiliation to notice. But "Mary" remains a presence in his poems; his real wife he calls her when questioned by his fans--not an idea that commends itself to his legal wife, who is tormented besides by the painful realisation that poetry brings in even less money than labouring. She nags him at length, but with some virtuosity: "Sleep on your own--you have the pleasure of getting kids, you have the worry of feeding them." She has throughout this knack of yoking images: granting Clare his right to a drink, she defines the question as one of "letting your glass empty afore your purse."

Bridget Turner makes the most of such lines as she does of the character's whole progress--from brisk girl to stony shrew to stranger, visiting her husband just once in the asylum because someone has paid her fare. Some other actors are equally adept with good material: John Normington with the quaverings of the clergyman, Bill Fraser with the complacencies of a poetaster admiral, asserting that some of Clare's amorous verses are too warm ever for the bedroom, "and I've been round the world." The best of Mr Bond's writing has matchless stage presence; his carved prose must be the envy and the goal of half the playwrights in Britain.

For all that, the play halts; nothing binds it. A gamekeeper early declares the need for "keepers of people," anticipating Clare's incarceration by the best part of two acts. The lord, mellowed, or perhaps simply tired by the last scene, notes that his son has fulfilled the parson's prophecy: he is "in love with his factories." But these are literary felicities; they do not amount to a theatrical structure.

The play is meant, I think, as a panoramic indictment of greed; apart from Clare himself, all the characters are, with varying degrees of volition, its prisoner. Mary searching for silver while Clare searches for her, the villagers stripping the parson, the gentry stripping the villagers. On the fringes are prizefighters breaking themselves down for money; off-stage are Clare's publishers unloading on him his unsold books.

The protagonist of Mr Bond's last play Bingo was an earlier poet, Shakespeare, depicted as the victim of his own acquiescence in the rise of capitalism. Clare is a victim, period, and easy to sentimentalise. Lunatic, lover and poet, peasant and social critic: he has something for everyone. But he is too slim a character (and too tardily developed) to unite the action. So the play--which is considerably more varied than Bingo--appears even more static. Nor is it much activated by the grey performance of Tom Courtenay, cast fatally to sensitive type; or by Peter Gill's production in which the muttering subfusc style falsely fathered on Brecht--and now deemed suitable for all plays set in the past or in changing locales or both--begins to approach self-parody.

* * *

I thought we had done for the Theatre at New End, but no, here we trudge again to the playhouse opposite the hospital (and converted from a mortuary). Trudging is the mode on stage as well; hopeful new management or not, David Edgar's Death Story is rather less interesting than the Anouilh Electra play with which the old gang kicked off. This one too retells an old story, Romeo and Juliet, divided within a modern city in which the Montagues are craftsmen and the Capulets financiers. An alien military force tries cynically to keep them off the streets; Mr Edgar must mean us to think of Ulster, but he hardly explores the parallel (and a modern town disrupted just by two families is not very credible).

His best moments are sour jokes on Shakespeare: Juliet writhing in an exhibitionist nightmare while waiting for Romeo, Romeo impotent on the night; it is probably healthy to be reminded that the two had imperfect bodies as well as perfect voices. Mr Edgar manages a good Mercutio of suicidal impulse (well played by Terry Palmer) and winds up with a thrice-repeated version of the lovers' suicide to show us how easy it has always been for us to lap up personal tragedy instead of facing the real truth about sectarian warfare. I trust that makes you feel guilty.

* * *

Ronnie Scott's Jazz Haven in Soho has been temporarily captured for the theatre in the early evening, through the agency of the Sadista Sisters, four female persons who sing very well--and act less adroitly--pungent little rock-songs and sketches about feminine stereotypes. Particularly arresting is a stripper who turns out to be heavily anaphrodisiacally pregnant. The attitude towards men (equally trapped by stereotypes) is altogether less helpful than seems to have been intended.

The Greenwich revival of Coward's Fallen Angels is frothy, neatly set and over before you know it. This particularly applies to the two heroines' famous scene of alcoholic reminiscence; if you wait for the scandal, you wait all night. Eileen Atkins and Judy Parfitt do a conscientious job (Miss Atkins in particular is more fetching than she has been in ages, and more feathery than I would ever have imagined), but conscience, alas, cannot make Cowards of us all. Joyce Grant, at least, has no truck with it, turning what was written as modest scene-stealing into grand larceny. I missed this production's first night by going to watch Charles Pierce working over the queens of Hollywood; somehow I feel the two experiences might have been profitably and entertainingly combined.

records.title: In the marriage trap
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man
records.body:
LAST year I attacked a production of a Franz Kroetz play for transferring its action from Bavaria to London, on the apparent assumption that no audience can take any interest in a situation farther away than its own backyard. This adherence to fashionable dogma effectively destroyed much of the play's fibre.

Now at Hampstead there is another Kroetz play; and from its title Morecambe you may guess that it too has been given a local injection. And there goes one more critical theory, for in this case the text has been so resourcefully transplanted that the play stands and the critic kneels.

Today, of course, the name Morecambe has two connotations, and Jane Brenton's translation exploits both of them. The play concerns a young marriage, and the two partners begin the evening by expressing admiration for Morecambe, near Wise and, associated with this, a desire to visit Morecambe, near Lancaster. It is not made too clear whether this would mean popping into the next town, or taking a long trip by Inter-City. The second sounds more probable; the dialogue and its delivery, in Annabel Leventon's production, are very London.

Whatever the distance, it increases in the course of the play; Morecambe, which would once have been a nice place to visit, becomes an impossible goal. So do a lot of other things. He works as a delivery driver, she in a shop. But their finances are precariously balanced, and an accidental pregnancy is enough to unsettle them fatally. Almost the husband's first thought is of an abortion; the wife resists and though she lets him arrange an appointment she ends up refusing to keep it.

Despite this the tone of the relationship and of the play is remarkably cheerful. A happy marriage is a rare phenomenon in a good play, and given the acting of Lesley Joseph and Philip Sayer one would be tempted to call this a perfect match. Sometimes, of course, it frays; there is a memorable pub scene in which she has to seek him out in the gents (the only place she can get a word alone with him) in order to beg him to spend no more of their substance on drinks for his mates. The very brightness and kindness of the relationship makes the situation hurt the more. In the most memorable scene the two of them, accepting the inevitability of parenthood, go through their budget wondering which items are the most expendable, and knowing throughout that in fact nearly everything will have to be. I don't know how it sounds in Deutsch Marks but it rings fearfully true in sterling. (Though while immediacy is in question: I don't find that when a play touches on my own problems I concentrate on it harder; I am more likely to embark on trains of thought of my own.)

Kroetz may be sorrowing that his characters have wrapped up so much of their happiness in consumer goods, or he may be raging that so basic a thing as birth should prevent them from doing so any longer. Decide for yourselves; the important thing is that you will want to. Both the trap and its inmates are solid and inescapable; the play resonates accordingly.

* * *

The difference between Morecambe and John McGrath's Yobbo Nowt, presented by the 7:84 company at the Shaw, is the difference between a created work and an enjoyable piece of theatrical journalism. Mr McGrath also deals with a woman trapped by pregnancy: in her case, into marriage with a man who leaves her some 17 years later with two adolescent kids, no job and no qualifications. Her encounters with the National Assistance lady, very sweet and smiling and deadly, are excellently done as lemony revue-sketches. Eventually she lands work in a factory, finds she is being exploited, and decides to find out about the system that is doing it to her. The investigation becomes, as she says, her hobby; but the more questions she asks, the more predictable become the answers. Suspense disappears; and so, with the leaden cartooning of the one Establishment figure in the show, does conflict.

Meanwhile the vanished husband reappears and is dismissed, our heroine having had her consciousness raised in matters of sex as well as class. Altogether she shapes up into an indomitably faultless heroine, on the lines of The Mother; and though Mr McGrath's play lacks the odious sentimentality of Brecht's it is equally one-sided. It rambles, too, without attaining to the picaresque quality of his earlier Fish in the Sea. It is saved by the spirit of the cast, and especially by their musicianship. The evening is packed with songs, all of them well performed. Mark Brown's music happily utilises a collection of pop styles, and Mr McGrath's lyrics, in this instance, are sharper than his dialogue. An aggressive number disposing of the love generation (if any of it is still around) is particularly good.

* * *

The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (ICA) is, as you would expect from the Pip Simmons Group, more like a nightmare. Based, how faithfully I cannot say, on a Dostoevsky short story, it puts an intending suicide to sleep, conjures up for him a series of painful or pleasurable hallucinations, and lets him wake up to the conclusion that life is pretty good after all if approached in the right spirit: sentiments of a singalong, which in fact is how the show ends. All the same, anyone joining in will have been had. There are fangs behind the smile. Even more disturbingly there is a leer.

In the middle of the dream, blending wit and enchantment, is the most idyllic tableau to be found on a London stage: a Polynesian paradise, represented by palms, bare-breasted girls, a couple of doves, a fruit vendor and a zany but harmonious addition--an old man knitting in a deck-chair and a live chicken. The scene is, of course, created only to be destroyed--which would be fair enough except that the cynicism is cranked up in excess of the situation.

* * *

Lonsdale's On Approval, revived at the Haymarket, begins as dead drawing-room comedy. Then it moves its four characters to Scotland where the air is much more bracing. Two of them, a rich woman and an impoverished Duke, are intolerable; gradually the two others realise the fact. Edward Hardwicke and Jennie Linden manage decency without dullness (Miss Linden even runs to a little sparkle) but in Frank Hauser's snappy and thoroughbred production the running is naturally made by the two monsters. They differ in approach. Geraldine McEwan, unbelievably white of face and thin of limb, is a terror from the start; but then she can afford to be while Edward Woodward, with only blood to recommend him, has to lace his way into awfulness.

Miss McEwan is like a sea-creature, jealously guarding her own rock, thrashing out with her tentacles whenever someone comes too near for decorous comfort or absents himself too far for speedy service. She can stretch her voice like elastic; some of the things she does with it are indeed scarcely human.

Edward Woodward, with his odd mixture of threat and drawl, has never been funnier. The ending, which maroons the two of them for an indefinite period in a snowbound house, reveals that Lonsdale saw Hell in much the same terms as Jean-Paul Sartre. Concerning the influence of the English boulevardiers of the twenties on the French philosophers of the forties, much work has still to be done.

records.title: Danniella and the dragon
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Danniella and the dragon

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the latest offerings from Danny La Rue and Charles Marowitz.

A YEAR ago the London Casino returned to live entertainment with a pantomime, Cinderella. Though excellent in most respects, this flunked the principal requirements of a modern Christmas show by failing to run until Easter. So this year no chances have been taken and the Casino has requisitioned the services of Danny La Rue, the surest draw in the West End. The show's title--though this is of the merest academic interest--is Queen Danniella.

For the past three Christmases I have been trying to explain the conventions of pantomime to my Canadian wife. I have had little success, and Queen Danniella makes the task harder than ever. It has virtually no story. Digression is of course the staple diet of pantomime, but this one has nothing to digress from. It has, to be sure, some stock situations: there is the usual quest in which all the good or funny characters venture into the castle of the bad or serious ones. Mr La Rue as Danniella, whose queendom is in hock, gets lost in a forest glade where she (I am running into trouble with personal pronouns) meets an admittedly sweet baby dragon. But the charm of irrelevant episodes like this is traditionally that of playing truant from the main action; when school has been closed up truancy loses much of its appeal.

Mr La Rue for the adults, fragments of narrative and slapstick for the kids, and some indeterminate pop for everyone or no one: that must have been the formula. It is, I suppose, only a logical culmination of the process which has been overtaking the cavernous West End panto for years. But at a matinee performance the calculations seemed upset; there were plenty of empty seats and those that were full were mainly full of children. Now whatever the advances of juvenile sophistication (signalised by a shrill cry of "Rape" from the back stalls when some villain made off with Sheila White's extremely tough Princess), Mr La Rue's characteristic double entendres are not likely to mean too much to the under-twelves. He went devoutly through his patter, and through Bryan Blackburn's lyrics (which contribute to theatrical history by rhyming "Gielgud" with "feel good" and don't ask me to explain the context or we'll never get home), but it was all done with subdued desperation.

In fact Mr La Rue was up against it; and in these circumstances he strangely seemed far more likeable than when playing to a full and sycophantic house at the Prince of Wales. His manner is always professional, and in this show his professionalism is manna. I have never seen a performer get through the community singing bit with more address or less embarrassment.

I even, when the panto-pretence was finally discarded for a prolonged star-turn, enjoyed his impersonations--done, remember, to an audience that can never have heard of Carmen Miranda or even of Marlene Dietrich. (He also does the Marilyn Monroe of Some Like It Hot, flanked by two other guys pretending to be Tony Curtis and Jack Lemmon pretending to be girls. Even Shakespeare never thought of that juxtaposition.) He has the legs for Grable and he wears the frocks as ever with superb panache--though the problem of how to occupy the stage while he is changing them has been solved even more miserably than usual. (By the way, could someone be hired before next Christmas to teach the pantomime chorus just one new step--or alternatively to drown them. Everybody knows these routines bore the kids; but whom are they supposed to entertain?)

The whole production stinks of compromise, but Mr La Rue--especially after you have spent an evening hearing Charles Pierce bitching at the ladies to whom he owes his livelihood--is very pleasant. He is, in fairness, less funny than Mr Pierce; next Christmas perhaps the two of them could do the Ugly Sisters.

* * *

Charles Marowitz, of all directors, respects his author. It takes only a workaday trust in Shakespeare to assume that his plays will make sense if the lines are delivered in the order their author set down, but to believe that they will still be effective with their running-order jumbled requires true fanaticism. It also requires of course that your audience, if they are to enjoy themselves, must bring prior knowledge to the theatre with them.

As this is true of Mr Marowitz's Shakespearean collages, so it is of his latest work. Artaud at Rodez (Open Space) is a phantasmagoric view of the French theatrical theorist and madman Antonin Artaud, Rodez being the asylum in which he spent some of the latest years of his life. That, and a deal else, I learned from Mr Marowitz's compilation but it was not enough. The production lacks flair, but it might succeed as an illustrated lecture if only we were told more; if, for example, some attempt were made to distinguish between Artaud's Theatre of Cruelty and its common interpretation as a theatre of sadism. The line is perhaps a thin one, and Artaud himself probably smudged it, but it ought at some stage of the evening to be drawn.

The show makes no bones, and a few good jokes, of the misinterpretation of Artaud's ideas by his disciples, but since those ideas are never presented to us he comes over as just another victim. As such he is well and feverishly played by Clive Merrison.

* * *

I missed Beetles and Buckman when they played the Mermaid this year, but I will do my best to catch them when they return to the boards in February at the Mayfair. Catch is the appropriate word; they are a pair of doctor-comedians, and for their current season at Quaglino's Beetles (Chris) has pulled the ultimate medical joke by going down with hepatitis, leaving Buckman (Robert) to carry the act on his own. This he does most appealingly, revealing himself as a unique commodity in Britain: an overtly literate stand-up clown, the first since Jonathan Miller.

His humour is far less surreal than was Mr Miller's; though it has a touch of what I can only call solid whimsy, in the most recent Cambridge tradition: hence a rousing sea-shanty about working in a public library. And though he does not actually cut anybody, he is sharp: he even creates an endearing critic, one who having left his concert tickets behind, nevertheless followed the pianist he was sent to review to the restaurant of his choice and there timidly admired the technique of a virtuoso "trained to be equally at home with spoon and fork." Geniality flows from Dr Buckman; go and see him, unless of course you are ill.

records.title: Return of Annie Oakley
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
IT IS always good to see an audience enjoying itself, and this is the main delight afforded by the Nottingham Playhouse production of Annie Get Your Gun.

It is cheering too to find that a major rep can fill its house with a modern classic. Actually revivals of the best post-war musicals have been a profitable commonplace for some time now; the regions have bristled with Kiss Me Kate and Guys and Dolls. But Annie is a comparative rarity, and I approached it warily.

The story goes that when somebody, during the show's original New York run, described it as old-fashioned, its composer, the imperturbable Irving Berlin, retorted: "That's right, a good old-fashioned smash." For him it certainly was; the score is justly considered his masterpiece. From "Doing What Comes Naturally" to "No Business Like Show Business" and on again to "They Say It's Wonderful," it seems to consist of nothing but hits.

But Annie is a comparative rarity, and I approached it warily. The Nottingham programme lists just one unfamiliar song-title, "I'll Share It All With You," whose obscurity must result from its being a holy terror to sing. Its complications, which happen very fast, are not what one expects of Mr Berlin: a reminder that this composer, so often taken for granted, in fact confounded expectation throughout his career.

Despite its technical originality, however, "I'll Share It All With You" is generally a very traditional kind of musical comedy number. It is a comedy love-song for the show's two second leads; there are numbers in Show Boat which fulfil exactly the same function. Annie came 20 years after Show Boat, but architecturally it has not advanced a step further. Modern enough to boast a story, it is still not sure what to do with it.

Annie Oakley, sharpest of shooters from the backwoods, becomes the heroine of a conventional backstage romance. She might, what is more, be back of just about any stage. (Not for nothing has "Show Business" become an all-purpose anthem.) Playhouse patrons, looking at the publicity and the programme covers, might be forgiven for thinking that they are off to see the Wild West show; but the book makes little of the ambience (beyond a few random jokes about Indians) and the production much less.

There is altogether a distressing baldness about the show at Nottingham; it consists of little more than the songs successively happening; and though they are enough to make a pleasant evening they also make an unsatisfying one. The script does remarkably little to set them up; the hero, Frank Butler, has hardly got his sights on Annie before he starts in about the girl that he marries having to be as pink and as white as a nurseree. I can imagine a production and performance so effervescent as to fill out the gaps, as the authors doubtless trusted they would; you can probably imagine it too; at the Playhouse you have to.

The most distinguished element of the evening is David Collis's open set, but this, though stark and stylish, is also a downer. It looks brilliantly economical; but brilliant economy is not really what one wants of a good old-fashioned smash. The one really joyous number, "I Got the Sun in the Morning," significantly deploys enough actors--virtually the entire cast--to obliterate the background. This, too, is the only point at which the band wakes up, spurred on perhaps by an arrangement which, like the tune itself, has not much to do with the Old West, but a great deal to do with swing. Annie is a forties musical and this song rejoices in the fact. It makes a lovely noise.

But this kind of volume and vivacity is noticeably absent from the other songs, most of them solos or duets for the leading couple. The show is essentially a duel for egomaniacs; shortcomings in staging, decor and choreography could all be redeemed by justified assurance from the performers. But John Price shambles apologetically through Frank Butler, his defences down from the start; and though Ursula Smith acts Annie rather well, this virtue, affecting only the dialogue, is of strictly limited use. Her voice is a throaty purr (at least it was last Monday), charming for a ballad like "I Got Lost in his Arms" (the best song in the score, incidentally, winding its melody up tight before releasing it), but fatally devoid of brass. So when the two of them square up to what should be a classic encounter ("anything you can do I can do better--no you can't--yes I can" and all that), nothing much happens.

The plot is interesting at this point though; Annie, having lost Frank by her irritating habit of outgunning him, purposely shoots below her best and gets him back. And this in a sex discrimination week: throw in the comic book Indians (a diminutive Sitting Bull must, to judge from his jokes, have been as much Jew as Sioux) and you have a stimulatingly reactionary entertainment.

* * *

The Oxford Playhouse, also in seasonal flight from tradition, has come up with an elaborate re-telling by Frank Marcus of Beauty and the Beast. Its comic diversions are mostly elephantine; a quasi-dame only just rescued by Hugh Paddick, a monstrously coy French fairy not rescued at all, a black postman who sings his messages. Others are potentially interesting: the postman is turned into a mountebank's symbol of the noble savage; this is obviously meant to illuminate the main plot, but it is difficult to see how. It comes over as filler; and the production has the heaviness which seems the hallmark of the new regime at Oxford.

But though Mr Marcus takes a long time to get to his real story, there is some magic in its eventual telling: in Terence Evans's bewilderment as Beauty's father lost in the Beast's castle and in the immaculate priggishness, not at all repellent, of Debbie Bowen's Beauty. There are her attempts to teach the Beast (Christopher Gable, piquant casting) to dance, and, most satisfyingly logical, her dismay when he turns into a prince. She misses his furriness.

* * *

In The Everest Hotel (Bush), Snoo Wilson transports three girl singers, rock-and-rolling in the service of the Lord and more particularly the Pope, from the Himalayas to Portugal by a route I found it difficult to follow. As usual Mr Wilson's writing ("what a life--you turn round and it's winter") is abrupt and kaleidoscopic; it is possible to see why those who like him like him very much. His own production is visually attractive in an off-hand way; but the casualness encouraged by the tiny theatre does little for clarity. The play seems to have two points: one is the performance of Janet Chappell, the other is faith, its desirability and its evanescence. Do not, however, quote me on that.

records.title: Starkness--and farce
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Starkness--and farce

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'The Ik' and Ben Travers's 'Plunder'.

THERE is no way in which the theatre can escape from its allegiance to effect; to inducing an emotion or enforcing a moral. Everything placed before an audience is a show, Peter Brook's production of The Ik (Roundhouse) as much as the National Theatre revival of Ben Travers's Plunder (Old Vic). Indeed, in terms of the unfamiliar demands it makes on its actors, Plunder may well be the more adventurous production of the two.

Many of us clapped at the end of The Ik; those who did not looked at us reproachfully. They expected us, I think, to be too numbed for so frivolous a response; and they could point to the integrity of a production which never raises its voice, literally or metaphorically, to back them up. But starkness is an effect, like any other; the refusal blatantly to shock or move an audience is the latest way of trying to do both.

In The Ik six actors offer their own image, born of travel in Africa and experiment in Paris, of the lives of a Ugandan tribe who have been denied their traditional existence as hunters and left to starve. They are old at 20; only the cleverest predators survive. They are dying out, since procreation is too much effort for them; their few remaining pleasures include cheating and teasing the anthropologist Colin Turnbull (on whose book The Mountain People the play is based), whose efforts to record them with notebook, tape and whirring cine-camera lend the production a solemn comic ground-base.

The play is given in English, but since the cast are international their speeches have a peculiar tone; they seem quite effortlessly alien. They really do appear indifferent to the public gaze; hence their fascination for Turnbull and for us. They are people who expect nothing and will take anything; they and the production have, in consequence, a unique rhythm. Everything is arbitrary, everything is inevitable.

Seeing them in Paris last year I described them as representing "irreducible, shuffling, nerveless humanity." I will now stand by the adjectives, but not the noun; I no longer feel inclined to generalise or to identify. The reaction that that is how we will all behave is obvious and true, but facile; a case, like that of Barry Collins's Judgment, which nobody would want to question. I doubt if that was one of Mr Brook's major preoccupations anyway; all he is really asking us to do is to look at, and be entertained by, the Ik, or by an ingenious, original, and consistent method of presenting them. (One of them, played by a constantly grinning Japanese actor, has the wiliness of a traditional clown; we loved him.) In other words, he makes voyeurs of us; as theatre always does.

I am not belittling him. What he gives us to gaze at is often stunning. A typical scene shows a woman luring a child with the promise of food held over a fire, withdrawing it and letting him burn his fingers. The production is if anything more sombre than it was in Paris, where the galleries, crevices and mountainous back wall of the Bouffes-du-Nord (interesting Mr Brook should finally have pitched his tent in a theatre, however dilapidated) offered a more exploitable, enjoyable space than the Roundhouse.

One formerly mesmerising sequence--the Ik roaring out "Rock of Ages" to earn food from visiting missionaries--now seems comparatively perfunctory. Mr Brook has a habit of dismissing his own work as soon as it is done, so perhaps the spectator is not to blame if he also finds the work less impressive on a second viewing. It may even be that Mr Brook, in masochistic mood, deliberately truncated the scene so that we would not be impressed. But we were: less than before, perhaps, but still incurably.

* * *

The most obvious thing to be said about the revival of Plunder is probably the most important. This is a play fashioned 50 years ago for an established firm of personality comedians; there is only a limited amount that mere acting can do for it now.

Many of the jokes depend on insult, the kind that is funniest when a family rapport connects the players and extends into the auditorium. Guesting on the Morecambe and Wise Show is about the nearest that National Theatre actors are likely to have come to the style required. One of the characters is a mountainous, fat and mountainously unpleasant lady. Everyone who comes into contact with her remarks on her girth ("You'll have to go a long way to get round me"--"I'd have to take a taxi"), but one-off casting is bound to make such sallies seem not so much rude as repetitive.

Actually at the National the situation is worse than it need be since Dandy Nichols, though she has the looks for the part, has nothing like the force. The play gets off to a good start with an abrupt proposal of marriage by an ungainly young man called Veal. But once we are past this nicely timed example of calf-love the character becomes the butt of all sorts of remarks about his resemblance to an egg. As played by Trevor Ray he is quite a good egg, but we have no cause to relish his humiliation as audiences in the twenties and long thereafter were accustomed to expect and enjoy the doing-down of Robertson Hare.

So it goes, right up the scale. Dinsdale Landen, playing a silly ass inveigled into becoming a cracksman, is technically superb, falling down on a bed (the victim of his own chloroform) or, always the mark of a fine athletic farceur, up a flight of stairs. But when he is questioned by the police, though an exquisite funniness seems to hang in the air, it never materialises. Mr Landen duly tangles up his sentences, his hearers and himself in slippery knots, tied by a blend of innocence, funk and bravado. But the lines seem to call for an unearthly abandon of silliness which could only be begotten by long practice upon matchless individuality.

Most of the other performers are allowed the fun of venality; they are all grabbing inheritances, marrying for money, robbing and blackmailing one another; and when the police are called in, their methods (particularly those of Derek Newark as an inspector of daunting solidity) are far from charming. For an English farce this is a pretty tough play and it ends with its protagonists apparently getting away with robbery and murder. Only apparently though; we gasp for a moment before realising that there are mitigating circumstances on both counts. If it is an amoral piece, it is so by cheery accident rather than (as in Joe Orton's similarly titled and much influenced Loot) insidious design.

Leading Mr Landen into temptation is Frank Finlay as a more experienced gentleman-thief. The outlines of this character are firmer than the others, and Mr Finlay, after some initial sloth, fits briskly inside them. His sang-froid when up before the law is irreproachable; this is a merrier version of his memorable Iago, an elegant shark. And the shark has pretty teeth, dear, and Mr Finlay is no kid when it comes to flashing the old molars. He dazzles.

There are two perfect scenes in Michael Blakemore's production--the burglary and Mr Finlay's interrogation--and much of the rest is adroitly handled. The first act is unduly slow, but much of the eccentric wit of Mr Travers's dialogue (which, of its period, I prefer to Coward's) has been preserved. Most of the disappointments are forgivable in the circumstances: Plunder may be the essence of a magnificent entertainment, but I doubt if today that essence can be bottled.

records.title: Austrian attitudes
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Austrian attitudes

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THIS week has brought us two German, or at any rate Germanic, works, sponsored in missionary mood by the Goethe Institute. I wish the Institute would get its facts right: Magic Afternoon (Bush) is not the second but the third of Wolfgang Bauer's plays to be seen over here, and Schnitzler's Anatol (Open Space) has certainly not had to wait till now for its British premiere. Both no doubt are enterprising choices but the area is not quite as unknown as press releases and programmes would have us believe.

Magic Afternoon will actually seem comfortingly familiar to anyone who attended the same author's Ghosts at Hampstead last year. It is both tighter and shorter than its predecessor (two blessings) but it occupies the same territory, and is similarly concerned with violent delights which have, but naturally, violent ends. Once again the characters are young layabouts; I am sorry to sound censorious but I could hardly disapprove of them more than their author does and laying about is undeniably what, most of the time, they do.

In Herb Greer's translation and Barbara Markham's production they have been pretty well acclimatised to London. In a dank bed-sit, in the low days of 1967, a would-be writer keeps a discreet distance from his typewriter ("everything," he admits, "is one big lazy excuse") while his Swedish girl-friend rows with him, jeers at him, and asks to be taken out. Since the evening paper advertises no suitable movie, she seems doomed to stay in. From time to time they put on a record ("Concrete and Clay," "In the Midnight Hour") and make love. These are not exactly joyful encounters; either the partners are mouthing the lyrics, eyes closed and more or less unconscious, or they are pummelling each other, escalating rapidly from playfulness to brutality. She gets hurt. Another couple take possession of the room and there is a repeat performance, ending in a broken nose. The play finishes in outright mayhem.

The build is logical, the rhythms fine, the ambience recognisable and the characters--as performed by Gregory Floy, Katja Kersten, Jack Galloway and Holly Wilson--broadly but firmly drawn. They seem out of key only when the text gets them playing word-games and piling on literary references and hinting that they are aware of their own status as dramatic fictions. Here it seems that a portentous schematic original has been--in two senses--naturalised, and the joins show. Beyond this there is a grinding quality about the writing: evidence goes on accumulating long after the verdict has been reached. Perhaps the author is exercising his own past, but why, at this date and length, pick on 1967? The characters are notably apolitical, and perhaps the implication is that we are in at the death of an unthinking Bohemianism which the events of the following year were to smash and awaken forever. I only said perhaps, and having offered the diagnosis I have to dissociate myself from it; Bauer's people are still around, no more lovable even when politicised.

The Goethe Institutionals are no narrow chauvinists; Wolfgang Bauer is Austrian while Schnitzler, as is well known, invented Vienna. His silvery reputation abroad has suffered from an act of self-censorship. He wrote a masterpiece--the parade of couplings generally known as La Ronde--which earned him the unwanted reputation of a purveyor of erotica; he therefore forbade the play to be performed while its copyright endured.

Anatol was his first play; it too is an assembly of sketches and it shows why the comparative explicitness of the later piece became necessary. Anatol is a roue whose prowess, from what we see and what we hear discussed, seems to consist more in luring women to the supper-table than into bed. Central European theatre is the only theatre that knows how to eat, and this play duly presents a set-piece in a restaurant, where Anatol's love (who is leaving him) tucks gluttonously into her last meal at his expense.

All his roses exhibit some variety of thorn; they are too insensitive, or too predatory, or too forgetful, or too protective of their reputations. There are six of them in the present version (a lively one, by Frank Marcus) and all are played by Prunella Scales. She distinguishes them magnificently, the brisk ingenue from the fastidious bourgeoise, the masterful, breathily enchanting circus-rider from the delicately emotional wife, trying to focus and hold on to some finer feeling. Only once does she resort to caricature in an effort to find a new character; but the variables in the performance are ultimately less important than its common factor, which is vitality. The actress is continuously alight.

Versatility might, paradoxically, benefit Anatol himself. There is one scene whose disillusion recalls that of The Misanthrope but Anatol is no Alceste; he reacts not with anger but with wry acceptance. Derek Godfrey does this beautifully but he meets his other rebuffs in much the same spirit. He is adept at exposing the hopeful vanity of youth peering through the mask of worldly middle age. But Anatol, according to Schnitzler's stage directions, was a young man; the melancholy is that for all his proclaimed ideals, he is an ageing lecher in spirit.

records.title: Fourth time luckier
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Fourth time luckier

THE RSC production of Man is Man, currently on view at the Roundhouse Downstairs, is quite a good show. I do not say this lightly; I have assisted at three previous renditions of this early Brecht, and I did not anticipate any great pleasure from a fourth.

The play is the account of a transformation; in Brecht's mythical British India an inoffensive packer named Galy Gay is made over into "a human war-machine." Responsible for the metamorphosis are three soldiers who have mislaid a comrade and dread what will happen should they turn up on parade without him. For the sake of their safety Galy Gay must become Private Jeremiah Jip. The real Jip has spent the intervening time locked up in a pagoda, the prisoner of a huckstering priest who passes him off to his congregation as a god, to the great benefit of the collection-box.

Galy Gay's story proves that a man can be made to believe anything of himself; Jip's that other people can be made to believe anything of him. A third variation is offered by the character of Sergeant Fairchild, he of whose inspection the soldiers are so mightily afeared. Finding that sexual desire (which overtakes him whenever it rains) turns him from the "tiger of Kilkoa" to a mere man, he castrates himself to preserve his identity. The most resonant moment in the play (its resemblance to an episode in Peer Gynt is doubtless coincidental) occurs when Galy Gay witnesses this mutilation and decides that if that is what truth to oneself entails, he will stay malleable.

Brecht keeps the three stories going relentlessly; just as you think you are free of one of them, it recurs. For all that, there are loose ends; the Sergeant becomes steadily less formidable as the play proceeds, the soldiers' plight accordingly less desperate. But they go on working over Galy Gay just the same; they may not themselves be compulsive manipulators but their author is. The process involves much debate over the sale of an elephant; actually, two men under a grey blanket. The feebleness of the deception (which is enacted at great length) is held to be its point; the merest whiff of commercial advantage is enough to blind our hero to any trickery.

I would not dwell on the heavy handedness of this complacently cynical piece (it is, after all, far from Brecht's best) had I not been so frequently exposed to it. It appeals apparently to many people; there is a strain of audience that likes blatancy, enjoys repetition, suspects subtlety, and gets a kick out of denying its own intelligence. Howard Davies's production, though, panders to this response less than most. It is very light and quick on its feet; the opening episode--the soldiers' attack on the priest's pagoda--is particularly deft.

It is really the soldiers who drive the play, and two of them here are outstanding: Bob Peck, large, pungent and authoritative, like a well-cooked dish of tripe and onions, and Sid Livingstone, a small sly worrying terrier with something of the amazed serenity of Eric Morecambe. Geoffrey Hutchings is the blank-sheet protagonist, sent permanently packing, and Ben Kingsley gives himself and the audience a good time as the priest.

There is also much musical pleasure; Guy Woolfenden has composed a new setting for the "Cannon Song" (familiar from The Threepenny Opera), which ingeniously circles Weill's version without ever quite stepping on it; and his other contributions are so good that I often wished the actors would junk the play and just go on singing. I blenched though at the final chorus which would make of a violent unloving play a simple anti-war tract. I might take it from the 7:84 company, but not from the RSC, all lined up, with their committed faces on.

* * *

Another morality play, of earlier date, has been revived in Leatherhead, to celebrate the place's twenty-fifth anniversary as a theatre town. (The present Thorndike Theatre, comfortable and impressive, is still fairly new.) The play is Tom Taylor's The Ticket-of-Leave Man, a bridge between Victorian melodrama and problem play, the problem being that of a convict, released for what must have been extraordinarily good conduct and looking in this production remarkably well on it, whose efforts to go straight are continually thwarted: not, unfortunately for the credit of the piece, by society but by his old colleagues.

The ambience is still nearer to Oliver Twist than to Galsworthy's Justice, and Geoffrey Edwards's production looks appropriately Dickensian; the final stage picture, with the play's kind old gentleman seen in profile, benevolently inclined, might have been drawn by Cruikshank. Stuart M. Stanley's sets are excellent throughout; I only regretted the decision to place them within a stylised Victorian proscenium: This signalled that nobody was taking the play seriously, though two performances--Christopher Strauli's as the hero and, better still, Rosemary Williams's as his girl--seemed not to have been let in on the joke and were all the richer for it.

Some of the characters are actually meant to be funny, but if there is a way of making them so, it has not been discovered here. The play suffers, like Brecht's, from the author's determination to keep all his actors constantly employed; their antics protract the evening unduly. But--again like Brecht's--it perks up when there is a story to be told or a song to be sung.

* * *

E. A. Whitehead's Old Flames remains a theatrical black mass more potent than Jean Genet ever celebrated, though it is less compelling in London than it was in the studio space of the New Vic in Bristol. The small proscenium stage of the Arts surprisingly forces it into a naturalistic mould that gets us asking awkward questions: a man literally devoured by his mother and his two wives is a matter for faith rather than sober proof. As a character, though, he is thoroughly plausible and Gary Bond slithers through the role as masterfully as before. He dominates the first half of the play, damning himself (neither I nor Mr Whitehead choose our metaphors lightly) out of his own mouth; in the second, the women damn him out of theirs, and this section belongs to Judy Cornwell, at first a compact comedienne kicking up her heels in erotic reminiscence, then blazing in anger at the threatened waste of her life, and finally freezing her mother-in-law in hate and futility further gone in than her own.

The London first-night audience by the way was considerably more inhibited than the Bristol matrons who surrounded me when I first saw it and who laughed hot and cold throughout. If they were shocked, it was not in their sensibilities but in their souls.

records.title: Going off the rails
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Going off the rails

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

The flaws in John Osborne's Watch It Come Down (the National Theatre's last production at the Old Vic) are manifest and manifold. You could, if you felt traditional, drive a coach-and-four through them. Mr Osborne himself has done something of the kind, only his chosen vehicle is a train. Though referred to as the weekly goods, it crosses the stage twice, within a span of two days. This is typical.

The train passes by what was once a station, but has now been converted into a house. It belongs to Ben Prosser, a film-director of uncertain distinction who 'must have been barmy to buy this place'. His wife Sally tells us that in the very first line; she goes on to fill us in on the details of the menage. There is Ben's old mother, forever offstage and generally forgotten. There is Sally's sister Shirley, a painter, whose presence Ben tolerates because, says Sally, rather clumsily, 'he still has a daft mystical itch that she might be the enigmatic tally to me.' She does appear, though she says virtually nothing. 'She looms quite impressively, though.'

There is another girl called Jo, described in Mr Osborne's usual clotted jargon as 'the sort of randy tongue-in-the-lip' romantic Ben thinks he missed out in his search for the Holy Groin.' There is Glen, an old, dying homosexual writer whom Jo is nursing. And there is a younger pouf (the favoured word in the Osborne old-theatrical milieu) named Raymond who is Sally's help and confidant. He listens to Sally giving out all this information in the opening scene, and shows remarkable patience considering that he must know all of it already.

This, even for a writer who has always been conspicuously bad at narrative, is exposition of staggering baldness. But if one half of the mind condemns the ineptitude, another succumbs to its charm: enough to make one wish that Mr Osborne would stop trying to provide a naturalistic frame for his diatribes and return to the patterned simplicity of A Sense of Detachment.

Watch It Come Down offers both plot and pattern. Neither is fully developed and the chances are that they throttle each other. Virtually nothing is made of the railway setting; one assumes that it represents a desperate nostalgia which Sally ascribes to Ben, but which occasionally gathers over the play like a cloud without much reference to character. Outside the station lies a hostile world; the Prossers are hated (and, we presume, envied) by their neighbours, who employ 'yobboes' first to kill Ben's dog, then to attack the place.

Mr Osborne has no charity for the present (the twentieth century is his major villain. England both its victim and its partner-in-crime), but he has plenty of bile to spare for the sawn-off segment of the past living on the right side of the tracks. There is generalised approval for wise, doomed, honourable Glen and for all-loving Jo, but more specific attitudes are vitriolic. The main focus is the marriage of Ben and Sally, a running sore. Their battles are the play's most immediate source of life. It seems that they are faking a separation, to see what effect it will have on the rest of the menage, but this idea is not pursued. Glen duly expires, and Jo throws herself under the precipitate goods, though whether in despair at the death of love or the persistence of hate is unclear.

Michael Gough plays Glen propped up in bed dispensing prickly benevolence with infirm authority; and Susan Fleetwood's Jo is the image of affection, like a large, warm and beautiful sheepdog. Their scenes read sticky, but act touching: even a lesbian passage of arms, which Miss Fleetwood shares with Jill Bennett's Sally, and which relates to nothing which precedes or follows it. For the rest Miss Bennett plays the usual pinched bitch she and Mr Osborne have evolved between them with more variety than usual; Frank Finlay builds a careful characterisation as Ben, haggard and slightly epicene. Their scenes together are the most nasal on the London stage.

It used to be claimed for Mr Osborne that he did not mince words; but this in fact is precisely what he does. The language, straining for virility, collapses into spiteful heaps. 'Your unlistening, constant rant,' (Ben to Sally) is both an example and an apt description. Ben's first wife (Rowena Cooper), coming in from outside, makes a brief refreshing contrast, tweedily forthright; otherwise everyone, whether blessing or cursing, sounds alike. But if the tone hardly alters, the tempo does, and Bill Bryden's production rings all the changes. Even his inability to make us believe in the offstage characters is turned to account. Mr Osborne's precious group are all we have and for the duration we accept them--not in spite but because of the limitations and the tricks. Though the play corresponds to nothing that I know or credit, though its reverberations are extremely shaky, it somehow manages to impose itself as truth.

* * *

At least it shines by comparison with other new work. Roger Milner's You'll Never Be Michel Angelo (Hampstead) is an aimless series of jokes, with few ideas and those above its station. Robin Bailey, still among our most polished comedians, walks tall throughout. This piece was first seen at the Edinburgh Traverse, which now houses Hector Macmillan's The Gay Gorbals, peopled by stereotypes slightly closer to life than Mr Milner's whimsies, but even more wearing.

The Glasgow Citizens' Theatre, which is really in the Gorbals, has in the past few years gained a bright and lurid reputation. Its publicity symbol--a drag Shakespeare--suggests the ambience; so does the splendid cheek which last year offered Seneca's Thyestes in repertory with Sailor Beware.
