I caught a bold pair of classics last weekend.

Middleton's The Changeling suggested that the Citizens' style was reaching the point of self-parody. The designer, Philip Prowse, was also the director and he offered an image more suited to a generalised idea of Jacobean tragedy, steamy and decadent, than to this particular play. Middleton depicts evil encroaching on normality, but nobody setting foot on Mr Prowse's latticed stage could sanely have expected to get off alive. Individual Citizens' actors (James Aubrey, Mike Gwilym, David Yelland) have shone of late in other companies, but a concentration of slim, saturnine young men can be confusing; I could not tell the minor characters apart. Some things were striking: the central scene between the careless Beatrice and De Flores, the scorned agent who becomes her ravisher (here played as a stolid white-suited slug), is infallible, and was here succeeded by a ritualised rape; Beatrice (a mettlesome performance by Johanna Kirby) surrendered, mysterious Spaniards danced what I took to be the last tango in Valencia. A beggar crawled around muttering Flores para los muertos, reminding us at once of the hero's name, the play's location and the director's existence, all things I would be happy to take for granted.

Goldoni's Mirandolina was another kind of camp, but more fun: a neat comedy of female superiority with Suzanne Bertish as glowingly attractive, if not quite as practical, as a heroine should be; a radiantly decaying Venetian set by Mr Prowse; much witty allusion imported into the text by the director, Robert David Macdonald; and an outstanding performance by Jonathan Hyde, dusty and raddled as an impoverished sponging marquis, gleaming with wit and underpinned, as such acting always must be, by ineffable dignity.

records.title: Simple Stratford
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Simple Stratford

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

ANNUALLY, it seems, Stratford remodels its stage and announces its longest season ever. The latter resource must soon die a natural death - not even the Arts Council can be relied on to provide a year with more than 52 weeks - but the former has indefinite possibilities. Having missed the Roman plays of 1972, I have often thought wistfully of the spectacular machinery installed for their benefit. Apparently I shall never see it in operation: Stratford, like everywhere else, is into simplicity.

This year it is into Elizabethan simplicity. The stage juts decisively into the auditorium, and the front stalls have been rearranged so that the audience may sit on either side of its protrusion. But one hardly thinks of it as an open stage in the manner of Stratford, Ontario, or its stunted child, Chichester. It is in fact very enclosed by terraces. The concentric circles - upper and dress - no longer stop precipitously in mid-wall. They reach round the sides of the acting area, becoming part of the set, and meet at the back to become once more the preserve of the audience. One thinks of this stage in terms of balconies, so it is appropriate that the first play given there should be Romeo and Juliet.

Actually the balcony in this play is a separate construction, standing out from the timbered surround but harmonising with it; the scene fits into this structure with unusual aptness. The full picture, designed by John Napier, is maybe the most cunning yet devised for this house. It is reminiscent, not only of Shakespeare's own stage, but of the tiered scaffolded settings devised at Stratford by Tanya Moiseiwitsch in the forties and fifties (I've seen photographs). But it has a warmth probably lacking then, and whose absence I mourn in the new Lyttelton on the South Bank.

For this we thank not only Mr Napier, but the patrons at the rear who complete the ring and must be rewarded by splendid views of the actors' backs and the crowns of their heads. Only David Waller as Friar Laurence is charitable enough ("we still have known thee for a holy man") to toss the odd fragment of soliloquy in their direction. I take it that their seats are cheap and that the company has tacitly adopted the principle expounded by Dame Edna Everage in addressing her audience, i.e., you get what you pay for.

This time round, you get a lot of it. When the chorus, a nice young man in denim, made the usual promise of "the two hours' traffic of our stage," someone near me uttered a disbelieving grunt. He must have been to a preview; the premiere lasted nearer four hours than two, which, for a supposedly fast-moving action on a permanent set, is a very long time. In a way, perhaps, Chorus tells the truth: one hour, if not two, seems taken up with traffic (as opposed to drama) and the jams are frequent.

In fact, for all its austerity, this is at heart a normally complicated RSC production, full of comings, goings and elaborate standing-still. Some of these are helpful. The opening brawl is excellent; the ball, which involves a masque of Cupid, presented by Romeo's party with Benvolio shooting toy arrows into the company, is festive, though it has made its point long before the lovers' meeting. Perhaps the directors (Trevor Nunn with Barry Kyle) have had their happiest inspiration when Juliet is discovered, doped on her bridal bed; her marriage escort arrives in full revelry, dancing and piping, turning ironically to lament.

The subsequent altercation between the unemployed musicians and the clown Peter is played with both parties in a foul temper and shouting a time-dishonoured method of dealing with Shakespeare's comedy when you cannot figure out how to make it funny. Earlier on, Richard Griffiths is rather good as Peter, doing his stuff with a burly perplexed intensity, not to say an accent, that amusingly recalls Albert Finney's Hamlet.

Mr Griffiths connects with the audience better than many of those in more obviously rewarding roles. The most regrettable quality of this production - and the most surprising, considering what a platform stage is supposed to do for a play - is its remoteness. Marie Kean, though in no way startling, sets the nurse's words snugly to Irish rhythms, Michael Pennington's Mercutio is dangerously alive at the approach of death, but his earlier scenes are casualties of the production's busy-ness: instead of building a relationship with Romeo and Benvolio, he has to go through exhausting routines for the entertainment of a crowd of extras. He is far more fantastical than the Tybalt whose affectations he despises. The best of the supports, by a long way, is John Woodvine's Capulet, hearty, possessive, tyrannic, and momentously forgiving. Largely through him, the reconciliation of the two families becomes unwontedly affecting.

Affecting, too, is Francesca Annis's Juliet, a slender flame but a true one. Her heights are the traditional ones of the potion, where she is really frightening, and the balcony, where she is really in love. While she is confident and generous, Ian McKellen's Romeo is bewildered by his luck: a blushing youth hoping for favour and then basking in it, surprised even by the mood that tips with silver all the fruit-tree tops.

An actor who in his mid-thirties essays Romeo must expect double-edged compliments: having acknowledged him the best adolescent of his generation, I must express familiar misgivings. He is given to sulks, which suit some of Romeo but not all; he defies the stars with a violent twist of his mouth, sounding like tragedy and looking like toothache. Like Miss Annis, he is good at dread, hurrying a line to its end with a kind of vocal shiver. Pillared sets are a permanent temptation to him, though I suppose that Romeo might well be given to posing in picturesque loops.

* * *

Having noted that last year's Merry Wives of Windsor has come to the Aldwych in, on the whole, improved fettle, I pass to our second most established provincial company. The Bristol Old Vic now has three auditoria: as many as the National, with the bonus that at Bristol all three are operational. All are currently given over to the work of Aleksei Arbuzov, monarch of the Moscow boulevards, whose The Promise also conquered London a few years back. That play is revived in Bristol's studio, while its two larger theatres are occupied by pieces strange to us.

I remember The Promise as unfulfilling; I was not much taken by the new lot either. Evening Light (Theatre Royal) is the more beguiling of the two; its appeal largely suggested by its title, it moves magically from a newspaper office to the porch of a country house to the river bank of the Volga, whose vistas have inspired John McMurray to design the most effective propaganda for the long-neglected backcloth that I have seen in years. The lighting is by a Mr Shakespeare (Robert A.) and worthy of the name.

Arbuzov's atmosphere and technique - though not, unfortunately, his vision - are Chekhovian. But Daniel Massey lacks energy (one of your mournful Russians) and Sheila Reid works too hard to convey automatic enchantment. Felicity Kendal cannot only convey it, she is it; and Arbuzov's Once Upon A Time (Little Theatre) is lucky to have her. It also has Michael Hordern, whose special line in beaming testiness, though not unfamiliar, ginger ups the text valuably. The play, about the invigorating effect of young Miss K on old Mr H, is set in a puppet shop; but it may just be memories of children's ballet that keep you waiting for the dolls, if nothing else, to spring into life.

* * *

The eighteenth-century Royal, by the way, remains a jewelled delight, effortlessly uniting the audience in just the manner Stratford has to strive for. The Little is not delightful. Nor is the Wimbledon Theatre, though it is far from little. It makes the Actors' Company look diminished. By the standards of two years ago, they may be anyhow, but they give a reasonable account of Widowers' Houses, which was Shaw's first play and, it occasionally seems to me, his best. Its satire is ruthless and absolutely unfused, its development - making an absolute virtue of its author's inexperience - as volatile as a jumping-cracker.

records.title: Much Ado in India
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Much Ado in India

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN at Stratford.

OBVIOUSLY the prospect of Donald Sinden and Judi Dench in Much Ado About Nothing (Stratford) was enticing, but it also prompted misgivings.

Miss Dench, we knew, would be funny and enchanting, but with so much going for her and virtually nothing going against her, it was difficult to imagine her as a plausible spinster. For this is what Beatrice is: not a bachelor girl, which would imply choice, but a woman who, both being of and living in a marriageable age, sees her contemporaries and juniors go to the world's end, accompanied by her own cry of "Heigh ho for a husband."

Miss Dench is not, on the face of her, a plausible occupant of any shelf anywhere. Stratford's last two Beatrices were, in different ways, alarming; they frightened off all but the exceptional man. In a world of Claudios they needed the Benedick. But Miss Dench is not a scarer; you could imagine her rejecting suitors, but never failing to attract them.

She copes unimaginably well. Her strategy is, at first, to damp herself down; her dress is drab and her wit sour rather than sparkling. Her gibes at Benedick are meant to hurt, not to entertain; their first encounter is played, unusually, without spectators. It yields intensity but not much laughter, and I began to fear that we would see another comedy crucified.

Relief and enlightenment came on a couple of lines, rather obscure and generally ignored, which hint at a previous, scarring involvement between the two protagonists. In John Barton's production, Miss Dench pulls this suggestion to the front of the play. We see what is gnawing her, sympathise and relax. When she melts, the effect is breathtaking. Miss Dench is always inspiring sentences like that, but her means for doing so seem simple enough; she merely injects into a hush a few lines denoting surrender and spoken with an unquestioning directness that inspires a kindred feeling in the audience. But I wish I knew how she created a hush in the first place; can there be more to it than concentration? I know, though, that while her spark and bubble make her a fine comic actress, it is these moments that silently proclaim her great.

We weep for happiness at Beatrice's conversion, having already laughed at Benedick's, which is enormously coy. Mr Barton has set the play in an outpost of the British Raj; there are gains and losses, but one of the gains is a dinner gong furiously struck by Miss Dench, when dispatched to summon Mr Sinden for tiffin. Benedick's desperate efforts to find signs of love in her ("There's a double meaning in that") have never, in my experience, been more hilarious.

His new passion is still, at this stage, a joke. It does not deepen until the church scene. Beatrice, enraged at Claudio's rejection of her cousin, falls--an inspirational touch--to sweeping up the confetti; she must, instinctively, do something. Benedick has to fight hard to reclaim her; has in fact to declare his love to her unyielding back; and his agreement to challenge Claudio is the natural development. He has been moved and stung into seriousness, and he grows. Mr Sinden conveys all these transformations beautifully.

With the happy ending secure, the two of them can afford to play a bit; in their mockery they almost return to first base. But this time it is a game, and if Benedick remains, in his airy way, something of a male chauvinist pig, he is obviously ripe--in the imagery of this production--for sticking. One mark of Miss Dench's supremacy in comedy is my invariable delight at seeing her get her man; Which, considering my feelings in the matter, is generous of me. The theatre must be an ennobling place.

Mr Barton's production is already fine and will probably be finer. The stage is thick with relationships: full of detail but not submerged in it. Some characters are dull, but others stand out as seldom before: the waiting women, for instance, with Margaret (Eliza Ward), the witty, flirtatious chambermaid, and Ursula (Marilyn Taylerson), a genteel lady's companion with an earnest enthusiasm for pleasures and plotting. Don John (Ian McDiarmid) is earnest too, and wholly original: curly-haired and studious, obviously sent out to the Army against his will and bitterly resenting it. Claudio (Richard Durden) is conventional but none the worse for it, convention being the key of his character.

In some ways the production is a companion to Mr Barton's Othello, also set in an outpost of the Empire; in others--notably its awareness that in Much Ado people are always awaiting, then attending, or recovering from a party--it resembles Franco Zeffirelli's National Theatre version. But it has wit and consistency of its own. (I have actually seen one Much Ado that wasn't set in the nineteenth century; it was something of a revelation.) The chosen medium has the drawback of making marriage seem the exception rather than the rule, which strikes at the play's ethos and diminishes Don Pedro's isolation at the end. I found myself, too, wondering precisely where on this subcontinent place names like Aragon and Messina might be found.

The lower orders are all loyal natives, which lends strange conviction to John Woodvine's Dogberry, both in his struggles with the English language and his pride in it. His friend Verges is a Briton, which seems inconsistent, but maybe the actor had trouble with the accent. Plainly the National's Phaedra has established a new route for the classics; they must all be shipped off to India at least once, so that they may learn what it means to be British.

* * *

Colonialism lingers on in The Soul of the White Ant (Bush), a brilliant play in which Snoo Wilson regains the lightness of touch which he--or perhaps his directors--seemed to have mislaid since The Pleasure Principle. Dusty Hughes's production hits the right note of hard insouciance; everything seems inconsequential as it happens, and then reveals its meaning. This is the first of Mr Wilson's plays in which I have known, from moment to moment, what was going on. Clive Merrison, fresh from impersonating Artaud at the Open Space, is now Eugene Marais, a South African writer with wide-ranging ideas about termites. Mr Wilson's interest in cracked theorists is greater than mine, but even if the idea of South Africa as a giant ant-heap fails to grab you, the rest of the play should. Example: two white women pregnant after bathing in a river full of a black house-boy's sperm thrown there after a spell in a fridge, where it had to be kept since the donor could hardly give it to his wife, she being, by law, miles away. Mr Wilson's characters are all sad, all white, all funny; Lynda Marchal, who builds a shapeless, battered character outwards from her accent, leads a cast in full control of style and meaning.

* * *

How the Other Half Loves has been regarded as a profitable skeleton in Alan Ayckbourn's cupboard; it rattled through a long West End run without actually pleasing anyone; least of all, it was rumoured, the author. The blame was placed on Robert Morley for turning a comedy of subtle social differences into a burlesque about the large gulf between himself and everybody else.

The Actors' Company at Wimbledon save the play's honour, revealing it as a trial run for Absurd Person Singular and in many ways its superior. It is more honestly farcical in its machinery, which is never allowed to run down but never obscures the characters.

* * *

At the Round House Downstairs, The Measures Taken is early Brecht adopting an aggressively anti-humanitarian stance in an attempt to prove himself more Communist than the Party chairman. His better feelings betray him; or maybe ours do. The Exception and the Rule, played second, is one of his best fables; several varieties of fear and self-interest accumulate through it to be exposed, with a sweet but mirthless smile, in one of the author's best ironic trial scenes. The Mutable Theatre Company, despite their name, do better with the direct statements of the first play than the inscrutable twists of the second.

records.title: Soldiers Upstairs
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Soldiers Upstairs

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE Royal Court's Theatre Upstairs is in business again, and the reopening production is worth the climb. Yesterday's News deals with the contribution of British mercenaries to the civil war in Angola. It is a show for talking heads and, in one or two cases, for some revealingly fidgety hands. Seven actors sit in a row, facing the audience, and deliver monologues which they themselves have culled (with the assistance of Jeremy Seabrook) from documentary material and interviews. Four of them represent actual mercenaries, of varying degrees of professionalism; the other three have more distant interests in Angola.

Only five of the cast are on stage to begin with. The two toughest soldiers arrive late, their looks uncompromising enough to suggest momentarily that this is a raid. They take their places at the end of the line and the central position accordingly shifts. Before it was occupied by a voluble lady journalist; now it belongs to Keith Jones, a 17-year-old recruit at first believed dead in Colonel Callan's massacre but later discovered to have survived.

He has, it seems, less to say than anyone; he sits hunched forward, and his ears, protruding before his cropped hair, seem to be propelling him further to the front. If he is the man in the middle, the others have all to some extent shaped his destiny: at one end his more hardened colleagues from the SAS and the paras, at the other, Roche, the man who recruited him. Nearer to him sit more domestic influences: a girlfriend, the reporter who got him into the papers having commandeered the rights to his story by moving in on his parents, and a stockbroker concerned with British investments in Africa.

These last two confuse the piece a bit. The girl has one bitter outburst about Keith's misguided ideas of playing at soldiers, but she seems too slight and too particular. The stockbroker, by contrast, seems too generalised; there is more to be said about economic interests in Angola than the play has time for, and his streaks of individuality--he was once an actor and may be one again--do not compensate. He never quite makes it as either a person or a type.

It is none the less an informative, scary and riveting evening: not about Angola but about Britain. The tone of the production (by William Gaskill and Max Stafford-Clark, for Joint Stock) is unremittingly level. Will Knightley's bewilderment as Keith becomes recognisable as native violence: a state which the real soldiers (Paul Kember and David Rintoul) have by now stonily transcended, their frustrations thickened into a way of life. Less reachable is Philip McGough's Roche, whose departure, in scowling fury, is as disconcerting as the arrival of the other two. Perhaps because these three characters are the least familiar, their performances are the most persuasively real. The others are actors' distillations, not larger but more insistently revealing than life; Gillian Barge, who excels in playing harried professional women, has her best and best-taken opportunity since The National Health as the journalist, alternately brandishing and tripping over her own nervousness.

* * *

This has been a good week for rooms above. The Bush (over a pub) offers Franz Xaver Kroetz's Geisterbahn, a sequel to his Stallerhof. Spastic Beppi, whom we saw impregnated by a farm-hand in the first play, has now had her baby, and the birth seems to have mellowed everyone considerably. This may partly be due to changes of cast: only Penelope Lee as Beppi's mother remains from before, even more creased and more desperately tired but with more sorrow than anger in her eyes. Her husband (Mike Pratt) looks positively benign, while Sepp (Peter Sproule), the discharged farm-worker, previously played as a man in whom gentleness occasionally surfaced, has been transformed by fatherhood, and dies a kindly martyr's death (to cancer and Social Security).

Beppi herself has more than doubled her output of words; she can not only talk to her baby but can deliver a poem over Sepp's body. This moment, and a couple of others, are unwontedly sentimental for Kroetz; he may be trying to get more out of these characters than they will render him, and some strain shows too in David Samourai's production, which is occasionally mannered in its stillness. Pictorially, though, it improves even on its predecessor: a series of bleak interiors takes shape, the actors harshly posed against walls that may once have been white. Harshly but not pitilessly: even when Kroetz appears to be wallowing in desolation, past the making of his points, there is some surprising human action at the end of it. He does not deal in automata.

Beppi's slow gyrations, as she fights against putting her child in a home, are touchingly executed by Jenny Twigge; hers is less of a virtuoso display than her predecessor's (if only because Beppi is now less of a case), but her decision to give the baby up--and her concern lest it should suffer for her negligence--is acted, as it is written, with stunning humanity. It is not the end of the play; what is, it would be worth your while to discover.

* * *

In the fifties, when they spoke of American playwrights, it was Tennessee Williams, Arthur Miller and William Inge. Inge's plays never reached London, except as films, and he is dead now; but his Bus Stop has finally arrived at the Phoenix as (appropriately) a vehicle ridden by Lee Remick and Keir Dullea: she as a Kansas City bar-room singer, he as the cowboy who fell for her at first glance and is abducting her to Montana on that basis (not to mention on that bus) but is temporarily halted, first by snow, and then by the suggestion that she may not actually like him.

They both do well, but the conventions of the play demand that we should will them to come together at the end, and I could not oblige. The film craftily began with the cowboy, and so got us on his side. The play starts with Cherie, stating her case, plaintively but firmly, against her boorish pursuer, and nothing that happened later persuaded me she was wrong. Other couples dispose themselves around Saul Radomsky's roadside diner (which looks as if it ought to be authentic) and Vivian Matalon's production takes good care of the counterpoint. The play really centres on a young waitress, watching it all as part of growing up; Jenny Quayle, who was promising but wrong in The Gingerbread Lady, is here fulfilling and right. The play is not badly contrived; but it is contrived.

* * *

At the Palladium last week Joel Grey did his MC numbers from Cabaret; their chill, their zest and their authority were undiminished. What was diminished was the rest of his act, which was compact of just the kind of showbiz bonhomie that Cabaret undercuts. Mr Grey does not need this kind of charm (just as well, since he hasn't actually got it); he has colossal energy, and is the fleetest performer I have ever seen, electric even when changing his shoes: one pair with taps and one without. He was supported by Johnny Hackett, a better than average Northern comic, and the Brotherhood of Man, a shiny gang of Eurovision song contestants for whom "slickening" would be the right portmanteau word.

records.title: Farewell to that old acid dream
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Farewell to that old acid dream

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

AT ONE point in David Hare's Teeth 'n' Smiles (now transferred from the Royal Court to Wyndham's) the following words occur: "It's not worth saying--nothing's worth saying--it's all so obvious." I know the feeling; nobody wants to be caught being obvious, that's obvious.

The situation--a rock group playing at a Cambridge May Ball in the last year of the sixties--automatically suggests a theme: the confrontation of two cultures. Mr Hare defuses our expectations on this score by more or less eliminating one side. Cambridge is represented on stage by one porter and one harmless medical student with ambitions of becoming a drop-out (after he's passed his exams).

If he is the opposition, then the battle is already won, the enemy within the gates. Only they are in no state to fight. The group is on the verge of breaking-up, their lead singer--self-cast in the self-destructive mould of Garland or Joplin--falling apart from drink. Our student asks her whether she believes that pop is any challenge to the established order; she obviously regards it as a silly question. So, I guess, does the author. But I have to guess because he is chary of making statements, even about not making statements.

A strange self-mockery permeates the evening. Sometimes it seems like irony; often, like the hedging of bets. A songwriter who escaped from the old values (he quit this same college) and is still attached to them (he lounges around singing Cole Porter) proclaims that "the acid dream is over," then undercuts himself by adding "it said so in the Daily Express," finally caps it all by telling the singer "but you and I still want to say something." What they want to say, he doesn't say, and she certainly isn't telling.

Mr Hare has perceived that the acid dream was never any use, but this perception is difficult to make into a play, at least into a play with this setting, so sometimes he forgets it and settles for the shadow of a conflict instead. He lets his characters jeer at themselves for paying so much attention to their exhibitionist star, who will survive, while forgetting their stoned bass guitarist, who won't. But after all, the author is the one who gave them the concern, pushed the lady into the centre of the play, and--since he is his own director--engaged Helen Mirren for the role, gave her the limelight, the billing and our attention. He then keeps telling us how boring she is (the character, not Miss Mirren, who is furiously good) as if by way of atonement. He also pads the evening out by engaging her in a romantic triangle which--despite sympathetic playing from Martin Shaw and Gay Hamilton as its other sides--never begins to take hold.

I suspect, too, that he became fascinated in researching the play by the life-style of the band, and threw in more detail than his story required. This, however, is his salvation; much of his dialogue is brilliant and its last-gasp cynicism has its own momentum and its own mood. These keep the play alive most of the time.

The production seems both less comfortable and more uncompromising in the West End than at its cosy old home in Sloane Square. (Its relation to its audience rather resembles that of its characters to Cambridge. I even heard shocked gasps; I only wish the shock had been caused by something more disturbing than the odd four-letter word.) The band's first number now sounds, as it should, really bad: a difficult effect to achieve in a straight play, where any outburst of music is generally welcome. They act contrastingly well, but the two most successful characters are Antony Sher's student, who significantly never finishes a sentence, because its ludicrousness always strikes him en route, and Dave King's manager, smilingly jaundiced about absolutely everything. If the play has a heart, he, effortlessly delivering all the best lines, is it.

* * *

Athol Fugard has also directed a play of his own which came to London last week: Dimetos (Comedy), of which I saw half, but heard much less, in Edinburgh last year. This time I stayed till the end: you do not walk out on Paul Scofield, who is awe-inspiringly audible and whose acting is inclined to suggest that he has a hotline to the Almighty. On this occasion he gives a great display, craggy and troubled, rather than a great performance, Mr Fugard having provided him with a situation rather than a character. Derived from an obscure passage in Camus, it presents a man paralysed by guilt over the suicide of his niece, after whom he lusted. He did not assault her; he merely upset her by playing the voyeur.

The second part of the play, which is Dimetos's agony and redemption, is considerably the better, but it sinks under the delusion that a writer may create a myth simply by taking thought. Camus may have achieved it in a casual paragraph, but Mr Fugard, excluding domestic detail in favour of conscientious metaphor, denies his play a chance of life.

records.title: Vague views
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Vague views

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

LAST WEEK I got my first glimpse of the St Georges Theatre in Islington, dedicated to putting Shakespeare back where he belongs. The externals are plain: quaint music, doublet and hose, and an apron stage. This, of course, is the easy part; it brings us no nearer to an understanding of how the Elizabethans thought. If we are to find out, we will have to give the matter a lot more investigation than George Murcell, the director of the theatre and of its new Romeo and Juliet, can reasonably be expected to have had time for.

When he declares that Shakespeare's characters were 'bounded by certain attitudes and beliefs relative to his time and not by modern political, ethical and psychological factors', he is talking obvious sense, though there may be more overlap between the two sensibilities than he allows. But he then goes on to tilt at productions which make 'Hamlet an Oedipus complex melancholic and Julius Caesar a fascist dictator in the Hitler mode.' But those are not today's distortions; they belong to the thirties, when the second was tried out by Orson Welles and the first by Tyrone Guthrie -- whom, funnily enough, Mr Murcell names as one of his mentors.

His views on modern Shakespeare production seem, in short, a bit vague. The chronology of Mr Murcell's own career and his invocation of Guthrie and Michael Benthall suggest to me that they really boil down to a feeling that Shakespeare was getting on very nicely in the 1950s until Peter Hall and the Royal Shakespeare Company came along and spoiled everything. This is quite a widespread attitude within the profession and among theatregoers; having myself received my theatrical education at the Old Vic in the fifties, I may still unconsciously regard that style as the norm, and everything else as a mutation. But when I think clearly, I can see that it was no more 'authentic' or 'Elizabethan' than what has displaced it.

There have, God knows, been absurdities perpetrated in the name of 'making Shakespeare relevant.' (Actually I don't believe that you can make a play relevant; either it is or it isn't. I doubt if you can even 'bring out' its relevance, though probably you can, accidentally or on purpose, obscure it.) But basically Mr Murcell is bugged less by modern directors' treatment of Shakespeare than by their treatment of actors. The dominance of the major companies has led to the disenfranchisement, in the name of some rather academic conceptions of theatrical taste, of a whole parade of players. Some, like Mr Murcell himself, have gone rapidly through these companies and come out the other side. Others have never got in; in these terms, Mr Murcell has a lot going for him.

However sympathetic many of us may be to the RSC ethic (which is what we read about), we have become increasingly resistant to the RSC mannerisms (which are what we actually see). Here Mr Murcell's 'Romeo' scores heavily over this year's production at Stratford. It is refreshing to find that double-entendres can hit their mark without laborious underlining; that a clown (Ronnie Stevens) can be a clown and not an angry underdog; and that the young men of Verona do not have to be irredeemably vicious. David Collings's Mercutio is even quite likeable; his Queen Mab speech, in the displaced lyrical tradition, for once makes atmospheric sense.

Peter McEnery's Romeo is interestingly tough; he does not actually duel with Tybalt and Paris, just goes up to them and stabs them. Sarah Badel's Juliet is tough, too, though this is more an inbuilt facet of her personality than of her interpretation. The two are at war, but it is a thrilling battle and since all Miss Badel's skill and intelligence are exercised in Juliet's cause, not her own, she has some ecstatic moments; her stillness after her one night with Romeo is very moving. She is hampered by a miscast Nurse (Rosemary Leach) who comes on like her older sister; altogether too bright and personable to sort with the text.

C. Walter Hodges's permanent set may have the prescribed number of balconies and alcoves, but is garishly coloured and looks strangely insubstantial. Mr Murcell directs for the open stage by stringing his actors across it, even in conversational scenes. Extras, reacting, look lost; routine naturalism is occasionally disturbed for the sake of a picturesque but improbable grouping. There is not, in short, much style, but there is plainness and energy, and for 'Romeo,' a narrative play, this works better than the more rarefied treatments we are used to.

I can see that it would have done less well for Twelfth Night, a mood piece, though I doubt if the St Georges production of the play (which I missed) was worse than the one that opened last week at Chichester. Keith Michell, like Mr Murcell an artistic director at large on his own stage for the first time, opts for regulation Chichester gaiety: lots of romping but no actual comedy. High life is pallid, low life denatured: Barbara Windsor's Maria even looks flat-chested. Gordon Jackson's Malvolio proves, for the second time this season, that this actor is no soloist.

In its last stages the production lurches surprisingly towards melancholy, allowing Tony Robinson to suggest that his Feste might have been quite interesting. Bill Fraser, Michele Dotrice and Charles Keating also have moments. Mr Michell places important scenes in corners of the stage, leaving the centre to attendants in whose reactions, with no ill will towards them, I was not much interested. There being so much Shakespeare, I defer Stratford's new Winter's Tale until next week.

After the achievements of Mike Leigh and Hull Truck there is an onus on improvised drama to prove that it can do things written drama cannot; Gin Trap (Bush) had me yearning for a playwright to bring the characters together, stop their conversation wandering (non-communication is no longer news) and focus a few themes. About to type, through force of habit, that the acting was good though, I realise that will not do for this kind of play and that the failure of Cecily Hobbs's tight-lipped baby-basher to make her lines convincing must be laid at her door as well as that of her directors (Sarah Anderson and Sheila Kelly). Other characters are competently observed and the ending is quiet but immensely forceful.

records.title: Musgraves dancing
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
I saw Sybil Thorndike only once on the stage: as the Nurse in the famous Chichester 'Uncle Vanya,' in which she was magnificent. I never met her. All the same, I feel this week as though I have suffered a personal loss.

The Family Dance (Criterion), by a new dramatist, Felicity Browne, is about a celebration-hop in the Berkshire home of a stockbroker called Ben Musgrave. Musgraves and dancing seem to go together in the theatre, though I doubt if John Arden's stony serjeant would relish the idea of a stockbroker for a descendant. At that, Ben is the only one of the new Musgraves to do any work at all. His brother, his sister, and their respective spouses live off his earnings in what he describes as 'a family commune.'

There are also, of course, children; it is they and their friends who are actually having the ball, though they are at it offstage; we are in the kitchen (a large one, of course) watching their elders collapse from underwork. It takes them in different ways: sister Diana has become the kind of hearty tyrant who, if our playwrights are to be trusted, may be found beneath every roof in the Home Counties, brother Toby has taken spinelessly to drink, and Ben's wife Sophie marks the evening's half-way point by gulping down an overdose of sleeping-pills.

Before taking this step, Sophie has asked Ben for a divorce, only to receive the reply--a witty one, I thought--that having been married for 17 years she might as well stick it out to the end. Miss Browne displays a great talent for the stylish display of selfishness; it is obvious that Ben has assumed the role of universal breadwinner largely in order to put the family in his debt. In Alec McCowen's bravura performance he careers around the stage looking for grievances, upbraiding his brother for a weakling, and his wife for a bad boiler of eggs and an even worse lay.

These bad manners are diverting, but they are not remotely believable. Or rather, they are only remotely believable: fine in long-shot, but not in close-up. Regarded as a verbal ballet of family discord, the play is very entertaining. Miss Browne has an eye as well as an ear and by putting Sophie, played waifishly by Annette Crosbie, into a biscuit-coloured dress ('the same colour as the rest of you,' says her sister-in-law, possibly meaning well) she isolates her effectively.

But she cannot get inside Sophie's character; cannot explain why she has stuck with Ben so long, or why, having done so, she should want to leave now. Indeed, despite the efforts of Miss Crosbie, Michael Bryant and Judy Parfitt (whose main contribution to the proceedings is to look handsome in green), the more downtrodden members of the menage never come to life.

The monsters, so glitteringly played by Mr McCowen and Helen Lindsay, overpower them. If their performances sometimes seem a bit relentless, the writing gives them little option. Nobody should accuse Miss Browne of glamourising family life or even Berkshire; when sentimentality breaks in, it is the character's, not the author's. But once we have agreed with her that the situation she presents is indeed unpleasant, there is little left for us to do. It is a watchable play, but not an energising one.

* * *

Anyway, there is hope for Miss Browne, as once there was, I suppose, for John Mortimer. However, Mr Mortimer is now one of the strangest phenomena in the English theatre: a brand-name dramatist for nearly 20 years, with only one play to his credit ('A Voyage Round My Father') that was even half-way good. There have also been some tolerable sketches: one of them is the second half of the double-bill Heaven and Hell (Greenwich). 'Hell's funny,' as we used to say in the sixties; heaven though, as tenuously dramatised in the curtain-raiser, is a drag and, as usual, difficult to believe in. The evening does offer Denholm Elliott, Peter Woodthorpe and Eleanor Bron; and, of course, many evenings offer less.

* * *

The Winter's Tale (Stratford) seemed promising, directed by John Barton 'with Trevor Nunn.' Mr Nunn staged this play excellently a few years ago and this season's 'Much Ado About Nothing' showed Mr Barton at the top of his form. But with the permanent Elizabethan set (of which the RSC seem already to have repented) masked in with furs and hieroglyphs, and the actors furry as well, this is dehydrated Shakespeare, the earnest tanning of a monster play.

Talking of monsters, this is the play in which a character exits, 'pursued by a bear'; at Stratford he merely finds himself confronted by what looks like a walking totem-pole, which escorts him offstage with the apparent intention of taking his name and address. Not surprisingly a subsequent speech describing his dismemberment by the bear is neither credible nor funny. (Funniness may be assumed to have been among the author's intentions, since he entrusted the speech to a character called the Clown. Another RSC director, Terry Hands, has recently declared in print that Shakespeare never means what he says. This is as simplistic as claiming that he always does.)

Throughout the evening the cast seemed engaged in ritual games which they probably understand, but which leave the audience in the cold. There are good performances, of course: Barbara Leigh-Hunt a formidably nannyish Paulina, David Waller's warming first moments as the Shepherd, Marilyn Taylerson as statuesque a Hermione as could be imagined, and even Florizel and Perdita no worse than usual. Above all, Ian McKellen's Leontes is splendid; the actor's technical control (which in Shakespeare has never been more evident) throws into relief the character's disarray. As Leontes's lucidity goes, Mr McKellen's increases, the course of each shaft of jealousy precisely plotted. Particularly revealing is his clinging to his son, counterbalancing his revulsion from his wife.

* * *

Robert Stephens in Othello (Regent's Park) is similarly exact, though his jealous transports are messier. I always forget just how powerful an actor Mr Stephens is, but there are speeches here whose weight he cannot shift. But I should like to see him try again, under a roof (since my Elizabethanism is by no means fanatical) and with an Iago who has a finer sense of rhythm than Edward Fox.

* * *

Liza of Lambeth (Shaftesbury) is the latest overweight British musical based on an Edwardian novel: Maugham this time. It has one good idea (the substitution of short comic monologues for full-blown songs) and seems to despise its own insistence on Cockney jollity (big number: 'Going Down to Chingford on a Chara.'); it compensates with overpowering slum sets, and must be the dingiest musical ever. The authors offer us no reason to be interested in their heroine, and Angela Richards, poor girl, cannot make the deficiency good.

* * *

The rock 'n' roll musical Leave Him to Heaven (New London) is also divided; its starting-point is a Stan Freberg musical parody, but while Freberg hated rock, the authors here do not. How much was intended as a mockery and how much as straight nostalgia I cannot guess, but there is no doubt that nostalgia wins. Even a song as awful as the necrophile 'Tell Laura I Love Her' has grown charm with the decades. Brian Protheroe has awesome energy as the teenage idol and his rendition of 'Chantilly Lace,' the era's very best song, is irresistible.

records.title: East of Broadway
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
East of Broadway

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a New York original.

DESPITE all pressures the New York commercial theatre remains more interesting than its counterpart in London. The pressures are certainly still there, and mounting; Broadway claims to have been enjoying a boom in the past couple of years, but however well the successful shows are doing, an uncomfortable number of theatres remain empty.

Nor would I assert that much of what goes on is very good; hardly ever, though, is it as unambitiously bad as much of what now occupies the West End. I have yet to discover the American equivalent of 'Murder at the Vicarage' or 'No Sex Please, We're British.' Most crucially, Broadway benefits from New York's lack of institutionalised theatre on the scale of the National Theatre or the RSC. (I am not claiming that this is a desirable situation or even, for very much longer, an economically feasible one.) For the moment, the best theatrical talent is still on Broadway, since it has nowhere else to go.

Occasionally, therefore, Broadway mounts an original work of a size and quality the West End has long forgotten--not that it always gets much thanks for it. The latest Harold Prince-Stephen Sondheim musical, Pacific Overtures, is about to close after a six-month run, never having recovered from its tepid reception at the hands of the local reviewers. It is unlikely to be seen in London, which is doubly sad, as all the English people I know who have seen the show or heard the score have loved it. I saw it twice within a week and thought it staggeringly good. Its setting is Japan, its subject the opening-up of that country in the mid-nineteenth century to trade with the West, America having taken the initiative in the matter by standing four battleships off the Nipponese coast. The commander of this expedition described his duties as the making of 'pacific overtures,' a euphemism which escalates the title of the show into, by my count, a five-way pun. Wit permeates the entire show. All the characters, Westerners included, are played by Oriental actors (many of them admittedly born in America) and it makes free and eclectic use of Japanese--mainly Kabuki--stage conventions: a narrator with accompanying musicians, an entry-ramp, men playing women. Screens are the basis of Boris Aronson's sets: maybe the finest that even he has designed. They make the show a bountiful gift of air and space.

The wedding of Kabuki techniques to Broadway skills produces of course a bastard form. But this is perfectly appropriate, since the subject of the show is bastardisation. Its upshot is the assumption by the Japanese of Western manners and--in a final jump to the present--their phenomenal victory at the West's own commercial game. A closing number balances the account: for most of the evening Eastern rhythms have been adapted by an American director, choreographer and composer; finally we watch American rhythms sung and danced by an Oriental cast--an ending which vindicates the American theatre's right to meddle with this subject and these styles.

As it is told, this is the most moving of the Prince-Sondheim shows. (I don't know whether Mr Prince considers himself a Brechtian, but I take alienation to mean not that emotion should be denied, but that it should be rigorously inspected.) The central character--a minor samurai employed as an intermediary with the invaders--is played by an actor called Isao Sato, who has a most beguiling quality: wry, tender, and quizzically hopeful. One song, 'A Bowler Hat,' which details his capitulation over the years to Western ideas and Western dress, he performs with surpassing delicacy. Indeed, not the least of the skills this show proves the Japanese to have acquired is that of acting in musical comedy; the level of performance is very high.

A couple of Mr Sondheim's lyrics unconvincingly credit some Japanese ladies with a fluent Manhattan wit (a multiple pastiche number for predatory European ambassadors is another, and a hilarious, matter), but his music--full of sweet dissonances, and haunting, angular melodies, has never sounded more individual or more dramatically apt. One song entitled 'Someone in a Tree' concerns, if you please, the impossibility of knowing the truth about any historical event, and the fading of an old man's memory--all set to a surging, questing rhythm that had me on the edge of my seat with excitement. And there is one song of farewell called 'There is No Other Way,' accompanied by a dance of floating silk, which--in sight, sound and sense--is as beautiful as anything I remember in the musical theatre. It can be heard in London--though diminished without the visual element--in the Sondheim compilation at the Mermaid, as can another song--a sailor's trio--actually done better here than in New York.

By way of consolation, Pacific Overtures has just been filmed for television, Japanese television, of course.

records.title: Waiting for Hickey
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Waiting for Hickey

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on revivals of O'Neill, Chekhov, Coward and Feydeau.

O'NEILL'S The Iceman Cometh (Aldwych) is the fountainhead of postwar American drama, the archetype of all the plays in which characters sit in bars or cafés or roadside diners or junkies' pads, interact and wait. It also has a considerable number of relatives living abroad; Samuel Beckett's bums waiting for Godot are in much the same predicament as O'Neill's waiting for Hickey, the travelling salesman. Beckett, however, let his characters off lightly; Godot never arrives. Hickey does show up and his acolytes barely survive his coming. That finally they do survive it is the cruellest thing in the play.

Iceman represents the underside of pop Americana: of Damon Runyon and of Clap hands, here comes Charlie. See the smile on all those hungry faces. They can tell that he's a buyer from the wide and open spaces. The men in Harry Hope's saloon, New York 1912, have permanently thirsty faces and Harry himself is usually pickled enough for his clients to grab themselves all the booze they want. Hickey's arrival will save them the trouble of scrounging; besides, a fresh face is always welcome if you never go out of doors.

O'Neill, writing in 1939, was again recalling his own youth. The claim most frequently made for him is that having touched bottom himself he was able to portray his fellows without any touch of patronage. Exploitation, though, can take many forms, and however much O'Neill may have respected his characters he had few qualms about moving them abruptly from one convention to another. Having set them up as individuals he turns them in his last act into a chorus; suddenly they start talking in unison. Harry becomes the chorus leader and Norman Rodway, who has kept his nose infallibly to the ground in Howard Davies's production, suddenly starts to intone. Visually Mr Davies manages the transition well; the drained, battered faces - 15 in a row - look like a rotting tapestry. Aurally it grates, and for the first time O'Neill's notorious deficiencies as a writer (generally more noticeable on the page than the stage) begin to obtrude.

The jolt is nasty, but the play survives it. Partly it does so by virtue of its length; it plays for four and a quarter hours. O'Neill gives himself room to stumble and get up again; and while a bad long play is insupportable, a good one is, from the audience's point of view, addictive. And because they give the actors a chance to dig their heels in, extended group pieces like this are almost invariably well performed.

The massive structure gives O'Neill the space to grade his characters. All of them are victims of a single disease; unable to face reality, each protects himself with a pipe-dream. At the centre is Harry, believing that one day he will take a walk outside. Around him are his clients, part refugees, part spongers, each with a past that serves also as an imaginary future.

Regarding them with pity and contempt is Larry, whose lack of illusion is itself an illusion. He is generally taken for the play's commentator, but even he is overseen by the barman, Rocky, the play's nearest approach to a man of the world; after all, he has a job, he can leave when he's not working and if he runs a couple of whores, they are only a sideline. His illusions are the hardest to crack because hardest to pin down. As Rob Hoskins plays him, Rocky is almost the centre of the play; certainly he is its pacemaker.

To them comes Hickey in the guise of an evangelist; he has seen through his own pipe-dream and wishes to cure them of theirs. He persuades each of them to try to realise his dream; predictably they all come back to the saloon, sobbing. They and the world have no use for each other. But this is Hickey's plan; what he has come to spread is not happiness but misery. (He deceives himself about this of course: he has merely traded one pipe-dream for another. O'Neill's philosophy may have been schematic, but its application necessarily involved him in greater subtleties than he may have envisaged.) The ground keeps opening. He has killed his wife. For a moment he even faces the fact that he hated her; then he lies to deny it, and his denial sets the bums free. They can claim that he was mad, that they obeyed him only to humour him, and that everything is as it was. If you like happy endings, hurry to the Aldwych.

* * *

The last developments can be hard to follow; O'Neill seems to regard illusion and reality as solid wedges to be moved around like chessmen. What is more, all the characters seem to know the rules. There is a parallel action involving young Parritt, who has shopped his mother as Hickey has killed his wife, and who comes to confess to Larry as Hickey comes to confess to the bums.

This is the area least well handled in the writing and in this production. Kenneth Cranham, usually an attacking actor, seems ill-at-ease with Parritt's whimpering passivity and plight. Patrick Stewart easily holds the stage; he does not make Larry's mental processes any too interesting. The rest, in Chris Dyer's set, high and wide if not handsome, is splendour. Alan Tilvern's Hickey is a perfect messenger of death, with slicked-down hair, slicked-down voice, and features locked in the permanent sneer bequeathed by years of successful salesmanship. The others - especially John Warner, Gary Bond and Richard Simpson - make their lurchings between the bottle and the door horribly involving. In its detail, more than its theory, the play rubs a universal sore; and in its attitude to hope (it exists in the saloon as in the proprietor's name and it depends on deception) it satirises tragedy, making it the archetypal modern play.

* * *

Not the greatest though: that is Chekhov's Three Sisters, which at the Cambridge is accorded, in Jonathan Miller's production transferred from Guildford, by far its best performance in my experience. There is at least one transcendent sequence: Natasha's proprietorial stalk around the sisters' bedroom in the third act is satirically reprised by Irena. Olga and Masha fall about; the trio are a laughing unity and the harmony prompts Masha to tell, still laughing, of her love for Vershinin.

Janet Suzman is magnificent as Masha; her reactions throughout are pointed but never planted. The flow of her performance is virtually unbroken. Nigel Davenport, partnering her, helps her to make sense; he is fleshily attractive, opportunist, a bit shabby. He philosophises because that is the thing to do, and he covertly laughs at those (like the doomed Trozonbach) who do it seriously.

The play takes shape, too, as an outsiders' revenge; Natasha and Solyony, both snubbed in the first act, naturally cause havoc later. June Ritchie's Natasha, in particular, is excellently rounded. Angela Down's Irena is refreshingly hard; she does not languish for Moscow, she merely wants it to hurry up. Mr Miller sacrifices intermediate climaxes (one or two, to be honest, I rather missed) for the sake of the last outburst, which comes hard and fast. Susan Engel puts more despair into Olga's last speech than I have ever heard before. Sebastian Shaw's doctor and Antony Brown's schoolmaster are particularly distinguished.

* * *

Blithe Spirit (Lyttelton) turns out more ghostly than might have been intended. Harold Pinter's production firmly outlines the marital discomfort at the base of the play, but he has little opportunity to build on it; and both Coward's prose and his artistic snobbery, the central character is a novelist with little good to say of anyone who isn't, seem petty and, what is worse, routine. A great Madame Arcati might save the day, as she saved the film, but Elizabeth Spriggs is no Margaret Rutherford. She has played too many eccentrics to conquer: the part from without, not enough to take it from within.

Maria Aitken has the right style - compounded of a witty drawl and a long, long back - for Elvira; Rowena Cooper deals professionally with Ruth's good lines, but cannot salvage the bad, which predominate; and Richard Johnson is dull. I think the production should be faster, but I imagine Mr Pinter trusts the text more than I do.

* * *

Nobody involved in Signed and Sealed (Comedy) seems to trust it at all, which is understandable. It is the least inventive farce ever to reach our stage under the name of Feydeau. If I had a line or two left, I could even summarise its plot.

records.title: Lessons of a crisp factory
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Some of My Best Friends Are Husbands
records.body:
Lessons of a crisp factory

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

JOSEF FRANK, as I learned last week, was one of those hanged in Prague in 1952 after the Slansky show-trials. In his new play, Weapons of Happiness (Lyttelton) Howard Brenton imagines Frank, surviving, somehow, coming to England and working, now in a potato-crisp factory, in South London. It will be seen that, historically speaking, Mr Brenton's Frank is a ghost; dramatically, too. "I don't sleep," he tells us at curtain-rise. "I walk about London."

The crisp business is in turmoil. The factory is small, family owned and running down. Its work-force seems to consist entirely of kids and old men. Prominent among the kids is Janice, whose political education began early with a book called "The Evil That Was Lenin." ("Think it was meant to put me off. 'Stead it put me on.") Discovering that the management has plans to sell out she organises a workers' occupation. She does not organise it very well; and her forces have to decamp through the sewers. Anyway her own politicisation, though fervent, has never seemed very secure ("Couldn't understand a word. But I believed in it") and she has not managed to communicate much in the way of ideology to her followers, who are driven by gut-discontent, gut-hatred, and--at the decisive moment--alcohol. Besides this they have neither the finance nor the contacts to take over the machines and make crisps themselves.

It is Frank who points this out to them; but it needs no ghost to come from the grave to tell us that this attempt at revolt was foredoomed. Mr Brenton's full-length plays are characteristically organised around two disparate blocks of experience; in Magnificence his worlds collide with immense force, in The Churchill Play they remain obstinately apart. In Weapons of Happiness they are brought together but there is no impact. Frank, both in the writing and in Frank Finlay's performance, is carefully opaque. We are shown his past as well as his present; there are flashbacks to his days as a Czech Minister negotiating with Mikoyan and socialising with Stalin; monologues about his torture and interrogation. These of course are harrowing, but ever since Darkness at Noon, never mind The Gulag Archipelago, they have been within the grasp of any competent writer who cared to use them. And Mr Brenton does not use them to any new effect; he leaves us feeling (a) that in the light of experiences like these, English ideas of revolution look childish and (b) that the idea of socialist revolution has anyway been irredeemably tarnished. These conclusions might be reached by any liberal, and I doubt if they are what Mr Brenton had in mind.

When Janice, in the last line of the play, recalls Frank, she merely says of him, "He was a Communist." And that line, coming as and when it does, sounds like a declaration both of love and honour; but it can hardly counter-balance what has gone before. There is more swimming about in the play than has been resolved or made clear. Half of the evening works, though, as a furious lampoon on a decaying corner of capitalism. It is like Mr Brenton to choose a crisp-factory for his area of conflict, and to make the owner the victim of his own ingenuity ("It was the pork chop flavour that finally did for me") in the fight against "the monoliths of the crunch world." Michael Medwin has the best of Mr Brenton's dialogue (brisk, grotesque and concrete as ever) and does well by it; he is pitiable and amusing. Julie Covington, too, is excellent as Janice; compact and composed, frank, exact and enigmatic, she proves herself here (as she promised a couple of years ago in The Pleasure Principle) the most distinctive contemporary young actress we have.

There are some excess characters: a deaf-and-dumb boy who is not used for cheap effect but is not used for much else either, and Mr Medwin's unsatisfied spouse. (If industrialists could make love to their wives, would that solve everything?) But Mr Brenton still takes as much delight in stage images, and his director David Hare takes as much care over them, as in their Portable Theatre days. Operating now at the other extreme, using all of the National Theatre that works, they convey the same cool pleasure in stretching and challenging the available resources. Not every play can offer both a scene in the London Planetarium and the spectacle of cartons of crisps hurled on to the stage to vomit forth their contents.

* * *

A redoubtable company of underactors, guided by a television director, fall predictably foul of Webster's The White Devil (Old Vic). The setting would be nondescript were it not for a brace of swing-doors downstage which inescapably suggest the lobby of an hotel with delusions of grandeur; the costumes have the same seediness, the same unspecified modernity. Everything and everybody is undercut, which is part of the effect Webster presumably aimed for, but by no means all of it. He was obviously fascinated by his luxurious assembly of homicides, and the moral judgments he delivered were considerably more complex and evasive than the puritanical disapproval, compromised by prurience, conveyed by this production almost before it has started. The amount of mumbling and gabbling indulged in is phenomenal.

Michael Lindsay-Hogg's production does actually manage some things unexpectedly well; one is a contest in melancholia between a couple of the play's numerous villains which dissolves when one of them receives good news and explodes with laughter; another is the portrayal of the boy-prince Giovanni. Glenda Jackson gives a small but accurate account of the title role, but she cannot hold the play together; neither can Jack Shepherd, who as Flamineo has the most chance. He establishes a properly confidential relationship with the audience but none with anybody else; he seems to comment on his own villainy without ever executing it. So the most varied and rewarding role in English drama fades into nothing. James Villiers does better as Bracciano, whom he just manages to keep believable as a sulky, possessive head prefect. Frances de la Tour is properly ambiguous as the seeming-virtuous Isabella, and Jonathan Pryce hovers to some effect as the cut-throat Lodovico. The end of the play is left confused; one character even escapes, most apocryphally, with her life.

* * *

The following night another TV director, Jack Gold, succeeded triumphantly in making another diabolical (if considerably more tractable) play command the stage. Indeed Tom Conti, leaning handsomely and languorously against the door on first entrance, looks more like The Devil's Disciple (Aldwych) than anybody reading the lines Shaw provided for his conventional romantic ne'er-do-well might imagine possible. Mr Conti and Mr Gold have been as assiduous with the play's wit as with its avowed melodrama; and the RSC have cast the play up to, indeed some way above, the hilt. The deployment of John Wood as General Burgoyne, whose every line is an infallible wisecrack, is definitely luxury casting and is of course pure delight; Mr Wood, like Mr Conti, announces his intention with his first movement, which is to lie full-length upon a table and gaze upward with lazy, insolent defiance. Even the emotions of the besotted Mrs Anderson get scrupulous attention from Estelle Kohler. T. P. McKenna has a roaring time as her transfigured mate, and I must mention Patrick Godfrey's perfect butt of a major, if only because I always mean to mention Mr Godfrey when dealing with this company and nearly always have to squeeze him out. I should remind you that the play is set in the American War of Independence and that this seems to be topical: military bands play patriotic airs on fifes.

* * *

At the Mermaid Hugh Leonard has adapted a Labiche farce under the title Some of My Best Friends Are Husbands, and may well have interfered with it. I suspect, though, that he is less the culprit than the director, James Grout, who permits his stars, Patrick Cargill and Moira Redmond, to give performances that have everything to do with actors' panic and nothing with that of the characters. Hugh Paddick nearly redeems the occasion as a masochistic, hypochondriac and possibly fetishistic cuckold; he fills the character to the brim but never over. The same tact and good sense is evidenced in smaller roles by Granville Saxton and Peter Bourke. It is also exercised by absolutely everybody in Donkey's Years (Globe), an unmitigatedly glorious farce by Michael Frayn to which I must return next week.
production_title: Some of My Best Friends Are Husbands

records.title: Trucking in from Hull
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Trucking in from Hull

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

ONE member of the Hull Truck Company claims in his programme biography to have been thrown out of LAMDA; another made a similar exit from Manchester Polytechnic School of Theatre. It is tempting to call Hull Truck a dropouts' group; that phrase belongs of course to the last decade, but it is no less appropriate on that account. The Truckers' most engaging quality is their independence of fashion. They are not themselves anachronistic; the characters they present may be nostalgic for the 1960s, but then that is one of the distinguishing marks of the 1970s.

So, at least, our playwrights keep telling us; Stephen Poliakoff's disc-jockey in City Sugar blamed his present cynicism on the wreck of his past dreams. Mr Poliakoff's Leicester looked like hell; Mike Bradwell's Hull (it is Mr Bradwell who drives the Truck) is more companionable. It tastes of keg beer and instant coffee, and it is unquestionably a university town; whatever their actual status, whatever their age, its inhabitants are leading a student life. They talk, since Hull Truck's plays are improvised, a great deal.

Their last show, Oh What, derived its unity from its characters' enslavement to past enthusiasms. Something of the same theme persists in their latest, Bridget's House, seen last week at the Young Vic, but here it seems peripheral, almost a mannerism. There is a difference - the characters are aware of passing time, they are consciously nostalgic - and there is pleasure to be derived from hearing pop-fans scrupulously distinguishing between the trends of the sixties and the early sixties. There is a pleasant song on the subject, too. (Hull Truck's use of music as commentary between scenes might one day lead us to a real native musical.) But it seems a long-winded, conventional way of establishing the two participants as, in Bridget's words, "emotional cripples."

Bridget is their landlady, as she is to most of the cast, and her estimate of them all is the same. It is the play's business to make us see that the words apply just as strongly to her. The trouble is that we can see this from the start. Bridget is an embittered divorcee, who has collected three properties by way of alimony. A psychology lecturer pursues her; she rejects him and takes a musician to bed, to the fury of his girlfriend.

Sexual situations are even more vulnerable than political ones to dramatists' distortion; the group improvisation method is a good way of preserving balance: We can see everybody behaving badly, weakly, embarrassingly, and no favourites are played. The dialogue is extraordinarily tight (theoretically it may vary in performance, but on the first night it seemed to have cast-iron consistency) and, most unusually in an improvised play, the actors know when to shut up.

Quite often the wit is sharp enough to make you wonder if Hull Truck are harbouring a playwright on the premises. The construction, though, cures you of that idea; Bridget's House, unlike Oh What, tells a story, and cannot raise interest in its outcome. It also differs from its predecessor in concentrating on middle-class characters and it has difficulty getting on terms with them, though David Hatton's lecturer is a clever study in ratty frustration. Rachel Bell's Bridget is clever, too, and as far as possible from her adenoidal tripper in Oh What. Here she shatters egos in a voice coated with iodine, stretches a leg across the lap of her intended with the brazen timing of a Maggie Smith.

This kind of acting (and I state it with no prejudice; in fact with all the approval of enjoyment) is, in the strictest sense, artificial, and needs a text to support it. If Hull Truck are going literary, Miss Bell, their most distinctive player, is going to get there first. The show is due at the Bush in November and the smaller space (though the Young Vic is hardly the Palladium) may suit it better. If the script of Bridget's House were written down, it would undoubtedly make a better read than that of The Canning Town Cowboy (Half Moon). This has an author, Shane Connaughton, and he brings off a few bright gags, but the play really consists of a single, rather arbitrary, conceit extended over a stretch of conventional community-theatre material. A ball of string is being unwound and it might be cut off at virtually any point. The hero is an East Ender who wants to be, and dresses like, a Wild Westerner; his non-conformity is the vehicle for some mild satire on bank clerks, policemen and such that might just as well exist without him. The acting is brash and genial, though it totters whenever the performers try to get a grip on surfaces too thin to allow them a foothold. Jill Richards, urgent and disdainful as the hero's girl, stands firmer than anyone else, though John Joyce, in various guises, grapples well.

* * *

The Only Way Out (Theatre Upstairs) is by George Thatcher, serving a life-sentence on a murder charge, having originally been condemned to death. It deals with a man in the early stages of the same situation: in the condemned cell, awaiting his appeal, protesting that he was framed, prophesying that the law, though it will spare his life, will be far too careful of its own ever to declare him innocent. Some of the action - notably the defiance of a bullying screw - comes over as wish-fulfilment, but most of it, in a well-controlled production by David Halliwell, is starkly convincing.

The inevitable bond between the prisoner and his unvarying attendants is traced without sentimentality or overt bitterness. Only his outline of his defence rings false: not the matter, but the manner. This may be how Mr Thatcher thinks now, but not how he, or anyone, would have spoken then; the pat phrases sink the actor, Brian Croucher, though earlier he is excellent, his accustomed casualness hardened into last-ditch defiance. I don't know if Mr Thatcher has another play in him, but it might be worth the while of a subsidised theatre to find out.

* * *

A few words of tribute to Side by Side by Sondheim (now at Wyndham's; I was away when it first opened at the Mermaid). Stephen Sondheim's best songs are built on fine gradations of tone and meaning, and the singers here are often more scrupulously aware of them than were the original interpreters. The duets - David Kernan and Millicent Martin in You Must Meet My Wife from A Little Night Music, or Mr Kernan and Julia McKenzie in Barcelona, the marvellous song of sleepy seduction from Company - become, as they should be, musicalised conversations. The emphasis is maybe too exclusively on sour urban wit (there are occasional cheerful songs in the Sondheim oeuvre), but Miss McKenzie, sad and hopeful, mines deep into Broadway Baby, the song of an unemployed showgirl, so that it passes pastiche and says, more movingly and economically, everything that is in A Chorus Line.

records.title: Mr. Harrison takes a train
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Mr. Harrison takes a train

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

The day after seeing M Perrichon's Travels (Chichester) I snatched a copy of The Selective Ego and was rewarded by the discovery that James Agate had been presented with a copy of this very play when about to board a train for Southampton, en route for New York. He did not, apparently, say much in the way of thank you, being mindful of M. Perrichon's odious habit of making speeches on railway stations, something about which Mme Perrichon had to speak to him severely.

Fate having made me a present of this information, I thought it only fair to pass it on. Anyway, it raises two points of interest. One: the incident occurred in 1937 when Labiche's comedy, written in 1860, was apparently a quotable classic. It was not, however, given an English production until last Tuesday. Two: now that it has reached us, the railway station seems almost its main reason for existence.

The director, Patrick Garland, and his designer, Eileen Diss, have expended enormous effort on re-creating for us the Gare de Lyon, where M. Perrichon's travels begin. Upstage a facade is projected; downstage arches are erected; smoke voluminously billows at the moment of departure; and Bill Fraser, our theatre's prime representative of bilious uniformed officialdom, slowly and resentfully combines the roles of porter and ticket-salesman, thereby occasioning factotum jokes which Labiche never invented but should have.

Mr Fraser's presence, together with that of a brass band to play us in (was the Gare de Lyon really such a fun-palace?), recalls the National Theatre's version of that other picaresque comedy The Captain of Kopenick. Mr Garland's production suffers in the comparison, since the play belies its title; having made such a fuss over dispatching Perrichon from Paris it follows him to Switzerland (land of merry alpenhorns and gemutlich hoteliers) for one scene only, then gets him home and belatedly settles into situation farce.

There is a continuous plot-line, concerning the efforts of two fairly indistinguishable young men to win Perrichon's daughter, but it hardly matters. What does matter, and might unify the evening, is Perrichon himself, a successful coach-builder who, as one of his employees cantankerously remarks, can ride in his own coach, to such a pass has French society now come. Perrichon, in other words, is a type of the emergent bourgeois, and at Chichester he is played by Rex Harrison, an actor who represents the bourgeoisie after a comfortable century in the saddle.

When buying his ticket for Switzerland, Mr Harrison tells us that he has never travelled before; this is an obvious lie, and Labiche's text compels him to go on fibbing for most of the evening. Perrichon is continually beset by hazards that scare the life out of him, but that Mr Harrison could shrug his way through; as a result the actor goes through the evening looking thoroughly ill-at-ease, but not the right kind of ill-at-ease.

In other roles, Mr Harrison has presented an ironist's complacency; Perrichon's complacency, however, is that of the buffoon, leading him into the solemn verbosity that alerted Agate. If it is his vice, it is also his armour, and it is linked to a meanness that gives the play some distinction as satire. Misadventuring on the Matterhorn, he is rescued from a crevasse by one of his daughter's suitors; a moment later he himself performs a similar service for the other. He much prefers the man he saved to the man who saved him; in gratitude, as in all else, he would rather be a creditor than a debtor.

Maybe this joke could sustain a whole play, but since neither Mr Garland (whose invention runs dangerously low as the evening proceeds) nor Mr Harrison gives it an honest try it is impossible to say. Mr Harrison does have a very touching few moments at the end, when Perrichon is told the truth about himself. Clive Francis, who was good in The Circle a couple of weeks ago, and Andrew Sachs do spirited work as the rivals; and Tony Robinson, suggesting Bob Cratchit gone mouldy a few years after Scrooge's reclamation, is fine as the captious clerk.

* * *

Little birds are bathing
Crocodiles in cream
Like a happy dream.
Like, but not so lasting:
Crocodiles when fasting
Are not all they seem.

That squib of Lewis Carroll's gives a tone as well as a title to Crocodiles In Cream (Mermaid), a one-man show devised by David Horlock, who directs it, and Michael Rothwell, who performs it. Carroll's verse and his fiction are subtly joined to his life and letters (I mean his correspondence) to reveal a man for whom existence was a perpetual jol, every Snark a Boojum.

Insufficient allowance is made, perhaps, for the success of his comic mask; when Mr Rothwell goes into extracts from Alice or recites 'Hiawatha's Photographing' ('From his shoulder Hiawatha/Took the camera of rosewood/Made of sliding, folding rosewood'), he eliminates the breeziness and concentrates on the melancholy. This makes him, of course, a magnificent Mock Turtle, a source of truly beautiful soup; and he holds the stage impressively throughout, with scarcely a moment's boredom.

Carroll cuts a more interesting figure than does the Roman satirist Juvenal in another solo turn, Juvenalia, which has just ended a run at the Bush, but may return; since the actor concerned is named Callow, the possibilities for punning seem limitless. Simon C. delivers the material in the style of a nightclub comic; in one of the dingier boites on the Appian Way, the kind you might drop into for compensation after a gladiatorial show with a low mortality rate. His flashing teeth and glasses, and his transfixingly chatty manner, suggest a Ronnie Corbett grown physically upwards and outwards and dyspeptically in all directions.

He comes out of it very well, better than his author. Juvenal's invective at the state of things in Rome (flattery, nymphomania and atrocious cooking) is pungent all right and if you want to think it topical you may; but it is very generalised.
