I never believed in the people to whom the satires were addressed (I always used to have difficulty with this particular convention when faced with Latin poetry at school) and I detected no specific concern. Juvenal is always compared with Swift, but his narcissistic vituperation runs the icy passion of the Modest Proposal a very poor second.

records.title: The gull flies again
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The gull flies again

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

Touching down in London for the first time in at least a fortnight, The Seagull (Duke of York's) can still spring the occasional surprise. Some of these are due to Mark Woolgar's unusually forthright adaptation; it may not signify much in London in 1976, but this is the first time in my experience that the language of Chekhov's heroines has caught up with that of Eliza Doolittle. One might be hearing much of the play for the first time; a compliment which Chekhov generally attracts and for which his various translators must take great credit.

Mr Woolgar's production, which has been brought in from Derby Playhouse, is as brisk and emphatic as his adaptation, which at least makes it a refreshing contrast to the curiously flat version which Lindsay Anderson directed earlier this year for the Lyric Theatre Company. (Whatever, by the way, happened to the Lyric Theatre Company?) True, there is no Helen Mirren in St Martin's Lane and I thought at first that Georgina Hale's Nina, curly and girlish, was going to be awful; she rattled off Konstantin's play as if it were meaningless (Nina may well have been defeated by it; but surely she put up a fight; at this point she wants to please Konstantin and impress his mother.)

Later on, Miss Hale begins to display real insight: she harps nervously and obsessively on the words 'fame' and 'glamour,' clasps her hands in adoring imitation of her idol Arkadina, directly anticipates -- with her fevered complaint that her head is spinning -- the dementia of the last act. This is played with a haunting self-mockery, if without the bedrock determination that allowed Miss Mirren to make final sense of the play.

Asked in the first act to recite something from Konstantin's play, Nina refuses to oblige; her cry of 'it's so boring' amounts almost to a long-range death-warrant for its author. Gabrielle Lloyd's Masha, who made the request in a solitary bright-eyed moment, sinks back into her usual bleariness, pushed a little further towards her hopeless marriage with Medviedenko, whose long-suffering futility is here given unusually sharp definition by Dennis Denny.

Their relationship, which foreshadows and inverts (since here it is the man who is baby-besotted), the ghastly union of Andrei and Natasha in Three Sisters, emerges more strongly in each new production of The Seagull.

Coarsening through the play, Miss Lloyd still preserves the thread of her feeling for Konstantin; it is she who pricks up her ears at his off-stage piano-playing, and she who knows immediately that he has shot himself.

Completing the play's sardonic picture of youth is Richard O'Callaghan's Konstantin, the best I have seen. He whines, he snivels, he hardly grows up, but there is passion and perception in him, however ludicrous, and he freshens the speeches about finding new theatrical forms without disguising their naivete.

He is also locked into his relation with his mother; when he quotes Hamlet at her he does so with real venom, the venom of absolute dependence. This Oedipal Konstantin might have fitted well into Jonathan Miller's production a couple of years ago. (When Seagulls come, they come not single spies.)

The elders fare less well; Mr Woolgar's emphasis on the primary colours in Chekhov makes them seem garish. Denis Holmes's Shamrayev shamelessly shouts (Mr Holmes was a notable quietist with the RSC, so maybe he is compensating now) and though Sheila Ballantine's Arkadina is a ruthless and witty study of a desperately dominating woman (whose main defence against time is her wig), this may be a part which really needs a star. This is especially so when a star is actually to hand in another role. Alan Bates's Trigorin is not a selfish performance, but it hardly fits; he is acting more elaborately than anyone else (perhaps more subtly, but in this context it is difficult to tell), gesturing and stammering more. The character never quite appears.

* * *

T. Zee (Royal Court), credited to Richard O'Brien and Richard Hartley, is the successor to Mr O'Brien's Rocky Horror Show, but completely lacks its lightness of touch. It also marks a partial return, after the skill and delicacy of Peter Gill's Small Change, to the hallowed Court tradition of high-minded bungling.

The stage is so destructively cluttered that the actors have no room to do anything but sing undistinguished songs into their hand-mikes, which gets monotonous. Even when the music stops, the lyrics seem to continue, since the script is written in doggerel couplets; anyone sensitive to rhyme will find himself in pain.

Mr O'Brien has written an awful part for himself as a knock-kneed anthropologist exploring the ruins of Los Angeles, and a better one for his lady companion, Belinda Sinclair, who can and does sing. Warren Clarke as Tarzan, into whose company they fall, also has an unexpectedly winning country-and-western way; most of what goodwill is going in Nicholas Wright's production accrues to him. The action takes place on a sort of giant pin-table in a libidinous inferno, peopled by the debris of Hollywood. But this time Mr O'Brien has forgotten satire and settled for celebratory camp. Nothing happens, fortissimo.

* * *

Four To One (Young Vic) is a first play by the excellent National Theatre actor Gawn Grainger which his colleagues seem to enjoy playing. It has less to offer its audience since it is inclusively constructed, despite a final sprint, and tends to an aesthetic of group menace and a theory of violence already familiar. Only its setting -- the back room of a pub, reserved for poker players -- and the resultant atmosphere of sour camaraderie seem to derive from Mr Grainger's experience of life rather than of other plays.

It is on this run that the cast fasten; I would guess that actors spend more time in pubs than most. As a National Theatre phenomenon -- casting Derek Newark, Pip Hinton, Trevor Ray, Mark McManus and Simon Ward an untrammelled opportunity to display their prowess and keep in training -- the occasion is fairly encouraging.

* * *

The cast of Seven Girls (Open Space) work in a harder, less accessible environment which they recreate brilliantly. Lynne Monahan, drugged and unreachable, Katherine Haber, ferocious, and Linda Regan, lost and terrified, head a flock of caged Swedish nightingales, inmates of a reformatory for teenagers run on humanitarian lines which inexorably crush humanely. The play, written and directed by Carl-Johan Seth, is scrupulously fair to its keepers, and the two sides come together to create an image of a life rigid in outline and unpredictable in event. There are perhaps more characters than we can take in, and the play asks too much to focus our concentration, but go along and grab what you can.

records.title: Clouds over Cuba
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Clouds over Cuba

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

The theme of Michael Frayn's Clouds (Hampstead) may best be considered in the light of two exchanges between Hamlet and Polonius. The first, concerning what might be called the cumulative effects of cumulus, demonstrated that a cloud might assume the shape, given goodwill or gullibility in the beholder, of a camel, a weasel or a whale. The other consists of the question 'what do you read, my lord?' and the answer, concrete without being specific, 'words, words, words.' Words, like clouds, can mean anything.

This is hardly a new idea, even in the theatre; indeed the theatre might be considered its natural home. Life can be presented as a continual banana-skin joke: every man the prisoner of his own preconceptions and continually stumbling over his neighbour's. One of the best Jacobean comedies (Chapman's The Widow's Tears) was described by a critic as 'irony made visible' and that, in his own kinder fashion, is what Mr Frayn gives us in Clouds, a comedy in the classic line.

Clouds is set in Cuba, and most of its characters are writers. We therefore have a locale which acts as a litmus for contrasting prejudices, and protagonists whose lives are dedicated to articulating them. We meet a male journalist sent out by one of the Sunday supplements, and a lady novelist despatched by the other. (It is not too difficult to guess which scribe belongs to which paper.)

The gentleman, given an enchantingly bilious acidity by Nigel Hawthorne, is inclined to slight the achievements of the revolution, and even more inclined to slight those of his competitor. 'Isn't it typical of that lot,' he inquires at a moment of easily won exasperation, 'to send out some manic-depressive amateur.' He then proceeds to exclaim 'Oh God!' three times. There is no great passion in the exclamations; they are rattled off in a vein almost of self-caricature. For a moment I suspected Mr Hawthorne of stylising his performance, then realised that in fact he was giving a wholly realistic performance of a man who stylises his own life.

Amateur or not, Barbara Ferris's hackette is inclined to get the stories that Mr Hawthorne misses: obviously, human interest still means something. But she too has her bad moments, usually descending on her in the morning when 'you know you can't get to the next day till you've been all the way through this one.'

Joined to these two are an American academic about to add another to his long line of enthusiastic publications on the new Cuba ('another country floating free of money and greed'); they are guided from farm to factory to incipient city by a cheerful driver who is mostly silent (since he has no English and the play little Spanish) and a government guide, beautifully portrayed by Paul Chapman, who is considerably more voluble but whose habit of beginning every sentence with 'I think' helps to give the play its peculiarly unnerving quality.

Every scene is a game of cross-purposes, and the play is in fact staged by Michael Rudman as a series of games; half-a-dozen chairs are continually rearranged to form the set. The only thing to be said against this format is that, smacking of revue, it lacks a little in narrative excitement. The play's many virtues do not include suspense.

They do, however, include surprise. Each of the four men is concerned to make a play for Miss Ferris and it seems to be only by accident that she ultimately (or, not to give too much away, penultimately) is matched with her compatriot, Mr Hawthorne. She claims she planned it, but why believe her? One of Mr Frayn's achievements is to provide the first convincing love-scenes to reach our stage in years but, the play being what it is, the love presented is conditional and much undermined. Our hero is very distressed by our heroine's habit of using him for copy, noting his words as he says them. There are recurrent choric scenes in which the characters are seen frantically typing or fretfully scribbling, ostensibly about Cuba, but actually about one another. They are the play's method, and ours, of keeping score.

At one point a dispute occurs over what Mr Hawthorne, with elaborate casualness, refers to as 'labour-camps'; the American prefers the expression 'work-camps.' Miss Ferris, belatedly surfacing, only hears the word labour and accordingly asks about the Cuban attitude to abortion. Mr Frayn's word-play is less effervescent than Tom Stoppard's, but even more acute; his view of the middle-classes better humoured than Alan Ayckbourn's (and his farce accordingly less mechanically expert), but his satire even more accurate.

* * *

Like Clouds, Troilus and Cressida (Stratford) is an open-ended play. In his celebrated, and lamentably influential, production some years ago, John Barton reduced its various moods to garish nihilism. His new version (co-directed with Barry Kyle) goes some way towards making amends. His Prologue (John Nettles, who doubles as Thersites) is properly sardonic, mocking the 'fair beholders' with the inevitably limited amount that may be 'digested in a play': the last word spat out.

Troilus and Cressida themselves can seldom have been so well played. Both of them are emotional gourmets, precocious sophisticates. Mike Gwilym smiles through both his expectation and his misery, Francesca Annis, both when holding off and giving in, palpably enjoys being a girl. But too many of the previous production's excesses linger on: trimmed and played against this season's sturdy permanent set, they lack even the courage of their own convictions.

Robin Ellis goes gamely through the flamboyant motions expected of this vicious bisexual Achilles, but seems, possibly to his credit, distrustful of them. Tony Church is a lucid enough Ulysses (though his best moment is silent as he shudders at Thersites's cackling that will outlast all his diplomacy); his famous comparison of Time to 'a fashionable host . . . with his arms outstretched as he would fly' finds amusing echo in David Waller's Pandarus, who flutters everywhere.

But neither of these performances is fully realised, and the rest are mostly mediocre. When the actors are dull, who cares what brilliant ideas the directors may have had, especially when one suspects that they may be partly responsible for pinioning the players.

* * *

In Mustapha Matura's Bread (Drum Arts Centre at the Young Vic), an unproduced black playwright declares that he would like to eat Shakespeare; learning that there is only pasta in the house, he settles for Pirandello. And Mr Matura in fact offers us a Pirandellian entertainment; his hero's play takes shape before us, showing us greed, revenge and extortion in Trinidad to match those the outer action depicts in London. Writing, acting and direction are all better in Trinidad, though the same players feature in both halves. Gordon Case, good as the creator, is even better as his creation.

records.title: Dear old Pal
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Dear old Pal

A LAST-MINUTE change of plan by the Edinburgh Festival and the English Stage Company (for which they blame each other) resulted in audiences turning up at the Royal Lyceum for the new David Storey and being greeted instead by an old Richard Rodgers.

Some of them departed in dudgeon and with their money back, thus dampening the proceedings even before they could proceed. As punters they had the right; though of course no responsible critic would countenance them. Even if we forget that Mr Rodgers must have given more widespread pleasure than any other theatre writer alive, it is difficult to believe that anyone seriously regards him as a lesser artist than Mr Storey.

Pal Joey, the last-but-one of the musicals on which Mr Rodgers collaborated with Lorenz Hart, is generally reckoned to be a seminal piece. I know of no American musical prior to its premiere in 1940 which stuck so conscientiously to its own line; the story it tells and the manner of the telling are both uncommonly bleak.

The script was fashioned by John O'Hara from his own short stories. Joey is a night-club compere who performs more notably in bed than on the floor. Rescued from oblivion by the wife of a Chicago tycoon who had made his bread in bread, he's dropped right back there when his protectress, who has staked him to his own club, is blackmailed by a gangster. Clubland is seen as an extension of the underworld. This show never tries to compromise by making its characters lovable.

This results, admittedly, in a certain monotony. O'Hara was not a particularly adroit dramatist and the second half, when the screws begin to turn, is heavy going. Nor, judged simply as a collection of songs, does the score - apart, perhaps, from Bewitched - rank with the best of Rodgers and Hart. They seemed to have jumped at this assignment with masochistic enthusiasm; the brassiness of Rodgers's music is unique in his work, but it is brusque rather than astringent and the melodies are run of the mill. Hart's lyrics are uneven; after a career of writing what were essentially one-shots, he faced the demands of character and situation with more determination than resource. Even Bewitched, in its unexpurgated version the confession of a nymphomaniac, overflows its context while other numbers fail to fill theirs. Partly this is because they lack proper support from the book. Partly it is because every song in this show is in form a conventional prop, and partly at Edinburgh it is the fault of the production. It comes from the Oxford Playhouse and will probably look better when it returns there, but as a Festival offering it is shrivelled.

Some blame also adheres to Time, which might be defeated if the performers could take possession of the material. Here only one of them does: Anna Quayle, aggressively deadpan, splendidly renders Zip, a satire on the intellectual aspirations of Gypsy Rose Lee. We see far too little of Miss Quayle these days; nor do we see much in this show, since this one mock strip is her only contribution to it.

Many of the other numbers are actually nightclub routines, and not intended to be very good ones. It may have given the authors an excuse for writing below their best, but Philip Hedley's production grants them a kind of remorseless integrity. We spend all evening in the club, done up in bricks the colour of tandoori chicken; all other locations are insets. At his best, Mr Hedley creates the bustle of a real timeless and placeless rehearsal (though the jokes are in the text rather than the staging). If the nightclub numbers are to be purposely bad, the straight songs must compensate, and here they do not. Bob Sherman's Joey is a talented performance but wrong; tall, fair and teasing, he almost makes Joey's stories of a college education believable. They should be incredible; what gives Joey his appeal (and also limits it) is not his plausibility but his barefaced cheek; he is a real no-hoper. There is an atmosphere in the staging, but none in the performances; no challenge in Pat Kirkwood's predatress, no menace in Dick Wilson's gangster. And when he has Mr Sherman break into a couple of unscheduled choruses of The Lady is a Tramp (same composers, different show), Mr Hedley sacrifices even his own credibility.

* * *

Ever since 1947, the Assembly Hall has proved a fit setting for moral comedy. It is a wonder that Measure for Measure (staged by the Birmingham Rep) has never been seen there before. In his programme note, the director, Stuart Burge, claims the comedy to be as important as the morality, and for once programme and production agree.

The scenes of regulation humour are not - despite the warm presence of Russell Hunter, an impudently strutting Pompey - unwontedly hilarious. But the blustering irony of David Suchet's Lucio leaves its mark on the stricter characters, particularly on the Duke whom Bernard Lloyd presents as a glib, roguish manipulator, taking to the Friar's hood (Shakespeare's friars being always something akin to pandars) as if he were born to it. He bounds genially from plot to revelation; but the relish he projects is more properly the author's than the character's.

In getting us to giggle at the Duke's schemes, Mr Burge ignores the fact that, in the main, they work; both Angelo and Isabella are respectively knocked off their perches, and, being knocked, learn charity. Anna Calder-Marshall's voice and manner, at once shy and decisive, do very well for Isabella; the rebukes of overreaching authority have never sounded more searing.

When David Burke's Angelo lunged, there were shocked gasps from the stalls, and the laughers were surely right; Mr Burke's interpretation, if a trifle stodgy (a kind of blank verse Malvolio), in no way diminished the agony. When he whispered of his gravity "wherein - let no man hear me - I take pride," he was as vulnerable to ridicule as to contempt. He shows, too, a powerful talent for self-abasement, dropping to the deck overcome by guilt or desire. This Angelo's puritanism was not perhaps of the livid sort to conquer a city, even Edinburgh, and the play lost accordingly part of its full power. But many productions have fallen further.

records.title: In praise of the Devil
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
In praise of the Devil

THEATRICALLY this year's Edinburgh Festival is the best I have known in four years' service. The Assembly Hall, tightened by Birmingham Rep's Measure for Measure, is positively glorified by its setting. The Devil is an Ass, Peter Barnes's streamlining of a particularly rare Ben Jonson, is less fortunate in its surroundings but nearly as good.

Mr Barnes has helped the text on its way by simplifying its intrigues, cherishing its most durable jokes, and adding a few of his own. He has, for example, made repeated and increasingly hilarious references to a valued but absent gentleman-usher, making a running gag out of what in Jonson was at best (the character in question being called Ambler) a strolling one. He has rendered the same service, on a larger scale, to a more important character, the devil himself. Jonson's hero is a hopeful fiend called Pug, who begs Satan for a day on Earth to gull humanity. Set down in Jonson's London, a town composed entirely of knaves and fools, he finds himself, unexpectedly but repeatedly, of the latter party. Satan had warned him how it would be on Earth, how far behind hypocritical mankind had left the Devil ("they have their Vices there, most like to Virtues"); he is even forced to rescue his protege from jail.

Together they make a final return, survey humanity which they find crouching in attitudes of corruption as if posing for a Breughel; they determine to find new worlds where devils are still devils and men still eat apples rather than each other; they will quit Earth, "this plague-spot of the cosmos."

That last phrase does not sound Jonsonian (it tries too hard). Nor is it; the entire episode is Mr Barnes's own and the archness of the writing is a price worth paying for the new shapeliness of the action. Jonson let his devils dwindle and vanish, but his adapter helps Bernard Lloyd to play a magniloquent Satan, and rescues Chris Ryan's pugnacious Pug from the law of diminishing returns. As he progresses through the Satanic mill, clumping and straddling in his human shape, trying to get laid or just get lucky, his frustrations build.

The terrestrial society that torments him is composed, as usual in Jonson, of gullible inventors, confident tricksters and painted ladies. Mr Barnes and his director, Stuart Burge, manage to persuade us that this constitutes a sustained version of corruption, rather than five acts of inveterate (and invertebrate) grumbling. Charlatan-in-chief is Meercraft, described by Jonson as "a Projector"; Russell Hunter does indeed project, very forcefully, what it would be nice to know Meercraft might be like when off duty.

The principal victim is an ambitious bumpkin named FitzDottrel; Jonson, almost alone among comic dramatists, has no affection for his dupes, and the part is accordingly well-roared by Peter Vaughan, who is an unusual combination - fanged and greasy. The supporting cast usefully includes David Burke as a quiet and stony factotum brimming with uncracked smiles and Alan Rickman, who speaks breathtaking verse while in drag, which may have been nothing in the seventeenth century, but calls for attention now. Robin Archer's costumes do London up proud and Hell up something sumptuous.

* * *

Japan's Bunraku Puppet Theatre (Royal Lyceum) is hypnotic, with the rider that hypnotism inhibits detailed response. Each puppet is controlled by three hooded but otherwise very visible figures about twice its own size. The dolls constantly seem to be about to break free, and at the curtain calls, which they take with shameless abandon, they appear to have succeeded. (One of them looks strangely like Rab Roy, perhaps in homage to Scotland.) At the side of the stage a narrator chants the stories; one feels sorry for the Japanese audiences who, understanding him, must miss the full exoticism of the entertainment.

Language uncomprehended is more deliberately employed by the La Mama Company of New York performing Greek tragedy in the long, bare gymnasium of Moray House College. The director, Andrei Serban, begins from the position that every translation of these plays, ornate or colloquial, sounds forced. Mr Serban goes back to the original Greek, not merely undeterred but encouraged by the fact that his actors do not understand it; it is enough that they understand the emotion behind each speech.

This would seem to be a recipe for bad generalised acting, but in fact Mr Serban's belief in a feral power residing in sound rather than sense turns out to be justified; as Andromache, whose young son is taken from her and murdered in The Trojan Women, Priscilla Smith emits a strange keening screech as if she were expelling a demon that had taken refuge in the roof of her mouth. For this play Mr Serban has utilised Aztec and American Indian dialects as well as Greek; he owes much also to the universality of the play. (Next to The Bacchae, it is for good reasons the most performed of Greek tragedies.)

It is easy for us to identify with the captive Trojans, especially in this environmental staging in which we mill around while soldiers, bearing prisoners in wooden cages, divide our ranks. Euripides's subtlest and most acrid passage - the acquittal of Helen - has been transformed into something simpler, though exciting. Dirt and abuse are hurled at her, but she does not wriggle free; we see her executed.

Vocally and visually, this is a brilliant production; Mr Serban's broad effects are more than acceptable because he can convince us that this is a play about ourselves. But he cannot do that with Sophocles' Electra, a play about a family, in which we need to apprehend details. The meeting of Orestes and Electra, accompanied by gentle but overwhelming bell-ringing from the chorus, is moving because there is power in the mere fact of reconciliation; not, it seems, in the mere fact of murder. We watch this play sitting down, and it pays to look to the sides, where scaffolding climbs the walls and actors climb the scaffolding. Few productions make such thrilling use of height; few spaces, of course, offer the scope.

On the fringe there is joyous story-telling by Shared Experience, the best group to emerge since Hull Truck, who specialise in dramatisations of the Arabian Nights. The piece I saw, Dalilah the Wily, features trickery on a scale (and in a good-humoured style) that would bemuse even Jonson. It is performed at great speed, with a minimum of costumes and props, and a maximum of character-transformation by the six actors, who are liable to switch roles in consecutive speeches. Ensuring our complicity, without a hint of blackmail, they raise the comic temperature to heights rarely experienced.

Of two shows at The Traverse, Kibbo Kift, billed as a rock song-cycle, suffers from the limitations of its style and of its subject: a breakaway Boy Scout group of the thirties that went political, to be reviled from Left and Right; only when it gets to broader issues - what makes men join movements - does it become really interesting, and it gets to them late. Still, it is something to see a middle-aged actor belting rock with the power and wit displayed here by Godfrey Jackman.

In Richard Crane's Nero and the Golden House, Mr Jackman plays St Peter and gets crucified. Mr Crane, with a rage and authority beyond anything I have found in his earlier plays, here counterpoints the birth of Christianity with the death of Nero, a self-made god who failed to pass the test of resurrection. Welded to this is the conflict of two modes of kingship: one sober and authoritarian, the other capricious, light and playful. That last is the operative word; the Golden House is Nero's own theatre (actor and author, his name should have been Orson Welles) and there are two plays within the play. The intricate structure, supported by language that rings, chimes and sparkles, and unbeatably directed by Chris Parr, must be reassembled in London.

records.title: Triumphant tragedy
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Triumphant tragedy

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE Royal Shakespeare Company must sigh by now with boredom at each new rave bequeathed it for a comedy or history, but the ecstasy-file on its treatment of the tragedies is comparatively thin. Trevor Nunn's production of Macbeth with Nicol Williamson two years ago was expected to add to it but fell short; and when it was remounted at the Aldwych, all stripped and shorn, it disappointed more; its simplicity seemed false and merely modish.

Mr Nunn's third attempt is also in a fashionable mould. Staged in Stratford's small acting chamber, the Other Place, it is in the line of Buzz Goodbody's miniature Hamlet. That is a good line, though, and Mr Nunn surpasses his model while leaving his own earlier Macbeth far behind. To find a match for this new production with Ian McKellen in the lead, you have to go back 14 years to the Paul Scofield-Peter Brook King Lear; and the new offering, being less tendentious, may even have the edge.

On the square of floor that serves as a stage, a circle is outlined in black. Around it stand a few potent props: a kingly robe, a thunder sheet, and also some boxes on the circumference, for the cast (a hardworked 16) to sit on. While some are performing in the middle of the circle, others watch from outside, but not at random: the spectators are carefully chosen. The witches observe Macbeth as he damns himself, Macduff is just outside the arena when his family are murdered within it. These are all familiar devices, at Stratford and elsewhere; what is impressive is not the invention, but the selection and refinement.

'How is't with me when every noise appals me,' asks Macbeth near the beginning of his progress; at the end, the measure of his fall is that he has grown impervious to sound. Mr Nunn keeps us in a state of grace throughout, alert to every noise from the scratching of the murderers at Lady Macduff's door to the subtlest change of tone from the actors, who supply so much energy, intelligence and concentration that an adequate critique would need as many lines as the play. The atmospherics are superb; the play gets into your bones.

What makes the production unassailable is that its antennae are directly tuned to the script. I have laughed before at Mr Nunn's literal way with imagery, but here his correlatives are not only exact, but stunningly imaginative. Macbeth at Dunsinane stands beneath a single light bulb; on 'I 'gin to be aweary of the sun,' he shoves it, sets it swinging backwards and forwards, so that it illuminates his face only on alternate beats; seizing it again, he shines it on to a talisman kept in his hand since his last meeting with the witches to remind himself of their ambiguous guarantee of his invulnerability.

When he speaks of his bloodstained hands that 'pluck out mine eyes,' Mr McKellen looks as if he might well blind himself with his jabbing fingers. His hands are the key to his performance; at first they are alert and sensitive; when he meets the witches they tense and stiffen, bunched fists inside black military gloves. At the end, they are lifeless; they have gone, with his conscience and his sensibilities, into decay and he knows it.

Macbeth knows everything; he is the most self-aware of tragic heroes, and the play makes us free of his mind. (Here of course lies its greatness--not, as we were told at school, in the piling up of external symbols of chaos to point a perfectly obvious moral.) Mr McKellen grants him, too, a certain courtliness, even wit; not merely the horror but the absurdity of his actions strikes him from the outset, and he can regard his downfall as an inexorable joke.

Allowing his wife to pace him is amusing; she pulls him along a road he would travel anyway and he can allow himself scruples, knowing she will be there to mop them up. Once her prosaic, limited ambition is achieved, she is of no more use to him and he shrugs her off; 'she should have died hereafter' is a moment of exasperation that dares our laughter. He can retreat within himself in a second; he is, as they all say, 'rapt,' a few feet away from us and impenetrable.

At the banquet, quizzing the murderer, he switches instantaneously from host to conspirator and back, playing a game with retribution (as once with ambition) until it overwhelms him and he caves fearsomely in. Mr McKellen, with the reputation of a self-consciously Sensitive Plant, is actually surprisingly burly: a believable fighter and a bulwark worth undermining. This time he never slackens or wallows, freshens the most jaded lines; 'tomorrow and tomorrow' are separated by a silent chasm, beyond which wait sickening vistas of despair. If not absolutely my ideal Macbeth (too much the toy of fate, not assertive enough in his final battle), he is the best I have seen.

Judi Dench, with fewer professional demons to exorcise than Mr McKellen (since she can hardly open her mouth without exuding spontaneity) edges her ring of confidence with steel; murder, as she counsels it, sounds the most sensible thing in the world. And when sleepwalking she emits a hoarse, racking sob which equals (without benefit of Aztec) the vocal exertions in La Mama's Trojan Women. It prompts the line 'Her heart is sorely charged'; the triumph of both protagonists is that their passions live up to the claims made for them in the text.

The supporting playing is the best all round at Stratford for years; Ian McDiarmid doubles an unusually funny Porter (hands thrust deep into his breeches) with an equally unusual Ross, a temporising civil servant with briefcase: the production has modern trappings but--apart from stockings on the murderers' faces--they are tactful.

* * *

Ivanov (Aldwych) gives Anton Chekhov a score of three London plays, equal with Ben Travers (we're all delighted for you, Tony, and Alan Ayckbourn is livid). Unlike its author's later works, it has an unequivocal star role, a man defeated for reasons which John Wood, executing a series of showy but incomprehensible verbal arabesques, hardly gets round to explaining; he emerges as the 'superfluous man' Chekhov explicitly said he shouldn't be.

He is driven to suicide by a couple of idealists; one (played by Mia Farrow who can be wide-eyed like nobody else) wants to marry him, the other to expose him. Kenneth Cranham is good in this role but his drunkenness at the end, coupled with Mr Wood's vagueness, defuses the conflict. David Jones's production offers touching work from Estelle Kohler and some sharp genre painting, when the local gentry, Carol Gillies bristling at their head, are en fete. But most of the cast seem to be playing in competition, and by different rules at that. Carl Davis's music is uncommonly, and most helpfully, bouncy.

records.title: Keeping good company
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Keeping good company

MANCHESTER, a city fortunate in its public buildings, has developed the noble habit of housing theatres inside them. The town rep can be found downstairs in the public library; now the Royal Exchange - disused as such since 1968 - houses a company which should be among the best in the land.

At its head is Michael Elliott, a stage and television director who commands a respect almost unique; I have never heard a professional word against him. He and his associate Caspar Wrede ran the 59 Theatre Company which, in the year of its name, made history at the Lyric, Hammersmith, and incidentally provided me with one of the most valuable pieces of my theatrical education; the lucidity and the humanity of the productions, and the steady dynamism of the acting, made it the first ensemble I had seen, and still among the best. It predated the National and the RSC, and its choice of plays still shames them: it introduced us, right off the bat, to Buchner's Danton's Death and Ibsen's Brand.

The same group came together for the last pre-National season at the Old Vic (Mr Elliott having also directed the unforgettable Vanessa Redgrave As You Like It at Stratford) and reformed, a decade after its inception, as the 69 Company, playing in various Mancunian strongholds: the University, the Cathedral and a tent pitched in the same Exchange where they have now erected what they call their "module" and which looks indeed very like a spaceship: an aspiring glass-and-steel heptagon, designed purely for acting and watching plays.

All interval activities are confined to the surrounding Great Hall, which constitutes the most spacious theatre foyer I have entered. The relation of foyer to auditorium is greatly enriched by their reciprocal visibility.

The stage is in the round (still a rare form in this country) and unusual in playing to three levels of spectators; the encircling galleries above give it - what everybody seems to be after this year - an Elizabethan look. In all, the combination of building and personnel raises expectation to an extraordinary level. This week's two opening productions, however, leave me still anticipating.

Clever though it is, it shreds the comedy, which is underplayed, though over-directed throughout; the characters are one-joke creations, and though it may be the actors' prerogative to humanise them, the outlines need to be firmly drawn first.

Patricia Routledge's Mrs Malaprop is no dragon but a quivering jelly which melts before it is properly set, and Susan Tracy's Lydia has difficulties with the Languish. Trevor Peacock's Acres is an energetic routine lumpkin, Christopher Gable makes a cheerful Jack, and James Maxwell, one of the original heroes of 59, executes some nice gradations of parental tyranny which his gentleness as an actor deprives of conviction. Tom Courtenay as the self-tormenting Falkland has the most command, but even he stops disappointingly short. It seemed a long evening.

The second offering, Heinrich von Kleist's The Prince of Homburg, is more interesting but scarcely more felicitous. Visually, in fact, it is a disaster; one accepts that on this stage actors may be masked by other actors, but to hem them in with designers' paraphernalia seems perverse. It is also, in this case, hideous; sets and props are a pattern of squared-off cylinders, as indeed are the costumes, which at close quarters (as in this theatre we are all supposed to be) are uncomfortable for both parties.

In the first half of Mr Wrede's production, when the stage is full of campaigning troops, it is often difficult to tell what is going on; the second act does sharpen considerably, though there is still an over-plus of throatily hopeful acting in the commissioned ranks of the Prussian army.

The Prince of Homburg is the kind of European classic one imagines being tossed around at planning meetings of the National and the RSC and guiltily forgotten; in staging its British premiere (it was written in 1811), the Royal Exchange Company is honouring its best traditions. The play is a heroic comedy, alternately reminiscent of Measure for Measure, Arms and the Man and A Midsummer Night's Dream.

The Prince, bewitched by visions of military glory and his general's niece, leads a triumphant cavalry charge which happens to be against orders. The Elector - a wise and crinkly performance by Mr Maxwell, but subject again to iron deficiency - condemns him to death, but grants him a pardon on condition he requests it. This the Prince, after one attack of funk, declines to do, and he is saved only when the Elector is convinced by his officers that the Prince's heroics are actually his responsibility - which one takes to mean that of the entire military caste and its ethic.

The play ends with the Prince raised shoulder-high by his companions and blinking in bewilderment, a mood which finds Mr Courtenay at his most communicative. He has made a mannerism of economy the way some actors do of excess.

This complex play, with more curves than I have mentioned, feels like a masterpiece. I honour the company for its choice and the philosophy underlying it, but both this and The Rivals (also concerned, satirically, with love and honour) demand a rigorous re-establishment of convention if they are to work on a new stage. Physical closeness does not always mean intimacy; I could have tripped the actors up in The Prince of Homburg, but I felt a long way from the play.

* * *

A rather more recent German work, Peter Handke's They Are Dying Out (Young Vic), shows us a business king, aptly named Quitt, who, by breaking trading agreements, ruins his competitors. What, they wonder, has got into him; and the answer, roughly, is Life. He notices things; his conversation is crammed with discrete phenomena, and his awareness of them breaks him down.

Unfortunately for our concentration, everybody else in the play talks in the same way, down to a small shareholder who disrupts AGMs like Judy Holliday in The Solid Gold Cadillac. William Russell, in the taxing role of Quitt, looks taxed; Paul Imbusch, a fat tycoon, and Martin Friend, a thin one, have bite, but not enough to make the words into swords. For his director, Handke needs a showman, but in John Russell Brown he gets a scholar; Handke plus Brown, all mind, makes no matter.

* * *

Denis Cannan, a neglected playwright who started in the early fifties (which is surely forgivable), has a new play, Dear Daddy, which London should see, though not necessarily in the production on view at the Oxford Playhouse. I caught it, admittedly, at a deserted Friday matinee when everybody except Phyllis Calvert (unaccustomedly besotted and bedraggled) imposed West End rhythms, with which the play has nothing to do, even though it deals with a middle class man of letters who has failed professionally, maritally (twice) and paternally. Mr Cannan impales two generations of selfishness; his material is family rituals and family memories, understood but never indulged.

records.title: Moral gymnastics
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Moral gymnastics

THEATRE

Robert Cushman on a Stoppard revival and a new play by Storey

FOUR years after leaping into prominence at the Old Vic, Tom Stoppard's Jumpers has arrived at the Lyttelton. Jumpers is the play about the professor of moral philosophy, possessed of a hare called Thumper, a tortoise called Pat and a wife called Dotty; he accidentally impales the first, treads on the second and, horror-struck, calls out for help from the third.

She has already spent much of the play making a similar request of him, and for a not totally dissimilar reason. She too is in receipt of a corpse and she has a suspicion that she may, at a party the previous evening, have murdered a logician and a gymnast, they being the same person. How are we doing?

The moral philosopher, a George Moore (as opposed to the George Moore), has ignored his wife's cries in the interest of what he considers a greater good, that good being goodness itself. He is preparing a debating speech to prove the existence of God, under two heads: as creator and as moral source. The first gives him comparatively little trouble (his argument seems watertight, though no more or less so than A. J. Ayer's rebuttal of it printed in the programme), but the second causes him real frustration.

He can dispose of semantic obstacles, such as the confusing use of the word 'good' in both ethical and aesthetic judgments, but this is just cape-work: immensely adroit and amusing cape-work, Mr Stoppard being the writer he is and George the beneficiary of the fact. But to bring off the kill, George has, in strictly moral terms, to answer his own question, 'what is so good about good?' and he can never quite find the right words, though he convinces us that they must somewhere exist. He does, however, find the right cry, even if it costs him a hare and a tortoise.

Michael Hordern, repeating his original and definitive performance, finds the passion as well as the oddity in George; his attempts to articulate his faith are rather moving. Elsewhere he prepares his speech in a series of beaming spurts, taking brief self-hugging trips around the stage whenever inspiration strikes, rounding off his sentences with a triumphant nasal swoop--vocal italics--whenever he wishes, by pointing a contemporary metaphor to rout the forces of trendiness on their own ground.

Leading these forces is Archie, vice-chancellor of George's university, for whom attempts to arrive at the roots of morality have little significance. Incidentally a man of means, he is primarily a man of ends, and ruthless in attaining them. His interests are wide; to please him, philosophers are athletes.

George, of course, is out of step on both counts. George is a duffer, Archie is omnipotent, and the play foresees a government of Archies. (Though the spirit of the work is joyous and funny, its import is black.) Mr Stoppard seems happier, though, with failure than success; I have seen two good actors play Archie (Graham Crowden last time, Julian Glover this) and they both came out wooden.

Between the two men is Dotty, an ex-musical comedy star who broke down when man reached the moon, thereby outdating most of her repertoire and other human values besides. This conceit has always seemed the least plausible thing in the play; the kind of violence and selfishness adduced long antedate space travel and Dotty's collapse seems arbitrary.

Julie Covington gets more conviction into it than I had hoped; she is disturbed where Diana Rigg was dizzy, with no loss of wit and with a great gain in singing. (Dotty's kind of star, by the way, has hardly existed in Britain since the 1940s.) One sensitive piece of rewriting brings her a fraction nearer to George (wishing him good luck with his speech) than before; the play seems more hopeful for the addition.

There are many other convolutions. If the form of the play is eccentric--a stretched monologue balancing a compressed plot--it is still effective, and the jokes, which bind the structure, are irresistible. The author, having discovered philosophy himself, makes us an exuberant present of it and the pleasure is contagious.

Peter Wood's production has expanded, literally and metaphorically, to fill the Lyttelton stage to the best advantage yet; the final scene incorporates a song and dance around Miss Covington which looks like a parody of the closing number in A Chorus Line--or perhaps like the object of which that number is itself a parody. The tune is 'Sentimental Journey.' Mr Stoppard stands out among contemporary playwrights for his generosity and acumen in giving us something to hum on our way home.

* * *

Two other comedies this week incorporate familiar songs in the gaps between scenes. In David Storey's Mother's Day (Royal Court) they are meant for whimsical comments on the action, though the connection becomes increasingly tangential as the evening proceeds, a symptom of growing desperation all round. The typical menage of Mr Storey's plays--embittered mothers, embattled fathers, and children in all varieties of peculiarity--have long hovered on the brink of farce, and it was sensible enough to push them over.

Now, too, Mr Storey can gaily expend all the narrative resources he has been withholding over the years; the play is never actually boring. But it is very effortful; as if the author had heard about farce and had set out to do right by it, but lacked the spirit. He employs Ortonesque shock tactics but turns them into running gags; and the two devices defeat each other.

Mother has bred a daughter whom she always addresses as 'liar' and keeps in a cupboard, and a son who elaborately rapes every woman he meets, and two other siblings who marry each other. Greed is heavily featured and there is probably an implicit moral about all families being like this. Betty Marsden manages one brilliant double-take, Jane Carr does her usual plump and proper schoolgirl dissolving in pleasure, Alun Armstrong has a dainty lour, and David Rydall (once of Jumpers) adds a touch of smouldering class. There is some awkwardness in Robert Kidd's production, but nothing really inexcusable.

* * *

The holes in Same Time Next Year (Prince of Wales) are filled by music typical of the period 1951-76, over which span a couple spend annual adulterous weekends. We witness six and see a strong if specialised kind of love developing.

The first half I found coy and irritating, stuffed with wisecracks that belonged not to the characters but to the author, Bernard Slade, and more particularly to his Broadway audience. Thereafter he is less indulgent, more observant; the fads and causes of the last decade pass before us, and if they are not very deeply considered that is probably true to the part they played in most people's lives.

You do not really have to believe in the relationship; it has been contrived as a theatrical means of keeping tabs on the participants, and in the woman's case at least the evidence mounts interestingly up; a shy starter, she develops in a rush and formidably. The curve is beautifully plotted by Frances Cuka, plumply convincing at every age. Michael Crawford takes on a slim distinction at about 40; but until then he gives a piping, laboured performance. Since they always meet in the same hotel room (which, they are careful to point out, never changes) and since no one else appears, the outgoings on this show must be minimal. The incomings are expected to be colossal.

records.title: The naked and the bed
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The naked and the bed

Robert Cushman in London and Stratford

THE title Carte Blanche, which might well have been bestowed on a musical version of A Streetcar Named Desire, is affixed instead at the Phoenix to a new revue, the long-delayed successor to Oh! Calcutta!

Revue is a form that has fallen into disuse in the past 15 years; its skills have rusted, and the rust is all over Carte Blanche. The endings of most of the sketches are visible some way in advance, and the foreknowledge is not as a rule encouraging. The strongest card of revue has always been diversity; but though this show employs a formidable muster of writers--from Paul Verlaine down to Molly Parkin--it confines them to a single subject. That the subject happens to be sex cannot in itself prevent monotony.

Nor is there the compensating virtue of a consistent point of view: each writer gets through as best he can, like a panel-game contestant requested to fill a given time on a given topic. Unthinking hedonist propaganda the show is certainly not; some of the numbers are very black. One of the more effective depicts the female body as a toothless, eyeless cadaver primped up to fool the eternally gullible male. Another concerns a geriatric orgy, and might theoretically earn marks for bravery, the sexual needs of the old being a subject we are generally reluctant to consider. The trouble is that the author shares our reluctance; treating his characters as zombies, he comes up with the feeblest item in the show.

Elsewhere sex is shown as something rather laughable and degrading, indulged in by the upper classes and showing them to be no better than the rest of us. It is never shown to involve affection, or indeed much emotion of any kind. Its dramatic possibilities are thus severely limited.

Flesh and blood actors on a stage have limited potential as fantasy material; they and their medium are so specific. The odds against seeing someone you fancy doing something you fancy are pretty heavy. It happened to me in Carte Blanche only once; in refusing further details I imitate the reticence of the authors who take no credit for particular scenes. I was also touched by one scene (a lesbian seduction blushingly narrated by Jean Warren in the best performance of the evening), amused by a couple of the jokes, and dazzled by some of the lighting effects--particularly the patterns projected on to the actors' bodies in the opening sequence.

Sado-masochism is in, homosexuality, despite the advance publicity, is not much emphasised except as an ingredient in threesomes, which are dwelt on frequently enough to suggest evangelism; Troilist and Crusader, perhaps. The hearty humours of Oh! Calcutta! have been left behind, but the new landscape has not been very clearly charted. In selecting material, Kenneth Tynan must have lowered his critical standards considerably; and neither the staging nor most of the performers reflect much credit on Clifford Williams's direction.

* * *

I drag in Mr Williams unfairly at the end to serve as a bridge. His celebrated Stratford staging of The Comedy of Errors has finally been replaced, but is still worth remembering, most of all perhaps for the maniac fervour with which Diana Rigg as the jealous Adriana berated her supposed husband (Alec McCowen) to be greeted, after 50 passionate lines or so, by the puzzled inquiry, 'speak you to me, fair dame?' In Trevor Nunn's new production at Stratford, Judi Dench preserves the intensity and Roger Rees the bewilderment and the scene is nearly as funny as ever. But while in Mr Williams's production it was one of a steady stream of laughs emanating from the text, in Mr Nunn's it is comparatively isolated.

Mr Nunn has turned the play into a half-cock musical; individual lines balloon into songs and dances after which we return to find the play exactly where we left it--except that we cannot quite remember where that was. With a story as intricate as this one that is fatal, and by the end I had lost interest; if the play were to work as a musical it would need a more ruthless adaptation, and a more distinctive score than Guy Woolfenden has provided. (Under the title The Boys from Syracuse, it has in the past received both.)

Many of the performances are pleasurable, and made more so by our awareness that this is the famous RSC letting its hair down. (The evening indeed depends on this knowledge.) Michael Williams as one Dromio is a virtuoso gagman, and Nickolas Grace as the other a fair singing-and-leaping match for him. Mike Gwilym makes a long piece of plotting into a farcical-forensic showpiece and Francesca Annis's Luciana is charmingly myopic. Richard Griffiths, an accident-prone Officer, is both the victim and the beneficiary of much invention. But the effects are not cumulative, and festive song and handshakes all round at the close--recalling other productions in and out of Stratford--are no compensation.

Meanwhile the RSC company continues to triumph at Stratford's Other Place, where David Edgar's Destiny is a wide-ranging examination of the far Right in Britain now. It begins simply, with the independence of India, whose returning British troops furnish Mr Edgar with many of his main characters; and it ends simplistically. But what comes between is astonishingly complex; no play of this generation has had so powerful a sense of the criss-crossing of ideologies. 'Drop the wog-bashing and it could be Tribune,' complains a National Socialist of the manifesto drawn up by a National Socialist.

The man for whom they have least time is the local Conservative, whose Labour opponent is brought by his wife to realise that racism cannot be laughed away; it exists in unfanatical British minds. A Left activist looks at a Right, and reports that it was like looking in a mirror. The spirit, and the peculiar passion, of the play are crystallised by an old officer who speaks of the terrible moment 'when you realise you have more regard for your enemies than those you view as friends.'

This speech, which is nearly crushed by tears, is the crown of a superb ramrod-spirited performance by Michael Pennington. Bob Peck as a Fascist visionary and Ian McDiarmid as a Fascist dupe add to their already remarkable records. Ron Daniels's production gives sharp and solid reality to a script short on human detail and even sometimes on narrative, but brilliantly adept in scenes of debate, manipulation and intellectual shock.

* * *

There is something of the same excitement in Joint Stock's Light Shining in Buckinghamshire (Theatre Upstairs). Caryl Churchill has delved into seventeenth-century records to uncover a revolution crushed almost at the birth of the middle-class. Her subjects are the extremist sects--Diggers, Levellers, Ranters--suppressed by the Cromwell, whose victory they had helped to win. As a set-piece we have the Putney Debate with Cromwell (played fairly and very squarely by Colin McCormack) listening, not unsympathetically, merely uncomprehendingly, to their suggestions and demands. (Can he believe his ears? Do they really want votes?)

Miss Churchill's linking-passages are a bit strained, so that one's thoughts turn to such matters as the decline in colloquial speech over three centuries, but she illuminates both the nature of Puritanism (restraint twin-brother to licence) and the irregular jumping course of history.

records.title: In triumph
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
In triumph

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the opening of the Olivier Theatre

WE are owed three National Theatres and last week, after much bilking, the second and largest instalment of the debt was redeemed. The Olivier Theatre opened in grand style.

I mean that quite literally; few playwrights have cultivated grandeur as assiduously as Marlowe in Tamburlaine the Great. Since it is written in two parts (here performed together in a trifling four and a half hours) and covers a deal of time and space, it qualifies in our usual loose definition as an epic. But it will satisfy sterner criteria as well; it is as close to Homer as to Hollywood.

It is an inordinately regal play. Tamburlaine's great celebration of ambition has its climax, 'The sweet fruition of an earthly crown,' and Marlowe's dramaturgy shows how far he endorsed his hero's sentiments. To be allowed a speech of any length in this play it is necessary to be a king, or at the least a captive princess. The only character allowed to break this rule is Tamburlaine himself, who, in his earliest days as a Scythian bandit, reels off a couple of arias which win him, at two blows, a fiancee and a lieutenant-in-chief.

Plainly, if Marlovian decorum is to be kept, such a man is born to be king, and so it proves. Reaching the Persian throne at the end of Act Two, he remains there until the penultimate speech of Act Ten. (Two parts, remember.) All that stands between him and the play's last words is death, the only comer he cannot defeat.

The intervening action has shown him defeating all other challengers. He is particularly successful against the Turks, whose Emperor, Bajazeth, he captures and humiliates in Part One. In Part Two his main opponent is Bajazeth's son, Callapine, who continually escapes him, though leaving behind a train of tormented allies.

Bajazeth is starved, climbed over (literally) and kept in a cage, against whose bars he finally brains himself. This shows us Tamburlaine in a comparatively genial mood, like a schoolboy realising his wildest bullying dreams. In Part Two a certain sourness sets in; when the captive kings he has harnessed to his chariot prove unable to draw him more than 20 miles a day he sounds genuinely disappointed in them: disappointed, too, that the game is proving less fun than it promised to be.

Marlowe was 23 when he wrote the play, and English drama comparably young; at a later stage of development such enthusiastic cruelty would be intolerable. Here it is seductive; the play draws you into Tamburlaine's ruthlessness, makes you one with it. You find yourself hoping that he will remain invincible: you do not want so perfect a pattern of victory to be spoiled.

You do not even want him to be merciful, and spare those he has threatened with destruction; if he did that he would break his word and Tamburlaine is pre-eminently truthful. His main complaint against Bajazeth is that 'Turks are full of brags and menace more than they can well perform.' Tamburlaine performs all that he menaces; you might even call him chivalrous, since he never strikes without warning. Indeed, if his adversaries would only listen to him and surrender or go home we could go home too; there would be no play.

Only two things can halt Tamburlaine: love and death. Both are once-in-a-lifetime experiences (since as regards the one he is that kind of guy and as regards the other we all are), so the course of most of the play is even, almost soothing. The spaciousness of the full text wards off the tedium that an abridged version, with the incidents jumping upon one another's backs, might produce.

The main acting-area of the Olivier is a wide ring crowned by a circular lighting-grid; the audience sit in an arc. Peter Hall has grouped his actors to reflect these patterns; though there are 51 names in the cast, the stage is never crowded until the curtain-call. Ranks of golden mannequins represent armies, waiting in the background while their generals harangue one another.

The staging is fluent, logical and very simple; the set, a huge pair of dark sliding doors, with deep vistas behind. Battles are represented by percussive music and widening red spotlights; red takes over as the evening progresses and throats are graphically cut. Actors unexpectedly involve the audience: 'and so would you, my masters, would you not,' says Tamburlaine to us of his desire to be king, though in the text he might be addressing his followers.

Marlowe's drama, says Mr Hall, stems from the morality tradition: hence the stylisation. I wonder, though, if Marlowe thought of it as stylisation, or if he thought of it at all; it may have been his notion of naturalism. I imagine he wanted his horrors rough and hearty; here the carthorse-kings (including the saintly Robert Eddison) are given crowns of thorns and devotional poses. But I do not think you can make Tamburlaine, or Marlowe himself, into Antichrist.

Marlowe's recorded views on Jesus are similar to Jens Thorsen's, but his plays are surprisingly orthodox; his attitude may have been dislike rather than disbelief. There is a faithless Christian in Tamburlaine, but he is punished and Christ is accorded the credit. Tamburlaine is partial to Christians and implacable against the Turks who persecute them. Himself a Muhammadan, he finally rejects his prophet for 'The God that sits in heaven, if any god. For he is God alone and none but he.'

I don't want to push it; Marlowe is capable of expressing any number of views, and barely bothers to reconcile them. When he is not partaking in Tamburlaine's sadism, he can let other characters condemn it in unobjectionable compassionate terms before returning with added relish. One character--Tamburlaine's bride--gives voice to both feelings indiscriminately; Susan Fleetwood tries hard for consistency, but it is wasted effort.

Albert Finney brilliantly encompasses the gamester in Tamburlaine, the blazing eyes and more blazing cheek, takes full advantage of the brief, friendly descents into prose and drives resourcefully through hundreds of end-stopped iambics; only as the hundreds mount into thousands does his grip slacken. Love and death defeat him, too, both agony and ecstasy eluding him. He is a springy, earthbound performance, but I do not know who could better it.

Once again he is matched against Denis Quilley, who doubled Claudius and the Ghost in Hamlet, and is now, as Bajazeth and Callapine, again his own relation. He rides the verse finely, but is miscast: too likeable, for all his booming, for the old Turk and too old for the young one. If Callapine is Tamburlaine's contemporary, the tension of their relationship vanishes; Marlowe was better at relationships than Mr Hall will allow.

Barbara Jefford goes mad in a split second, the right way to do it; Philip Locke gets every sympathy for the King of Persia, a rational coward. Six Virgins of Damascus in Part One are Turkish Concubines in Part Two: the way of all flesh.

Tamburlaine, true to form, has annihilated the week's opposition. Romeo and Juliet (Shaw) was, at the preview I attended, unusually bad, except for the fights, the skeletons in the churchyard, and some stabbing moments from Angela Pleasence. Yahoo (Queen's), a Swift biography-anthology?, offers Alec Guinness on his knees as the King of Lilliput for a blissful couple of minutes, fear popping in his eyes and indignation crinkling in his lips; but erect for a good deal longer and as blandly Hibernian as Bing Crosby singing 'Galway Bay.' Best of the bunch is Scribes (Greenwich) by Barrie Keeffe, a naturalistic piece about a newspaper before, during and after a strike; in the way of soap-opera, it grows on you and is jauntily acted.

records.title: Feydeau's potty farce
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Feydeau's potty farce

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

I APPROACHED The Frontiers of Farce (Old Vic) as one approaches frontiers generally, with trepidation. The title conceals a double-bill and a programme note. On the bill are a Feydeau and a Wedekind; they have been adapted and directed by Peter Barnes, and the note is by Barnes as well. Its tone is earnestly pugnacious, its import that farce, in the hands of a few masters, may be an instrument for scourging the bourgeoisie--or, failing their availability, the theatre audience.

In his own plays, The Ruling Class and The Bewitched, Mr Barnes has tried to use it for such an end and has tried too hard. But he has performed valuable ambassadorial work on behalf of the dead. His adaptation of Jonson's The Devil Is an Ass (now at Birmingham) is one example; his current offering is two more. Or at least, one and a half more.

The Purging is among the one-act pieces which rescued Feydeau's career. To my surprise, it justifies the claims Mr Barnes makes for it; it is hilarious, which might be expected, and it is uncompromising, which might not. In fact it restores a faith in Feydeau which a succession of swirling, over-decorated productions of his full-length plays had virtually destroyed. Michael Annals's set looks as if someone had gone over the customary art-nouveau decor with paint-stripper, leaving only the accustomed drawing-room shape intact. The dramatic structure has been similarly streamlined, though at least one familiar device remains; thirsty or desperate characters grab the nearest fluid, which invariably turns out to be a particularly disgusting medicine.

In this case, it is a laxative; Follavoine fils is constipated and Follavoine pere finds his working-day disturbed by the demands of Follavoine mere that daddy should make baby take his physic. Since the job Follavoine has on hand involves the sale of a huge consignment of chamber-pots, it will be seen that the piece possesses an unquestionable unity of tone. The flight to the bedroom is replaced by the flight to the lavatory; the Palais Royal meets the excremental vision.

The two modes unite in the performance of Leonard Rossiter, which is uninhibited in style and totally controlled in technique. He is the mercantile spirit made flesh, consumed with avarice and corseted by respectability; he and his wife (Dilys Laye in curl-papers and a terrible temper) alternate the roles of bully and victim, in a subtler version of marriage than Feydeau usually gives us; they might be prototypes of Mr and Mrs Basil Fawlty, and Mr Rossiter's rage, like a supply of supposedly unbreakable porcelain smashed to smithereens in an impromptu scientific test, is in a class with John Cleese's: inspired vaudeville which never ceases to be drama.

* * *

He goes even more picturesquely berserk in the Wedekind piece, The Singer, as a composer in the finest musical frenzy since Jimmy Durante's on the day he found the lost chord. But with this piece Mr Barnes's enthusiasm has overreached itself; the Feydeau may stand on the frontiers of farce, but Wedekind is outside the territory altogether. One or two ladies are hidden in a hotel-room and there is an unexpected death, but the substance of the piece is not action but argument: the plea of an idolised operatic tenor that art in general and his in particular is overrated by the fans, nice though it is to have the adulation and the money.

The role might benefit from a more extravagant performance than it gets from the steady and sensible John Stride, but Wedekind hammers some obvious points and Mr Barnes, who can be as uncritical of his idols as any opera-fancier, seems more than ready to indulge him. This is a piece to be collected; its predecessor (in which John Phillips is a model of affronted dignity) is to be relished.

* * *

So is The Circle, which has come from Chichester to the Haymarket. It seems, behind that chocolate-box proscenium, more conventional than before; but Maugham's involvement with the society he criticises has its own satisfying irony. This is very much a social play; there is one character whose sole function is to make a fourth at bridge.

The acting is among the best in the West End, though both the leading ladies are a shade defensive; Googie Withers is emphatically aware of her laugh-lines and Susan Hampshire switches on her smile within two seconds of her entrance. The men are unassailable: Bill Fraser's chuntering reveals all the regrets that folding flesh is heir to, Clive Francis is touchingly brash, John McCallum shows us a smugly witty raisonneur hoist with his own petard, and Martin Jarvis, bringing a beautiful style to insensitivity, is an apt son for him. Mr Jarvis plays Miss Hampshire's husband, and those who once wept at their failure to get together in The Forsyte Saga may now take heart. It would never have worked.

* * *

The Royal Shakespeare Company's detente season at the Aldwych has so far shown America (The Iceman Cometh, The Devil's Disciple) to be a more entertaining dramatic locale than Russia (The Zykovs, Ivanov). Terry Hands's production of Aleksi Arbuzov's Old World leaves the score unaltered, though it is a superior piece of staging, evoking the world of a sanatorium with great wrought-iron gates and looming models standing in for a supporting cast. These embellishments almost persuade you that something is going on, but the impression does not survive the interval.

There was an old lady from Riga; or at least an old lady from Moscow who came to an establishment in Riga and proceeded to entrap the director. Their relationship proceeds at unremarkable length; she recalls her past as a circus performer demoted to the box-office, he recalls his dead wife. At one point they dance the Charleston, and since they happen to be Peggy Ashcroft and Anthony Quayle and we are not accustomed to seeing them in such circumstances, they bring the house down.

This attack of the cutes outdoes anything in the much-scorned Same Time Next Year and the play does not offer nearly as many compensations; the sugar-content of the final scene exceeds anything on Broadway. There is nothing to quarrel with in the performances except the waste involved.

* * *

Far more worthwhile is Colin Bennett's Soon (Bush), an array of 20 or so scenes prophesying triumph or apocalypse, depending which side you are on. Which side the author is on is not clear; he appears very hung-up on hatred and even more so on mysticism. The base of the play is the successful attempts of some women prisoners to shake the walls by choral thinking. Characters are apt to express hostility not just to the present system but to all civilisation since the Greeks. A girl arguing against violence gets less sympathy than anyone else on stage, but it is notable that no-one ever gets round to countering her arguments.

At the heart of the play is one man's subversive attempt to throw money into Wimpy bars or fried chicken parlours (the mythology is confused) without taking any food in exchange. The wit of this goes beyond the general mood of starry-eyed desperation and Nick Edmett's wild-eyed exploitation of the audience's proximity makes his performance literally the most challenging I have seen.

records.title: Putting Daddy in the dock
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: An' Me Wi' A Bad Leg Tae
records.body:
Putting Daddy in the dock

by Robert Cushman

THE leading character of Denis Cannan's Dear Daddy (Ambassadors) is not always affectionately addressed as the title might suggest. Three of the cast are his children and they seem uneasy about what to call him. They seem uneasy about him altogether, and he knows it. His impulse is to blame it on them, or on youth generally. 'It's a sad generation that doesn't know what to call its parents' is his phrase for it.

He has a phrase for everything. His name is Bernard, and he is very verbal. In one of his aspects he bears out Howard Brenton's claim that the West End is the theatre of envy. I was certainly jealous of Bernard's collection of books; the towering shelves were enough to get me going. They dominate a set which bears witness to good things having come Bernard's way in the past.

Recently, though, they have stopped coming; and envy drops dead at the foot of the library steps. His brood, now in their twenties, have come to sign over to him money that was being kept in trust for them. Filial duty done, they spend the rest of the play remembering, in a long crescendo of bitterness, the details of life with father. Mother drops in to help them; she is Bernard's first wife, who was drying out at a nearby health-farm and just happened to be passing. (Mr Cannan is a bit cavalier about mustering his forces; the action presupposes an ever-open front door.)

All together they accuse him of surpassing, patronising selfishness; of subduing their personalities to his own, of always being ready to crush them with a quotation, of taking from them and never giving. Ex-wife claims that he laughed her out of her own career in children's publishing; present wife, who at first seems wholesomely inclined to avoid the battle, confirms that he has done the same to her talent for making clothes: 'It's known as "My sewing!"' As for the children, Charles, the youngest, a trainee teacher, is comparatively gentle but owes his survival to a girl-friend who is, by the family's standards, hopelessly unsophisticated; nothing exposes them more than their efforts to be friendly to her and Charles himself is shaping up to be as exploitative as his father. Brother Billy is a nondescript drop-out, Daddy's favourite butt; sister Gillian, who attracts and dispenses more venom than anyone else on stage, is an espouser of causes, and a ferocious victim, sexual and social, making more money as a typist than she ever could with her degree. (It could be the theme-song of a generation: women who are making it without men: divorcees, widows, unmarried mothers, etc.)

* * *

There is a poignant wedding of theatre to title: An' Me Wi' A Bad Leg Tae at the Theatre Upstairs. A Puerto Rican girl in A Chorus Line refused to change her name 'because I figured ethnic was in.' In response to Billy Connolly's first play, she figured wrong.

Mr Connolly is among the nakedest emperors to ride into London for some time. A soldier bound for Germany returns to the family hearth in Glasgow, and sets off some sub-O'Casey rowing, philosophising, boozing and raging, leading a clansman to a dead end, punctuated by spotlit monologues as a guarantee of seriousness. There is a rich and subtle portrait of a drunk by Bill Paterson, whose complexion sets you thinking of rubies or beetroot, and some good old jokes: 'I fought with Monty.' 'You could never get on with anyone.' There is even the one in which X says that he didn't come here to be insulted and Y replies as Y has immemorially replied. The innocent delight of most of the Press seems the innocentest thing on view.

* * *

Frank Dunlop's production of Antony and Cleopatra (Young Vic) is vigorous and fast. Delphine Seyrig's Cleopatra is vigorous and intelligent. Michael Graham Cox's Antony is vigorous. You will gather that all this, though welcome, is insufficient. Except in one scene, the soldiers' litany as Hercules, fares so well, the play is denied its wonder, hence its grandeur, hence its breadth, hence finally its point.

* * *

That a comedian as gifted as Ron Moody should have failed, for 15 years, to find himself a viable vehicle suggests a certain self-destructiveness. On the evidence of The Showman (Theatre Royal, Stratford) his fault may be excessive diffidence. In this musical of The Bells Mr Moody plays not the tormented villain Mathias, but the purely ancillary role of the hypnotist; his elaborate routines confuse the issue but cannot, unfortunately, stop the show. The score confirms that musical merit has nothing to do with memorability; though I fled at the interval two tunes pursued me pitilessly. Perhaps I should have stayed, but as Mr Moody said after a particularly strenuous exhibition of goodwill, Qu'est-ce que vous voulez, blood?

records.title: National disappointment
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
National disappointment

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Goldoni at the Olivier Theatre.

THE Venetian Carlo Goldoni, Italy's most celebrated comic playwright, is high on the list of neglected writers whom critics like myself are constantly nagging the National Theatre to resurrect. This week, at the Olivier, they obliged us, in theory at least; in practice they annoyed us considerably. Il Campiello ('The Public Square') is as faint an evening's entertainment as this company can ever have offered.

Goldoni's career began in the mid-eighteenth century when Italian theatre was dominated by the stereotypes of the commedia dell'arte; his first success came in persuading its performers to act his texts instead of their own improvisations. Later he broke further out by discarding stock characters and plots and writing about his own society. Even by our own standards Il Campiello is unconventional, jettisoning narrative and character in favour of community and locale.

Dramatic interest is equally split among nine people who live on three sides of the square. (Who or what lies behind the fourth wall we never discover.) Three old widows and four youngsters play games, quarrel, rampage, enjoy themselves; at the end one boy and girl are married and another couple betrothed. A more sedate young lady and her bearish guardian make up the number; she considers herself a few notches above her neighbours, and he cannot stand any of them. He comes from Naples, and this seems to involve a class as well as a territorial difference, reinforced by the arrival of a Neapolitan count who seems remarkably well pleased by just about everyone.

Bill Bryden's production attempts a miniature re-enactment of Goldoni's own progress. There are puppet-shows in the foyer and a carnival procession through the stalls as the lights go down, corresponding to the commedia inheritance that Goldoni never thoroughly abandoned. Then flats are erected round the stage, representing the houses in the square and the play, more or less realistic, begins. The trouble is that both styles seem half-hearted; the cavorting in the audience is more noisy than vital, and there is more volume than energy about the main action as well.
