records.title: Loose lady in the dock
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Loose lady in the dock

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN ranges from Rattigan to Shakespeare.

Terence Rattigan's Cause Célèbre (Her Majesty's) is by way of being a triumph for the traditional West End play. I say "by way of being," since, though the Rattigan vessel sails securely enough into port at the end of the evening, its early passage is pretty rough. There are even moments when it looks like capsizing.

The weaknesses which, with a becoming sorrow, I noted down en route divide in retrospect into two categories: those which turn out to be strengths in crafty disguise and those which just lie there helpless.

To take the latter first: Rattigan's heroine is Alma Rattenbury, a suspected murderess of the 1930s, whose feckless bewildered charm melts even those most prejudiced against her; I wish Rattigan had found some other means of making this point than providing her with a stony-faced wardress who draws sentimental sighs from the audience when she consents to address the prisoner by her first name, and is her devoted friend thereafter.

Then there is the matter of Edith and her circle. Edith, I should explain, is forewoman of the jury at Alma's trial and her story is told in tandem with Alma's. Alma lives in Bournemouth, Rattigan's cockpit of gentility (cf. Separate Tables); Edith wants to move there now that she has rid herself of her husband. Ridding herself of her husband - by bashing him on the head or getting her teenage lover to do so - is what Alma is being had up for; Edith has merely divorced hers for infidelity. Alma, the loosest of loose women, is everything that Edith, upright and uptight, most abominates. Edith's thin-blooded upper-middle circumstances are the kind with which young playwrights today are likeliest to come unstuck; it is a shock to find Rattigan too resorting, probably unawares, to caricature. "Jury service ... my dear, how too frightful," says Edith's confidante as the plot gets under way. "He was only about 40 when, you started ... having headaches," she goes on apropos Edith's old man. Edith picks up the Significant Pause habit, while laying her soul conveniently bare: "I never did care much for that ... side of things."

But we are already on the verge of the play's deceptive faults and actual successes. The juxtaposition of the two protagonists comes in the end to something very impressive; both are brought unsparingly to a desperation which seems inevitable rather than just a playwright's whim. Though Rattigan seems at times to be putting his leading actresses through some fatiguing hoops, he makes it worth their while, and they respond in kind. Edith's son, aroused by the newspaper accounts of Alma, goes out to get laid and contracts VD; this gives Helen Lindsay the opportunity to play a minor Mrs Alving and she rises steadily from there. Alma, passionate and bedraggled, is ideally served by the butterfly vulnerability of Glynis Johns. On a more relaxing level there is a showcase role for a KC (descended from the one in The Winslow Boy), with holes in his socks and invincible courtroom command: Kenneth Griffith, heading a covey of television notables, plays him with the right Rattigan blend of sensitivity and shamelessness.

The trial scene, by the way, makes great use of flashback; this would seem to be a disastrous idea, fatal to the infallible tensions of the courtroom. In fact it makes the play, providing scenes that are not only gripping in themselves but propel the characters forward to the point where each must jettison her most cherished image of herself. Rattigan's celebrated technical mastery usually leaves me cold; here it knocked me out. This is certainly the best of his recent plays; it may be the best of them all.

* * *

And so we leave the commercial theatre, remarking only that Lonsdale's On Approval is back yet again - at the Vaudeville - and that Kenneth More and Patricia Routledge are too mild a pair of holy terrors to dissuade us from heeding the play's title and sending it back to the management with a curt note.

Meanwhile, at the Open Space, E. A. Whitehead's long-awaited Mecca proves a disappointment, an "is that all?" kind of play. Like Cause Célèbre, it is a schematic piece with an unobjectionable moral about tolerance and hypocrisy, particularly sexual; the difference is that Mr Whitehead's characters never transcend their frame. They are brought to a pretty pass, rather than a transfixingly ugly one.

Six British holiday-makers (two couples, two singles) are at a holiday-camp in Morocco, protected from the natives by barbed wire and broken glass; one girl strays outside and is raped. Her compatriots turn on a native boy they think responsible and beat him to death. Their very smooth Moroccan courier eventually agrees to fly them safely out, at a stiff price; soon, he says icily, Morocco will reach their dubious standard of civilisation, but they should stay away till then. As if to bear him out, the muezzin sounds, reminding us that some people still have standards.

Earlier we have seen our tourists drink cheap red wine and eat oranges, wince at Moroccan poverty, quarrel over their own various degrees of permissiveness, make variously successful passes at one another. Most of the author's bile is reserved for a childless career-woman. Played by Judy Cornwell, who was one of Mr Whitehead's Old Flames, she takes respectable feminist arguments, brandishes and degrades them, tearing apart an unsatisfactory lover and reacting to the report of rape with the self-righteousness of a lynch-mob. The dialogue, well-tempered in Jonathan Hales's production, flows with malignant ease, but none of the people are more than attitudes and some - notably Miss Cornwell's homosexual husband - are less.

* * *

I suspect that while rehearsing The Alchemist Trevor Nunn actually found the philosopher's stone. If King Lear at the Aldwych was an improvement on its Stratford self, Romeo and Juliet is a transmutation. I never thought to be so moved by this play: by the reconciliation at the end (with the stilling of John Woodvine's raging Capulet) as well as by the lovers. Francesca Annis plays the potion scene with terrifying immediacy, as she plays her love-passages with enchanting immediacy. The balcony scene, as she and Ian McKellen act it, is funny as well as magical; hyperbole made flesh.

This is a great production, partly because it is so abundantly witty; the play is as conceited as its contemporary Love's Labour's Lost. So Michael Pennington's Queen Mab speech is mockery and celebration at once, and this whole performance brilliantly blends Mercutio's loneliness and camaraderie. The stage is crammed with meaning, in relationships and in individual performances (Miss Annis fairly oozes with it). It extends to the clown, Peter Richard Griffiths, with his Bottom, has come to full comic mastery. He is a walking slow-burn.

Bow Down (Cottesloe) must leave in the main to Peter Heyworth, merely congratulating Tony Harrison on bringing a beautiful macabre poem to our attention and skilfully exploiting its variants, and Harrison Birtwistle on his most supportively dramatic score: to date, Walter Donohue's production is both witty and scary, though inclining to artiness when all else fails. Actors and musicians share responsibilities and look very intense about it; we should inform them that the same thing is being done very light-heartedly on Broadway in I Love My Wife.

records.title: Mabel's back in town
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Mabel's back in town

ROBERT CUSHMAN meets a great supper-club singer.

MABEL MERCER, who is to popular singing what Elisabeth Schwarzkopf is to lieder, is in London until the end of the month, singing in a newly opened room at the Playboy Club. I should warn or reassure you though that there is no singer in the world who sounds less a vocalising bunny than Miss Mercer.

She is, to begin with, one of those comfortable people (Fred Astaire is another) who, having been born in 1900, are as old as the century. Then, too, she is richly cosmopolitan; her career gathered momentum in Paris, peaked and consolidated in New York, but she was born and grew up in England. (Her father, though, was black American.) North-country vowels come through in her conversation if not in her singing. They have been reasserting themselves, she says, since she has been back in Britain.

This is the first time she has been here since 1938. Just before that she went to New York for a short engagement and found that the war prevented her return to Europe. So a brief trip was extended almost to infinity. Ironically the lady from the old world became the paragon and the prototype of American supper-club singers.

The supper-club was described by Whitney Balliett, jazz critic of the New Yorker, as "that royal relative of the night-club" and ideally should combine elegance and intimacy; the second is indispensable. It has never taken root here, and even in New York it came close to dying out in the sixties. Recently there has been a small revival, and the New York entertainment listings are themselves again.

Show-songs (generally the unhackneyed ones) are the essence of their repertoire; a singer usually begins by plunging through the catalogues, then as years pass refines the list down to the songs which -- through her choice or that of her public -- have accumulated around her and will not be dislodged. The programme I heard Mabel sing at the Playboy on Tuesday was almost identical to one I heard her offer in a plush New York hotel two years ago -- including Porter, Coward, Rodgers and Hart. Many of the songs she had recorded during a spate of LP activity in the fifties. They still sound fresh; her tone and her bearing acknowledge them to be classics, but no performance is jaded.

She calls them "songs of sentiment," and the sentiments tend to be concern and regret rather than passion -- although she is able to infuse passion into them. Her version of "Send in the Clowns" almost sums up her art; the recurring title-phrase is treated differently each time it comes round; it begins nonchalant and ends up fierce. She also insists, more firmly than any other singer, on this song as a waltz: a rhythm to which she is peculiarly sensitive. She reiterates that she is not a jazz singer; certainly she has none of the trappings, but her sense of time and of beat, though never thundered forth, is infallible.

A sleeve-note once described her as a "one-woman faculty" for American popular singing. She herself is sceptical. "I've often wondered about this. All performers are very aware of other performers; we all learn from each other. I used to sing songs that weren't popular -- unusual songs -- and maybe that was the attraction."

We talked on Monday -- the day of her opening -- with the room still apparently being constructed around her, our conversation punctuated by the arrival of bouquets. The message on one of them read, "Love and welcome back from your old fan of Tony's days -- John Gielgud." Tony's was her first New York booking, and she stayed there for nine years.

Her next engagements were for seven and three years respectively. You knew where to find her, and this permanence she regards as the most important ingredient of her success. "I was a sort of link, generation to generation. I sneaked into everybody's family. It's a warm feeling."

People come and request songs with memories, and "when your voice cracks up on you, it doesn't matter."

The voice has not in fact cracked as much as some reports (including her own) would have it; yes, she talks portions of her songs, but she sings more, and still with power. Uniquely among singers she does not stand at a mike, jump around or even perch on a stool; she sits on a gilt chair. "I got to sitting down all the time when I found it made people more at ease." It also gives her great control; her hands, too, sing.

Her accompanist is a mellifluous gentlemanly pianist named Jimmy Lyon; they have worked together for seven years. (More permanence; one "piano-player" served her for 16 years.) Her earlier fans must have told their grandchildren; her audiences are surprisingly young. Every night someone at the Playboy is sure to call out "welcome back"; I wish to be associated with that sentiment.

records.title: Thrones, coffins and roses
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Thrones, coffins and roses

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the 'Henry' cycle at Stratford

THE three parts of Henry VI (Stratford upon Avon) might be subtitled 'War and Peace and War Again.' They take up the history of England where Henry V leaves off (the RSC has in fact remounted its successful production of that play).

Part one wraps up the Hundred Years War; the French conquests amassed by King Hal slip successively through the fingers of those of his relatives assigned to guard them. They blame their defeats on Joan of Arc and witchcraft, but occasional flashbacks to the home front clue us in to the real reason; the English nobles are becoming factious, i.e. they are hanging around the Temple Garden plucking white and red roses and picking up sides according to horticultural preference.

The occasional throne, coffin or, of course, rose bush is carried on or off Farrah's set as required, but for most of Terry Hands's production the stage is deep, bare and threatening.

Part Two is largely devoted to the gentler pursuits of court intrigue; this is the only section of the trilogy in which the actors get to stand still. Men still die, but in their beds: stabbed or smothered, usually. Mr Hands has staged this one on an ironically bright expanse of greensward, divided by a rope barrier. On one side King, Queen and courtiers perambulate; on the other the lower classes gawp.

As the evening proceeds they make their presence felt first as comic relief, then as the threatening embodiment of riot. After half time they swarm on to the field, uniting both roles in a fierce and bloody enactment of Jack Cade's rebellion. (Object: the abolition of privilege and literacy, not necessarily in that order.) But Cade is merely a front; behind him stands the Duke of York, equipped with a watertight if complicated claim to the Crown, and determined to enforce it. In the last scene of the play, the Wars of the Roses break out.

In Part Three we fade to black again. The action is almost continuous butchery, the stage barer than ever. The mortality rate is such that one actor dies twice before the cycle has reached its first interval, and only four characters go through all three plays: Henry VI himself, best described by Sellar and Yeatman as 'such a Good Man that he was thought to be a saint or alternatively -- especially by the barons -- an imbecile,' his termagant Queen Margaret, and their opponents York and Warwick.

The plays are the earliest Shakespeare and Part One the most primitive of all; no play in the English repertoire is as dependent on pure narrative drive, and the company swing it enthusiastically and infectiously. Many of them, however, seem too lightweight for Part Two, a more rewarding play but dependent on the clash of personality (as opposed to that more complex thing, character). In Part Three they begin, understandably, to get tired.

The last instalment, chiefly concerned with hacking its way through history, lacks definition. Nevertheless, as written, it contains three great scenes. First is the capture, humiliation and death of York at the hands of Margaret. This finds Helen Mirren at her best. She lacks the reserves for her pounding attacks on Henry (the most spectacularly henpecked husband in English drama), but her treatment of York is subtler, crueller, and Miss Mirren paces it with sexual relish. Emrys James, though luxuriantly sniffing at his white rose, presents York as a twisted dandy, a believable conspirator but no soldier, and unable to pour out his heart since he plainly has none.

Secondly, there is the battle of Towton, where Henry witnesses the reality of civil war: two soldiers of whom one has unwittingly killed his own father and the other his son. The scene is badly staged, but the trouble lies deeper; Mr Hands has given us an emblematic treatment of the surrounding action: if, say, the text reads 'Enter Northumberland,' then Northumberland enters, without military support. The commons, so active in Part Two, have vanished, leaving us no sense of the context from which the unfortunate homicides have sprung.

Finally comes Henry's confrontation with his spiritual opposite, the future Richard III. Their duet is classically influenced: Alan Howard's Scofield-tremolo versus the Olivier-yelp of Anton Lesser, a tense and springy newcomer.

Mr Howard's Henry is actually neither saint nor imbecile; he is not even a particularly Good Man, though he is certainly a very nice one. He is an innocent (Mr Howard has discovered a staggeringly virginal walk) who loses his illusions very quickly but gains all the time in intelligence. He can out-observe any man in the realm but he cannot act on his insights. He is recognisably his father's son (Mr Howard having now tilted his Agincourt routine as far towards introspection as is humanly possible, and maybe farther); but with a paralysing extra layer of sensitivity.

This is Mr Howard's best performance, and its final intensity is a perfectly believable trigger for Richard's rage. The murder done, we are plunged back to the newly established court of Richard's brother, Edward IV, who prophesies peace and orders that the royal band stop playing dreadful marches and switch to delightful measures. Unfortunately nobody in the palace knows the steps, and we end on a charmingly sardonic note -- or will, when Mr Hands has got the staging sorted out. For most of the three nights his invention hardly flags.

He has still, though, to get his company together. It has three elements: (a) such RSC trusties as the unshakably stalwart Jeffery Dench and such more recent recruits as Oliver Ford-Davies and Stephen Jenn; both developing finely; (b) experienced classicists from other stables, notably Julian Glover, a commonsense Warwick with moments of grandeur, and Graham Crowden, though his eccentric authority sits oddly on the sanest man at court; (c) actors from all over, and all ages, having a bash.

These last vary greatly, but the verse -- which is confoundedly regular -- often defeats them. I liked Jack Klaff's vacillating Clarence, Charlotte Cornwell's Joan, and as the fighting Talbots, fils et pere, Ian Gelder and David Swift. Alfred Lynch has a cheerful go at Edward, but is much better as a gentle chorus in Henry V; James Laurenson, looking like Geronimo, is a bloodcurdling Cade, but not very funny; the horror of his scenes is there, but not the music hall.

Interest in these plays is very recent; I, stripling as I am, have witnessed most of its twentieth-century stage history with my own eyes. As we entered the lists for Part One, the critic of the Sunday Times, after we had duly struck each other across the cheek with our red and white blooms, inquired if I had seen The Wars of the Roses, the Peter Hall-John Barton adaptation that made history in 1963. I had; and, magnificent though it was and fondly as I recall it, I now recognise that it planted RSC mannerisms that are only just disappearing. It did not just edit, it editorialised, flaunting ironies that are merely implicit in the original and encouraging a flamboyantly acting style still apparent in Mr James and occasionally in Mr Howard.

But before that came a Birmingham Rep-Old Vic production, played with a down-centre vigour now hard to find. Too many of this cast cannot raise their voices without having their words disappear through the roof; it can't all be the fault of the Stratford acoustics. There was besides much nervousness evident last week; much fluffing, leaping of cues, and upsetting of furniture. That will obviously mend; meanwhile, Mr Hands has displayed great courage, great faith and great imagination. A rave review is struggling within me and, though I cannot conscientiously let it out just yet, I shall keep it on ice.

Alan Howard is interviewed in today's Colour Magazine.

records.title: Of liberty and damnation
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Of liberty and damnation

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN revives Stratford, Manchester and London.

While the Stratford-upon-Avon main house takes us to the Middle Ages, the Other Place is going Renaissance. A notable seventeenth-century tragedy has been revived in modern dress, while by way of balance a modern play by a contemporary playwright has gone to work on sixteenth-century Florence in period costume.

Paul Thompson's The Lorenzaccio Story is not, strictly speaking, a new play. It is based on the Lorenzaccio written in the 1830s by Alfred de Musset. Musset's piece is saturated in revolutionary disenchantment and has all the hallmarks (dozens of brief elaborate scenes, banquets for 40 people, horses) of the insouciantly unstageable. Looked at another way it cries out to be staged, and one can imagine Franco Zeffirelli putting it across as a lush Medici documentary or Terry Hands as a masque of death.

Its subject is the assassination of a young debauched Duke by Lorenzo, his cousin, friend and procurer. Lorenzo has always wanted to be a tyrannicide, but to fulfil his ambition has had to get so close to his victim as to take on his colouring. Few Florentines will trust him and none will take him seriously.

Before committing the murder he tries to rouse the leading Republicans; they tell him to go home and stop playing the fool. Earlier he confesses to Filippo Strozzi, the local leader of progressive opinion, that his project has become an end in itself; he will go through with it, but he has no hope that it will lead to a better society and no interest in constructing one.

Mr Thompson retains both these scenes and they are the best in his play. Elsewhere he seems an efficient craftsman, though his personality is none too easy to make out. Musset's play seems simultaneously to have appealed to him and to have got up his nose. Lorenzo's fatalism is retained more or less undoctored, though in both writers it is an elaborate form of words rather than a dramatised process and the new words are much flatter than the old. He is also more explicit, and harsher, with Strozzi the liberal aesthete (well played by David Swift) roundly condemned by his own son, who ends up leading a students' revolt: a foredoomed gesture but, it is suggested, a noble one.

Nor that this son is faultless; he shrugs off Florentine poverty as no concern of his. This attitude was shared, incidentally, by Musset, for whom ducal tyranny seemed mainly to consist of treading on the toes of old-established families and seducing their women. Mr Thompson throws in some economic colouring, writing up the roles of two trade-conscious bourgeois onlookers and having Lorenzo fall victim to a poor man who needs the reward money: a fate our hero accepts with his usual cankered equanimity.

Musset, endorsing Lorenzo's despair, got close to tragedy; Mr Thompson, relishing but not quite following it, winds up with cynicism. Peter McEnery, long, lean, and lank-haired, looks conscientiously depraved, yet his overstatement of the corruption suggests that he does not really believe in it. James Laurenson, less effortful and more contained, gives the Duke a poisonous romantic flair; he is one of those rare actors made for Jacobean tragedy.

* * *

It would be good, for example, to see him in Ford's 'Tis Pity She's a Whore, the other Other Place play. As it is the most Italianate performance in this story of incest and butchery in Parma is given (as an expatriate Spaniard, oddly enough) by Geoffrey Hutchings: grey hair neatly combed, stocky and menacing in his blue pin-stripes, definitely a man of respect. And also of religion; when he learns of the bedding of brother and sister, his response ("to what a height of liberty and damnation hath the devil trained our age") is quiet and heartfelt; staggered, he looks for comfort to one of the religious pictures which dot the stage.

Though Ron Daniels's production lays great stress on the transgressed orthodox code, it comes out with no clear attitude towards it; friars seem to be good and helpful, cardinals bad and grasping. (Here he is true to his author; there is a book to be written on the shifting attitudes of Elizabethan drama to the Catholic Church, treated as venal superstition or moral authority, often within the same play.)

The plots and sub-plots are laid out neatly, but neither Simon Rouse nor Barbara Kellerman are up to the leading roles, though he at least attempts to grapple with Giovanni's rising insanity and she lends Annabella a pleasing teasing quality, like a girl trying to convince herself that she is having an ordinary affair with ordinary rules. Mr Hutchings apart, the play belongs to Tim Wylton, emerging from his Bardolph make-up to play the fool Bergetto, whose death signifies that the play is getting down to business.

* * *

Having given us life with father as seen by Peter Nichols and John Mortimer, the British stage has delayed in bringing us Hugh Leonard's Da (King's Head), who proves the best of three: an unstoppably winsome eccentric, rejoicing in a pension of 19 shillings a week because it comes from the Quality, and provoking from his son the anguished comment, "If you knocked him down in a motorcar he'd thank you for the lift."

Even within this convention I found Eamon Kelly's old man excessively invertebrate, but I have never gone much on Irish charm; I prefer the steelier, worldlier Irish actor of whom Tony Doyle (playing Mr Leonard or his surrogate) is the finest specimen since T. P. McKenna. Mike McCabe, touchingly blank-faced, acts out the struggle of his younger self in quest of a job or (the best and funniest scene in the play) a girl; Kevin Moore is beautifully shockable as a contemporary who never made the break.

Whatever the structural differences between a play and a musical, it is unwise to use for the latter a story that would not pass muster for the former. That is the lesson of Trevor Peacock's Leaping Ginger (Royal Exchange, Manchester). Which hangs some attractive numbers - including ensembles which approach the Sondheim standard of musicalised conversation - on a frayed and indeterminate fable about a young ex-con falling foul of big business man (assumed to be his moral inferior though the case is never proved) and in love with his rehabilitation officer. She is black, though the show only registers the fact too late to make anything of it but portentous melodrama. Malcolm Rennie's villain is the only performance with much personality, but Graham Murray's production makes the best use yet of this theatre and its stereophonic sound effects.

To the Cottesloe comes Steven Berkoff's production of Steven Berkoff's East starring Steven Berkoff. The use of pastiche blank verse for this black impression of the East End is still irritating (an endless repetition of the anachronism joke), but the mime remains excellent and two prose passages - Anna Nygh's outcry against male domination and Barry Philips's bitter saga of life in the rag trade - deserve to be classics.

Previously at the Cottesloe we had Chris Harris in Kemp's Jig, a one-man show about the Elizabethan comic who left the Lord Chamberlain's Men to dance to Norwich in nine days. Mr Harris is now on the road himself and worth catching if he rigs your way; less for his own clowning or the narrative of his travels than for his recurrent memories of his feud with a snuffling, scratching Shakespeare.

records.title: Murder, rape, and politics
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Murder, rape, and politics

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on plays by Howard Barker, John Mortimer and Shaw

The Royal Shakespeare Company's Warehouse in Covent Garden - formerly a rehearsal room and making few bones about it - is now open for business. Last week the critics were let in for a sight of That Good Between Us, a two-year-old piece by Howard Barker, the least doctrinaire of our youngish romantics, the readiest both to exploit "chaos" (a word he himself employs) and to be appalled by it.

That may sound a disreputable combination, but it has a respectable enough lineage. The greatest English practitioners were the Jacobeans, but they covered themselves by setting their blood-boltered scenes either in the past or in Italy. The eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Romantics - often more thoughtful writers - did the same: cf. Musset's Lorenzaccio, also currently aired by the RSC, though in an adaptation which substitutes for the author's voice that of any writer of the 1970s. (Interpreting a classic has come increasingly to mean asking it to tell us things we already know rather than letting us be disturbed by its otherness.)

In his present play Mr Barker deals, like Musset or Webster, in rape, murder, temporising sententious politicians, inefficient conspirators, stormily lascivious ladies and ambitious, discontented spies. The difference is that Mr Barker's setting is not fairyland; his action happens not only here, but now, or at least - since he posits such mutations from the present order as a female Home Secretary and an army almost wholly devoted to strike-breaking - in a few minutes' time.

Useless to accuse Mr Barker of melodrama: he has only to point to the headlines. The trouble is that the play's texture remains that of the headlines; its people are very thin, creatures of their author's hectic pessimism, which they are obligingly good at verbalising. There is wit at work here; an agent named Godber is allowed to offer exactly the same rhetorical credentials - viz, the disillusion awaiting a bright grammar-school boy when offering himself for Government work - as when infiltrating military subversives in the course of that work. Fine; but he sounds in the same note of brittle toughness throughout the play; obviously he thinks it's clever. His author, unfortunately, seems to think it's real.

He is the middle man of a trio: above him spymaster Knatchbull, fond of a handicapped daughter, respectful of the existing order and prosaically ruthless in the protection of both; below is McPhee, the tartan yob, bound in service to Knatchbull, won over by the opposition's talk of freedom, and finally hunted by both sides. All three are expertly played: by John Nettles, the young master of hard, bright social deviance, Patrick Stewart in his cosy commissar's vein and Ian McDiarmid, king of the underdogs. His McPhee is as wild as his shopman in Destiny was respectable; he gets his full naked height and yells triumphantly "what sounds like 'I ...? Some new rough beast, swimming towards Bethlehem, to be born?'"

Barbara Leigh-Hunt as the Home Secretary has two humane and eloquent speeches, one on Fascism, the other on sex: the second is belied by her daughter, who jumps into bed with Godber while despising him, and the first by her own action in licensing murder and muzzling the Press. Since this is accompanied by a full complement of moral qualms, one wants to know in more detail the circumstances which prompt her to it. Doomwatch drama has become a mannerism, almost a reflex, and it comes here with full trimmings: a stageful of debris, dialogue to match, and a marginally relevant gang-bang, graphically staged. Some of it grips; Mr Barker's generation of playwrights differs from its predecessors in providing stories, and this one, confusing at once, is worked out with jigsaw precision. But there is the scent of bravado about it all, natural perhaps in a classical company always sensitive to any charge of respectability.

* * *

My favourite line in John Mortimer's The Bells of Hell, in its one-act form at Greenwich, was the closer, "he's a gentleman," applied by the rector's wife to the (literal) Prince of Darkness who had seduced her, and who had temporarily restored her husband's faith by filling his fridge with loaves and fishes. At the Garrick the finale has turned to frantic gyrations backed by fireworks, and the rest of the play has been similarly coarsened. Two new characters have attenuated the plot and have pushed the wife's awakening, which once was crucial, to the side of the stage.

Phyllida Law may well be for general purposes a better actress than Eleanor Bron, but following in Miss Bron's steps without her caricaturist's line she just seems to be over-acting. Peter Woodthorpe's floppy rector, Tony Britton's hearty curate, and Trevor Baxter's efflorescent bishop, are all hard-working performances worked too hard, and the same fault overtakes the small but amusing situation at the heart of the play.

* * *

Shaw's The Apple Cart furnishes Chichester's statutory good production for the year. Keith Michell's Magnus has charm, tact and a good memory - the basic requirements - and his Cabinet is excellently filled; you can even tell them apart, which is more, I fancy, than the author could manage most of the time. In the approved feature roles are Paul Hardwick as a jovial and innocent Boanerges, June Jago, whose attack on the Breakages Corporation is as usual the highspot of the play, and Nigel Stock, whose Prime Minister is a guileful assembly of celebrated mannerisms, timed to a turn or done to a T or both. The very secretaries (Brian Spink and Adam Bareham) are excellent, setting the tone for a stylish examination of monarchy, symbol and reality.

It is not their fault that no such thing emerges. Magnus's royalty, as Shaw said himself, is incidental; what counts is his individuality, but since no-one else is allowed any, the contest lacks bite. I spent some time wondering whether Penelope Keith was wasted or just miscast as Orinthia the Beloved; finally, settling on both. Miss Keith is a supremely businesslike actress, and Orinthia had no time for business.

records.title: The ship-builder crippled by guilt
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The ship-builder crippled by guilt

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on two RSC productions

Did you ever hear the one about Ibsen and his wife? They were about to leave Norway for their long self-imposed exile in Germany, and they were rushing for the boat. They were late, and Ibsen warned Mrs Ibsen not to look back, but she did and she turned into a pillar of the community.

Ibsen never got over it; he blamed himself. And that story - which may not, I admit, be the literal truth - reminds us of the deep seam of guilt that runs throughout his work. From Brand to When We Dead Awaken his heroes fulfil themselves at the expense of their women, and the knowledge cripples them. Dramatically the women have their revenge. The protagonist of The Pillars of the Community (Aldwych) is Consul Bernick, the kingpin of a small and profoundly insular Norwegian town, grown rich as a ship-builder and now hoping to make millions in railway speculation. But he is off-stage for the most resonant scene in the play. Lona Hessel, whom Bernick once loved and whom he abandoned for a more advantageous match, has returned from America to make him face the lies on which his success has been founded. In John Barton's production Judi Dench plays Lona; she makes a flamboyant entrance (she has been caught up in a circus parade) and no actress could more efficiently dispense the fresh air Lona declares to be her new gift to her home town.

For most of the evening the burden passes to Bernick's sister Martha, whom Patricia Brown plays with exquisite tact. She had loved Johan, the man who took the rap for Bernick's misdeeds (seduction and embezzlement) and to whom Lona has subsequently devoted her life. The two women quietly, smilingly, recognise their kinship, and the texture of the play is poignantly enriched.

Add to them the neglected Mrs Bernick (Eliza Ward) and the orphaned girl (Marjorie Bland) patronised by everyone in sight and you have a quartet (the respectable ladies of the town serving as chorus) whose griefs and grievances - never proclaimed and never whined for - raise the play above the problematics of Bernick's own conscience.

Not that this melodrama fails to excite; though Ibsen would come to write it, it still counts as an early play. It belongs to the period of his second start, and precedes the oppressively perfect masterpieces. Max Beerbohm, vetoing The Lady from the Sea, said that though Ibsen's technique still dazzled, his ideas were sadly dated. For us the situation has changed; the ideas, more complex and self-critical than Beerbohm imagined, still live, but the technique prevents us from getting at them. One winces at the prospect of going to Ghosts, Hedda Gabler or Rosmersholm, seeing the jigsaws fitted together all over again. This play takes a deal of exposition to be swallowed, but thereafter the story - as opposed to the theme - moves in an exhilarating straight line. Its ending, to be sure, might seem abrupt. The mere mention of yet another site being allocated for a shopping centre - particularly, of course, when it happens to be in the middle of some delightful locality - is almost always greeted with feelings of real dread.

Bernick, who has been willing to send a ship to the bottom in order to rid himself of the visitors from the past who threaten his future, is redeemed by the near-loss of his young son and makes a public confession of his own guilt. It is possible, however, to argue that he makes a better thing financially out of repentance than he could have done out of continued sinning. This is the line the RSC takes, and it is probably wise; the facts allow it and the straight ending would seem unbearably flatulent. We are nudged rather heavily, though.

Ian McKellen leaves it an open question whether Bernick at the end is a machiavel or a self-deceiver. He is perhaps too flighty and nervous for so stolid a community to have adopted him as a figurehead. They would have wanted a Doric pillar, and Mr McKellen with his fluting is Corinthian. But on these lines he plays magnificently, especially when under stress. It is great to see an Ibsen hero who loses his temper instead of staying buttoned-up.

Michael Annals's setting brings us yet further from the Ibsen mausoleum; out go the horsehair sofas and in come the cane-bottomed chairs with which the RSC has been wont to furnish its Gorky dachas. There are big airy windows (we are after all beside the seaside) and the whole fits with amazing but appropriate snugness into the Shakespearian timbers of the season's permanent set.

* * *

Those Aldwych actors excluded from the community are to be found at the Warehouse, offering naught for our comfort. C. P. Taylor's Bandits is marginally bleaker than Howard Barker's That Good Between Us the previous week, if only because its characters speak and behave as they would, rather than as their author would like them to.

I offer this reassurance, and the promise of an overpowering final scene, to help get you through a hard evening. For his study of urban blight, Newcastle brand, Mr Taylor has turned, as the movies often do, to the police records. The bandits are the one-armed kind (a selection mount guard at the back) and their avatars, two of whom are run in for the murder of a third. But the culprit, according to Mr Taylor, was a mineworker and ex-soldier acting out of jealousy, sexual and financial, and also perhaps out of the ashes of his own largely discarded communism.

This last bit comes over as an author's mannerism; however motivation is not everything, whatever they may have told you in drama school, and Bob Peck makes the killer's gangling animosity a sufficient dramatic fact in itself. Paul Moriarty's all-over trembles as his victim make up unequivocally the best image of physical terror I have ever seen on a stage. Behind them the cops, investigating the murder, uncover a world - that of the bystanders as well as the crooks - fit for anyone to reject: a world of which they themselves are of course a part. If the common-coin expletives of the dialogue sound grotesque on the lips of the superintendent (Hubert Rees), that is the point; he is the arch-matter and the characters' philosophy (by "Z-Cars" out of Samuel Beckett) is ludicrously inapposite to his job.

* * *

Steven Berkoff's London Theatre Group was briefly at the Cottesloe in its version of Kafka's Metamorphosis; Terry McGinty won all hearts as the mutant whose dung-beetlehood could hardly be less horrible than life with his family. This point was heavily underscored by turning them into grotesques with voices like slowed-down gramophone records. This distanced and allowed for cunning gradations between theatre and mime. It made for something like dehumanised theatre, but felt, on its own terms, faultless.

The Elizabethan stage at the St George's turns up trumps for The Merry Wives of Windsor; it looks pleasant in itself and is architecturally helpful, even realistic (the case for its appropriateness in plays not set in Elizabethan households is still unproven). The social detail in the dialogue comes off best, particularly from David Horovitch's Slender, with his wistful talk of bear-baiting. Otherwise the production, though full of bustle, is dour; Falstaff is subdued and though the wives seem to live next door to each other, one country and the other county.

records.title: The three Irish Maries
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The three Irish Maries

THE AUTHOR'S name is Mary O'Malley, the theatre the Royal Court and the play is called Once a Catholic, so you approach expecting another glum patch from the Irish litterati, drenched in Catholicism and philosophy. Not a bit of it; on offer is an insouciantly funny piece about the growing pains of three 17-year-old girls at a convent school in the neighbourhood of Willesden Junction.

The three girls are all called Mary - like every other girl in their class, apart from a token Maria. Mary McGinty is going out with a local Ted. (The date is 1956.) Mary Gallagher is having a pretty intense relationship with a Catholic boy who fancies himself for the priesthood; and so it is piquant that it is Mary G who has lost her virginity by the end of the play while Mary McG has picked up a proposal of marriage.

The third girl, Mary Mooney - who seems to represent the author - has one brief encounter which leaves her in a state of shuddering surprise, but otherwise the chief man in her life is the school music-teacher, who wants her to become a singer. He too makes her shudder. She is the innocent of the trio, and also the fall-girl: a string of unfortunate coincidences leaves the staff with the impression that she, of all of them, is the incipient scarlet woman.

Miss O'Malley's play is put together rather amateurishly; in the first scene the girls' form-mistress (a performance of ripe simplicity by Pat Heywood) warns them of the GCE perils ahead, promising 'a very heavy burden of homework' and advises that 'no one ever passed any exam of their own accord - only prayer can help you.' Exam results prove crucial to the play's resolution, but in the stretch between the subject is entirely dropped. The author, one feels, might pay more attention to her lessons and less to sex. It is, of course, a more easily stageable subject, and Miss O'Malley, taking the situation as it comes, treats it with great good humour, some invention, and considerable tact. We see nothing of the girls' parents but still get a full picture of their homelives. If Derek the Ted is conventional, Cuthbert the would-be cleric is an original, given by Mike Grady his full measure of preening insecurity. And if the situations are predictable the jokes (or two-thirds of them) are not.

For non-Catholics the play has of course a considerable voyeuristic appeal, but one which produces smiles rather than tears. Nostalgia is similarly handled: fed but not pampered. Mike Ockrent's production is physically awkward but it has the authentic smell of repression and school gravy; and though it is time Jane Carr (who has more or less cornered the market in plump, prim adolescence) was allowed to grow up she makes the mooniest of Maries.

The second half of the title we can of course fill in for ourselves; not so the action to which it corresponds, and one would like to know how these girls - rebellious but still indoctrinated - coped after they had left school. It might make a more challenging play.

* * *

The Roundhouse, as currently occupied by Joint Stock, lives up to its name; the audience surround at any rate, three-quarters of the acting area. For Howard Brenton's Epsom Downs this consists of a dazzling green slope; up and down it move some 50 characters. Not, unfortunately, all at the same time; nine actors play all the roles, and though this is clever of them it does result in the audience getting the worst of both worlds: no massed scenes and no characters to hold on to. The moment you begin to take an interest in someone, he is off to change into someone else.

So the play is afflicted by a monotony of rhythm and by the surprisingly low pressure of the writing. This new Derby Day canvas may be Mr Brenton's most genial play, but it is also his weakest.

Critics, noting the coexistence of knights, shopkeepers and beggars in Jacobean comedies, like to refer to them as 'pictures of a hierarchical society.' Epsom Downs is open to the same indulgent misrepresentation, presenting as it does the Aga Khan, a Socialist peer, bookies, punters, trainers, horses (fetchingly impersonated by nude harnessed actors, one of whom brings the house down with the bashful admission that he's an outside chance), a gypsy and a stable-boy: these last two for that dear old thing, the love interest. But it only presents them; and the ghost of Emily Davison, the suffragette who once threw herself under the royal horse, stalks the scene to little effect leaving us only with the vague feeling that it is a good idea to throw yourself under racing hooves on days of celebration. Cf. Mr Brenton's Magnificence: 'Disrupt the spectacle. The obscene parade.'

But the nearest to obscenity in his depiction of the Derby is the amount of litter dropped in an excellently-staged spectators' galop while the race is on, to be picked up at the end by inmates of the local mental home. (Good of the actors not to leave it to the stage-staff.) Otherwise the best scenes involve a poor family risking their all on a desperate flutter. They include Gillian Barge as a splendidly horrible three-year-old (girl not horse) and Simon Callow, a polished comedian seen in a new and homelier light.

* * *

Otherwise it has been a week of old favourites. Edward Bond's Bingo (Warehouse) has been rescued from the mumbling mummer-set which has previously shrouded its minor characters and much of its action in unfathomable mystery. The RSC is rich at the moment in striking young actors named Paul (this is as far as I am prepared to go in spotting trends); the Messrs Brooke, Shelley and Moriarty all illumine their roles and the play. Patrick Stewart, than whom Saturn himself could hardly be more saturnine, plays Mr Bond's suicidal Shakespeare; strong while establishing his despair, monotonous when reiterating it.

This is largely the play's fault, but it distributes its guilt with more complexity than I had suspected; the Puritan parricide who in leading the anti-enclosure men fulfils the Shakespearean prophecy of chaos ('the rude son shall strike the father dead') is a fascinating study in self-righteousness. So is Judith Shakespeare, not malicious but lethally unimaginative; Meg Davies's performance matches her Regan and I doubt if the connection is fortuitous.

For Barry Collins's Judgement (Cottesloe) too I now have more respect, though there is more of literature and less of humanity in Ben Kingsley's rendition of this marathon monologue than there was in Colin Blakely's. To suggest so persuasively the actions and reactions of seven men, abandoned and reduced to cannibalism, is a considerable imaginative feat, though Mr Collins cannot leave his ironies well alone; after using the word 'delicacies' he has to draw our attention to it.

Tales from the Vienna Woods (Olivier) remains the National's best show, though the replacement of Kate Nelligan by the perky Brenda Blethyn leaves it more schematic, less tragically turbulent, than before. All the same, to see the bathers plunge daintily into the Danube or the stage revolve twice over, apparently through sheer joie de vivre, is to realise how much the theatre customarily denies us, and to see the death-dealing grandmother leave the stage proclaiming her own immortality is to feel the dead hand of the ritualised past on your spine. Always a Catholic.

records.title: Making you blub
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Schweyk in the Second World War
records.body:
Making you blub

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

TERENCE RATTIGAN'S In Praise of Love was once a double bill and, like most, not very popular. As is common practice (cf. 'The Bells of Hell') its more successful half was torn from its mate and forced to live alone, first on Broadway and now at Bromley's new Churchill Theatre (christened perhaps in memory of the Blitz; it is certainly as subterranean as an air-raid shelter, though more comfortable).

The new play has been permitted to retain the family name, which in fact suits it better than did its former title, 'After Lydia.' It is a piece in which theme is more important than character. Plot comes in last though what little there is is deftly handled; the exposition relayed to a patient best friend (American as such sticks always are in posh plays now, perhaps because Englishmen can no longer afford to travel long enough to get out of touch) needs a determined swallow, but there is nothing actually painful about it. Though the play must have been padded to fill out an evening, the swelling is not easy to detect, and the tension remains.

Lydia is an Estonian refugee, married just after the war to a London literary critic, and now dying of leukaemia. She refuses to tell him on the grounds that he, as a public-school Englishman, is quite unfit to cope, either practically or emotionally, with the prospect of losing her. He in fact knows the score, thinks she doesn't, and is trying to hide it from her by intensifying his natural boorishness.

Lydia has altogether to do a good deal of suffering and Sylvia Syms sometimes sinks beneath it. She bobs up again, though, in the scenes that obviously lie closest to the dramatist's heart, denouncing the society in which she finds herself ("English bad form lies not in showing emotions but in having any emotions at all") and brushing aside ideological differences as irrelevant to human feelings.

In its beleaguered old age West End drama is becoming very didactic; Rattigan's heroine and his title make up a statement of belief. A statement, too, which he has the craft to justify. Lydia's husband says of good writers that "they all make you blub somewhere" and proceeds to make the point on his own creator's behalf. He has begun, inevitably, really to love his wife when about to lose her, and Alfred Marks releases the banked-up hesitant tears to fine effect. He, too, is miscast (he might pass for a self-made bookman, but never for a Wykehamist and Oxonian), but in the end it hardly matters. If this piece and 'Cause Celebre' are indeed to be Rattigan's last, they stand in the best tradition of final plays: summaries and experiments.

* * *

At the other extreme Nigel Baldwin comes on very strong with Sudlow's Dawn. With this play Upstairs and 'Once a Catholic' below, the Royal Court is accommodating two attention-grabbing playwrights; both are in residence, which suggests sharp thinking on the part of some committee or other.

Mr Baldwin's title is ambiguous; Sudlow is a mild young mental case, rescued from rock-bottom cafe employment to attend on a young lady of the suburbs (father a councillor) who is also, theoretically at least, a revolutionary and sees him as a cause. This agent of Sudlow's awakening is actually called Dawn; you will see that she is, strictly speaking, the titular figure, and she does indeed get most of Mr Baldwin's attention. She spouts and paints slogans, rows with her parents, rails at her carefully chosen working-class boyfriend for not living up to her preconceptions, idly seduces Sudlow, gets VD from him and goes to jail. (There are intermediate stages I've omitted.) Coming out, she goes to work in a strip-club, finds she can't take it and goes home, though not before her tender-mindedness has been exposed by a fellow-artiste.

The acting around here is very thin, but then so is the writing. Mr Baldwin goes on telling us things about Dawn which his first scene - the cafe pick-up - has made brilliantly clear. Meanwhile he skimps on Sudlow: a pity since Karl Johnson's frayed nervous puzzlement is riveting. ("I hate bringing people bad news," he says, announcing a scarcity of bacon sandwiches.)

If Mr Baldwin's point is that the dispossessed keep getting elbowed out and about by their self-appointed saviours he is party to the offence himself. (Actually he is unfair to Dawn; some of her activities sound useful, but they are given only passing mention.) Still, he never romanticises and, until the last scenes, you can't stop listening to him.

* * *

Part of Michael Hastings's thesis in For the West is that Amin plays up to his newspaper image: a point the President proved abundantly and fittingly last week by shooting actors in Uganda while Mr Hastings's view of him (mad and murderous, yes, but partly our creation and largely our responsibility) took the stage of the Cottesloe. History, in these circumstances, made drama pale, though, given Mr Hastings's emphasis, it was possible to applaud the faultless authenticity of the two British colonial types (Basil Henson upstanding and Roger Milner cowering, both with dignity) who made up half the cast.

Mr Hastings takes Amin seriously. Brecht in Schweyk in the Second World War (Warehouse) was less responsible; his Hitler is a strutting marionette (Nickolas Grace's eyeball-rolling is spectacular) anxious for the love of the little man.

When Schweyk, who is that person, meets Adolf he defies him, though the heroism of this action is limited (a) by the scene which is Russia with the Germans on the run and (b) by the mood which is allegorical. Early on, in occupied Czechoslovakia, he is concerned to keep his nose clean while still being moderately subversive. With these contradictory aims it is hardly surprising he gets in trouble, thereby impairing his mythological status as a survivor.

What Brecht was at is unclear, except to serve up individually funny scenes to help the war effort; in this he succeeds. Michael Williams's Schweyk is much influenced, to his benefit and our pleasure, by north-country comics; there is a bit of Eric Morecambe in him and a lot of Ted Ray.
