records.title: A pair so famous
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
EVER since Tyrone Guthrie first adapted Edinburgh's Assembly Hall to his own uses, Elizabethan staging has meant platform staging. Thirty years on, the Prospect company at the same address have drawn on another contemporary source, the cockpit. The raised stage has gone, who knows where, and so have the ecclesiastical seats -- known, from the sightlines they afforded, as Blind Pews -- from which the audience regarded it. We now look down, from hard tip-up chairs, on a square scooped-out space: visible, audible, accessible.

For Antony and Cleopatra it is backed by what the buffs call "the tiring-house facade", alcoved and balconied. In All for Love, Dryden's retelling of the same old story, this is encased by what, I suppose, are Restoration gates. Pauline Kael once laid it down as one of the few immutable cinematic rules that "all pictures set in ancient Egypt are ridiculous" and Prospect seem, with some reason, to believe the same of plays. So they have costumed each of their shows in the period of its author, with only a top dressing (i.e., the occasional funny hat) of classicism.

As Dryden's Antony John Turner resembles, at his first disconsolate appearance, a mad monk with a military past, but soon he is accoutred like -- prophetically if you examine the dates -- James II at the Boyne. The army of Antony assumes, when you see the plays together, almost allegorical significance; with his gear on Alex McCowen as Shakespeare's warrior seems a different man; if not quite (alas, and now read on) a different actor. Their respective mistresses get a worse deal from their dressmakers; why can't they, you wonder, slip into something more comfortable before getting down to empire-toppling?

I cannot altogether blame the designer for the miscarriage of this Antony and Cleopatra but I have to start somewhere. Toby Robertson's production has its key positions filled by four of our best actors; the fifth, Robert Eddison, is enticingly tripletongued as Soothsayer, Schoolmaster and Clown. Derek Jacobi's Caesar and Timothy West's Enobarbus are expected excellents; the former can be faulted only for being too icily politic in his summing up and the latter (a beery ranker instead of the usual staffman) for an undue briskness as commentator, delivering his verdicts as if having reached them before coming on stage.

They are both strong, sane, vividly witty actors; so of course is Mr McCowen and the play lacks something in temperamental contrast. That he can put his rivals down at the imperial summit is fine; the scenes where Antony is on top give him no trouble. But where Antony is massively careless he is meticulous, substituting an acerbic bonhomie for the mad generosity of the text; he is measured in a play whose terms are oceanic. "The false Egyptians have betrayed me" is not tragically inevitable but incredulous (like his Misanthrope).

Many fine actors so miscast would give up the ghost; Mr McCowen battles on, meets every challenge, encompasses every rage. Technically he is brilliant but technique cannot bridge the fatal gap between what he says and what he is.

He also seems on distant terms with Dorothy Tutin's Cleopatra. Their small quantities of shared stage time are largely devoted to mutual bitching. This of course is in the script, written for conditions which stylised, or just by-passed, displays of heterosexual passion. It may be that to lay the ghost of this play we shall have to call up that of the boy player. That is not a situation about which anyone can feel enthusiastic (though there is a hint of drag about Cleopatra's berouged maids here) so our actresses must continue to work overtime.

Unfortunately Dorothy Tutin, who looks on paper (and has been proclaimed in this paper) the ideal Cleopatra, goes by the book, and she really succeeds only with the spoilt teasing bits, jumping to wittily unflattering conclusions about her rival Octavia. The last scene is sort-of-impressive but no more; its rhythms when read are so majestic, yet so buoyant, you feel it should play itself. It is therefore of course lethally difficult.

All for Love is easier because more artificial; you can, as Frank Hauser has done here, go after a style and get it. The costumes help greatly and so do the wigs, I almost wrote Whigs, though Kenneth Gilbert's honest Ventidius is a solid country Tory. Mr Eddison's villainous Alexis is a politic schemer to the manner born; I couldn't actually follow all his plots but I enjoyed them. Barbara Jefford is an eloquent Queen, though she seemed surprised at just how nice a lady she is meant to be. Dryden's Cleopatra hardly betrays her lover at all; when she confronts Suzanne Bertish's blanched, jealous Octavia we get a contest of outraged virtues. There are laughs here I never expected; even Dryden might have got a surprise.

But the play is Antony's and Mr Turner does full justice to Stuart nobility if not always to Stuart wit. (Here oddly enough, Mr Cowen might have been better suited.) Set against Shakespeare's most accomplished but not greatest play, Dryden's, though virtuous, seems artificial for reasons that have nothing to do with Augustan decorum; Dryden came to dramatic blank verse too late, and had to work at it. His characters talk, not, like Shakespeare's, as they must but as they ought; an air of paraphrase hangs over the play, an air in which succeeding iambic dramas have virtually choked.

* * *

The Edinburgh fringe usually harbours a degree of funniness difficult to find elsewhere. This year's exemplar is Writers' Cramp (Carlton Studios), an account by a new hand, John Byrne, of the life and works of F. S. McDade, "poet, painter, philosopher and sage", who if he didn't exist should have. Mr Byrne specialises in delayed action puns. "How they shoot up," says McDade's ma of her grandchild, now a dope peddler. Think about it.

Also of a literary bent are Paines Plough, a touring group who are unique and expert and leave me cold. In David Pownall's Richard III Part II (Traverse) they investigate the perversion of history through a complex ingenious prism. Stephen Boxer plays Richard II well, George Orwell (as Prologue) better, and various archaic musical instruments hauntingly. He also composed.

Ian Watson's Mary (as in Queen of Scots) (Little Lyceum) brings the accursed vogue of jokey history to, I hope, its nadir. Pete Atkin's musical A & R (Traverse) confirms the decline of pop (all smiles and teeth) and has the air, if not the precise tone, of authenticity. The drama is rudimentary; songs are cued by such engaging lines as "I think I've got the chords in my notebook", but when they come they can be bewitching.

records.title: Tartan blues
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Tartan blues

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THERE was a good time to be had at the Edinburgh Festival. There was Carmen and the film festival and good company and Ian McKellen's Shakespeare recital. All of these except the last count for this column as hookey and the charming informality of Mr McKellen's performance really precludes criticism. It included by the way an image-by-image analysis of Mafia Macbeth's "Tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow" which is absolutely invaluable.

The main official drama in the festival's second week came from the Nottingham Playhouse company whose director, Richard Eyre, is about to depart for television. He will be missed; as the best director of new work to come along since Peter Gill. His two festival offerings, though, were unfortunate.

First was Stephen Lowe's Touched, about kindness and cruelty as demonstrated in working-class Nottingham and the world at large between VE and VJ Days - or from the discovery of Belsen to the blasting of Hiroshima. One moment the world is revolted by barbarism, and the next it is adding to the score. That is more or less Mr Lowe's pattern, epitomised by a young lady who develops a hysterical pregnancy when things look hopeful which subsides when they fade back to black. She believes the father to be an Italian PoW; a belief which brings her into great disfavour with her two sisters and almost to blows with her mother.

The most charitable explanation offered for her behaviour is that she is "touched," as in slightly mad. We in the audience, hearing her take off into gentle monologues about her hopes for a gentle future, are meant to feel touched, as in moved, but are likely to feel touched, as in cheated. She is a playwright's convenience, slow to emerge as the centre of the play, but irritatingly immovable once there. It is impossible to believe that, at the end of a six-year war, people chirped so self-consciously about a "new world." They must have been much too tired.

The rest of the play is routine back-fence naturalism, and I am not sure that Mr Eyre does it any service by poeticising it - in plain terms, slowing it down. If he were working with better material his production might well be extremely fine; in the circumstances it is indulgent. The same must go, really, for Marjorie Yates's performance in the leading role; she has quality - a reeling, obstinate fragility - but I wanted to kick her.

This was followed by Adrian Mitchell's White Suit Blues, which does for Mark Twain what Mr Mitchell's Tyger did for Blake i.e. it lets him spend most of his time shaking his fist, literally or figuratively; only when allowed to deliver a monologue, cheerfully demolishing the literary pretentions of Fenimore Cooper, does he come to life; here, of course, the words are Twain's own. The whole is framed in a vast humourless conceit about Twain going to heaven, finding it composed mainly of upper-class Englishmen, and gladly descending to hell. Religion, especially Christianity, is blamed for all its literally--cripples are "God's experiments."

The final scene seems to mean that if we were all jolly atheists, floating down the Mississippi surrounded by our loved ones (everyone, including Huck and Jim, on for the finale) pain would disappear. Mike Westbrook has provided a rousing antispiritual for the occasion and he does good service throughout; it's refreshing to encounter a score on the British stage that really sounds like music. But for a musical, indeed for anything meant actually to entertain an audience or at least keep it awake, Mr Eyre's production is uncommonly louring; it begins with the grey of a funeral and is black-avised hereafter. "Tyger" was at least jolly.

The Traverse has this year returned to its former resident playwright C. P. Taylor, who has provided two pieces collectively known as Walter, he being a Scots Jewish Socialist comedian, living in retirement that would be comfortable if only he wasn't ill. The comfort is afforded by a late success in a TV soap-opera, a series which, he says, achieved the impossible by uniting the Scottish press; they all hated it.

The play is constructed as a deathbed flashback with the various cultural errands of Walter's past alternating in his mind; one would like to say entwining, or even interacting, but in fact there is a peculiar recurring stasis about the play which, despite rich moments in the dialogue, exhausted me. I left half-way through Part Two, which at least enables me to declare the show a play and a half. Certainly Grant Hicks has designed a set and a half - a living-room so complete that there can be no excuse for demolishing it at the end of the run; it should be given to the homeless. Mr Hicks does more for the texture of the evening than the author or any of the actors, though Peter Kelly is resourceful in the lead, and Peter Lincoln engaging as an emblem of respectability.

It is possible that, among the hundreds of shows on the fringe, I missed a couple of masterpieces; what I saw was unhappily typified by The Player King, an attempt to graft we're-all-actors-really implications onto a commonplace and desperately protracted triangle story. If Writer's Cramp, reviewed last week, shows the virtues of the Edinburgh fringe; this exemplifies its vices: arch attempts at experiment for the titillation of audiences who, except at Festival time, don't get out much. It is almost saved by Neil Cunningham, an actor with the aplomb and precision of an emergent Alec McCowen, plus a touch of madness.

Back to London for Dean (Casino), which I tried to approach by forgetting the publicity and concentrating on the title: hoping that it might yet turn out to be a one-man show by Frank Sinatra's sleepy friend, or perhaps a saucily-christened musicalisation of one of Trollope's ecclesiastical novels. But no, it's James Dean all right, or rather all wrong. Dean may have been important for his talent or for his social influence; neither is explored here. It is merely a movieland success story with an unsurprising surprise ending. Probably they now wish they'd done Elvis Presley instead. He at least would have provided cues for song; there is no reason on earth or in Hollywood for the numbers here.

records.title: Liberty and banishment
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Liberty and banishment

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Stratford.

I visited The Old Country (Queen's) in a state of more than usual innocence. The publicity had been secretive, and I failed even to get a programme. All I knew when the curtain rose was that Alan Bennett had written it, and that Alec Guinness and Rachel Kempson were in it.

Sure enough there were Sir Alec and Miss Kempson married to each other, pottering around an odd-looking country villa (what a big veranda, and could those really be birch trees at the back?). They spoke of England in the special terms, distant yet possessive, familiar in the kind of play that habitually gets described as 'civilised'. There were many books, and the Guinness persona--here called Hilary--was appropriately literate. I began to wonder if he would ever stop being so serene; he can even be serenely irritated.

A young couple appeared, and were not, it seemed, too welcome. The boy was timidly ingratiating and the girl close-cropped and almost definitely foreign. I discovered in the interval that she was Heather Canning, so highly praised at the Aldwych a few years ago, and was surprised. Miss Kempson, noting Sir Alec's distaste, remarked that after the war he and his visitors had things in common. They were all, she said, traitors.

At which point the oddities in the situation came together, the villa revealed itself as having every right to resemble a dacha (earlier one wondered if the management had booked a Chekhov production by mistake) and the nostalgic meanings of the opening scene took on, retrospectively, an edge. I wished, and still do, that I could remember more of them.

Hilary the defector is visited, in his aching Russian retreat, by his sister and her husband, on a trip from the home country to take in the art (why else, they ask, does one travel anywhere?). Brother-in-law Duff is on the board of absolutely everything and also lectures on E. M. Forster. This prompts Hilary to endear himself to me for ever by asking just what 'only connect' is supposed to mean: the first time I have heard such doubts voiced in public. It could perhaps be done only by an exile.

There is no greater patriot than an expatriate, and Hilary plainly longs for home. Duff tries to persuade him to return, overestimating, it seems to me, both the amenities of Her Majesty's prisons (he compares them favourably to Trust Houses) and the compassion of the popular press. Hilary, though he never gives such a vulgarly practical reason, seems reluctant; perhaps, for all its discomforts, his present life of acidulous nostalgia fits him better than any other. It certainly suits his author, who has found just about the perfect framework for his preferred style and subject.

There are many delights. Guinness rouses himself from his elegant stupor to express real wit, real pain, each intensifying the other. Asked to come back, he sits with his eyes closed, as if suffering from some cosmic headache; then he turns slightly and the set of his shoulders shows that everything is hopeless.

Duff, as written by Mr Bennett and acted by John Phillips, is a monumental inside job on the establishment. Mr Phillips is intelligent and immovable and silly, vastly proud of a self-fostered and probably imaginary reputation as a maverick ('I have the name of being a little difficile') and very sad inside.

When Hilary remarks, apropos his 14-year absence, 'I'm so out of it,' Duff, with no such excuse, is plainly in the same predicament. He is in himself a whole television series on Civilisation. Both men are well mated, Miss Kempson being all patience and contempt, Faith Brook all glass. 'You're lucky,' she says, 'eating so simply. We would, only it's so complicated.'

I have quoted shamelessly and could continue; the one-liners beat the set pieces, which I would rather hear delivered by the author, out of context. They cannot keep the play going; Mr Bennett seems one of those playwrights (like T. S. Eliot) who can tell a story, but cannot make it matter. His natural mode is irony, and it is sadly characteristic of him that he proclaims the fact; Hilary says he will give it up and has failed within two minutes. It happens to be the dramatic quality to which I am most attracted, but I like it to be made flesh.

* * *

As You Like It (Stratford) presents us with the two faces of Trevor Nunn. The showbiz Nunn, late of the Comedy of Errors, turns as much of the show as possible into a musical. Likely bits of dialogue are sung--a bad idea, though an increasingly common one, since good dialogue is different in shape and pressure from a good lyric--and the real songs are turned, care of Gillian Lynne, into production numbers. This is fine, and 'A Lover and His Lass' becomes a properly joyous prelude to the closing nuptials. It even accommodates, very touchingly, the courtship of Oliver and Celia, which Shakespeare, to say the least, underwrote.

There is also the alert and scholarly Nunn, combing the text to amplify the story. Thus Orlando is allowed to practise his wrestling on an old Adam and even on the disguised Rosalind. (It is some tribute to Peter McEnery that he makes such an arrant bully likeable.) The stream of refugees to Arden is unending; Le Beau and Charles, the wrestler, both turn up there, on the strength of some longing lines uttered in their courtier days, and Duke Frederick's conversion (from sheer loneliness, I imagine) takes on a kind of logic.

'Now go we in content,' cries Celia, 'to liberty and not to banishment.' And Mr Nunn carefully juxtaposes the two. (So of course does Mr Bennett, who actually has a line about the Forest of Arden.) In winter Arden is palpably cold and Jaques seems the sanest man in the wood; come the spring, it rains coloured confetti, and his discomfiture--for in each of the comedies, someone has to get locked out--is inevitable.

In Shakespeare's own day, philosophy and musical comedy met in the masque, and this is Mr Nunn's solvent here, though he pushes it on a half century or more; cut-out forest with crooks for the shepherds (Phebe, sheepless, looks like Bo-Beep), an etched country chateau for Oliver, and the court of Versailles for the Duke, with Touchstone, jumping on in time, got up like Watteau's sad jester Gilles.

Hymen, who comes on to marry everyone at the end, now has a sung prologue, presiding at a dispute between Fortune and Nature. Rosalind and Celia, two scenes on, carefully enunciate their brief discussion of these two abstractions, but it remains an intellectual accretion, and though marriage is the climax of the play, it is not really its subject. Besides, the songs, the dances, and the costumes do not as yet become many of the actors.

If Nature means innate ability and Fortune acquired skills, Kate Nelligan's Rosalind is a natural, able with her superb whole-heartedness to rule a scene, but not to govern this stage, this language, and this over-complicated presentation. She is at her finest in the mock marriage where her page-boy masquerade disappears; it is always the woman whom we watch and for whom we feel. Emrys James's diseased Jaques similarly fails to ride the production. I liked him when he was on, but forgot him when he wasn't. Best of the rest are Judith Paris's Celia, Ian Gelder's Silvius, and David Shaw-Parker's unnervingly confident William.

records.title: Hitting the bullseyes
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Hitting the bullseyes

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on "The best Shakespeare production I have ever seen."

THIS has been a spectacular week for acting. It was so dominated by the RSC Macbeth, which reinforces at the Warehouse the impression it made last year at the Other Place. It is the best Shakespeare production I have ever seen, combining minute textual scrutiny with throat-seizing emotional power.

At Stratford I dispatched the supporting cast with a collective superlative. This time round I should like, gratefully, to name names. First the witches, a businesslike non-cackling trio, relying less on Satanic vision than malicious determination. Marie Kean, the peremptory ruler of the coven, receives grizzled support from Judith Harte; they are earthbound, with young Susan Drury--the initiate witch that wants hard use--their lifeline to the supernatural.

They exemplify many of the production's merits; alert to all possible contrasts, they can still merge their identities when required. They make their points quickly and firmly; they do not brandish new interpretations, they embody them. They are on easy prosaic terms with their high roles, but the roles themselves are so uneasy that we are constantly jolted into poetry.

Griffith Jones's white-haired Duncan is, unrestrainedly, a saint; but it is the content of his words, and the mind behind them, that matter. Malcolm as his heir he raises and then crushes Macbeth's hopes--that decides his fate. John Woodvine's Banquo scans the sour future of his lineage; "sons" and "children" as kings seduces him, as surely as it maddens Macbeth.

Bob Peck's Macduff is the steadiest of all; when he speaks of the ills "that strike heaven on the face" he is flintlike, hammerlike. The one non-vacillating character in the play, he balances not only Macbeth, but also Roger Rees's hopeful, doubtful Malcolm, and Ian McDiarmid's civil servant Ross. Greg Hicks's Seyton is a streamlined thug whom Macbeth adopts as confidant, when his murderous instincts begin to outstrip his wife's.

Judi Dench's Lady Macbeth in fact would kill Duncan and leave it at that. If her husband would be equally content, she might even get away with it. As it is, her breakdown is triggered more by his rejection than her conscience. Exhausted by the events of the banquet, she slumps to the ground. On "We are yet but young in deed," Macbeth pulls her violently up and half supports, half drags her off. The contact is a cruel parody of the embraces with which she softened him up to the initial murder. There is never any doubt she will succeed; she knows her man.

For Ian McKellen's Macbeth is worm-eaten from the start. For all his victor's smiles in the opening scenes, there is less courtliness about him than last year; our first glimpse into him comes when he tells Banquo, "Your children shall be kings." Envy is already there and, once loosed, it is a consumer. The note is sounded again in Mr McKellen's most scornful tones, once he is king; he has done it all "to make them kings? The seed of Banquo--kings?" It sickens him.

Envy reaches backwards, colouring the despair of "Duncan is in his grave." The words, and the mind behind them, are rancid; and it is this mood that takes possession of the last act. Practically everything disgusts him, and his only reason for fighting to the death is that the thought of subjection to Malcolm is the most disgusting of all.

Where Miss Dench succeeds with a carefully built characterisation, Mr McKellen is more unpredictable, flooding the play with energy as if it were an electric field. His alacrity goes physical: bravura; the autonomous bloodstained hand, the quaking leg when Birnam Wood approaches; we are present at the revelation of a consciousness and at the unfolding of a story that pales any horror film.

Trevor Nunn's production is bleak and simple; the goodies entering Dunsinane find it full of upturned orange boxes and discarded magic fetishes, and they end the play, not unnaturally, in weariness and disillusion.

There is little hope in the evening, but in the hitting of so many bull's-eyes there is enormous joy.

* * *

Meanwhile, back at the Other Place, Sheila Allen surrenders herself in Pam Gems's Queen Christina, seeking personal freedom as Swedish monarch (Act I), then, after abdication, all over Europe (Act II).

Miss Allen has a hearty, roguish, teasing approach to her quest ("Where are the blue stockings?" she demands, lifting the skirts of the Parisian femmes savantes) that you could swear was a put-on. The greatest joke of all is that it is real. Christina yearns in the end for the traditional maternal role of which she was robbed by a masculine upbringing. Do not overlook, however, that this was actually forced on her by a man--a father who desired a male heir as fervently as Henry VIII and was determined to make her into the next best thing.

The play is an argument for love, and against dogma. Appropriately breezy in presentation, it includes one violent scene worthy of the Jacobeans; certainly the best Jacobean play in years, never allowing events to obscure the character, though at some cost to narrative clarity. Among the supports, Tam Moore stands out as a cardinal, despatched sensibly short of unction.

* * *

There is the occasional rough edge to Miss Allen's performance; none at all to Julie Harris in The Belle of Amherst (Phoenix), a one-woman show about Emily Dickinson. You get little sense of the poems (which are slid into the whole with excessive unobtrusiveness), though much of the author's wonder at having written them.

This Emily, buttonholing the audience for two and a half hours, must be the most loquacious recluse on record. This is a brimful performance, graced with earnest wit, but since the script is not much (its peculiarly American schoolmarmishness might be more appropriate for Louisa M. Alcott), it is best to regard it as a magnificent audition. It allows Miss Harris to display the qualities of a great actress, down to a bewitching lightness of foot in running on for her calls--but not to harness them.

In Ronald Harwood's dramatisation, Evelyn Waugh's The Ordeal of Gilbert Pinfold (Royal Exchange, Manchester) has dramatic shape but no dramatic point. The torments, self-induced, of a Catholic writer hearing voices on a sea cruise are well set out and well directed by Michael Elliott, though I am disappointed that he should countenance so much sloppy acting. But they mean little, for Gilbert himself is established as nothing worse than a routine snob.

In the circumstances, Michael Hordern's tetchy benevolence is actually a hindrance. Alec Guinness was originally cast for the part, and he, in his aloof way, might have rooted it in a real spiritual ache.

records.title: Stars that don't shine
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Stars that don't shine

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on O'Casey, at the National Theatre

THE National Theatre production of The Plough and the Stars has set two platitudes warring against each other in my mind. The first is that foundations should be built upon; the second is the one about lightning not striking twice in the same place.

Bill Bryden's success with The Playboy of the Western World suggested a natural progression from Synge to O'Casey. On this occasion, though the contrary principle asserts itself; the plough lumbers forward, and the stars refuse to shine.

Much of the blame must go to O'Casey. Reaction to the Playboy was certainly coloured by Kenneth Tynan's reference, apropos of an earlier revival, to "quaint pastoral rumbskulls." I don't know that they are any worse than the quaint urban numbskulls who people O'Casey's drama, and at least Synge saw his characters steadily and unsentimentally.

O'Casey's are liable to turn, quite arbitrarily, into heroes. That's life, we are obviously meant to think; that's theatre, we actually respond. For, until they are needed to make some gesture or other, the Fluther Goods and Bessie Burgesses of this play function purely as comic relief. It is amazing, considering how high his reputation stands among modern clowns, how little the play -- as opposed to the stage-directions -- tells us about Fluther. His one characteristic -- his pretence that he has given up drinking -- is strictly from stock.

Cyril Cusack's performance of him here is discretion itself. He shows, uniquely in this cast, the ability to stand silent and yet, unmistakably, to belong. He can trip off a neat bit of alliteration ("fluther a feather of Fluther") and bring the house down.

But such a downbeat rendition can hardly carry the play; not in the face of the support -- ranging from pallor to outright nonentity -- that his colleagues offer here. Anna Manahan's mountainous Bessie is an exception, but even she plays the avenging angel to the exclusion of the squabbling street-trader. She attaches herself, in fact, to the "serious" half of the play, an area surely better avoided. Here dwell Jack and Nora Clitheroe, he devoted to the Irish Citizen Army, she to keeping him home and out of it. He is killed in the Easter Rising of 1916, she loses her baby and runs mad.

This last scene suggests how much of Bryden's dramaturgy O'Casey learned from Shakespeare. Shakespeare, however, left no characters safe from irony; the compartmentalisation of his plays is more apparent than real. O'Casey, carefully fencing off the Clitheroes, wound up with traditional melodrama. What, remembering her fine Pegeen Mike, can one say of Susan Fleetwood, the National's honorary Irishwoman, except that a character who talks of herself with such winsome consistency in the third person ("your little red-lipped Nora") scarcely allows the actress a way in.

All this might cease to matter if the play's essential counterpoint could be established; if the small dramas on stage could be highlighted by the greater events off. It might easier be done in a small cockpit theatre, but in the vast Olivier it is difficult to imagine an off-stage; everything has to happen on. The play accordingly becomes a failed epic; we hear occasionally about bloody street battles, mob orators or rampaging looters; we actually see three actors standing at the corner of a wide stage, unable to fill it with their own drama, let alone to suggest another one.

And O'Casey's fabled richness of dialogue becomes impossible to judge, since it is so difficult to hear; a fault which, in my insular way, I would blame less on the Olivier acoustics than on a team of Irish actors taking their own idiom for granted.

* * *

The production is marginally slower than Troilus and Cressida (Aldwych), but it's a close-run, or close-plodded, thing. For the first couple of scenes the Royal Shakespeareans seemed to be taking their time from some faulty metronome in the wings, one which so absorbed their attention that they hardly remembered to speak to one another.

As the evening proceeded they came to life a bit, though David Waller's Pandarus surrendered no jot of deliberation. He also retains (in a production that has, by and large, put away childish things since it left Stratford) some mirthless comic business with a phallic pillow. This play, too, is hampered by its stage; a far bigger piece than The Plough and the Stars, it might yet work suggestively well in a genuinely intimate area; here it has a goodly-sized one hemmed in by the season's permanent set.

Outsize Meccano strips inserted between the timbers do little to suggest either the plains or the palaces of Troy, and the whole thing has an undeniably shoddy air. Only one performance, Francesca Annis's Cressida, is a full-scale creation, but Tony Church (Ulysses) and John Nettles (Thersites) make the most of their set-pieces, as does Michael Pennington (Hector) when forced unwillingly to contemplate Troy's destruction.

At other moments, Mr Pennington retreats into recent RSC history and intones; so, too often, does Mike Gwilym as Troilus. He is best when intently outlining the limits of love; worst when lamenting its loss.

* * *

Willy Russell in Breeze-block Park (Mermaid) makes obvious points about consumerism, narrow-mindedness and family tyranny (all different faces of the same monster) as experienced on a northern council estate. He makes them, though, with considerable wit, even if it is not the bounding ingenious kind of the same stable's Funny Peculiar.

He has been almost too generous in the creation of his central monster, played by Wendy Craig with contagious relish if not always with total authenticity. The plot revolves around her daughter, who wants to leave her and experience the good life (long tables loaded with wine and cheese) with her student boy-friend. Mr Russell never actually says that this life will be as empty as the one she wants to leave, but the hint is there and, if taken, it enriches the play.

records.title: After all, it''s not Gomorrah
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
After all, it's not Gomorrah

ROBERT CUSHMAN meets the author of the latest Broadway musical to hit London.

THERE is a piece of musical comedy lore which states that the man at the piano surrounded by adoring beauties is the composer; the man biting his finger-nails, neglected in the corner of the room, is the lyricist. Where this leaves the librettist (or "book-writer") I'm not sure. Maybe he never gets invited to any parties.

The book of a musical is traditionally the element of the show that nobody notices. Nobody, that is, except the critics, who can usually be relied on to insult it. Michael Stewart, who wrote the book of I Love My Wife, a Broadway success which opens at the Prince of Wales this week, claims to have a scrapbook full of phrases like "lacks wit" and "despite a weak book by." He looks well enough, since the shows that won him these accolades include Hello Dolly and Bye Bye Birdie; he can afford to.

Recently, anyway, his cuttings-book has brightened; for I Love My Wife he wrote, for the first time, the lyrics as well as the script, and nobody has suggested that they are either weak or witless. Clive Barnes (late of the New York Times) called them "literate," which surprised Mr Stewart; not that he didn't agree, he was just used to Mr Barnes coming out and saying such things.

He spends much of his time in France, and a couple of years ago in Paris he saw there a comedy, by Luis Rego, on the subject of dutifully attempted wife-swapping. He liked the play, though he was less keen on its half-heartedly interpolated songs.

To turn the show into a proper musical, he bought the rights, and refused to relinquish them to a Broadway producer until he was signed to write the words: all the words. For composer he secured Cy Coleman, whose previous scores include Little Me and Sweet Charity and whose individual songs (like Witchcraft and The Best is Yet to Come) are the best recently written in the rhythmic propulsive Gershwin tradition. Coleman was working on another assignment (he still is) and Stewart persuaded him to take on this one by promising that it would only, as in the Paris version, involve half a dozen songs. It grew.

For all that it remains a small show: a cast of four, and a band of the same size, who create a precedent by taking on acting roles as well. This, Stewart cheerfully admits, is the only really experimental thing in the show, though it proved innovative enough to cause a distinct flurry even outside the actors' and musicians' unions. The show has come to London in the time-honoured commercial game, invoking the spirit of Annie. Despite their differing approaches, they are both reassuring shows. The story of I Love My Wife has been moved from France to Trenton, New Jersey, the protagonists rechristened Wally, Monica, Cleo and Alvin.

Alvin it is who states the impulse that moves them all: the desire to "cut loose and have a ball / With orgies relatively small / Because it's Trenton, after all / And not Gomorrah." Though the New York critics liked the show, and despite its immediate success, Stewart found a "guilty feeling" about these lyrics. It had been maybe 17 years, he said, happily, sharing whatever musical honours were to be had with the large-scale Annie.

It is Stewart's own, Seeing Rego's play in Paris he was struck by an "astonishing simple truth" which he could relate to his own homeland. "In the US we're so bombarded by the media with word of the permissive society. Even I have sat home feeling that things must be going on in every apartment in the building except my own."

Like Alvin, he finds two kinds of guilt (puritan and permissive) and they clash. "I think that's the secret of it. Most people are content to fantasise, then come up with some kind of rationalisation for the entire family. There's an innocence about it."

Richard Beckinsale, currently occupied with a similar theme but different tone of Funny Peculiar; Ben Cross, late of the RSC; and Michael Williams and Polly Adams are the London cast. The production is by Gene Saks, the choreography by Onna White.

Stewart thinks that the difficulties of casting a musical in London are overrated. In Paris they are insuperable. But he likes the French theatre. "It's like slipping back in time."

Soft-spoken, sandy haired and 47, Stewart sees the success of I Love My Wife as the end of seven lean years, following on the seven fat ones of Birdie and Dolly. Between Dolly and this one he has had only two Broadway shows, both flops. Now the telephone is ringing again and "the offers are up to one a week again--most of them for impossible shows."

He knows that, whatever the critics say, a musical cannot work without a good script. "Without what the book says--and God knows, it's hardly profound--I Love My Wife would just be a collection of 14 bright numbers; as an adapter I've never betrayed what the original author did it all for."

records.title: Happy impotence
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Are You Now, or Have You Ever Been?
records.body:
Happy impotence

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'I Love My Wife'

THE weaknesses in I Love My Wife (Prince of Wales) are fairly blatant.

Two couples in Trenton, New Jersey, decide with varying degrees of reluctance to celebrate Christmas Eve with an orgy. Husbands Alvin and Wally have some trouble persuading their spouses, Cleo and Monica, to play along, but finally break down their inhibitions by getting them high on marijuana.

The hash turns out to be modelling clay, and the game of four-in-a-bed is over before it has begun, since Alvin, who was always the shyest of the quartet, finds himself unable to perform with a woman not his wife. He sings the title song instead and Wally joins in.

This may be the first occasion on which impotence has constituted a happy ending; otherwise this musical is cut strictly to Broadway-type. It titillates with sex and drugs, but allows no consummation. The argument that these characters would, in fact, beat just that kind of retreat in real life is a powerful one, but they would surely have gone a little farther in experimentation first.

In order to keep them pure till the final curtain, Michael Stewart has had to pad out his slender story beyond its natural span. He does actually get his characters to bed, but he employs them, once there, in a series of coy slapstick routines which would be thoroughly embarrassing were they not so amusingly staged.

A note of praise having crept in at the end of that paragraph, I shall sustain it for most of what follows. My objections were raised more out of duty than conviction; I enjoyed the show mildly in New York last spring, and greatly in London last week. The British cast are not actually more accomplished than their American equivalents--in fact noticeably less. But their klutziness works for them.

I Love My Wife is a do-it-yourself musical; the four actors have to take care of the dancing and most of the singing, and the numbers are set up, out of dramatic context, as a series of essays in various pop genres. For the performers they are like rounds in a talent-contest and the bunch emerges slightly breathless but justifiably cheerful. Richard Beckinsale is the undoubted winner; his singing shapes steadily up towards a captivating rendition of the closer, and his comic timing--stonewalling until laughter becomes happily inescapable--is beautiful.

His Alvin is a different kind of slob from the one presented by his gifted predecessor, Lenny Baker; where Mr Baker gangled, he shambles, and where Mr Baker, even with a visibly unblemished skin, seemed ineradicably spotty, he is grinningly wholesome. Wally, the slickest of the foursome, gets a performance to match from Ben Cross; Deborah Fallender is an appealing and vocally stylish Cleo; and though Liz Robertson's Monica inclines to shrillness, she never really lets the side down.

Another quartet play piano, bass, drums, guitar, and the employees in Alvin's furniture-removal business. They are also a chorus; they are liable to break in brandishing their instruments (no, I don't suppose you can brandish a piano) and dressed, as the situation or the music may require, as tempting devils (with pretty red tails), reassuring Santas or simply as a band. They have their own share of musicians' charm--the appeal, like the actors, of being slightly out of their element.

Director (Gene Saks) and choreographer (Onna White) put the performers through some neat and funny paces; and everyone is buoyed up by Cy Coleman's sparkling score. Through rock, country, cod ballad, straight ballad, military march, buck and wing, and barrelhouse sing-along, Mr Coleman manages to keep faith with each convention while adding to it a lilt, a rhythmic pattern or a sense of fun that is entirely his own.

Mr Stewart's debut as a lyricist falls somewhere between the auspicious and the astounding; his images pile crisply and wittily up, many of his rhymes have a satisfying snap. What lyrics and music lack, however, is dramatic weight, which is partly an intrinsic failing and partly a comment on the action--which, in fact, is what they are designed to provide. But the action hardly calls for comment; it's too thin.

I am veering back to censure, so I shall end by humming a couple of the tunes to myself and assuring you that they make--after the hyped-up melodies of A Chorus Line and the denatured classics of Bubbling Brown Sugar--a very healthy sound.

* * *

Happy again, I turn from actors indulging in song-and-dance to a musical-comedy man giving a stunning home-straight performance. Bob Sherman appears in Are You Now, or Have You Ever Been? (May Fair) as the actor Larry Parks, who, to twist the irony a little further, became a star when he played, but did not sing, Al Jolson.

Soon afterwards his career crumbled as a result of his appearance before the House Un-American Activities Committee. Not that he was an unfriendly witness; he named names. They had to be wormed out of him though, and Mr Sherman gives an unforgettable performance, as real and immediate as the passing moment, of a man striving to make his judges set limits to his degradation.

Eric Bentley's play is taken verbatim from the records; it is concerned only with HUAC's siege of Broadway and Hollywood. A cast-member has recalled her disgust at hearing McCarthyism, HUAC's twin, described as the best goddamned television ever. I see what she means; all the same, I have to declare this piece very nearly the best goddamned theatre around.

I cannot imagine anyone failing to be gripped by it. Its three moods--of inquisition, confession and defiance--offer the actors immense opportunity and the response is the most direct we have enjoyed since Kennedy's Children. (Again the cast is mainly American.) There is not much heroism on view; the imprisoned Hollywood Ten are briefly dealt with, except for those who subsequently recanted.

Apart from Thomas Baptiste's ferocious Paul Robeson, we have to do mainly with uneasily repentant sinners, the more frightening since their brainwashing was largely self-administered, and petty persecutors; Ramsay Williams's chairman, a hoarse and thickset toad, is every Jack in any office.

* * *

The third Yankee import is The Dog Ran Away (Hampstead). The author, Brother Jonathan, is a monk who seems to be travelling all over, getting his plays put on, and his characters are hardly your conventional monasts either. There are three of them, in a Long Island house, with no visible sense of vocation--which could mean (a) that they have none or (b) that it exists too deep to require discussion.

One--probably a case of (a)--stays on and works; the other--a presumptive (b)--runs away like the symbolic hound of the title. They are both dully played, but their companion is more arresting; he is old and mad, and he is given by Robert Flemyng a performance so mannered that I wanted to follow the dog, but so artful that I had to stay.

I had the same divided feelings about the play: impatient that the subject was under-dramatised and under-explained, tempered with a respect not, I think, wholly inspired by the habit which--if his characters are any guide--Brother Jonathan hardly ever wears, even when home.

* * *

Phantom parody

KEEN fans of Phantom Captain, a group of controlled and grave actors who do what I can describe only as a sort of verbal performance art, will probably enjoy The Changeless Congress (King's Head), a parody of science fiction movies played first as a serious black-and-white thriller and then again as a Technicolor musical comedy--but its jokes and ideas were a bit thin for me. And I suspect that only Agatha Christie fanatics will hold their breath during A Murder Is Announced (Vaudeville), a plodding, if well-performed adaptation by Leslie Darbon which treads an interminable space of fishless water before it deigns to bait its hook.
production_title: Are You Now, or Have You Ever Been?

records.title: Doubts about Brecht
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Doubts about Brecht

ONE distinguishing mark of the well-intentioned critic is his tendency to wake in the middle of the night in a cold sweat, full of doubts about Brecht.

It has recently been possible to cast these doubts away on the grounds that we have only been seeing his minor plays. The Good Woman of Setzuan (Royal Court) puts an end to that. It does not, however, sweeten our dreams one whit.

Keith Hack's direction simplifies the play and confuses the audience. The main pitfall of The Good Woman is that its point may well seem to have been made before its story has even begun. Fifteen minutes in, we are well aware that the good nature of Shen Te, the prostitute made rich by a gift from the gods, will expose her to the rapacity of her neighbours; another 15, and we know that she can only be protected by her ruthless male cousin Shui Ta, actually herself in disguise. The interest lies in seeing Brecht spin out variations on his theme; each narrative complication embodies some new paradox. Hence the clear lights and cool playing of Brechtian tradition.

Confined as we have recently been to the earlier Brecht, a new tradition has grown up among us: violent, abrupt and formless. The Good Woman is accordingly performed on a set composed of oil-drums that come in for a fearsome banging during the trial-scene. When the spectators are not being deafened, they are being harangued, less from political passion than as an ego-trip for director and performers. (It is, of course, often difficult to tell these two motives apart.)

The poor people of Setzuan are given a set of sneering creepy-crawly performances. Only two elements of the presentation seem calculated to provide any pleasure: Stephen Oliver's Chinese Palm Court music, and Janet Suzman's pliant and imaginative performance of Shen Te. Miss Suzman's warmth (not really counterbalanced by her outline sketch of Shui Ta) underlines an implicit contradiction in the play; the very existence of a good woman shadows the author's materialism. Brecht himself was aware of the contradiction, and explored it in the scenes involving the gods, here mostly cut. In what remains they are shown, not merely as ineffectual moralists, but as seedy poseurs.

Divinity, all the same, has had a good run this week. The Mermaid have brought us The Fire That Consumes, originally La Ville dont le prince est un enfant, study of a Catholic boys' school between the wars rife with amities particulieres. Special friendships is a less resonant English substitute, and though this production restores the Puddle Dock tradition of putting neglected works on to the Mermaid stage, it also honours the less reputable practice of mugging them once they get there.

When the older schoolboy of the play's twosome proclaims his passion to be higher than that of Racine's Andromache, he clues us in as to feeling and style. They may not be attainable by an English cast; certainly the hearty juveniles of this version get nowhere near. With its ice melted the play looks for much of the time like a protracted and mealy-mouthed restatement of a theme once thought daring.

Only in the last act--a confrontation between the schoolmaster Abbe himself in love with the younger boy, and his Superior who brings the fact home to him--do the actors seem to have an idea what they are about. Even this scene, however, has been misconceived; it is directed not as a duel but as a bear-baiting, with an aggrieved Nigel Hawthorne circling around an impassive David William. And Mr Hawthorne is not really the actor either for the Abbe's profession of faith in human love or for his self-scourging at the end. We get at best the underside of the sympathetic housemaster in an English prep-school story.

Montherlant's play was banned for years by the author's own wish. It is well known that Dennis Potter's television play Brimstone and Treacle has been banned for a shorter period in opposite circumstances. A stage version has now been given an excellent production in the Crucible Studio, Sheffield.

Technically it gives no hint of its origin; the action stays in one room with no rambling. But it still, like most TV scripts in the theatre, lacks texture. Characters and situations, designed to be highlighted by the camera, now look opaque--simple without being clear. Teasing ambiguities turn into bald conundrums.

A diabolic young man, dead keen on house-cleaning (with a duster, indeed, hanging from his waist where his tail should be), invades the home of a teenage girl whom a street-accident has turned into a vegetable. He charms her mother, even for a moment her oppressive, guilt-ridden, Right-leaning father; while they are out of the house he rapes the girl. His action shocks her into recovery; whether this is intentional benevolence or an unexpected by-product we are not told. (I suspect the latter but choose for yourself which would be the more ironic.)

Why a devil should want to rape an unconscious girl is mysterious; he could hardly hope to get at her soul that way. We could--though it makes a less intriguing play that way--dismiss all thoughts of the supernatural, enjoy the dazzling display of soothing platitudes with which Mr Potter has furnished him, and take the Prince of Darkness for a hypocritical young man from the Festival of Light: Housewives' Choice made flesh. He doesn't just dispatch 'mumsy' to the flicks; he adjures her to catch up with The Sound of Music. At moments Mantovani fills the air. Media treacle is made to seem more hellish than traditional brimstone; I would just like to know if one has replaced the other or if they are working in cahoots. In this form the play is interesting without being exciting, frightening without being really gripping.

It is the first offering in a promising season of new plays at the Crucible. Meanwhile the Citizens, Glasgow, continue their hardly less enterprising season of old ones; plays we have never seen, plays we have never heard of. Currently Vautrin by Balzac, entombed since a one-night stand in 1840. Extreme sophistication of design (Philip Prowse offers a glorious Parisian mansion, visibly supported from without by a set of grubby planks, and changing at the billow of a few drapes into a Turkish-delight thieves' kitchen) combines oddly with school-play acting; very good school-play acting in the case of Mark Lewis, whose Vautrin is a brooding outcast master-criminal whose master-stroke is the adoption of his protege and adoptive son into one aristocratic family, and his marriage into a second.

The mixture suits the play; a melodrama that sweeps along with increasing velocity, so that even those who cannot rise to the occasion are swept up in it. Robert David Macdonald, director and translator, pulls all kinds of operatic tricks and, unbelievably, they work.

This rich food, however, is hardly more nourishing than the plain crust of Paul Copley's Pillion (Bush), set in what used to be, but as one character bitterly points out is no longer, the West Riding. This sets off, of course, an attack on bureaucracy wherever it works because the play's values are solidly in front of us.

A motor-bike mechanic's shed (realised in magnificent detail by Grant Hicks whose living-room in Walter at the Traverse was until now the premier realistic design of the year) becomes a workable equivalent of the wheelwright's shop Dr Leavis used to go on about. With its virtues, though, go a certain blinkered obstinacy, fully realised in Edward Peel's performance, the best, in Chris Parr's production, of an admirable bunch.

records.title: Words and rhythm
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Words and rhythm

ROBERT CUSHMAN talked to Crosby a few days before he died

IN A year fatal to superstars -- Callas, Stokowski, Elvis, Groucho -- Bing Crosby may well be missed as much as all the others put together. My one meeting with him occurred just 10 days before his death. I had gone to the Chelsea flat he occupied during his two-week season at the Palladium to talk to him about his deceased friend and colleague Johnny Mercer.

He was much occupied in planning future activities, including a trip to the Far East, and we had some difficulty in fixing a time. He finally agreed to see me at 10.30 in the morning: not, I would think, the best or most convenient hour for a 73-year-old singer working hard every night.

It was an unglamorous meeting; he was in pyjamas and dressing-gown, his baldness and his wrinkles were undisguised, he had a cold, and he had plainly not properly recovered from the fall that had threatened to put him out of action for good. But he was kind and courteous and amusing, and the way he spoke was fascinating.

Not just what he said, though his remarks bore out Shaw's dictum that a man describing others always describes himself; he dwelt on Mercer's feeling for jazz and his love of old vaudeville performers, on the ease and flexibility of his singing, his small-town upbringing, his loyalty to his family and his ability to appeal to both plain and fancy public.

This was a distinguishing mark of Crosby's own work; his corniest songs were distanced, saved from embarrassment, by urbanity and humour. He was often at his best in joky duets (with Mercer, Armstrong, Astaire, Hope, Sinatra) and he assured me that all the ad libs were genuine. The record companies just let them play around.

He had in fact an enormous affinity for language; he spoke to me of Mercer's "little jollities" and "jocosities" and those words, informally formal, illuminated much of his own appeal. He was one of the few American singers who could talk to an audience without becoming unbearably stilted. He slipped very naturally into the role of popular music's elder statesman, since his appeal was always reassuring rather than emotional.

Meeting him gave me clinching proof of his great ineradicable achievement; he established that in popular music the singing voice is valuable only as a natural extension of the speaking voice. That, incidentally, is why his sense of words and rhythm made him the best-liked comedian Tin Pan Alley ever gave to Hollywood.

records.title: And 'Rosmersholm' makes five
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
And 'Rosmersholm' makes five

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Ibsen, Shakespeare and Feydeau

IF statistics mean anything, the most important man in the West End theatre is Clifford Williams, director of five current productions. He is represented at the top end of the market by Wild Oats and The Old Country, at the bottom by Oh! Calcutta! and somewhere in the middle by Man and Superman and, as of last week, Rosmersholm (Haymarket).

No clinching conclusions may be drawn from this oeuvre other than that Mr Williams, like a good Briton, is better at plays than at musicals, happier with comedy than with tragedy, and conscientious about narrative. In his Rosmersholm you want at any rate to know what happens next, or, this being Ibsen, what happened last.

The production also boasts a striking portrayal by Frank Middlemass of Ulric Brendel; seizing on the line about this vagrant philosopher's association with actors, he turns him into a Scandinavian Crummles, fluent of hair and of tongue. He seems rather a wild mentor for the chronically sober Rosmer, but his two scenes ring out like nothing else in the play.

He amply performs the most crucial function of the Ibsenite intruder-figure--one coyly neglected in the text-books--which is to wake the audience up. As it happens the home he invades is more than usually soporific: this despite a distinguished Rosmer by Daniel Massey, shy, keen and bursting with conscience. The strongest thread in the play is his disillusion with the smug opportunism of the left, as with the defensive pomposities of the right. He still ends up, though, an undeniable sap; this may be inevitable, but I should still like to see a Rosmer played tough-mindedly against type, just as I should like to see a Kroll less stolid in his bigotry than Michael Aldridge's competent buffer. (Why not give him a touch of Ian Paisley? An Irish actor anyway might give the play a charge.)

The indications that Kroll is motivated by lust for Rebecca go for nothing here, as does the sexuality, and indeed the ambition, of Rebecca herself. Claire Bloom's performance is entirely neutral; she is a famous actress, Rebecca West is a famous role, and that's about it.

Perhaps she was intimidated by the sheer overloading of the play. Rebecca is a woman who drove a rival to suicide; she then feels remorse, as well she might. It hardly needs exposure to so elevated (and unspecified) a code as the Rosmer view of life to explain the fact. Ibsen in fact is engaging in double bluff; "the Rosmer view of life ennobles," so we have tragedy, "but it kills happiness," so we have a social drama about the evils of entrenched belief, and the two cancel each other out. The top dressing of incest, which so impressed Freud, merely adds to the confusion. Mr Williams tactfully dogs the footsteps of a play which needs to be firmly collared.

* * *

Ibsen usually gets higher marks than Shakespeare as a craftsman, but if Rosmersholm is the attempt, Coriolanus (Stratford) is the deed; and equally likely to confound its interpreters. A play so perfectly proportioned, so devoid of overflow, presents an unfriendly prospect. The central scenes of conflict between plebeians and patricians are an unrivalled dramatic picture of a society on the move, but the mass and energy of the text all too often contract and evaporate in the theatre. Terry Hands's production draws a neat diagram of the conflict, but turns a "mutiny" into a scrap. Perhaps the trouble is simply lack of manpower; anyway the production style is compact, typified by the presentation of the opening crowd as an orderly phalanx.

The play is ensconced in a familiar RSC mould (leathery costumes by Farrar) and Alan Howard's Coriolanus is a natural extension of his Henry V. From a man striving to turn himself into a war machine, he has become a war machine: also, and I mean no disparagement, a rhetoric machine. His clangorous tones are exactly tuned to this play's peculiar music, and some of his special effects--the echoing taunt of "Your voices," the incredulous long-drawn "sh" with which he picks up the presumptuous tribune's "Shall"--are thrilling, ingenious and appropriate.

One misses the excitement (as in Nicol Williamson's Coriolanus or Mr Howard's own Henry VI) of an actor going out to meet a role, and finding himself in the process, but that is the penalty of ideal casting. I have only two major cavils: (a) he fails to differentiate the happy warrior at Corioles from the disgruntled civilian whom he brilliantly embodies in Rome; (b) he gives little sign of the psychological wound that exposes him to his mother's entreaties--and Maxine Audley's Volumnia is not of sufficient stature to do the job alone.

The other actors group themselves round the leading man as the other characters round the hero. Jeffrey Dench's Cominius keeps an honest respectable distance, Graham Crowden's Menenius, though he scents one urbane possibility (which could be a director's touch), still gets insinuatingly close; only Julian Glover's Aufidius seems disposed to set up in competition, and, though commanding, he is canny enough to stay in his own less elevated yard. The tribunes, Tim Wylton and (especially good) Oliver Ford-Davies, go their own way, coolly toppling the protagonist before themselves succumbing to inflation.

* * *

Time was when the National Theatre offered the classiest laughs in London; what with Bedroom Farce and now The Lady from Maxim's (Lyttelton) time may be again. As a taxpayer I have no objection to subsidising Feydeau as rich, and as richly done, as this. There are perhaps no performances to compare in poetry with those of Geraldine McEwan and Edward Hardwicke in A Flea in Her Ear, though Mr Hardwicke is in this one too, very reliable if less hilarious without his cleft palate, and Sara Kestelman approaches Miss McEwan's standard of outraged propriety while adding an aggressiveness of her own.

She plays the pious spouse, subject to saintly visions, of a wild-living Paris doctor who gets entangled with a cabaret tart, whom he has to pass off as his wife in polite provincial society in order to appease his long-lost military uncle who believes ... I shall stop while I'm ahead, and commend Morag Hood's ebullience, Stephen Moore's pace, Michael Bryant's bluster (a turn-up for the casting directory), Timothy Davies's sketch of prolonged pubescence, Harry Lomax's welcome return as a dilapidated butler, and the drilling of Christopher Morahan's production, which was ruthless, doubtless.

* * *

Suicide in B Flat (Open Space) is one of Sam Shepard's doodles on American mythology, and more beguiling than most. A jazz musician may have killed himself, and the investigating fuzz suspect suicide due to creative exhaustion: "his improvisations were lasting for days on end." On the edge of the music and the detective story there transpires, inter alia, a Western; an arrow shot from one world transfixes a character in the next. Deborah Norton, as a lady bass player, again demonstrates her mastery of spaced-out soliloquy. Nobody else sounds quite right, but Christopher Benjamin's cop--bovine and juddery--looks absolutely marvellous.

Given a certain carbon-copy element which is inherent in the operation, the restoration is remarkably faithful.

records.title: Rampaging from Naples to Norwich
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Rampaging from Naples to Norwich

This week a play by the most important Italian playwright since Pirandello opens in London, directed by Zeffirelli. ROBERT CUSHMAN reports.

JOAN PLOWRIGHT and Colin Blakely are getting married again. They appear as husband and wife in Eduardo de Filippo's play Filumena which arrives in the West End (on Wednesday, at the Lyric) only a couple of weeks after Sidney Lumet's film of Equus, in which they are Peter Firth's parents.

Equus was shot in and around Toronto; and it was during one of the lulls in filming (since it takes time to turn the Canadian into the English landscape) that Miss Plowright first broached the subject of Filumena to Mr Blakely.

Her own acquaintance with de Filippo goes back to Saturday Sunday Monday, the penultimate production of the Olivier regime at the National Theatre, and one of its greatest successes. There was a warmth to it that took audiences completely by surprise. And indeed the audience response took the actors by surprise. As Joan Plowright tells it, after the first euphoric stage of rehearsal, "we got into a stalemate. We couldn't go further without an audience. There's no other playwright who needs audience contact so much." I suppose that's because Eduardo writes for a company of actors.

The use of the Christian name, by the way, is not green-room cosiness. De Filippo comes from Naples--he, in fact, personifies the Neapolitan theatre, and there he is, by his own desire, "Eduardo" to everyone. Apart from anyone else, it helps to differentiate him from his brother Peppino, who is, like him, an actor-manager. Both have been seen, with their companies, at World Theatre seasons in London. At one time, however, they acted together in Eduardo's plays, alongside their sister Titina--a magnificent actress, by all accounts, who created what we are coming to think of as the Joan Plowright parts.

Eduardo himself was once called by Gordon Craig the greatest actor alive, and his one appearance in London (in his own Napoli Millionaria) certainly revealed to us a formidable talent, with an amazing gift for making himself quietly at home on a stage and simply existing. He is also generally regarded as the most important Italian playwright since Pirandello, which adds up to as much prestige as any one man should be entrusted with.

Eduardo is now 77; Ben Travers, with whom he has recently struck up a great friendship, refers to him affectionately as "the old chap." (Mr Travers is 90). Though he speaks no English, Eduardo has been over for rehearsals of Filumena and was particularly delighted when the play, on its pre-London tour, seemed to go down well in Norwich. Naples to Norwich really augurs universality.

Filumena was actually the de Filippo play the National first thought of doing as its standard-piece in Italy (written in 1946), it was the only play of his that had crept into the English anthologies. Kenneth Tynan presented Miss Plowright with the only available translation, which she thought too bad to permit any judgment on the play. At this point, Franco Zeffirelli, who had wanted for years to introduce Eduardo's plays to Britain, announced the existence of the far more recent Saturday Sunday Monday. All de Filippo plays are rooted in family life and the family in this one is larger and more rambunctious than most, so it seemed a good bet for the National, then at one of its strongest periods as an ensemble, and so it proved.

The author gave his blessing, only remarking that Miss Plowright seemed too young for Rosa, the materfamilias (and virtuoso ragu cook) of the newer play, though she would be just right for Filumena. This bewildered the lady a little, since there's only about four years' distance between the characters, but she played Rosa to everyone's great satisfaction and, four years having indeed passed, has embarked on the other.

Once again Keith Waterhouse and Willis Hall have translated and Zeffirelli directs; this despite a well-publicised row between author and director after the Broadway failure of Saturday Sunday Monday, done with an ad-hoc cast, and resulting in pressurised caricature. Filumena, as it happens, is more of a star vehicle, and the weight rests on the two leads.

Mr Blakely plays a rich confectioner; Miss Plowright is his long-time mistress, an ex-prostitute who, just before the play begins, has tricked him into a deathbed wedding and then, infuriatingly, failed to die. ("A nice change to do a Neapolitan whore after that repressed lady in The Bed Before Yesterday.") Wife, whore or both, Filumena is emphatically a mother; and motherhood, rather than marriage, is the family piety invoked in the play.

Surprisingly, though they were both National Theatre luminaries over the same long period, the two stars have only been together in one play before. That was Saint Joan, in which Mr Blakely made a ghostly appearance as the English soldier in the epilogue. It hardly counts as a duet; he was able to stay home till nine, and made a civilised progress to the theatre while she was getting tried and burned.

Both players, by the way, are among those who have helped to make regional voices acceptable; he's Belfast, she's Scunthorpe. Part of the fun of Saturday Sunday Monday was hearing an Italian overlay on familiar accents; this was not, contrary to general belief, Zeffirelli's idea. ("You don't," he used to say, "put on Russian accents to do Chekhov.") But the actors found there was no other way to match up to the emotions. And anyway, there's a sense in which Zeffirelli asked for it; a sense in which Joan Plowright likens him to Sidney Lumet directing Equus. They both say: "I don't want any of this English good-taste acting. You can be appalling at the way you find yourself giving forth."

records.title: Explosions in Naples
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: The Fall of the House of Usher
records.body:
Explosions in Naples

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on de Filippo's Filumena

The initial situation of Eduardo de Filippo's Filumena (Lyric) is comic operatic. The Neapolitan prostitute Filumena Marturano, for 25 years the mistress of the rich Don Domenico Soriano, finally entraps him into marriage. Like Volpone or Gianni Schicchi, she takes to her bed. She seems to be dying and Domenico consents to make her happy in her last moments. The ceremony performed, Filumena jumps spryly from her couch.

This event is the most ravishingly theatrical, and also the least obviously credible, in the play. It happens offstage; not merely offstage, but before curtain-rise. What we first see is the volcanically quarrelling couple, flanked by their respective servants. De Filippo, with the craft of either great cunning or great simplicity, has had it all ways. We are given the measure of Filumena's determination, and the play acquires the flavour of classic comedy while remaining a realistic drama.

To see Filumena's stratagem in action would be to become involved in the sheer joy of deception, and thus to get the wrong idea about both the play and its heroine. For the lady differs from her ancestors in Italian comedy; in no way is she in the game for fun, any more than in her earlier years she was on it for fun. Born in the slums she has been prosaically dependent first on prostitution, and now on household trickery, to keep her head above water.

It turns out that she has been fooling Domenico for years. She has three grown sons whom she has brought up on his money and without his knowledge; without theirs, come to that. Her revelation of this fact turns the play into a prolonged family reunion: a joyous event with doubtful, bitter undertones.

One of the boys is Domenico's; she refuses to say which on the grounds that, at this stage, she wants no favouritism. By the end of the play their marriage is confirmed, as we always knew it would be, and Domenico has agreed to stop asking questions. But it is impossible to believe that he will be able to keep this promise; we are given a happy ending with the certainty of breakers ahead.

You have been out of the theatre for some time before this hits you. We actually end with Filumena, for the first time in her life, crying: a conclusion which, the adaptors, Keith Waterhouse and Willis Hall, and the director, Franco Zeffirelli, probably make more sentimental than it need be. A British audience, though, can hardly help abetting them. For us, these people are refreshingly exotic, and de Filippo sunnier than he probably seems to his compatriots.

For the most part, Zeffirelli works a refined version of the magic he exercised in Saturday, Sunday, Monday. This show is less of a carnival: like his author, Zeffirelli acknowledges farce, but does not exploit it; he gives us this time (in a verismo set by Raimonda Gaetani) something more believable and more moving. I almost wrote 'more restrained,' but in fact the production lacks nothing in explosiveness; and in Joan Plowright and Colin Blakely it has two of the most resourcefully passionate players on the British stage.

Mr Blakely starts on a high note of badgered belligerence; his rage at moments lifts him off the floor. And he has the measure of the play's greatest comic scene: Domenico quizzing his three putative heirs to find out which of them--as a singer, perhaps, or a womaniser--takes after him, and pulling up a chair to get a good look at the likeliest suspect.

The throb in Joan Plowright's voice makes it difficult to believe that she has never wept, but her banked-up furies are tremendous. She turns self-pity into honest, cleansing anger, and single-mindedness into generosity. Patricia Hayes as her confidante gives her fierce and funny encouragement, and Larry Noble is a philosophically downtrodden manservant whose every gesture reduces to a shrug. The three sons are fetching in their contrasts, and even more in their unanimity. London could hardly have found a better antidote to power cuts.

* * *

James Robson's The Factory Birds (Warehouse) is more or less defined by its title. We are shown men and women, mostly young but ageing fast, having their humanity blunted (they make machine parts for cleaning out battery hen-coops, and if that sounds gratuitously symbolic, reflect that somebody must be doing it) and, for the most part, acquiescing in it. In the last consideration lies the author's originality--he differentiates. I don't know his history, but it is hard not to identify him with the goaded, sensitive boy who in the end makes the break his loud-mouthed mates have always talked about. The loudest of them all is a self-proclaimed Casanova; the escaper is a virgin. The second act centres on an off-stage rape; and sexism, as the emblem and product of a shuttered life, is most on the author's mind.

None of this is controversial; but then none of it is deniable. The play's obvious weakness is monotony, but it is necessary and stops short of tedium. The play survives, in Bill Alexander's production, on its authenticity and its acting. Enforced companionship always brings out the best in actors, and there is of course the added kick that these are from the RSC, and so presumably used to higher things; Roger Rees is the most spectacular breaker of new and greasier ground, but there are no flies on any of the cast.

* * *

Nor are there any, once you accept a convention in which everyone talks like Valentine Dyall, in The Fall of the House of Usher, which last week was visible at the Cottesloe. Steven Berkoff's style of rigid fantastication actually suits Poe better than it did Kafka.

Alas, the flesh cannot be made to creep indefinitely, as Mr Berkoff seems to recognise, since he makes abrupt descents to the conversational for the odd camp laugh. But the music and movement are as accomplished as ever. Mr Berkoff arrestingly gives Roderick Usher the sound of a mechanical winch in the last stages of disrepair, and Shelley Lee, in her anguished groping from beyond the grave, is a quite transfixing Usherette.
