You're not really queer? say his friends incredulously, and Richie does have his moments of uncertainty. He shares a room with Billy, a nervous college graduate, and Roger, who is black and the best adjusted of the three. They are all privileged soldiers; the underside of the army is represented by Carlyle, also black, aggressively bisexual, and the only character with fully-formed intimations of cataclysm.

But foreshadowing it, he also hastens it on; ferociously disinclined to die for a country that has done nothing for him, trusting only in his senses, he contemptuously seduces Richie and then, cornered, knifes two men. He is festering America: sociologically a victim, dramatically a daemon. If he is the immediate future, the past is personified in two veteran sergeants, full of funny drunk stories; mainly about parachutes that failed to open.

The play is hardly flawless; when not actually letting blood it can be verbose or portentous. But it ranks (with Bedroom Farce and The Bundle) as one of the three best plays in London, and its awesome strength is preserved in Leslie Lawton's production. With no visible sweat Don Warrington brings the animal Carlyle to immediate life; James Aubrey, Jeffery Kissoon and Trevor Jones as the three new musketeers show us the fraying edge of civilisation.

American plays are welcome, apart from anything else, as a means of forcing our actors into hysteria; not, of course, that one wants it to become a habit, but the occasional confrontation must do them good. Simon Gray's The Rear Column (Globe) -- another military play, though the title might suggest a backward English equivalent of The Front Page -- has characters in equally desperate straits but more reticent about it. They go to pieces, they tell us they are going to pieces, occasionally they even display their symptoms, but they never make us feel their disintegration. Something tells me I should prefer Mr Gray, who is all subtlety and suggestion, to Mr Rabe, who lets most of it hang out, but I cannot concur.

The play's faults are not all necessarily the author's. One relates to fashion: his five principal characters are of the Victorian officer class and we are conditioned to expect either an expose or (exceptionally) a defence of their code. Mr Gray simply presents it, and our expectations (to which, for a couple of moments, he seems to subscribe) get in his way.

Another is due to history: the rear column is a back-up force for H. M. Stanley on his last expedition, left waiting for him in the Congo for more than a year, short of men and also of supplies, since Stanley has left them no explicit permission to break open provisions and the officer in charge, not wishing to be caught out by a greasy civilian, will do nothing without orders.

The length of their endurance is its essence, but it is difficult to dramatise; things get worse, but not different, character-conflicts recur. Since Mr Gray writes elegantly, knows his men and has an exotic setting going for him, the play is interesting in 10-minute bursts, but it never fulfils what it promises. Nor is the acting in Harold Pinter's production all that satisfying. Barry Foster underplays the CO's rigid lunacy, though Jeremy Irons as his second deals superbly with the play's central irony. Gentle and considerate, Uncle Osborne of Journey's End to his commander's battered Stanhope, he precipitates final moral breakdown by conniving at a cannibal feast among the locals. Is this, he asks, any worse than the flogging and killing they have all indulged in? A good question, not necessarily in need of an answer, but late in coming.

James Saunders's Bodies (Hampstead) has an awful first act in which two couples, dimly lit, remember mainly in soliloquy (a duologue is a great treat) their reciprocal adulteries. Act Two mercifully brings them together, turns up the lights, and contrasts the satisfaction found by one pair through encounter therapy (physical peace and satisfaction are all that matter, forget all yearnings) with the full-scale middle-class angst of the other.

Most of the latter belongs to Dinsdale Landen, and the play is really entirely within him, since he is about one-third on his antagonist's side and knows it. Given the few jokes of the first half, Mr Landen also has the gratifying rhetoric and self-torment of the second and deals nobly with both.

At the Royal Court a rather clumsy revival of The Bear, Chekhov's variant on the primal Widow-of-Ephesus theme (lady lured out of weeds into arms of impulsive wooer), precedes David Suchet's justly-praised solo rendition of The Kreutzer Sonata, Tolstoy's confession of an uxoricide. The story itself matters less than the misogyny beneath it, and that in its turn is dwarfed by the self-hatred that lies under all.

records.title: A quick guide to the London stage
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
A quick guide to the London stage

THEATRE

A QUICK guide to the London stage:-

A BED OF ROSES (Royal Court from 14 March): The improvising group Hull Truck in its most complex play yet. Excellent songs make it almost a musical - the new British genre.

THE CHERRY ORCHARD (Olivier): Half-successful production, graced by Dorothy Tutin, Albert Finney, Ben Kingsley, Susan Fleetwood, and a nippy new translation by Michael Frayn.

THE ELOCUTION OF BENJAMIN FRANKLIN (Mayfair): Gordon Chater's tour-de-force solo in a wittily written Australian piece about the inoffensive 'transvestite terror' of Sydney; innocent but confined.

PRIVATES ON PARADE (Piccadilly): Improved transfer of Peter Nichols's concert-party memoirs; possibly the funniest show in London, and the best of the almost-musicals. Denis Quilley plays gay, and Nigel Hawthorne very straight.

SAINT JOAN (Old Vic): Eileen Atkins defying hell and breasting high water to deliver a wholly consistent interpretation, backed by a sensible production.

THE REAR COLUMN (Queen's): Caught in the Congo, somewhere between 'Journey's End' and 'Waiting for Godot,' five Victorian officers in Simon Gray's latest go to pieces, victims of the heat, the natives, their absent commander, H. M. Stanley and each other. Handsome and sort of civilised, but long.

STREAMERS (Roundhouse): More military, Americans this time, waiting for Vietnam while doing a better job on one another than the Cong ever could. Our strongest introduction yet to David Rabe, writer of plays and winner of prizes.

Robert Cushman

records.title: Down with clowns
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
WHEN A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum was in trouble in Washington, its fortunes were saved by the addition of a new opening number, a sort of declaration of intent:

Nothing with kings,
Nothing with crowns,
Bring on the lovers, liars and clowns.

The new musical Kings and Clowns (Phoenix), as you may gather from its title, sets out to shatter such rigid demarcations but makes, by gross default, a powerful case for artistic apartheid. After 400 years Sir Philip Sidney, who strongly objected to having clowns thrust in by the heels among tragical matters, has been vindicated.

The aim of Leslie Bricusse's show seems to be to demonstrate that every king is actually a clown, and Henry VIII an ordinary bloke with six wives or a kingdom just like you or I. One has, though, to be tentative in judging its intentions; this show too ran into trouble on the road, less happily resolved. It arrives in town, for one thing, with no one credited for its book.

Once upon a time someone known anagrammatically as Tom Rimer is believed to have been involved; those with a head for this sort of thing have declared him to be Lara Murtin, and I would like to believe him responsible for a powerful speech in which Henry declares his need for a woman who will love him through all his physical infirmities, which are graphically described. This, in its grotesquely credible self-pity, must be what the show was designed to be about. That, however, was probably a long time ago; what is evident now is a desire to get through the evening somehow, anyhow.

I seem to remember that Peter Hall was once slated to direct, and Bernard Delfont to present, a musical called "Great Harry." I know that years ago Sandy Wilson wrote a show on the same subject. More recently on Broadway Richard Rodgers had a King Hal musical called "Rex," short-lived and soporific.

This catalogue of doom suggests that there may be something wrong with this king as a subject. You can have a go at Tudor history and get bogged down, or you can pretend that all Henry ever did was get married. This is the way of Kings and Clowns and it is very monotonous, the same situation repeated half a dozen times, with a scoreboard at the side of the stage to ram the point home and stop us hoping for anything else to happen.

Well, they try. The past and future wives are kept around, a chorus of blithe spirits, to comment on whichever happens to be the present incumbent. Halfway through Act Two, with Catherine Parr at last installed, we are whisked alarmingly back to number one. The ladies have been well cast and each goes through her assigned routine with spunk and, I imagine, the desperate hope of something better next time.

Dilys Watling, as Anne Boleyn, a red-feathered vamp, sort of strips and Anna Quayle, one of the worst-served talents on our stage, delivers Anne of Cleves's bad jokes with such ferocious aplomb that it seems churlish to wish her some good ones. Frank Finlay manages to keep his head above these unaccustomed waters, trouping spryly and tunefully enough to earn a booking with Morecambe and Wise next Christmas. (Have they done Henry VIII yet?) Ray C. Davis barnstorms bravely as the king's jester and, I suppose, his alter ego.

That last suggestion, I know, sounds pretentious, but it is one of the show's troubles that it is not brave enough to be wholly mindless. The man is a fool-and-bring-on-the-girls idea harks back to Mr Bricusse's big success with Anthony Newley, "Stop the World--I Want to Get Off." That was a dreadful show, an idiot's idea of satire; but it had a line and kept to it and some took it for art.

Traces remain here; John Napier, bringing with him some left-over horses' heads from "Equus," has designed a set that seems meant to be sparse and spectacular and is just tacky. (The musical really is an area where looks can kill.) If the choreography is the worst single ingredient of the evening, the direction (by Mel Shapiro) can hardly have provided much incentive; the opening has the cast playing boomp-a-daisy on a strip of stage too small for them--which at least gives the audience fair warning.

As for Mr Bricusse, he perhaps is the real Tom Rimer--he depends on jingle rather than sense to hold his lyrics together, so can hardly afford such clinkers as "morality" and "fidelity." His music varies from the tinkle to the portentous, a combination believed to have great efficacy in the winning of Oscars, and known in pop circles as middle of the road; the show, bankrolled and masterminded by the American Hilliard Elkins, is just middle of the ocean, a damp, dangerous place to be.

* * *

In the first scene of Robert Holman's Outside the Whale (Bush) a short passage from George Orwell's "Down and Out in Paris and London" is read to us; it sounds concerned but faintly patronising. Later a clerk who has nicked a few copies from the Gollancz office prepares to sell them in order to survive; that, it is hinted, is the only social good the book can do.

This, and a few noises on the grapevine, suggest that the play is an attack on Orwell. He may be, in the words of his most famous essay, "inside the whale" ("very comfortable, cosy, homelike"--and oblivious), but there are others who cannot afford the luxury. Mr Holman, however, is a gentle as well as an allusive writer and his central scenes, which show Orwell actually on the road with a tramp, are far from lethal. Obviously the two come from different worlds; certainly they cannot communicate, maybe (but so what?) Orwell is working out his own hang-ups, but the real interest lies in the humour and tenderness of the writing--particularly in a prize scene where the tramp, wrapping himself in scowls and in newspaper, takes a much dreaded bath.

Chris Parr's direction is superb here, as are the performances of Godfrey Jackman and Mark Penfold. The time-scheme is fragmented and the play itself fragmentary, but there are other scenes which show the same mastery of muted domestic discord (though protracted here) as Mr Holman's "German Skerries." He is an oddball writer, and valuable.

* * *

Julian Mitchell's Half Life has arrived in the West End, still witty, still indeterminate, unless you can take one Don's disappointment as a metaphor for the failure of a civilisation. (Some can, apparently.) John Gielgud is now in command, though still too kind for his role; Lockwood West has arrived as his manservant, Richard Pearson has put down roots; otherwise the supporting acting has gone off.

records.title: Dying to be dead
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
MOST OF US have made a theoretical decision about a point, either of pain or disability, at which we would consider life to be no longer worth living.

We have probably been aware that, in practice, a kind of sliding scale would operate and that, even were death to be had for the asking, we would keep postponing the request. We would hang on to life because, having got through one day, we might as well endure another. Habit itself would numb us. But that, too, is a terrifying proposition, enough to make suicide seem an enticing prospect: at least from afar off.

Nothing is likelier to involve an audience than the emotion I can best describe as there-but-for-the-grace-of-Goddishness; and I have never felt it operating more intensely than at Whose Life is it Anyway? (Mermaid). I have rarely been so gripped, my attention has never wandered less, and I have never felt so conscious that everyone in the house was reacting as I was.

We were all rooting for Brian Clark's hero, a sculptor whom a motor accident had paralysed from the waist down, and our sympathy took the unaccustomed form of wanting him to die. It was what he himself wanted, and in making this choice he was toting a load for all of us. Nor does the decision cost him, as far as we are shown, much of an effort; his struggles are all with the world beyond his bed. His chief antagonist is the consultant in charge of his case in whom a professional disinclination to sacrifice a patient's life combines with the general feeling of society that suicide must be essentially wrong and who can point in all honesty to similar victims who have survived into a kind of content.

This doctor, in the writing and in Richard Leech's performance, is allowed dignity and intelligence; Mr Clark is fair minded. But mind is not everything, and his heart, his guts and his wit are all on the other side. Ken, the sculptor, is both funny and attractive; to top it all he is played by Tom Conti, whose more extravagant mannerisms have of course been forcibly eliminated by the physical circumstances of a role which otherwise allows unlimited scope to his peculiar gift: that of making other people feel not merely sorry for his sufferings but guilty about them. He is at once abrasively self-pitying and damnably charming. The self-pity in this case is wholly justified, which should set up even more complicated vibrations but in fact results in a moral landslide.

There is a curious discontinuity here; long after Mr Clark's theme has been established, his plot goes on reiterating it. The consultant invokes the Mental Health Act to retain his control of Ken (a man who can logically argue that he wants to die must be insane is the Catch-22 argument) and Ken's solicitor responds by trying for a writ of Habeas Corpus. All is resolved in the judge's chambers (which for the nonce are located at Ken's bedside) and the decision remains in doubt till the very last moment.

The play works in fact as a thriller in addition to its effectiveness as polemic (and I believe it to be one of the very small body of plays which, because it articulates widely held feelings, might have a genuine social effect). It scores, too, in Ken's reactions to impending vegetation; particularly his bitter awareness that sexual desire does indeed outlive performance and that he is beginning to think and talk like a dirty old man.

Craft and dialogue are generally excellent. The analysis of the nature and function of hospital routine (institutional repressiveness at, in all senses, its purest) is fair enough, but Peter Nichols and Trevor Griffiths have done it better. There are too many lay figures among the supporting characters, notably the sympathetic lady doctor (Jane Asher) and the solicitor who, with surprising speed, takes Ken's part. The weaknesses can be felt at the time, but they do not interfere with the enjoyment.

* * *

A couple of years ago Mr Conti was involved in a singularly luckless attempt at Moliere's Don Juan. This play finally gets its English deserts at Greenwich in a production and translation by David Thompson.

Mr Thompson is probably the most underrated director in the British theatre; at least I have yet to hear anyone imperiously demand that he should be given his own theatre. He could make better use of it than most. No phrases flash out at you from his translation but the whole is singularly well-knit. There are no obvious visual coups either, but there is constant satisfaction.

Peter Rice's set is dominated by a great pair of doors and these, open or closed, are a continual source of satisfaction. A pair of carved saints at either side of the stage admirably set the religious background about which Moliere was so enticingly non-committal. There is plenty of orthodox sentiment in the play, most of it in the form of moral missiles aimed at the hero, but neither he nor his opponents are at all endearing.

The production's main merit is the obvious one that the actors are permitted to inhabit the play, rather than to wander uncomfortably through it. Frank Barrie's Juan, the height of cool, is matched with a dwarfish Sganarelle (Peter O'Farrell), common sense compromised by cowardice: the prototype comic servant, in fact. His famous cry for his wages, with his master dead, shows us Mr Thompson at his most tactful. It is not a moment; it does not crush us with Savage Irony; it has actually been pared down, but it haunts.

* * *

And so for a plunge into the cesspool. That is how Orwell introduced his essay on No Orchids for Miss Blandish and the Glasgow Citizens' company, as might be expected, take the plunge with enthusiasm. This is in fact their best production I have seen, piling on the tension, the sex, the cynicism, the violence, the madness and the drugs in a manner calculated, if the longed-for crunch ever comes, to drive Agatha Christie wincing from the West End.

And if the cast seem young and their accents well-intentioned but bizarre, then that does not crush us with fits too; James Hadley Chase, as I was reminded last week, never himself set foot in the States. His America is like the Jacobeans' Italy, a gloating fantasy; and the comparison certainly fits here. In this version all crosses are doubled and only one character survives the bloodbath: a private eye who closes the evening with Marlovian (Philip, not Kit) moralising.

If bits of Robert David Macdonald's adaptation are incongruously high-flown, his direction is exhilaratingly high-flying. The morality may be pernicious, but it is free of the hypocrisy that Moliere castigated more effectively in Juan than in Tartuffe. The sharks all eat each other; whose death is it anyway?

records.title: Mr Deeds goes to prison
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Mr Deeds goes to prison

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Nottingham, Manchester and London.

On the occasion of Richard Eyre's departure from the directorship of Nottingham Playhouse, four worthy playwrights, all in their time beneficiaries of his regime, have had a whip-round. The total of their contributions is a play called Deeds; described as 'by Howard Brenton and Trevor Griffiths with Ken Campbell and David Hare.'

There are belligerent, bewildered passages that suggest Brenton, others with a northern wit that could be Griffiths. Underneath everything is a wild anger, not exempt from sentimentality, that could be anybody's except, curiously, Griffiths's; his rages are generally more practical. Nor is he usually given, though most of his contemporaries are, to the profusion of incident that marks this play: it is not called Deeds for nothing.

Actually a pun is involved; the hero is called Ken Deed (say it fast) and the play is his quest. There is also a Mrs Deed and, briefly, a baby Deed. The child's death from dehydration is attributed to its being fed on powdered milk, wrongly made up, though Ken only learns this from hospital gossip. (The consultant either didn't know or wouldn't tell: strange behaviour, either way.)

Trying to get, by the nearest means, at the truth about the fatal concoction, he wrecks a supermarket and is sent to prison. Refusing his mates' advice to appeal, he devotes his time inside learning 'to climb': an accomplishment which later enables him to spy on a board-room meeting on the offending firm of Nuzzles Milk and later to break in on their master-mind in his Savoy suite and force him to sign a kind of confession. He also lobbies his MP and a supposedly friendly minister, to no effect, and finally decides to end it all by drowning himself in a railway-truckful of Nuzzles. In the nick of time his wife Mary reappears and persuades him that steeplejacking and self-immolation are no way to make a revolution.

As proof of guilt, the authors resort to showing us their villain frolicking in a bath with a couple of call-girls. Ken on the other hand is healthily monogamous--and at the end of the play Mary is carrying his second child, promising to raise him as a properly indoctrinated avenger. The Puritan backlash is gaining ground in unexpected places--though perhaps the authors are less against pleasure than the fact that it's the rich what gets it.

Mary seems actually a scarcely less exasperating character than Ken; she has communicated with him only through a riddling note, while working things out for herself. But her mental processes, which take place offstage, might have been more interesting than his--might even have included a measure of self-reproach since, however confusing the label on the tin, she was the one who misread it.

The best recent political plays have explored a specific issue and let it reverberate. Deeds skips the issue and jumps to the reverberations which, accordingly, do not reverberate. I doubt if any of the collaborators would have worked so sloppily on his own. The play, with its constant changes of scene, makes a good leaving present for Mr Eyre and he has unwrapped it, greatly aided by his designer, John Gunter, with justified enthusiasm. There is satisfaction in seeing so convincing a rail-yard; and a real thrill when an apparently genuine lift heaves in to view on the revolve, so that we see it first three-quarters on, then in full frontal. (The National Theatre should be so lucky.) The cast oblige too, with Mick Ford in full control of Ken's inflamed doggedness. His linking soliloquies, spotlit downstage, have the impact of a screen close-up; that sounds easy, but I have never seen it managed before. It remains true that a bad epic play is less boring than a bad naturalistic play, but that is a last-ditch justification; did anyone feel Comedians to be confined because it took place in a couple of rooms?

* * *

The Deeds intend to breed a killer. The idea of justified murder was tried out in the thirties (theatrically, I mean) by Irwin Shaw in The Gentle People, revived at the Royal Exchange, Manchester. Two refugees, a Jew and a Greek, face another expropriation by a Brooklyn gangster who demands protection for not sinking their treasured fishing-boat. They pay; he demands more. One of them protests; he gets beaten up. The worms really turn; and get away with it.

The unlikeliness of this, particularly the last part, is carefully pointed up; the play is an ironic fable for the age of appeasement--or a sane man's Arsenic and Old Lace; the killers being so endearing and all. They get added justification when the hood (if he's really a mobster, incidentally, where's his mob?) gets to messing around with the Jew's daughter--and she, incredibly, goes along with him, despite being fully in the know. Even Shylock never had it so bad. The play moves too slowly for our tastes (its three acts should be redivided into two), but it does move, and tickle. The Royal Exchange again proves its aptitude for plays set mainly on boats; John Bennett and Harry Landis as the goodies do well against flabby opposition.

Still with murder: at the Roundhouse Downstairs The Boston Strangler speaks disturbingly, mainly in his own words; the actor, John Cunningham, makes him Everyman. There are also some bits that the credited author, Mike Stott, must have written: brief businesslike re-enactments of the stranglings and precedent rapes, determinedly un-titillating, each of the 13 victims being played by the same actress who, mentally at least, is not infinitely undressable. An odd entertainment but, since it grapples with some kind of truth, not contemptible.

records.title: Slices of nostalgia
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Slices of nostalgia

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on some 'showbiz nonsense.'

IN A backward-looking week the most palatable nostalgia was served up by Ginger Rogers at the Palladium. She starts of course with a huge advantage, having an unusually large slice of the past at her command. I mean, as they say, no disrespect; Miss Rogers makes no secret of her years, and besides, better preserved Ginge you could hardly hope to find.

It is still unusual to find a director credited for a variety act but Miss Rogers lists one, and with reason. Onna White's staging is a masterpiece of tact and timing. We begin with a few clips from the Rogers-Astaire movies. As the screen is whisked away a voice, surprisingly strong, starts up in the wings on the verse of "Night and Day" and you suspect that everything is going to be all right.

What follows is illustrated, and selective, autobiography. It is not without its irritations. The narrative is glutinously written and archly delivered; you wait for some hint that the lady is sending herself up but there is never a crinkle. Miss Rogers bounds from sentence to sentence, from name to famous name, and indeed from side to side of the stage; she is very enthusiastic about her own career and the enthusiasm becomes contagious. She speaks of herself, with wistful compassion, as a frightened teenager about to play her first major role on Broadway: 1930, this was. The show only happened to be Gershwin's "Girl Crazy," and her two solo numbers were merely "Embraceable You" and "But Not for Me." She sings them, again very well. (She curiously fails to mention another newcomer in that cast who got an even bigger hand and whose name was Ethel Merman.)

So to Hollywood and the Busby Berkeley era: "Forty-Second Street" and "Gold Diggers of 1933" (the best) and producers making unscheduled appearances in rehearsal rooms ("Why, come in ... oh, Mr Zanuck") and forcing our heroine to go right ahead and sing "We're in the Money" in baby-talk. So much history. We are dazzled. And she hasn't even started with Astaire yet.

When she does get to the great partnership she dwells with suitable emphasis on the composers and lyricists involved. She goes into a Kern and Gershwin selection (Irving Berlin is reserved for special treatment later) and something surprising happened. I know these songs, really, too well; and I had expected to do no more than nod approvingly as each one washed over me. But I actually listened. Her authority is complete; for the first time I could accept her as, in her own right, a star.

The screen is lowered again for extracts from "Kitty Foyle" and "Roxie Hart," ostensibly so that we may appreciate Miss Rogers's extra-musical range, but really so that she can change. Only then does she, to any extent, dance. Her gowns actually prevent us from seeing, with any clarity, what she is doing with her feet but she can certainly glide. Though she likes to refer in tones of hushed mischief to the gamine she once was, her stage persona now is all great lady: the hardness of edge, and the craziness, that were so valuable in the flicks have gone. But the whole act is beautifully integrated.

Donald O'Connor, who precedes her, seems unsure of what the justification for his appearance is supposed to be. This is sad, for on the evidence of his films I would have supposed him to be, in strict terms, the more talented of the two. But he lacks the one great advantage which Miss Rogers exploits; he is not a legend. Just once, perhaps--doing "Make 'Em Laugh" in "Singin' in the Rain"--he attained greatness, but that routine could scarcely be reproduced on a stage, even were Mr O'Connor 25 years younger. (He used to be as dapper as Danny Kaye; he's now as fleshy as Mickey Rooney.) And then he was always stuck as hero's best friend, whether the hero was Gene Kelly or Francis the Talking Mule.

Anyway, he has to work, not just be. Where Miss Rogers cannily pretends to be breathless, he gets breathless in grisly earnest. I suspect that he could still structure an act around his singing, which was always better than that of most hoofers, but the structuring had better be done quickly.

* * *

Kismet (Shaftesbury) is generally described by both friends and foes as a great slice of Turkish Delight. All then depends on your taste-buds; it is not my favourite brand of candy but there is nothing wrong with the preparation, which is baubly and bangly though not particularly beady; I imagine that the original leading man, Alfred Drake, was a more determined charlatan-beggar-poet than John Reardon, who plays the role here. But his singing is good and round, as is that of Lorna Dallas as his daughter and Joan Diener as an irresistible (and unresisted) temptress.

There is lively choreography. Dervishing is apparently a less specialised trade than I had supposed; anyway, most of the locals are good for a whirl. The composer, as is well known, was Borodin, who didn't know what he was doing at the time; he is unlikely to write another musical but if he does I should like to hear more of his rhythm numbers and less of his ballads, "Not Since Nineveh" being far more congenial to my ear than "Stranger in Paradise."

* * *

At the Roundhouse a Dutch group, Hauser Orkater, have brought something bewilderingly entitled The Hunch. I may be paranoid but my own hunch is that the show is satirising precisely the kind of showbiz nonsense to which I have devoted so much space this week. Otherwise I wouldn't care to explain it. It contains inconsequential poems considerably delivered in English (the accent makes them sound Brooklynese), a striptease by a female impersonator alarmed to discover unwanted body-hair, and a great deal of loud, vengeful rock.

Nine of the ten actors get together at the end for a deafening drum ensemble; I remembered how Duke Ellington used urbanely to remark, after percussion solos, that "a drum was a woman" and wondered if this had any bearing on the tendency of Hauser Orkater to keep their womenfolk in what the programme refers to as "the blue object" and which actually looks like a jerry-built washing-machine with the occasional limb protruding from its port-hole. It contrasts pleasingly with the stage-floor which is made up of bright red slats. Recommended to those who like primary colours, aural and visual; others will fidget.

records.title: The best of Bruce
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The best of Bruce

THE acting profession is getting uppity. The first night of The Travelling Music Show (Her Majesty's) ended with Bruce Forsyth coolly informing us that, though we had disappointed him at first, by the second half we had pulled ourselves together and made some kind of audience of ourselves, was how he put it. It had been, he implied, uphill work.

I don't think he knows when he's well-off. Two points should be quickly made. First, I enjoyed the show very much. Second, Mr Forsyth is probably the best thing that subsequent audiences fresh out of their coaches will eat from his hand instead of gnawing at it. If returned, he will presumably get the Bruce of Beat the Clock and The Generation Game. We had something better, something too more in accord with what the show seems intended to be about.

Careful. Those theatre journals which conscientiously reprint the logbooks of assistant directors working on experimental productions in Warsaw might do us all a service if they could let us know just what befell The Travelling Music Show on tour. We were led to believe that it would be a showcase for the collected works of Leslie Bricusse and Anthony Newley. Many of their songs are surtitles (nothing, alas, from Mr Bricusse's first and best score, Lady at the Wheel) but they are neither explored nor exploited. They might be any songs: in fact it is part of the scheme of the show that they should, to an extent, be done badly.

Mr Forsyth plays Fred, a Limelight entertainer and family man, gambolling all but bringing London a revue about itself. He has a supporting cast of five, of whom one absents herself from the premiere. So the show goes on, with the others frantically covering for her. Their plight is amusingly and economically illustrated in an opening number which is brightly staged and has a gap. Throughout the evening we are whisked very smoothly from backstage where the cast are panicking, to onstage where they are triumphing.

Well, three of them are. Fred's wife and Fred's daughter and some young man or other step into assorted breaches, in assorted dresses, and knock 'em dead. (It says here. No, really, they do all right.) Another young man is played by the amazing, malleable Derek Griffiths, who announces at the beginning that he's never been on a stage before. I can think of no performer of whom that seems less likely. In Round the Horne once there was a sketch about an unknown who went on in a concert-party, with no experience, no rehearsal, and would you believe it, he was absolutely diabolical. This is Mr Griffiths's role here, though a man of his parts can hardly keep that up all night, and he is allowed some delightful reprises.

Fred meanwhile, with fame to win and fortune to keep, goes through the night in a spirit of desperate aggression, brilliantly embodied by Mr Forsyth, all talents bristling. He plays magisterially off a recalcitrant house. Yes, he tells his colleagues, they're a nice audience; there is no viciousness in them. That's a beautiful line. Is it in the script? Is there a script? Is the show's structure a springboard or a safety net?

Tucked away in Burt Shevelove's production are some happy digs (mainly costume changes) at the bits of theatrical ingenuity that are plainly tending towards mayhem, have to be forcibly rerouted in the interests of the next plot. But the show is a triumph of more than ingenuity; the Papal scenes approach magnificence, and the madhouse episode actually attains it.

* * *

Lark Rise

Lark Rise (Cottesloe) also conscripts its audiences: those at least who stand and mingle with the players on the ground floor. This, like The Passion last year, is a promenade production. Watching them from above, I was fascinated by their ebb and flow; I've seen far less interesting movement from companies who've rehearsed. In one scene nine men go, do allegiances; to me a meadow, advancing in a straight line on the punters who respond with a first-rate impromptu mime of the parting of the Red Sea. Later some of them allow themselves, with due bashfulness, to be dragooned into joining in a children's tug-of-war game; and at the close there is country dancing.

Keith Dewhurst has dramatised the first part of Flora Thompson's rural trilogy, Lark Rise to Candleford, ingeniously shaping its scattered details of milk, wood, fashion, into an account of a single day in the life of an Oxfordshire hamlet in the 1890s. The family who are meant to be at the centre of it (one of its indistinctive features: the faint performance by Laurence Hanman as the boy), but the periphery is alive and the directors, Bill Bryden and Sebastian Graham-Jones, have moulded some excellent groups. It makes a pleasing and informative entertainment, marred only by the hint of do-goodery that seems to afflict any show involving folk-songs.

* * *

The Duchess of Malfi / The Second Mrs Tanqueray / Eejits

Julia Blalock, grappling with three ambiguous heroines at once, fuses them by main force; if her trial scene is exaggeratedly impudent (she might as well poke out her tongue at her judges), her final passion makes amends. The whole cast, under Philip Prowse's direction, breathe in the poisoned Renaissance air like petrol fumes.

At the Sheffield Crucible, Peter James has directed an almost violently unstuffy revival of Pinero's The Second Mrs Tanqueray; Mel Martin and Richard Easton emote with a fury and velocity that are exhilarating even when they exceed credibility.

Meanwhile in the Crucible's studio Ron Hutchinson's Eejits, a successor to his Says I, Says He, this time dealing with emigrant or second-generation Irishmen, each a poor imitation of the wrong kind of thing entirely. This means they drink, swear, quarrel and shoot past the point of monotony (and are fully, though not disgracefully, indulged in this production). Mr Hutchinson remains, how you say, promising.

If Rayner Bourton's script had chosen to follow this line it might have given us something which the Stone's could never have managed themselves. As it is the show turns out to be a harmless but rather limp little offering.

records.title: On stage
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
On stage

ROBERT CUSHMAN'S quick guide to London theatre.

In a desolate London scene one recent offering has been outstanding:--

WHOSE LIFE IS IT ANYWAY? (Mermaid, until Saturday; returns for a further run on 24 April): Brian Clark's gripping hospital piece asks whether or not a crippled Tom Conti should be allowed to take his own life. You almost expect the lights to go on, and the audience to be canvassed for opinions.

* * *

And one reasonable:--

KISMET (Shaftesbury): 25-year-old Turkish bath of a musical, old-fashioned even then, but tuppence-colourful and well sung.

* * *

A few golden oldies:--

THE ELOCUTION OF BENJAMIN FRANKLIN (Mayfair): Australia's most celebrated play; Gordon Chater's performance in Steve Spears's sparkling monologue of a transvestite is a tour-de-faiblesse.

* * *

FILUMENA (Lyric): De Filippo comedy, one of Naples' staples, given a funny and moving Zeffirelli production, with Joan Plowright and Colin Blakely.

* * *

MACBETH (Young Vic): The fabled Trevor Nunn-Ian McKellen-Judi Dench production transfers to a slightly larger theatre.

* * *

PRIVATES ON PARADE (Piccadilly): Life in a post-war troop concert-party, staged that way, too. Seems to have come out lighter than the author (Peter Nichols) intended, but no one else will worry. Taken all round, probably the most amusing show in town.

* * *

SIDE BY SIDE BY SONDHEIM (Garrick): The best theatre-songs of this generation, intelligently anthologised.

records.title: The soup tastes good
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The soup tastes good

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a Wesker revival and a new Ayckbourn.

IN THE FIFTIES Arnold Wesker's Chicken Soup with Barley (Shaw) made a terrific impact by presenting on stage people who talked seriously about politics. We are used now to seeing people who talk seriously of nothing else; the rare compulsion of the play at this date is that they really are people -- and the real treat, that Mr Wesker writes without a trace of contempt for them, his audience or himself.

The personal appeal of the play now far outweighs the polemical. At its centre is Sarah Kahn, an East End Jewish matriarch and a lifelong Communist; we eavesdrop on her, her family and their friends over a 20-year span, from the invasion of Whitechapel by Mosley's Blackshirts to that of Hungary by Khrushchev's tanks. Sarah is the only person on the stage whose commitment survives this last event: a fidelity made possible through ignorance. We are informed that she never read a word of economic theory all her life; someone told her that socialism meant love and she believed them.

This credulity seems, on one level, admirable; on another it is just foolish. And Sarah's folly both enriches and damages the play. The damage comes when Mr Wesker, pulling himself together and remembering where he is, seems -- as in Sarah's ringing curtain line, 'If you don't care, you'll die' -- to put his full weight behind her.

The enrichment is more pervasive, and it fills the play with ambiguities. For Sarah's husband, Harry, has emphatically not cared; and he, if not quite physically dead, is a mental and spiritual corpse. Having suffered a couple of strokes, he is a shambling, incontinent wreck. Whether his wife's enthusiastic bullying -- which she offers as proof of how she fought all her life -- has propelled him to this point, or whether he would have reached it anyway, is left an open question.

She emerges as a particularly fascinating type of the woman who loves humanity at the expense of those near her. Not that she neglects her family: her charity does not only begin at home, it is rooted there. It is very practical; at almost every moment of the play food is being cooked or eaten or a kettle brewed. But it is a charity fatally divorced from tolerance.

So her friends, while respecting her, are glad to get away -- geographically and, as their faith crumbles, politically. Her daughter goes the same way. Her son -- who seems in his awkward posturing to represent the author's revenge on his younger self -- wonders repeatedly which of his parents he takes after.

* * *

A number of younger playwrights might have imposed a neater ideological pattern on this story but they could not have given us the Kahns. Anthony Cornish's production is journeyman work in some ways (people keep going on strange exploratory walks round their own livingroom), but, through the performances of Barbara Young and Martin Friend, it releases the play's real strength. Jack Chissick, who ages particularly well, stands out among the comrades.

There is actually a clearer political polarisation visible in Alan Ayckbourn's Ten Times Table (Globe). The opposition in Chicken Soup is kept off-stage; Mr Ayckbourn offers a Tory lady, a young Marxist schoolteacher and several indeterminates between, all of them sitting on a committee to organise a village festival. However, the play is literally a departure. Having explored kitchen, bedroom, livingroom and garden shed, Mr Ayckbourn has finally left home.

The journey has done little to impair his faculties. The meetings are faultlessly done, the absentee members almost as vivid as those present. The festival hinges on the re-enactment of a local legend: the massacre 200 years ago of the Pendon Twelve, the village's own Peterloo. Each faction espouses its own side of the cause; at the close the peasantry, clad in new home-made jerkins, take on the establishment, led by a drunken Earl of Dorset unsteadily mounted on a hobby horse (in private life the earl is in electrical goods).

The farce of the last scene is a let-down after the preceding high, or at least uppish, comedy; a reversal of the situation at the Scarborough premiere last year, where the company, though expert and enthusiastic, were often too young for their roles. Two who were not have been brought to London and more than repay the trust: Christopher Godwin as a brusquely demented dog-breeder, a Mad Mitch of the North Riding, and Diane Bull as the teacher's self-effacing lady who converses mainly in mumbles. (This part has been beautifully observed.)

The London contingent -- recruited from the middle-brow, middle-weight, middle-income actors for whom Mr Ayckbourn has done so much and vice versa -- are not all so exciting; Benjamin Whitrow and Tenniel Evans give, by their own standards, routine performances and Julia McKenzie is cast not so much against type as against form; her success in Side by Side by Sondheim came in emotional rather than comic numbers and her best moment here is a breakdown.

Paul Eddington, however, radiates well-modulated bewilderment from the chair, Stephanie Fayerman is thoroughly convincing as a turncoat, and Mateylock Gibbs, dealt all the best lines as a deaf but spirited old lady, plays them excellently to the accompaniment of a brilliantly benevolent beam.

* * *

Last year, when reviewing Illuminatus! I remarked that its success confounded most of the arguments against transferring novels to the stage; all you needed was time. I didn't know that I was being inspirational; apparently, though, I confirmed Mike Alfreds, director of Shared Experience, in his determination to bring Bleak House (Theatre Upstairs) to the stage in four full-length instalments. On the evidence of the first I can only thank Mr Alfreds for proving me so right and himself and his company so talented. The secret of the enterprise lies in the group's name; having enjoyed the novel, they pass their pleasure on to us. I shall explain how when I have seen the cycle entire.

In the meantime I merely recommend and pass on to Manchester, where the old dramatising method -- gallons into pint pot -- has been followed with Crime and Punishment (Royal Exchange). To the credit of Paul Bailey, his piece is a play, rather than a series of snippets. Each short scene has shape and momentum.

But there are crucial failings; Mr Bailey eschews soliloquy, so we are denied an insight into Raskolnikov's mind until the murder is done, after which everyone starts explaining it to us, too late for us to take an interest. Then there is the playing. The magnificent Leo McKern is on hand as the investigating inspector (a ministering as well as an avenging angel), but Tom Courtenay brays excessively as Raskolnikov.

Michael Elliott has perhaps the finest moral sense of any director in the English theatre but he seems compelled to express it through spineless actors and weepy actresses. Perhaps it is unfair to pick on the good prostitute Sonya; she is an impossible character, but Shared Experience managed to bring the priggish Esther Summerson alive and even likeable. It is easy of course to leaven Dickens with humour while leaving the nightmare intact. No one, certainly not Mr Elliott, would try it with Dostoevsky?

records.title: Driven quite mad by peace
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Driven quite mad by peace

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on David Hare's new play and a Japanese company.

DAVID HARE'S Plenty (Lyttelton) is described in a programme note as a history play. The history comes in two varieties: Social and Case.

We skim the years between 1943 and 1962. At the first extremity Susan, aged 17, is seen working as a courier to the resistance in France. She then pursues a varied, but generally disastrous, peacetime career; much of it spent married to a junior diplomat, apparently fated to remain junior for ever. There are occasional references to ration-cards and such; but as far as the actual style of the dialogue is concerned, time stands still, strongly suggesting the disenchanted 1970s--particularly the version of them familiar on our best-regarded stages.

Two outside events are mentioned: the Festival of Britain, a symbol of manufactured national reassurance, and Suez, standing for disaster. The latter is in fact the first act-curtain, and it is a flashpoint for Susan. But for us, and for the play, it seems too obvious, too isolated; we know, by now, what to think about Suez.

Susan takes it at the time as a welcome portent. "Everything is up for grabs, we will see some changes." She is reiterating, in opposite terms, an optimism she also expresses on a peaceful French day at the end of the war: "There will be days and days and days like this." There won't and there aren't. If you think things look good, they change; if change itself looks good, it doesn't happen.

The problem with using these dramatic poles is that it hardly matters what you put between them. Almost any evidence will support you. So Susan's own story comes over as arbitrary, both in itself and its relation to external events. Suez gives her a chance to lash out at the Foreign Office; when her husband's career seems blocked she has another go. We can all agree that the Foreign Office represents Britain at its most British, and for a few moments it seems clear what the play is meant to be about. Then the picture clouds again.

The trouble with Susan as a mouthpiece is that you never know where, intellectually, her attacks are coming from; she becomes a front for generalised disaffection, and what cannot be unloaded on her is transferred to her scarcely individualised sidekick Alice. They generate between them a few laughs and a good many more sardonic chuckles. They belong in spirit with the heroes and heroines of John Osborne.

Mr Hare is of course a far more controlled writer than Mr Osborne. He remembers to attack his protagonists; he does so, in fact, with icy ferocity. Susan's wartime record, the implicit justification for her intransigence, also gets blamed for it; you didn't talk to people much in the resistance and sex was an encounter of strangers. The pressures of peace drive her mad, literally, and marriage hardly helps. She ruins her husband's career, but even this matters less than it should, since we never know what his job meant to him anyway. Late on he denounces her for her selfishness and delivers, from the audience's point of view, the most satisfying tirade of the night.

The good will earned by his delivery of this speech brought Stephen Moore (though he is excellent throughout) the warmest of responses at the curtain-call. It feels like the last word on Susan; but since the play proceeds for another two scenes it obviously isn't. Like the singer in Mr Hare's Teeth 'n' Smiles, she is indulged, castigated, then indulged again. There is a fine line between irony and equivocation, and the play ends up on the wrong side of it. Susan has witty moments, even moving moments, but she never comes through whole and alive.

She does work, though, as a whopping part for Kate Nelligan, who gives a performance of shattering composure which when itself shattered--as when suddenly clinging, feet off the ground, to a fellow-agent, or in the frantic measured declaration "I am in temporary need of this room"--genuinely disturbing. Julie Covington pounces voraciously on the scraps Miss Nelligan leaves over and shows a welcome ability to transcend not just her own period but her own age-group; she gets visibly solider as the evening progresses.

There is much good miniature work as well: Basil Henson and Frederick Treves as soft and hard FO chiefs, David Schofield and Lindsay Duncan as the losing youth of two decades. There is no lack of accomplishment in the playing, in Hayden Griffin's sets, or, apart from an occasional stateliness (possibly endemic to the Lyttelton), in Mr Hare's direction. No lack of accomplishment, come to that, in his writing. It is not a wasted or unexciting evening; merely a frustrating one.

* * *

The Japanese company Tenjosajiki has come to Riverside Studios with Directions to Servants, title from Swift, substance a sequence of stunning images of sadomasochism; something in which we can all take an interest, though not necessarily when served neat for two hours.

I have a recurring problem with the Theatre of Stunning Images tout court; I am mightily impressed for 10 minutes, I then go on being impressed, but am bored as well. (As with Tadeusz Kantor's more quiescent The Dead Class at the same address a year ago.) If the human condition is really being stripped bare, then the human condition has been overrated. That the director Shuji Terayama is a master (that seems the right word) and that he commands an intrepid group of automata is undeniable. This is dead-end theatre; but you should see it once, and now is probably the time.

* * *

Royce Ryton's comedy The Unvarnished Truth (Phoenix) has an incredible plot. It becomes clear that this is its point (sounds of critics striking their heads on the floor as rugs are pulled from under them), but I don't see why the characters have to be incredible as well. Under such circumstances laughter, on any continuing basis, becomes difficult; when it does come, it induces self-hatred.

The leading players, Tim Brooke-Taylor and Graeme Garden, have slight stage personalities, though Mr Garden purveys an endearing brand of casual panic. Jonathan Lynn's production, logistically good, is disfigured by some of the worst supporting acting in London. I am forbidden to tell the story, but, what the hell, it involves death and a completely new brand of sexual discrimination. There.

* * *

At Salisbury's newish and attractive Playhouse, I caught, not having been inculcated, a new kiddie-rock epic called Gilgamesh, he being an extremely primeval Sumerian hero--or hero as the opening couplet has it. Since there is no dialogue, that kind of aural torture goes on all night. The music includes occasional relieving bits of pastiche. There are cute lighting effects; there is cute everything.

records.title: Kamikaze tactician
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Kamikaze tactician

ROBERT CUSHMAN profiles one of Britain's most influential theatre directors who is now turning his talents to television.

THE theatre of the decade for new work -- the Royal Court, if you like, of the 1970s -- has not been in London at all.

For the past five years Nottingham Playhouse has been a centre for writing and acting, brittle in style but wide in scope; that has influenced the Court itself, the National Theatre and such fringe companies as Joint Stock. It has also touched television; and the Playhouse director during this period, Richard Eyre, has now in fact moved on to the BBC as a producer of Play for Today.

Eyre, who is 35, began his professional life as an actor. Even that, he insists, was an accident; he had intended to become a journalist. Certainly he always wanted to write, and it had occurred to him that he might well at some point write for the theatre. When he went up to Cambridge in 1961 involvement in university theatre seemed a good method of preparation. So for three years he acted -- in, it must be added, extremely good company. So at least it seemed to me, viewing his generation through dazzled freshman eyes two years later. Robin Ellis, Michael Pennington, John Shrapnel are among his acting contemporaries who have made professionally good.

I have memories of standing around in some undefined and probably unnecessary capacity (in the professional theatre I could at least have made the tea) on a production of The Caretaker; Eyre was the tough brother, Shrapnel the lobotomised one, and the tramp was Jonathan Lynn, who now also runs a rep (at Cambridge, in fact). Neither Eyre nor Lynn directed anything much as students, though; Eyre actually directed a film, which he now describes as "a 16mm. piece of avant-garbage." Cambridge meanwhile was full, as it always is, of people who thought they were going to be directors. Hardly any of them have succeeded.

The turnabout for Eyre came soon afterwards at Leicester, where he was appearing in The Boy Friend, delivering "a collector's piece of coarse acting -- no, that's overrating it. Acting is the most depressing job in the world, if you realise you can't do it." To stave off depression, he organised some of his colleagues into a Sunday night production of The Knack, which was successful enough for Clive Perry, the boss of the theatre, to face him with the brusque and unexpected question, "Well, which are you going to be, an actor or a director?"

Put that way, there was really very little choice. Eyre went, prophetically, to Nottingham, assisting John Neville on a couple of plays that eventually toured the Far East. He did freelance productions for the Liverpool Everyman and the 7.84 company, and in slack times worked as drama editor for a publishing firm and even, I assure you, as a theatre critic for The Scotsman.

That figures because it was in Edinburgh that his directing reputation was really established. He worked at the Lyceum there for his old mentor Clive Perry, and as Perry turned more and more towards administration Eyre began doing the bulk of the productions. He ran through many of the standard classics (including all four major Chekhovs) and began, as well, to find himself as a director of new plays. It was in this role that he came into prominence when he took over in Nottingham: first (in January 1973) as deputy for the incumbent director, Stuart Burge, and then in his own right. "I've always been interested in writers. Why, some of my best friends. . . ."

One of them, David Hare, went with him to the Playhouse in the first instance as literary manager; and Brassneck, written by Hare and Howard Brenton, was the first world premiere of Eyre's regime, a social comedy built to the capacious scale of the Playhouse stage and auditorium. (It is one rep without a studio for new work to be banished to.) The success of this play, followed by Brenton's Churchill Play and Trevor Griffiths's Comedians (which Eyre, with reason, counts as "a contemporary classic"), established Nottingham as the home theatre of the new generation of public playwrights: a generation too young for the Royal Court and too ambitious for the fringe.

They are also writers in demand elsewhere, and to lure them to Nottingham Eyre pursued what he calls "a kamikaze policy." I said, "Write a play and I guarantee I'll put it on." I could offer them a definite commitment and, with hindsight, I'd defend having done every one of them." The list also includes Stephen Lowe's Touched, which I disliked but which Eyre regards "with great pride: a play about Nottingham, by a Nottingham author, but ambitious, not parochial."

The play is set at the close of World War Two, which reflects not only the author's but the director's preoccupation with the last 30 years. "Brassneck" covered the period from the Labour victory of 1945 to the end of the Poulson era -- the crucible out of which our present state has crystallised." Eyre grew up in Devon, sheltered, he insists, with little knowledge of the theatre or of real life. Going north, he says, made him realise there really were two nations -- and I don't mean England and Scotland." At Nottingham he had to function virtually as a liaison official between theatre and city.

As well as writers Eyre has developed some tough, quirky actors ("Comedians" was a terrific ensemble production). "It's a real pleasure going to work with a group of people, friends." His wife, Sue Birtwistle, runs the Playhouse's Theatre-in-Education company, and there are times when she's had as large a company as me. I'll miss keeping open house for them all." He may even mean this. The Eyres' Nottingham home is extremely pleasant, and the move to London has made house-hunting a far greater headache than script-hunting.

He has in fact a number of scripts lined up for his television series. He got the BBC offer last June; James Cellan Jones, the Head of Plays, was looking for scripts from contemporary writers, and though no one, least of all the man concerned, ever knows precisely how these things work, it seems reasonable to assume that Eyre has been commandeered to continue his Nottingham work for a wider audience.

Certainly some writing links are being maintained. Trevor Griffiths is writing a film. (Eyre has been contracted to do 10 plays, two films and eight in the studio.) Scripts have been commissioned from other theatre writers -- Robert Holman, Barrie Keeffe, John McGrath -- and also from novelist Tom Clarke. Clarke's piece is the first to go into production: a play about apartheid, but set here, and dealing with our responsibility for it. If the series has a unity, it should lie in Eyre's concern with the way public behaviour hinges on the private and vice versa.

He alternates between relief and regret at ceasing to run a theatre, though after five years relief seems uppermost. He's glad not to be directing for a bit, though he will handle one TV play himself, probably next year. When I talked to him he had just made the common discovery that "watching other people's filming is very boring," but, like most people who have got within yards of all the fascinating hardware of TV, he has not done badly with hardware on the stage and there seems no reason why his Nottingham style ("highly wrought detail alongside the spectacular") should not transfer from one medium to another.

records.title: Return of Don Juan
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Don Juan Comes Back from the War
records.body:
Return of Don Juan

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on plays by Horvath, Shaw and Shakespeare.

ODON von Horvath's Don Juan Comes Back from the War (Cottesloe) was a casualty of the aborted season of Juans planned for the National Theatre.

As it happens, the recent Greenwich production of Moliere's entry in this hallowed competition has provided the context originally envisaged for the South Bank. It's been nice to see both plays, but they have not illuminated each other much. Perhaps they would have done if we had seen them under the same roof, but I am more inclined to regret that the Horvath play reaches us so long after the disappearance of its parent production, Tales from the Vienna Woods.

This Don Juan is the kind of stripped allusive play that dramatists traditionally turn out in their last years. Horvath was still young when he wrote it; he was, all the same, only two years from his death, and the nature of the play - which is death-haunted - is enough to make you believe in premonitions. It assumes the world of soured romanticism more elaborately presented in Vienna Woods. It also assumes, without providing very much detail, the period of hyper-inflation that followed in Germany on the end of the First World War. But this should be no trouble. In 1936, when the play was written, it was recent history; for us, it is myth and more potent than most.

Horvath's Juan belongs to the great twentieth-century line of disenchanted, almost passive libertines: the object, not the instigator, of the chase. He is the only man in a cast of 13; and the dozen actresses play an average of three roles each. In those circumstances no wonder he's Don Juan.

Juan's charm leads him to financial as well as amatory success; in a world where cafe bills mount casually into millions he emerges top of the heap. Much of the play (which is only 90 minutes long) is taken up with the recriminations of the women who throw themselves at him; recriminations aimed at one another as much as at him. A fragmented picture is built up of a society which actually is not fragmented at all; at every level, its preoccupations are grimly uniform.

The play moves into its highest gear, however, when city intrigues are left behind and Juan goes in search of the one girl whom, in pre-war days, he loved and betrayed. We have known from the start that she is dead; have met her grandmother who, from a distance, offers Juan real hatred; from everyone else he gets only spite. He ends, in a scene that reaffirms Horvath's power of infusing melodrama with new life, by his girl's snow-covered grave. He is a doomed figure whose fate has already been prefigured in one brief and dazzling scene: the decapitation of a snowman. Some of the earlier scenes are laboured, but the ending is theatrical poetry as fine as anything since Chekhov.

This beautiful, perplexing play is given a capable if rather tight-lipped production by Stewart Trotter, superbly served by Christopher Hampton's translation and by the mournfully magnetic Daniel Massey. The National Theatre seraglio paraded for the occasion includes such favourites as Polly Adams, Helen Ryan, and the Susans Fleetwood and Littler; but of the many varieties of female bitterness on view it is Janet Whiteside's that strikes home the hardest.

* * *

Love, war and their general unfairness are further irradiated, in an excellent Greenwich production of Arms and the Man. Robert Chetwyn's staging has been condemned as 'un-Shavian.' That, to my mind, is its strength; Mr Chetwyn forsakes the usual rattling tempo and the resultant automatic laughs, and finds real sex, therefore real romance, therefore real comedy.

One actually wanted to see Raina and Bluntschli, the destined lovers, brought together; and Felicity Kendal, in her best performance to date, flashes with bewitching aplomb from Raina's affectations to her blunt realism. Lewis Fiander's Bluntschli, her mirror-image, has to bide his time; the deliberate pacing does rather dampen his jokes (which are most of his role) in the first act; but they allow him to command the stage as the comic judge, and finally the comic victim, of the later scenes. Sergius is unfortunate, neither a real nor a chocolate soldier, but Ursula Mohan as the maid Louka is suitably provocative (which in this play means sensible) and the bewilderments of Major Petkoff become, in Frank Middlemass's hands, the pivot of the plot if not the entire play.

* * *

Not much love of course in the three parts of Henry 6 (as the Aldwych insists on billing this scholar-king, though he was surely at least as good a Latinist as his father V); though all the war you could desire. There is not too much virtue in seeing all three on the same day; unlike The Wars of the Roses aeons ago, they have not been shaped for cumulative effect. Though Terry Hands's production is almost endlessly resourceful (and had better be), he cannot, in remaining so faithful to the text, avoid repeating himself.

Part Two is certainly the best play; a magnificent animation of court intrigue in the long truce between foreign and civil wars. But the most enjoyable is Part One; a glorious re-ordering of history to the playwright's own convenience. Part Three, with even more carnage, plods more; full of battles the author had to include rather than those he wanted, and conducted for much of the time in bellicose but strangely bloodless one-liners.

Its four great scenes are glimpses of another world; two of them - Henry's yearnings for peace on Towton field, and, most especially, his murder by the incipient Richard III - have ripened since Stratford; Alan Howard, fine in the first, is inspired in the second, embracing death while somehow remaining a human sacrifice, not a suicide. Earlier on he delivered less a characterisation than a commentary on the play roughly from Henry's point of view. (Did he want the laughter that greeted the words 'poor soul' severed from their followers - on hearing that one of his subjects had been born at Bury?)

Many performances have gained in amplitude: Anton Lesser's Crookback, Julian Glover's Warwick, Emrys James's York now twitching less, and David Swift's bulldog Talbot, a part once played similarly and as well by his brother Clive. (The Talbots are one race who go always to the Swift.) I am puzzled by a new Stratford puritanism, which decrees that rhetoric shall be ladled out to the audience in full frontal, while jokes, as in the Jack Cade scenes, are coyly hidden. These, to keep the best till last, are democratically-written plays in which any actor, soldier or messenger, can find himself for a moment carrying the show; hardly anybody in this team drops it.

* * *

At the other extreme Alec McCowen holds the Mermaid himself with his rendition of St Mark's Gospel. Mr McCowen is an actor of unexampled lucidity and a master of two opposed modes - the rhetorical and the quizzical. In this performance the two fuse into a kind of defiant humour, an acceptance of mystery that tackles doubt head on. The most powerful line in the evening, a hammering shout, is 'help thou mine unbelief.' That, from an actor to an audience, is the most potent prayer of all.
