records.title: All-or-nothing epic
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
All-or-nothing epic

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Ibsen's 'Brand' at the National.

THE fascination of Ibsen's Brand (Olivier) is the impossibility of determining where the ice breaks.

The implacable Norwegian priest in his glacial mountain parish works necessary wonders in stiffening the souls and spines of his flock. He does much the same to his own neck. By the end of the play his vocation has resulted in the deaths of his wife and child and his own exile; stoned by the formerly faithful. A mad girl, finding him broken and bleeding, takes him for Christ. A moment later, in highly symbolic circumstances, he is killed by an avalanche, while a disembodied voice proclaims the God of Love: thus presumably letting Brand know where he went wrong.

We may know where, but how about when? There is no identifiable moment at which beneficent rigour shades over into inhuman presumption. Even at their most repellent, Brand's actions are in some way defensible; the balance of forces is more perfect than in any play since 'The Bacchae.'

That much is theory, and necessarily vague. The practice, unfortunately, is hardly more specific. The programme (the most informative at the National in some time) quotes Ibsen's declaration "that Brand is a priest is really immaterial; the demand of All or Nothing is valid for all aspects of life." Brand, he said, might just as well be "a sculptor or a politician" (as in subsequent plays -- all variants of this one -- he actually became).

This is all very well, but it means that we see very little of Brand, so to speak, actually on the job; he vocalises about his duties and responsibilities, but he never defines them. He calls for sacrifices, but, except when dealing with his immediate family, he refuses to explain not only what they're for, but what they are.

He is in fact the idea of intransigence, and as such quite at home in an epic poem -- which is actually what Ibsen wrote. But since it is in dialogue it is bound to be staged, and, since it is by Ibsen, it can, with the right actor, work. It did so at Hammersmith 20 years ago when Brand was gauntly and explosively played by -- I almost wrote "the late" -- Patrick McGoohan, since his subsequent career has been another tragedy of waste.

But the incumbent pastor is Michael Bryant, whose strengths lie in humanity and understatement. Probably no actor can play Brand without visibly and audibly goading himself, but with Mr Bryant the ends -- which is italic quoting -- fails to justify the means.

His adversaries, the crowd, are largely at the mercy of Ralph Koltai's ingeniously sliding set. When it is, so to speak, at full tilt, the groupings look interesting; on the flat they are painfully limp. The director, Christopher Morahan, staged some good massed scenes in 'State of Revolution,' but that was in the Lyttelton; if the future of our classic theatre lies on vast open stages like the Olivier, our directors will have to acquire new skills. (Or perhaps re-acquire old ones: I write this fresh from reading 'Astonish Us in the Morning,' an inspiring collection of tributes to Tyrone Guthrie, who was both the prophet and the great showman of the open stage, and who left a gap as yet unfilled.)

I have to add to all this the information that the performance lasts close on four hours. However, persevere. There is a salty new translation by Geoffrey Hill, unexpectedly funny (I look forward, after a suitable break for refreshment, to Mr Hill's 'Peer Gynt') and varied in its rhythms, thereby offering fidelity to its source and opportunity -- too seldom seized -- to its interpreters.

There are also good middle-reach performances: Patience Collier makes an ashen irruption as the hero's avaricious mother, and, as the Mayor, Robert Stephens is quite stunning in his cunning. As written, this local politician is vigorous but a type; Mr Stephens, turning all his idiosyncrasies to account, does him full emblematic justice but humanises him as well, giving his author more than he asks but nothing he cannot accommodate. Previous acting versions have dispensed with Ibsen's topical satire; here it seems the most pertinent part of the evening.

* * *

In Prospect's Twelfth Night (Old Vic) Sir Andrew refers to a "dun-coloured stock" instead of a flame-coloured one. He has to, clad as he is in a pair of 1920s ducks from the Ben Travers collection. This woke me up to the fact that this is a modern-dress production; earlier I'd taken it for granted. (It would take something really revolutionary -- a doublet-and-hose, say -- to really jerk me out of my seat.)

You will gather that I know this text too well; were I less jaded I might have got more out of this show, in which the funny bits are done funny and the melancholy bits melancholy, the latter winning out, since the comics are unintuitive while the tragics have on their side Eileen Atkins's wise Viola, Louise Purnell's frightened Olivia and -- as her lugubrious soulmate and our master of ceremonies -- Robert Eddison. He is actually playing the fool, but it is difficult to wish him other than he is. His is the final and the finest moment of the play, when the wind and the rain song ends in "we'll strive to please you every day" and "we" turn out to be the Prospect company promising not only scattered showers but the rest of their season.

* * *

The sisters of Tom McGrath's play at Stratford East are three in number, and they aren't ever going to get to Moscow. Or anywhere else they might want to go. Their hopes are blighted almost before they are expressed. They are East End schoolgirls, only friends really: One Pakistani, one West Indian, one working-class. (Well, of course, they're all working-class but the script's descriptive powers don't run to a third adjective.)

It is the kind of play that seems to have been researched rather than written: lively and apparently accurate; but aimless. When creativity does take over, the results are jarring. Most of the scenes alternate schoolroom and playground; as blackboard jungles go, this is a mild one. The teacher even manages to make himself heard, though the script may have intended more riot than the production achieves. A show whose most convincing moment is a fit of vomiting has surely got its priorities wrong somewhere. Among the cast Tim Stern, in fierce black specs, fetchingly suggests the teenage Harold Pinter (or a teenage Harold Pinter), pauses and all.

* * *

A Cool Million (Open Space, transferred from the Half Moon) is the same kind of theatre in fantasy-time. Based (freely, I imagine) on a Nathanael West novel, it charts the downfall of innocence in a strange region of depression America, somewhere between Mid-West and Deep South. There are bright, sharp moments, mostly occurring in Andy Smith's pastiche songs, wittily and meticulously written and engagingly performed.

In the same category is a monologue, of doubtful provenance, from Michael Irving as an Indian chief who has a gesture for every word, and delivers both simultaneously. Benny Young makes an appealing male ingenue of the hero Lemuel Pitkin, who loses a couple of organs, a few limbs and finally his life in pursuit of the American dream, duped by a Fascist party which finally claims to have saved America from sophistication. On the evidence of this show they have done a thorough job.

Last week, in reviewing 'Henry VI,' I read Bury for Berwick. Obsequious apologies to the burgesses of both towns, to all my readers, and to the entire Royal Shakespeare Company. In self-defence, it sounded like Bury. But I should have looked it up.

records.title: Disorderly conduct
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The new Stratford-upon-Avon season offered a brace of unexpected prologues.

The Tempest began with an apology from its director, Clifford Williams, for the breakdown of the theatre's computerised switchboard into which the play's lighting-cues had been irrecoverably locked. Two nights later, Jonathan Pryce, billed as Petruchio in The Taming of the Shrew, was observed, apparently drunk and certainly disorderly in the stalls, coming up very rough with a programme seller who was attempting to tame him--and who looked to my puzzled eyes very like Paola Dionisotti his destined Katharina. So, Shakespeare's last comedy and one of his first, with nothing much in common except a final preoccupation with concord and the difficulties of achieving it: which means, of course, they have everything in common. It is a theme of which both productions are aware, though in style they are as different as the plays themselves. To simplify unfairly: Michael Bogdanov's Shrew is good and mod; Mr Williams's Tempest is trad and bad. I don't know how much The Tempest suffered on its first night from the torch batteries and the tallow candles; Ralph Koltai's set, an anonymous wasteland, might have been transformed by proper illumination, but on its own it is featureless. Mr Williams's main success, and one not to be underrated, is his arrangement of the immensely difficult final scene with its six separate groups of characters.

Paul Brooke's unregenerate Antonio (the only fat Shakespearean villain I have ever seen) stands or sits aloof from the general rejoicing. Prospero--a performance of extraordinary kindness by Michael Hordern--realises that, where his brother is concerned, he has failed; but the awareness goes for little since the production fails to blend all the characters into the same play.

There is little tension among the courtiers, no more than routine ardour from the lovers, and, O Jupiter, how weary are the spirits. And where are the clowns? There ought to be clowns.

There is, however, an impeccable Ariel--an extraterrestrial Jeeves--by Ian Charleson, who deals beautifully with the most haunting songs Guy Woolfenden has ever composed.

David Suchet seems as Caliban to have broken through the barrier that separates a reliable from an exciting actor, though his grudge against Prospero is difficult to understand as they are both such thoroughly nice people. (This is actually the most charitable Shakespeare production in years, and if only for that, I would love to see it come together.) Mr Hordern shows no bitterness towards Caliban which, read it how you will, robs the play of a dimension. Otherwise this is a Prospero well within sight of greatness: a study in love, loss and--supremely--resignation. He effectively surrenders his powers on the line 'They shall be themselves,' restoring to his enemies their freewill in full awareness of what they are likely to do with it. It is, more than incidentally, a performance free of mannerism and vocally glorious.

To return to Mr Pryce, whom we left duffing up the hired help. He clambers on stage claiming his name is Christopher Sly, and offering a free translation of Sly's actual lines ('I'll pheeze you in faith' becomes 'No bloody woman's going to tell me what to do'). He personally demolishes a pretty period set (arches and fountains and things). It is never seen again.

Enter, as in Shakespeare's Induction, a Lord, who proposes to dress Sly up as another Lord. A page boy (Mr Suchet, looking disgusted) is got up as his lady. Then, though no players have been announced, The Taming of the Shrew starts; Mr Pryce is (a) bemused, (b) embroiled, (c) Petruchio. The show is now plainly his dream, but at what point it began--or why, before the play proper, he should talk modern and everyone else Elizabethan--I couldn't say.

However, if what follows is sometimes lacking in finesse and even--given its premises--in invention, it is full of interest. The play becomes a man's vision of revenge on a woman. This is not a love-at-first-sight Shrew; there is a spark between them, even some fun, but he torments her, and she suffers, in earnest.

Miss Dionisotti gets round her big repentance speech partly by personalising it (as both her husband and her playwright instruct her), but most of all by taking it literally. When she says she will put her hand beneath her husband's foot she does so--and he, moved and a little appalled, withdraws the foot. You are left distrusting the partnership while liking the partners. Mr Pryce confirms his supremacy among our theatre's horde of bovver-boys, but apart from that this tearaway performance is nearly all--not quite, since he mutters a bit--that could be wished; he is an actor with rhetoric at his command, and a deadly quiet at his core.

The production--done in real modern dress, not the usual pop artifact--is justifiably very money-conscious. Baptista assesses the competing bids for his daughter's hand on a mechanical calculator. When Tranio makes his big offer, it blows up under the strain.

For the closing wager on their wives' obedience, the men sit round a green-baize table, handy for brandy and also for roulette. Petruchio, the winner, remembers to rake in the chips; Baptista conscientiously writes a large cheque for the reformed Kate's second dowry. The production is intelligently ambiguous about the play's ethics; 'Peace it bodes and love and quiet life' as Petruchio says, but only on masculine, mercantile terms.

The production is played up stairways and across catwalks: a severe contemporary ambience to replace the one that Mr Pryce destroys. Both set and performance are concerned to make us rethink the play. They are also concerned with enjoyment, which is enhanced by a motor-bike, as dubious a horse as ever staggered upon two pairs of actors' legs, and a thoroughly delicious Bianca from Zoe Wanamaker. Messrs Brooke (Baptista), Suchet (Grumio) and Charleson (Tranio) reappear with honour.

* * *

Some of the hardest-hearted men I know, not all of them critics, have yielded to Annie (Victoria Palace) and I propose to join them. It is the story, derived from a legendary cartoon strip, of a little girl who escapes from an orphanage, is adopted by a billionaire, and very sensibly hangs in there. Since she conquers him at first sight and they just go on liking each other, the show does lack a little intention. True, there's a kidnap bid, and Annie just happens to suggest the New Deal to President Roosevelt, but that doesn't add up to what you would call a plot.

I could also object that Charles Strouse's score steadily declines from a promising start; that Martin Charnin's lyrics are far less adroit than his direction, and that a Kurt Weill chorus of the unemployed has nothing to do with the rest of the show, which is firmly in favour of wealth--and which shows, in David Mitchell's super-efficient sets, just what can be done with it.

Efficiency is of course the conquering element: that and a shrewdness in treating Annie and her protector (an increasingly confident Stratford Johns) with perfect seriousness while poking fun at nearly everything else. Thomas Meehan's script includes a delightful parody of a Depression radio show, complete with invisible ventriloquist, 'masked announcer' and closely harmonised exhortations to smile.

Andrea McArdle, a rather large Orphan Annie, has come from Broadway for a few weeks; Dorothy Loudon, who played her chief oppressor with bewitching shamelessness, has unfortunately stayed at home, but her replacement, Sheila Hancock, is game. The show has half a dozen thoroughly drilled singing-and-dancing moppets and the dog. But it doesn't hedge its bets; it also has two teddy bears.

* * *

The Homecoming (Garrick) is a streamlined revival of Harold Pinter's most concentratedly vicious play. Kevin Billington's production captures all of its abundant humour; Timothy West's simian ex-butcher trades exquisite insults with his sons; Michael Kitchen, poncing, and Roger Lloyd Pack punch-drunk. The family tensions are hypnotic; purest Pinter. The sexual fighting works less well, with Gemma Jones an unconvincing temptress. But the real trouble here is that these characters exist only in a continuous present. Whenever we are told things about their past the trouble is not that we don't believe, but that we don't want to know.

records.title: Aboard the good ship Snoo
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Aboard the good ship Snoo

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN finds excitement at the Court.

THEY are raising spirits at the Royal Court; mine among them.

Snoo Wilson's The Glad Hand should do more to restore this theatre's reputation than any play in years. It concerns a man who tries to summon up the Antichrist; and the one thing that can be predicted of such a quest is that it will always succeed. If you believe in monsters or in scapegoats you will find them.

Mr Wilson's snark-hunter is a South African capitalist called Ritsaat, who credits the Antichrist with the dissemination of Marxism. To root out him and it he charters a ship; fills it up with actors, a playwright, a CIA man, an electronics freak, and a family of villainous Irish domestics; and sets off in the direction of Cuba.

I'm sorry, this isn't making sense. But the play does, perfectly, so I'll try again. The thing is, Ritsaat believes that the Antichrist was last sighted in 1885 during a cowboys' strike (this -- the strike, I mean -- really happened) in Wyoming. He's not going there, of course, directly. But he hopes, within the propitious geometric confines of the Bermuda Triangle, to perform a play about the strike whose vibes will be so powerful as to propel him and his quarry towards each other.

Sceptics like me have sometimes fallen foul of Mr Wilson's concern with the occult; here he makes it easy for us. Like Tom Stoppard he sets up impossible situations and explains them; and his wit in this piece has a Stoppardian exhilaration. Then, again, if Ritsaat is an exploiter he is also exploited; his psychic surgeon is a self-confessed charlatan. We expect, maybe dread, a magical explosion; it is deferred and deferred until we mentally discount it; finally, with the full weight of the play behind it, it explodes, bringing what have seemed random or playful elements into new alignment.

Meanwhile we have been entertained with brilliant variations on the all-in-the-same-boat theme; and, in the second act, with the promised play-within-the-play. Much of this is parody of the didactic strike-breaking dramas, all short scenes and starvation, usually served up in community theatres. The sheriff, traditionally moustached, is the reactionary villain ('cowboys don't belong in unions, cowboys belong in bars'), but his opponent's speech is genuinely stirring stuff -- enhanced, not nullified, by the complexity that surrounds it. (Its speaker is, in the outside play, distinctly unsavoury.)

Another drama of labour unrest takes place on board, directed against Ritsaat himself, who must be the most disarming dictator-figure in modern drama. Antony Sher, who is shaping up into a truly remarkable actor, plays him crew-cut, trim-bearded, humourless, and implacably eager.

The last time I felt this excitement at the Court was with Howard Brenton's Magnificence, directed, like this play, by Max Stafford-Clark. The production here has some of his Joint Stock characteristics; off-centre but still precise, it is in its way a social panorama. (An American girl, sort of passing through, defines the English disease as 'standing around leaning on unsprayed car doors,' which is really all that needs to be said, though some writers say it at greater length.) The cast -- Tony Rohr, Julie Waters and Will Knightley are among them -- leap on the play, and win the freest laughter I have offered any play in ages.

* * *

Additional proof is provided by Per Olov Enquist's The Tribades (Hampstead), which shows us Strindberg hysterically asserting his own masculinity in the face of an affair between two actresses, one of them his wife. Peter Woodthorpe and Susan Hampshire make -- in the Strindbergian sense -- an admirable married couple; that is to say they bitch beautifully. But of course Strindberg's miseries have already been exhaustively dramatised by Strindberg and this piece is pretty heavy for a footnote. I suppose, and dread, that young American playwrights are already hard at work on O'Neill.

* * *

The Club (Regent) is the latest girlie show; seven ladies portray the inhabitants (five members, two staff) of a male enclave in fin-de-siecle New York. They sing ballads glorifying women and tell bar-room jokes reviling them; the point is accurately made that these are opposite sides of the same limited attitude. That is established in about 10 minutes; afterwards everything, as in most musicals, depends on performance level.

In the successful off-Broadway production, staged with great spirit and resource along a projecting ramp, this was very high. In Tony Tanner's London version, performed on a handsome but constricting set, the cast don't seem to know where to put themselves. They have to (a) sing and dance (b) look male (c) sound American. The only performer to succeed in all categories is Linda Thorson, who should take the town as a man about it. The material would sound far sourer if performed by men; I am grateful that the author, Eve Merriam, tried for something more delicate, but not even androgyny is a guaranteed source of theatrical interest.

* * *

Sandy Wilson's The Clapham Wonder (Marlowe, Canterbury) is about levitation: an intractable subject, even for a musical, and surrounded by domestic misery to which Mr Wilson's polite, jolly style is totally unsuited. Pip Simmons's adaptation of The Tempest (Riverside Studios) has more unity than some straight versions, largely owing to its sandy set. Most Shakespearean cut-ups end up as parodies, and this one is at least good-humoured.

records.title: Old pals act
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Peter Allen at Madisons Supper Room
records.body:
Old pals act

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

ONE OF the postulates of Ben Travers's Plunder (Lyttelton) is that our two heroes, Freddy Malone and D'Arcy Tuck, were at school together.

The memory inspires them both; it prompts D'Arcy to help Freddy in his house-breaking, jewel robbing schemes (the house is actually Freddy's own, but the rocks certainly aren't) and it prevents Freddy from bashing D'Arcy's silly head in. John Standing now plays Malone to Dinsdale Landen's Tuck, and as the two of them loll against a table, breathing insouciant defiance of all who have not had their advantages, their common background is easy to credit.

Two years ago, when Frank Finlay played Freddy as a shark with apparent South American connections, this vital element was missing. But Mr Finlay had a pace, bite and attack which were extremely valuable; and which, on his opening night at least, were not supplied by his successor. Mr Standing let the side down (no other phrase will do) and there is no actor of whom I would have expected it less.

Mr Landen, however, has refined his performance to the point of ineffability. I never really knew what this was before, but it seems to involve a centre parting, much brilliantine, more good will and a perfect innocent balance between love and avarice. He has sacrificed a few first act laughs in the interests of clear narrative and characterisation, while gaining many in his Scotland Yard interrogation, which is now the pearl it should be (His Majesty's police help to polish it) and is triumphant as ever in the actual commission of crime. Michael Blakemore's direction of both these scenes is masterful.

Derek Newark, Polly Adams (a cut-glass heroine) and Trevor Ray have also survived to advantage, and Peggy Mount has arrived as a harridan worth defying and a decided gain to boot.

* * *

The Open Space's American season continues with a visiting show, a genuine piece of rubbish called The Ball Game, which takes farcical satire to be the art of dismembering dummies. It has Deborah Norton characterising hard and strong, and Maureen Lipman, who is so appealing that any man must yearn to rush out into the night (apparently a dangerous proceeding in Pittsburgh, where the action is laid) and find a better play for her.

* * *

You get a higher class of Americana at Madisons Supper Room, a much needed new resort at Camden Lock, where Gotham, a trio offering skilled close harmony singing and more questionable close harmony jokes, have given place to Peter Allen, who smiles and cavorts at the piano like some inspired combination of Liberace and Jerry Lee Lewis while giving enthusiastic voice to his own songs, which are usually rhythmic and sometimes touching. Gotham mostly offered old songs; Mr Allen offers new ones which sound like old, and much better than such things have a right to be.

records.title: Shakespeare As I Like It
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Shakespeare As I Like It

ROBERT CUSHMAN reports on the Berlin Theatre Festival.

WEST BERLIN seems to be a city in a continual state of arts festival; rather as if, having lost its role of capital, it felt compelled to acquire a new one as West Germany's purveyor of cultural hospitality.

The Berlin Theatertreffen, a three-week event closing today, is itself an assertion of the German theatre's identity: more particularly of the identity of its directors. A jury have chosen 10 productions from Germany's subsidised output over the previous year. Once they have come to Berlin (only two of this year's offerings actually originated there), the critical function passes to the audience who are the most vocal connoisseurs I have encountered.

A pretty way-out production of Goethe's Iphigenia in Tauris was greeted with cheers and boos of equal volume. I assumed that the barrackers were conservatives who objected to seeing Goethe staged on a setting suggestive of a bomb-site. A colleague, wiser than I in the ways of Berliners, told me that they were actually radicals who objected to seeing Goethe staged at all.

Of the two Berlin productions granted entrance to the festival, one, expectedly, was the work of Peter Stein. Surprisingly, however, it was not his celebrated version of As You Like It, though this show has probably made more noise in the world than any other German product since the decline of the Berliner Ensemble. It was, however, still on view and I took myself to it. Or rather was taken: the show is performed in an outlying film studio and a special bus is laid on from mid-town.

On arrival, you are ushered through a series of outhouses into the first playing-space: a long white room, crammed and balustraded, where the audience stand huddled to watch the play's first pre-Arden scenes. If the intention is to make us feel like members of the court then it fails, but there is enough in the action itself to hold us. After 40 minutes the doors open and we are off to Arden. We walk for five minutes or more through a maze of passages, hung about with details from the Elizabethan World Picture, and emerge properly footsore and expectant into a mind-blowing Forest of Arden: a cross between Disneyland and the tree-walk in the Battersea Pleasure Gardens. This time we can sit down: just as well, since the entertainment lasts for three more uninterrupted hours. But then in Arden you lose track of time; there's no clock in the forest.

The production has a tremendous primitive appeal; the studio set is a huge toy and we yearn sometimes for the actors to be turned off it so we can play there ourselves. But the treatment of the play itself is sophisticated and meticulous.

There is no uniformity to Stein's greenwood; Audrey may be realistically churning butter in one corner of it, while Phebe and Silvius are adopting conscious pastoral poses in another. This simultaneity (tentatively explored over here by Terry Hands and Pip Simmons) is an enormously valuable technique for staging Shakespeare. It allows us - like the best imagistic criticism - to see a play's world whole. And Stein does it without sacrificing the narrative; indeed he enhances it, bringing off stage-events before our eyes, right down to the invasion of Arden by the usurper's army. This might not work with the original text (Shakespeare's rhythms put up their own defence against intrusion), but a translation can afford to be explanatory.

The production is steeped in Elizabethan lore: the only reason I can think of for its exclusion from the official festival canon. Official opinion seems to prefer its classics dragged into the twentieth century, though preferably not kicking and screaming. The only piece to be really manhandled was Kleist's Prince of Homburg, whose directors (guests from East Berlin) devoted the evening to a tedious demonstration of their own dislike of the Prussian militarism in which the play is admittedly steeped. This was a night on which boos outweighed cheers - and on which one of the directors made his own charming intervention from the stalls, to point out that a crucial effect (actually the raising of a curtain, which is about as crucial as you can get) wasn't working properly.

Even here, however, there was visual imagination at work, even if of a monotonously louring kind. The production came from Hamburg, which also offered a straight version of Ghosts (a play it is difficult to imagine done crooked), which still outpaced most British productions in its fanatical attention to detail. Oswald, at his first appearance, slid down the banisters to illustrate his Bohemianism, but stopped halfway - to illustrate his debility.

Even the most libertarian productions displayed a firm sense of responsibility to their texts. The Iphigenia was directed by the highly regarded Claus Peymann of Stuttgart (though soon to be of Bochum following a political quarrel with his employers), who seized on the play's contrast between civilisation and savagery. Goethe's treatment of Euripides is a rather smug Enlightenment rebuke to ancient barbarism. Peymann makes Iphigenia into a prim but genuinely troubled keeper of the Hellenic conscience, her brother Orestes into an unscrupulous adventurer and their adversary Thoas into a half-emancipated Caliban dazzled by Iphigenia, who gags disgustedly when he hears of the refinements of human sacrifice practised by her ancestors of the House of Atreus.

Roland Schafer, of Dusseldorf, mounted Schiller's Kabale und Liebe, a domestic prose tragedy which the comparatively poor are ruined by the undoubtedly rich. The contrast between ranks is fairly simplistically pointed up by housing the former on a cramped bit of forestage and the latter on the vast expanses behind, but the production is informed by a remarkable poetic delicacy. The hero and heroine die of poisoned love and poisoned lemonade; in the first scene both the love and the lemonade flow freely and the long-range forecast is very touching.

These are all old plays. New ones were sparsely represented, though Trilogy des Wiedersehens by Botho Strauss turned up in two manifestations (it's been done all over); I saw Stein's Schaubuhne version which offered the best ensemble playing of the festival. The play, set at the opening of a 'capitalist realist' art exhibition, would be a natural for Hampstead, since it's crammed not only with the discreet charm of the bourgeoisie (and Stein's production is quite Bunuelian), but with its wit and its hang-ups as well. The Schaubuhne is a large adaptable room; the play was performed, with consummate naturalism, in one corner of it.

I had a tonic week, and a reassuring one: reassuring since I detected little of the self-congratulation and coterie ingratiation that might be expected to dog a theatre in thrall to directorial concepts; directors in thrall to designers; concepts and designers in thrall to huge budgets. Subsidies make ours look shameful, but nobody seems to have been corrupted by them. I have my doubts as to whether the British theatre could muster 10 comparable productions for a similar annual event, but the only way to find out is to try.

records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: I Was Sitting On My Patio This Guy Appeared I Thought I Was Hallucinating
records.body:
Howard's trumpet concerto

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the RSC's Coriolanus and the National's Macbeth.

THE ONLY thing lacking in the Royal Shakespeare Company production of Coriolanus (Aldwych) is variety; it is rather like a concerto for trumpet and brass band.

There can be no question that Alan Howard is ideally cast in the title role, and little doubt that he delivers the performance of his career. Even more impressive than his physical energy, or his ability when spreadeagled (there's a Roman thought) between the gates of Corioles to become an emblem of war, is his vocal stamina. He sounds the play's tintinnabulous music not only without flagging, but without ever admitting that flagging might ever be a possibility. He has, too, the exact measure of Coriolanus's embarrassment when put to the task of vote-catching, and of the fury to which this leads him. For a moment, when he has acceded to his mother's request to spare Rome, he is even moving.

Not quite moving enough, though if you regard this moment as the climax of the play -- as I (to confess my own bias) have regarded it since seeing Nicol Williamson crack almost visibly apart under the strain, Maxine Audley's Volumnia is now wittier and more robust than at Stratford, but the mother-son relationship is still underplayed. Other conflicts are well taken care of: Julian Glover's Aufidius dogs Mr Howard's footsteps, and even his tricks of voice, like envy personified, but still with enough grace to justify his last-minute repentance. Among the hero's teammates, Graham Crowden is a juicy Menenius and the ever-reliable Jeffrey Dench an admirable Cominius.

There is a vigorous crowd as well: though their scenes (including one they have pinched from a different group of characters altogether) are lacking in relaxation. Everyone on stage seems to be infected by the fierce restlessness of the protagonist. No director is more sensitive to the nuances of rhetoric (they do exist) than Terry Hands; which makes him the nonpareil conductor for nine-tenths of this score. Only the grace-notes escape him.

* * *

This Coriolanus is a production realised through sensitivity to language; I imagine that the National's Macbeth (Olivier) had similar ambitions -- though played as it is on a huge neutral platform (as opposed to the familiar leathery world of Farrar's Rome at the Aldwych) it must have hoped for a flexible style rather than a uniform one.

There are occasional touches of innovative spectacle; years ago, pondering an undernourished banquet scene, I wrote that "one day I would like to see this party staged as if it were worth breaking up." This time, with catering apparently by Simpsons-in-the-Glen, it has been; though I must admit that this does less for the play than I had hoped.

Another departure is the inclusion of the goddess Hecat, the witches' commanding officer, whose jingling cues for song and dance (here taken in full) have generally been regarded as un-Shakespearean. Now that I have heard them I have to agree. Obviously I could not have reached this conclusion unless I had heard them, so I must be grateful for the opportunity, but they do seem to me to do fundamental harm to the play.

They set up a chain of dependence: Hecat dominates the Witches, they dominate Macbeth. He becomes their creature, largely unaware of what is happening to him, and by that much less interesting. He seems rather thick; events take him by surprise. Only at the end, when he becomes a savage fatalistic clown, does Albert Finney's performance take hold, though by now crime and the destinies have so knocked him out of shape that he seems more like Richard III.

Otherwise Peter Hall's production appears mainly concerned with getting people on and off stage. The best that can be said of it is that it provides a launching-pad for the occasional brief solo flight: Dorothy Tutin's invocation of the spirits, Nicky Henson's deadpan confession as Malcolm to all possible sins, Robin Bailey's moments of suspicion as Banquo, and pointed interventions by Lennox, Angus and the Third Witch. Imagination has seized up.

Listed as co-director is John Russell Brown, the National's head of scripts and author of Free Shakespeare. I don't know if his ideas are workable, but I do not see why they shouldn't be tried. They are not here though; as I recall they involved having no director (here there are two), short texts (here we have every line) and informal playing-spaces (here it's the Olivier, even unto its very back wall).

Macbeth is, paradoxically, a powerful argument for enlarging the National's subsidy, allowing it to do more plays so the failures matter less and even (with some of the pressure off) become less frequent.

One day Byron's Cain could work well in the Olivier, though the London Planetarium might suit it better. Its central scene is designated as "the abyss of space"; in it Lucifer tempts Cain away from the religion of his father, plays on his disgust at the newly-introduced idea of death, softens him up for his own thing as a killer. Byron may not have been a natural dramatist, but he excelled the other Romantics as a writer of dialogue; and some of his pungency is captured in a miniature production by the literally-named Company of Three at the White Hart, Hammersmith. The piece provides the rare and satisfying experience of a writer finding the right myth. It ends today.

David Rudkin in The Sons of Light (Warehouse) writes his own myth. I pronounced the play an unsalvageable failure when I first saw it at Newcastle and must now recant, blaming my error -- against the author's own declared admiration -- on an incomprehensible production. Ron Daniels's present direction is extremely lucid and has the best teamwork this branch of the RSC has yet exhibited.

Set in one of the remotest Scottish islands, the play exhibits two kinds of repression; an unseen landowner keeps the islanders in spiritual darkness while sanctioning an underworld complex in which enslavement is, in the name of science, given horrifically exact embodiment. To the island come a new pastor and his three sons, who finally succeed in liberating both strata -- and, incidentally, in freeing an island girl from possession, otherwise called schizophrenia.

This character, a crouching compendium of obsessions, is the cause of much indulgence on Mr Rudkin's part (though discreetly played by Charlotte Cornwell); indeed as the evening proceeds his fevered language gets the better of him -- and he seems unable to recognise that his sinister scientist is a stock figure: Dr Strangelove with legs. But on a narrative level he goes on inventing almost to the end (the conclusion is disappointingly pat) and that is reason enough for applause.

* * *

After all these words, more words. For though Robert Wilson's show, I Was Sitting On My Patio This Guy Appeared I Thought I Was Hallucinating (Royal Court), seems to be an assault on verbal theatre, it uses the enemy's weapons and, committed to misusing them, makes them tedious. Mr Wilson's interest in theatre is said to have begun with a visit to The Homecoming; he was fascinated by the introductory movement, "and then this play had to start." The same summary will do for his own piece.

records.body:
Theatre-from A to W

ROBERT CUSHMAN'S quick guide to the London stage.

ANNIE (Victoria Palace): Triumphantly shameless musical--orphans, dogs, hissable villains, exhilarating scenery, unlimited knowhow.

* * *

BRAND (Olivier): Gruelling assault on an almost unscalable Ibsen; "worthy" has to be the word, though Robert Stephens's Mayor transcends it; the play itself is a rarity worth grabbing.

* * *

THE HOMECOMING (Garrick): Good Pinter revival in which the play comes over as unabashed black comedy.

* * *

PLENTY (Lyttelton): Fine performances from Kate Nelligan and Stephen Moore in David Hare's chronicle of a war heroine's failure to adjust to the next 10 years.

* * *

TEN TIMES TABLE (Globe): Alan Ayckbourn finally gets out of the house and into local politics.

* * *

WHOSE LIFE IS IT ANYWAY? (Savoy): Thoroughly gripping statement of the case for euthanasia transfers from the Mermaid. (At the Westminster, Malcolm Muggeridge is presenting the case against.)

records.title: Drama for actors and orchestra
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Drama for actors and orchestra

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on plays by Stoppard, Wesker and Strindberg.

WHEN the Tom Stoppard-Andre Previn piece Every Good Boy Deserves Favour (Mermaid) first surfaced as a one-night bash at the Royal Festival Hall, I complained that it contained scenes anyone might have written. I am now not sure what I meant. I don't think that I was trying to father any of the dialogue on Mr Previn, or for that matter any of the orchestral interludes on Mr Stoppard. But I was bothered by the new aura of respectability that seemed to have descended on the playwright: by the spectacle of Mr Stoppard finally getting in line and writing about a specific political abuse -- in this case the confinement of Russian dissidents in mental hospitals. We are not short of plays about oppression (though the ones we generally see are not set in Russia) and the scenes in which the boy Sasha, whose father Alexander Ivanov is just such a prisoner of conscience, is bullied and harangued by his schoolteacher, came over as routine slices of protest.

Blame the verbal (as opposed to musical) acoustics of the Festival Hall, or just my obtuseness. These scenes, though more sparely written than we expect of Mr Stoppard, are in his authentic echo-chamber style, re-stating and re-arranging themes from elsewhere in the play. The continual exhilarating paradox of his work is that its linguistic exuberance always turns out to be strictly functional. Every joke doubles back on itself. Even without a band behind him, he is the most musical playwright we have.

All the same, the actual choice or alignment of themes varies in conviction from play to play. 'EGBDF' was born, we are told, of a compulsion (write about dissidence) and a commission (write for actors and orchestra). Dissidence suggests dissonance; and Ivanov shares his cell with a namesake, a real madman who believes he owns an orchestra. But their association seems to be more a matter of the authors than of their jailers. It lacks the inevitability of the philosopher-gymnast equation in Jumpers. (The philosopher-footballer tie-up in Professional Foul falls somewhere between the two.) The musical patter is mostly beguiling, though the inclusion of the glockenspiel joke ('Not to speak of the glockenspiel.' 'The glockenspiel?' 'I asked you not to speak of it') suggests that the playwright's imagination was working at less than full pressure.

Still, Stoppard at his second-best surpasses most playwrights at their first. Ivanov's encounters with the psychiatrist (Frank Windsor) who will declare him sane if he admits to madness recall Catch-22; but it is probably impossible to write comprehensively of the modern world without doing that. The same psychiatrist is a part-time violinist, which makes his attempts to grapple with his other patient's delusions doubly fruitful.

Ivanov's account of the reasons for his incarceration is, in John Woodvine's stoical performance, both funny and moving -- and exactly judged for being spoken against self. So is, or was, music. And the ending is majestic. The brilliant doctor of semantics who has ordered the joint confinement of the two Ivanovs ends up by mistaking one for the other and releasing both. To the pleasure of seeing authority hoist with its own petard (and a hopeful comment on totalitarian stupidity) is added the satisfaction of poetic justice -- but the music tells us that it is only poetic. It is not how things usually happen. This has all the irony of the Threepenny Opera finale, without the grinding obviousness.

Ian McDiarmid gives a sprightly account of the musical maniac, whose delusions seem to have lost some of their grandeur. Once he owned the LSO; now he has a smaller outfit known appropriately (since they all sport tails) as the Mermaid Chamber Orchestra. The scaling-down, to my ear at least, actually enhances Mr Previn's score. A final point: if a playwright wishes to fire us against injustice or the waste of life he must first convince us, in the quality of his own work, that life is worth living anyway. Mr Stoppard's gaiety is a moral quality in itself.

* * *

So is, or was, Arnold Wesker's; the enduring quality of his Chicken Soup trilogy has proved to be its family comedy -- which, since Mr Wesker writes of all his characters as though they were his relations, has infinitely wide reverberations. The farm-working Bryants of Roots are as rounded, and as respectfully-treated, as the Jewish, Socialist Kahns of Chicken Soup with Barley, who have more of the right ideas but are hardly more efficient at putting them into practice. It is even arguable that Mrs Bryan's apathy does less harm to her offspring than Mrs Kahn's commitment; at least Mr Wesker seems more optimistic about Beatie Bryant's future than about anyone else's.

The third instalment, I'm Talking About Jerusalem (Shaw), is, despite lively passages, an anti-climax. It returns us to the Kahns' daughter Ada and her husband Dave, who move to Norfolk after the war to make and sell furniture. After 15 years, they acknowledge failure and return to London. The play, like all such finales, has to devote some of its energy to mopping-up. This makes for untidiness, but also for the best writing of the evening: if we crane forward for news of characters from the other plays.

Ada's horrified account of a visit to her stricken father is, as delivered by Adrienne Posta, the most powerful sequence. But the play disappoints, not because its upshot is pessimistic but because that depression is never faced or argued out. Confrontations are promised but not delivered. The acting, too, Miss Posta apart, is weak; play and production hinder each other. The Shaw revivals have always lagged behind the detailed realism the scripts demand; here the direction has not caught up, but the play has dropped back to meet it.

* * *

Strindberg fans are always trying to sell their idol's plays as comedies; the RSC revival of The Dance of Death does this more whole-heartedly than any before, more than the National Theatre version which was hampered by the difference in scale between Laurence Olivier and Geraldine McEwan. Sheila Allen and Emrys James (whose performance, though complete in itself, suggests an inadvertent parody of Olivier's) are far better matched; each takes it in turn to deride the other's boasted sufferings.

The trick to getting laughs from Strindberg is to play fast, so that the miseries always seem outpaced by the lamentations; the disparity can be very funny. I enjoyed it very much, though I doubt if the author would have. The news that Mr James (as his surrogate) had expired murmuring 'forgive them for they know not what they do' brought the Aldwych down. But Strindberg, of course, was imagining for himself a moment of stunning nobility; he had the genius to recognise his own self-pity, but that never stopped him indulging it.

* * *

Marivaux was a far more disturbing (because outwardly more dispassionate) observer of the sexes: a butterfly with steel wing-tips. His L'Heureux Stratageme has been revived -- premiered, rather -- at Chichester, done into pastiche Restoration prose by John Bowen with a title -- The Inconstant Couple -- to match. There is obvious strain involved for adapter, players and audience; but there are also rewards. In particular, Keith Baxter gives a finely puzzled account of an honest man amazed at the lengths and depths to which he will go to win the hand of a flirtatious spouse.

The lady in question is Sian Phillips, cast against her stage personality, which is resolutely opposed to artifice. Morag Hood, however, confirms herself the wittiest classical comedienne to emerge since Maggie Smith. The other performances in Noel Willman's production deploy stock period devices, but never without thought or indeed without effect.

records.title: Black boxed
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Black boxed

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Stratford.

AT LAST new young directors seem to be emerging capable of working on the main stage at Stratford.

After Michael Bogdanov's Taming of the Shrew comes Measure for Measure from Barry Kyle, who has collaborated with his seniors on the RSC's larger stages, but has confined his previous solo work to their miniature spaces. His present production bears the marks of his confinement; there were times when I felt that all concerned would have been happy to have been transported down the road to the Other Place. It is not, physically or emotionally, an expansive production.

Christopher Morley, who designed the celebrated white box in which so many Stratford productions were set in the sixties, now returns with a black box. The final scene, played virtually on a forestage, could also use more people; the economies that have reduced the RSC's acting strength are unfortunate for those plays (Coriolanus is another) which deal with public events.

So much for strictures: in most respects Mr Kyle's is an auspicious debut. Other directors have done interesting things with this play, but he is the first in my experience to get it right. The most famous lines in Measure are the ones about "proud man, dressed in a little brief authority" and the keyword is dressed.

When Angelo first comes before us he is a Cromwellian Puritan, all neat in black jerkin; promoted to Duke (Temporary Acting), he puts on the ducal robe of justice: a long white thing, decorated with red motifs that look like licking flames. It doesn't actually change his nature, but it brings dormant qualities to life. There seems, too, to be a strange kinship between this garment and the prison uniform -- short white tunic, also splashed with red -- worn by convicted fornicators like Claudio. Isabella arrives at her convent with a suitcase, and she carefully assumes her nun's habit before going out to encounter Angelo. In the circumstances his seducer's line ("If you are a woman show it now/by putting on the destined livery") could hardly be more fitting or, for her, more shocking. The Duke, disguised as a friar, surprises himself with how easily the right words come to him. Pompey, promoted to headsman (also Temporary Acting), assumes the full black gear. And at the end of the scale, Barnardine, the play's one natural man, he who refuses to die even if it means upsetting the plots of both his Duke and his author, appears stark naked.

For most of the characters the play is a voyage of self-discovery; an unsentimental education ending, like its lighter counterpart As You Like It, in a quartet of marriages. Michael Pennington's Duke visibly improvises his schemes; neither God nor the devil (both approaches have been tried), but a witty juvenile lead whose urbanity can terrify both the Puritan Angelo and the libertine Lucio, but also enables him to forgive them.

Jonathan Pryce's Angelo is as much victim as villain: horribly shy, a theorist (probably with a first in law) wrecked by the complications of actual practice. Paola Dionisotti's Isabella is his female equivalent, as much her brother's judge as his advocate. She giggles when she tells of her mock-assignation with Angelo; it's the first time she's had to talk of such things and she seems to have stumbled on a new world.

Both John Nettles's Lucio and Richard Griffiths's Pompey are excellently communicative. Mr Griffiths is one of your deliberate fops. His pimp shines with quiet professional pride.

* * *

At the Other Place, a new playwright, Peter Whelan, gives us Captain Swing, he being a populist leader who terrified the landowners of Britain in 1830. He may or may not have existed -- and he may or may not appear in the play. A wandering wounded man is assumed by some aggrieved Sussex villagers to be the very Swing, but is never collected enough to confirm or deny it. It suits both sides to believe that he is; the people can use him as a symbol, the gentry can catch and kill him.

The odd man out is the village wheelwright, who believes in peaceful protest. "The people keep the law -- those who govern break it" is his credo, uttered at first with pride and finally -- when the troops have been sent in and he has been sent to the hulks -- with anguish. Negotiation is fine, but it don't mean a thing if it ain't got that Swing.

On this evidence, the play seems an orthodox plea for violent change. In practice it comes over differently, since so much sympathy adheres to the gradualist (especially as played by David Bradley) and so much contempt to the extremists: an Irish infiltrator who escapes with a whole skin and the village whore who discovers the crypto-Captain and whose possessiveness (she will allow no doctor near him) effectively kills him. Only the Dragoons commander (David Lyon) matches the wheelwright, since he too is allowed the benefit of his own doubts.

In setting and atmosphere the play recalls Serjeant Musgrave's Dance and it is shot through with a similar promise: verbal -- as where Swing speaks of an army raised "from under the fields of King Corn's kingdom" -- and theatrical. There is a powerful, if structurally confusing, scene in which the villagers beard the parson in his church, cut Christ down from the cross and adopt the figure as their own. Bill Alexander's production, played all over the tiny theatre, enfolds the audience; it has wrap-around excitement.

records.title: Ben Jonson to Bruce Forsyth
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Ben Jonson to Bruce Forsyth

ROBERT CUSHMAN'S quick guide to London theatre.

BARTHOLOMEW FAIR (Young Vic): Slapdash production of Jonson's masterpiece that nevertheless makes the jokes funny and the moral clear.

* * *

CORIOLANUS (Aldwych): Strong performance by the RSC Brass Ensemble; Alan Howard blows the solo trumpet.

* * *

EVERY GOOD BOY DESERVES FAVOUR (Mermaid): The Stoppard-Previn parable of musical dissidence and political dissonance; probably the wittiest piece ever to be set in a mental hospital.

* * *

EVITA (Prince Edward): Hal Prince's production stunning, but the result still seems partially locked inside its authors' heads.

* * *

FLYING BLIND (Royal Court): A tragical farce about the farcical tragedy of Northern Ireland. Indispensable.

* * *

PLUNDER (Lyttelton): A revival of the revival of Ben Travers's 1920s farce; Dinsdale Landen the most cracking of gentlemen cracksmen.

* * *

ST MARK'S GOSPEL (Comedy): Last week of Alec McCowen's infinitely accomplished solo performance, before he goes to spread the word to the heathen of New York.

* * *

THE TRAVELLING MUSIC SHOW (Her Majesty's): Has only two more weeks to travel. Bruce Forsyth is worth seeing; and only masochists will regret that the show isn't really a Newley-Bricusse songbook.

records.title: Dying flames
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Dying flames

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Stratford.

ALL THE characters in The Lady's Not for Burning (Old Vic) speak alike. That was noted when the play was first done just after the war. Christopher Fry admitted the point, but made light of it. After all, he said, people in real life all talk alike as well.

That is as true as it is disarming. But it does not follow that we all think or feel alike. Drama would be impossible if we did and dialogue, however uniform it may be, ought to clue us in to the rifts beneath. But the characters in The Lady seem to have no inner lives; all they have to offer are words, many of them now devalued by time.

I had hoped to be exhilarated by verbal ingenuity, if not actually by poetry. In the event I was fatigued by archness. Poetry concentrates, but Mr Fry's verse only decorates. Sometimes it even obscures. It is as if the conceits of Love's Labour's Lost were allowed five acts to themselves with no messenger of death to sober them up.

Death indeed hangs over Mr Fry's plot -- a war-shocked medieval soldier wants to be hanged, a suspected witch does not want to be burned -- but it makes no difference to what we actually hear. They rattle on regardless. They fall in love, of course, and are spared. "I love you," says Thomas the soldier, "but the world's not changed." A finely balanced conclusion which fails to resonate because "the world" has been kept firmly offstage.

Thomas, gazing into the wings, sums it up as "all nitwittery": a mincing phrase for the horrors of 1400 either more or less exactly, and even more so for those from which the world had just emerged when the play was written. Derek Jacobi and Eileen Atkins thread their lines well, but there is no romance between them, and Mr Jacobi seems too lightweight to be suicidal.

George Baker's production plods, offering single sparks instead of explosions, but it gives the actors room to work and the famous funny lines remain potent; in fact, they keep the evening afloat. "You always think you can do things better than your mother," says Brenda Bruce, cross but patient, to a fractious son who claims to have been reborn; and brings down the house.

Miss Bruce's timing and her unfussed professionalism are something of a revelation; Robert Eddison could hardly be that now, but his wispy Chaplain is perfect, again. Michael Thomas is promisingly good-humoured as a subsidiary lover, and Ronnie Stevens is a gleeful late arrival, bearing the welcome gifts of drunkenness, prose, and even the odd four-letter word. Has Mr Fry been rewriting, or was he an early unsung battler against the censor? The programme, piquantly enough, champions Mr Fry against the purveyors of "building-site dialogue."

* * *

I have my own objections to obscenity in the theatre, particularly in the West End. In A Family (Haymarket) a young girl tells her grandfather to fuck off, and the first-night audience fell about at the naughtiness of it all. It is the only such lapse in Ronald Harwood's curious play; the rest is literary, not only in style but in structure. The characters have their bearings only in the author's head; the climax is a flashback. You wonder why they couldn't have dragged out the skeleton in the first place.

The title is the play: one to which we can all, if you like, relate but which we resist because it has been done so often before. Mr Harwood's clan, besides, are marooned between archetype and special case -- and also, in Casper Wrede's nebulous production, between Jew and Gentile. It has besides a cast of solitaries: Paul Scofield, Harry Andrews, Irene Handl et al are, like most stars, natural orphans. Only Trevor Peacock looks attached and he, as it happens, is meant to be a foundling, connected only by marriage.

There is building-site dialogue to spare in Savage Amusement (Warehouse) and much of it could be spared. It is true that indiscriminate obscenity limits human potential; it certainly limits dramatic potential, since every time a row brews up the dialogue becomes predictable. To be fair, Peter Flannery's characters are meant to be limited -- they have in fact little choice -- but the distance between them and their author often gets blurred; convenience writing takes over.

These are blots on a compelling evening. We are in Manchester in 1982. The chalked slogan that reached our newspapers last week -- "Hulme is a prison" -- are out of date. It is now part wilderness, part concentration camp -- one of the areas abandoned by an authoritarian government which has brought back the birch, overhauled the social security regulations and staffed its offices with disembodied voices.

It is depressingly convincing, but Mr Flannery adds a dimension: we focus on a quartet of squatters, of whom one is an anthropology student, drawing unflattering comparisons between civilisation and savagery. Meanwhile we see a home-grown savage emerging: an 18-year-old scavenger blind to all except the most immediate loyalties, not so much learning survival as embodying it.

Played with fierce vacancy by David Threlfall, he is a powerful social and dramatic fact. Around him a debate rages between a drop-out who admires him and a pragmatist who deplores him; the author tries to be fair, but cannot help indulging the first and despising the second. There are awkward explanatory speeches and stageworn relationships. But the structure is deceptively cunning, the territory new and John Caird's production grimly sympathetic.

The old Manchester school is well represented at Greenwich by a revival of Stanley Houghton's classic Hindle Wakes, in which the mill-owner's son gets a working girl into trouble and she takes all breaths away by refusing to marry him. Robert Kidd's production is uneven, with one character misconceived, another miscast and Frances Viner smiling too readily as the heroine. But John Gill and Anne Dyson make her parents a fine couple of sanctimonious graspers, Tom Chadbon skilfully navigates the shallows of her intended and Mark Dignam gets much, though not all, of his father's doggedness. The odd suggestion of The Fosdyke Saga ("don't forget the old saying -- there's three generations from clogs to clogs") is rather charming.

* * *

In The Merchant of Venice (Other Place, Stratford), Patrick Stewart's Shylock, an unemphatic and unaccented businessman, is the most convincing I have seen. In the trial scene he follows the play's comic logic and cringes. Silently he begs mercy from Antonio; nods assent when commanded to become a Christian. I don't know if John Barton intended this to be as distressing as I found it; perhaps his production, like this year's Shrew, is concerned to expose the play's unpleasantness.

The whole Shylock menage is authoritatively handled with a silkily tormenting Tubal (Raymond Westwell) and a silk-hatted one-man band of a Launcelot Gobbo (Hilton McRae) -- like Harpo Marx given voice. Marjorie Bland's Portia reacts beautifully to her suitors from a distance, but on closer acquaintance freezes over; John Nettles, however, effectively conquers his accustomed sneer as Bassanio.

records.title: Putting Henry James on stage
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Putting Henry James on stage

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'The Aspern Papers'

THIS year's Chichester programme includes two plays from the West End season of 1959.

I imagine that '59 is seen as a haven of reassurance: the last year before the barriers went down and the Visigoths of the sixties started fanning out from Sloane Square, writing their new plays, forming their new companies and building their new theatres -- Chichester, for example.

I can get quite nostalgic about it myself. 1959 was the year in which I began regular theatregoing, and I remember it as the last date on which the commercial theatre still had a substantial share of the best new plays. The Aspern Papers, Michael Redgrave's adaptation of the Henry James novella, was among them; though at the time I was less taken with the play than with the acting of Flora Robson, Beatrix Lehmann and Redgrave himself.

The Chichester revival would be justified purely as a seventieth birthday tribute to one of our greatest actors, but it also reveals him as having written an almost perfect play: probably a minor classic. It must certainly be the shapeliest of all attempts to put a novel on stage; it unfolds in five scenes, not one of which is weighed down by more narrative than it can plausibly carry.

To a peeling Venetian palazzo comes Harry Jarvis, an American literary sleuth, on fire with the scholar's passion. His quarry is a near-centenarian expatriate lady, once the mistress of the deceased Jeffrey Aspern, H. J.'s own candidate for the role of great American poet. Hugging Aspern's literary and emotional relics to herself, the lady is appropriately dragonish. H. J. proposes to circumvent her by making love to her middle-aged spinster niece; and since he has all the charm of indifference (the pursuit of letters having absorbed his sexuality) and she the vulnerability of seclusion, he seems set fair to succeed.

He does actually get his hands on the papers, only to be surprised by the aunt. "You publishing scoundrel," she calls him -- obviously the filthiest term in her vocabulary -- and drops from the excitement. The treasures pass to the niece, who makes it discreetly plain that he may have them only as part of her dowry. He jibs at this; maybe he would change his mind, but he is not given the chance. The Aspern papers go into the fire.

As usual with James, the American, who thinks himself the sophisticate, proves the innocent; he may plan emotional blackmail, but it is the Venetian ladies who practise it. That he gets even as far as he does is to the credit of his ambitious and unscrupulous Italian valet: a good supporting performance by Keith Drinkel to balance an uneasily patronising one by Irene Hamilton as the hero's conductress.

Cathleen Nesbitt is (as who would not be?) a less-terrifying old lady than Miss Lehmann, but she is also a wittier; she gains her victories in hand-to-hand combat. Her big moment of discovery is badly mistimed in David William's production. The particular heights of the original performances -- Redgrave's suavely brutal disengagement, Dame Flora's brief blossoming, when taken out for the evening -- are missing too. But there is a compensating strength of detail in Kenneth Haigh's calculating brashness and in Jill Bennett's, who has the recluse's efficiency as well as her innocence. When the pair at last elude each other, the emotional geometry is exactly outlined. And the climax, with Miss Bennett in effect burning her lover's child, reminds us what a good Hedda she was, and also of how zealous an Ibsenite was James himself.

* * *

Irish Eyes and English Tears (Theatre Upstairs) begins, in time-hallowed fashion, with a group of young roughs harassing an old tramp. Just to prove that this is 1978, he is busking (singing the title song in fact) and they are on their way to a football match. One of them, who runs with the pack out of discontent but is discontented with that too, saves the old man from being beaten up and strikes up a friendship with him.

Brian Hayes plays the tramp, Karl Johnson his protector; both maintain a constant sense of surprised awareness throughout the evening. They are strongly supported; at half-time I found myself wondering what would happen to these actors when they grew up. The author, Nigel Baldwin, turns out to have similar preoccupations; his young loner is merely a younger version of his old dosser and in fact ends the play like him, settling down for the night wrapped in newspaper.

The young, in fact, are older than we think; one of the best-drawn characters is an unmarried mother of 31, still playing the games of her previous decade and earlier. "Teenagers" you think when you first look at the cast; they aren't, but there is nothing else they want to be. The highspot of Ian Kellgren's production is a scene on the terraces: the cast bunched together, each over-reacting in his own way, with the tramp, taken along, standing dazed among them. The gallery set looks amazingly like a prison. The West End seems to have latched on to the documentary craze as once was, but at this date, and at these prices, who will care?

Mr Baldwin chips incisively away at his subject; his lines ring true and make patterns. But he is not yet a builder; too much happens between the scenes, with a crucial reversal in the interval. The tramp is adopted by the rest of the gang; spruced up at a jumble sale, he is unrecognisable as his former self -- and in fact the more we learn of his descent the less credible it seems. The kids meanwhile interact convincingly and compellingly (Annie Hayes and Alfred Molina are especially good) grabbing us more securely than the foreground action ever does.

records.title: In at the death of the joke
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
In at the death of the joke

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

REVUE returned to the London theatre last week though not, I suspect, for long. Two shows were offered, their titles radiating honest hopelessness. At the Bush In at the Death; at Hampstead Beyond a Joke. They can say those again.

The Bush show is a Dying Newspaper. Dusty Hughes, the Diaghilev of Goldhawk Road, enjoined some half-dozen dramatists to bring him songs and sketches inspired by stories in the public prints. Whether he really meant them all to find their inspiration in minor disaster stories, is open to doubt. But that is where they went and what they came back with; and Mr Hughes himself has entered into the spirit of the thing by writing a number called Ghouls about a family who buzzard off, picnic hampers at the ready, at the first tinkle of the passing bell, frequently beating the ambulance men to the scene of the catastrophe.

Setting the evening's tone, Mr Hughes also puts himself, his team and his audience on the spot. We are necrophiles for the night; but why, after all, is it wrong to be young and ghoulish? The evening's fatal lapses are not of taste but of technique. Too much goes on too long; the numbers repeat themselves and one another. Mr Hughes's family group seems largely interchangeable with the one invented by Ron Hutchinson to populate a sketch about How to Survive when living in Belfast. You subject your oul da over the years to multiple amputation, and collect the insurance on each limb. That is not a bad idea (in context, I mean) but Mr Hutchinson hugs it to himself for ages, in the meantime grossly overestimating the comic potential of the phrase "the all-Belfast Ruby Murray look-alike contest." I reckon those words are good for only one laugh; which you have now had.

Of the other writers involved, Ken Campbell is at his most heavy-handed and Snoo Wilson at his least penetrable. Nigel Baldwin contributes the most substantial of the episodes, reiterating the strengths and weaknesses of his full-length work; his dialogue way above average, his themes and characters cowering from the light.

A newcomer, Victoria Wood, is responsible for most of the songs, notably a snappily rhymed lament for Guy the gorilla (the nearest the show gets to lampooning a world figure) and a really haunting, worrying piece called Abortion (the nearest it gets to real feeling). She also appears, early on, as a gleefully malignant schoolboy, an aura she never quite sheds.

Otherwise the actors are as the writers, known talents failing to make an impression: even Clive Merrison, even Alison Fiske. The glowing exception is Julie Walters, who is developing a cherishable line in Fairly Emancipated Women, ready for a giggle but capable of instant recoil when the new limits are overstepped.

* * *

In at the Death suffers from having only one subject; the show at Hampstead, far worse, has none at all. Its participants are making jokes about jokes. They are appealing, that is, to their audience's nostalgia; my own was tickled by the final number which is a cod-opera about brigands. I have never met a brigand but I have met several cod-operas and I like being reminded of them. I have less affection for numbers about pompous young men who take girls to restaurants and are defeated by the French words on the menu, and for men with high-pitched voices who make xenophobic remarks while sitting on benches.

Beyond a Joke has a cast of three, most of it called Rowan Atkinson. Mr Atkinson has eyebrows, curly hair, a lower lip, and timing. These are all good things, but they are not in themselves hilarious; though Michael Rudman, the indulgent director, looks to believe that they are. Mr Atkinson is not a natural charmer; he needs material, and only once does he get it, as a schoolmaster contemptuously informing his class of the number of jokes to be found in Shakespeare.

The other performers are Elspeth Walker, a Valkyrie, and Peter Wilson, a straight man. There are two musicians, one of whom sings two inaudible songs. The influence of television is apparent in the lack of punchlines; unfortunately there are no electronic tricks to compensate. The show wants to please, which is nice of it, and is totally uncommitted, indeed unaware; which should make the post-68 playwrights who talk so proudly of "our generation" realise how old they, we, are getting. There's a new lot coming up and they don't care. This collection emerged, recently, from Oxford; it is not true that university humour has stood still for 10 years. It has gone round in a circle, and is tired.

* * *

In Cambridge, things are brighter, not to say older; the Arts company having revived Thornton Wilder's The Matchmaker (1955) which afterwards became Hello Dolly and had already been at least four other plays. Wilder's eclectic dramatic reading may account for the smallness of his output; not only must it have taken up his time, he may have found the weight of tradition inhibiting.

In this case he blends farce with moral comedy, and though it would be false to claim he gets the best of both worlds, he blended them attractively.

For his setting he chose elitist New York, thereby guaranteeing, as far as I am concerned, instant enchantment: enhanced in Jonathan Lynn's production by judicious musical interludes and in Saul Radomsky's designs by a captivating abundance of stripes.

The play, carefully filled with stock characters (healthy stock, of course), should be cast up to the nines; some of the small parts here are at sixes and sevens. But most positions are well held: Bernard Spear, Leueen Willoughby, Angus MacInnes, Tom Kleh, Richard Simpson all lift the spirits and Vivienne Martin, playing slyly and confidently along in the first three acts, emerges in the fourth as a dazzling Dolly. The play arrives with all the credentials of a classic: the production proves them to be fully in order.

records.title: Theatre round-up
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Theatre round-up

ROBERT CUSHMAN'S quick guide to the London theatre

American Buffalo (Cottesloe): David Mamet, fairly new, fairly white American hope, makes poetry out of verbal and physical junk: some longueurs but an intelligent production with Dave King masterly.

* * *

The Dance of Death (Aldwych): Strindberg's marital tango rendered as funny as its fans have always claimed; Emrys James in fine bull-frog form.

* * *

Hindle Wakes (Greenwich): The founding regime at Greenwich goes out in glory with a Manchester classic.

* * *

Irish Eyes and English Tears (Theatre Upstairs): Nigel Baldwin is a playwright who has found his voice but not as yet his mouthpieces. See also "In at the Death" reviewed this week.

* * *

The Lady's Not For Burning (Old Vic): A necessary if disappointing revival. Fry can still be gloriously funny but the depths are non-existent.

* * *

Privates on Parade (Piccadilly): A fortnight left to see Peter Nichols's ENSA - and - after comedy, much reviled by the gay lobby who haven't noticed that all the characters are stereotypes, and meant to be Fun.

* * *

Savage Amusement (Warehouse): Vision of the near future, actually more 'savage' than amusing. Author Peter Flannery is the opposite of Nigel Baldwin: his story compels while his language flounders. David Threlfall is an actor to watch and impossible not to.

* * *

Every Good Boy Deserves Favour (Mermaid): The Stoppard-Previn parable of musical dissidence and political dissonance; probably the wittiest piece ever to be set in a mental hospital.

records.title: Law student, singer, dissident
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Are You Now or Have You Ever Been?
records.body:
Law student, singer, dissident

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Chichester

NOBODY would describe Paul Robeson (Her Majesty's) as a play: nobody, that is, except the author, Phillip Hayes Dean. Or maybe it was just the programme's fault.

Anyway what Mr Dean has to offer is a monologue in which James Earl Jones takes us from Robeson's days as a student at Rutgers almost up to his death. No other actors appear and Mr Dean perforce makes much use of the imaginary conversation; it is a relief when Mr Jones is allowed recourse to simple reminiscence or straightforward oratory.

With him on stage is an accompanist, the superbly dapper Burt Wallace. When Mr Jones's Robeson walks offstage after refusing to sing for a segregated audience in Kansas City, Mr Wallace stalks after him with magnificent hauteur. He looks demonic, so it is perhaps appropriate that when a second voice is at last admitted he should provide it in the collective role of Robeson's adversaries at the House Un-American Activities Committee. This is the second time that this hearing has been re-enacted on the London stage; the first was last year's HUAC documentary 'Are You Now or Have You Ever Been?'

The instructiveness of the evening overrides its weaknesses. Most of us will have two or three isolated images of Robeson in our minds -- the law student, the singer of 'Ol' Man River,' the dissident banned from foreign travel -- surrounded by large chronological blanks. This show enables us to fit them together, and to watch the development of a man's awareness.

At Rutgers he defends himself against racial prejudice with all the strength of his body, his voice and his wits. He becomes a football hero; proving to the whites that they cannot do without him. Later, having discovered his vocation as a performer almost by accident, he becomes a culture hero on a similar basis. In New York, at the time of the abortive 'Harlem Renaissance,' he begins to relate his own struggles to those of all black Americans. He comes to London with 'Show Boat,' remains there for most of the thirties, and his political horizons begin to widen further. Messrs Jones and Dean are excellent at balancing innocence and experience.

Ideological confidence usually entails selective blindness; though he had enormous provocation, Robeson was guilty of doublethink over the Soviet invasion of Hungary. The format of this show prevents it from examining this point; more seriously it denies us much of an insight into Robeson's private life. At one point he accuses his wife of not understanding him; we never, of course, get to hear her reply.

In some ways the brief glimpse we got of him in 'Are You Now' was more revealing than this full-length performance, perhaps because he was played there by a singer, Thomas Baptiste, whose delivery convinced us that, however considerable his other achievements, the source of Robeson's charisma was his voice: not just its power but its dignity. It made him impossible to ignore or, I would guess, to argue with.

Mr Jones gets the right startling note within seconds of opening his mouth, but he cannot keep it up all night; he and Mr Wallace do a charming relaxed duet of 'Nobody Knows You When You're Down and Out,' but for the most part Robeson's singing has to be taken for granted. At the preview I saw, Mr Jones was still feeling his way and the show's rhythms often went awry; but he is clearly a masterly actor, alert to every nuance of humour, and with regal authority. He, like Robeson, could withstand a more searching examination than Mr Dean's and still emerge intact.

Some of my most cherished Feydeau memories do not concern slamming doors or bouncing beds. They are sudden cynical moments of truth: the confession of the Lothario in 'A Flea in Her Ear,' that "I know what's expected of me, but I don't know how to make it new"; or the lament in 'Hotel Paradiso' of the would-be adulterer suddenly stricken by indigestion: "This would happen when my wife's not here to help."

* * *
