There are no such cris du coeur in Look After Lulu (Chichester); more importantly, there is no solid ground from which they could spring. The keynote of Noel Coward's version of 'Occupe-toi d'Amelie' is struck at the end of Act Two. What, somebody asks, is going on here? Geraldine McEwan as Lulu responds with a brief and accurate resume of the story so far. "This," says her interlocutor, "is becoming farcical." Curtain. In other words we get a scornful commentary on the idea of French farce; and who in echt Feydeau would be able to come up with a synopsis?

Lulu is a cocotte, temporarily abandoned by her lover to the care of a friend. When her old protector finds her in bed with her new one he takes signal revenge; he persuades them into a mock-marriage which turns out to be genuine. The marriage scene itself, performed by an authentic magistrate whom everyone believes to be a fraud, is a set-piece of considerable merit; this scene of orchestrated disbelief is the only credible thing in the evening.

Of course with two comic masters at war some sparks fly. The actors are required to play in two styles at once. Some decline, like Fenella Fielding who performs in her own manner, and Kenneth Haigh who hardly performs at all. Geraldine McEwan reconciles them best; ironically enough the virtuous indignation she deployed so marvellously as the bourgeoisie of 'A Flea in Her Ear' also suits Coward's Lulu, for whom sex is just a matter of double-entendres. I doubt if she has much in common with Feydeau's Amelie, who would be businesslike and half the age. Still, Miss McEwan looks beautiful and sounds funny. Clive Francis shines too as the unwilling husband; his performance is a model of economy (i.e., he is in a state of permanent slump). Nigel Stock gets closer than anyone to true Parisian determination, bolstered as it happens, by hilarious Dutch vowels. I wish Chichester had mounted a real translation; it's one thing to revive West End successes, but 'Lulu' (which dates, like 'The Aspern Papers,' from 1959) was a West End flop. 'Lulu' is high comic art compared to Philip Magdalen's Boo Hoo (Open Space). Here are a trio of Miami hookers, each forcing the actress concerned on to the aggressive-defensive. Georgina Hale affects a belligerent squeal, Estelle Kohler a Monroevian pout and Janet Suzman -- the most successful of the three -- a world-weary brashness. She could probably sail through the entire Katharine Hepburn repertoire.

While this trio compare incomes, plot to kill their husbands, disclose unexpected relationships or drop references to the state of the Nation (desperate jabs in the direction of satire), we look at Timian Alsaker's set, which incorporates a Buddha that opens out into a cocktail cabinet and a table on three stockinged legs: the evening's sum total of wit.
production_title: Are You Now or Have You Ever Been?

records.title: Back to New Orleans
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Back to New Orleans

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Tennessee Williams and Shakespeare

DO YOU KNOW what it means to miss New Orleans? Tennessee Williams does and over the years his public have come to share the feeling. We have all wished him a return to the quality of A Streetcar Named Desire and if the quality, then why not the locale? Vieux Carré (Piccadilly) returns us to both; and there has hardly been a more satisfying evening in the West End since the revival of Streetcar at this same theatre.

While we are harking back, we may as well recall Mr Williams's other classic, The Glass Menagerie. Vieux Carré inherits its technique of first-person narration. Indeed, however centrally placed, the Writer is less a character in Vieux Carré than an extension of the Tom, now come a reasonably long way from St Louis if not, I would guess, very far at all from Tennessee.

One calls the setting a rooming-house by courtesy. The landlady Mrs Wire professes to think highly of it but her tenants refer to cubicles rather than rooms. Their comfort is not increased by Mrs Wire's practice of sleeping on a camp bed in the hall, all the better to see them from. She disapproves, volubly, of all of them: of the tubercular painter Nightingale who seduces the Writer; of Jane the genteel youngish New Yorker shacked up with a stud from a strip-joint; even of the two pathetic old ladies who stray about a kitchen when they sniff home-made chicken gumbo. They do this, oddly, in the middle of the night, but as they explain, 'our light bulbs are burned out so we can't tell day from night anymore.'

The Writer gets more of her tongue than any of them but he also gets more of her indulgence. He even works for her for a time, rustling up customers for her 25 cent bargain dinners. The slogan 'eat for a quarter in the quarter' may count as his first published work.

Half-way through the evening Mrs Wire wreaks vengeance on her basement lodgers, who have broken the terms of their lease by holding orgies (she says), and pours down boiling water upon them through a gap in the floorboards. For this she is taken to court and fined. I could not see that this event, however centrally placed, had much effect on the rest of the action, but you do not go to Vieux Carré for its plot. You go rather to hear the author, frank and relaxed, raising self-plagiarism to new heights and admitting it in his title. The process has had a rejuvenating effect on his dialogue, which has never been funnier. (It is in fact the best comic writing in London.)

There is now a refreshing wryness about his treatment of sex, homo and hetero; it still permits passion but banishes melodrama. Jane is a miniature re-working of Blanche Dubois, but considerably easier to take; she does not pose, and she is afforded no convenient black-outs. You see her hating herself and her lover, and succumbing; you also see why. Mr Williams the black romancer is still in evidence, in a long speech about a beautiful woman -- 'the champagne girl' -- devoured by dogs, but it is a necessary hideousness: an emblem of the world from which Mrs Wire's establishment provides at least a kind of shelter.

Vieux Carré is also a tribute -- maybe an unconscious one -- to a form of stagecraft long in disuse but still potent: the theatre of Elia Kazan, where music faded in and out at the precise atmospheric moment, houses were seen in section (sometimes, as here, with the aid of a revolve) and characters moved effortlessly into pools of light with retrospective intent.

In Keith Hack's loving production (there's a phrase I never expected to write) it is served by actors obviously overjoyed to have, for once, something to act. Richard Kane is perhaps a bit fuzzy as Nightingale and Jonathan Kent's bedroom champ may try too hard, though his efforts are usually rewarded. But Sylvia Miles is a barbed and electric Mrs Wire and Sheila Gish was hauntingly bruised as Jane. (Her subsequent exit from the part greatly surprised me; she seemed perfectly in tune with it.) Neither lady, blessedly, is pathetic.

The Writer is Karl Johnson, hitherto known in the complete works of Nigel Baldwin at the Theatre Upstairs, and possessed of a curiously compelling face, ratlike but vulnerable, and of a personality to match: open and inscrutable. For Mr Williams's surrogate, moving towards professional detachment, he is a perfect and imaginative choice.

* * *

More riches at Stratford: John Barton's production of Love's Labour's Lost is the season's best so far (though his Merchant runs it close) -- not so much a discovery of unknown riches as a clear demonstration that those in which we always believed do actually exist. Mr Barton directs it as a play about four undergraduates who forsake the world because they are afraid to face it, are thrown by the arrival of four ladies, try to get the love-game together, are made ludicrous by the disclosure of their pretensions, try to put a good face on things, think they have succeeded and are defeated by the arrival of an unalterable reality, Death.

None of this, I am aware, is news, but I have never seen it lived so thoroughly before; never heard such delight taken in the scholars' affectations, felt the mood change so palpably at the last, or known a Berowne keep so precise a balance between badinage and lyricism, sense and surrender, as Michael Pennington. (He starts as a disembodied intelligence, merely accomplished, and grows.) Backing him is a delightfully timid King from Richard Griffiths, as hesitant as he has in former roles been solid, and opposed is a Princess (Carmen du Sautoy in a spectacular ginger wig) who though she can teach him something of life, is visibly learning herself.

The finest touch of the evening comes in the show of the Nine Worthies: one of the performing clowns lets his spear droop; the Princess comes forward to help him, and the King to help her; a three-way rapprochement. Allan Hendrick is a marvellously assured Costard, and there is a parkful of talent besides, the extremes of experience meeting in Michael Hordern's Armado, who is rather like Quixote, and Jo James's page, who is nothing at all like Sancho. There is a soothing arboreal set (most uncharacteristic of its designer Ralph Koltai) and the action, mostly taking place on an oblong forestage, gets closer to the audience than is usually believed, in this theatre, to be possible.

* * *

Ken Campbell's The Great Caper was claimed by some to be ahead of its time when first seen at the Royal Court. Maybe it was just ahead of me. Anyway I found the current revival at the ICA far funnier, even though Mike Bradwell's production is considerably less polished than the improvised work on which the company, Hull Truck, has made its name. Mr Campbell's mystical-farcical tirades are delivered with the right offhanded delight, though the actors sometimes seem foxed by the absence of anything much to say. Meanwhile. There is action, oh yes there is action, and it takes strange shapes, but it doesn't come round very often.

Michael Abbensetts's Alterations (New End) is also dependent on its verbals, which again are well dispensed. Twenty years ago it would have been a Jewish play; now the minority group trying to get a footing in and through the rag-trade are West Indians, and at their best they can be similarly salty. The central situation -- a man working himself and his colleagues and his marriage to exhaustion -- never takes proper root, but the sparks fly around it with reasonable frequency.

records.title: Visitors from Russia
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Visitors from Russia

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE Malaya Bronnaya Company from Moscow have brought to the Lyceum a brace of programme-note productions. Our own directors no longer tell us so earnestly what they are trying to do, though one or two of them would probably like to.

Anatoli Efros presents a determined face to the plays he directs: to Gogol's The Marriage (not, he says disarmingly, "a precious find for the theatre of our time") and Turgenev's A Month in the Country ("a good play, delicately . . . written. But what is good writing and what is delicacy?").

We are likely to find the Turgenev more enjoyable because more familiar; there is no fun in seeing a classic desecrated if you don't know it in the first place. The Marriage should, perhaps, be trimmed and presented as half a double bill. Efros, though, has elongated it through the introduction of dumb-shows.

The play has a soliloquising heroine (it also has a soliloquising hero with a soliloquising best friend) and whatever she imagines, we see. She compares the merits of her four suitors and they appear: a typical Gogolian rout of snobs, hangers-on and minor civil servants, lined up patiently on a bench like long-delayed commuters. When she has made her choice she thinks of the future and of children; a dozen of them promptly appear. Her intended must have had similar premonitions, for he bolts. Gogol has him jump out of a window. Efros lets us see him land, and scramble into a waiting landau.

In this line of experimentation the Russians lag far behind the Germans, the French and even the British. Efros's actual staging is clumsy; his scenic ideas waylay his actors. But he has the priceless director's gift of making his performers think, and he has an excellent company to work on.

Olga Yakovleva, though capable of considerable physical exertion (a graceful backward bound and pirouette across the stage when proposed to), makes the disappointed bride a figure of great poignancy: far more than I can find in the text. Nor can I see the point of ending the play with a menacing wedding cortege, symbolising precisely the plight that the characters have escaped. Disdaining the trappings of farce, Efros has substituted those of melodrama; his production is hard-hitting but soft-centred.

His Month in the Country also has some violent externals; it takes place mostly on a wrought-iron semi-circular garden seat mounted on a revolve and set regularly spinning. At the end (comes, I suppose, the Revolution) silent, sinister functionaries close in, dismantle the set and even rob the self-pitying chatelaine Natalie of the child's kite she has been cradling (Yakovleva has just treated us to another virtuoso athletic display, this time denoting grief). Clearly, the giddy whirl of the land-owning classes is about to come to an end.

While it lasts, however, Efros gives us a hard, clear look at it: not, however, a callous one. Natalia says to her lover Rakitin that his conversation is like lace-making, beautiful but arid, less attractive than a drink of cold water on a hot day. It is easy to get lost in Turgenev's tapestry; Efros pours on the cold water instead. Yakovleva's blonde Natalia is attractive, sympathetic, potentially passionate -- like a film star ageing into mother roles, sometimes with relish, more often with resentment. Her menfolk restore one's faith in Russian male acting (rather shaken by The Marriage). Crowning all is Leonid Bronevoy's doctor, whom you might label an eccentric were he not so robustly confident that he creates his own world around him. It is understandable that Efros should want to transcend "Russian realism" but the rest of the world cannot wish him too much luck since for us that label denotes something so satisfying and so all-inclusive; these actors confirm all our most favourable prejudices.

* * *

The official festival this year is either Russian or Shakespearean. The RSC have entries in both sections, stopping off at Daniel Stewart's and Melville College ("patrons asked not to smoke in the school gymnasium") with their fit-up version of Three Sisters and Twelfth Night, the latter a nicely framed production.

It begins with Viola gazing fascinatedly through a mirror at the Illyrians: Olivia on one of her devotional trips to her mother's grave, Sir Toby grumpily bringing up the rear. The link between clowns and romantics is established, to be severed at the end; as Feste sings his last song the lovers embrace while the outcasts -- just about everybody else -- are sent packing with broken heads, or hearts, or both. Magic.

What goes between is lively but not always especially coherent. Viola (Emily Richard) and Olivia (Suzanne Bertish) are bright but lightweight though what they really lack is practice, nine times out of ten the determining factor in acting Shakespeare. Apart from Edward Petheridge's subtly felt mocking Orsino, habit is here on the side of the comics, who include the best couple Belch and Aguecheek I have seen.

Roger Rees's Andrew is a blazered incompetent with a Hitlerian forelock, who knows he is being strung along but cannot help himself. A kind word will do wonders with him, and it is just his luck that Ian McKellen's Toby knows when to apply it. This Toby, except when dealing with his niece, has an answer for everyone, a splendid, habitual air of innocence and a lachrymose family pride ("am I not consanguineous"), flaring into real anger with the upstart Malvolio (Bob Peck), whose romantic scene ("this does make some obstruction in the blood, this cross-gartering") is an excellent mixture of lust and cramp. Add a sad but not suicidal Feste (Christopher Hancock) and a fine deadpan Fabian (Clyde Pollitt).

In the Assembly Hall Shakespeare also rules but not OK: not at least in The Tempest done in modern dress which, since the play has so little explicit action, could hardly matter less either way. I still don't know how Ariel should be costumed but I can now add streaky body stocking to the list of discarded alternatives. The fairies in A Midsummer Night's Dream are similarly got up, though Taylerson's Titania -- more becomingly. This, despite kebab house music, is altogether a far more agreeable production, rarely stirring the imagination but amusing and efficient at ground level.

The Traverse have their usual massive festival repertoire. I saw Robert Holman's Rooting presenting the human face of The Archers, passions boiling and subsiding and just going on down on the farm among real pigs, whose presence has a soothing, distancing effect on the human action.

There is an annexe, the Other Traverse, which looks and unfortunately sounds barnlike: hence missed subtleties of John Byrne's The Slab Boys though those around me laughed enough to persuade me that the author of Writer's Cramp had lost none of his wit in moving to a factory setting, drawn from his own youth. The acting of both Traverse plays is, at worst, immaculate.

records.title: Passion and the playwrights
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Passion and the playwrights

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'The Changeling' and 'The Philanderer'

THE playwrights of three eras last week redelivered their views on sex: views in the main deeply discouraging.

For Middleton and Rowley in The Changeling (1652), passion is an aberration born of ugliness and/or self-absorption and issuing in murder; best symbolised by the caperings of madmen. For Shaw in The Philanderer (1893) it is a character deformation bred especially in women by the false values of society and opposable only by a planned heartlessness almost equally indefensible. Only Aphra Behn in The Rover (1677) suggests that it might be the basis of an enjoyable relationship.

The Changeling (Riverside Studios) has not been seen in London for 16 years and its return is a joy and a relief. There is no verse played outside Shakespeare possessed of such natural resonance; none in which a man can declare "Can you weep fate from its determin'd purpose? So soon may you weep me" without making you feel, as Webster would, or even Jonson, that he knows he is rising to a great moment. The Changeling is in fact a play of unusual plausibility, if you can swallow (as the heroine has to) the odd, dubiously scientific virginity-test.

Beatrice, daughter of the governor of Valencia, falls in love with a handsome stranger, just after becoming engaged to someone else. To rid herself of her superfluous fiance she hires a villainously plain (and in her eyes plainly villainous) servant De Flores, whom she has hitherto humiliated. He cannot believe his luck; he has always, and hopelessly, wanted her -- now he can have her. The scene in which he claims her, making plain what she has done and where it has placed her (she being stronger on maidenly indignation than moral imagination), is an unmatched duet, an explosive series of revelations. Only the central scenes of Measure for Measure compare with it.

Criticism of the play has tended to take Beatrice at her own valuation: an innocent ruined by a tempter. (How dare De Flores poke his ugly mug round the door, just as she happens to be contemplating murder?) Performance upsets this; you could make out a good case for De Flores being the victim (a dab hand at murder, admittedly, but there is no suggestion that he does it very often) whom she corrupts. At any rate, he gains the theatrical sympathy that always goes to a realist; he knows what he is doing whereas Beatrice maintains a self-centred ignorance. Treating others as objects she keeps talking, as he contemptuously points out, of her "honour." It is this counterpoint that keeps the play darting about on its feet until the end.

The play's other surprise is its sub-plot, which acts far better than it reads. It is set in a mad-house, where gallants disguised as patients lay siege to the keeper's wife, who knows, unlike Beatrice, how to get rid of them. In Peter Gill's production these scenes are kept not only lively (special credit to David Troughton as a cynical clown who has his own stab at defloration) but relevant: at one point the two leading ladies pass each other as like ships in the night as you could ever hope to see on dry land.

Mr Gill's direction, on a wide, grim, flagstoned stage, has exemplary clarity and considerable emotional force. It lacks however in wit; it moves too deliberately both for the double-entendres which mine the text and for the giddy capriciousness of Beatrice that springs the action. She is an actress's problem -- a shallow character who suffers -- and Emma Piper offers a sedate though accurate sketch rather than a full portrait.

Brian Cox's De Flores emerges more likeably than even I would have expected: a strong, wracking performance if limited in its choice of notes. (A word in memory of the late Robert Shaw who gave his best performance in the role at the Royal Court in 1961 -- in a production that actually smacked far less of the Court than this one does.)

Julia Craven in The Philanderer might be Beatrice's lineal descendant; both ladies have indulgent fathers and latch on furiously to the men of their choice. Julia's tactics stop short of murder, though she speaks of it; her method is to throw tantrums and make scenes. Often they work, though a rival responds to them with a roof-raising line: "Do you suppose I am a man, to be imposed on by this sort of rubbish?"

At the Lyttelton, Penelope Wilton plays Julia in accordance with that response: as a calculating neurotic, keenly and hilariously observed. Christopher Morahan's production, the National's best this year, realises the play admirably down to its last stage direction, which happens to be "the rest look at Julia with concern, and even a little awe, feeling for the first time the presence of a keen sorrow." It is arguable that we should have felt it earlier, and that our laughter should have been edged with discomfort, but that is a small point. (Or rather, it's a large one, but it doesn't matter.)

The philanderer himself is another casualty of the sex-war: more engaging (like De Flores), since he has both wit and common sense, but studiously cold. He is a sexless satyr, and if such a thing cannot exist in nature it can in Shaw. Dinsdale Landen (bearded and sandalled, but not Irish or, as far as I could discern, vegetarian or teetotal) plays him with consummate airiness. Basil Henson again demonstrates his command of the military virtues, Barbara Flynn is a taking younger sister (an apprentice New Woman) and John Standing is the embodiment of stuffy shyness as an amorous doctor, discoverer of "Paramore's Disease" and, by the grace of a pun, one of its prime victims.

Shaw thought paramour's disease curable, though the continuing topicality of this, his second play, suggests he may have been mistaken. Middleton and Rowley thought it might be halted, at least in sensible people who spoke prose in sub-plots. The best Restoration playwrights took it for granted, and welcomed it.

* * *

Where, these past years, has Aphra been? I once recommended The Rover to a theatre that was mounting a season of plays by women; if such a category exists, this is its prime exhibit. The best thing about it, though, is that you don't stop to consider the sex of its author; its sympathies are boundless, and its humour unsentimentally acute, despite a plethora of moonlight duels. Its rover is a practising philanderer who ends up with a girl designed to be a nun; there can have been few such lovers in the history of vocational guidance. It is given a lacklustre performance at the Mercury, Colchester; it, and its fortunes, should revive.

The Salisbury Playhouse looks almost identical to the Mercury, but its stage is currently more expertly occupied. Two things happen in Hardy's Under the Green-wood Tree as rendered for the stage by Patrick Garland: a young man wins the hand of the local schoolteacher, and the church string band, mainly composed of his relatives, are ejected from their place in favour of one of them newfangled harmoniums. Their story, and particularly their music, takes precedence; once you have got the hang of it, the method is very agreeable.

Kevin Moore gives a charming account of the vicar who loses the girl but gets the organ, and Frank Shelley as the oldest inhabitant acts, sings and plays his instrument with equal authority.

records.title: Racing to destruction
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Racing to destruction

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the revival of Inadmissible Evidence.

JOHN OSBORNE must have had to dredge a bit to find the unfavourable reviews of Inadmissible Evidence quoted in the programme for the present Royal Court revival. It is, after all, his junction play, offering something for everybody; for some, it is the first work of his maturity, for others the last flaring of his youthful promise. (This was 1964, seven years after Look Back in Anger.)

I would identify myself with the first faction. Mr Osborne's subsequent road has been a rocky one, but he has at least shown a lively awareness of who his enemies are (I speak as one of them); before that, he was merely snorting with the crowd.

Inadmissible Evidence is, of all its author's plays, the one in which the chief character shuts up for the shortest length of time. This is despite the fact that he is very rarely alone on the stage, and despite the further fact that his companions are very far from being stooges. The play covers two days inside the life, the office and the head (these are frequently overlapping zones) of Bill Maitland, solicitor.

Nicol Williamson was marvellous in the role 14 years ago, and he is so again now: his is one of the key performances of our time. But a remarkable aspect of this production (directed by the author) is its supporting playing, the best I have ever seen in an Osborne play. Clive Swift as Maitland's managing clerk, offering him sympathy discreetly measured out so as to escape involvement, Deborah Norton a waxen fury as his departing secretary, Rowena Roberts provocatively normal as his telephonist, Paul Greenwood and Marjorie Yates figures of spectral pain as the clients whom he hears with an embarrassing degree of concern since he is projecting his own agonies on to them: all are alive, and their humanity - in the face of all that Maitland can say to or about them - is the best rebuke to his self-absorption. What is more, he knows it. Maitland starts out with the feeling that everybody is against him (this morning he couldn't even get a taxi) and by the end of the play he has had the fact abundantly proved. Everybody leaves or rejects him: his staff, his mistress (more overlapping), his daughter, his wife.

Through it all he talks, with increasing desperation and increasing speed. The most impressive feature of Mr Williamson's performance is its constantly accelerating rhythm; you actually feel a mind racing towards breaking-point. And when his voice is not working, his hands are, convulsively.

The weakest passages in the play are the most self-consciously public: the opening dream sequence, which is paradoxically full of clumsy assaults on bureaucratised Progress, and Maitland's celebrated diatribe (to his daughter) on the subject of Youth, Modern. Otherwise Maitland, given more rope than any other Osborne protagonist, obligingly strangles himself.

He is, however, worth mourning for. Though dauntingly selfish, he is not unloving; that in fact is his downfall. It would be a short-sighted woman who railed at the play merely because it has a sexually exploitative hero. A thoroughly sensitive, responsible, caring man would however be entitled to reject the character and the play. I don't know anybody like that myself.

* * *

In a book called The Season, published a few years back, William Goldman analysed the Broadway phenomenon of the Snob Hit, an annual event - imported from Britain - producing rave reviews, bored audiences and large dividends - plus, every year, a competing set of unsuccessful transplants ending up as Snob Flops. The Americans now have their revenge in the shape of the Camp Hit (or, as it might be, Flop), exemplified by Dracula (Shaftesbury).

This is a 1920s dramatisation (credited, in almost invisible print, to Hamilton Deane and John L. Balderston) revived in New York last year with enormous success due to (a) Edward Gorey's sets - blown-up Gothic illustrations, magnificently stylish and guaranteed to obliterate almost anything that might pass as acting; (b) an uncanny display of wit and beauty by Frank Langella in the title role; (c) the perennial and, when done by Americans, perennially effective stock-Englishman joke, applied to everyone else in the cast.

The London replica has lost (b) and (c). Terence Stamp's Count flashes his cloak with elan, but has no presence beyond that, while Dennis Rosa's production, being conceived in opposition to the text, positively demands that the other roles be played badly. Miscasting would help, but these actors have not been miscast. They have to work at it.

All of them are, in some sense, Bats - a motif that can be found all over (a), whose splendours become in this context, embarrassments. Actually Mr Rosa's style might do better for the rival import, The Passion of Dracula, which was written as a joke. In the current state of the theatre, two Draculae are, at the most liberal estimate, one too many.

* * *

For genuine camp go to the New End, where in Arthur Whitney's A Tribute to Lilli Lamont the phenomenon is both anatomised and exemplified. The anatomising is done by introducing us to a New York fan-club (membership five), whose chairman has turned his obsession with movie memorabilia into a small business. The exemplar of camp is Gloria Grahame, who plays the object of their affection and who acts, as befits a cinematic lady, in short bursts: most of them craftily to synchronise with the dramatic points.

Miss Grahame seems a little surprised to find herself on a stage, but game to play along and to exploit the fact; the same is true, in her rather similar circumstances, of Miss Lamont. Her admirers, cleverly delineated as types (especially the autograph-hunter ruthless in his pursuit of famous persons), get out of hand when the author attempts to exploit them; it is not, after all, an inexhaustible subject and the second half goes downhill. Good performances by Don Fellows and Gordon Sterne.

I have a feeling that Tom McGrath's The Android Circuit (ICA) also belongs in the camp category. It is a harmless piece of SF whimsy, about the last man and his encounter with an exhaustively programmed female robot. Attractively acted, sometimes funny and - at just over an hour - over-extended.

At the Old Vic there is a likeable and finally exhilarating production of The Rivals - not a play I ever expected to be exhilarated by. All the characters are walking jokes, the one difference of each one is zestfully presented; they add up to a satisfying pattern and also tell a good story. The novelettish imaginings of Lydia Languish are beautifully done by Isla Blair; so are the humorous stratagems of her lover by Christopher Neame. Anthony Quayle as his father mingles apoplectic fits with reminiscent lusts; Margaret Courtenay, who took over Mrs Malaprop at short notice (an unenviable task in this of all roles - suppose she got the words right?) turns her mannerisms into obsessions and those obsessions into a personality.

records.title: Rudman's final fling
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Rudman's final fling

ROBERT CUSHMAN on "a cracker" of a comedy by Michael Hastings.

MICHAEL HASTINGS'S Gloo Joo is rumoured to be Michael Rudman's last production as director of the Hampstead Theatre.

Though I join with all the world in applauding the friendliness of Mr Rudman's five-year regime at Swiss Cottage, I have generally found his actual choice of plays to be glum.

There have been exceptions, of course: two plays by Michael Frayn, one by Pam Gems, and now, at the last, a cracker. The show-piece of Mr Hastings's play is a Jewish wedding, different from most that have been seen on our stages in that the bride is African, the groom Jamaican and the setting an immigration office at Gatwick Airport, whose two functionaries are currently trebling as witnesses, congregation and upholders of the handy portable canopy brought along (together with a celebratory bottle of sherry) by the officiating rabbi.

The assembly are required of course to wear hats, and here the bridegroom can oblige. What living he has, he makes from selling woolly football caps, dealing impartially with supporters of all teams; he now produces a couple of samples. Very funny they look. Mr Hastings here reveals himself as a superb farcical engineer. His hero, Meadowlark Warner, reveals himself as a superb opportunist.

That is his role throughout. The play occurs on what he calls repeatedly "the greatest day of his life." It happens to be the day decided on by the authorities for his deportation; he is forcibly removed from Brixton to Gatwick and is in imminent danger of further travel. He has, however, provided himself with a pair of fiancees.

The first, who is Irish, he discards as having the wrong-coloured passport. (Meadowlark, I should warn you, is a racist.) The second lady is far more eligible and, her patrial status having been approved to the satisfaction of all parties, the ceremony is performed in the exotic circumstances already described. A necessary (though imperfect) coda shows Meadowlark finally meeting his match. His new wife demands to be supported. "From now on," she says immortally, "you'll line up at the social security like everybody else."

The play makes manifest the racial jokes that underlay Trevor Griffiths's Comedians. Meadowlark has lines (one, for example, about not wanting to go to Jamaica because he can meet quite enough Jamaicans in London) that no white character would be entrusted with. When he needs suddenly to claim Jewishness he pours out a glorious flood of nonsense about something called the Black Temple of Nimrod; but his real appeal is to the brotherhood of the persecuted. Meanwhile the immigration officers look on with fascinating (and subtly interchangeable) degrees of callousness and sympathy.

Mr Rudman's flawlessly zippy production is propelled by Oscar James's bounding, fluently Meadowlark and anchored by Antony Brown and Dave Hill as his guardians. Mr Brown, the more punctilious of the two, is an especial delight during the wedding; permanently desirous of mopping his brow, but hampered by the lack of an available hand.

This is, according to the programme, Mr Hastings's ninth play; having missed all but one of the other eight I cannot guess whether he has it in him to give us more comedies as refreshing as this. But then I don't know whether Snoo Wilson will ever give us another Glad Hand, Bill Morrison another Flying Blind, or Mike Stott (the next Hampstead attraction) another Funny Peculiar. Counting blessings rather than pre-natal chickens, I can only celebrate the existence of a new and penetrating genre of social farce.

* * *

Stephen Poliakoff is not among its practitioners. He does not make many jokes. But neither is he weighed down with solemnity or self-hatred. Shout Across the River (Warehouse) adds to his patented collection of grisly fun-centres: there are scenes in an ice-cream parlour (not such a bad place, actually) and in a multi-barred pub, "the biggest pleasure centre for 20 miles." More importantly he shows an increasing mastery of inner terror.

A mother, only 35, has a problem daughter, suspended from school for every imaginable offence. So much for the first scene; in the second, it transpires the daughter, only 15, has a problem mother, who has hardly left the house for six months. Daughter proposes, in the week left her before removal to an approved school, to take mother in hand. How much of her action is due to concern and how much to malice (for she has to be cruel to be kind and would very likely be cruel anyway) is unclear; and the mother's acquiescence is not too easy to swallow.

There are indeed many unexplained details; we don't know what the family lives on and Mr Poliakoff has inflicted on himself a peculiarly refined version of the eternal exposition problem; characters who live together are continually discovering things they should have known for years. He has yet in fact to find a satisfying connecting path between the interior and exterior landscapes he charts with such acuteness. But the effort of belief is this time worth making; the jumping, twisting dialogue is compulsive.

Besides, the upshot is unprecedented. Daughter screams that they are living at the worst time ever and mother, defying all current theatrical custom, refuses to believe it. Having been lured out into the world she finds she can take it. The shout across the river between the generations (or is it merely between the characters south of the Thames and the audience north of it) is, against all augury, successful. Lynn Farleigh gives a wonderfully illuminating account of the mother. Gwyneth Strong is superbly sharp-edged in opposition and support.

* * *

A pair of similarly damaged lives are depicted, but hardly explored, in David Storey's Sisters (Royal Exchange, Manchester); unlike Mr Poliakoff, Mr Storey shows no strain in his writing, but the result -- wringing wan jokes out of a suburban brothel, family-owned -- slips away as soon as heard.

Trevor Nunn's production of As You Like It (Aldwych) still lacks a final roundness and sureness in performance, but a show that was half-good at Stratford is now three-quarters excellent. Mr Nunn excels both at bringing joy and at criticising it; the Forest of Arden is mocked even while celebrated. Oliver Ford Davies (Duke) and Jeffery Dench (Adam) are prodigies of self-deprecation. Alan David's Touchstone, funny nearly all the time, and Emerys James's Jaques, the prototypal Eeyore, are greatly improved performances, and Charlotte Cornwell's Rosalind is most seriously and charmingly in love.

Other newcomers are Cherie Lunghi, a phenomenally witty Celia, and Jane Carr, whose lumpy schoolgirl act does notably well for Phoebe. The changes in the weather (from "blow, blow, thou winter wind" to "sweet lovers love the spring") are exactly and most musically noted, and much of the play is in them.

records.title: Restoration house party
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Restoration house party

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a Congreve revival and a new play by David Mercer.

CONGREVE'S The Double Dealer (Olivier) has the reputation of a neglected classic. Actually, compared to some I could mention, it's a repertory standard. It touches down about once every 10 years and I, who have measured out my life in revivals of minor classics, am usually in its path. Since nobody should be required to summarise the plot of this play more than once in his lifetime I may draw, in what follows, on my own previous writings on the subject.

Right then. The Double Dealer, in the words of Ray Charles, ain't nothin' but a house-party. Lord Touchwood has invited some friends down to celebrate the betrothal of his nephew Mellefont to Cynthia, an arrangement which pleases hardly anyone.

Lady Touchwood, Lord T's wife, fancies Mellefont, as does Lady Plyant who is not Cynthia's mother, merely the second wife of her father, who by the way is Lady Touchwood's brother. Cynthia meanwhile is desired by Maskwell, the kind of friend with whom Mellefont doesn't need enemies. There are also Lord and Lady Froth, but they keep themselves very much to themselves.

I have known the Froths, a pair of litterateurs who have met their perfect match in each other, to dominate the play: a perfect image of the Hampstead or Blackheath couple who meet at a party, find themselves in complete intellectual sympathy, and go to bed on the discovery. Here they are subdued, though Nicholas Selby, at least, captures the lord's complacent solemnity (reining back all intrusive smiles) and Brenda Blethyn's flirtatious lady fits neatly into the evening's principal pattern.

There are four women in the play, and three of them are nymphomaniacs (or, to put it in Restoration terms, married). Cynthia, a coolly intelligent little number in Judi Bowker's performance, looks at them and decides that her match at least will turn out different. Of her three errant sisters, if Lady Froth is a creature of satiric farce, Lady Plyant ascends to high lubricious comedy: her lines, as cooed and purred by Dorothy Tutin, are the poetry of double entendre. Finally, there is Lady Touchwood, in whom passion and jealousy come close to madness, and whom Sara Kestelman in a grandly unabashed reading (her best yet, I think) turns into a pale-faced compound of Phedre and Lady Macbeth.

To each lady at least one gentleman. (There are also a couple of spare gallants to carry messages and make up the occasional threesome.) The most complicated is Maskwell, whose quirk is to tell his dupes what he is going to do to them before he does it. Robert Stephens adds a further twist; his professions of conscience are not all bluff. Glassy-faced, glassy-voiced, he blenches momentarily at the thought of betraying his friend, bedding his protector's wife, yet again. As a tragi-comic creation, he almost unifies the play. (A double dealer works wonders.)

Ironically, I suppose, he is dressed in white (cream, anyway), while Mellefont, the goody, goes about in black, thereby pre-empting his own final disguise as a chaplain (a necessary prelude to marriage, in this kind of play). Lord Touchwood is central to the plot, but peripheral to the play; Ralph Richardson cannot bring him to life until the end, when he, too, has a triumphant stab at intrigue.

I have now cleared the decks for Michael Bryant, who plays Miss Tutin's spouse, an ill-used knight kept in sexual and social subjection, and convinced that it is for his own good. Occasionally he stirs into revolt, but gently rebukes himself. There is a quiet war within him; no word can escape him without being gravely weighed. He has one longish speech describing his state of life (he lies trussed up at night, so that his wife will not be disturbed by his advances), which Mr Bryant breaks up into sections of two words each. Each phrase gets a laugh. His is the most huggable performance I have seen for ages.

Tanya Moiseiwitsch has set the play on a timbered baronial staircase, a solid comfort to behold. It comes equipped with carved heads for decoration, secret passages and exit-windows for action, and a revolve to transport us to the bedroom (and the motivation) behind the display. It leaves the acting-area a bit cramped; a great deal seems shoved into a corner.

Peter Wood's direction suffers from a giggly beginning and a huddled, hurried end, but its middle is stuffed with accomplishment. The variations in style hardly matter (the text invites them - some critics seem to want everyone to give the same performance); the variations in pressure do. There is not the solid mellow enchantment of Mr Wood's Love for Love, but if you relax with it the good things will come to you.

* * *

"We are not," hollers an English upper-middle-class drunk in the wake of a Russian defector who is defecting back again, "a valid statistical sample." There is no reason for Cousin Vladimir (Aldwych) to leave England on account of the collection of soaks to whom he has been exposed on his brief visit - especially since he himself is no heroic dissident, but an industrial swindler a step or so ahead of the police.

The common complaint against David Mercer's play has been phrased in much his own words; if these people are not typical, what is the point of arranging the encounter? It begins to fade when you try to imagine a social group who might give Vladimir a better run for his roubles; disenchantment would surely set in somewhere. The flaw is rather that Mr Mercer's bleak honesty about both sides amounts to a meeting of negatives: a subject, possibly, but for a shorter play than this. Once you have grasped the point that life in Britain may be preferable to life in the Soviet Union but we shouldn't get smug about it, there is not much to take in, apart from exceptional articulateness. But the drinking-gang are not fascinating (not even their leader, an ex-physicist who gets Vladimir asylum by marrying his cousin) and the evening becomes a replay of The Iceman Cometh? (a houseful of lushes embracing and then rejecting a false saviour) without O'Neill's widening single-mindedness to hold it together. The acting is all right, which means not right enough.

The second agoraphobic mum in two weeks turns up in Anne Commire's Shay (King's Head). As a case-study, this American lady, afraid to meet people because she knows that she can talk to them only too readily, is far more believable at first sight than Stephen Poliakoff's Croydon recluse in Shout Across the River, but has nothing like the same imagination or intensity to guide her thereafter.

Shay herself may be disturbing, but the play is cosy. Libby Morris gives her plenty of guts, plenty of despair, but there is no jelly in her; the lady's tic is a showbiz compulsion, but when Miss Morris sings along with a Lena Horne record she does it so well that you wonder what she can be worried about.

records.title: The call of the sea
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The call of the sea

SHE WAS only a lighthouse-keeper's daughter, but her passions were way off the beam.

Ellida, the heroine of Ibsen's The Lady From The Sea (Royal Exchange, Manchester), has a marine complex, presumably inherited, that caused her during a youth spent in the frozen north to fall in love with a sailor. He vanished, with a murder charge hanging over him, and she became the second wife of a doctor from the south.

Here she lives, loving her husband, but unable to communicate with him or with his two resentful daughters. Besides, the sea keeps calling her: most audibly in Michael Elliott's production, where the cry of the breakers and cries of (I am assured) whales and dolphins come at you from all sides in the highest of theatrical fidelity. They sound real enough for a dream and they are complemented by Laurie Dennett's set which is largely composed of water.

Dr Wangel lives by a fjord and the action here takes place on a series of moveable jetties. Stage-hands wade in between the acts to shift them around; one even planted a tree which obscures an important conversation in the succeeding scene. But it is soon uprooted, and everything else is clear: this is the most visually satisfying production yet staged at this theatre.

It is also by far the best acted. It is a paradox that this play, which would seem to have the most tenuous and unlikely plot of any Ibsen, has also the greatest feeling for the everyday life of a household. The affairs of the doctor's daughters are set, in almost Chekhovian counterpoint, to those of their stepmother. Ellida believes that in marrying she may have sacrificed her freedom for the sake of an illusory security; Bolette, the elder girl, is shown doing the same in agreeing to marry her old tutor, who is himself merely transferring his affections from Ellida herself. Meanwhile young Hilde (the future predator of The Master Builder) amuses herself in teasing a sculptor who looks to the hopeless but ennobling longing he must surely inspire in every young woman he meets.

Against these illusions are set the claims of a perfectly real lover, Ellida rejects him - to summarise brutally - only after the doctor has set her free to make her own decision. She then subsides, quietly hymning the joys of responsibility. That seems glib when you read it but Vanessa Redgrave and Graham Crowden make it not only credible, but moving.

Mr Crowden, who starts with the advantage of being in his angular way an exceptionally endearing actor, visibly grapples with his own possessiveness, thereby generating a powerful electricity of his own, quite enough to counterbalance the seafarer's magic. Miss Redgrave can make you share her belief in any number of impossible things; happiness, bewilderment, loneliness, loss, and happiness again suffuse her every inch. (Her height, given the intensity with which she works, may be her greatest asset.) She gives an amazingly unstrained performance.

The play belongs to her; she has played Ellida in New York, and years ago in London she played Bolette. The memory of that performance lends resonance to the parallel between the characters in the present production. Sherrie Hewson's Bolette, initially a modest lump, grows steadily in strength and definition through the evening, as does Lynsey Baxter's Hilde, the only character actually to get her feet wet. She trails them in the water while effectively seducing the sculptor, who is amusingly played by Christopher Good.

There should be other bouquets for John Franklyn Robbins's tutor, Michael Byrne's stranger and for Ronald Herdman as a choric Jack-of-all-trades, who dissolves play and production in a single call. Seventeen years ago Miss Redgrave and Mr Elliott gave us the As You Like It of a generation; their joint return to form could hardly be happier.

* * *

On the strength of Gemini, still running on Broadway, I would rate Albert Innaurato the best of the new transatlantic playwrights. Hampstead, the Royal Court and the Cottesloe should be knifing one another for the rights. Meanwhile the Bush has sent us Benno Blimpie, an earlier play which, like Gemini, shows us a world of Italian immigrants with a sensitive and fat boy at its centre, but is earlier, shorter, more schematic and more self-indulgently ugly. Benno Blimpie has the soul of an artist, but the shape and the appetite of the Michelin man. And with no rosetted restaurant available in the district, he has to gorge himself on junk food.

Discarded wrappers and empty cartons lie in heaps around him as he looks back on his life: arrested by his mother, neglected by his father, bullied and insulted by the other kids - especially by a 13-year-old nymph, who seduces and robs his grandfather. Watching this last experience 26 years later, he intervenes until he is assaulted by a gang of youths in a playground. Realising that the world has no other use for his body, and none at all for his mind, he sets out to eat himself to death.

It is a limited view of the world, but Mr Innaurato can impose it for the duration; his writing commands wit as well as grotesquerie and the two are balanced here in Lynda Marchal's swashbuckling production. Michael Poole's groping, pathetic old man; Robbie Coltrane, pain and indignation battling across his face, does a sympathetic job on Benno.

An Evening With Dave Allen (Vaudeville) is time well spent with a modest but masterly comedian. I'm not too sure what comics get up to in Ireland, but over here Mr Allen seems to belong less to the tradition of the English standup gag man than to that of the loose American conversationalist: homely Will Rogers crossed with liberal Mort Sahl. Not incendiary Lenny Bruce, though: one conceivably anti-gay joke aside, Mr Allen, who is in favour of tolerance and against bigotry (sexual, religious, political), says little that today's West End is likely to find controversial.

I was tempted to write him down at first as better than his material, but this would hardly do since he rolls his own. Sometimes he pursues a subject too far and too mechanically, but one or two of his riffs - for example his plain man's gloss on the story of Noah - are inspired. He is very likeable, which has got to be the intention.

Lumiere and Son are ahead of most performance art groups in that they can actually perform. All five of them can move and talk with conviction. The severe limitations of their medium are thus exposed more clearly than usual. They can present an issue - in this case the constrictions of a guilt-ridden social order - in pretty pictorial terms, but they cannot explore it.

Lacking faith in words, they patronise their characters, who are made to scan like inarticulate slobs, no worse than the patronage of much conventional drama, but it is to me more tedious. They too are likeable, but I am not sure that that is the intention. Their show is called Nightfall and it can be found at the Theatre Upstairs.

records.title: Finite variety
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Finite variety

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Peter Brook's new production of Antony and Cleopatra.

PETER BROOK's production of Antony and Cleopatra (Stratford-on-Avon) is an excellent evening's entertainment; don't let anyone tell you different. All the same, Tuesday's audience was definitely underwhelmed.

Mr Brook is now generally felt to have a historic function at Stratford: about once a decade, he arrives and changes everything. This time it seems at first glance that the company has been ahead of him; his production fits as neatly as is possible on that stage, into the intimate "chamber" mould that the RSC has pioneered in the Other Place.

But I forget: Mr Brook has already practised this half-way-house staging at the Bouffes-du-Nord in Paris, where his French Timon of Athens was a beautiful piece of storytelling. Using the native text of Antony, he is more constricted, though actually the production's greatest merit is its unremitting concentration on the text - a virtue not uniquely Brookish, but as much to be praised in him as in John Barton or Trevor Nunn within the RSC or Peter Gill (who may well be Mr Brook's heir) without it.

Sally Jacobs's set is bounded on the sides by movable trestles and at the back by glass screens. It is a set more practical than pretty (and at that it is more attractive than the costumes, which include a generous assortment of striped nightwear and turn at least one attendant Egyptian into a Desert Song Bedouin), but it proves itself in the notoriously difficult monument scenes; with no split-level pretences the dying Antony can simply be hauled horizontally to Cleopatra wrapped in her and her women's scarves.

Earlier, the battle scenes are suggested by the hurling of blood upon the screens - the only stand-out shock effect in the production, unless you count the carousal on Pompey's galley which works, like some of the best scenes in Evita, by going on just the vital bit longer and more, intensely than you would think possible. (Richard Peaslee's music, here and throughout, has unusual distinction.)

Otherwise the startling moments are all in the acting; they begin when Antony and Enobarbus break into helpless joyful laughter at the news that Antony's wife is dead. The episode brands Patrick Stewart's Enobarbus not (as is usual) as the keeper of his general's conscience, but as his junior partner in dissipation. "Now he'll outstare the lightning" is spoken in admiration, even though followed by his realistic plan for desertion. The conflict eventually and graphically kills him. He prefaces his anthology description of Cleopatra with a proprietorial "I will tell you," as who should say, you ain't heard nothing yet.

Even more complex is Jonathan Pryce's Octavius. Maecenas talks of Caesar seeing himself in Antony's spacious mirror. This is the relationship played by Mr Pryce: at first dazzled by his senior partner, tempted by him into surprising levity; then sobering up in horror, regarding him increasingly as an example to be studied, dreaded and destroyed. "He calls me boy," he cries exultantly on receiving Antony's craziest message (and using it as a paper kite): as who should say, he's really blown it now.

David Suchet, completing a fine season, finds more in Pompey than could have been suspected; he, unlike Caesar, gives way to his own generosity and dies of it. Then there are Paul Brooke's complacently agreeable Lepidus, Paul Moriarty's Menas, Paola Dionisotti and Juliet Stevenson as Charmian and Iras, Richard Griffiths unrecognisably straight as Cleopatra's messenger and himself again as the Clown (the only actor I have known to take Shakespeare at his word and make the asp-man red-nosed funny), Raymond Westwell's old soldier drawing, or so I guess, on his Churchill at the Other Place, Marjorie Bland's Octavia is colder than necessary, but really only two performances disappoint.

You guessed. It would be presumptuous to dictate terms for the playing of Antony and Cleopatra. But there are clues; both are defined by other characters' attitudes towards them. (That is why I have dwelt on the supporting playing; its superb quality is not luxury but a necessity. All of these actors have at some time to carry the baton.)

The story dictates that almost everyone in the play shall be in thrall to Antony and he to Cleopatra. Here it isn't believable. Alan Howard gets Antony's madness (suicidal in his determination to fight by sea, by sea, which words he burns up), but not his child- or god-like magnanimity. He is a loner: still Coriolanus. Glenda Jackson meanwhile is still Elizabeth I, capable of a superb death-scene (she is transformed, as she should be, from the moment she enters the monument) and of a breathtaking thunder-and-lightning transformation when the messenger tells her of Antony's marriage. (When he flees, she throws a knife after him.) But Cleopatra's sexuality is left in abeyance, where in fact Shakespeare himself left it. He, using the code of the boy-player, could afford to: we cannot.

Accepting that, we can feel with and applaud her - can appreciate, as we cannot with the lovers up the road, how a bitch can inspire devotion. The cheers that were stifled at Antony rang out next night for Pam Gems's Piaf (Other Place). Miss Gems is an imperfect playwright, but man, I mean woman, I mean person, can she ever write parts for actresses. To Alison Fiske's Fish and Sheila Allen's Queen Christina must now be added Jane Lapotaire's Edith - "Ede" as her friends on the Parisian streets call her. This little sparrow is a sparrer.

The play follows her from cheerful, foul-mouthed whoredom to loneliness-at-the-top; drugs and desperation and car accidents, caused by her inability to keep her hands off the men at the wheel. Sometimes she lashes out at the middle class (whatever that may be) and occasionally Miss Gems seems inclined to humour her, but in general what makes the play is the author's realisation that - with whatever provocation and whatever excuse - it was Piaf who destroyed Piaf.

Actually our warmth to her gets mixed in with our warmth towards Miss Lapotaire, whose success here is the most involving since Angela Lansbury's in Gypsy. Even her early chirpy vulgarity (in partnership with an irresistible Zoe Wanamaker) is unsentimental and the ageing, done without change of costume or make-up, is almost consummate - though she cannot quite manage the gnarled imperiousness that you hear in Piaf's records.

Her numbers are the only gash in an otherwise seamless assumption; though she sings well, gentility invades her voice. But her shakes as she approaches the mike in later days are relentlessly truthful. There are good sideline performances by Ian Charleson and Allan Hendrick; others in Howard Davies's baldly staged production confirm that Mr Brook has scooped Stratford's acting pool.

Another fabled lady: Celestina, the classic raddled bawd of the Spanish fifteenth-century classic, bravely revived at the Sheffield Crucible. Bravely because Fernando de Rojas's piece, in a jewelled Elizabethan translation, is not a play but a series of dialogues. Only in the last act, after hours have passed, does Charles Lewsen's production begin to stand on its own feet, aided by a heroine (Pamela Stephenson) who passes from virgin to voluptuary in record time. Bill Stewart's bravo is also a help; Antonia Pemberton's Celestina, though serviceable, comes far short of legend.

* * *

Baby business

MARY and Joe are a young married couple who are trying to conceive a baby; their next-door neighbours, a lesbian couple named Georgina and Sandy, want a child as well. Georgina resorts to AID (Artificial Insemination by Donor) after a failed pregnancy by more natural means; while Mary decides that she doesn't really want a baby after all.

I can't help wondering what Gloria Graham and her mum, two of the first-night audience at Michelene Wandor's AID Thy Neighbour (Theatre at New End), made of it all. Ms Wandor's play for Women's Aid sets out (1) to show us how nice lesbians really are (indeed they're just like those two nice young women next door) and (2) to argue for lesbian motherhood.

Ms Wandor does all right with her first premise, but falls down rather in her second, where she bases her argument, in a way Mary Whitehouse wouldn't dream of doing, on the wickedness of the other side. This is incarnated in the person of a woman journalist attempting to write a series (code term: Operation Dyke) criticising AID for lesbians.

The journalist arrives for supper at their house equipped with a hidden tape recorder. Georgina and Sandy, apprised of her mission, have armed themselves in turn with a camera, and they use the photographs of the drunken Geraldine ("just call me Gerald") to blackmail her out of writing her series. Although the supper scene - with each party hiding her clandestine instrument and the couple adopting exaggeratedly masculine and feminine roles - reaches a classic moment of farce, the blackmailing is a rather unhappy argument for Ms Wandor's cause. Sara Bowes makes a sympathetically confused lesbian-baiter.

records.title: Body, mind and soul
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Body, mind and soul

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Terry Hands's new production of The Changeling.

RIVERSIDE Studios' production of The Changeling was good; the Aldwych production is better.

It is, for a start, much steamier. Perhaps this has been overdone, but the faults in Terry Hands's staging are on the right side and they are redeemed by two outstanding virtues. One is the close attention paid to the play's verbal wit; puns are not just decoration, they are the vital material of a play about changing states - spiritual, physical, psychological. The other, closely allied to the first, is the performance of Diana Quick as Beatrice, with whose body, mind and soul the play is principally concerned.

Usually the interest in this play passes to De Flores, the servant whom she has unconsciously seduced long before circumstances cause her to make explicit overtures to him, who all too knowingly seduces her. His is an uncommonly grateful role for an actor; a good De Flores can justify The Changeling as a good Iago can justify Othello. He will, all the same, leave the heart of the play untouched - as happened at Riverside, and years ago at the Royal Court.

Those earlier Beatrices were blanks; Miss Quick bangs over every phrase of the character's development (rather too hard at times - one thing the performance lacks is a flowing line). At first she is a spoiled child, impatient both of her official fiance and of De Flores's offensive ugliness, which she construes as a personal insult. "The next good mood I find my father in," she declares, sounding in the play's marvellously conversational verse the imperious note of debutantes down the ages, "I'll get him quite discarded."

Needing his services as a murderer (what else could he be fit for?) she becomes exaggeratedly affectionate, removing her shawl to reveal a good proportion of her bosom: no wonder he thinks he is dreaming. It is of course absurd that she could then profess dismay when he claims her as his reward, but it is quite believable. Beatrice is very weak on assessing the consequences of her actions; hence her revulsion when De Flores produces the dead man's finger as evidence of mission accomplished.

Miss Quick gives full value to Beatrice's evasions - her crushingly ironic appeal to her modesty, for example. Her degradation, half enjoyed, is done with similar conviction. She is married in effigy to her beloved Alsemero, while at the back of the stage her actual body is enthusiastically humped by De Flores. Her complaint, "this fellow has undone me endlessly," wearily delivered, becomes an hilarious double entendre that Middleton (of Middleton and Rowley, playwrights) would surely have approved.

De Flores, meanwhile, is reduced in scale; Emrys James has perhaps played too many villains, too many malcontents. Here he acts almost in the abstract, giving us all the man's logic, but nothing of his suffering. But the supporting cast are uniformly good, notably Julian Glover and Charles Dance as the Piracquo brothers - murdered Alonzo and avenging Tomazo - a pair of blond grandees in a predominantly brunette world.

In Mr Dance's rendition, Tomazo's passion, like those of Beatrice and De Flores, approaches madness - as it should, since these respectable blank-verse people are set against the disreputable prose population who only play at madness and who themselves are placed among certified, locked-up lunatics. Mr Hands keeps these gibbering on stage throughout the final scenes; and he runs out of things for them to do (one berserk caper is much like another). But, before this, he has animated the intrigues and brought out their pertinence with considerable flair.

Here too we have a besieged heroine (spirited Charlotte Cornwell), but one who can deal with her situation. Here we have another eavesdropping servant, a would-be villain whom Barrie Rutter turns to genial farce. And here we have virtuoso essays in feigned dementia by John McEnery and Stephen Jenn, both haunting and funny. Mr Hands takes on the entire Jacobean apparatus, dumb shows and ghosts and all (throwing in a particularly good banquet en route) and makes it live.

The past is recalled with comparable skill, though in vastly different style, in the current Riverside attraction, Joint Stock's The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists. Stephen Lowe's adaptation of Robert Tressell's novel concentrates on men at work, counterpointing the possible joys of house painting in 1906, and the actual humiliations.

Rankling with the men as much as their starvation wages is the fact of being forced to do a job in half the time necessary to do it well. The chief revolutionary among them is also the finest craftsman; so absolute are his demands that he almost holds aloof when his fellows finally take collective action with limited aims. Their rising, at once tentative and effective, ends William Gaskill's production on a magnificent note, tense, expectant and satisfying; a miraculous balance of forces.

In the main play the seven actors constituting the workforce double as bosses and onlookers - sometimes stepping before our eyes from one role to another. These moments are strangely exciting, as are the repeated assumptions by each of them of the character of foreman, achieved simply by donning a suit. This only misfires when the man commits suicide - the result of the multiple performance is to prohibit not only empathy at this point but simple interest.

In general the fluid direction sets off performances of exemplary solidity - the best case yet for Joint Stock's participatory methods. They have made the book their own (it takes on an independent life unexampled among stage versions of novels) without ever betraying it.

* * *

However, two playwrights with talented pasts (and, quite possibly, futures) are giving trouble at present. The title character of David Pownall's An Audience Called Edouard (Greenwich) is Manet, though he never appears. He is looking, with us, at an animated canvas of his Dejeuner sur l'Herbe, whose four figures have broken for an extended chat. They are joined by two other figures, one of them Karl Marx - an obvious threat to their Second Empire existence. So, in another way, is Manet himself (and they, the sitters, what with strikes on the Suez Canal and personal problems, aren't too happy either) but battle is never joined; the stasis inherent in the original idea is never transcended.

The main interest of Alan Strachan's production is its capacity to come up with tableaux that look every bit as provocative as Manet's own; indeed, consulting a picture book at the theatre bookstall, it is possible to indulge in the pleasingly heretical thought that Edouard got it all wrong and his naked figure looks nothing like Susan Hampshire.

In Ballroom (Young Vic Studio) Terence Greer shows us, at numbing length, a couple of Ionesco automata (the sum of their own prejudices and therefore dramatically dead) taking out their deficiencies on their children, who revolt. The play is set in the thirties; among the things for which the characters are apparently blamed is the rise of Nazi Germany. This, since it yields guaranteed shudders, is cheap as well as inflated. Mr Greer seems to be paying off old scores; it's rather late in the century to be satirising the appeal of Shirley Temple. There are some passages of bravura writing, and the acting in Mel Smith's production is well tuned and, when opportunity permits, lively.

* * *

At the Open Space, Beckett has directed an extraordinary Krapp in Rick Cluchey, an ex-con whose San Quentin Drama Workshop grew out of the affinity of Beckett's plays to prison life. Cluchey's is the bleakest, most soulless and terrifying Krapp I have seen: a nightmare vision who unveils his (half) banana with godless joy and is tetchy to the point of violence. He is a ghost, the un-dead, and as foreign to the younger, articulate self of the tapes as that self would be to the impoverished scarecrow who shuffles before us.

Endgame, the other half of the bill, was directed by Cluchey in consultation with Samuel Beckett, an association that apparently lasted 10 days but left the members of the troupe satisfied that this was Beckett's production. Nevertheless, the result is much less successful (as it is, for me, a less successful play), despite some beautifully musical exchanges.

records.title: More murder
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
More murder

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Simon Gray's Molly and King Lear.

A FEW belated thoughts on David Jones's recent article in this newspaper concerning the relative merits of stage and television drama.

First, he is undoubtedly right when he says that a great deal of professional theatre is done essentially to impress other theatre professionals; it is surprising, though, that he considers the situation in television to be any different.

Talk to any TV writer or director working on anything more ambitious than Coronation Street (and I am not sure I should make even that qualification) and you will find his standards to be every bit as rarefied and inbred as those of his theatrical counterparts. This does not imply indifference to either viewing or box office figures. Aesthetic attitudes, though, are largely determined by who you drink with, and few punters find their way into the studio bar-rooms.

Again, Mr Jones correctly attributes the fragmentation of stage drama into numberless short scenes to the influence of television; he omits to mention that, except in the rare case of an Edward Bond, this is not a blessing but a curse. Finally it remains true that a television play is a smaller (not necessarily lesser) thing than a stage play; it can more easily arouse intense interest in a miniature subject.

Which brings me to Simon Gray's Molly (Comedy), a stage version of his teleplay Death of a Teddy Bear; a good and clever piece, but one which now leaves its audience with an uncomfortable feeling of confinement; its subject is not quite large enough to fill its space.

It is based, like Terence Rattigan's Cause Celebre, on the Alma Rattenbury murder case, and though Mr Gray's characterisation is considerably more subtle and detailed than Rattigan's, and he completely avoids the platitudes to which Rattigan sometimes resorted, his is still the less powerful piece. The subject seems to matter less to him. And Rattigan's instinct in providing a parallel plot to the Rattenbury story itself is now vindicated; it made the experience worth going out for.

Still, given that you have got yourself into the theatre in the first place, there is plenty to enjoy in Molly. Mr Gray has restructured the story around four characters--all, as Molly (his Alma) says, essentially children. There is Molly herself, the unproductive amateur songwriter, once divorced, now back from Canada with her new husband and "needing her sex." There is Teddy, the deaf and ailing mate who cannot give it to her (and never has), but who spanks her instead. There is Olly, the young chauffeur-gardener, "not quite right in the head," to whom she turns for relief and who has the bad luck to fall in love with her as a result. And there is Evy, the housekeeper, censorious but faithful, and also in love with Molly.

They make a sad collection (bleak you would call it if Mr Gray's style were a little more expansive). Olly's is the only consummated passion among them and it causes him to murder Teddy. For Molly actually loves Teddy, and it is the last-minute revelation of this fact (as he bleeds to death) that furnishes, as in Rattigan, the strongest moment in the play. Mr Gray's heroine is far less dependent on her lover than Rattigan's; she may need him physically, but she could always find another and she never hesitates to pull rank. At the end of the play, with both men dead, she settles down with Evy for--presumably--another lifetime of passion denied.

Stephen Hollis's production puts the play, firmly but discreetly, into what we must now recognise (give the telly its due) as the Dennis Potter 1930s. The period is perhaps most palpably there in the pinched, waddling vowels that Billie Whitelaw employs for Molly's silly coaxing moods. It is plain that she despises this part of herself (the refrain "pretty please with sugar on it" takes on a thicker layer of disgust each time it appears), but this cannot quite conceal a discontinuity with the woman of the world who appears when Molly sets about subduing her admirers.

Miss Whitelaw in effect offers two stunning performances: less satisfying than one would be, but still the most powerful female acting seen in London this year. She gets good support from Barbara Atkinson and Anthony Allen; T. P. McKenna as Teddy offers no more than routine testiness until his end approaches; then he takes off into a splendid tirade.

* * *

Prospect's King Lear (Old Vic) begins with thunder, causing the unwary to suspect that the first half of the play has disappeared. A couple more cliches follow. When Lear swears at Cordelia all present drop on their knees and shield their faces with their arms. Gloucester in the next scene should enter talking to himself; here he addresses his rambling remarks to an attendant, who then has to exit as if he has received some kind of instruction. After this the production disappears and the actors are left to their own devices.

These are frequently oversimple, but Christopher Neame and Isla Blair make a glamorous couple of Edmund and Regan, while Trevor Martin as Kent does the basso rugged honesty bit better than any actor I know.

Anthony Quayle's Lear is incomplete; he has the raw power for the rages, but not the transfusing variety. What he does convey, often very movingly, is the sense of a mind long set and forced to reorder itself. There is a military directness about him; when he calls on Nature to dry up his daughter's womb or speaks, admitting his ignorance, of the terrors of the earth, then he means what he says. "I would not be mad" is apprehensive, lightly tearful, so that "I shall go mad" a little later is hopelessly, crushingly logical.

I have known no actor make more than Mr Quayle unfussily does of Lear's gentlest moments: his concern for the Fool or his sudden fear of "the little dogs ... Trey, Blanch and Sweetheart." This is a very English Lear who, whatever his failings with people, must always have been wonderful with animals.

records.title: Musical musings
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Musical musings

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Bar Mitzvah Boy.

AS I WAS saying, television plays, however meritorious, usually seem thin when translated to the theatre. One obvious way of thickening them, though, is to turn them into musicals; make them, that is to say, into wholly different animals. Let us consider Bar Mitzvah Boy (Her Majesty's).

The man who professes, when musicalising a play, to be doing it with the utmost respect for the original should be mistrusted. If you feel that way about a play you should leave it alone. Really you need the instincts of a vandal, prepared to change not only the shape of your source but its values as well.

These are just principles, understand; it is difficult to be that cavalier in practice, especially if your point of departure is something as estimable as Jack Rosenthal's teleplay. Since Mr Rosenthal has himself written the book of the musical the problems must have been peculiarly delicate: should he have remained true to himself and who, in this new state of affairs, was himself anyway?

Bar Mitzvah Boy has actually turned out a thoroughly professional musical (it doesn't look like an accident, which, since it is a predominantly British show, makes a pleasant change), but it is difficult to watch it without feeling a bit torn: half willing the author to be ruthless, half regretting the changes he actually has made.

The story remains the same: a 13-year-old Jewish boy runs out of the confirmation ceremony that is supposed to turn him into a man because the exemplars of manhood he has before him--his father, grandfather, and incipient brother-in-law--seem very poor advertisements for the product. His family are aghast; not only has he desecrated a religious ceremony, he has also (and, it seems, far more importantly) forced them to cancel the extremely expensive dinner-dance that was to follow. The officiating rabbi finds a Biblical text that enables them to have their celebrations (and the show, incidentally, its finale). Young Eliot makes his bar mitzvah speech; he has threatened--and here, I think, we depart from the original--to unmask the failings of his elders but he refrains, on the grounds that "it is less important to know the truth about people than to understand it": an unexceptionable sentiment, but a disappointing substitute for the bitter-sweet observation that Mr Rosenthal once kept going until the final credits.

I am breaking my own rule, blaming him for infidelity. But I have to, since he has not made enough changes to put such considerations out of court. Much of his dialogue, if not identical to what was televised, is at any rate as witty and as accurate. But there are considerable foreshortenings of character. Only Eliot's father, among his male elders, is given much scope: a testy taxi-driver forever complaining of the crippling expenses into which he has been inveigled.
