Grandfather has only one brief, rambling scene and an energetic song-and-dance ("The Harolds of This World") is no real substitute for the gentle but ruthless expose to which Eliot's sister's boyfriend, an unturning worm, was initially subjected.

So we do not feel the long-term reasons for the boy's flight--though the moment itself is tersely and tellingly presented with some of his relatives' more fatuous remarks superimposed on the boy's mind as they go through their assigned portions of the synagogue service. The musical in fact makes one point about Eliot's alienation more trenchantly than the play: that he is involved in a religious ceremony whose significance to everyone else seems purely social. Being a musical, though, it seems constrained to give excessive emphasis to the Jewish mother joke, which was far funnier when it was played down.

As a story musical, hewing near to an established dramatic line, the show suffers from some familiar drawbacks; the songs may sometimes intensify the situation, but they rarely propel them any farther than has already been managed by dialogue. There are a couple of marvellous moments in the score; get them when a character comes on and, immediately and without warning, sings; that does move things along. Jule Styne still writes better brassy music than anyone else around, and a pair of initially sticky ballads are rescued by cunningly bright reprises.

The other Americans involved are Martin Charnin, the highly efficient director, and the choreographer Peter Gennaro, whose first act knees-up (the one sequence in which the show unquestionably justifies itself) may be the most invigorating use ever made of a British chorus. The principals, too, are ours. I especially liked Harry Towb's cabbie, alternately shamefaced and acerbic, and the unnervingly confident Eliot of Barry Angel. In sum: there was probably no crying need to musicalise Bar Mitzvah Boy, but as the new Jewish proverb has it, if we tried living on necessities we'd probably starve.

* * *

Jesse and the Bandit Queen (Roundhouse Downstairs) is an off-Broadway success by David Freeman. Jesse is James; the bandit queen is Belle Starr, his female counterpart. The two of them play out their lives and deaths for us, occasionally stepping into each other's roles and even clothing. (There are psychological reasons for this, too fatiguing to explain.) They have their moments, but I wish they knew more people; it would have been pleasant had someone else dropped in from time to time. Annabel Leventon is certainly a belle, and very likely a star.

records.title: Scooping up Africa
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: A Trick to Catch the Old One
records.body:
Scooping up Africa

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Stoppard's latest play.

IT can sometimes be difficult to persuade people of the unbroken continuity of Tom Stoppard's work; and he doesn't help either, dividing his stuff into the real heavies and the "nuts and-bolts" comedies.

His new one, Night and Day (Phoenix), has affinities to that second workmanlike category (it is, just as a story, much the tensest play he has written), but its size and its ambitions place it with Jumpers and Travesties. And yet it takes off from a moment in the impenitently lightweight Dirty Linen: the one in which the delectable Mrs Gotobed advises her roomful of lovers not to worry what the Press might say about them. After all, she maintains, the readers don't really care, and the journalists are mainly concerned to impress themselves and each other.

Ruth, the heroine of Night and Day, puts the same case, more emotively. She is the wife of a senior mining official in the imaginary African country of Kambawe, a State with--depending on your point of view--a secession or a rebellion or a liberation problem. From the Sunday Globe in Britain come three journalists to cover the story: a photographer and two reporters. One of the reporters, Jacob Milne, is actually a young freelance who has got lucky and secured an exclusive interview with the rebel leader. This does not please his counterpart Dick Wagner, a hard-bitten Australian. (That is very likely how he would describe himself, but I must admit that the cliche rolled quite effortlessly off my typewriter, which seems to prove some of Mr Stoppard's points for him.)

Dick is a strong union man; Jacob isn't, having resigned over a strike at his former paper, the Grimsby Messenger. Dick informs London of this, demands that Jacob be taken off the story. His demand is refused, but it sets off a labour dispute, and next Sunday the Globe fails to appear, which is not quite what Dick wanted, since this time he has the scoop. It doesn't matter much to Jacob anyway; he's dead, shot in--for want of a better word--action.

It is this last event that sets off Ruth's tirade. It's all bloody ego ... as far as I'm concerned Jake died for the product. She, as it happens, was some way to being in love with him, though it is Wagner whom--just once in London--she had bedded; at the final disillusioned curtain, she looks like repeating the performance. "A lady," she had said earlier, "might go to bed with a chap once ... but twice ... a lady might think she'd been taken for a tart." (The structural ironies in this play are fewer than in most of Mr Stoppard's but they are crushers.)

Anyway, and shades of The Front Page, both men are less enamoured of her than of their jobs, symbolised in a very practical manner by her husband's shining Telex machine. I am not sure exactly what Mr Stoppard intends us to make of Ruth; he gives her more than he has given any other woman. She has charm, wit, beauty, music, some passion, much self-mockery; alone in the cast, she has a direct line to the audience.

She is played with an abundance of all the qualities mentioned above, by Diana Rigg, whose personal blend of sad secrecy with devastating attack has never been more highly charged. But somewhere her roles of commentator and protagonist have got tangled up. It would make sense if her problems were the same as the journalists' and she just happened to see them more clearly, but that isn't how it comes out.

She gets a lot of the "civilised-values" speeches, siding with Jacob against Wagner over the journalists' closed-shop. This seems loaded. Jacob is given an attractive boy-scout performance by Peter Machin and Miss Rigg is Miss Rigg; against them John Thaw's Wagner, forceful though he is (over-forceful for the first half-hour, in which his accent seems to consume most of his attention), has no chance. And the argument is trivialised; the reduction of workers' solidarity to protective squabbles over differentials is a sadder and more complex thing than the play admits; so is the newspaper industry itself.

When the play widens to consider the whole question of a free Press, its value, its abuse and its psychology, it achieves kaleidoscopic brilliance: from particular painful barbs ("rubbish journalism is produced by people doing their best work") to sweeping proclamations. And even Ruth's last outburst has its coda: when the denimed cameraman (played by William Marlowe with, well, photographic accuracy) admits her case, but adds to it the rider that reportage is some small insurance against tyranny. "Information is light." And he should know about light.

You can set against this the blunt honesty of Olu Jacob's African president, or the precise amount of Press freedom that he, a despot but not a madman, can tolerate. The amount of imaginative (as opposed to intellectual) sympathy in this portrayal is something new for Mr Stoppard. The jokes are disarmingly good as ever. (He even gets away with having Wagner called Strauss by a composer joke, but a composer called Richard joke.) It is an elating evening.

* * *

The Glasgow Citizens' company have always been heedless of immortality, but it is cavalier, even by their standards, to have jettisoned their version of The Spanish Tragedy after a mere eight performances. As expected they got Kyd's primal shocker (the foundation-stone of the Elizabethan theatre) exhilaratingly right. Despite some allegations, they did not even muck around with the text very much; the alleged additions were mostly of contemporary origin and helped to make the story clearer. (Some reviewers have strange ideas about the plays of this period; one chastised Terry Hands for introducing a ghost into The Changeling. That house was haunted long before the RSC reopened it.) Death comes easy in The Spanish Tragedy, most staggeringly in the final scene: a play within a play where the deaths are real and the victims expire to enthusiastic audience applause. At Glasgow it seemed inevitable.

A Trick to Catch the Old One (Theatre Clwyd, Mold) usually seems arbitrary. This is another Middleton, this time a city comedy of cheating and more cheating. In Scotland they played in modern dress and one gave it hardly a second thought; in Wales they did the same, and seemed to be trying to prove something. Michael Hucks's production lacked comic gusto; its rival usurers were tame figures.

The production only came to life when most serious; when the play's peculiar male morality carelessly turned a courtesan to a victim, or when an extraneous miser (a Dickensian figure) expired in a haze of greed and avarice, quietly mourned by his housekeeper, to whom Ilona Linthwaite gave remarkable depth in very little space.

A good week for transfers: the joyous Gloo Joo to the Criterion; DHL, the Lawrence show praised by Victoria Radin at Edinburgh, to the New End; and to the Prince of Wales, prior to Broadway, Alan Ayckbourn's Bedroom Farce, which may be my favourite play of the past five years: not necessarily the best, though I can think of none which achieves its aims more completely, or in which every word works more efficiently.

Three and a half marriages are laid hilariously, sharply, but quite unpatronisingly, bare. The missing half is the distrait Susannah, who has now defeated three actresses: Delia Lindsay finds truth in her, but not much humour, perhaps because Mr Ayckbourn forgot to leave her any. With her mate Trevor, however (of whom I was also inclined to complain on first acquaintance), he has done wonders, and Stephen Moore--appealing with his whole length to every interlocuter, even when the conversation is being conducted by telephone--does even more.

records.title: Play it again, Jule
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Play it again, Jule

ROBERT CUSHMAN talks to Jule Styne, composer of 'Bar Mitzvah Boy'

JULE STYNE is 73 years old, short and very active. When I first met him four years ago, backstage at a theatre in Toronto, I took him to be a 50-year-old who, if he kept jumping around like that, would certainly give himself ulcers. He tended to jump in time to his own music, and that music was generally very rhythmic, coming as it did from Gypsy, the most highly-regarded of the 29 musicals he has composed. Currently it is more likely to be that of Bar Mitzvah Boy, the latest in the line and the first to be launched in London rather than New York.

Two more British musicals are lined up for him--if, that is, he can overcome the impression left him by some of the Bar Mitzvah Boy reviews that there is an unbridgeable gulf between himself and the British critics. "What we call honest sentiment," he says in equally honest puzzlement, "you call schmaltz."

Among currently practising Broadway composers only Richard Rodgers has a more extensive and impressive catalogue. The Styne shows include Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, Bells are Ringing, and Funny Girl. And there has also been a long list of song-hits, many of them written for the movies in the forties before his theatrical career got under way.

Stephen Sondheim, who was his lyricist on Gypsy, says that Styne's fecundity of invention is extraordinary. "He'd rather write a completely new song than re-write an old one." He prefers not to work at the piano. He was a child-prodigy pianist, and it seems to have been his size that kept him from an adult concert career (his hands weren't big enough). So playing remains for him a different kind of work from writing--and separating the two allows him to concentrate on melody.

All the same, when he does get to the piano--at a party, perhaps--interesting and fruitful things can happen. What started as an improvised parody of the economic, repetitive songs of Vincent Youmans (Tea for Two, I Want to Be Happy) ended up as Just in Time, the big hit of Bells are Ringing. Then there was Time after Time, one of his Hollywood songs, sung by Frank Sinatra in a 1947 movie. Alec Wilder in his indispensable book American Popular Song describes it as "his best song ... It bespeaks personal involvement and great warmth."

It is doubtful if Mr Wilder realises the exact nature of that involvement. Styne tells it like this. "A lot of us used to go round to Sinatra's house and play parlour-games, to try and keep his marriage together. One day Sinatra asked if anyone had heard any of the songs Jerome Kern was meant to be composing for the show that Irving Berlin eventually wrote as Annie Get Your Gun. I said I had--I don't know why, actually I hadn't heard a note. So they said, play us one.

"I couldn't go back on it. I crossed to the piano, honest to God not knowing what I was going to play, only that it had to be in the style of Kern. I sat down, and I improvised the first eight bars of Time After Time. Then right on, through to the end. And everybody said 'it's wonderful, that Kern, he's done it again.' And having made the tune up, I couldn't remember it. But Sammy Cahn could, and he wrote a lyric to it."

Despite such casual triumphs, Styne left Hollywood for Broadway "to become a composer instead of just a songwriter." Though most of his early shows were successes, it took him some time to achieve this to his own satisfaction. Jerome Robbins staged his sixth show, a musical version of Peter Pan. "Robbins taught me to use music to underline the plot and develop the characters."

So what, applying these standards, could music add to Jack Rosenthal's television play Bar Mitzvah Boy? Well, according to Styne, "emotion, vitality, and a new dimension for Eliot, the boy whose bar mitzvah it is." According to the critics, a certain softness. Maybe there is not so much disagreement there. The new dimension, in Eliot mainly, involves his relationship with his cab-driver father who, late in the evening, sings him a conciliatory ballad called The Sun Shines Out of Your Eyes.

But Styne insists that family affection is what the love musical stage could best add to the story, and insists that it means a great deal to him personally. "When my son had his bar mitzvah he had a hard time too. But I got through to him by telling him what an important experience it had been for me. This is my Jewish show; I'm paying a personal debt."

Which does not quite make up for a certain stickiness in the way the song, like the parents' duet, We've Done All Right, comes across on stage. However: I went along to the recording of the original cast LP and found that, out of visual context, both grew on me appealingly. They sounded like more than respectable additions to his list of ballads.

"You hear that?" he said during a short Hebraic chanting section from the first number, in which Eliot is jauntily lectured by his rabbi on his doubts about the coming ceremony. "There's the whole guts of Jack's story in that music. In America I would have got credit for that." He didn't spend too much time brooding on it, though. One of his first jobs was as a vocal coach and he still has the instincts. He continually disappeared into the studio to admonish or encourage the performers. "The trouble is, when they get in front of a microphone they think they're singers. I need actor-singers; I can't stand singer-singers."

When you watch a musical in rehearsal it's difficult to believe that it could ever fail: all that vivacity, all that discipline. When Bar Mitzvah Boy was being rehearsed in London I asked Styne whether he saw himself having to write new material during the Manchester try-out. He was confident that no more would be needed.

I saw a few minutes of a number about catering arrangements: "When it's once in a lifetime, when it's your little boy/You don't want to settle for, say, the Savoy." It seemed fun (lyrics by Don Black, who is philosophical about being ignored in reviews), but it perished on the road (if Manchester is the road). "It didn't add up," says Styne, "a one-joke song." They replaced it with a yet more rousing chorus called The Bar Mitzvah of Eliot Green (pom-pom).

Maybe that should have been the title song. Styne now thinks their greatest mistake was keeping the TV title; it invited irrelevant considerations about fidelity to the original. How sore is he at the carpers? "Listen. I believe in the critic-system. If it wasn't for you fellas, everything would run forever and we'd never get any new shows on." He's done all right.

records.title: Brook''s ''Mesure pour Mesure
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Brook's 'Mesure pour Mesure'

Theatre

by Robert Cushman

TALKING or writing about the theatre over the past few years, Peter Brook has always come back to Measure for Measure. Now at his Paris theatre, the Bouffes-du-Nord, he has come back to it in another, literal sense.

In 1950 he directed a production of this play at Stratford which those who saw it still recall with rapture. In his book The Empty Space Mr Brook writes of 'a base world . . . the disgusting, stinking world of medieval Vienna . . . we must animate all this stretch of the play as the roughest comedy we can make . . . the rough is in prose, the rest in verse . . . if we iron Shakespeare into any one typography of theatre we lose the real meaning of the play.' The italics are mine; I believe that sentence to be of vital importance in the consideration of almost any Shakespeare play.

But it does not altogether apply to the 'Mesure pour Mesure' Mr Brook has staged in Paris, since Jean-Claude Carriere's French adaptation ignores the 'clear signal' (Mr Brook's phrase) that Shakespeare gives when the play is about to jump tracks: it is all in prose, and clipped declarative prose at that. It speeds the action along and Mr Brook's direction moves at a matching clip. No longer a confusion, the play remains a puzzle. There are no glaring contradictions in it--Angelo and Mistress Overdone belong to the same hard, clear world--but there is no overriding coherence either. Everyone is himself, firmly drawn, without apology or explanation.

This even applies to the one character for whom most directors feel compelled to invent a rationale. Shakespeare gave the Duke little personality but it is customary to make him the vehicle of an interpretation, agent of Providence or greasy manipulator. Francois Marthouret, a dazzling actor, sticks to the basics of charm and authority.

Mr Brook may have had in mind a legend of justice--the most powerful tableau of the evening consists of the three judges--Duke, Angelo and Escalus standing side by side--but his production says surprisingly little about it, or about the twin subject of mercy. Isabella pauses long before agreeing to beg for Angelo's life, but her hesitation lacks the explosive effect it apparently had in 1950. There can be no doubt that Clementine Amouroux's crew-cut Isabella will do the decent thing; youthfully idealistic (and, for the role, ideally young), she lacks rigidity or spiritual pride.

The most complex performance is Bruce Myers's Angelo, which moves easily from self-satisfaction to self-hatred by (and this is something of a revelation) a comic route; the clean thrust of the translation puts a hard edge on the revolving paradox of his situation.

But then the whole company is, as ever, commandingly unfussed, notably Maurice Benichou's sleek, chic Lucio and Andreas Katsulas's huge, and hugely ingratiating, Pompey. There is some viciousness in M. Benichou, but M. Katsulas seems harmless. Theirs is not the reeking world of which Mr Brook has written, but then in this neat 'Mesure' his ideal 'Measure' has gone by default. On this occasion he has stretched the mind, not blown it.

* * *

The Catalan company La Claca, who have brought their Mori el Merma to the Riverside Studios, are like nothing we have seen since the Bread and Puppet Theatre who were the best group to come out of the American explosion of the sixties. La Claca are as charming and more powerful. They communicate enormous gaiety and they make with it a powerful statement on the nature of dictatorship which widens into an image of any and every power-structure. They are, in every sense, essential theatre.

Which is strange since their method here is very specialised. Actors in this production are the slaves of the designer. This is contrary to most theories of theatrical well-being, though the fact that the designer is Joan Miro might earn them an indulgence even were the work less successful than it is.

Miro has constructed a series of giant grotesque machines; the actors inhabit and propel them. Thus is created for example a sort of Michelin man whose bulk has descended to his buttocks and who sports a blue hawk-head with a red fluffy beak. He is followed on stage by a companion monster, bigger yet, with enormously long black pneumatic arms. Ruling them all is something elephantine: something with a trunk anyway. They are all initially endearing (like the more sinister of the Muppets) and it is an achievement of the show that by the end it has made these floppy funsters seem irredeemably horrible. They are attended and fawned over by grey-suited flunkeys with black ties and false noses, and they tyrannise over a race of beaked sea-green figures, unprepossessing but inoffensive.

A sequence in which one of these is dismembered while the monarch's consort, hugely girlish, disports herself with a skipping-rope recalls the torture-scene in Edward Bond's Lear, and is far less questionable. Nor is it easy to forget the sight of the lady rocking her boring spouse to sleep. Those children's books about Babar, king of the jungle, will never seem so innocent again. The actors occasionally break out from behind their masks; one, for example, is allowed a final gesture of contempt for the old regime which is understandable but artistically regrettable; the point was already made.

* * *

The Comings and Goings of Mike Stott's new play at Hampstead are part of a halting mating-dance. Most of the characters are concerned to leave their partners, and the process turns out to be easy but unprofitable; something, or someone equally unsatisfactory will usually transpire instead. Either way it doesn't matter much. The arbitrariness of the pattern infects the play itself, at least where plotting is concerned; the action takes place in a single flat to which a surprising number of people have access. Mr Stott is meticulous in telling us what their jobs are--they tend geriatrics, sell biscuits, plan cities, research Norse myths--and in no case does it matter; he places us all, whatever our social or sexual orientation, in the same boat.

The play's energy resides in its language, which is full of fine twisting flourishes. John Normington is rather too restrained an actor to take full advantage of his choric role as the Viking expert, but Lindsay Duncan as a hearty county girl trying earnestly to untie her tongue and describe her first orgasm is tremendously funny (and no caricature incidentally), and so is Paul Jesson as her awakener who could not be more surprised.

Snoo Wilson's A Greenish Man (Bush) is a goodish play; like Mr Stott's piece it is both concerned with and afflicted by half-heartedness. Mr Wilson's is the more considerable talent; so his play is the more frustrating. It concerns various would-be adherents of the IRA domiciled in Kilburn, including one who is plainly an overgrown leprechaun. The only untainted character is a little girl; she is called Deirdre and dances on tables, and I think she represents Ireland. The play keeps promising to become really enjoyable; the production, which always seems a beat behind, doesn't help much.

records.title: Giving us the works
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: The Complete Dramatic Works of William Shakespeare
records.body:
Giving us the works

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the BBC's six-year Shakespeare project.

STARTING on BBC2 tonight, a new series called The Complete Dramatic Works of William Shakespeare. Independent Television gave you his life; now watch while the BBC gives you the works. I wonder if the theme-tune will be released as a single.

Romeo and Juliet is the starter, so there's a popular beginning for you. On the two succeeding Sundays will come Richard II and As You Like It. Then in February three more: Julius Caesar, Measure for Measure, Henry VIII. And so on for six years. He wrote 37 dramatic works so it almost makes a neat sum.

Shakespeare has been a staple of BBC television drama throughout its existence. Some plays (Romeo is one of them) have turned up with almost monotonous regularity; others (Henry VIII is one of them) will receive their TV premieres during this series. The climate has changed, though, in the last 15 or so years.

There was once a tacit assumption that adapted stage plays had to form the basis of the TV drama output. There is now a far from tacit orthodoxy to the effect that theatre plays are unwelcome intruders on the screen, to be reluctantly tolerated until the audience that enjoys them perishes from anaemia. Such plays, to get on the air at all, must be housed in well-appointed ghettoes bearing such titles as Play of the Month--and that label is itself revealing. I can remember when there was a stage play on every week.

I do not particularly mourn all this. The purists may conceivably, despite their stridency, be in the right and I myself am hardly starved of theatre. Viewers who do not have my job may possibly feel differently and some of them must surely have noticed that a workmanlike tradition of presenting classics on TV has long since died. It peaked in 1960 with the history series An Age of Kings (which, perhaps not coincidentally, was one of the last great flings of live television) and died soon after.

As productions have got less frequent they have also become glossier; where once they took their tone from the Old Vic they now take it from Chichester. They have about them a definite air of classy makeshift. That is the situation that The Complete Works will inherit, and it is rather well demonstrated by the casting of the leading roles. At the centre, youth and inexperience (Juliet in fact is played by a schoolgirl); on the periphery as the Chorus (all 28 lines of him) John Gielgud.

It may work beautifully; I merely note it as a sign of the times. The producer of the series Cedric Messina (founding father of Play of the Month) claims quite rightly that to have Gielgud speak the series' opening lines is not merely sound showmanship but symbolically apt: homage is paid to another great tradition--and will be again when Gielgud plays John of Gaunt to the Richard II of Derek Jacobi who played the part excellently on radio last year--though one suspects that it was more his international triumph in I Claudius that prompted the casting here.

Messina is engagingly aware of the slightly anachronistic figure he cuts in fashionable media circles: "I'm in conflict with the elitists and the television drama pundits all the time. It doesn't bother me. I'm a populist. When I was a child in South Africa the only way one could hear plays was on the radio."

He now wants television to perform the same introductory or enlightening function. May I say that I myself am witness that it can. My own enthusiasm for Shakespeare--which preceded my enthusiasm for the theatre--was sparked when I was horribly young by a children's television version of a cut Midsummer Night's Dream (no lovers, just clowns and fairies) starring Robert Atkins. I have never recovered.

So good luck to Mr Messina (who by the way has produced in his time a Seagull and a School for Scandal finer than any I have seen in the theatre) and to the worldwide marketing operation that has made his project possible. But I shall hope for productions that do not glory too much in not being modern dress versions, or eccentric interpretations (Mr Messina's disclaimers) if only because productions so self-denying frequently end up as far from the centre of the play--and therefore as eccentric--as any others.

There is no pretence that definitive versions are being attempted (Richard Pasco's Jaques is the only stage performance to be transcribed for posterity and the export market in the first batch) but considering how many millions are going to see them they will perforce become definitive. They will corner the Shakespearean market for longer than their six-year span. They had better be good.

records.title: Chicago chuffer
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: To the Happiness Of Us All
records.body:
Chicago chuffer

ROBERT CUSHMAN on theatre in New York and Toronto.

A LONDON director, on whose latest production I had cast some mild aspersions, wrote me a kind and forbearing letter suggesting that I seek theatrical refreshment in New York, where at least I might see some good musicals. Such solicitude towards my tenderest spot touched me deeply. I received his letter on Wednesday 29 November; Thursday I was on the plane. To tell the truth I was going anyway.

* * *

Friday. Three musicals have dominated 1978 on Broadway: Dancin', Ain't Misbehavin' and On the 20th Century. The last of these has been generally dismissed as old-fashioned, being the only one to possess a traditional book, with a plot and all. It derives from the celebrated thirties movie, about an actor-producer trying to lure a former protegee back into his arms and on to his stage, and is admittedly tired.

But it all happens on a train, chuffing from Chicago to New York and representing, as designed by Robin Wagner, both the apotheosis of Art Deco and a mechanical delight. Its freight includes a new star, Judy Kaye, who is a spunkily funny coloratura. The train and Miss Kaye set the tone of Harold Prince's unexpectedly playful staging which reflects the benign showbiz nostalgia of the best MGM musicals -- all written, like the show, by Betty Comden and Adolph Green. I enjoyed it.

* * *

Saturday. The matinee of Eubie, the latest anthology show, celebrating Eubie Blake, now 95, son of slaves, composer of "I'm Just Wild About Harry" and much else. Like most such combinations, it started off-Broadway and moved on. It now boasts an energetic black cast and audience, the latter comparatively new to Broadway, the former traditional. Musically the show moves from rag-time grace to overblown soul (everyone trying to sound like Lou Rawls or Diana Ross); theatrically it is slight, but it holds.

In the evening downtown to Joseph Papp's subsidised power house, the Public Theatre (a complex with more components than the National) for a workshop production of Thomas Babe's latest, Fathers and Sons, a disappointment after A Prayer for my Daughter, since it extends that play's tendency towards verbosity while sacrificing both its movement and its powerful verismo. It's a Western fantasia; Wild Bill Hickock meets and is gunned down by his unacknowledged bastard. That's really all, although Calamity Jane and many others follow in attendance.

The production, however economical, is crowded and handsome, though too many lines (and Mr Babe still writes good ones) are yelled into oblivion. Why does a city whose every waitress and cab driver seems gifted with perfect comic timing support so much heavy-handed acting? Richard Chamberlain's Wild Bill is a stylish and heroic exception.

* * *

Sunday. The Sabbath matinee is a splendid institution, and I went happily to Dancin', Bob Fosse's tribute to his trade, hoping to swallow bile summoned up by Mr Fosse's Chicago. Well, there is one exhilarating set of routines -- done to Benny Goodman's swing classic "Sing, Sing, Sing" -- and those American kids can certainly (but who doubted it?) dance. But the whole is uninspired, and often worse: witness an erotic number that looks like a reject from "Oh! Calcutta!" and linking figures who say there will be no story or dialogue, and say what each scene intends, and go on saying, archly and witlessly. My teeth were constantly on edge.

In the evening, back to the Public for the last night of a sell-out -- in all senses, according to the local scribes. Now when a show gets merely bad reviews, the chances are it is merely bad. When the boys club it to the ground and then jump on its stomach, it usually has something going for it. So it is with E. L. Doctorow's first play, Drinks Before Dinner. It is not a model of dramatic excellence or even of intellectual consistency. It works only through words, but these are witty where the play lampoons Manhattan chic, and terrifying when it veers towards a vision of the apocalypse.

A rich New Yorker, invited to dine with half a dozen of his peers, pulls a gun on the guest of honour, a high Government official. His pretext is that he believes that the end of the world -- at least of his world -- is at hand; his victim corroborates all his suspicions and even elaborates on them. Christopher Plummer, whom I have never seen better, and Josef Sommer, whom I have never seen, play an exquisite game of cat and mouse. Tony Walton provides a set of literally incredible elegance.

* * *

Monday. Neil Simon's Chapter Two has been widely hailed as a bad play, and indeed its first half (particularly the wisecracks) bears the painful stamp of truth. But Mr Simon cannot act as tough towards his central couple -- a hastily remarried widower and divorcee -- as he would obviously like, and so fumbles and pads in the second act. I don't think he is pandering to his audience; he's pandering to himself.

* * *

Tuesday. Off-Broadway, Sam Shepard's new one, Buried Child. Recommended for those who can take or leave him alone. Ghastly black comic revelations in rural America, reminding some of The Homecoming and me of Cold Comfort Farm. I didn't much care about the skeletons, since I never believed in the cupboard, but the incidence of individual laughs and shudders is praiseworthily high.

* * *

Wednesday matinee. Finally make it to Ain't Misbehavin', the town's hottest ticket apart from Annie. Disappointment probably inevitable. This Fats Waller medley, obviously inspired by Eubie, which is less slickly staged but now has the higher performance level. Waller's wry joking has inevitably been coarsened, but the show is still likeable; if I'd come across it unheralded, I would probably have loved it. Both Dancin' and Ain't Misbehavin' are comin' to London, which somehow ain't that excitin'.

* * *

Thursday. A treat. Bondini's, a downtown restaurant, has a mini revue whose title, To the Happiness Of Us All, is the only uninspired thing about it. Peggy Beatty, an aggressively genteel soprano, Norman Rollings, a bald and sinister singer-pianist, and a strange, sultry lady cellist billed as Miss Faun provide a wildly unpredictable entertainment that begins as spoof operetta and sends out tentacles in all directions. Mission fulfilled: this is New York's best musical.

I write this while anticipating Ballroom, Michael Bennett's first show since A Chorus Line and mulling over the profound thoughts (whither America?) that are supposed to occur to critics on their foreign travels. Meanwhile I shelter in Toronto, where the big playhouses offer British or American exports (current attraction, John Gielgud in Half Life), but where, in stark contrast to navel-gazing New York, a bristling fringe is consciously (often self-consciously) nationalistic.

One small theatre, the Tarragon, goes looking for a Canadian identity on the highways with a country music show called 18 Wheels about long-distance truck driving: a marvellous subject but, on this static showing, a difficult one to stage. Another locally respected company, Theatre Passe Muraille, is due to visit England next year, though not, I hope, with Les Maudits Anglais, a clumsy joke about cultural warfare in Quebec.

The same topic is hilariously treated by Toronto's resident revue team, The Second City, as are airlines, the Post Office, TV news (slogan -- "If it happened today, it's news to us") and inevitably the Prime Minister. (Theirs, I mean). Nothing very new about the targets, but the company's elan is immense; I've seen no funnier revue in years.
production_title: To the Happiness Of Us All

records.title: Fun in Saratoga
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Fun in Saratoga

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the Royal Shakespeare Company's seasonal treat

LET ME clue you in on Saratoga (Aldwych). A battle was fought there, but that is of no account. It boasts one of America's most celebrated race-courses, and that begins to matter. It is, or was, a great spa, and that is of crucial importance. Bronson Howard's comedy was premiered in New York in 1870 and reached the English stage four years later re-titled Brighton.

Howard, of whom apart from this production and its programme I know nothing, has apparently been called the Dean of American Drama. At the time he was writing, American Drama was still a small faculty, under heavy transatlantic influence. This, his second play, is a routine period piece, a comedy of manners ageing into heavily plotted comedy of intrigue. The characters are types, and frankly engagingly acknowledged as such. They have come to Saratoga to take the waters and each other. The younger ones enjoy themselves; their elders look on with a kind of tolerant disgust. "Call this travelling for pleasure?" asks one heavy father repeatedly. On the whole I would.

This show is another in the Royal Shakespeare Company's line of seasonal treats - London Assurance, Sherlock Holmes, Wild Oats. Like its predecessors, it celebrates the glories of stock theatre. You take a piece just slightly above the rut of its time and treat it, not disrespectfully, certainly not mockingly, but playfully. In fact such teasing as goes on is not so much of the work in hand as of the actors and the audience for enjoying it. Something atavistic in both factions responds to the material with huge enthusiasm; there are no depths to be explored, but there is a story to be told and followed and fun to be had - the kind of fun that probably drew us to the theatre in the first place.

Charmingly coloured by Jocelyn Herbert, Ronald Eyre's production is delectable, full of comic ripples. Some of these exist outside the action proper; Mr Eyre has taken a trio of waiters - "coloured gentlemen" they call themselves - and let them sing and strut between the acts, to tunes more or less of the period. Bert Williams's gloriously misanthropic Nobody ("Tain't never got nothin' from nobody") becomes the evening's theme song. (It is currently the most exposed of songs in town, since it figures also in Bubbling Brown Sugar.) Just before the last scene, when he is in serious trouble - I shan't of course give away the plot, but the play's sub-title is Pistols for Seven - Dennis Waterman as the multiply susceptible hero joins the ensemble to terrific effect. Aggrieved desperation has seldom been so funnily or rhythmically conveyed. This is actually the high-point of Mr Waterman's performance, which elsewhere tends to timidity. He does not so much offset the gaucherie of James Laurenson (playing his earnest best friend) as reproach it.

The ladies are the best of the evening. Mr Waterman is in love with two of them; only Maxine Audley as somebody's mother escapes his attentions and she is such a glamorous, stylish matriarch that the omission is difficult to understand. The amorous complications, by the way, can generally be seen coming half an act away; that is possibly the sign of a well-made play. Among the girls Joanna McCallum, who is very tall, pairs pleasantly with Polly James, who is the opposite and extremely determined: she gets her man with the aid of a late Victorian contact ad. There is also Cherie Lunghi as a beauteous young wife; she and her spouse (Jeffery Dench) are played - impeccably - as Southerners, conceivably because their name is Carter.

In the cameo reaches of the cast, which are extensive, I noted Billie Brown as a hobbledehoy (a word for which there is sadly little call nowadays) and David Shaw-Parker as an exhibiting artist. The first act is set in a gallery and promises sharper satire than accrues in the later stretches, which are merely comfortable. But there is bubble in the play presaging the next 50 years in which American comedy frothed and steamed ahead while the English variety died on its feet. But we are better curators than they are.

In New York the previous week I found that few had heard of the play or its author; one exception was Richmond Crinkley, the director-designate of the hitherto bedevilled repertory at Lincoln Centre, and one of his aims is to explore the American repertoire for himself without waiting to be scooped by London.

Mr Crinkley is an impresario, not a director, but he has assembled a formidable artistic board, ranging from Woody Allen to Robin Phillips. One hopes he can keep them together (or, if it would be more tactful, apart), since he faces a city where straight drama is in a horrendous way - though not quite as awful as a telephonic misunderstanding over my copy last week may have led you to believe: Neil Simon's Chapter Two has not been hailed as a bad play but as his best. I disagree, but not that emphatically.

For all his capitulations, Mr Simon writes with as much psychological seriousness as any of his compatriots; social seriousness is hardly to be found. The glibness of much British political drama is repellent, but it is preferable to the prevailing Broadway. This can be amusing, and sometimes it is enlarged by a few frames and is dubbed "myth-making," which makes it sound headier than it is. Hence the continued ascendancy of Sam Shepard - regarded by a promising writer like Thomas Babe as a continuing fount of inspiration - and the quick decline of David Mamet from genuinely theatrical plays to plays about the theatre.

This last tendency has been noted, with some disquiet, by Edgar, author of Destiny, currently on a year's sabbatical over there and, as far as I could tell, half-confused, half-delighted. The tendency is particularly noticeable in the musicals, to which one continually recurs. This isn't just my frivolity; a conversation with the sternest American playwright is apt to terminate in the revelation that he was first turned on by My Fair Lady or Guys and Dolls. But these days they keep cannibalising themselves.

This is true even of Michael Bennett's Ballroom, which, though it has a dowdy ordinary man-and-woman story, is really a celebration of dance. Mr Bennett, of course, handles this aspect superbly, drowning out the story and even the song in the process. I think he would like to eliminate song in fact, but the Broadway audience might not buy it. More interesting to me was A Broadway Musical (terrible title - tell people you've been to see it and they say "Which one?"), which is a sustained joke about a bad play being turned into a worse show.

The weakness is that the authors never quite admit to themselves or to us just how bad either is; there ought to be a revelatory last scene. But Charles Strouse has written a better score than for his blockbusters Applause and Annie, and Lee Adams's lyrics generally begin with funny ideas, even though they don't sustain them. It's good-humoured and I hope it gets past the critics; I saw it in preview, amid awful rumours, which gave the backstage calamity scenes an engagingly macabre quality.

Back in London, the King's Head has the best Canadian play I have seen. George F. Walker's Zastrozzi, the Master of Discipline is about a self-proclaimed sinner and saint who, philosophically speaking, need each other. All shades in between are, in a gory last scene, eliminated. I can imagine a production more attuned to sex 'n' violence than Kenneth Chubb's, but - in the performances of John Castle and especially Antony Milner - his is witty. Toronto here beats New York at its own bizarre game.

records.title: On such a night
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
On such a night

ROBERT CUSHMAN on theatre in 1978 -- a good year for actresses and new plays.

TO BEGIN, as ever, with the National Theatre.

I lifted a sad eye to a noticeboard announcing the evening's attractions. The Woman was on in the Olivier, The Philanderer in the Lyttelton, and American Buffalo in the Cottesloe: two excellent new plays (one large, one small) and a first-class revival. On such a night the National is obviously doing what we ask of it: providing three of the best.

Some bitter fruit might have yielded me dustier answers, but the averages have got unsteadily higher over the year. There are just two cautionary notes. One concerns the output of new plays; the other is the regular appearance in the Cottesloe repertoire of mercilessly boring new plays. To Lost Worlds and The World Turned Upside Down must be added the current Christmas attraction, Herod, a brief and stunningly undramatic nativity piece. The occasional animal noise, and a group called The People Show, plodding at the back and at the end of the hall, somehow add to the depression. Good is being forcibly done to us, and pedagogy cannot save it.

The Woman is a post-Civil War panorama with Diggers digging and Ranters ranting and Levellers not getting level. It was an astonishing production of a difficult play. The language has a rough grandeur and the images are carved large; the theatre around it seemed momentarily to have recovered a public size. I can understand people not liking Edward Bond's play The Woman, though I think they miss something; I am baffled by the negative responses to his staging of it, which is powerful and also great to look at.

The National's plans for next year look exciting; I was always a sucker for Press-releases. As for the opposition, the Stratford season has been underrated. Love's Labour's Lost reaffirmed John Barton's grand mastery of Shakespearean comedy, Michael Bogdanov mounted a sparky Shrew, and Peter Brook's Antony and Cleopatra was at any rate the best production of the play most of us have seen.

The Aldwych's record with new native plays was watery--as usual. In nearly 20 years' occupancy there have been few of note: since Peter Hall departed, taking Harold Pinter with him, hardly any. The energies of the directorate have been focused elsewhere, Terry Hands having in his time directed everything which does not actually stand still and a group of actors were, as always, responding. The Caretaker, here given a tight and succulent production, packed much more bite than the Philanderer which, together with the slightly perchier Double Dealer, restored the approach which frankly is the national approach to middleweight comedy, i.e. two-thirds of the effective repertoire.

The rich performances, with Congreve, along with those of Robert Stephens in Brand and Susan Fleetwood in The Cherry Orchard, reminded us of another of the proper pleasures of posh theatre: that of watching a front-rank actor blow a supporting role up to his own proportions, enriching the texture of a play without damaging its fabric. Trevor Nunn may object, but the incidence of individual laughs and shudders is praiseworthily high.

Heroic acting--and this is serious--has been at a discount: Mr Bryant succeeded as Sir Paul but not as Brand, Albert Finney as Lopakhin but not as Macbeth. But the Olivier has seen one heroic production. The London and Stratford studios, by contrast, have bombarded us, and generally to good effect. In The Bundle the RSC had an even better Bond than the National; we assisted at the development of Pam Gems, Stephen Poliakoff and (turning creatively to adaptation) David Edgar; and new authors called Peter--Flannery, Whelan, Atkin--proved as thick (on the ground, I mean) as directors used to be.

This activity yielded some fine performances (Mike Gwilym as Basho, Peter McEnery as Albie Sachs, excelled themselves) and one, Jane Lapotaire's Piaf, for which the only word is formidable. It works even better if you italicise it. There was nothing quite as exciting in the main houses, though Alan Howard tightened his grip on Coriolanus and Jonathan Pryce came on strong. Ian McKellen, leading theatrical commando raids on unresisting villages, should have disarmed them with his Toby Belch.

As must be clear by now, male acting has been subdued; only Nicol Williamson, reliving the agonies of Inadmissible Evidence at the Court, lit rockets. But actresses were something else: Miss Lapotaire's outburst as Piaf has already been noted, and Vanessa Redgrave in Ibsen provided one of the strongest stage experiences of the year. Diana Rigg in Stoppard's Night and Day, Penelope Wilton in Betrayal, and Susan Fleetwood in The Cherry Orchard were different kinds of command. The year of the feminist? Not quite, but it was certainly the year in which actresses and new plays most often gave the theatre its charge.

records.title: England''s a prison?
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
England's a prison?

Theatre

by Robert Cushman

The late great songwriter Johnny Mercer once hit on the unfortunate idea that love was like a game of poker, and pursued the image through 32 whole bars. The dramatist's equivalent of the "Love is like" routine is the "England is like" game. Howard Barker's The Hang of the Gaol (Warehouse) is the latest round.

I spent a large part of the evening trying to pretend that this wasn't the case, and that Mr Barker was interested in the burnt-out moorland prison he calls Middenhurst for its own sweet sake. The jig was up, though, when a character referred to England and his ability to get the hang of the place, thus referring us back to the title and telling us what it meant.

More specific guidance is provided by the only prisoner to appear in the play who says in effect that the British Empire will endure for as long as there are prisons in the land. Since there are jails in every country in the world, and since even in this country they predate the existence of empire by some centuries, this seems to me an extremely shaky argument.

I will grant you that imperialist habits of thought still permeate the way we run our institutions, and that it is in prisons that we are likely to find those habits at their nastiest. That, though, seems a disappointingly small point. A spectacular set-designer might help to give the image the magnitude it seeks, but that is obviously off the cards at the Warehouse.

The play centres on the investigations that follow the fire. On hand to be questioned are the governor and his wife, a pair of warders (one mild, one bitter) and that solitary trusty, keeping the governor's dogs and feigning madness. From their combined testimony we gather that Middenhurst has been on the verge of disruption, owing to the governor's controversial methods and the contempt this has aroused in all hands. The cons, if I got it right, felt patronised, and the screws of course felt betrayed.

The inquiry scenes themselves swing along nicely in good judicial fashion, reaching a climax when the youngest member of the tribunal of three finds himself taking a brutal pleasure in interrogation and, conscience-stricken, begins comparing himself to Himmler. His chief, in the best line in the play, tells him that it does all men good to confront the insect in themselves so long as they do not, like Himmler, grow to love it. But the consolation proves ineffective, and junior rushes off to live like a wild man, thus dangerously upping the number of moorland madmen at large in the play, and demonstrating how a spark of dramatic life may be snuffed out by inflation.

Meanwhile his mentor maintains a pose of alcoholic crustiness (unpredictable but incorruptible like a committed Dr Cameron) and lusts in a forlorn way after his remaining colleague (a woman). There are also two self-satisfied arson experts - a comic duo responsible for the play's few laughs - and, controlling all, a Labour Home Secretary who naturally occupies the lowest place of all in the author's sympathies. The governor and his wife may be ridiculous, and their privilege questionable, but Mr Barker allows them integrity and even style; their just-left-of-centre opponent is merely grasping. You will, if you go to the theatre much, have met him before.

There are on offer some pithy thoughts on the immorality of punishment, and the play's imagery is certainly unified. Scatology is the link; begin with the name Middenhurst, and go on from there. But a play like this, where neither character nor dialogue are believable or pretend to be, desperately needs a strong fable; and this Mr Barker has not supplied. He brings his actors on in varying combinations, but the configurations seem arbitrary. There is, to put it at its most basic, nobody whom one is particularly glad to see. I don't mean they aren't credible or likeable; I mean they have no energy.

This is true even of the senior inquirer, invested by Fulton Mackay with his usual measure of frazzled Caledonian insistence. Mr Mackay is always a compelling actor but I liked him best in that other prison drama, Porridge, where the demands of TV comedy caused him to hurry on a bit. Left to himself he is apt to add 10 minutes to any play's running time. Nicholas Le Prevost elaborates on his particular speciality, the smart but nervous grammar-school boy fallen among bullies; while Nigel Terry, darkly mumbling, has another go at his. Gaye Brown, on the other hand, is cast rewardingly against type; the lady she plays could never be described as a good-time girl.

* * *

It would obviously be unfair to judge Ken Campbell's projected 10-part sci-fi epic The Warp (ICA) by the first night of its first instalment. At least I hope it would be unfair, since what I saw was mostly terrible. The acting, even by Mr Campbell's informal standards, was sloppy; I was relieved when a first-night cry of "Speak up for God's sake" turned out to have come from the maestro himself. (It worked too. Instant direction.)

Neil Oram's script, as so far revealed, plays like a pale copy of Illuminatus: conspiracy theories are adumbrated and the questing hero, a would-be poet, is passed on from one baffling guru to another; one grew to dread the announcement that someone had an interesting friend they wanted him to meet. There are also beddable girls for him to enjoy and policemen to stop him doing it (the number of arrests in this play must constitute an all-time record).

Only Jim Broadbent among the actors seemed to me to match Mr Campbell's exalted standards of frenzy. But the staging offers some promise of fun to come; the play is performed on a series of stages placed end-to-end around the walls of the hall. It chases you clockwise round the room; in fact I must confess to wondering what happens next. (Will I succumb? Watch this space.)

* * *

The heroine of Shaw's very late play The Millionairess (Haymarket) is required to be simultaneously bossy and enchanting. Penelope Keith can be bossy and hilarious (as in The Norman Conquests) or vulnerable and enchanting (as in Donkey's Years); the new combination is beyond her, though she manages both elements by turns and looks a treat; her giraffe height functions in the production almost as mobile sculpture.

Her colleagues mostly vary from grotesque to dull (Nigel Hawthorne performing needless prodigies of self-effacement), though Charles Kay has a pretty style as her chosen mate, the Egyptian doctor whom he plays, perhaps inevitably, as Peter Sellers' Indian. (Donald Pleasence once did so on television. And some movie producer saw him, and cast Mr Sellers in a film version, opposite Sophia Loren. Goodness gracious both of them.)

The play is a problem since its dialogue has sparkle far in excess of its weight. The piece races along, and the audience are left wondering what it is all for. At its heart, though, is a very powerful conceit; the heroine Epifania is sexy because rich: a lineal descendant of Portia in The Merchant of Venice and encumbered by much the same kind of paternal will. She is cold and challenging; so is the play.

records.title: Living in the present
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Living in the present

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

NOW IT comes on the winter of 1979 and there is much snow on the ground, and also ice, and it is a miserable time for one and all, and many citizens and even theatres are compelled to do the best they can.

There is one theatre in East London called the Half Moon, which is formerly a synagogue in the days when there is a big call for such places in East London and what do they put on but a show which is entitled Guys and Dolls and which is well known to be a musical comedy whose plot is lifted from one of the short stories written by Damon Runyon. This Runyon writes many such tales back in the 1930s, and is such a guy, as hates and despises the use of the past tense. This tense is in fact employed more than somewhat in Guys and Dolls but I excuse it since the stage is well known to be a bastard art form, while the musical comedy stage has practically nothing legitimate about it whatsoever.

Personally I greet the arrival of this show with much enthusiasm for many citizens of my acquaintance regard it as the best musical they ever see, including many who never actually see it at all. The thing is, it is first staged in London in 1953 at an hour when many of my friends are tucked up in their beds, with their mammas maybe singing lullabies to them; and I myself do not see it at this date though afterwards I play the record maybe a hundred times, and also take two or three ganders at the movie. One way and another I feel pretty well acquainted with Guys and Dolls and I wish to say I never expect to see it performed in an ex-synagogue by a cast of seven. But the Half Moon is what is called an art theatre, with few potatoes to spare, and its patrons are very tolerant.

A guy named Shakespeare once says to make a virtue of necessity or some such; and Robert Walker, who directs this item, is very virtuous, in fact he is practically a saint. Many characters in this show are gamblers, and one or two are no better than common criminals, and it will be a dreadful thing if any honest guys or dolls in the audience admire them or find them romantic. But Mr Walker sets them all in a barroom which maybe once sees better days, though personally I will not like to bet on it; and he brings them all on very slow and sour, and sends them all off even slower and sourer, and one way and another he seems to think the show is what they call a black comedy though this is by no means the case.

Furthermore, he cuts out some of the best jokes from Abe Burrows's dialogue, though the book is still the funniest ever written, for Broadway at that. But Mr Walker knows what he is doing and is bigger than me, or at least broader, so I do not pursue it.

At first he seems to have 10 actors, only three of them turn out to be nothing but musicians; though one of this trio is liable to leave his piano and stand on a box to impersonate Big Jule who comes from Chicago and who many inhabitants of Manhattan wish will return there on account of his hasty temper. Also visiting town is Sky Masterson, the renowned sportsman, who falls in love with a Salvation Army doll, though neither of them, according to the song, is ever in love before; Barrie Houghton, who plays Sky, is as rat-faced a juvenile lead as ever I wish to see, but of course this is part of the intention, and he is slick and oily and also sings pretty good.

Maurice Colbourne, who shrugs in a very eloquent manner, plays Nathan Detroit, who runs a floating crap-game and on occasion that attracts much opprobrium from the coppers, and also from Miss Adelaide, who is Nathan's fiancee of 14 years' standing, though to hear her tell it standing is not her usual position. Adelaide gets to sing about her plight as a female who is "getting a kind of a name for herself and the name ain't his," which is maybe the most comical line any lyricist ever writes.

Adelaide is played by Maggie Steed, a long lady who honks very high-toned and has plenty of attack and makes me laugh ha-ha practically every time she opens her mouth. There is also a guy named Robin Hooper who plays seven roles, male and female, which means he is frequently on stage with himself and has to keep changing his hat. He sings a quiet ditty called "More I Cannot Wish You," which is such a touching ballad as you would not expect Frank Loesser to write, he being famous for such comedy numbers as "Take Back Your Mink," performed by Adelaide and the Hot Box Girls, only three, and "Sit Down, You're Rockin' the Boat." But such chorus numbers as "Luck Be a Lady" and "Sit Down, You're Rockin' the Boat" are done with great ingenuity, and also glee; and it is of course a great testimony to Guys and Dolls that it can lose so much weight and still live.

* * *

A month or so ago I am sitting in a restaurant on 72nd Street with David Edgar, the playwright, talking of his piece Mary Barnes which opens in Birmingham last year and is to transfer to the Royal Court where it arrives last week. "You are," he says to me, "the only critic who notices that the play is not only about alternative methods of psychotherapy but about the counter-culture generally. But," he says, "I see that you say this subject is skimpily treated and I rewrite the play accordingly."

I will not of course mention such a conversation, being a modest guy at all times, if this aspect does not strike me as being far more effectively handled this time round. But I am puzzled, for I do not notice any extra scenes or speeches; in fact I suspect Mr Edgar trims his play, reducing the social and historical background to scale and stepping up the ironies. Hugo, the Supershrink, who many spectators believe to be none other than R. D. Laing, is played by Donald Sumpter, who is teasing and testing and also cool. Simon Callow meanwhile is kind and furious as Eddie who guides and coaxes Mary Barnes through her ascent from schizophrenia; and Patti Love's Mary is so complete that I get a shock when she takes her curtain-call since by then I honestly forget she is an actress.

Up above Mary Barnes, in the Theatre Upstairs, there is Ron Hutchinson's Anchorman, which also comes from what is called the Midlands, namely from Coventry. Now Mary Barnes is such a play as turns pain into pleasure by illuminating it, but Anchorman keeps everything dark, including the audience. Four British soldiers, who will be considered very rough customers even in the army, are present at the end of the world, or at least of this society, though of course not being dramatic critics they have little experience of such cataclysms, and panic accordingly.

The production is on the dingy side, and is such an event as a scribe like Ambrose Hammer, who dearly loves to heave the old harpoon into actors, will enjoy reviewing; but I am kind-hearted and wish no part of such action, so I shut up.

records.title: Screaming the house down
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: A Day in Hollywood, a Night in the Ukraine
records.body:
Screaming the house down

Theatre

Robert Cushman on a Joe Orton revival

The programme for the revival of Joe Orton's The Erpingham Camp (King's Head) sports a paragraph by the author's biographer, John Lahr, claiming the piece as Orton's great transition farce, paving the way for What the Butler Saw and second to it in merit. This, I think, is a case of biographer's bias. The Erpingham Camp is an aggressive and exuberant work, but is also repetitious.

Erpingham is a holiday camp supremo, whose subjects rebel with bloody, and to him fatal, results. "You've struck a figure of authority," says a scandalised redcoat when his chief comes under fire, approximately, the tenth time the joke has been made with half the play still to go. That Orton should have been locked into it was perhaps unavoidable given the play's premise. The camp represents the connivance of the British in their own humiliation (patronised, ballooned and bingoed into grateful submission) and the image can hardly be quarrelled with.

Orton himself, though, seems just a little too delighted with it, and the self-satisfaction shows through, particularly in a small theatre where the audience gets to share it. There is not after all much overlap between the clientele of the King's Head and that of Butlin's. The play was written for commercial television when it must have seemed far more courageously subversive.

There is still much mileage to be had from the rebellious campers, who talk mainly in headline bromides. The rising comes about when an ambitious redcoat, newly in charge of entertainments, organises a screaming contest, into which one young woman enters so enthusiastically that he has to slap her to quieten her down. Her husband, dressed for other festive purposes as Tarzan of the Apes, takes this to heart; he had married her against the odds ("Our love was banned") and, what is far more, she is pregnant. He leads the mob "for the gratification of those in the family way everywhere"; Orton spins endless verbal variations on this theme and the satire - in a society and a theatre much oppressed by slogan - is extremely satisfying.

Said to derive from The Bacchae (but then, what doesn't?), the play asks for a larger production than Islington can offer; starved of accompanying spectacle, the glibness that Orton himself recognised as his own weakest spot is more noticeable. But there is still plenty of verve and intelligence in Stewart Trotter's staging, and a prime performance of Erpingham himself, domineering and grossly epicene, by Peter Vaughan.

* * *

Jennifer Phillips's Daughters of Men (Hampstead) was once a neat radio script. On stage it seems attenuated. There are large gaps in our acquaintance with the characters, while much of what we are shown is gratuitous - and, in Nancy Meckler's production, remarkably sluggish. The main conflict is between the estranged couple for possession of their daughter. The wife, an artist's agent, seems set to keep her; financially at least she is better equipped than her husband. The issue was left teasingly in doubt for most of the original; expanded for the stage - or rather with the same material gone over more slothfully - it merely drags.

The main story is framed by an interview between the wife and a social security official; stagecraft seems to amount to giving Frances de la Tour time to change her clothes while switching between past and present. Miss de la Tour has a couple of minutes of stylised verbal comedy on the subject of toothpaste; otherwise her gifts are wasted, indeed positively misplaced. With nothing to give her pouting angularity a charge, she just mopes through the evening. (I kept wishing she were playing the self-tormenting heroine of Bedroom Farce; she might bring it off like nobody else.) Two other prominent actresses, Anna Carteret and Annabel Leventon, are spectacularly wasted (Miss Leventon never even moves) and there are a couple of wretched performances further down.

* * *

Dick Vosburgh wrote the lyrics to a very funny song called "I love a film cliche," which has led a flourishing underground life for some years now. It crops up in the first half of his double-headed entertainment A Day in Hollywood, a Night in the Ukraine (New End) and it is the key to the entire enterprise. I quote: "I love the dialogue/like 'Please don't shoot my dog/Rusty couldn't have eaten those sheep'." That, in its mocking affection, is the spirit of film-buffery.

It hangs pretty limp in A Day in Hollywood, where the elements tend to cancel each other out. There are jokes about Nelson Eddy being dumb enough to turn down a Cole Porter song; the song itself, "In the Still of the Night," is then sung perfectly straight, to a beautiful accompaniment provided by Frank Lazarus. Mr Vosburgh's taste in movie music is impeccable, but he has gone to strange lengths to get in on the stage.

There are pleasures: Paddie O'Neil doing faultless imitations of Bette Davis and (especially) Ethel Merman, a performance of "Thanks for the Memory" that stakes a claim for Leo Robin as the most underrated lyricist in America, a Depression medley including a powerful "Remember my Forgotten Man" from Maureen Scott and a charmingly wistful "With Plenty of Money and You" from Mr Lazarus. But it all needs more shape and purpose, firmer direction and a choreographer. Also more stage space, since what there is at the New End is being held in reserve for A Night in the Ukraine.

This is much jollier, being Chekhov's The Bear as it might have been done by the Marx Brothers. There is, I must admit, something self-defeating about it; you can hardly parody the Marxes, you can only compete with them. Mr Vosburgh has hit off the style to perfection and many of his cracks are every bit as good as S. J. Perelman's: Chico of Margaret Dumont - "She's a-more than unhappy, she's a-house-broken"; Groucho of Chico - "I'm afraid this story has an unhappy ending, folks, he doesn't die"; Harpo of Groucho - any number of toots on a motor horn.

The song of self-introduction which Messrs Vosburgh and Lazarus have dreamed up for Groucho as Serge B. Samovar, the crooked lawyer, is quite perfect, and this unimpersonatable performer is actually brought off uncannily well by John Bay. Sheila Steafel's Harpo actually goes beyond imitation, having the delicacy and gusto of a genuine creation. And Mr Lazarus's Chico signals a welcome triple talent: as composer, pianist and Italian. There are two funny lovers as well. That it has all been done before is the evening's limitation, but also its glory.

* * *

The Grand Magic Circus are back in town, this time at the Shaftesbury which barn they almost succeed in humanising. I never tire of listening to their presiding genius, Jerome Savary, bidding us a mournful but obviously genuine welcome in his individually elongated English. ("Tonighter we are performing the entire show in Breetsher.") He looks and sounds like a mad undertaker, though for much of this show he is dressed as a Caliph, this show being 1001 Nights.

Scheherazade is explicitly disowned (things, we are given to understand, never work out as happily as that), but the GMC's technique of stopping and starting stories within the stories can get irritating. Chinese boxes full of shaggy dogs. The music and spectacle are well meant, as are the performances, but the really interesting objects are likely to be mechanical; a giant American eagle, for example, which comes down, I think, to illustrate a fable about capitalism. I would also like to mention a pantomime camel.

records.title: Rocking the future / Theatre round-up
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Rocking the future

IN A week of bits and pieces the most substantial fragment made its appearance at the Bush. This was The Cockroach that Ate Cincinnati, presented by Hull Truck but differing greatly from that company's familiar group improvisations. This show has a script, and only one performer.

The performer is Alan Aldred, who in A Bed of Roses gave a memorable impersonation of a man with a plate in his head. He was glowering, unpredictable and rather frightening. Psychopathic hints similarly abound in his current vehicle, but they are softened by humour. Mr Aldred has formidable comic timing, but of course he owes something to his writer, Alan Williams. In fact Messrs Williams and Aldred are the same man and freely admit the fact, but their subterfuge does allow them a double entry in what would otherwise be an undercrowded programme.

The title may remind you of a notably unfunny comedy song of the last decade, The Eggplant that Ate Chicago. Such references are constant; our monologuist is a pop-fancier of the fifties and sixties who has found his faith destroyed in the seventies. He has had a vision, or at least he has heard voices. On record, untraceable in any catalogue, he has made out, between the grooves, what he describes as 'a prophecy of the future of rock from 1968 to 1983.' It includes, you may note with whatever response you feel appropriate, the death of Elton John.

Disillusion becomes retrospective; the reputations of the past come up for consideration and are rapidly and ruthlessly dismissed. I must admit that I have never understood why a whole generation -- my own, to add to the confusion -- should have supposed for a moment that rock could provide them with a moral and political programme, and should even furnish leaders to put its tenets into effect. No betrayal can ever have been more clearly foreseeable.

Mr Williams does not do much to explain such a state of mind, but at least he evokes it powerfully and wittily. It is worth going to the Bush to hear, delivered with curling relish, the definitive put-down of Bob Dylan and his worshippers. A poet who didn't know what he was writing down from one stanza to the next -- we were lucky to find him. Evocative name-dropping ('there wasn't really that much to Wayne Fontana and the Mindbenders') duly sets the nostalgia-glands working, as Mr Aldred recalls a youth spent playing his Woolworth Dansette record-player, clearly a gesture of rebellion in a household where Classics Illustrated were the only permitted comics.

Messrs Aldred and Williams lost me in their second half when a misty pretentiousness set in ('son of man -- Manson,' it went) suggesting that the Dylan influence had gone ineradicably deep. But the fun and the anger, while they last, are good value.

They will not however be available at the Bush until 5 February, for one week only; I was admitted to a press preview. Holding the stage until then is something called The Paranormal Review, which I cannot recommend too highly. In fact I am not sure that I can recommend it at all. It purports to be a meeting of the Charles Flynn Society, who collect rationally inexplicable phenomena. They present items from their collection in the form of dramatised sketches, most of which go wrong. The entertainment lies in their confusion when this occurs.

We are presented in fact with a pretty traditional form of backstage humour, to which the occult trimmings are strictly irrelevant. Indeed, since the Charles Flynn societaires are repeatedly shown up as incompetent fools the veriest sceptic (me, for instance) is likely to find all his prejudices confirmed. He will also laugh some if (again like me) he is a sucker for offhandedly delivered theatrical gags. Whether the odd bits that are funny justify the bits that aren't must be a matter of personal taste. There is not much polish in the performances, though Paul McDowell (what, Whispering Paul of the Temperance Seven?) makes a pleasantly wooden compere.

My reaction to The Putney Debates (Cottesloe: one more performance, on Wednesday), was anticipated more than a century ago by Lord Melbourne, who said of an amateur performance of a Ben Jonson play got up by Dickens that, though he knew it was going to be dull, he did not expect it to be 'quite as damnably dull as it was.'

This enterprise, a pendant to The World Turned Upside Down, involves 11 National Theatre actors in reading extracts from the deliberations of Cromwell's New Model Army shortly before their final defeat of Charles I. They were engaged in discussing just how revolutionary they were prepared to be, and notions of the necessity or immorality of property were freely tossed around. So you can't say that the ideas have lost all interest, and there is a sporting attempt to make Cromwell (quite the least radical man on hand) sound like the Prime Minister.

But the readings are appallingly slovenly and quite unco-ordinated. No actor establishes a relationship with the previous speaker; each in turn plunges in, splashes about for a couple of sentences hoping his personality will buoy him up, and then sinks. It is impossible for the audience to know what they're talking about, since they seem ignorant of it themselves. They wear civvies; though period costumes might at least make the proceedings look more appetising and would not, in the circumstances of the current repertory, cost anything.

I don't know if the Roundhouse Downstairs is the most morgue-like theatre in town, or whether successive offerings merely make it seem so. Latest occupants are a callow troupe who seem, to put it charitably, out of their depth with Pantagleize, a satirical fantasy from between the wars by the Belgian playwright Michel de Ghelderode. Centring on a simpleton who blunders into and through a revolution, it now seems unbearably arch.

The translation doesn't help, though, while the performance merely confirms that plays which are at once old, substantial and unfashionable are likeliest to be tackled by companies unequal to the job. A rotten week. Like the man said, I'm waiting for the weather to break so's I can get out of London and see some theatre.

* * *

Theatre round-up

THE CHANGELING (Aldwych): Steamily persuasive production of a Jacobean blood-and-lust masterpiece. Diana Quick excels herself as the fair murderess.

CLOUDS (Duke of York's): British Sunday paper journalists go junketing in Cuba and find that everything is in the eye of the beholder. Michael Frayn's best play yet.

THE DOUBLE DEALER (Olivier): The National Theatre regains its grip on Restoration comedy. Michael Bryant and Dorothy Tutin are going to be legends.

EGO JOO (Criterion): Michael Hastings's quick-witted farce on how to become a legal immigrant in one easy wedding.

MARY BARNES (Royal Court): Patti Love gives a stunning performance as a young nurse whose deliverance from schizophrenia (courtesy of R. D. Laing) has been dramatised by David Edgar with a judicious blend of irony and concern.

THE PHILANDERER (Lyttelton): Sparkling revival of Shaw's second play and one of his best; Dinsdale Landen plays, more or less, G.B.S. himself, the author being in a merrily self-scourging mood.

SARATOGA (Aldwych): Early American comedy that may never be revived again, but which Ronald Eyre and his company have made the occasion for a fine frolic that includes some of the best song and dance in town.

STRIFE (Olivier): A very pleasant surprise: Galsworthy's strike drama may lack something as a tract on industrial relations, but in Christopher Morahan's granite-hard production, it lives as a study of human obstinacy on the grand scale -- which is just how the author intended it.
