Toss of the coin

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Alan Ayckbourn's new play(s).

ALAN AYCKBOURN'S Sisterly Feelings (Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round, Scarborough) is at base a play in four scenes. However there are complications.

Mr Ayckbourn has written alternative versions of the second and third scenes, or rather he has written one alternative version of each. However, either variant of Scene Two is playable with either version of Scene Three. The play can be seen four times, with the spectator getting a different show on each occasion. I hope this is clear.

I went twice, which allowed me to collect the entire text while missing out on some of the juggling. I gather that the arrangements I saw are referred to among the Scarborough players as "the Abigail play" and "the Dorcas play." Abigail and Dorcas are the sisters with whose feelings we are concerned, and though Abigail is a housewife and Dorcas works in local radio (producer of two half-hour shows a week) they bear more than a passing resemblance to Goneril and Regan. They have a ga-ga dad, and a mother: in fact they are on their way back from her funeral when we first meet them. Above all there is a young man whom they both fancy, though unlike Shakespeare's Edmund he is in no sense a bastard. He is Simon, their brother's girl-friend's brother, a clean-limbed young man and also chivalrous.

At the end of Scene One there is some question as to with which of the two he will walk home. In the end the matter is decided by the toss of a coin (and that toss, which incidentally is left to chance in performance) decides the content of the second scene. For the walk home is the prelude to an affair.

Scene Two, whatever happens, is a picnic, and the feasters are the same either way, but their relationships obviously differ. The end of this scene provides another moment of choice that determines the nature of Scene Three; Simon may either be having it off with the same flame or with her rival. That Scene Four should be exactly the same, whatever has happened, is of course its own ironic comment. Abigail and Dorcas may pride themselves on their dissimilarities, but nobody else can notice any; to their despised future sister-in-law, for example, they are both "hopelessly neurotic and out of touch."

The one crucial difference between them is that Abigail is married; and since Mr Ayckbourn sees his people less in terms of character than in terms of domestic circumstance this is more than enough to justify his peculiar strategy. That the Abigail play works the better of the two is a tribute to the old-fashioned rules, both social and dramatic. Much depends, of course, on the quality of the cuckold. Here Abigail is in luck; her husband Patrick is an exemplary mixture of cynicism and complaisance. Professing complete tolerance of his wife's activities, he so contrives, with the utmost politeness, to make her life an embarrassment, while Simon, despite the obvious need for discretion, comes close to duffing him up. He is, besides, most incisively characterised as a man besotted with his job, his house and his car, particularly when they involve mechanical extras.

By contrast, Stafford, the gentleman whom Dorcas betrays ("Dorcas's thing," her father calls him), is a stereotype of the half-baked far Left intellectual already worked over (to rather better purpose) in Mr Ayckbourn's Ten Times Table. His jealousy takes far less inventive turns than Patrick's. Scene Three offers a choice of Abigail and Simon going tramping, or Dorcas offloading her cross-country race with Simon one of the favourites. Again Abigail offers the playgoer a better deal: acute situation comedy as opposed to overworked farce.

All scenes take place in a remote corner of Pendon Common. Pendon was also the scene of Ten Times Table and I suspect Mr Ayckbourn thinks of it as home. I wish Mr Ayckbourn had allowed his heroines one head-on collision, rather than confining them to polite fencing with undertones, but overall this related comedy is excellent value. As usual, the author's production offers resonances generally inaudible in London where, with rare exceptions, star casting has obscured his characters' unblinking ordinariness.

At Scarborough the audience take up where the play leaves off - and they are in no way patronised. After all, they get better new work on a regular basis, than can be found at any other regional theatre, in perfectly judged productions. Alison Skilbeck's Abigail, James Bate's Patrick and Robin Herford's Simon are splendidly recognisable.

* * *

The Glasgow Citizens, operating at the opposite aesthetic extreme, are offering Jean Cocteau's Orpheus - not the play, but a staged version of the film. Geoffrey Cauley, directing and designing, has set it among black cubes so highly polished that they act as mirrors, this being Cocteau's image (questionable but reasonably arresting) of the passage to death. Death is actually personified here as a lady in black; Orpheus falls in love with her, and she quite unconstitutionally with him.

Eurydice, though visually linked to her husband by the fact that they both wear red (nobody else dresses that warm), has no chance, which rather robs the evening of dramatic tension. It becomes an exercise in style: an envious choice for the Citizens, but rather an empty one. The acting is more dangerously underpowered than it has been there of late, with only Jack Elliott as Death's unwilling assistant impressing himself among a crowd of palely beautiful young creatures of both sexes. But then everyone is overshadowed by the open white Rolls, of Cocteau's own vintage, which is the underworld's gift to Orpheus and an irresistible bribe if ever I saw one.

records.title: Bad temper
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Bad temper

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'A Fair Quarrel' at the National.

THE National Theatre continues its season of plays with turbulent titles. Strife, Betrayal, and The World Turned Upside Down are succeeded by A Fair Quarrel (Olivier). No doubt this bellicosity suits the times, but it reflects all previous ages as well. In the entire world repertoire the only beatifically named play that comes to mind is Aristophanes's Peace, a very long time ago.

Otherwise the world's drama is crammed with bad temper. There are three courses of it in A Fair Quarrel, which comes from Middleton and Rowley, the Jacobean firm who gave you The Changeling. Critics have pronounced that its separate plots are bound together by their concern with codes of behaviour under strain. It is difficult to imagine any story that wouldn't somewhere support that interpretation, but we may give the scholars two out of three.

Plot A, which is about duelling, is indeed parodied by Plot C, which deals with the 'roaring boys' who made a cult out of rowdiness and in one scene even give lessons in it. Plot B, though, leads a discrete, if not discreet, existence and is concerned with a girl courted against her will. All these juxtapositions involve the authors in some odd time-keeping; a heroine goes through the greater part of pregnancy, and is brought to bed, while a hero is strolling back from the field of honour. 'No wonder his mother worries.'

Her honour, I should explain, is itself in question. Young Captain Ager is called by his colonel a 'son of a whore' and, as was expected, challenges him immediately. Lady Ager, not wanting to see her boy carved up, blushingly (and quite falsely) admits to having slipped in her time, and the captain sets off prepared to apologise. His antagonist promptly calls him a coward, the captain's reflexes are reawakened and the fight is on again.

The Jacobeans, while regarding such behaviour as something of a joke and more of a public nuisance, would still have found it understandable. To us, unless we are properly instructed, it is only a joke; and the only time when a perplexed first-night audience felt the ground firm beneath its feet was when it could laugh at Nicky Henson's Captain striking noble attitudes.

William Gaskill's production is very clear; you can hear most of the words and the actors seem unusually convinced of what they mean. They also know what the issues are; to a man they jump whenever their reputations are called in question. But though clarity is an essential basis for a revival, it is not enough and this play -- no masterwork, but an entertaining genre-piece -- needs filling out. Some of the social detail that Mr Gaskill used to supply in Restoration comedy might be helpful, along with actions that explored and projected the characters' passions instead of just tastefully indicating them. The actors come mainly from Joint Stock (and are therefore, according to current doctrine, beyond criticism), but for this play, on this stage, they look under-powered.

The stage is part of the trouble -- this is another main house production with its heart in the studio. On this occasion, the back of the Olivier platform has been given over to the audience, which may cut down on the stage's intimidating vastness, but makes the house itself the biggest arena theatre east of Hollywood Bowl. The acting area is a timbered rectangle with a hole in its middle: a large trapdoor which the actors, thus democratically prevented from taking the centre of the stage, warily circumnavigate.

Those who make the strongest impression are those previously in residence: Mr Henson, and Dermot Crowley as a creepy physician. Among the insurgents, Fred Pearson has a good swagger as the Colonel and Marjorie Yates a nicely judged vulgarity as a bawd. I honestly believe plays like A Fair Quarrel should be revived, and I realise that I have not greatly assisted their chances this morning. But they can be done.

* * *

The staging of Tommy (Queen's) reopens some questions which one might have thought buried. It is boldly billed as a 'rock musical' and is one of the few of its kind to deserve the name. Hence of course its failure; rock cannot co-exist with drama, since the first depends on repetition and the second on variety. Whenever a supposed rock-score has been praised in the theatre it has been for its 'eclecticism': i.e., it has got away from rock as far and often as possible. (This has often been the case with pop music outside the theatre as well.)

But Tommy is sanctified as The Who's masterwork, a hit on records and filmed by Ken Russell (they deserved each other), so we get it now with its rhythms crushingly unvaried, its decibels ringing and Pete Townshend's atrocious lyrics generally inaudible -- which does nothing for the plot but something for the sensibilities. (Mr Townshend is not, as you might think, proudly indifferent to rhyme; when he can think up 'sorrow-tomorrow' couplets, however lame, he shoves it in.)

It is not altogether the authors' fault; Tommy, after all, wasn't written for the stage. To put it there is brutally (the right word) to expose its masochistic narcissism: here is the hero as deaf, dumb and blind boy, here he is as teenage idol, and here finally as crucified star. Filling in the visual details can't be easy; apart from some spectacular laser-work, this production settles for third-hand eroticism. If a couple of nurses have to appear they naturally flash their suspenders.

To show you how original it plans to be, the show begins by having its cast clamber down scaffolding in their leotards while clouds float across the back-projected sky. Things that on the record were just meretriciously menacing are here clumsily nasty; his relatives' sexual assaults on Tommy are played for laughs. (Bob Grant makes Uncle Ernie a perverted Bruce Forsyth.) Allan Love mimes quite touchingly in the opening scenes; but when his faculties are restored he has to grab a hand-mike just like everybody else. Character conflict in those constricted circumstances is hardly possible. Listen, people, nobody in America writes rock scores for the theatre any more, and they know far more about musicals than you.

* * *

It is a relief to turn to Talent (ICA), a cheeky title but something for the sensibilities. Victoria Wood, as author and performer, fully justifies. She is already the best songwriter we have, the best refreshing melodist to wry, funny, concrete lyrics, and she may have it in her to be our best female playwright (if we are to encourage such distinctions). Her present piece, though short, has perhaps too many personal memories pushed into it; but her dialogue lives and breathes, and though she can be sour -- she writes of northern working-girls with dead-end prospects -- she is resilient, and accompanies sexy, ambitious Julie, would-be singer, to a club talent contest.

As the night in the dismal dressing-room proceeds, Julie learns that she has nothing to hope for, while Maureen's prospects, briefly expanding, subside as quickly. Hazel Clyne, brittle and edgy, gets both Julie's selfishness and her vulnerability. The show is an object-lesson in making upbeat theatre out of downbeat material without ever falsifying it.

records.title: American cancer ward
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
American cancer ward

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a Pulitzer Prize play.

THERE is a perpetual conspiracy in American drama to wring cosiness out of terror.

Soap opera is part of that story; but not all of it: soap of itself has always seemed to me a reasonably healthy phenomenon, since to simplify emotion is not necessarily to anaesthetise it. Soap knows its place. But Hollywood movies on 'important' or 'sensitive' subjects do not. And neither do the plays or novels from which they derive. Michael Cristofer's The Shadow Box was a Broadway success in 1977 and won the Pulitzer Prize. It has now been given its British premiere at the Arts Theatre, Cambridge.

It is about death. Three terminal cancer patients are living in some kind of medically supervised settlement, each in his or her own chalet. There is a restless-minded author, now living with a young male hustler and forced to cope with the sudden reappearance of his wife; There is a contrastingly uncomplicated working man whose wife has so far withheld the truth of his condition from their guitar-playing son. There is a rasping old woman, shunted round in a wheelchair by one daughter and anxious only for news of another. One faces the inevitable with resentment, another with resignation; and the third oscillates between.

Each has quite enough personal and family problems to be going on with, and these are duly aired. Where British drama generally avoids confrontation, American drama seeks it out (this will do as a generalisation about our private lives as well) so there is much hand-to-hand and heart-to-heart.

As domestic drama this is all conventional and innocuous if a bit dull (there being an overwrought gentility about much of the dialogue that recalls the suffering days of Bette Davis), but Mr Cristofer has of course the built-in gimmick of mortality. He has also -- and this is where my reservations harden into hostility -- a narrator. He introduces us to the sufferers; he is not, he insists, a doctor. Or rather: "We're not your doctors," he says, blandly and infuriatingly assuming the role of audience spokesman.

This device is given little scope -- the characters are informed of our presence, blink, and then retire behind their fourth wall -- but it is enough to bestow on the evening the aura of cutely earnest experimentation. Our fugleman sits there, wise and smiling and impotent, but we are back with the worst of Thornton Wilder -- as it might be, "The Skin of Our Town." "Joe," he says, summoning his first specimen, and you would not have thought a writer could sprinkle so much sugar on a monosyllable. At the end, the company, Jobs and comforters together, give up on action and address us on the wisdom and necessity of acceptance. After everything else, Mr Cristofer throws a tone poem at us.

The play has gained in one signal respect since I saw it in New York. The word "cancer" is now actually mentioned. It also has the benefit of a production by Jonathan Lynn which is -- until the closing stages -- livelier and less reverential than the original, and of a magnificently clean-cut performance by Madge Ryan as the senior patient (an easy role in which to be self-indulgent while still attracting good notices). Dick Wilson and Sheila Allen fill the family chalet with its proper measure of sympathy and bafflement.

The writer's menage is the most clumsily contrived and the fullest of reproaches. Anthony Bate is too restrained and trained for it and June Ritchie too emphatic; James Aubrey as the cuckoo in their nest begins splendidly, goes to pieces when the character does, but retrieves himself in time for the final curtain.

* * *

Tom Kempinski's Flashpoint (Mayfair) returns us to another traditional form: the enclosed army melodrama. Those with long enough memories will recall "The Long and the Short and the Tall," especially when confronted by the central character, the tough, foul-mouthed barrack buffoon who turns out to have the right moral instincts. The place is Ulster and the time "next year." Martial law has been imposed, a hutful of squaddies await the morning on which they are to shoot a convicted deserter. Some regard the prospect with indifference, one at least with positive pleasure, and one cracks up. He in effect hijacks the hut, turning the rifle on his mates and demanding the cancellation of the execution as the price of their lives.

Up to this point the play has dragged at comic-documentary level; now it jumps to life and -- despite some repetitious writing -- stays jumping, even treating us to a couple of prize twists at the end. Nothing much is said about the Northern Ireland situation, except that it is probably insoluble; nothing much about the British Army, except that it is as likely to be brutalised by war as any other. To go one further, and deduce a "troops out" message, requires a considerable talent for unassisted extrapolation. (A soldier after all might well baulk at shooting one of his own, whatever the ethics of the conflict.) The actors take full advantage of both the tensions and the humour, Tony Selby romping home in the plum role.

* * *

The Albany Empire is a community theatre in Deptford, which burned to the ground in July after presenting a cabaret show with an anti-racialist slant. "Controversy," say the company, "rages as to the cause." The theatre has now been rebuilt and I wish I could welcome the reopening production. But One Gun Salute, which purports to be a lament for the welfare state, is the dregs of agit-prop. Not that you could accuse it of unfairness to its opponents: it never keeps its eye on any object long enough to find any attitudes at all. Attempting to chronicle the disillusion of a social security official, it never lets you get a look at him, and its choice of surrounding incidents is arbitrary to the point of factitious non-existence. Messy acting, desperate music and a lamely allegorical structure complete the picture.

* * *

Michael Hastings's Full Frontal (Theatre Upstairs), a black African applies for membership of the National Front. His life is unhappy and he needs scapegoats, so his application does have a bizarre logic. He has no time for West Indians and is rather like Mr Hastings's Meadowlark Warner (from "Gloo Joo") in reverse.

But unlike Meadowlark he has no plot, and not very much wit, to keep him going; the piece is a monologue, Mr Hastings having kept the listening Front official off-stage. He has in fact forfeited the boldness of his conception, tacitly acknowledging that though it sounds a brightly provocative notion, it will not stand the test of actual dramatisation. All we get is another hard-luck story, though it's pleasant to hear it delivered by Winston Ntshona, who was once the plumper half of the "Sizwe Bansi" duo, but now seems pretty slim and twice as fluent.

records.title: The Demon Barber
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas
records.body:
The Demon Barber

Theatre

Robert Cushman on Sondheim's 'Sweeney Todd' in New York--and the Louisville festival.

I WROTE at the end of last year about a Broadway musical called 'A Broadway Musical' and wondered whether it would get past the New York critics.

It didn't; it died at birth. A pity, for though horribly confused, it was still appealing; it both dramatised and exemplified the lunacies of putting on a show in the face of murderous economics, artistic bewilderment and the theatrical withering of the popular song. It would have been pleasantly symbolic to have it around, welcoming subsequent arrivals with a deranged grin on its face.

For still they come. The blockbusters continue to bust blocks: 'Annie' and 'Ain't Misbehavin'' and grand-daddy 'Grease.' All in a row on 44th Street stand the choreographic musicals, 'Ballroom' and 'Dancin'' and 'A Chorus Line,' almost making a sentence. Then there is 'The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas,' a success and possibly the worst little musical in the world. It has country music and is stupid.

Of 1979's early comers, 'The Grand Tour' starring Joel Grey as a Jew on the run through occupied Europe, died young, possibly because its narrative techniques were old-fashioned, possibly because the world was not waiting for the musical-comedy version of 'Holocaust,' possibly because the authors (the 'Hello Dolly' team of Michael Stewart and Jerry Herman) hadn't realised that that was what they were getting into. 'They're Playing Our Song' looks like surviving, it being this season's Neil Simon two-hander embellished by smart production and negligible songs; its first half is bright, its second--in which the audience is invited to take an interest in a relationship it hardly knew existed--discouraging.

The palm would have to go to 'Whoopee,' a cheerful exhumation (the best of its kind I've seen) from 1928, were it not for the advent of a show differing in everything but expertise: the Stephen Sondheim-Harold Prince 'Sweeney Todd.'

This, too, might count as an exhumation (it is full of graveyard imagery and there are a couple of diggers on stage at the start to set the mood), since it brings to Broadway the fabled Demon Barber of Fleet Street. The source of the musical is a version by the English playwright Christopher Bond staged at Stratford East in 1973. Mr Bond took the central penny-gaff situation--the cut-throat artist practising above a pie-shop and supplying it with cheap and easy meat--and gave it with a beginning out of 'The Count of Monte-Cristo' and an end out of Elizabethan tragedy.

His Todd is an escaped convict, sentenced to transportation on a trumped-up charge so that the judge could have unimpeded access to Mrs Todd. Our barber returns years later to find his wife a suicide and his daughter, now adolescent, the judge's ward. He plans revenge.

The convict's return is a familiar Dickensian motif, and this 'Sweeney Todd' has more of the spirit of Dickens--the nightmare spirit of 'Oliver Twist'--than any show based on the novel. It presents Victorian London as a plague-spot. Eugene Lee's set, which just about takes over the vast and antiseptic Uris Theatre, is a combination of chapel (with organ), street and--overwhelmingly--factory; and a factory whistle sounds unnervingly at each curve of the plot.

The veneer of social criticism, though, is less important than the passion beneath. Len Cariou's death's-head Sweeney is a magnificent study of a monomaniac--and, in its bitter frantic clarity, the best rendition of a Sondheim score I have heard. It is a musical frenzy that carries Sweeney across the bridge from specific to general bloodlust, but the process is prefigured when he first appears, singing in a low, terse staccato: 'There's a place in the world like a great big pit/And the vermin of the world inhabit it/And it goes by the name of London.'

There is more to the score, and the show, than this: a laconic humour ('So what if none of their souls were saved/They went to their maker impeccably shaved') which expands to epic proportions with Angela Lansbury's pie-woman, looking with her hair piled high in unruly braids, like a monstrous tabby-cat. She and Todd make a marvellously complementary pair of villains: she jolly and practical, he the visionary and thwarted romantic. The tenderest strains of the evening sound around the barber's chair, as he regards his instruments ('my friends') or prepares to use them. This goes beyond grotesquerie or easy irony to a feeling for the criminal as outcast that is absolutely true to the underside of Victorian literature.

More conventional romance comes off less well: Todd's daughter and her sailor-lover are indeterminate figures. They can afford to be, in Bond's play (which reads as elegant, funny and gripping pastiche), but not amid the far greater density of this musical. I should add that Bond's plotting is excellent and the final retributive section of the show--in dialogue, song and Harold Prince's staging--stunning. There is no choreography, but there is consummate choral work. (The show is at least three-quarters sung.) I am sure there is a large, mainly young, audience for this show: the problem is getting them to Broadway. London must see it; it is as near as anyone has come to writing the great British musical.

It is a good season for Victorian misfits. The play of the moment is Bernard Pomerance's 'The Elephant Man' (seen last year at Hampstead) with its caustic use of a painfully intelligent freak as a moral measuring-rod for the society around him. A pellucid production is about to transfer from off-Broadway.

The other touted play is Arthur Kopit's 'Wings,' which begins as an interesting attempt to represent linguistically the dislocation caused by a stroke but falls apart when the author gets down to cases. (Just like Neil Simon.)

Recent American drama is a desert of promise; what is lacking is mature performance. Off-Broadway now has to compete for its white hopes with the increasingly prosperous regional theatre movement. In Louisville, Kentucky (home of Muhammad Ali and Colonel Sanders), the Actors Playhouse last week concluded its third festival of new plays. The theatre, housed in an old bank building, boasts two stages and, for the festival, a very good company. They have also found (and launched as far as New York) a local playwright, Marsha Norman, though her contribution this year was unimpressive: a play about a circus that just looked as though someone had sat down and doggedly written a play about a circus.

Slightly better were a double bill of musicals based on one-act Shaw plays (though performance style proved a problem here) and a programme of playlets entitled 'Holidays' contributed by 10 prominent dramatists, several of whom appeared to have dug out old scripts and written in a few lines about the Fourth of July or whatever.

A new playwright, Beth Henley, offered us 'Crimes of the Heart'; I never quite overcame my disappointment at finding that her piece, about three Mississippi sisters with problems, was not after all going to be a gothic comedy, since it started out that way. Miss Henley went some way towards reclaiming the domestic hearth (or, this being a kitchen play, stove) for respectable drama, but the antique associations proved overpowering.

The find of the festival was James McLure, whose two plays, 'Lone Star' and 'Pvt. Wars,' turned out to be exhilaratingly funny on old subjects, like growing up in Texas, and comparatively new ones, like looking back on war-service in Vietnam; this last hitherto a taboo subject, for laughter. Mr McLure writes cross-talk that builds; he could become a major comic writer, which would be fine, or relax into being a gag man, which wouldn't be so bad either.
production_title: The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas

productions: A Day in Hollywood, A Night in the Ukraine
records.body:
Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN's round-up of the London stage:-

Betrayal (Lyttelton): Harold Pinter's straightforward (though played backwards) triangle drama. This critic was disappointed, but there have been enough intelligent demurs for it to be worth your attention.

A Chorus Line (Drury Lane): Mostly exhilarating (and, by the way, superbly lit) musical now approaching the final chorus.

A Day in Hollywood, A Night in the Ukraine (New End): After regaling us with movie songs and anecdotes, a talented cast--notably Sheila Steafel as Harpo--play at being the Marx Brothers playing Chekhov. Accurate and therefore funny. Last week.

Filumena (Lyric): Barbara Jefford has temporarily replaced Joan Plowright as the fiery Italian ex-whore and eternal mother, and should be ideal.

Flashpoint (Mayfair): Gripping if not over-profound military melodrama set in Northern Ireland.

Night and Day (Phoenix): Erroneously hailed as a new departure for Tom Stoppard, it actually follows logically from his previous works. It presents a clash of principles: the feminine, and that of Press freedom.

The Ordeal of Gilbert Pinfold (Roundhouse): Michael Hordern is far too nice to be an acceptable Evelyn Waugh surrogate, but he is always worth watching on his own account and the production marks the welcome arrival in London of Manchester's Royal Exchange company.

records.title: Tolstoy at the National
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Hoagy, Bix and Wolfgang Beethoven Bunkhaus
records.body:
Tolstoy at the National

THE most surprising feature of Tolstoy's comedy The Fruits of Enlightenment (Olivier) is its mildness.

It was written late in its author's life at a time when he was denouncing all sexuality while wrestling unsuccessfully with his own; and while he bore the scars of battles with the peasants who had stubbornly refused to do what he thought was good for them.

Art, presumably, purifies. There is not a trace of sex-hatred in The Fruits of Enlightenment. Indeed, there is hardly any sex at all, only the conventionalised courtship of a maid and kitchen boy. As for the peasants, they seem to have been conceived in accordance with the beautiful visions in their author's head rather than with the reality on which he kept stumbling.

The play presents a trio of them, come to Moscow to buy land on credit from the master of the house, who would rather have cash. The plot turns on their efforts to get the bargain made on their own terms; the dramatic interest hangs on their bewildered sceptical reaction to the fashionable life of which they are the temporary spectators, and to the absurdities of that life itself.

The master believes in spiritualism, and the marriageable maidservant, by passing her boyfriend off as a medium, rigs a seance in the peasants' interests. The translator, Michael Frayn, has by his own account transferred the seance from the play's three-quarter mark to its end, thus keeping the story going, giving us the real climax, and sparing us a final act consisting mainly of comings and goings. It sounds reasonable, but I suspect that he has miscalculated; the comings and goings are the most enjoyable part of the play, while the story is thin and gains nothing from being protracted.

Mr Frayn's introduction to the published text (reprinted, with tactful abridgements, in the National Theatre programme) is engagingly frank about the play's defects. He acknowledges that the peasants are sentimentalised ("two of them are comic characters, one of them is sturdily outspoken"--I'm still not sure which is which) and that Tolstoy's jibes at the credulity of the educated classes weigh a little heavy at times too. He might have added that the whole menage--mother is a fussy hypochondriac, the son is a wastrel, the daughter is a blue stocking (or at any rate is outspoken and wears spectacles)--is hardly the occasion of trenchant satire, despite the amount of stage time that it takes up.

The Master is described by Tolstoy as "in the English sense a 'gentleman'"; and it is of course in the English manner of golden eccentricity--benevolent, slightly touched, and disregarding people even in the act of radiating good will at them--that Ralph Richardson plays. John Harding and Selina Cadell make him a bright pair of offspring, but everything in this area of the play seems forced; however hard and fast the actors talk, the play moves slowly.

There is, though, an intermediate layer to the play: that of the servants, who regard their employers with varying degrees of envy, amazement and, just occasionally, hatred. (The mutterings of an old cashiered cook, who has crept back to sleep on the kitchen stove, make one wish that Tolstoy had written a more splenetic play.) They also have a tremendous nostalgia for the land, sparked off by the arrival of the peasants. The lovers in particular can hardly wait to get back there and the fatherly valet wants a place kept warm for him.

As a displaced pastoral, the play has resonance if not exactly urgency; and there are good performances below stairs from Brenda Blethyn, Peter Copley, Peter Needham and Greg Hicks, whose Cossack dance is the best thing in the show. It may seem glib to blame Christopher Morahan's production for a general lack of Russian-ness (and I have no idea how he could have overcome the deficiency), but the play does seem to lack a necessary context. One notes yet again that the Olivier stage is a powerful devourer of detail.

* * *

Hoagy, Bix and Wolfgang Beethoven Bunkhaus (King's Head) is Adrian Mitchell's latest spasm of slightly dramatised hero worship. Hoagy is Carmichael of course, Bix is Beiderbecke, and Bunkhaus, we are given to understand, is their Indiana college pal William Monkhaus, a surrealist poet who re-christens Hoagy "Hogwash McCorkle" on sight. He talks that way all the time. An exasperatingly fey creation, he seems to be driving his actor (Murray Melvin) to distraction. Bix is fey in another fashion; white-faced and appealing, in Sylvester McCoy's performance, and naturally doomed. The play seems to be searching for somebody or something to blame for his dissolution, but not even Paul Whiteman (played, along with half a dozen other parts, very well by Roland Oliver) can quite make it as an exploiting villain.

I spent the evening waiting with increasing impatience for the music, which, of course, is lovely: most of Mr Carmichael's best songs are delivered with modest insouciance by John Vine, who actually bears a helpful facial resemblance to the patient young Hoagy, and with measured punch by Nicola McAuliffe, whose "Washboard Blues" is magnificent. The play, to use a suitable Dixieland word, rambles.

* * *

So, in effect if not in structure, does John Byrne's Normal Service (Hampstead), which is set in the design department of a Scottish commercial television company in the fifties. The author has a firmer controlling idea than is immediately apparent. He manages entrances and exits less mechanically than he did in The Slab Boys and he gets a sheaf of solid performances, notably from Garfield Morgan and Richard Wilson. But Mr Frayn's Alphabetic Order has rather spoiled the market for typical day-in-the-office plays, and Mr Byrne's dialogue is not funny enough (not consistently, anyway) nor his characters' passing troubles arresting enough, to make me sit through another one. I am rather sad, remembering the vaudeville of his Writers' Cramp, to see him buckling down to naturalism so soon.

* * *

Frederick Harrison's Subjects for Interrogation (Bush) is a double bill of cautionary parables about the breeding of torturers. The first is pre-packaged, an argument between a young terrorist and a gently mannered sensory depriver who have nothing to say to each other and at great length, and you may as well miss it. Be on time, though, for the second, in which an average unemployed man (most convincingly played by David Hargreaves) is put through the ordeal of putting someone else through one. Three characters--judge, tormentor and victim--make up a scale susceptible to gripping and cunning variations. The play also works, a lot of the time, as a parlour game, which is more than you can say for most plays.
