(She's vocally secure, too: a pleasure to report.) Denis Lawson, appealing but not likeable, wisecracking on the edge of an abyss he senses but won't confront, has Joey sized up; his blank-faced clockwork hoofing is a treat.

So is most of Stuart Hopps's choreography, which picks off a series of tired floor-show routines with venomous enthusiasm. All his seven dancing girls can act, or maybe it's the other way round; anyway they're individuals, especially Susan Kyd's smart cookie and Jane Gurnett's dumb ox. Dodging in and out between episodes, they contribute much to the atmosphere -- mostly hard-boiled but sometimes a bit runny -- as do Jean Hart's lady journalist and Christopher Muncke's club-owner who shrugs through the show with the air of a man who could outperform the lot of them if only he had a number.

The textual history of Pal Joey is of Shakespearean complexity. Mr Walker has collated Good and Bad Quartos (plus his own interpolations), sensibly, barring some solecisms in the lyric-readings. (Details on request.) There is a six-piece band and good glitzy costumes.

records.title: Planetary passions
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Planetary passions

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on `The Life of Galileo' and `Othello.'

IN an interview a couple of years ago Howard Brenton described himself as `an anti-Brechtian, a Left anti-Brechtian.' Now here he is as the translator of Brecht's Life of Galileo (Olivier): a play whose central event, fittingly enough, is a recantation.

There should be joy on the South Bank, if not actually in heaven, since Mr Brenton's version is mostly excellent. Its clarity is in line with the best aspects of the play and of John Dexter's production. This play, with a Renaissance European setting, has an Oriental delight in contemplation beyond anything to be found in Brecht's Eastern fables. Galileo, his disciples and his enemies are united by their passion for thought: by its shape as much as its substance.

I remember Mr Brenton, in his former mood, complaining that `The Caucasian Chalk Circle' didn't connect with the class struggle. I don't know; it features kindly exploited peasants and unpleasant masked landowners, and I'm not sure that `Galileo' gets much further. The play posits that the Inquisition's real objection to the physicist was not that his cosmology contradicted that of the Bible, but that in removing the earth from the centre of the universe it greatly diminished the prestige, celestial and terrestrial, of the princes of the church, and gave the masses ideas above their station.

Sometimes this is believable; a young monk, who almost against his will becomes Galileo's pupil, has a good speech about his parents, happy in their poverty, because they consider it part of a divine order. But once the scene is over you begin to wonder (in line with Brechtian theory but not with the thrust of the play) whether their faith would be much affected either way by the position of the planets. Tom Stoppard is not a playwright one would ordinarily compare with Brecht, but this play resembles `Jumpers' in overrating the influence of astronomy on personal conduct.

For the most part Brecht keeps the people offstage; when they do arrive they celebrate Galileo's ideas in a carnival scene which has rather more impact as spectacle (though it's oddly underdone in this production) than as argument. Mr Brenton suggests that Galileo's smuggled truths are a metaphor for Communism in our day. You can just as well equate them, if you start to think that way, with any other minority creed: with Christianity in Russia, for example. Actually, in the sharp early scene where Galileo debates with the orthodox thinkers, the traditionalists in their eloquent appeal to the beautiful symmetry of their received ideas sound more like Marxists than Galileo ever does.

Our hero is in fact transcendently selfish; that is what unifies his character and the play. In the last scene Brecht, disturbed by the atom bomb, gives him a social conscience: `I believe the only aim of science is to relieve the toil of human existence.' That's a noble aim, but it is as unlikely to inspire a great scientist as a great artist. It hardly squares with the Galileo whose opinion of other people is governed solely by whether they help or impede his work. Knowledge (as Brecht's own pupil Friedrich Durrenmatt was to point out in `The Physicists') is a neutral, therefore dangerous, force; Brecht wants to tame and moralise it. As usual he evades tragedy.

The play lives as a clean piece of story-telling, and as a celebration of genius. Mr Dexter's production, in which even Galileo's legs-akimbo stance at his wash-basin looks like a geometrical figure, does full justice to the first but little to the second. Michael Gambon, who plays the lead, is an actor of great skill and subtlety who excels in depicting the character's ageing process, and in elucidating his thoughts. But he has to try hard (in plain terms, to shout) in order to convey energy and the returns rapidly diminish. (I will muzzle the unworthy suspicion that Brecht protested so much about Galileo's sensuality because he couldn't actually dramatise it.)

Selina Cadell meticulously traces the development of Galileo's daughter from ingenue to jailer, but much of the acting is disappointing. On the principle of chastising the best-loved, let me pick on Simon Callow and Stephen Moore. Mr Callow plays the peasant monk as an urban mooncalf. Mr Moore negates his imaginative casting as an Inquisitor of Shavian gentleness by utilising his familiar spaced-out timing to get Ayckbournian laughs.

* * *

In Othello (Aldwych) Cassio's rhetorical wish that Jove might watch over the Moor is incongruously turned into a formal prayer. That is the only gaffe I could discover in Ronald Eyre's superbly lucid, detailed, eloquent and moving production. Relationships are tangible; the outbreaks of violence have the shock of inevitability; movements are always revealing. Othello, entering the Senate, makes straight for the military briefing table.

Some of the deepest obscenities of his degradation escape Donald Sinden, but he brilliantly captures the boyish innocence and uncorks a fine passion. Burnishing his voice, he reveals it as an instrument of unsuspected virtuosity; his clubman's warmth has given way to a suave authority that can turn `the goodness of the night upon you' into a genuine benison, disturbing in its confidence.

While his assurance cracks, that of Bob Peck's Iago hardens; he ends as a squatting statue of satisfied malevolence. The solidity of the character merges with that of the actor who discovers new conversational riches in every line without ever veering from his course. What tortures Othello most is Iago's conscientious matter-of-factness about Desdemona's infidelity; Mr Peck worries him into madness. These two performances, in opposed but complementary modes, are not only a magnificently interdependent Othello and Iago but golden examples of the strengths of contemporary verse-acting.

* * *

Writer's Cramp--which to these southern ears is John Byrne's most congenial play--has resurfaced at Hampstead, enriched all round. A prologue comments on the growing fame of F. S. McDade, Scots bookman and no-hoper, since this tribute was first unveiled three Edinburgh Festivals ago. Mr Byrne, with an eye as sharp as his ear for risible detail, has himself designed a McDade Memorial Corner, fit for the most painful of illustrated literary lecturettes. The cast of three has reassembled, with John Bett's narrator even more of a Muggeridge, discoursing in a silky wheeze that makes every word of praise come out as a disparagement.

Mr Bett doubles as McDade's flighty mother, sublimely. Alex Norton reads the poems, in tones of surprised disgust, and also plays a uniquely unnerving prison warder impinging on one of our hero's frequent darkest hours. F.S. himself, going from school to death-bed without so much as a change of blazer or moustache, is Bill Paterson, as a virtuoso blend of swaggerer and mendicant.

* * *

A full-stage revival of Elmer Rice's The Adding Machine, which in 1923 domesticated expressionism to the American marital front, would probably expose the play unkindly. The pocket production at the Gate, Notting Hill, allows us to take it as an elegant little joke, with enjoyable soliloquies for the nagging Mrs Zero and for her biddable spouse who turns murderer when automation pushes him off his counting-house stool. He goes to heaven, where he is revealed (and reviled) as the essence of wage-slave. He also meets another murderer, endearingly done by Mike Burnside, a plump and dignified comedian, like a louder Richard Griffiths.

records.title: From Titus to Virginia
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
From Titus to Virginia

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN reports on a recent visit to the Stratford Festival, Ontario, whose company will be visiting London later this year.

I CAME to Canada, as I generally do, via New York, where the temperature was 10 intolerable degrees higher than it was in Stratford, Ontario. America, though, pursued me: the surrounding conversation suggested that the Stratford Shakespeare Festival gets much of its clientele from south of the border.

Brows were furrowed over Pelican editions of the coming evening's play, which happened to be 'Titus Andronicus.' 'Titus has cut his hand off. Can someone tell me why?' 'It's an act of atonement,' suggested someone not quite accurately. I wondered what they would make of the cannibal feast that closed the show. The conscientious continued to bone up, glancing enviously around as friends wandered away in search of ice cream.

The American connection does much for the alertness of Stratford's audience: also, of course, for its box office. In other ways, it saps Canada's theatre. The best Canadian talent gets lured to Broadway or Hollywood, even occasionally to London. (I don't know what can be done about this: natives can hardly be forbidden to leave the country. The alternative strategy, favoured by protectionists, of stopping other actors from coming in seems to me counter-productive.)

This is the Englishman Robin Phillips's sixth season as Stratford's director; the Festival Theatre's platform stage retains its magic, and he has unequalled ability to make it swirl. He has more bodies at his beck than any director could find in Britain, outside an opera house, and he pours them onto the stage. Maybe it was unfortunate that both his Shakespearean productions on offer during my stay were comedies, 'Twelfth Night' and 'Much Ado About Nothing' -- in which charm and movement, though certainly secured, seemed to have become ends in themselves. In 'Twelfth Night' the only moments of real resonance came when Stratford's doyen, William Hutt (who has been with the company since its inception in 1953), burst gravely into song as Feste, making -- as the finest theatre always does -- an eternal moment out of the evanescent.

In 'Much Ado' Mr Phillips has oddly done one of his crowd numbers on the church scene: a couple of dozen people seem to be in on the secret of Hero's 'death,' and it is inconceivable that not one of them would have blabbed. But in general this is a most solid production, blessed with foresight: even an initially unfunny Dogberry turns out to be holding himself in readiness for the revelation that he is an ass. The imported stars, as in previous seasons, are Brian Bedford and Maggie Smith; and they complement each other well. Mr Bedford's Benedick is firmly and stolidly a soldier (as his Malvolio is firmly and modestly a steward); he provides the anchorage and Miss Smith the pyrotechnics. Her Beatrice is a woman blessed with wit and passion and almost afraid of her own endowments -- in fact, a classic Maggie Smith performance. Stratford seems to have honed both her skills and her insecurities -- each perfectly timed riposte is prefaced by an unnecessary (and anachronistic) interjection: 'Well,' 'Do you know?', and 'I mean.' Maybe she doesn't know she is doing it: her talent is what makes her mannerisms so irritating. Her gift for self-deprecation -- dispatching her own wisecracks to the ground with a flick of the wrist -- permeates 'Virginia,' the festival's most-trumpeted new play. It happens to be dead wrong for the ineffable Virginia Woolf, who can never have seen a joke against herself in the whole of her life, but it saves Edna O'Brien's piece from complete inertia.

This is a play about sensitive literary people with sensitive literary problems acted out in sensitive literary writing against sensitive literary music. The three characters -- Virginia, husband Leonard and intrusive V. Sackville-West -- are grouped in Mr Phillips's production like ghosts from Harold Pinter's 'Old Times.' One expected better from this author and this director, if not, to be honest, from this subject.

Another three-hander, 'Bosoms and Neglect' (hot from failure in New York), is the work of America's most frustrating playwright, John Guare; frustrating because his wit and his perceptions hardly ever cohere. Here are an octogenarian woman, trying to deny that she has breast-cancer, her bookworm son, and his new-found lady-love, who, like him, is deeply into literature and deeper into analysis. Many of Mr Guare's sallies are funny, but as they pile up they group themselves into variants of the New York psychiatrist joke or -- with the old lady at the other end of play -- of the idea of salty old age, eccentric but indomitable. Each has been done to death, though the second at least gives the cue for a knock-down performance from Kate Reid.

So back to Shakespeare and to Mr Bedford's production of 'Titus,' simple but powerful, with everyone in the right place at the right time, and the play actually seeming to have something to do with Imperial Rome. Mr Hutt marks time during Titus's authoritarian phase, but in the onset and then the retreat of madness, with every line an ironic shaft, he is very fine. Other performances run the gamut -- too common at Stratford -- from vigorous-anonymous through serviceable-dutiful to ambitious-atrocious.

Mr Phillips's new production of 'King Lear,' with Peter Ustinov had yet to open when I left. It will, however, be seen later this year in London at the Haymarket. Next year at Stratford the power structure changes; Mr Phillips remains in command, but he will now have a phalanx of associate directors including Len Cariou, the Canadian actor who was Broadway's Sweeney Todd, and English-born Pam Brighton, who has recently scored a great success with her own conflated version of the 'Henry VI' plays.

records.title: Lucifer on a fork-lift truck
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: A New Way to Pay Old Debts
records.body:
Lucifer on a fork-lift truck

EDINBURGH FESTIVAL 1980

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the National Theatre's 'Passion' at the Assembly Hall.

THE pews have been removed from the Assembly Hall, and the ground-level is one great playing-space, where the audience, and even the actors, can disport themselves.

Ira Gershwin said it forty-odd years ago:

Each girl and boy alike,
Sharing joy alike,
Feels that Passion'll
Soon be National.

Here is the National Theatre production of The Passion, drawn from the York Mystery Cycle, and familiar from three years' appearances at the Cottesloe, now fitted out with a first part of equal length. This has been labelled Creation to Nativity, though, in the abrupt and rather frustrating manner of the Mysteries themselves, it gives up the Old Testament narrative halfway through Genesis and jumps straight on to the Annunciation.

Jesus's story takes up the last play-and-a-half, but in this version it has little contact with what has gone before. We are given a human drama issuing in a cry of despair. There is no resurrection, no judgment; only a curt statement of belief delivered by Brian Glover in a miner's helmet, whose beaming lamp provides the most original lighting effect in contemporary theatre.

But this moment hardly returns us to the beginnings of the first play, where Mr Glover is God: a businesslike deity as he goes about creating everything, glimpsed through a warming forest of lanterns somewhere up among the rafters of the Assembly Hall. In an even finer burst of visual inventiveness Lucifer (Jack Shepherd--the medieval guilds of glovers and shepherds would be proud to see their descendants carrying on their traditions in such surroundings) delivers his doomed challenge from a red plush armchair, perched halfway up a forklift truck. Perdition is a rapid descent into a smoke-filled tub, which is then whirled fiercely around the hall like an outsize dodgem car.

Such toys as these are the modern equivalent of the pageant-wagons on which the plays were originally performed (the medieval theatre was machine-mad, far closer in spirit to Drury Lane than to the Warehouse) and Bill Bryden's production resembles the RSC's The Greeks in being an all-purpose raid on whatever aspects of the ancient tradition may be made to serve a modern turn. It is unprincipled in all respects save the most important, that of telling the story. The means vary, even the promenading audience perform a different function in each half. In the first play they are employed as witnesses of the performance, in the second of the events themselves.

The new piece is in fact a patchwork, episodic where its sequel is centrifugal. Humanity only breaks in with Dave Hill's Joseph, honestly aghast at the news of his wife's pregnancy. It is maintained in the famous episode, interpolated from the Wakefield Cycle, of Mak the sheep-stealer. (Somebody should write a ballad of Mak the crook.) This astonishing playlet, with its story of a sheep hopefully passed off as a newborn child ("What the devil is this, he has a long snout") parodies the Nativity as a prelude to celebrating it.

Its equivalent in the second half is the scene of the grimly practical torturers at the Crucifixion, a triumph of unselfconscious sophistication. The Assembly Hall acoustics are not too kind to extended conversation-pieces like these, but actors with tirades--notably Mr Hill's John the Baptist and Mr Shepherd's Judas, registering resentment in alliteration--rise splendidly above them while the Albion Band contribute at least two smashing numbers.

Another smashing number begins the Canadian production, Billy Bishop Goes to War (Moray House Gymnasium): a quietly mocking lament, with simple but artful rhymes for the generation who went off to die in World War One. It is sung by the complete cast, which is to say Eric Peterson and John Gray; Mr Gray also plays the piano and wrote the show. He comes up subsequently with nothing as good. This story of Canada's most productive (or destructive) air-ace masters all the ironies about the simultaneous horror and exhilaration of combat and the patronising attitude of the British establishment towards its colonial cannon-fodder, but it does little more than lay them efficiently out. Mr Peterson plays all the parts well.

I might have enjoyed it more had I not visited the Traverse that afternoon to see Barry Collins's The Iceman, another monologue about a survivor of the same war with scars left this time by class rather than race, and seeking to erase them or himself by undertaking a solo ascent of Everest. Chris Ettridge, the actor here, does nothing wrong, and neither, in strict literary terms, does Mr Collins. But theatrically it is a deadening exercise. A one-character play with a subtext is, I suppose, possible, but in practice we have to believe what the character says. There is no undercutting, no conflict. We know the man has weaknesses all right, but only because he tells us.

I began to yearn, after these two shows, for the spectacle of a couple of actors talking to each other. The Tarnished Phoenix (St Cecilia's Hall) offered two actors, side by side reading--Ian McKellen as D. H. Lawrence and Sheila Allen as Frieda. Mr McKellen can give me enormous pleasure when immersed in a character or when he is simply being himself--as here in a few carefully artless sentences of welcome--but he was mostly betwixt and between: compelling admiration when turning the ending of "Snake" ("I have something to expiate: a pettiness") into a cadenza of disgust, but defusing Lawrence's intolerably censorious outbursts against people assuredly no worse than himself with a self-deprecation completely alien to them. Miss Allen got closer to the iron self-righteousness in "How beastly the bourgeois," though some of her other selections were, at the first performance, less assured (she was deputising at short notice for Janet Suzman).

The fringe are offering two Jacobean rarities, Massinger's A New Way to Pay Old Debts (the Priory Theatre Company) and Middleton and Dekker's The Roaring Girl (Cambridge University Mummers). The amateurs do far better than the professionals, and this only partly because they have the richer play. Massinger's piece, for centuries a stage and schoolroom classic, has fallen into disuse and it does emerge here as thinly as disconcerting to realise that the legendary extortioner-villain, Sir Giles Overreach, never stands a chance of grinding anyone's face in dust: they're all on to him from the start of Act One. The production is inspiringly stylised; because his name merely denotes his job: he's a watchman.

The Cambridge Players have correctly deduced that characters with allegorical monikers (as it might be, Dapper or Trapdoor) had better be played as real people. This they do, with assurance in a pleasing variety of styles: it is possible to make a book on which of these players is bound for the Half Moon, which for the Olivier, and which for the issue desk of the nearest public library.

records.title: Panache from Poland
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Panache from Poland

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'official' and fringe theatre.

THE Polish painter-director Tadeusz Kantor has been back in Edinburgh, this time at the Moray House Gymnasium.

The approach to the audience is appropriately strenuous. There are no intervals, and a notice in the foyer proclaims that no late-comers will be admitted. This might be admirable if it were being done for the sake of the spectators. Actually the people being considered are the performers, so the edict counts as self-indulgence. More specifically it is an attempt to intimidate us into feeling privileged to be there.

Kantor's Wielopole Wielopole does in fact come off as something special. It is presented to us an evocation of the director's own childhood; and he himself is on stage throughout--the very picture of the Central European genius in shiny black suit and open-neck white shirt--to keep his memories in order. Mostly they revolve around the army and the church. Kantor's uncle is recalled as the priest of the village that gives the play its title, his father as one of a group of conscripts who for a long time merely stand and crouch ominously in a corner. They might be papier-mache: when they spring into life they are deeply alarming--and remain so for the rest of the action.

The priest seems to be blessing and encouraging the soldiers as they go to fight. When, later on, they turn on him and--all seven of them--bayonet him, this is something of a judgment and rather more of a moral and political truth. (They that live by the sword, etc.) We see uncle and father marching happily side by side, one with his weapons, the other with his Cross. The Cross, which is huge, later becomes a more oppressive burden. The priest staggers under it, like Christ en route to Calvary. But round and round with it he goes and it comes to dominate the play.

Crucifixion is certainly an apt enough image for twentieth-century Poland. All the same, the Catholic iconography had me confused, for I had always imagined Kantor to be Jewish: and confusion was compounded when one of the players (Kantor's wife in fact) appeared as a rabbi.

Had I understood the dialogue (one forgets that Kantor uses words, but he does), I might have been able to fit the pieces together. As it is I have to report a spectacle of undoubted panache and authority, but repetitive. The same pictures keep revolving through the evening at increasing speed. I don't know whether this is intended to illustrate the frenzied workings of memory or simply to pulverise the audience. Very loud music suggests the latter.

Of course if you really want to direct your actors while they are actually at it, you become a puppeteer. At the National Arts Centre in Ottawa they apparently specialise in marionette versions of nineteenth-century classics. The obvious candidate would be A Doll's House, but they have brought us Buchner's Woyzeck and Strindberg's A Dream Play.

The treatment of Woyzeck is elaborately structured to emphasise the elements of social and military exploitation. Soldiers enter and are barked at in German. When they have been thoroughly cowed, they are issued with puppets whom they have to control. Sitting above are a quartet of nobs (3m, 1f) who control them, announcing the scenes and reading the dialogue. Meanwhile the puppets oppress one another, with Woyzeck himself, a piteous sight with his bald lantern head and skeletal features, at the bottom of the heap.

Only the doll playing Marie seems miscast, making her a Hollywood vamp, and the execution is immaculate: the hero being a barber, there is plenty of opportunity for fancy handwork. But a drama which deals with the hounding of a man till he becomes a thing loses some of its impetus if he is a thing to start with.

In Le Songe (the Strindberg is done in French) all is sedate and beautifully modulated, and the piece loses its only interest--its phantasmagoria of changing scenes. It is also slow. But dreams are fast: ask Mr Kantor. The text is read by a series of actors, each in turn imitating the god Indra, whose daughter, on the main stage below, descends to earth to find that man is unhappy and has to do the washing-up. That, mercilessly reiterated, is Strindberg's message: one that can still find takers. Le Songe is ended, but la maladie lingers on.

After all this I looked forward to the flesh, bone and overflow of Henry IV, Parts 1 and 2 (Daniel Stewart's and Melville College). This RSC touring production, directed by Bill Alexander, captures a good measure of them. Alfred Marks's Falstaff gains in assurance all the way. The more complicated verbal architecture defeats him, but he is a wizard with one-liners, with impatient eye-rollings, with audience contact, and with comic situations: the ensemble scenes in Eastcheap build firmly outwards from him.

He has two striking female team-mates, though their styles hardly blend. Barbara Jefford's Quickly is an elaborate, textually observant assemblage of optimistically genteel vowels: Patti Love's Doll is jaggedly at odds with the rhythm, but her first drunken entrance is magnificent. Among the straights, Stuart Wilson's Hotspur (apart from looking and sounding like Richard III) has the same kind of problems as Mr Marks: Hotspur can hardly stop talking, and it sometimes seems that Mr Wilson can hardly start. But he develops great charm, especially in the scenes with Juliet Stevenson as his wife (this must have been how the marriage in The Taming of the Shrew turned out), and the baiting of Glendower can scarcely have been better done.

Mr Alexander seems, for an RSC cadet, uncommonly alive to comic nuance, and he lets the plays' two worlds (epitomised in a set composed of banners and barrels) unobtrusively illuminate each other. The thieves "make the commonwealth their boots" and so do the rebels, stomping all over a map of England. The Welsh foxiness of Bernard Lloyd's Henry recalls Emrys James's five years ago, but is less showy and allows the king nobility as well: David Rintoul's Hal is resonant but hollow. In general, company experience tells: as in John Burgess's politic Northumberland doubled with a properly actorish Pistol, and in David Shaw-Parker's string of roles, culminating in a Justice Silence who looks, in his modified balaclava, like a pantomime mole and blinks like one too.

One-man shows better be funny. Three on the fringe are: (1) Three Men in a Boat (at Buster Brown's). Jeremy Nicholas beautifully times the infallible jokes and also manages to place and accommodate the passages of fatuous moralising without patronising them. (2) The Third Nam (Heriot-Watt Theatre). In this play, credited to Bill Stair, Tony Robinson is a prodigy of naturalness as a company manager left to carry the show alone, and also conveys numerous misgivings about the spare-part section of humanity that he embodies. (3) Here's a Funny Thing (Viewforth Centre). John Bardon impersonates Max Miller to, apart from a slight lack of expansiveness, the life. The patter works and Mr Bardon stills the house with unmarked poignancy in the biographical section.

The Traverse, with money scarce, offers fewer plays than formerly and, as usual, quality slips with quantity. John Anderson's Snapshots is Forties-Fifties Americana, growing-up-in-New-York division, the hero too insubstantial to give it point. Song and dance erupt too late. There are some entertaining scenes and matching performances from Tucker McGuire and Ramsay Williams as crabbed age, Robin Pappas as youth, Janene Possell somewhere in between and Lou Hirsch all over.

Wielopole Wielopole can be seen at the Riverside Studios, Hammersmith, from 3-14 September.

records.title: Double toil and trouble
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Pack Up All Your Cares And Woe
records.body:
Double toil and trouble

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London, Sheffield, Glasgow and Edinburgh.

PETER O'TOOLE has not acted a major Shakespearean role for 17 years. Bryan Forbes has not directed in the theatre before. Macbeth (Old Vic) is a very difficult play. So much for excuses.

The designer is new as well, though his set looks decidedly old: standard-issue rostra approached by what you might call the general run of steps, the only playful variant being the daunting height of the bottom rung, on which somebody is going to come to grief before the end of the season. Surveying this structure, and noting too the grubby William the Conqueror costumes, I settled down nostalgically to a one-foot-up, one-foot-down evening. Expectations were dashed, however, as Mr Forbes's production began to take on a quite untraditional identity of its own.

He stretches, for starters, one of Shakespeare's briefest plays to more than three hours' playing time. Built up permanent sets are meant at least to permit of unbroken transitions from scene to scene. Here there are constant blackouts, filled with optimistically spooky music, and lifting to reveal a stage on which, puzzlingly, almost nothing has changed. Occasionally a few dead bodies will have disentangled themselves from the picturesque poses in which they have been cluttering up the place; and the prospect may be altered by the loss or gain of a stool.

A Cross is momentarily suspended, to show that someone has noticed the play's Christian imagery, though this perceptiveness does not extend to the English scene; Malcolm and Macduff conduct their heart-searchings beneath a fully-manned gibbet. This is the single most curious stroke of the evening, though the presentation of the witches as one of the sexier sister acts on the blasted-heath circuit runs it close.

A more defensible idea, made risible by the shaky tone of the production generally, is the voluminous bloodiness of Macbeth's hands, and subsequently of Banquo's ghost. Either sight would be enough to send the protagonist into a coma. Unfortunately Mr O'Toole has been in this state from the outset, so he has nowhere to go. Chances are he loves the play, but his performance suggests that he is taking some kind of personal revenge on it, methodically draining it of sense and variety. His last line comes out as 'And damned be him that first cries hold e-nough'; and though the pounding beat may suit Macbeth in extremis, he has given much the same emphasis to all the words he has encountered on the way.

Eccentric rhythms reminiscent of Ralph Richardson are relayed to us in the fretful tones of Malcolm Muggeridge, with a few intimations of the self-disgust found in the role by Ian McKellen. Mr O'Toole's conception seems to be that of a man somnambulant with guilt from the first, waking only to occasional extremes of laughing sadism or cringing terror. These are effective but they are very occasional. They are belied too by his physical glamour, which is unchanging.

Nobody else in the cast seems able to get through to him. They try various methods. Frances Tomelty's Lady Macbeth -- almost a Fourth Witch -- goes for sex, but elicits hardly a twitch in return. Brian Blessed's roaring Banquo slaps his noble partner's back a great deal. All, reacting to the rhetorical vacuum at the centre, try helplessly to be conversational; the only possible reply to poor Lennox's aggrieved 'Our chimneys were blown down' would be 'Well fancy that.'

Dudley Sutton's Macduff is a bit wild; when Macbeth's very convincing severed head was brought on at the end it looked so convincing one feared that, somewhere in the wings, Mr Sutton had lost control. Even as it was, Murphy's Law ran riot on the first night; lines were muffed and furniture bumped into. In the shambles John Tordoff's businesslike Third Murderer survived best.

* * *

The Macbeth set might almost have done for Alan Ayckbourn's Taking Steps (Lyric), which takes place on various levels of a decaying mansion. Here the ascents and descents are all mimed within Michael Rudman's production -- startling lack of finesse. This, like much else in the play, must have worked much better in-the-round, at Mr Ayckbourn's own unpretentious theatre in Scarborough. The play is a mixture of the light and dark Ayckbourn, the light farcically predominating until the end, when we are left, too abruptly, to consider how unhappy all the characters are.

One of them is, in his own words, 'a very successful man,' who accordingly wants to live 'in a very big house.' Dinsdale Landen plays him heavy handedly, though he gets drunk with some panache. His wife, whom he claims (probably correctly) to have saved from a deeply undistinguished career as a dancer, cannot decide whether or not to leave him. Nicola Pagett, in unaccustomed waters, begins very brightly, but the role gives out on her.

The supports have better chances: Paul Chapman a stylishly doleful chorus as a man born to be deserted, and Michael Maloney winning hearts as a solicitor who has difficulty finishing his sentences. He, with a girl of similar temperament, provides a fairly touching sub-plot, but the theme -- of manipulation and resistance thereto -- emerges unhelpfully late.

There is a good quota of laughs: as a writer of comic dialogue Mr Ayckbourn just keeps improving. But mechanically he is way off form: his developments are foreseeable without being inevitable. The play is dedicated to Ben Travers (and Mr Landen draws on his own performance in Plunder), but the Travers airiness has less and less in common with the cracking suburbia which Mr Ayckbourn's characters, waving and drowning, nowadays inhabit.

* * *

Pack Up All Your Cares And Woe (King's Head) is cabaret rather than theatre, and I'm not complaining. Bertice Reading, the salvation of Only In America, overflows the stage, her songs and her much-vaunted collection of outrageously-fringed dresses. She belongs with Ethel Waters and Pearl Bailey among the very best singer-comediennes. She is one of the few major black performers who do not seem to be employed in The Wiz (Crucible, Sheffield), the Harlem version of The Wizard of Oz, which I greatly enjoyed in New York for its spirit, its exuberant performance and its imaginative staging.

Not enough of this remains. Peter James's production has some impressive mechanical effects, but it never fills the scene. Gillian Gregory's choreography consists largely of people stepping in and out of holes in the stage. Much of the self-kidding quality of William F. Brown's script survives, though you sometimes have to listen hard for it.

We are thrown back too much on the story (which was always a good one, but is not the point of this particular exercise) and on Charlie Smalls's score which, despite a few soothing or spirited numbers, is desperately uninventive. This show too boasts glamorous witches: Debra Bishop's Addaperle (a good one) is enjoyably mischievous, and also shares the vocal honours with Celena Duncan's Dorothy and with Peter Straker's rocking falsetto in the title role.

Les Saxon rattles impressively as the Tinman, and Derek Griffiths as the scarecrow and Oscar James (though he is apparently not a singer) as the Cowardly Lion have charm. It is difficult too to resist a show in which the wicked witch, having listed her enemies, is told by one of her henchmen (a signifying monkey), 'you don't get on with anyone.' Suckers for anthropomorphic humour will enjoy themselves, but the going is too often slow.

* * *

Phillip Prowse of the Glasgow Citizens has designed one of his most ravishing sets yet for Goldoni's The Battlefield, a white cathedral transformed into a heap of martial rubble. This is a comedy more about being fair in war than in love. The visuals give it abstract impressiveness, but the piece never really gets out from under. It is heavily played, whether the immediate objective be laughs or shudders, though Gordon Hammersley as a noble cripple reaches both goals without too much obtrusive effort.

Glasgow is only a short hop from Edinburgh, from which a brief final thought on the Festival Fringe -- it is one of the last strongholds of bookish theatre. Richard Crane's trophied Vanity, an exercise in verse forms, is very literary. Even such a show as Lumiere and Son's Circus Lumiere is weighed down with words, the acts being linked with a ponderously arch commentary. The turns themselves comment on traditional routines, mostly by sending them up. The mind-reading act is hilarious. This Circus works out of a blue tent; if it appears on your horizon it is worth entering.

records.title: The trouble with Timon
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The trouble with Timon

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Stratford-on-Avon and London.

THE hero of Timon of Athens (Other Place, Stratford-on-Avon) may be said to come in three sizes.

First, he is the feted spendthrift, inviting all Athens to dinner, and sending every man home with a ruinously expensive present: the willing patron of every hack artist who knows how to turn a dedication. When his friends fail him, some dunning him for debts he has no means of paying and the others refusing to help tide him over, he becomes for a brief space an active avenger; though his revenge is mild by Jacobean standards--consisting as it does of throwing one final party in which the entire bill of fare is lukewarm water, served directly in the visitors' faces--it is set off by yards of vituperative rhetoric.

Apparently finding words more satisfying than action, Timon settles for them in the last long section of the play. Taking up residence in the wilderness, he looks for roots and finds gold. Word spreads and all his former acquaintances come to see him. They are told, at glittering length, to get stuffed. Nothing much actually happens, except that an army marches on Athens but decides at the last moment not to sack it, and that Timon himself abruptly dies.

All the action of the play is concentrated in its first half: most of the recognisable humanity as well. Timon's banquets, the ebb and flow of creditors in his halls, the chat of servants deploring the avaricious ways of their masters, bustle with life. This play, presumably written in the wake of Antony and Cleopatra and Coriolanus, has the same fearsome naturalistic energy contained within the disciplining form of verse. A technical advance on the overflowing prose of equivalent scenes in Henry IV, it is extraordinarily hard to bring off in the theatre. Either the form is softened or the content leaks away; we are left with senseless spectacle or (likelier nowadays) the husk of the dialogue, all moral but no meaning.

Ron Daniels's studio production, lacking space and manpower, can hardly give us more than a diagram; with this year's underweight (or at least underexperienced) Stratford company, he misses out on much of the verbal colouring as well. Character contrasts are flattened out; the professional cynic Apemantus (deftly done by John Carlisle) emerges as a disinterested commentator rather than as a special form of parasite with an axe of his own to grind. When Timon goes broke the atmosphere sharpens; his slippery friends are well contrasted, the scenes in which each in turn bows out of his obligations coming over as ironic comedy. An abacus, worked by each financier in turn, dominates the stage.

The final feast (I almost called it the last supper--a reference which directors have employed in other plays with less justification, but which Mr Daniels avoids) takes the pressure up further, and--against all the rules, since they merely repeat the same theme over and over--the wilderness scenes prove very fine.

They are played against a background of fishing-nets and jetties; Timon says that he will make his grave by the sea, and having spoken his last words, two scenes before the final curtain, he pulls a net over his head and, for the remainder of the play, just sits there. It is an oddly satisfying finish, lending shape and definition to a play that could peter out and fizzle. Richard Pasco gives it the authentic accent of finality.

Mr Pasco is a sympathetic actor and I would have expected him to be happiest in the hospitable early scenes--where, in fact, he misses the hectic size of Timon's bounty. But he has the measure, if not quite the pulse, of the avenging Timon, and he discovers not only force but variety in the last phase.

He even finds enjoyment: this Timon gets a kick out of painting his face and discomfiting his second wave of flatterers. And he preserves a thread to the earlier scenes by suggesting that Timon is a disappointed idealist. His credo--"I am Misanthropos and hate mankind"--is delivered with his eyes rolled towards Heaven: "What wouldst thou do with the world?" is a genuine helpless question.

He cannot, though, actually explain the part or the play. We never get an insight into Timon's mind until his mind has begun to go, never discover what fuelled his early recklessness. Hence the unending debates as to whether the play is satiric comedy or tragedy; it changes gear halfway. We look first at the hero, then with him, and the two viewpoints are never reconciled.

Clearly Shakespeare enjoyed pouring out misanthropy, and we can enjoy listening to it, but it is no wonder the play comes to a dead stop. Every one of Timon's themes is more roundly and inclusively treated elsewhere: ingratitude in King Lear, superhuman generosity in Antony and Cleopatra, exile in Coriolanus. Even Timon's sexual disillusion (directed at a couple of courtesans, presented here with generous decolletage) merely scratches the itch of Troilus and Cressida.

* * *

Lancelot and Guinevere (Old Vic) comes over as the Timothy West show. Mr West plays Malory, apparently thrown into prison just after finishing Morte d'Arthur, and intent on revising the last chapters which he proceeds to read aloud from a script whose aspect suggests that Caxton's printing methods were more advanced than we have thought.

This Malory is a man who knows he has hold of a good story, but who cannot reconcile its lofty ideals with his own. Sometimes this leads him into laments on the decline of contemporary morality (Malory is thought to have been imprisoned for rape), more often into mockery of his work's absurdity. Comic details are either emphasised or invented. 'It was on a Monday,' says Mr West at his most urbane of some heroic moment, and the irrelevance of it tickles greatly. So, of course, does the invariable lucidity of his delivery; only a final agonised cry at Arthur's death cannot be fitted in.

He's all right though; he has a character. The rest of the cast, first seen lying on the floor, pick themselves up to become things in his dream, acting out his story as if it were some medieval equivalent of Simon Says. When Malory says Guinevere screamed, Guinevere screams; when he says Mordred laughed, Mordred has a go. The sound and lighting effects behave in the same way, and it gets a bit repetitive.

The trouble is this version (adaptor Gordon Honeycombe, director Martin Jenkins) never allows them separate identities; it sticks to the original and Malory was no dramatist--not even a novelist. Maureen O'Brien's Guinevere comes over as a teaser of inordinate primness, Bryan Marshall's Lancelot as a lump, David Sumner's Arthur as a cipher. The casting of Bernard Bresslaw as an abductor suggests that the drift towards comic relief was premeditated, the behaviour of the Old Vic lighting on the second night that the Macbeth curse is not yet lifted.

* * *

Roger McGough's Life-Swappers (Roundhouse), in which a couple of couples are rather literally on the H. G. Wells notion that if you don't like your life you can change it, is a collection of amiable jokes that eventually capitulates to whimsy. Some good actors--Christopher Ryan and Peter Dennis, especially--help to fight it off, but they are also combating an unconscionably slow production.

records.title: The case for dirty hands
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The case for dirty hands

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Exeter.

IT is possible at Lillian Hellman's Watch on the Rhine (Lyttelton) to appreciate the impact it had on its audiences in 1941.

The play is an arraignment of American isolationism. It addresses itself to, and concerns itself with, the well-heeled. A Washington widow, bright and liberal, and her middle-aged son, similar, are visited by the daughter of the family and her husband, a German who has spent the previous seven years as an anti-Nazi agent.

He hears that three of his comrades have been captured, and prepares to return in order to obtain their release by bribing the guards. ("It has been done before.") First, though, he has to deal with another emigre, a Romanian count who has discovered his identity and is blackmailing him. He kills his man; and his in-laws, confronted by the deed, realise its necessity and become accessories to it.

The point is not that they have learned the truth about the nature of Fascism--they already knew it--but that they have discovered how to fight it. The implication is that America can afford to dirty its hands a little. ("I'm not put together with flour paste," says mother to son. "And neither are you--I am happy to learn.")

Three cheers for that old New England stock. For the Washington drawing-room where the action happens could be in any comfortable cultured Yankee city. For 20 years it was the scene of every American play that was neither broad farce nor grinding expose. Even now, as it approaches dilapidation, Edward Albee can call it home. It is the ground on which middlebrow Americans expected to see issues debated, wisecracks exchanged, marriages saved or sundered. Miss Hellman obliges on all these counts. In doing so she hit her audience where it lived, or at least where it would like to have lived, but she also risked becoming a slave of the mechanism she employed.

That, in fact, is what happens. The play centres on Jessica the chatelaine and we are shown her relations with her butler, with her lady companion and with the memory of her worshipped husband. Some of this may be necessary to clue us into the character and milieu, but it threatens to run off with the play--or rather to lumber off with it; since these are not really the things on her mind, Miss Hellman cannot invest them with much urgency.

The blackmailer's marital problems likewise appear as a heavy-handed method of letting us know that he is a cad. We are kept waiting a long time for the exciting, and perfectly valid, melodrama that is Miss Hellman's proper medium. For us too there is the knowledge that, though she was doubtless more aware than most people, she either didn't know the half or wasn't telling. It is impossible to believe that captured resisters, high on the Nazi wanted lists, could be rescued, or that they would be left alive long enough for anyone to try. The blandness the author castigates has invaded her play.

The acting in Mike Ockrent's production is mostly excellent. Peggy Ashcroft times her characterisation immaculately; it is not complete until she has spoken her last dismissively determined line, whose ingredients are salt, ice and perfect breeding. John Quayle, gangling over her, troubled but confident, is the shy bookman to the quietly philandering life. Of the intruders, Susan Engel's black-avised calm modulates beautifully into caring warmth, while David Burke is a shambling marvel of a hero.

* * *

Rodgers and Hammerstein's Oklahoma (Palace), which first reached Broadway two years later, is a completer work. The songs may not carry the story--it is light enough to need no help beyond the dialogue's--but they are responsible for mood and colour, for something of character, and (in the title song and "The Farmer and the Cowman") for the theme: the opening-up of the West.

It is undeniably odd (and nothing to do with accents) to hear British performers declare quite so ringingly and repeatedly that the land they belong to is grand; it's like pillaging a national anthem. But when these performers hurl their bodies through the air in the second act barn-dance they are magnificent. I don't remember this exhilaration from last year's Leicester opening; all the dancing in fact has improved beyond recognition. The dream ballet has gained in force and point; the ensemble of aspiring flirts in "Many a New Day" is enchanting; everyone acts and reacts fit to bust.

The songs may be inserted a trifle stolidly into the script, but once there they irradiate their context and each other. Recurring in fragments they make a musical world, and a theatrical one. The balladeering in this production is riper than we are used to. John Diedrich's Curly makes a stirring noise and Rosamund Shelley's Laurey a pretty one, but she can be flat and he florid, declaring three times that everythin's yoin' his way, and once that the breeze is so busy it don't miss a tray.

Acting is done by Alfred Molina's dark and disturbing Jud Fry, Linal Haft's funny shrugging peddler, and Madge Ryan's Aunt Eller, churning her butter in the opening tableau so serenely that she obviously knows she is part of a myth. The legend is secured for me in the second song, "The Surrey with the Fringe on Top," when she and Laurey, hypnotised, echo Curly's "Don't you wisht y'd go on ferever." Yes.

* * *

Maybe the bravest production of the year has been in Exeter Cathedral, where the Northcott Company tried Hardy's Napoleonic epic The Dynasts (three parts, dozens of acts, hundreds of scenes). The evening began dispiritingly; first came an interpolated folk-dirge about all the fighting being at the expense of the labouring man, which may be true but has nothing to do with the case presented by Hardy who was then allowed his first line, hideously mis-scanned. ("What of the immanent Will and Its design?" What indeed?) It is doubtful if anyone unfamiliar with the text knew what the inimitably turgid choric spirits were about. The driven humans too were often caricatured (mad, sick, terrified George III allowed no pathos), but Ian Reddington's Bonaparte emerged as an engaging, even innocent, opportunist and the others gradually got into line.

Hardy's extraordinary cinematographic stage-directions ("the various battalions are marched away in their respective directions") had, of course, to be ignored; adaptor-designer Hugh Durrant and director Crispin Thomas shaped what remained as a pageant. Each warring nation was equipped with its own booth, and they met and contended on a ramp stretched the length of the nave. We, surrendering to the size and ambition and even to some of the pity and terror, tracked the action, Cottesloe-promenade style. If ever the National want a piece to exercise all three of its auditoria simultaneously, this is it.

records.title: Mine eyes dazzle
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Mine eyes dazzle

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Webster and Priestley

ADRIAN NOBLE is an assistant with the RSC who has been let out to do a production of The Duchess of Malfi at the Royal Exchange, Manchester.

He seems to have a complete understanding of play and space--both of them tricky--and has used each to bring out the strengths of the other. The arena stage is left uncluttered; a thick strip of carpet along its diameter is enough to suggest the poisoned courts of Webster's action.

At the beginning the honest steward Antonio describes, for his even more honest chum, Delio, the dispositions of the three siblings--Duke, Duchess, Cardinal--with whom his own life is about to become fatally entwined. For a moment the story stops, with each participant bathed in his own pool of illumination; and an effect which might seem ludicrously studied on a proscenium, or even a platform, stage here seems completely right.

Again, there is the episode in which crazy Duke Ferdinand visits his imprisoned sister and leaves her with, as she thinks, the severed hand of her husband, Antonio. We are near enough to the action for it to be played in complete darkness without losing us, as both credibility and atmosphere demand.

As with light, so with sound: the Exchange has its own aural equivalent of Sensurround, an enveloping acoustic. Moments of defiance or determination--charged single lines--are pitched to wake the obliging Exchange echo. For some more sustained passages--the elegy spoken by Bosola, the prince's hit-man, in the disguise of a sexton, and his earlier briefing by Ferdinand--the actors have, I assume, been equipped with throat-mikes; certainly the effect is unearthly, and yet totally persuasive.

The rediscovery of the Jacobeans--and of the means to do them justice--has been the most encouraging development in the British theatre in the last couple of years, and it is to the poetry that this production is finally keyed.

This has nothing to do with golden voices, everything with a considered imaginative approach to Webster's pervasive wit. He was the nearest of all the playwrights to the metaphysical poets; and The Duchess's swooning of Antonio is carried out as a series of geometrical conceits. 'All discord, without this circumference, is only to be pitied,' says Helen Mirren's Duchess, spreading her arms. Hers is not a great performance, but it is captivating and ultimately moving.

Mike Gwilym delays Ferdinand's madness until the rebuke to Bosola, 'Why didst thou not pity her?' which, though crazy in context, is natural and even gentle in delivery. This becomes the keynote of his performance. Sane, he is a routine neurotic villain; mad, he develops a highly disturbing charm.

Julian Curry makes a suave and secular Cardinal, and Peter Postlethwaite establishes the worth, the bewilderment, and the timidity of the declassed Antonio. Bob Hoskins admirably performs the basic duty of any Bosola--that of keeping us with him through the moral twists that corkscrew through Webster's universe; but his subdued Cockney lacks the vocal flexibility to make the journey exhilarating. Bosola is an escaped galley-slave, but he is also a decayed gentleman. It could be one of the play's ironies that he is actually better-born than the Antonio he half admires, half despises.

* * *

There is a revival of comparable merit at Greenwich where Alan Strachan shows J. B. Priestley's Time and the Conways to be a play three-quarters superb. This is the one which jumps from 1919 to 1937 and back again. In Act One a northern middle-class family--widowed mother, four daughters, two sons--enjoys and celebrates itself; in Act Two it confronts financial ruin and the failure of all social and marital hopes; in Act Three it returns to happiness while the audience smugly ponders how little the characters know and spots the seeds of the approaching debacle.

This makes for some admittedly crude dramaturgy (the nadir comes when the youngest daughter, whom we know will soon die, cries out that she is going to live) but it is saved by the efficiency and penetration of Mr Priestley's writing. The second act is as tough and chilling a sequence as any British playwright has brought off this century. Beyond praise is the interweaving of the personal and political so that Madge, the spinster schoolmistress who put her trust in the League of Nations, stands for a whole generation of disappointed liberalism; while her mother--outmoded even in her own time--clings to her wastrel soldier son who is 'the same sort' and the most reactionary of them all.

Meanwhile the despised new industrialist--an Antonio who refused to be intimidated--turns out the most successful and unpleasant of all, exerting a nameless tyranny over the once-proud Conway daughter who was unwary enough to marry him.

It is a pity that Mr Priestley felt obliged to wrap up a quite legitimate use of flash-back-and-forward in spurious mysticism about time, with a soothing bit of Blake to make everything cosy. Reduced to common sense the moral is that yesterday's pleasure is no less real than today's pain, and that tomorrow they will be equally part of the past. But the theatre, of its nature, insists that the present is all-important, and indeed Mr Priestley's specific practice here contradicts his theory.

The effect of Act Three depends on our already knowing--from Act Two--what is really going to happen and regarding it as all-important. However, the theorising only takes a couple of minutes and what remains in Mr Strachan's production is excellently modulated, placed and--despite some self-conscious throbbing as the actors approach the significant and/or juicy bits--played.

* * *

Some of John Dankworth's tunes for Colette (Comedy) are very attractive; but his lyrics run to such couplets as 'You'll see Puccini and Zola/Toulouse Lautrec in his bowler.' This in a number called, I'm afraid, 'Paree.' Even this might conceivably be saved by flashy production but Wendy Toye's idea of excitement is to send sequins of light winking round the stage. Even a goodish lyrical idea--as in 'I'm about to make the same mistake ... more than 17 times'--is run coyly into the ground, and then reprised.

Nor can the songs find any support from the book; Mr Dankworth merely supplies a series of limp uncharacterised sketches taking Colette from pigtails to arthritis, via three husbands (all played, together with a lesbian girl-friend, by Kenneth Nelson) and a trip on the Normandie apparently undertaken only so that Glen Laine, looking forward to visiting New York cabarets, can do a Dietrich impersonation. (For this she left home?)

Miss Laine has an agreeable stage presence and her singing, warm-voiced as ever, is less flighty than usual; only once does she resort to bluesy melismatics. They are misplaced but one can understand the desire to bring in some excitement somehow. The narrator, very tactful, is John Moffatt, in a red smoking-jacket, to go with the heroine's little red room. Occasionally the lighting goes the same colour and Tim Goodchild's elegant set takes on the complexion of a tandoori chicken. Or, perhaps more appropriately, a tandoori turkey.

* * *

The Passion has returned to the Cottesloe. Part One (Creation to Nativity) must rank as the most inventive of Bill Bryden's promenade productions, and the most engaging in its involvement of the audience; it is far tighter, not to say more audible, at home than at the Assembly Hall in Edinburgh. If the text seems sometimes thin, blame the Middle Ages.

records.title: Muzak in the air
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Muzak in the air

NEIL SIMON'S musical They're Playing Our Song (Shaftesbury) concerns an affair between a composer and lyricist, which at least adds a new twist to the perennial question of which comes first, the words or the music.

I call it Mr Simon's musical, since the book is more important than the score. This may seem odd, given the avocations of the characters -- who are reputedly based on Marvin Hamlisch and Carole Bayer Sager, the composer and lyricist of the show -- but disappointingly little is made of the working relationship. Vernon Gersch and Sonia Walske might be any urban couple in a Neil Simon comedy; there is nothing here of the fantasy or broad satire with which Mr Simon has extended his range in his previous musical scripts: Little Me, Sweet Charity, Promises Promises.

But the form still takes its toll; the songs are Mr Simon's alibi for digging less deep than he otherwise might. The first act, which is glad preparation for the affair, is enjoyable; the second, which is relationship and break-up, gets frustrating. Mr Simon won't tell us anything. All we learn is that Sonia has a dependent ex-boyfriend called Leon who won't let go; and phones up at unearthly hours. She keeps rushing to his side and is late for appointments; so she's a kook. Of Vernon we're told nothing; or rather we're told that he's an obsessive perfectionist but we never see it. Leon (Leon Petsky, I can just see him) is the plot.

He's also one of two running gags. The other concerns Sonia's wardrobe. She has an actress friend who gives her old costumes, so she can talk about her "Cherry Orchard" dress, or the one from "Pippin." This turns out to be an arresting affair with a halter-top and nothing but fringe below. Gemma Craven looks stunning in it; Tom Conti has fun primly arranging the bits. But both these jokes are shamelessly over-exploited.

I'm a fan of the Simon wisecrack; it's not only funny but truthful, a natural defence for people who lead with their nerves and guard with their intellects. There are a couple of deathless ones here about Vernon's broken-down car and the American Automobile Association.

But this doesn't make a play; or, really, a musical. Just one scene breaks out; Vernon and Sonia, on their first date, hear their biggest individual hits, back to back, and go into the title number -- much the strongest in the score -- and thence off to bed. Success is an aphrodisiac; there is a point musically and theatrically made. But otherwise the songs are just wan decoration; Mr Hamlisch's music is spineless (theatre music may be predestined for muzak but the ghastly end doesn't have to be met so eagerly halfway) and Miss Sager's words anonymous. I played the American cast album recently and found that, despite having seen the show in New York, I couldn't place any of the songs; they had no dramatic weight.

Mr Conti as Vernon has some excellent physical comedy, notably a sequence in which his hands close round a bottle, impelled by a sudden urge to brain his beloved; but the burdens of singing (which he does perfectly adequately) and an American accent seem to constrict his acting. Miss Craven, cool and level-headed, is hardly a natural for Sonia but she is maybe our best actress-singer. They make a good dancing pair: he funnily self-absorbed and angular, she flowing and dynamic. Each protagonist is equipped with a trio of alter egos, mainly there to provide an excuse for a disco sound; the cues for their appearances steadily get thinner and more irritating. There are no other visible characters. The sleek original production has grown somewhat tattered in transit but Douglas W. Schmidt's sets, mainly black and-white projections, retain their sheen.

* * *

I wonder if Sonia and Vernon would work as vehicles for Victoria Wood and the Great Soprendo, whose Funny Turns (King's Head) is the best entertainment in London though I must admit that it tells us little about the state of their marriage. The Soprendo is an actor pretending to be an oily Mediterranean pretending to be a magician, both pretences succeeding magnificently well and each serving the other in fighting off the stupor that may result from the contemplation of total competence. I generally find conjurers boring but the Soprendo knows when to muff a couple of tricks and to subdue his audience with barbed-wire patter. ("Thank you," he murmurs with murderous obsequiousness, "for that applau.")

His is the first half, Miss Wood's the second. Her repertoire of songs is not growing as fast as might be wished, and I can't quite concur with the colleague who declared that she purposely avoids writing memorable tunes; I reckon she wouldn't mind one or two. But at least her melodies support her lyrics, the only ones I know to combine traditional rhyming and metrical skill with mordantly funny observation of today's Britain seen as part supermarket, part surgical ward. She manages, as writer and singer, to be warmly dismissive; as stand-up comic she spoils an excellent run of gags about her native Morecambe by fast nervous delivery; once she slips into a persona (as a patronising W.I. chairman) she is much happier.

* * *

The first half of Jeeves Takes Charge (Fortune) I was inclined to write off as an impossibility; I suppose Bertie Wooster, in the flesh, would be the guffawing chump that Edward Duke makes of him but what has flesh to do with Wodehouse anyway? Bertie is not a man but an angel, truly ineffable; Mr Duke makes him undeniably effable. The Wooster style is swift and light, beyond the power of any actor to capture at a pitch suitable for the human ear.

In Act Two, however, Mr Duke turns, far more happily, to Aunt Dahlia being ungainsayable and Gussie Fink-Nottle handing out school prizes with a gap between his teeth as wide -- to judge by his lisp -- as the hyphen between Fink and Nottle. Here, too, Gillian Lynne's direction desists from underlining every word with a gesture and turns to the discovery of a tap-dancing style suitable for the young master. There is a charming Art Deco set: the kind in which every cupboard looks like a fridge.

* * *

You will have noticed that everything so far discussed is, at biggest, a duologue. Here's another. In Vaclav Havel's Protest (Orange Tree) a Czech writer smoothly argues himself out of signing a petition while a released dissident (played by Frank Moorey like the spirit of conscience) hears him with infuriating compassion. You think Havel may be trapping himself into a tract; he shows his stature with a tartly theatrical ending. The companion piece by his compatriot Pavel Kohout, The Licence, is a group piece on the same theme, more plainly laid out and more obviously a parable. Havel you take as literal truth.

* * *

Just now at the Half Moon in Pal Joey they were asking (or would have been if they had kept to the original lyric which I understand has been restored in the transfer to the Albery) "will Saroyan ever write a great play?" A negative answer is returned at the same theatre by Playthings, a set of yet more duologues between actors representing inanimate objects. The conflicts -- of ceiling and floor, lampshade and hat-rack -- and so on -- reflect human jockeying for position, and at the end we are treated to the brief sermon on man's destructive nature you might expect from an author of advanced years and whimsical disposition.

If I've made it sound dreadful so has he, but it somehow manages to be pleasing as well. The cast are admirable, notably Thick Wilson as, among other things, a clove of garlic whose very image he manages to look in a bunched green tunic credited -- if that is what "illustrations" means -- to Andy Warhol. Let us now praise famous men and women: the adroit director is Mai Zetterling.

records.title: Feathered friends
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
CAPTAIN Jack BOYLE picks up a book belonging to his daughter and reads off the contents with disgust: "A Doll's House? Ghosts? The Wild Duck." Kid's stuff.

The laugh this got on the first night of Juno and the Paycock (Aldwych) may have had something to do with an awareness, at least in the professional section of the house, that a production of The Wild Duck was opening that same night at the Lyric, Hammersmith, and would shortly have to be caught up with.

The two plays have much in common. Each centres on a windbag's family, kept more or less on the rails by a realistic self-sacrificing wife. Each ends with the death of a child, sacrificed to somebody else's notion of idealism. O'Casey's Johnny Boyle, caught up in the most vicious and ludicrous stage of the Irish struggle, is shot by former comrades. Ibsen's Hedvig Ekdal shoots herself because she believes her father hates her.

On the surface the O'Casey play is the darker. Johnny's death breaks up his home. His mother Juno, who also has a pregnant deserted daughter on her hands, walks out on Captain Jack for good. Hedvig's suicide at least has the effect of drawing her parents closer together. There is however Dr Relling, the play's raisonneur, on hand to assure us that Hjalmar Ekdal's fine words over his daughter's corpse are only fine words and will lead to no new attitude. Nobody dares to say that of Juno's final oration. It moves us and in moving us comforts us. The Wild Duck is bleakly ironic to its roots, and there is little in Juno to match it.

The trick of the comedy in Juno is to preserve the human reality: to prevent it from becoming a dance of symbols expressing a doubtless universal truth but totally unbelievable as dramatic action. Trevor Nunn and Michael Blakemore manage these complementary assignments superbly. From now on if anybody asks what I want from the theatre I propose to answer "intelligent showmanship" and to offer these two directors as exemplars.

Mr Nunn takes Juno very deliberately; the assumption is that every moment counts, and that there is juice to be extracted from every action. Sometimes it is comic juice; there is an extended sequence early in Act One when Norman Rodway's poem of the hippo is interrupted at almost every line by a succession of bizarre visitors. You observe the precise workings of his relationship with John Rogan's Joxer who watches him ceaselessly to observe how best to flatter and cave in. Rodway's Captain Jack is actually dangerous, and is funny to the exact extent that he is dangerous.

Mr Rodway could scarcely be more remote from one's image of a man of integrity; the startling core of his performance is his violent tirade when he learns of his daughter's condition. His drunkenness is hilarious and his selfishness horrifying; the comedy and horror go together. Judi Dench's Juno also makes the comedy work, both in her tart rebukes to her husband and when she suddenly is given the frightfully important job of reading the will in the second act. But underlying everything in her performance is an immense practicality; everybody's sweetheart is now everybody's mother. As for her last familiar lament, doubt that at your peril.

The welding process is extended in Gerard Murphy's Johnny who is kept in focus throughout, tormented by life inside and out of the tenement room, and maddened as much by the jollity as by the horror. Dearbhla Molloy as his sister undergoes something of the same progress, and her two suitors are sharply drawn by Bryan Murray and Frank Grimes. All the characters save Juno are romancers; Johnny's "a principle's a principle" is the reflection of his father's imaginary career at sea. O'Casey deplored both; Ibsen would probably have condoned the Captain's fancies as a life-lie on a par with Hjalmar Ekdal's imaginary invention.

The trouble with Ibsen's play is that its idealist Gregers Werle and his idol Hjalmar are an unlikely combination. It would take a great fool not to see through Hjalmar, so Gregers is a great fool. This coalition might come about, and might well produce disastrous results, but it seems rather a specialised base from which to proclaim universal truths. Mr Blakemore's production sets energetically about normalising the two of them. Jim Norton gives full weight, and some reason, to Gregers's hatred of his father; he becomes one of the walking wounded with his own kind of plausibility. Richard Briers's Hjalmar has a stocky self-satisfaction that just might, in a suitable light, be mistaken for sincerity. When he goes to pieces he does so with surprising fervour; his comedy and tragedy are of a piece and ingrown. They almost co-exist in time; Hjalmar too is a comic set-piece over his breakfast and Ibsen, after all, a bolder playwright, brings it right up to the moment of disaster.

The domestic sphere is maintained by Nerys Hughes's Gina, and above all by the Hedvig of Michele Wade, who is a plain, bespectacled and fanciful schoolgirl. Not only does she not sentimentalise the play, but she actively robs it of symbolism. When this Hedvig talks about the depths of the ocean you can hear her mind wrapping itself lovingly around the books she has read. Gerald James makes a welcome Dr Relling, and Frances Cuka is quite outstandingly good as the kind and worldly Mrs Sorby; the solid relationships she establishes (with Gina especially) in two brief appearances exemplify the strength of the evening.

* * *

David Mercer's The Limits of Love is, posthumously, at the Warehouse. It presents an economically comfortable menage a trois; valid, since it is smashed by a newcomer who turns out to have been one man's analyst. Mercer gives them tirades that are moving, revealing; take your choice, but he never seems to have the characters properly in his sights; they are good for what he can get out of them at any moment (rather like Neil Simon with his one-liners and ultimately no more informative).

The lady in the case comes off particularly badly; Susan Fleetwood spits and preaches, but she is not given a life. John Shrapnel adds electricity every time he appears, as a bouncing bisexual don, though the bisexuality is hard to credit and the bounce rather close to professional foul. Bob Peck as an outrageously (to everyone else) passive cellist has a tellingly individual line in stump; Edward Petherbridge alone makes his memories of unseen characters in the past seem pressingly important in the present.

records.title: Hard times for the Celts
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Hard times for the Celts

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on plays by Howard Brenton, Nigel Williams, Alan Bennett and Alan Ayckbourn.

HOWARD BRENTON'S The Romans in Britain (Olivier) is about imperialism. Its last event, chronologically, is the shooting of an English army major by Irish republicans.

As he is dragged off he shouts, "When will peace come?" His killers are not impressed: "What right does he have to stand in a field in Ireland and talk of the horrors of war? What nation ever learnt from the sufferings it inflicted on others? What did the Roman Empire give to the people it enslaved? Concrete."

That sounds uncomfortably like the Judaean Liberation Front in "Monty Python's Life of Brian" excoriating all the enemy's works except transport, sanitation and public safety. Overlapping with the 1980 scenes in Mr Brenton's play are two moments from ancient British history: the arrival of the Romans in 54 BC under Julius Caesar, and that of the Saxons 550 years later. Caught in the middle every time are the Celts: their homes burned, their crops destroyed, their women raped and - as is made graphically apparent - their men too. The Roman invasion takes up most of the first act; it is a fine moment when, just before the interval, Caesar's army returns to the stage this time dressed in khaki.

Unfortunately we never progress far beyond that moment of plus ca change. Mr Brenton has written a fierce, funny and maddeningly inconclusive play. All he has to say in the end is that conquest causes suffering and ought not to be allowed. He brings off his version of Celtic civilisation - not exactly an easy subject - with vigour and ingenuity, but the only time we feel ourselves inside a man's head is when we meet Caesar, meticulously grooming himself for history.

Mr Brenton's Celts incidentally (including a couple of comic Ancient Irish who begin the play) are no models of moral behaviour. They kill strangers on sight and would obviously be as murderous as their conquerors if they had the fire-power. The dim view of humanity taken throughout suggests that war breeds imperialism rather than the other way about, and that both are basic to human nature rather than unexplained mutations of it.

I agree with this, but I don't think it's what Mr Brenton set out to prove. Anyway he seems to be enjoying himself with the play's omnipresent violence: gloating not so much over the thing itself as over his ability to make the audience sit through it. Michael Bogdanov's production solves most of the play's problems (with a couple of farcical lapses) and incorporates good acting from Michael Bryant as Caesar; from Stephan Moore as the major and James Hayes as his nemesis; and from John Normington and James Carter as the clowns.

* * *

Nigel Williams in Sugar and Spice (Royal Court) repeats the pattern of his last play "Line 'Em." A belligerent character harangues everyone for an act; after the interval the opposition arrives, and does its own sounding-off. In this case the initial focus is a teenage punk, Sharon, who arrives with friends in the flat of a Chelsea tart and arranges the ritual humiliation of a boy who has been following them with obvious designs on one of them.

Both as written and played (by Toyah Willcox) Sharon is quirkier, and more compelling than Mr Williams's last mouthpiece, and the aggro she expresses is real and painfully rooted. But apart from the fact that she goes on too long, she is not believable; she is too ornately articulate for her background, and her background is the point of the play. I will take Mr Williams's word that he is not trying to write naturalistically, but I think he chooses the wrong subjects to get stylish over.

Anyway there is nothing hieratic about Bill Alexander's production, which tries, with varying success, to find convincing things for the other characters to do while listening. (Text and production have sketched out individual lives for them, but they only function in fits and starts.) The acting too is variable, to put it politely; the actor who inherits the rhetoric in Act Two seems to have no idea what to do with it. There is action as well as talk: boys and girls alike being maddened by their sexual conditioning, a broken whisky bottle is flashed and so are quantities of male and female flesh.

The delectable Gwyneth Strong (coping admirably with a bewilderingly inconsistent role) is slowly stripped in Act Two; this, given the play's moral drift, is having your cheese-cake and eating it. There is an entertaining performance by Carole Hayman as the unwilling hostess, wondering why the sexes can't just get on together. If she says it once, she says it a hundred times. All concerned spend quantities of time volubly reacting to situations and ideas that are never actually established.

* * *

From the Howards and Nigels of subsidised youth to the Alans of free enterprise. Not that no wires are crossed between the two: last week I witnessed two bodies dubiously dead, two unanswered 999 calls, and two young ladies proclaiming, "I'm a slag." Well one, being from the north, says "I'm a slag, me."
