She figures in Alan Bennett's Enjoy (Vaudeville), and her parents' fond belief that she is a respectable secretary is one instance of their incurable (and exhaustively paraded) silliness. Their bland acceptance of the news that she is off to Saudi Arabia to marry a prince tells us more about them than about their author's allegiance to the post-Orton comic mode, in which the joke consists of taking outrageous events for granted.

Mr Bennett provides a few hilarious variants; nevertheless his first act had me furious. He seemed to be patronising his characters and his central device was cumbrous; he introduces into his protagonists' decaying Leeds home a silent official who will take notes on their behaviour that may help in resettling them. ("Don't take this down yet, we're not being typical yet.") Later one recognises Mr Bennett's strategy; resettlement turns out to mean incarceration in a museum of local working-class culture, a sort of human zoo, for mum, and in a home for dad, paralysed by a car-crash and a juvenile assault.

The sour taste, in fact, is intentional. So, yes, this is an uncompromising play for today's West End; and, yes, it is finely acted by Joan Plowright (though Beryl Reid could do it more effortlessly) and Colin Blakely (though to cast so vibrant an actor as a physical and spiritual cripple is a definite waste), finely supported by Susan Littler (she's the slag, her) and Liz Smith; and, yes, Mr Bennett is a superior writer. Not really though a writer of plays; his characters are museum exhibits, well displayed but with no interior life, and they are presented to us at exorbitant length.

* * *

Alan Ayckbourn seems to keep writing the same play. I don't mean that he repeats himself, but that he explores different areas of the same family canvas. Season's Greetings (Roundhouse) takes off from "Absurd Person Singular" by being about Christmas and from "Sisterly Feelings" by being about sisters. Again they fight over a man, but in this case one of them has only platonic (which does not mean unpassionate) designs. Marcia Warren plays her with a good blend of decisiveness and finesse. Other pearls are Ronald Herdman as a worm who turns, with unusual passion for these latitudes, on one of Mr Ayckbourn's fascistic lawmen, and Susan Uebel as his wife, a walking accident.

Some scenes are surprisingly pallid. But if you are collecting the Ayckbourn set, you would hardly want to miss an instalment.

records.title: Wood Fun
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Wood Fun

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Manchester.

VICTORIA WOOD is the greatest good fortune to have befallen the British musical in decades. Good Fun (King's Head), for which she wrote book, music and lyrics, lives wryly up to its title, but I don't believe in it. We need to know, from the start, just what conventions are being utilised, what kind of song Miss Wood is using, and why.

Her natural mode is confessional. Her characters explain and reveal themselves. These songs do not move the plot along: they halt it while amplifying - acutely and with a splendid ear for detail and for the humours of self-betrayal - the people in it. Liz, the heroine, tells us at curtain-rise that she is a middle-class do-gooder, working hard at benevolence in order to compensate for disappointed sexual and social ambitions. (Much of this, Miss Wood being skilful, is implied rather than stated.) Liz's perch is an arts centre ("an adaptable space," as she repeatedly explains) and her immediate project is a party with entertainment for 300 cystitis victims.

The preparations, which are not smooth, bring her into contact and conflict with a goofy librarian who fancies her and with her own adored, self-styled artist soiled with the last droppings of the alternative culture; not to mention a passing lady beautician, oppressively full of joie de vivre, a dolefully pregnant catering help (salads only), and an old school friend who, in Liz's words, has a much better time than ugly girls are entitled to, but seems jaundiced by it all.

Her number "I've had it up to here with men" ("I'd be happier, I know/If we could only go/From the foreplay straight to the cigarette") is already a standard in Miss Wood's own repertoire; that she also has a glorious store of one-liners may have something to do with Miss Wood having played the role herself in Sheffield.

I was the mug who complained, at that first production, that the male characters, not being allowed raw singing, were being given a raw and even prejudiced deal. Now the chaps do get to join in. The librarian is one half of a courtship duet which is a treat. He also joins in Liz's early morale-boosting routine about facing up to organisational problems ahead. So does his parasitic opposite number. This is disaster; the guy, as given to us, wouldn't be caught dead participating in well-drilled displays of enthusiasm. The assumption that any character may be dragooned into a number is part of our national musical-paralysis. When the author, like Miss Wood, has justified pretensions to be considered a playwright, it is fatal. Besides, the very idea of a concerted production number violates the implicit contract Miss Wood's other songs make with the audience. The show never recovers.

It does, though, provide many incidental pleasures. The theme of what men do to women, and more especially what women do to themselves with men in mind, is prettily dovetailed with the idea denoted in the title: pleasure, mostly imaginary, as a desperate panacea. The Northern background of fast food and minor bureaucracy - burgers and burghers - is impeccably observed; and nobody can beat Miss Wood at schoolhouse reminiscence.

The plotting is neat in conception, ineffectual in execution. There is, to scotch a growing rumour, no disparity between music and lyrics. When one is funny, the other is. Liz's last song is melodrama, words and music; a despairing solo for the unwilling mother is real drama. So does his parasitic ditto. Tina Marian's toughly melodious account of this role is one of London's two gains over Sheffield; the other is Kevin Moore's librarian. Paula Wilcox is pleasing as Liz, but the songs tax her and the production isn't much help. Nichola McAuliffe, by contrast, has more notes in her voice than the score can use, but she makes a neatly sardonic author's deputy.

* * *

The songs in The Streets of London (Her Majesty's) are discreet and enjoyable (music, Gary Carpenter; lyrics, Ian Barnett). The best of them, immaculately sung and strolled by Royce Mills, comes when we should be intent on the plot.

Boucicault, who wrote this roaring 1850s thriller, believed in throwing everything in. But new songs work, unavoidably, as a comment on the play rather than as a part of it, and there is rather too much comment already, especially in the audience, who on the first night were far more intent on enjoying themselves hissing the villain than on enjoying the play.

This was their loss, since the plot and stuffing of the piece are quite as entertaining as its conventions; three-sided reunions, double-suicide attempts, valiant sorties into blazing buildings, are affecting as well as rousing. William Squire is finely farouche as Gideon Bloodgood, unscrupulous banker, and Jane Wymark sublimely selfish as the daughter who is his only weakness; Michael Carter slinkily contorts voice and figure as a turning worm whose ambiguities show Boucicault at his inventive best. As usual the wrong'uns have the best of it; I would have turned the trio of odiously deserving poor into the snow without a moment's compunction. Diane Cilento's handsome and leisurely production knows which side its bread is buttered; the play may end with a prayer for the poor of London, but she caps it with a solid chorus in praise of gold.

* * *

Which brings us to Arthur Miller's The Price (Shaw), whose substance is a fight between two brothers, a cop and a doc, over the material and spiritual legacy of their father, who was ruined in the Depression and may or may not have needed their support thereafter.

Mr Miller, unusually among modern playwrights, is a humane and intelligent man of whom you might with some confidence inquire the time of day, and there are a good number of reliable insights, along with the carefully forged chain of memories. But you end up wondering why, if the dramatist knew so much about the characters' pasts, he couldn't have told us in the first place or better still why he couldn't have put that past on stage.

There is not much drama about the present; no sense that what these people learn will change their lives in any way. It is, by way of compensation, Mr Miller's funniest play; though this production is rather humourless. John Bennet depicts the gnawing pains of success successfully, and Frances Cuka manages not to play the policeman's wife as just an old grey nag: an achievement.

* * *

The Two Eugenes are not, as you might think, a pair of trick cyclists. They are O'Neill and Ionesco, two playwrights with historical status as innovators and "experimentalists" - maybe they were trick cyclists. Their plays revived as a double-bill at the Royal Exchange, Manchester, seem barren enough now. O'Neill's The Emperor Jones is chiefly notable for the blackface performance of a white actor, Peter Postlethwaite, as the Pullman attendant turned island dictator on the run in the jungle and encountering, in very sketchy hallucinatory form, his own fate and his people's. Monsieur Ionesco's The Chairs is the duologue for two nonagenarians with an incomprehensible message to bestow on an invisible audience. There is still some poignancy in their mutually supportive regrets, but they seem to go on for ever.

records.title: Busy beaux
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Busy beaux

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on new productions by the National Theatre and the R.S.C.

I WONDER if Peter Wood was scared as a child by a particularly bad production of a Restoration comedy.

When he directs one of them himself he seems to have in his mind the memory of two actors on an empty stage in pretty clothes just talking, talking, talking. Mr Wood has no intention of letting this happen in his own productions, which are extremely busy. In his staging of Vanbrugh's The Provok'd Wife (Lyttelton) actors have crossed the stage on floats, tavern songs have been carolled, before we even get to the first scene, which Vanbrugh wrote largely as a brace of soliloquies for the discontented married couple, Sir John and Lady Brute, but which is here transformed into an exchange of recriminations across the breakfast table.

An exchange between the two beaux, Constant and Heartfree, is enlivened by having one of them surprise the other at shaving. Even more mobile than the actors is the scenery. When Sir John, disguised as a woman, is on the run from the watch, the stage suddenly sprouts a set of chimney tops on which to conclude the chase. It is a charming effect, as are most of the others, but it does nothing to make the scene funnier. It fractures the rhythm.

The adornments have the curious effect both of prettying the play up and damping it down. At its black heart the play is the study of a misalliance from which neither party has the means or the courage to break. Watching this sad state are another pair, Heartfree and Bellinda, wondering whether to risk their intelligence on a similar venture. Watching them is an envious flirt, Lady Fancyfull, playing an outdated sexual game in which no one will join her. And in the outermost circle are the servants, pursuing their own intrigues with a jaundiced eye on their masters'.

The pattern takes some time to emerge here, though Mr Wood finally brings the threads together in an ice-ballet - the happiest of his scenic inventions - on the frozen banks of the Thames; no director is better at elaborate Restoration finales. By this time, too, his actors have come through. Peter Bourke and Brenda Blethyn supply a cynical ground-bass as the domestics, Michael Kitchen as Heartfree escapes from his earlier stolidity to let loose some wry calculations on the worth of a bachelor's freedom, and Dorothy Tutin, posing before the longest of mirrors, turns Lady Fancyfull (Affected? moi?) into a precursor of Miss Piggy, though unfortunately without the same volcanic temperament.

Sir John Brute seems written to be a squat and stupid tyrant; John Wood, being of a different shape and temper, misses out on much of the humour, but supplies some of his own. He analyses his own plight with a masochistic sharpness (and, as far as I could tell, with actual lines) not to be found in the original text; when scorned by his wife's lover his stupefaction speaks for all the cuckolds in comedy. John Gielgud once defined style as knowing what kind of play you're in; Mr Wood goes further and tells us.

There is a similar awareness in Geraldine McEwan's Lady Brute, whose command to her swain, "into the closet," in its sophisticated weariness, is itself worth the price of admission. Miss McEwan has the advantage that her author meant her to be intelligent; with Nicky Henson's admirably flexible Constant and Lindsay Duncan's Bellinda, she makes up a splendid trio of quizzical good sense.

The evening's highlight is a scene in which the two women lie together discussing their respective amours while Mr Kitchen tosses in another chamber on the other side of the stage. Two beds opposed: the picture could hardly be more apposite.

* * *

At almost exactly the same time, but across an ocean rather than a town, the Puritans who, to stretch a point, had left England because of plays like Vanbrugh's were building in Massachusetts the civilisation that was eventually to be the subject of Arthur Miller's The Crucible (Cottesloe). The Provok'd Wife was premiered in 1697; The Crucible is set in 1692. Now here they are, side by side, but still keeping their distance.

Bill Bryden's production of The Crucible is puritanical in tone as well as subject: sometimes achingly so. The first scene, in which it is determined that the teenage girls caught dancing in the woods are under the influence of witchcraft, is taken with an extreme slowness that should serve to highlight nuances, but in fact flattens them out.

The great compensation is that the piece emerges as something more than the drama of one brave man against the crowd. John Proctor, the enlightened farmer, is of the crowd, as much concerned as they with personal righteousness and tormented by his own failings; Mark McManus, choking back bitterness, is here finely partnered by Dinah Stabb as his wife, a walking conscience. There are other strong performances by J. G. Devlin and Tony Haygarth.

The girls were historically in their early teens. Mr Miller made them 17 and 18; most productions cast them in the twenties. I don't know how old Mr Bryden's actresses are, but they look and sound about 14, which adds to the horror of the story, but produces some toneless renditions of key scenes. It also underlines the author's equivocation about Abigail, the ringleader. She is not, considering her part in the action, onstage very much; but the plotting seems to ascribe to her almost sole responsibility for the Salem inferno. Other factors are hinted at but not explored. The subject in fact cracks out of the form, though this tension may be partly responsible for the play's undoubted power.

* * *

If Mr Miller warns against hunting witches, David Rudkin in Hansel and Gretel (Other Place, Stratford on Avon) counsels against ignoring them. His comic guignol version of what was already a pretty terrifying story has it in for everyone. Children are horrible, disruptive things whose parents wish to be rid of them. After dramatising, in Ashes, the misery of not having children, Mr Rudkin turns to the misery of having them. There's no pleasing some people. Mummy is worse than daddy; she turns out to be the witch's heir. Gretel is worse than Hansel; she collaborates, and deserts her brother.

The twin totems of Margaret Thatcher and Mary Whitehouse have made misogyny politically respectable, and both are duly invoked. The witch (a smashing performance by Brenda Bruce) informs her victims that she doesn't want their productivity impaired. "We," she says, "are people of quality, we take tea on the lawn." Invited to address a school she warns against the frightening effect of such stories as that of the Three Little Pigs, however salutary its message of self-help. (I detected, at this point, some hopping from hoof to hoof.) Barbara Kinghorn as the witch's daughter, Olive, who is literally faceless, grunts and squeaks as engagingly as her namesake, Popeye's girl, but on the whole, not having caught Mr Rudkin being funny before, I am not crazy to catch him at it again. For scares, however, he remains unrivalled.

records.title: Sweeney gets the chop
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Sweeney gets the chop

ROBERT CUSHMAN looks at the implications of a musical's demise.

YOU had better go to see Sweeney Todd. I hate writing that kind of sentence. I think I should be able to convey enthusiasm for a show without issuing instructions to readers. But this isn't a review, and the show has only two more weeks to run.

Quite possibly you will have seen Sweeney Todd already. It opened at Drury Lane in July, and though a four-month run for a major musical represents a commercial failure of ominous proportions (ominous because it will discourage further adventure), it still means more performances than are enjoyed by the average production at the National or the RSC. Maybe the number of the discerning has already been exhausted. But the feeling remains that there is an audience for this show that has not been reached.

I visited it a couple of Saturdays ago and there was a football crowd in. They listened raptly and cheered at the end. Whatever its subtleties, this is primary-coloured theatre with a strong story and a compelling score -- with these two qualities more than usually interdependent. The performance, with Denis Quilley as the demon barber and Sheila Hancock as Mrs Lovett slicing her pies and her syllables with manic precision, was more cohesive than ever.

According to Miss Hancock, houses, if less than full, have been young and enthusiastic. There may be some wishful thinking in the customary equation of youth and enlightenment, but the fans have not been the customary patrons for "Musicals at the Lane." Most London theatres lost their identity long since, but now Drury Lane seems to retain one, composed of memories of Ivor Novello, Rodgers and Hammerstein, and My Fair Lady. Hence the indignant, nostalgic letters to the London Evening Standard about this bloodthirsty tuneless show.

Tuneless? Let us grant that Stephen Sondheim does not write autonomous melodies in the fashion of Kern or Rodgers and that it might be a nicer world if he did. But where exactly is the competition? Evita? Annie? They're Playing Our Song? The current hits can hardly muster a distinguished tune between them. But they are forgiven -- by critics as well as audiences -- because at least they let you know that they would like to sound like the good old stuff. It is the shows with individual aspirations (On the Twentieth Century? is another example this year) that get shot down in flames.

Instant memorability is no criterion. (We can all, I imagine, remember tunes that we would rather forget.) There is a famous Broadway story about a critic in the Thirties who complained, on his way out of a new Jerome Kern show, that the songs were forgettable, especially the one about smoke getting in your eyes. Jule Styne once told me that it took him several hearings to grasp a Cole Porter song. Since the pop music business was then geared to the theatre, the necessary repetitions were available; the songs became hits and, eventually, standards. That connection has now been severed: pop means rock or muzak, and neither is dramatic.

Actually I think that if the music business could rid itself of the superstition that the only good show song is a love song, somebody might have had a hit with "The Ballad" of Sweeney Todd, whose function and impact in the show are analogous to those of "Mack the Knife," in The Threepenny Opera. Since it closes the show and has an insistent rhythm, audiences probably come out thinking they know it; since it also has some tricky modulations, they're probably wrong.

But what is important in the theatre is that the music should excite you when you hear it and that it should enhance the situation. Sondheim's music does this in spades and, besides, provides the experience, rare in any kind of theatre, of a writer developing while retaining an individual voice. And if you hear it a second time, either in the theatre or on record, you will not forget it.

Before the show even opened it was put down by John Mortimer, who complained in the Sunday Times that "show music" wasn't "either real classical or real pop. Why music should have to fall into one of those two categories (jazz, of which he must have heard, doesn't either) Mr Mortimer never explained. Compared with Porgy and Bess, the obvious test case, Sweeney Todd is musically informal. It isn't opera, and it's unfortunate that the amount of music it contains caused critics and publicists to bandy the word about and to prophesy a future for the show in the operatic repertoire. (If I were feeling really pugnacious, I would mutter something about the frivolity of a form that uses words while taking great pains to render them indistinguishable.)

Sweeney Todd is a dramatic theatre piece and -- since the subsidised theatre has yet to take musicals at all seriously -- a commercial theatre piece. It threw everyone into confusion. The popular reviewers, instead of saying whether they had enjoyed the show, speculated on whether it would be a hit. (That -- trying to make up the public's mind instead of your own -- is the real critical treason.)

I've heard it said, rightly I think, that it might have done better had it come to us from the Roundhouse or the fringe rather than from Broadway, dripping with Tonies. Evita (same producers and director) was able to survive, even thrive on, publicity overkill through the appeal of native authors and a pre-sold score; it's still the hottest ticket in London. Sweeney Todd fell foul of all our double standards -- at one end the Daily Mail daring its readers to like the show; at the other Time Out, whose initial review was favourable but who obviously felt it would not do to recommend a Broadway-West End product week after week. Pal Joey, being a transfer from the Half Moon, gets the nod.

Now there's a show with the right credentials. It shocked the New York critics in the Forties and the London critics in the Fifties. Now its cynicism -- which to its credit is unostentatious and ingrained -- feels like home. Critics who were only vaguely aware of the existence of Rodgers and Hart are understandably bowled over at discovering them.

Pal Joey is so enjoyable that it seems unkind to point out that it represents the team at their second best (Hart, the supposed sophisticate, is actually less at home in the milieu than Rodgers, the real toughie) and that the director, who at one point permits the words from one song to be sung to the tune from another, must have a tin ear. It's interesting that Pal Joey received a far better press than the revival of Oklahoma!, which really was, and remains, a landmark musical, even if its fresh air is currently less to our taste.

When critics don't expect to take a show seriously they imitate the skipper of the good ship Hesperus, and bring their little daughters along to keep them company; so it was on the first night at the Palace. But the show didn't need our good opinions (though it had mine). These revivals -- Oklahoma! and My Fair Lady and The King and I -- are invincibly and deservedly popular. They answer a real need; they dispense a genuine glow. In later shows -- from Hello Dolly! to They're Playing Our Song -- that glow has become synthetic: hence the importance of Sweeney Todd in offering a new satisfaction, sending you out not warm but tingling.

records.title: Committing high treason
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Committing high treason

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Stratford.

WALLACE SHAWN is a stocky dishevelled mole of a New York playwright best known here for the erotic farce A Thought in Three Parts. He also acts with - to judge from a performance in Machiavelli's Mandrake a couple of seasons ago - more enthusiasm than technique.

By his own account Mr Shawn took to acting to pay his bills. His own account is being rendered (at the Theatre Upstairs, until Wednesday) in an entertainment entitled My Dinner with Andre. Andre is Andre Gregory, once a famous off-Broadway director, but absent from the scene since the early 1970s. Like Mr Shawn he appears here as himself. The action, after some scene-setting remarks by Mr Shawn, consists of a restaurant conversation between the two.

Mr Shawn disarmingly admits that he was dreading the encounter, but planned to survive it by pumping Mr Gregory with questions and listening to the answers. As a performer, Mr Gregory combines maximum relaxation with minimum projection and the first half of the evening, before one adjusts to his level, is a bit of a trial. Mr Gregory tells of working on large-scale improvisations with Jerzy Grotowski in the Polish forests, of travelling to Tibet: experiences that have focused and confirmed his disillusion with America and with the theatre. He would like to submit audiences to experiences of similar intensity in the theatre, but he sees no way.

And here the evening becomes unusually exciting. Mr Shawn is provoked into reply, and comes through with shy, spluttering eloquence. Mr Gregory has apparently been preaching a sort of spiritual quiescence, somewhat intimidating Mr Shawn who says, "I'm not adequate just to be a human being"; he needs, he says, goals and actions. And small ones will do; as he says, it isn't practical to take everyone to Everest. "Why not enjoy the details?" he asks; getting up in the morning, being with your wife, having a cup of coffee.

He goes on to preach the highest theatrical treason and to reveal that he enjoys not only writing plays, but getting the reviews and reading about plays "and things about things about plays." He celebrates in fact all the trivia that theatrical gurus of every stamp have instructed us to despise. Generations of guilt fall away. I felt like cheering.

If we can stop worrying about the grandiose things power-hungry theatricals would like their shows to do to people, we can maybe get down to appreciating the smaller things it can do for them. (Audiences, you may notice, are the factor left out of nearly every theatrical manifesto.) I don't want to imply that Mr Gregory, especially when he starts speaking up to reply to Mr Shawn, is a mere bully - he's actually very charming - or that there is no common ground between the two of them. Mr Shawn has his full measure of unease, and Mr Gregory his of compassion. And he makes a mark; Mr Shawn scampers home to tell his wife every detail of their conversation. His mind has not been changed, but it has been coloured. Which is all that a play can do; and what this one does far better than most.

* * *

Edward Bond in The Guardian last week was attacking James Fenton of The Sunday Times for not liking The Romans in Britain. He obviously felt that more than Howard Brenton's play was at stake; he wanted reviewers to pick up sides, preferably his own. We are asked to supply blanket approval of one stream of work (Mr Bond differs from previous scourges of the Press in wanting rave reviews for his friends as well as himself) and blanket disapproval of another.

Academic critics may be able to oblige with this kind of partisanship, but regular reviewers cannot. We see too much, and are confounded by finding merits and faults in unsuspected quarters. We may start radical or reactionary, but we invariably end up liberal. I liked The Romans in Britain and I have liked most of Mr Bond's plays, but I have probably damned myself by liking Stoppard, Ayckbourn, Gray and Frayn as well.

Audiences tend to be as disobligingly catholic as reviewers; the all-or-nothing response craved by theatre people is rarely an honest possibility. A lady with a personal stake in the new Stratford productions of Richard II and Richard III told me during an interval that she wanted the shows to be either loved or hated. She's an old and dear friend and I hate to disoblige her, but I have to confess that though temperamentally out of tune with Terry Hands's hectically operatic approach, I thought these examples of it pretty good.

Mr Hands is an avowed enemy of realism and he can justifiably assert that these two early Shakespeare histories are stylised pieces, full of emblematic characters and elaborate verbal tropes. But I suspect that the war between realism and stylisation is a phony one. There never was a wholly realistic play or production, never will or can be. Complete stylisation is a possibility, but is unlikely.

In practice the two modes always co-exist, and if a text tilts in one direction it is the director's job to restore the balance. (I expect to contradict myself on this point, and rapidly.) For example: in the Flint Castle scene of Richard II, after Alan Howard as Richard has expressed his willingness to come down and surrender to Bolingbroke in the base court, he executes a highly unrealistic and acrobatically impressive walk down the wall of Farrah's burnished-copper set. This should be a stunning image, but though arresting it doesn't work because Richard has already made the point verbally and at formal length. What we need here is a nifty prosaic exit on one level and entrance on another.

Similarly Richard III's hoodwinking of the Lord Mayor of London is as written a pretty crude affair: it may be that instead of staging it as an outsize Punch and Judy show it might be better to opt for a sober treatment that might add a sense of Realpolitik.

Both productions are at their best in the scenes that follow these central episodes. In Richard II Mr Howard abandons the stinging and/or mournful approach most actors bring to the deposition. He is almost playful, even in comparing himself to Christ, and by so much the more disconcerting; he almost embarrasses Bolingbroke on to the throne, and it is plain that David Suchet's usurper (hitherto a plain and rather likeable opportunist) will never get over it. Mr Howard is almost coy when he looks at himself in the glass: over-powering when he breaks it to pieces. This may be the motif that links the two plays: R2 loves his own image, R3 hates it.

Mr Howard's Crookback goes heavily for deformity, taking the first soliloquy rewardingly at face value. His prize scene is the coronation, when he must heave himself painfully up the steps, and sits on them to take counsel from a diminutive page on the Princes' murder. He makes more than any actor I have seen of Richard's nightmare, prompted by a posse of ghosts who mark the climax of Mr Hands's boldly helter-skelter production. (The spirits of Rivers, Vaughan and Grey even get away with playing ring-a-ring-a-wars-of-the-roses.) The play also has the best of Stratford's support with Derek Godfrey a ruefully witty Buckingham, with an excellently charted relationship to Richard, Mr Suchet a helplessly sick king, Richard Pasco a resounding Clarence, Domini Blythe, Barbara Leigh-Hunt and Sinead Cusack a powerful pack of queens and Joe Melia, no less, turning unexpectedly up as Second Murderer.

* * *

Peter Buckman's All Together Now (Greenwich) finds a new source of drama: the tribulations and evolution of a local brass band. It is their actual music that provides the excitement, comic and dramatic as well as musical. The talk bits are routinely competent group-portraiture; none of the actors puts down roots in Peter Dews's production.

records.title: Dog Days in Vienna
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Dog Days in Vienna

ROBERT CUSHMAN visits an unusual outpost of British drama.

JUST two Sundays ago Simon Gray made his debut as a director with, as you would expect, one of his own plays.

What you might not expect is the location of his debut. It took place in Vienna; not, though, on one of the Austrian national stages, where Pinter and Stoppard are regularly unveiled in German translations under the batons of their original British directors. The Gray corpus has been seen in Vienna at a much smaller theatre, and in English.

Just about the first thing you see in the Vienna airport, if you have flown in from London, is a strategically-placed poster for Vienna's English Theatre. If you seek the theatre out, you find a modestly plush 250-seat house, described in the programme, with a proper respect for geography, as "the only full time, fully professional producer of English drama east of Great Britain." With the exception of the Donovan Maule Theatre in Nairobi (which makes a surprise appearance on the Spotlight list of British reps) it is British Equity's farthest outpost.

Its guiding spirit, however, is an Austrian named Franz Schafranek, a director (and former actor) married to an American actress, Ruth Brinkmann. She was born in Berlin, but her family came to America as refugees from the Nazis when she was three. It was, however, in Vienna that she met her husband, whose career had already taken in a year with Brecht's Berliner Ensemble and had most recently been working successfully in Sweden.

This, however, was one place where Miss Brinkmann had no desire to live; she wanted either to stay in Austria or to go back to America. Schafranek favoured Austria, but finding work there for an American actress was a problem. So he created some. In 1963 he presented her opposite Anthony Steel (remember Anthony Steel?) in a production of Dear Liar, the two-hander based on the letters of Shaw and Mrs Patrick Campbell.

He hoped for an audience of English-speaking tourists and found one. He also got rave notices in the Austrian Press. In the succeeding years he repeated the experiment, though for some time with less encouraging results. He was now offering plays of which, unlike Dear Liar, his audiences hadn't heard: an adaptation of the Edgar Lee Masters narrative poem Spoon River, or Gallows Humour by Jack Richardson, once regarded (along with Albee, Gelber and Kopit) as a promising American playwright. Only the memory of Dear Liar kept him going. (You might call it Brinkmanship.) Finally he hit on the right format: "modern classics."

From 1969 to 1973 the project operated in a basement theatre in Vienna's Amerika Haus. In 1974 it moved into its present quarters, in a building in the Josefsgasse, owned by the Teachers Association of Vienna, who undertook the renovation of the auditorium. It now operates a year-round season. (By his own account Schafranek never takes a holiday. He says that he tried two years ago, but found that after four days he couldn't stand it.)

Nine or 10 shows are put on every year. And the audience has grown far beyond the tourists. The Viennese come. (It is comforting or disconcerting for the British visitor to Vienna to find that everybody speaks English to him.) There is a subscription audience of 6,000. There is also a subsidy; between the Austrian Government and the city council the English Theatre receives £120,000 this year. By Austrian standards this is pretty small lager; total theatre subsidy in the country amounts to a hundred million. Between them, the Vienna State Opera and the Burgtheater (National Theatre) receive £45 million. As well as its home activities, the English Theatre mounts touring productions of set-texts for schools. Not Shakespeare though; nothing too elaborate.

The programme in the Josefsgasse is pretty much that of a British rep: Ayckbourn, Coward, Wilde, Neil Simon. In 1976 Schafranek brought off something of a coup by directing the world premiere of Tennessee Williams's The Red Devil Battery Sign. Last month, the English Theatre paid its first visit to London, when the Half Moon housed its production of another play by an American veteran, William Saroyan — the distinctly odd Playthings, directed by Mai Zetterling.

There is no permanent company; plays are cast individually in Britain. Like many people, Schafranek mourns a shortage of British directors: "You end up with television directors, and they hire television actors, and nobody can hear them." Top-line actors are hard to come by if you're not paying West End money, but every so often he nets some kind of star.

Joan Fontaine (remember Joan Fontaine?) did excellent business, though her unbudgeable choice of play (The Lion in Winter) was, Schafranek freely admits, "terrible." Anna Neagle, Siobhan McKenna and Peter Wyngarde have also appeared on English Theatre playbills, in very large type. Schafranek believes in promoting his assets. I doubt if any author has received more prominent billing than has Simon Gray on this occasion; his name as playwright, actually eclipses his name as director, not to mention the play itself.

The play is Dog Days, staged at the Oxford Playhouse in 1976, but never seen in London. Gray was persuaded to direct it after three other of his plays had been done in Vienna. This being his first production, he was especially nervous on the first night. (It really was the first night. There had only been a public dress rehearsal, attended by all the ambassadors in town. Embassies in Vienna are very hot on cultural patronage, and seating them according to their seniority is apparently a regular headache. The solution is to give them their own preview, letting them in on a first-come, first-served basis, and damning protocol.)

Reckoning on a quiet debut away from his compatriots, Gray was surprised, and not pleased, to find British critics in attendance. The production was rough-edged in some respects, but it was a great improvement on the rather dingy version in Oxford. Time had helped too; the play was written before Otherwise Engaged and there are similarities which make it look like a trial-run.

In both plays the central character is a publisher with a crumbling marriage, and with a shambling schoolmaster brother to act as a foil. In Otherwise Engaged the fraternal relationship is pushed to one side of the play. In Dog Days it is central. If the publisher here is not exactly Alan Bates, he has some pretensions to worldly and amatory success; the drift of the play is to prove that under the skin the brothers are — well, brothers.

The wit is less glacial than in Otherwise Engaged since the protagonist is much more obviously on the defensive; the play glitters less but touches more. Michael Byrne, who achieved his first success playing opposite Bates in Gray's Butley, is splendidly nervy in the lead.

Gray has carefully labelled the play "a period piece," mindful perhaps that though life in Muswell Hill and Chalk Farm, his chosen locales, has changed little in the past decade, it is fashionably considered bad form to write about it. Gray has a broad-faced resemblance to Howard Brenton and seems to occupy much the same position in fringe-theatre demonology as Brenton does on the left. The Viennese audience seemed puzzled by the play; its nuances are perhaps too English even for the English Theatre. But this tourist was glad he went.

records.title: Illuminating Labour
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Illuminating Labour

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Oxford.

HISTORY tells us that in the Forties and Fifties the Lyric, Hammersmith, performed a valuable function as a launching-pad for plays felt by their producers to be too specialised in appeal for a direct assault on the West End, but capable of being slipped in at a later date to raise the tone of the capital.

That category of plays has grown alarmingly; and it is more than encouraging that the new Lyric, as well as reproducing its predecessor's architecture and decoration, has inherited its policy. We cannot afford to lose it; nobody else is doing the job. No other London theatre could so appropriately have taken the chance on Peter Jenkins's first play; and before dissecting it I had better say that Illuminations is an auspicious debut. It cracks along, taking character, plot and dialogue in its stride. What it doesn't have is unity, which may be appropriate, since Mr Jenkins is writing about the Labour Party, but isn't helpful. He seems to be writing three plays at once.

First there is an allegory, treating equally of the state of the party, of the nation, and of Blackpool, which is where, during a party conference, the play is set. A head porter delivers an opening monologue about how nothing ever changes, whoever's in power; it turns out that he's referring mainly to the state of trade in the four-star hotel that employs him and shelters the delegates, but we can laugh ironically at that.

At curtain-fall a Labour Government has left office and all the characters link hands to sing, with varying degrees of enthusiasm, The Red Flag with the lights of the city winking garishly behind them. These devices might possibly work if they were marked boldly out from everything else, but Richard Cottrell's production tries instead to squeeze them in.

Then there is straight political debate. Late on we have a stand-up fight between two Ministers: on my right, smooth Martin Gale, on my left, rugged Ron Henriques. This is a fizzy scene with Mr Jenkins getting things off his chest through Martin while trying to be dramatically fair to Ron. But he is unfair, and not through any inequality of rhetoric. We don't know Ron; up to now this has been Martin's play, much the most substantial of the three on offer, and it is too late to change tracks.

Martin is Home Secretary, and under fire over public schools. He has a son at Charterhouse; actually his estranged wife is responsible for the boy's education, but his enemies don't know that and he won't talk about it. We're already into a specialised dramatic situation: specialised comic, in fact, since Mr Jenkins surrounds his hero with nice observations on the rigours of luxurious living away from home and with a lady journalist (very Sunday Times), whose indifference to what are supposed to be burning issues tellingly hits off disillusion chic.

And Martin himself, cursing room-service while donning a cap to go off and eat with the real people, is a risible figure, especially as played by Paul Eddington, a high comedian (one of our tallest in fact) whose gift for undercutting eventually extends to himself; fully capable of passion, he still carries absurdity with him. His entourage, consisting of Nigel Stock as an attendant trade-union baron and Bill Nighy as a rising young something, is excellently played; other performances, compounding the imbalance, range from competent to wretched. Mr Jenkins's illuminations are fitful but sparky.

* * *

Unemployment is mentioned. In Snoo Wilson's Space Ache (Tricycle, Kilburn) it's dramatised. Christine, a London teenager without prospects, elects to be deep-frozen for a million years in the hope that there will be a job, and a better world, when she thaws. However, due to some sort of foul-up on the space-craft that's supposed to be taking her, in a sealed canister, for safe-keeping, she revives, and this sends the ship right off course: dislocating most of the solar system, travelling sideways through time, and ending up on Neptune. (Look, I only like Mr Wilson's plays; I don't claim to follow all the details.)

Neptune turns out to be a super-Sybaritic sort of place where you play the fruit machines to obtain an orgasm (and get your arms cut off by the proprietor if you hit too many jackpots) and where pain, as a rare commodity, is highly valued. The health service is highly developed; the surgeons, as Shaw once suggested in The Doctor's Dilemma, pay you for the privilege of letting them cut you up. Chrissy gets rich from having an abortion, and decides anyway that she wants to live, now. (What do you know, Mr Wilson has written a sci-fi temperature-reversed version of The Lady's Not for Burning.)

All ends happy, in a sour kind of way, and Mr Wilson, along with a beguiling imagination and a supply of off-the-wall gags, offers a surprising amount of goodwill. This play is a doodle (the ship's crew are a prolonged RAF joke), but it is not a doddle and Kenneth Chubb's production, which comes untidily wrapped in silver foil, is not up to it. The actors are left, by and large, stranded; some of them may deserve it. Frances Barber as Chris survives best, which seems suitable. Mr Chubb's sloppiness is probably preferable to the solemnity this playwright used to elicit, but is no substitute for the precision he needs.

* * *

There was plenty of tacky acting too in the Oxford Playhouse production of Ariane Mnouchkine's Mephisto (the loss from the title role of Ian McDiarmid, replaced by the director Gordon McDougall, who isn't an actor and doesn't claim to be, was probably demoralising), but the play was worth seeing. Based on a novel by Klaus (son of Thomas) Mann it follows a group of actors and other artists in Germany from Hitler's defeat in 1923 to his ascension in 1933.

Most are Communists; the most vociferous, famous for his Mephistopheles and based on an actual and most celebrated figure, ends up going along with the Nazis, selling his soul, if you like, to himself. Earlier he had been the hardest of all, a bully in fact, on Nazi sympathisers; the play makes scrupulous moral distinctions, and its closing scenes, horrific without explicit horror, tear at you. It sprawls; its narrator seems its least necessary figure. It ends with a salute to the fallen; honourably, it is also a lament for the misled.

* * *

At least at the National Theatre there is a play with a full cast of ace performers. Mind you, in Harold Pinter's The Caretaker (Lyttelton), the last English classic, there are only three characters; and Warren Mitchell's tramp seems somewhat inhibited by his Welsh accent (which is necessary to the part; read the lines). He is an expert wheedler and, towards the close, a very nasty threat; and one realises, as in Death of a Salesman, what a contained actor he is. There are no stray bits of Warren Mitchell left flapping about at the edges; everything goes into the character.

Jonathan Pryce does a snaky virtuoso turn on Mick, oozing through his cadenzas in the kind of cockney (patented by Harold Steptoe) in which all sound seems to proceed from the gums. Kenneth Cranham meanwhile conveys a stilled aggression behind Aston's lobotomised calm; he is recognisably his brother's brother. This falls short of being a definitive production; Kenneth Ives's direction lacks defining power. But it impresses.

records.title: Dancing on rubble
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Dancing on rubble

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

AN-HISTORICAL play is being mounted, amid threats of censorship and closure. The objections centre around scenes of rape and mutilation; this is an invasion drama and the Celts are getting it.

We are not talking about The Romans in Britain. All this happens in The Irish Play, whose author, Ron Hutchinson, can hardly have foreseen how topical his piece would turn out to be. It has some resemblance to an earlier Howard Brenton work, The Churchill Play, with which it shares a director, Barry Kyle, and a theatre, the Warehouse. It is the most joyous new work I remember seeing at this address, and for its author — previously associated with the kind of verbal booze-ups he himself describes as "Irishry" — a great jump forward.

We are in an Irish club in Coventry where, for one night only, there is to be a break in the usual round of bingo and squawky country-and-western bands composed of the entertainment secretary's relatives. The members, or some of them, are presenting a home-brewed play about the twelfth-century Norman incursions which, due to betrayals and rivalries among the natives, set the tone for the ensuing 800 years of Irish history.

The young author's length of hair and the lady director's lack of bra arouse suspicion in the predominantly middle-aged breasts of the club committee, as does the fact that the club president — shortly up for re-election — favours the play and is actually appearing in it as Henry II and most of his barons.

Personal ambitions criss-cross with political protestations, patriotism, as Johnson should have said, being the first refuge of the expatriate. The compulsion to talk about Ireland while living in England is one that Mr Hutchinson shares with his characters. We are always being told (much to our surprise) that not enough plays are being written about Ireland, meaning Ulster and meaning, as a rule, a prescribed political viewpoint. The undying fatuity that a good play can be written about an Issue (and had damn well better be, or our authors will have to stay in and write it on the black-board) must bear hard upon an honest playwright; Mr Hutchinson dramatises the pressures in the committee scene that is the heart of the evening.

At one end of the table is the Socialist demanding that the oppressed peasants of the twelfth century be brought to recognise the advantages of the nationalisation of the means of production, distribution and exchange; at the other (slightly caricatured) the representative of the women's section declaring for the proprieties: "the women will have rape at a pinch but not language"; between them ("I won't take second place to anyone where republican fervour's involved — historically speaking of course") various shades of hypocrisy, sanctimony and self-interest.

Mr Hutchinson's structure is probably more cumbrous than he needs to make his points, and the motives of the increasingly fanatical president remain obscure. Perhaps he's just stage-struck. But the irruption into the clubmen's quarrels of rioting actors in medieval costume brilliantly dramatises the persistence of the past in the present; and when at the end the play-within-a-play takes over the stage-upon-a-stage (as in The Churchill Play and on much the same set), becomes as sombre as farcical.

Factions divide, the costume-trunk is impounded, bully-boys are brought in, the show goes on and the house comes down. There is a clutch of good performances from John Cowley's resident president to the little girl who, after asking, "Is it my turn now?", ends the play by dancing among the rubble, while accompanying herself on the pipe: a superb final image. Mr Hutchinson has written, literally, a play-and-a-half.

* * *

Seamus Finnegan's Act of Union (playing lunchtimes at the Soho Poly and transferring shortly to Action Space, Chenies Street) is the more approved kind of Irish play, set in Belfast. Its decent aim, well achieved, is to tell us what life is like there, emphasising the contradictions while acknowledging (in the words of Valerie Lilley's tart raconteuse housewife) "youse have a hard time understanding the easy bits."

* * *

Lunchtimes at the King's Head is a Schnitzler double-bill: a typical piece of bittersweet badinage called New Year's Eve, and a short story rendered by Stephen Oliver into a mini-opera, A Man of Feeling, with a lovely ironic curl (rather than twist) in its tail. Mr Oliver distinguishes himself as translator, librettist and composer (funny and astringent), Nichola McAuliffe and Oz Clarke as actors and singers. The opera, though not the play, is to go into the evening bill with Coward's Shadow Play next month.

* * *

The Biograph Girl (Phoenix) is Mary Pickford, though, she being dead and unavailable for interview, the publicity has focused on Lillian Gish. If this is confusing so is the show. Miss Pickford (who spends most of the time working for Paramount, not Biograph) shares stage-time with Miss Gish and the implacably visionary D. W. Griffith. Indeed they get more time than she does; or maybe it seems more. Sheila White's Mary is the best thing of the evening; while everyone else is stuffy and noble, she alone has bubble and edge. She gets one of those "Hello Dolly" numbers (which A Chorus Line should have killed) in which she smiles stage-centre while the male cast walk round her telling the world how wonderful she is.

In this context she deserves it, but even she gets murdered by the show. End of Act One she does a satirical number about her wholesome image, which she hates. Then she strips off curls and white frock, smiles wickedly, says "right, it's time to start living that dream" and struts into the wings as preparation for a stunning bad-girl number. Only there isn't one; she doesn't come back. Showbiz logic is denied, and dramatic logic never has a chance. All the show knows is that silents sure were a glamorous era and, hell, there must have been some tragedy, because the talkies came in and ended a lot of careers.

This last thought prompts a pleasantly plaintive trio for three fading stars. (One of them, Mack Sennett, was actually a director by this time, but the show, which models him on Donald O'Connor role in Singin' in the Rain, isn't bothered.) Earlier the composer, David Heneker, has furnished some sprightly enough tunes. But he has also thrown in a tawdry rock (or perhaps just rocky) golddiggers number, a ludicrously earnest chorale sung on the set of Intolerance and called Beyond Babel (given the straight-chinned, eyes-front treatment of Griffith and Company) and a Thirties torcher, school of These Foolish Things, in which D. W. unwisely attempts an exhaustive analysis of his decline in technical terms ("as we call it in the trade, we've reached the gentle fade").

Quality apart, these musical anachronisms have no place in a show which elsewhere plugs its period in a Charlestoning routine called Nineteen Twenty Five. Choreographer Irving Davies meanwhile knows two ways of staging a number. In one the whole company (12) comes downstage, stands sideways on, and does the train sequence, which involves gyrating while clutching the bottom of the person ahead. Soloists come downstage, face full front, sing and never move. After the British musicals that aimed insultingly low (Barnardo) or misguidedly high (Colette), we have — less awful but more painful — the one that sits and decomposes in the middle.

records.title: Fooling about with Hamlet
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby
records.body:
Fooling about with Hamlet

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE Footsbarn Company sounds as if it ought to be a band of German strolling players.

In fact it does stroll and is popular on the Continent. Its base though is Cornwall, and holidaymaking actors who have encountered it there have declared themselves so impressed that they were tempted to throw it all in and go footsbarnstorming themselves.

Last week Footsbarn's Hamlet marked the company's London debut (at the Golden Lane Theatre in the Barbican) and its first tussle with a received text. Generally they work up their own, and what they offered here was not exactly Shakespeare; rather, an acrobatic paraphrase. The favoured method of entry, on to a circular platform apparently covered in green baize, was the graceful pole-vault. Costumes veered from the Orient (Rosencrantz - there was no Guildenstern - looked like a down-at-heel mandarin), through Araby (Hamlet in his mourning state being sternly yashmaked), to Turkey, at which point it met up with the music which, though skilful and effective, recalled the sensation of being seated up by the juke-box in a kebab house.

The performance lasted only two hours, so much went. The first scene was mimed, crowned by the appearance of a horrifically bony ghost. To be or not to be was cut entirely (cheeky) and the other soliloquies pared to the bone. All other speeches were made easy. "Will you listen," said the Ghost, huffily re-interpreting the original "List, list, o list."

Some scenes were re-extended to give scope to the actors' talents for tumbling and funny voices: the gravediggers were upped to three, with a whole new routine; and the players became a collection of Chico Marxes. Melodrama was strong and so were visuals; at the close the bodies were covered by a great dust sheet, on which the lighting picked out a pattern of skulls.

Hamlet made little impression beyond some enthusiastic gibbering and cock-a-doodling when insane, but there was an Ophelia with a will of her own and a Polonius who, for the third time this year, came close to walking off with the play: an inveterate political shover, whether briefing a quintet of spies ("you follow my son Laertes and see what he gets up to") or boasting about his past ("I was in a play once, you know") and ending up spectacularly impaled on Hamlet's spear. In the end, though, I was left wondering what it was all for. There was enough of Hamlet left to arouse our interest in the story, not enough to maintain it.

* * *

Francis King, novelist and critic, has turned playwright with Far East (Belgrade, Coventry), based on his own experiences as a cultural representative in Japan. I have to take his word for the surprising innocence of a 21-year-old Japanese student-cum-houseboy living in with a British Council couple, tainted by their weary worldliness, seduced and then disillusioned by an English mission-girl. Having taken it, I was touched by the writing and by Richard Rees's performance; similarly, by Renu Setna (who is becoming our theatre's all-purpose Oriental) as an elderly Japanese Anglophile, quaking with politeness and declining a visit to England on the grounds that the country now won't be much like Jane Austen. Mr King is very good at marking out and exploiting cultural differences; but his British couple, structurally at the centre of his play, never rise from stereotype.

* * *

A male virgin twice the age of Mr King's is the hero of Rattle of a Simple Man (Savoy), Charles Dyer's West End success of 20 years ago, revived as a vehicle for Pauline Collins and John Alderton and belatedly collected by me. Innocence again comes off best, Messrs Alderton and Dyer (and the audience) empathising mightily with the Mancunian football fan who blunders into a night with a London tart and at curtain-fall is still deciding whether or not to go to bed with her. But if he is real, she is a creature of fantasy: in two senses, since she has to lie continually to make life bearable. She reeks of old psychological theory and dramatic practice, and not all Miss Collins's technique and general lovability can make her believable.

* * *

Nicholas Nickleby (Aldwych) is back in town, and everything else pales. The RSC has accustomed us to marathons: this, though, is their first comic epic. Over the past five years Trevor Nunn has been breeding a richly human company. Dickens seems, in retrospect, their logical goal.

Paradoxically, David Edgar's adaptation, which gets everything in, has more of an individual theatrical identity than more timidly selective versions have done. It is massive but also supple. Each group, each episode, painted in loving detail, is balanced against another and can be whisked away to make room for it. The closing stages of Part One - in which the Crummles' production of Romeo and Juliet is juxtaposed with the attempted seduction of Kate Nickleby, whose fate is momentarily much like Juliet's - is the purest theatrical wizardry.

Formally, indeed, Mr Edgar may well improve on Dickens; he makes the plot not an encumbrance to be stoically borne for the sake of glamorous interludes, but a source both of excitement and meaning.

Only in Dotheboys Hall do we feel the production straining to make points rather than making them. Maybe the use of grown-up actors instead of boys masks the real casual cruelty of the system; certainly Fulton Mackay's Squeers, like Ben Kingsley's before him, is oddly puritanical. Some performances (Jane Downs's Mrs Nickleby and John McEnery's Mantalini) have greatly improved.

Performances I praised before have matured with staggering assurance: Roger Rees's Nicholas, Edward Petherbridge's Newman Noggs exuding pent-up excitement from every clenched joint, David Threlfall's Smike, Bob Peck's double of Hawk and John Browdie (the latter incarnating all the qualities in the production that make one want to cheer), above all John Woodvine's Ralph, a smooth dark villain who greets disaster with an awesome change of gear. Watch how these actors, with the minimum of fuss, simply take and hold the stage - as, on a smaller scale, do Patrick Godfrey's crawling Kenwigs, Timothy Spall's face-stuffing junior Squeers, Janet Dale's painfully refined Mrs Wititterly, Nicholas Gecks's young lord and a dozen others.

Add an imposing double by Lila Kaye and a tremendous treble by Suzanne Bertish (whose sister Jane Bertish, by the way, is good in the play at Coventry). Welcome various newcomers: Christopher Benjamin a juicy Crummles (with the most affecting line in the piece) and Emily Richard and Harriet Walter bringing the heroines fully to life. Acknowledge the whirlwind energy brought to the beneficent Cheeryble menage by David Lloyd Meredith, Hubert Rees, Griffith Jones and Christopher Ravenscroft, while admitting that the flaw they represent in the logic of novel and play alike can never quite be glossed over.

Celebrate the set by John Napier and Dermot Hayes, a drama in itself, and the immense contribution of Stephen Oliver's music. Call down blessings on Mr Nunn and his co-director John Caird. Admit that you have still not done justice to the occasion, and decide that, in all probability, nobody ever will.
production_title: The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby

records.title: Dreaming of Hollywood
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Dreaming of Hollywood

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Leicester.

PETER PRINCE'S Television Times (Warehouse) are hard times for all concerned. The malaise of TV drama is defined as the wish of all concerned that they were making movies instead.

Accordingly we watch a long-established team -- author, director, producer, actor and make-up girl -- at work on the series they hope, wanly, will prove at least to be the prelude to Hollywood: a weekly canter through English history, the kind of project in which, as someone says, the characters inevitably end up telling each other that this place must be Runnymede.

The playwright is the nearest thing on hand to a protagonist, going through marital and professional crises simultaneously. He is given a nervily attractive performance by Karl Johnson, but he is moved into the centre of the piece too late, and out of it too early. Mr Prince seems to be creating problems for him as a means of keeping the show going. Interest is more firmly held by group-portraiture: Richard O'Callaghan as the producer and Ron Cook as the director are a pair of fey, insecure opportunists much given to elaborate parades of petulant despair.

An opening sequence of general paranoia in the control-room is fun; so is a closing lampoon of the BAFTA awards. What goes between is pettiness that Mr Prince observes well enough, but about which he seems neither especially angry nor especially amused. Neither, in consequence, do we. If the aim was to present one medium to another, the result I think will be to increase mutual mistrust.

* * *

Bernard Kops's More Out Than In (Bush) is another play that presents a milieu, and tells us in effect to get on with it. Mr Kops's characters are mental patients, out of hospital but still leading a terrified institutionalised life in a Margate boarding-house. The pity becomes a parade of fixed smiles, and it takes a tough playwright -- a Chekhov or Ben Jonson -- to make that formula work. Mr Kops is far too kind to deal harshly with the deranged; he farms that duty out to his Dickensian landlady.

The production ladles out additional syrup, and the pierhead set usurps space without evoking it. Bill Stewart, with gap teeth and questing eyes, does as much for the principal sufferer as any actor could, but there is some narrow, monotonous acting going on around him.

* * *

Gigi (Haymarket, Leicester) is the stage version of the film musical of the dramatisation of Colette's novel. The first two stages are perhaps beyond recall, but the transition from film to theatre is always threatening. Stage performances, however good, can be replaced; but we know that Leslie Caron, Louis Jourdan, Hermione Gingold, Maurice Chevalier are still there on celluloid, and almost impossible to dislodge. Only one scene here imposes itself; Betty Marsden and Hugh Paddick sing I Remember It Well (as, with all their radio years together, they presumably do) with leisured, affectionate grace.

Everywhere else the production hurries, as if trying to catch some unattainable bus. There is style in Terry Parsons's settings but nowhere else; and on stage this American tourist's view of Paris -- so elegant, so vivacious, so naughty -- is cloying. (The Belle Epoque that Feydeau caricatured had the right idea.) The film got by uplifting views of fountains and statues; having David Firth walk round a post is no real substitute. There is one interesting addition to the score: a song of surrender for Gigi (Janet Shaw), the reluctant courtesan, that may be the most adventurous number Alan Jay Lerner and Frederick Loewe have written.

* * *

On the bank of London's river
Stands a theatre built of concrete,
Built of louring, greying concrete;
Where, to greet the festive season,
Actors who appeared but lately
Dressed as Celts, undressed as Druids
Now have changed their pigmentation,
Now assumed another warpaint.
(Body makeup by Max Factor?
Hard to tell; there is no credit.
Could this be the Hidden Factor?)
On they run in crouching posture,
Bending double, at the double;
(Which is quite a trick to master,
Guaranteed to put your back out);
Tell the tale of Hiawatha,
From the pen of Henry Wadsworth,
He the Fellow, he the Long One;
Though no longer than his poem,
Written in trochaic metre
With no rhyme but lots of rhythm,
As is known to every schoolboy
(Though it seems -- I blush to say it --
Not to every theatre critic);
And no longer than this sentence.
(Can you hear me, Bernard Levin?)
Three the stages in this complex,
In this highly complex complex;
And the play of Hiawatha,
Every afternoon and morning,
Currently adorns the largest:
The Olivier they named it,
Named it for our greatest actor,
He the baron, late of Brighton,
He the Moor and Jew of Venice,
Star of stage and magic lantern
Where he plays sadistic dentist
Or -- I cannot wait to see it --
Ailing father of Al Jolson
In remake of early talkie.
Very big and grand this actor;
Very big and grand his theatre;
And -- despite a smallish cast-list
And, I'd guess, a smallish cost-list --
This production big and grand too.
The adaptor and director --
First name Michael, last Bogdanov --
Specialises in such ventures:
Mystic poems, active poems,
Told for children but not childish.
Some reviewers brought their offspring;
Some brought other people's offspring.
Your reporter, Scrooge incarnate,
Sat without a young companion;
Noted, surly but approving,
How impeccable the silence,
How they watched and did not chatter,
How they listened without coughing.
Plot was not the main attraction;
For the tale was episodic,
Leaving you to muse and wonder
Why his tribe loved Hiawatha,
Just what made him so important.
Spectacle it was that held them,
From the farandole of kerchiefs --
Blue and green and white and yellow --
Through the fingers of the West Wind
(He was Hiawatha's papa)
To the figure of the white prophet,
Posed against a fiery circle,
Gun in hand and set to use it.
(There's a thought to send you home with.)
So to Marty Flood, designer.
Commendations for the teepee
That enveloped all the action,
Gave a focus and a meaning.
Hail the Great Bear, Mishe Mokwa,
Black and huge and slain in combat
(Though if we were meant to triumph
In the death of one so furry,
They don't know the British public:)
There was joking, there was dancing,
And a pretty Minnehaha,
She the interest romantic;
Plus the odd interpolation --
Nothing though to vex the spirit.
'Hiya, Minnie.' 'Hiya, Watha.'
This variety of crassness
Was conspicuous by absence.
I'm surprised you raised the question.
Let me end with something joyful.
Merry Christmas. No, that's next week.
Hang this up outside the theatre:
I enjoyed it. Honest Injun.

records.title: King's double
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
King's double

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE King's Head -- I speak with considerable personal bias -- has offered more consistent pleasure this year than almost any other London theatre. Their new double bill is a lovely finale.

The curtain-raiser is Stephen Oliver's brief opera, A Man of Feeling. Based on a story by Schnitzler, it finds a taut, mocking musical style to match the nervous elegance of its author. The title figure is a man who kills himself when he discovers that his mistress, an aspiring singer, is using him on medical advice as a therapeutic means of recovering her lost voice.

The action is flashback within flashback. Oz Clarke slips lightly between hero, doctors and executor, whose lament 'he was so nice, you know nice' -- a rising vocal line -- embodies Mr Oliver's vivacious flair for marrying his own words to his own music. Nichola McAuliffe gives a sportingly funny account of the peremptory canary.

After this, and playing further tricks with time, love and music, comes Shadow Play, one of the playlets Noel Coward wrote in the late Thirties as vehicles for himself and Gertrude Lawrence, mainly on the theme of how irresistibly sophisticatedly louche the two of them were. In many respects the piece is a compressed and softened version of 'Private Lives.' Here are Simon and Victoria Gayforth, obviously made for each other (or at least not noticeably made for anybody else), but on the brink of divorce.

Simon and Victoria do more than Elyot and Amanda to justify their privileged position; they sing and dance (to three of Coward's best songs, including the unanswerably insistent 'You Were There'), giving their impersonators the chance to play at being Fred and Ginger as well as Noel and Gertie.

John Standing and Estelle Kohler take it with communicated relish. The defiant smile, daring disbelief, flashed at the audience by Mr Standing tapping would conquer a coven of critics. His voice taps too. Some jazz singers are said to sing like instruments (horns usually); Mr Standing, urgently insisting 'Play, Orchestra, Play,' gives out like a rhythmic typewriter not much tone but plenty of beat. He is a bit like Rex Harrison, but a lot more like James Cagney.

With his jauntiness and his timing go something I doubt Coward himself could have equalled: a down-to-earth compassion. He guides Victoria back through her memories when she takes a mild overdose; the nostalgic trip -- fuelled by all that potent cheap music, dramatised in time-slips that seem refreshing even now -- saves their marriage. (Well, what else did you expect?)

Both players find a style of their own for the frightfully brittle badinage. I laughed more than I have at any Coward play in years. Miss Kohler, baring snowy teeth between vermilion lips, is a queen bee: sound all honey, sense all sting. The toughest baby-face since Nelson, she also contrives to be languorously vulnerable. Lizzie Romilly and Anthony Hyde are the interlopers; Miss McAuliffe (who acts contralto, though she sings soprano) and Malcolm Mudie are faithful friends. None of them misses a trick. Add to this an unexpected visual sheen (silky settings by Norman Coates) and fun choreography (David Toguri), and Peter Stevenson's production must count as the best Coward revival since the National's fabled 'Hay Fever.'

* * *

Probably only minor classics can receive such definitive productions. The National knocked off several of them in its early years; I propose to sidle into a consideration of the Old Vic's Trelawny of the Wells by recalling Pinero's play as it appeared on the same stage in 1965. That production originated at Chichester, whose open stage dictated that the changes of scene from actors' lodgings to West End drawing-room to theatre be carried out, most un-Victorianly, in full view of the audience. So one dramatic world appeared before our eyes as another vanished.

You could see and feel the movement of history; a play that was always charming became, for a few moments, great. An exchange about the inevitable tides of fashion (the new drama will in time be old) became both moving and healing: tragic in fact. And in this context the actors playing actors, striking as individuals, built up into a dazzling solid group.

Without this underpinning the play goes soft and, what is worse, slow; affectionate detail becomes obstructive clutter. In Timothy West's production the first scene, in which star actress Rose Trelawny leaves her fellow actors to become engaged to a swell, suffers particularly; most of the troupers have their moments, but they don't cohere or leave us wanting more. But the play is sparked by Pinero's nostalgia for the theatre of his youth, which we should be made to share. We should be made to love the jargon.

When Rose falls out with her posh prospective in-laws she returns to acting and finds she can no longer do it. Real life, among other rich, has spoiled her for make-believe (just the message for today's progressive drama with its class bias reversed) and a new kind of play must be written for her. Tom Wrench, downtrodden actor (back half of dragon in panto) obliges with a comedy called 'Life' and also reunites her with her fiance, who has gone off to be an actor himself, and who, Tom prophesies, may one day be as good as Kean; which, despite a perfectly presentable performance by the lad by David Shaughnessy, is coming it a bit strong.

This area of the play works better. Robert Lindsay is a possessed propulsive Wrench, heavily scarved and generally suggesting the school swot blossoming into a football hero; and Lynne Miller, despite some vocal gaucheries (a very modern Ms, Miss Miller) has a mystery and a conviction to her; there is a palpable churning within this Rose. Bill Fraser as the stern Vice-Chancellor chunters too mildly, but melts most touchingly. The scene in which he, who was once Kean-struck, discovers the old boy's sword in a trunk and tries out a few lines of Richard III, is infallible. I don't think it's sentimental. (More exactly, I don't care.)

To enjoy The Revolt (New End) you have to keep reminding yourself that it was written in 1870, and is thus a striking anticipation of modern feminism. A wife who has minded her husband's house, son and business for four years, determines to walk out and tells him why in detail. He reacts with equally voluble incomprehension; and after her departure he goes to pieces. But the author, Villiers de L'Isle Adam (best known for having rented Axel's Castle to Edmund Wilson), has a joker to play; the lady returns; their marriage has been a commercial contract, and she is now too irrevocably the businesswoman to break it.

Susan Hampshire gets a tremulous self-loathing into this revelation; Olivier Pierre, dangerously boyish, plays his solo with similar panache. Together they hardly connect, but Simone Benmussa's production (set by herself with great precision, especially in the matter of a wrought-iron hatstand) wants them to. They recite at each other.

records.title: Misfits--and marathons
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Misfits--and marathons

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN sums up the achievements of 1980.

IN New York a couple of years ago, at the time of Sweeney Todd and The Elephant Man, I remarked that it was a great season for shows about Victorian misfits.

Nineteen-eighty was the year in which both these productions reached central London stages, along with Nicholas Nickleby and The Streets of London. With The Ticket-of-Leave Man, a nineteenth-century melodrama spiced with social comment announced for production by the National Theatre, it is obvious that the trend still has some distance to run.

There is escapism at work, all right. The word has acquired murky connotations; youngish playwrights use it to mean taking the bread out of their mouths. What is being escaped from, though, is not contemporary life, but the general run of contemporary theatre. What Sweeney Todd and Nicholas Nickleby -- the undoubted peaks of the London year -- had to offer were size and intensity, together with the sure-footed craftsmanship of men who knew what they were doing, even though the ground was fresh to them, and who were extending themselves because their material demanded it.

They also capped the two most important streams of work in the English-speaking theatre of the past decade. Sweeney Todd was the fifth of the Harold Prince-Stephen Sondheim musicals; not quite the best (that, I think, was Pacific Overtures), but, in its narrative force and psychological power, the most expressive of its composer. Nicholas Nickleby gathered up everything that has been achieved by Trevor Nunn and his collaborators since the RSC turnabout of 1976.

In fact the line goes farther back than that. The Theatre Workshop actress Toni Palmer has recently speculated on the production's debt to Joan Littlewood; and it's true that the last show I can remember whose cast seemed so thoroughly committed to what they were presenting and how they were presenting it -- to be so much a part of the play -- was Oh What a Lovely War. In both cases the commitment stemmed from responsibility; they had worked up the material themselves.

They had not, however, written it; and it is here that the RSC's literary bias works in its favour. (The contrary animus practically killed Theatre Workshop.) It's amusing now to remember the beginnings of the fringe, the cries of the Sixties and early Seventies. No more masterpieces. We don't want art, we want events.

There was a certain force to them. Art, as the best critics -- Kenneth Tynan, Pauline Kael -- have realised, is a useless term, signifying whatever one approves of (and can hit other judges over the head with). A great production of a classic is a uniquely energising experience, for audience and participants, but most productions go from ordinary to painful. Who wouldn't rather have an event?

The trouble is you don't achieve one simply by dispensing with a script: the point has been proved, miserably and often. Nor do you get it by 'restructuring' an existing play; it has its own values which are likely to be stronger than those of any director. He may spoil it, but it will murder him, making nobody happy.

With Nicholas Nickleby, by luck or cunning and maybe unrepeatably, the RSC has found the perfect solution: a great text which, not being written in theatrical form, had to be restructured by its interpreters. The fact that our second greatest dramatic genius, the second source of energy in English literature, did not write plays has turned out a theatrical blessing. And, form apart, Dickens is the friendlier and more amenable of the two. (You don't really collaborate with Shakespeare. Ralph Richardson once said he found him too great a genius to be chummy.)

All that really stands in the way is length; most dramatisations squeeze out everything except plot, and a few catch-phrases.
