That marathon theatre disposes of the alleged incompatibility of the two forms was proved by Ken Campbell's version of Illuminatus. I said as much when reviewing it, apparently inspiring Mike Alfreds of Shared Experience to have a go at Bleak House, a production which I imagine influenced the RSC. (Why put a novel on the stage? To share the experience. The pleasure.) If the RSC's achievement exceeds Mr Alfreds's, that is partly because it offers a theatrical statement rather than a virtuoso demonstration that the thing can be done, and partly because of superior resources; in the end a show with 42 actors, a beehive set and lots of music is more fun.

There have been other RSC epics: The Wars of the Roses, the Terry Hands histories, and, also last year (a staggering thought in itself), The Greeks. We came out of them all happily, punchy, impressed and excited, and we applauded the actors. But we never felt it was their show; the concept came first. But then none of them was essentially comic.

To keep the comic spirit alive and at full pressure over eight and a half hours is an extraordinary achievement, and it induces a special exhilaration in the audience. The experience of Nicholas Nickleby is literally unique; though it was prefigured in Trevor Nunn's productions of The Comedy of Errors, The Alchemist and Once in a Lifetime. These were not just funny, but joyous; as his Romeo and Juliet, Macbeth, King Lear, Three Sisters, Juno and the Paycock were not just moving, but searing. What links them is an apparent concern for the human components: actors and audiences. (The range may explain why Nunn has never been accorded the cult-status of the puritan directors -- Lindsay Anderson, William Gaskill, Peter Gill.)

With Sweeney and Nickleby as beacons, we can survey the year for other shared experiences. Shared Experience's own five-man production of Cymbeline was certainly one; the year's best Shakespeare, and proof that the fringe can tackle the classics on its own terms but without resorting to grubby iconoclasm. Juno and The Greeks I've already mentioned. Adrian Noble's Duchess of Malfi was the best production yet at the Royal Exchange, Barry Kyle's Maid's Tragedy one of the best at the Other Place, and The Wild Duck an absorbing return to form for Michael Blakemore.

After which we get to individual performances; to Jonathan Pryce's Hamlet (I've cooled on the production itself, maybe in reaction to the ignorant claims made on its behalf by Christopher Logue, who was in it), to Julie Walters's exuberance in Educating Rita and Julia McKenzie's high notes in On the Twentieth Century, to the riveting calm of James Grout in Make and Break and Lindsay Duncan in Julius Caesar, and to Alec McCowen's breakdown in The Browning Version; the only performance that really turned me on at the National Theatre, whose year was seldom less than respectable, but hardly ever more.

That assessment includes The Romans in Britain, one of the better new plays of the year. Ron Hutchinson's The Irish Play was an ebullient advance with a stark ending, a child dancing in debris. (Some took it to be hopeful; if they're right, the play is as sentimental as its enemies make out.) Paul Kember's Not Quite Jerusalem was an arrival; other promising playwrights were critics (Dusty Hughes, Peter Jenkins, Francis King), which is charming. The best new play, Michael Frayn's Make and Break, was brave, sad and funny, but not quite a knock-out.

Nineteen-eighty was proof that it's possible to have a great year in the theatre without great new plays. If that weren't true, we'd all have cut our throats years ago.

records.title: A matter of adultery
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Of the Dying, of the Dead, of the Living
records.body:
A matter of adultery

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Peter Nichols's new `Passion Play.'

JOKE heard at a New York Christmas party. Moses comes down from Sinai with the Tablets and announces: `First the good news--I got 'em down to 10. Now the bad news--adultery's still in.'

It's still in the theatre as well; for good reason. The falling away of religious sanctions has, in a puzzling way, enriched rather than destroyed the subject. Peter Nichols's Passion Play (Aldwych)--which happens to end with a Christmas party--is about this paradox.

James, a restorer of old paintings, has for years been comfortably and faithfully married to Eleanor, who sings in a choir. Their children have left home. Kate, who is not quite old enough to be their daughter, determinedly seduces James. She is `the common-law widow' of their old friend Albert. His legal widow, Agnes, has never forgiven, and it is she who tells.

Benjamin Whitrow plays James and Billie Whitelaw, Eleanor. When Mr Whitrow returns home after his first night of shame--actually a brief and not too satisfactory evening--another actor, identically dressed, walks on stage with him. This is Anton Rodgers, who plays half of Mr Whitrow's consciousness; the half that prompts him in his alibis, watches to see how they are being received, and persuades him to continue the affair. When Miss Whitelaw has been wised up, she undergoes a similar process of amoebic fission, and acquires Eileen Atkins as a shadow sister, unable to forget and disinclined to forgive.

This is a fruitful but potentially irritating device and Mr Nichols handles it with great cunning. He refrains from springing it on us until we have become firmly involved with the characters as single persons, and he uses it to show how hopelessly confused they are. Kate, single-minded hedonist, and Agnes, unremittingly and puritanically vengeful, need no alter egos.

All the characters exist on artistic fringes--Kate is a not very good photographer; Albert was `a crusading editor'--but only James and Eleanor take their half-heartedness to heart. He spends his working days touching up old Christs, she her nights singing the St Matthew Passion; and all the puns, as you may judge from Mr Nichols's title, are deliberate. The verb `to come' starts echoing through the dialogue before so much as a finger has been--you should pardon the expression--laid.

James upbraids his Old Masters for the irrelevance of their creed to his present plight; while all that Bach--relayed on the radio--becomes a means of timing his exits from Kate's bed. For all his wit and penetration, Mr Nichols has never been a very neat dramatic architect, and though his irreligious imagery is suggestive, there is never a single moment at which it comes into sharp focus; the final Christmas tableau is superb, but for other reasons.

The second act, in which the affair, detected and over, starts up again, rambles somewhat; but though the play would be neater without it, it would also be poorer. James is reduced to declaring that he doesn't know what love means, and has probably never experienced it; but he's also capable of declaring love for both his wife and his mistress--and, in its moment, each of these contradictory avowals rings true, to him and to us.

Possibly what turns him on in Kate is not her sexuality but her rampant sexiness; and a feeling that he owes it to himself, at this late stage, to grab whatever experience is offered. It seems unfair of Eleanor to suffer pain in a world that is supposed to have abolished jealousy--and his attempts to placate her are among the most startling moments in the play. There is in fact quite enough in James to keep two actors employed; and when Mr Whitrow's precision gives way to the fleshiness of Mr Rodgers, we think of a thin man with a fat one trying to get out.

The actresses are a little less happy; each has a good scene of desperation--Miss Whitelaw's disillusioning, a suicide attempt for Miss Atkins--but Mr Nichols seems to be conscientiously trying with them, instead of being instinctively right, as he is with their spouses.

In fact Eleanor's best lines (she knows he's making secret phone calls because she can hear the change jingling in his track-suit pockets when he goes out jogging) all really relate to James. The revelation of her own past infidelity flies around with nowhere to go. Mike Ockrent's production--on a split-level set by Patrick Robertson with resonances domestic, social and psychological--is his smoothest to date.

* * *

`The ones that need to know about it, never know.' That's the Jewish proprietor of a Parisian tailoring business, on genocide. It's what ties together the two threads of Jean-Claude Grumberg's The Workshop (Hampstead), in which the day-to-day, year-to-year existence of a quintet of female employees, sewing and stitching, is counterpointed against memories of war.

We move from 1945 to 1952--when, as the boss says, complaining about low productivity, `we are no longer in the post-war period; we are now again in the pre-war period.' (He adds a reference to `the competition': `All those people who work better than us'.)

Perhaps counterpoint is too sophisticated a term; it might be more truthful to say simply that the two themes are alternated. The play, if one may judge from the author's programme note, has the special grace that just occasionally accrues to autobiographical drama; everything about it strikes true.

M. Grumberg is presumably the strikingly assured little boy who appears in the last scene to announce that his mother is too exhausted to come in today. Up till then she has been the nearest thing to a unifying figure; one of the workers, and the wife--in all likelihood the widow--of a Jewish deportee, trudging from office to office, hoping first for news, then for the form that will guarantee her a pension.

Lynn Farleigh plays her, movingly but quite unsentimentally, as a woman both oppressed and sustained by routine. It is a strength of play and performance that much of the time she is just one of the girls. (Occasionally she recites, but then so do the Misses Whitelaw and Atkins in Passion Play; since actresses don't come much better than these three, it must be some strange English female disease.)

The employer is a figure the author at first seems half inclined to despise but who ends up almost taking over the play; Lee Montague--he should only have more roles this good--pours out hangdog eloquence and bravura misery, matching his ulcers against a rival's dodgy heart. He is well served by Tom Kempinski's translation, which foists some weird phrases on the working class proper; but--except when occasionally abandoned to talk among themselves--the ensembles, under Nicolas Kent's direction, are fine.

* * *

Ekkehard Schall has returned to the Riverside Studios in another Brecht recital. Of the Dying, of the Dead, of the Living (last performance tonight).

This sly dapper man is recognisably a great actor from his businesslike entry. While his voice rasps or caresses, his body modestly transforms itself into an old man, a small boy, or the German soldier's wife peacocking in each bit of invisible finery sent her from the front. Poems which use the concentration camps as a pretext for slogans (what else caused them to be built?) always anger me, but in general the actor lets us see his father-in-law from his best, humorous side.

records.title: Exporting Amadeus
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: I'm Getting My Act Together and Taking It On the Road
A Day in Hollywood, a Night in the Ukraine
records.body:
Exporting Amadeus

ROBERT CUSHMAN reports on a recent visit to Broadway.

A dozen years ago, in an invaluable book called 'The Season,' William Goldman analysed the Broadway phenomenon of the Snob Hit.

'The Snob Hit,' wrote Goldman, 'is rooted in two false beliefs: (1) theatre is "good" for you and (2) British is better. The first accounts for so many Snob Hits being "lofty" in either subject matter or treatment, or both.'

A decline in the British export drive, coupled with rampant protectionism on the part of American Equity, has meant a falling-off in the supply. But the current season has produced a prize specimen. I refer of course to Amadeus, written by Peter Shaffer, staged--with all its National Theatre trappings intact--by Peter Hall, provided with three British actors (Ian McKellen, Tim Curry, Jane Seymour) in its leading roles, and treating of two characters as lofty as any snob could desire: Mozart and God.

I am beginning to sound patronising, one of the two sins besetting critics who write about Shaffer (the other is being senselessly ecstatic). Contemplating this account of the hatred of the self-proclaimed mediocrity Salieri for the genius Mozart, reviewers in both London and New York have proclaimed the thing impossible on the grounds that mediocrity would be incapable of recognising genius anyway and therefore would not be jealous.

The critics have enjoyed themselves defending Mozart (they appreciate him, of course, so there's no question of their being mediocre) against Shaffer's supposed portrayal of him as a foul-mouthed buffoon. Actually--and Tim Curry's effervescent performance makes this even clearer than in London--Shaffer's Mozart, consistently right in his judgments of his own work and everybody else's, is bright but fatally tactless. I don't know what Mozart was really like, but Shaffer's version convinces for the duration of the play. As a character he wears better than Salieri.

On the assumption that it could equally well apply to any great artist, I can accept as a metaphor the idea of Mozart as God's instrument. I could even, while listening to Paul Scofield's trumpeting on the London first night of Salieri's deity-defying speech, accept it as a dramatic fact; but not thereafter.

The play's major flaw is not intellectual, but structural; it has no second act. Salieri tells us that his quarrel is not with Mozart, but with God. God, however, has not been established; so we get a succession of scenes from Mozart's last years--scenes which, by the play's own rules, are irrelevant. It doesn't matter how great, even whether, Salieri did love him; his jealousy, once established, is never explored; it might be interesting, but the play has no time for anything so vulgar.

The much-bruited rewrites undertaken for New York and to be incorporated later this year in London make no essential difference. The greatest gain is the loss of Salieri's sepulchral manservants; one lay figure the better. A sequence on 'The Magic Flute,' and its antagonising of the Freemasons, adds to the anecdote, and also, of course, to the parade of greatest hits. A final encounter between Mozart and Salieri, made conclusive of the latter's masquerade as messenger of death, can hardly crown a relationship that never existed.

The New York audience, the night I went, gave the play a standing ovation. A cynical friend maintains that Broadway audiences always do this, to justify to themselves the mountainous cost of the evening out. My experience was different; I saw houses rise only to Ian McKellen and to Jim Dale in Barnum--another visiting star in a virtuoso role.

Neither as it happens is being seen at his best. McKellen is not yet at the stage where he can float through a role, using the fact of stardom for water-wings. Salieri offers him one emotion, plus elementary quick-changes from youth to old age. He wolfs that down in about 10 minutes and goes hungry for the rest of the evening.

Visually, Peter Hall's production is handsomer than his London version, though he has mislaid the running conceit of the play as opera. The antiphonal messengers called the Venticelli now sound--as they were originally described by Martin Esslin, who should know--like bad radio drama.

* * *

'Amadeus' apart, the straight play most approved by New York critics and audiences is Paul Osborn's Morning's at Seven, a quirky small-town comedy first staged (unsuccessfully) in 1939. It shows four sisters growing old vengefully.

The precise tone, one of delicate brutality, is difficult to establish, and it has eluded this production by Vivian Matalon, one-time director of Hampstead Theatre Club, before that an actor specialising in playing Americans and now in process of becoming one. The production is graced, all too consciously, by two senior movie stars, Maureen O'Sullivan and Teresa Wright; and the play turns into a homey soporific.

I had fears that Hugh Leonard's A Life, which I caught at the end of a brief run, would be another; it does include some facile juxtapositions of past and present, but its central character--a dry and dying civil servant--is written, and was played by Roy Dotrice (in a good play at last), with invigorating tartness.

Even more surprising was Mark Medoff's Children of a Lesser God, known locally as 'the deaf play'; I had avoided it on previous visits, scarred by earlier encounters with the mixture of earnestness and sentimentality Broadway reserves for the fashionable themes of sickness, disability and death. This piece, however, is honestly emotional: a love story--in fact. Phyllis Frelich, who is herself deaf, plays an embittered rebellious girl who marries her speech-teacher, a knock-out performance by David Ackroyd, who has to speak for both of them.

Clinical drama can be its own form of escapism, and it remains true that for plays that look out at America you have to go, selectively, off Broadway. Ted Tally, whose Captain Scott play, 'Terra Nova,' was seen at Chichester last year, tries contemporary satire in Coming Attractions, which takes a single obvious idea--murder can make a man a celebrity--and gives it a thorough pounding. There are good jokes (a judge asks, 'Is this a first offence? I mean, has he ever killed 30 people before?') and, against the odds, a chilling ending when the hero goes to the chair.

There are also songs, which prompts a consideration of small musicals. Off Broadway they can run eternally; I'm Getting My Act Together and Taking It On the Road (due in London soon) has been around for years, though not as many as its faded feminist pointmaking may suggest.

A marvellous miniature show called Tintypes, a musical history of melting-pot America pre-1914, went Broadway and died. Off-off Broadway, an hour's worth of Stephen Sondheim songs, written for and cut from other shows, were strung together under the title Marry Me a Little to depict, with very little forcing, the fears and fantasies of two impoverished young Brooklynites.

Some shows can expand and live. On the coldest Christmas Day for 100 years, with both the wind and the theatres going full blast, I saw A Day in Hollywood, a Night in the Ukraine, its singalong first-half transformed to advantage, its Marxist second feeling the lack of a feasible Groucho and Harpo, but still indestructibly funny. A hit on Broadway, as it never was in the West End, the show is perhaps the oddest offering yet laid on the shrine of nostalgia.

Most current musicals subscribe in some way. The latest revival is Brigadoon, surviving mainly on Frederick Loewe's score, a succession of ballads that outclasses his later music for 'My Fair Lady.' 'Barnum' is nothing, though Jim Dale, singing while crossing a tight-rope (two new accomplishments for him), inspires patriotic as well as hospitable affection. The spectacular 42nd Street, 22 girls tapping as the curtain rises, is impossible to resist or--a day later--to remember.

'42nd Street,' though, is already yesterday's sensation. The new one is, of all things, The Pirates of Penzance: a smash last year in Central Park and now warming up the inhuman Uris Theatre. Linda Ronstadt, singing beautifully, though not acting at all, may have been the initial draw, but the real driving force is Kevin Kline, an actor extraordinarily good-looking for a comedian or extraordinarily funny for a leading man, and wildly acrobatic for either; Burt Lancaster's Crimson Pirate with vocals. His contortions, and his good humour, seem to have infected the entire cast, chorus especially.

Wilford Leach's production is eclectic, with George Rose revivifying traditional Savoy routines while a synthesiser takes over the string parts in the pit. The original may be, in all senses, amplified, but it is never (well, not very often) contradicted. Snobs go--or stay--home.

A Day in Hollywood, a Night in the Ukraine

records.title: The Marathon Man
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The Marathon Man

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Shaw at the National.

Shaw used to patronise Shakespeare by declaring that his sound counted for far more than his sense: 'Tested by the brain it is ridiculous; tested by the ear it is sublime.' Those words, and their music, rebound heavily upon him in the National Theatre's production of Man and Superman (Olivier) in its five-hour entirety.

Two of those five hours are occupied by the play's third act; the one, generally cut, in which Jack Tanner, fleeing from London to Granada and points beyond in order to escape the marital clutches of Ann Whitefield, is held up by bandits in the Sierra Nevada and dreams of himself as a Don Juan governed by intellectual passions consigned to a sybaritic Hell ruled over by a Devil who greatly resembles the brigand chief, not least in being a good talker.

He is allotted one of Shaw's longest, wittiest and most persuasive speeches, on man's essential destructiveness. It goes right against the official Shavian ethic (the play was written in his most buoyant period) and is immediately countered by Juan, who proclaims that humanity is obsessed not by death but by ideals, and that what all these amount to is the drive to create ever more intelligent forms of life. He goes on arguing this for the rest of the scene, and gets only token rebuttals; for once Shaw seems disinclined to risk giving the Devil the best tunes.

The cliche is apposite; since what holds us in this scene--and it works, in Christopher Morahan's production, astonishingly well--are the melodies and rhythms of the prose. (There are also bursts of real music from, naturally, 'Don Giovanni': putting this play on alongside Amadeus suggests that a spirit of economy is beginning to haunt the South Bank.)

As Juan, Daniel Massey's natural musicality stands him in magnificent stead; his speaking, a sensuous pleasure in itself, is also a vehicle of character. He only loses the thread towards the end, when he gives up all pretence of talking to his companions and concentrates uninterruptedly on the audience. Michael Bryant, a Satanic maitre d'hotel, is his deceptive opponent, and the other participants--Penelope Wilton's Dona Ana, respectable even when damned, and Basil Henson as her father, still a man of stone on the outside, but all sentiment within--are likewise impeccable.

Ana says little, but she has the last word. The Devil, after Juan's departure, happens to mention the concept of the Superman leaving Ana, suddenly revealed as eternal woman, determined to give birth to it, which means finding the right father. Juan, who thought he was done with sex, is, to judge from the determined wonder in Miss Wilton's voice, doomed all over again; and by his own philosophy. At which point Tanner is here merely picked up and put down.

Thus we return to the social-sexual comedy generally known as 'Man and Superman' to find it--as Juan found Hell after a taste of heavenly contemplation--less amusing than it might be. Tanner's chat about the Life Force, Ann's compulsive wiles, may make more intellectual sense, but their accustomed comic energy is diminished. Maybe this is a matter of aesthetic disproportion; a sex comedy lasting five hours is excessive, even with overtones. But the production too is at fault; Mr Massey's doomed white-suited gyrations as the trap closes are exquisitely done but he is too helpless a victim from the start. Both he and Mr Henson (unstoned as Ramsden) could do with more Edwardian bluster, as Ralph Koltai's first-act set in battleship grey (limbering up for some glowing abstract transformations as the scene moves outwards) could do, at this stage, with more Edwardian solidity.

Miss Wilton, conversely, gives little sign of the girlish vulnerability that takes in most of the men. The production is, however, exceptionally clear; and the mother-wit of play and players guarantees considerable pleasure. Which reminds me that maybe the most creative performance is given by Antonia Pemberton as Ann's mother, scoffing sweets in the delight of hearing someone insult her child. The subsidiary romance--English ironclad and American innocent--is brightly handled by Anna Carteret and Greg Hicks.

* * *

Stanley Price's Moving (Queens) is a fairly pleasant comedy about the traumas of selling a house, flawed by pretentiousness, itself possibly the result of flagging invention. Maybe if Mr Price had been able to construct a farcically logical chain of events from the inability of his protagonists to decide between rival offers, despite the necessity to reach a quick completion over the house they want, he would not have felt obliged to pad out his second half with reflections on the property market as a reflection of middle-class values: a subject that should be pushed harder if touched at all, but is here merely picked up and put down.

As often happens in West End comedy, the funny lines have no connection to the situation; they are merely whimsical metaphors for whatever happens to have crossed the speaker's mind. Mr Price goes very easy on his characters; of course in real life most people do manage to dispose of their homes without having nervous breakdowns, but there are occasions when real life should be kept away from the theatre.

The standard pair in the middle are Peter Jeffrey, who seems very real, and Penelope Keith, who adds to her familiar skills a surprising capacity for tears. Roger Lloyd Pack is an enlivening presence as a decorator, with a sympathetic whine in his voice and furrows in his cheeks. Paul Scofield must have been like this when he played his dead common role in 'Expresso Bongo.'

* * *

Characters and situations closely related to the above but younger, appear in Jonathan Gems's Naked Robots (Warehouse). In both a young actress appears with an I've-just-had-an-abortion look on her face (defiant in the West End, woebegone on the fringe, which has always been the place for sentiment); Mr Gems's teen and twenties fashion freaks would like a decent place to live instead of one room piled high with mattresses, but it would cost them £40,000.

Mr Gems has written an unarguably terrible play which stubbornly, despite great provocation, refused to bore me. His characters are: a costume designer, a singer, a dope-pusher, a lost girl, and a rock manager; all sliding or slid, all with deeply conventional aspirations which the author gently satirises, but with which he seems to have no basic quarrel. Accordingly he might have given them a firm conventional structure to mirror and support them.

His current stop-go methods are underlined in John Caird's production, which gets no rhythm going and leaves five uneasy actors delivering possibly amusing lines into stony silence. Mr Gems has an excellent ear; you never groan at his dialogue as you do at some currently successful plays. The hero's profession has inspired Ultz to design spectacular costumes, as for a sci-fi panto cast with Michelin men.

* * *

A group called Cheek by Jowl announce a radical new version of 'Tis Pity She's a Whore (Theatre Space, Covent Garden). Well, they've cut a sub-plot, and they play in modern dress; but that's not new. What is, is the quiet conviction with which they invest the sober verse and lurid action, though limitations of space, skill and temperament promote a nagging or plain sulky delivery of potentially incendiary material. They should refrain from fully audible soliloquial ad-libs, which are not only an abomination which may not matter, but silly, which does.

records.title: Restoration vaudeville
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Restoration vaudeville

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Oxford.

The praise deservedly heaped on Peter Nichols's Passion Play has had one bemusing aspect. Mr Nichols has been widely credited with inventing the device of the on-stage alter ego: a strange claim when no less than half a dozen of them are cavorting about the stage--even if to no particular purpose--in They're Playing Our Song. Brian Friel's Philadelphia Here I Come!, built around an identical device, is of course ancient history: a dozen years old if it's a day. Even further back, authors used to save the management the cost of an extra actor by employing the aside. Asides came in two categories--the conspiratorial and the conscience-stricken--and the employment of both is the most rewarding feature of Vanbrugh's The Relapse, as revived at the Old Vic.

The Relapse is a late Restoration comedy (first production 1696) with honestly confused ideas about morality. The reformed rake Loveless has married the virtuous Amanda and is attracted by her friend Berinthia, who encourages him off to bed, to her satisfaction and to the author's obvious amusement and probable approval. Meanwhile Amanda is being pursued by everybody's old friend Worthy, but rejects him; again to cheers from her creator. The last scene, naturally, includes a masque, which proclaims that 'the joys of life and love are in variety.' (In this production the words are repeated at the final curtain.)

This variety might conceivably include fidelity: each to his or her own kick. But what turns Loveless on may--in fact, does--hurt Amanda; Vanbrugh is too truthful to deny this, too nervous to give it full expression. So dramatically their relationship, which starts the play, must crumble away; by the end we have no idea what they think of each other. But on the way through Vanbrugh has given Loveless his full share of conscience-stricken asides; they anticipate Mr Nichols's male double-act, and they are delivered by Richard Kay.

The divided lady--again as with Mr Nichols--is less well served; when called on for heart-searching, Maureen O'Brien delivers, but she has a habit of demonstrating a line, like a salesman, instead of speaking it. (She is lumbered with a newly written prologue, which makes agonisingly arch jokes about arts subsidy and, yet again, The Romans in Britain. The Relapse is a tough play to do, and it hardly needs extra handicaps.)

The main action tells us that some enjoy themselves, others suffer; the positions may be reversed and meantime the only unforgivable sins are to crow or to whine. This is the only link with the second action, whose central character, Lord Foppington, the self-made dandy, is guilty of the first offence and barely avoids the second.

Foppington begins the play as a specialty act--consulting and insulting an army of costumiers, reeling off the peacocking pleasures of his day--then develops into a person steely, selfish and unscrupulous beneath the enveloping wigs (one of them here the colour of a Florida grapefruit). John Nettles's performance, the surest of the evening, is best when he gets to the undercoating: his are the conspiratorial asides, with the audience as his partners in crime.

Both sections of the play are interesting, but this is almost an additional hazard; one continually resents being dragged away from either of them. Their rhythms, too, are totally different: one a tight-knit farcical intrigue, the other a discursive essay on sex. Maybe a director could find some striking visual metaphor to link them (Adrian Vaux's set here is a pleasingly discreet affair of black and white), but Michael Simpson is not much to be blamed for failing to find one. This, like most Restoration comedies, is a vaudeville bill and he has not--with a few promising exceptions, such as Julia Swift's bumpkin Hoyden, ambitious for London life and lust--the actors to fill it.

* * *

I suspect that one sign of a weak theatre is an obsessive verbal harping on class. It is a fine subject for comedy, as Vanbrugh shows without ever mentioning the subject.

Philip Barry's 1939 comedy The Philadelphia Story (Oxford Playhouse) does nothing but mention it, but has no way of transferring its talk into action. The immensely wealthy Tracy Lord decides not to marry her stuffy fiance (up from the mines into management), but to return to her first husband, C. K. Dexter-Haven, noted yachtsman. En route she has a flirtation with newspaperman Mike Connor, also up from poverty, and a touch embittered, but all right because he has style.

Barry's values are not so different from Vanbrugh's, but (a) Vanbrugh doesn't go on about them and (b) he justifies them in the texture of his writing. Barry's wit is woolly, and his passionate declarations painfully lush; he even, in passing, preaches. So at least it seems in Gordon McDougall's woefully ill-timed production; two film versions have suggested different, but they were suffused in stardust (incidentally adding two further layers of mythology to complicate the lives of future interpreters).

Only Robert Beatty and Tenniel Evans, in sideline roles, come off with complete credit; add, maybe, Paul Herzberg in a role axed from the movies to fatten the part of Dexter, who in his original emaciated state seems more chorus than protagonist. Lewis Fiander does well by the first function, but cannot rise to the second. Mike's frigidity is well dispensed by Alan Rickman, but it ends the entire role. Gayle Hunnicutt offers an intelligent reading of Tracy's lines, but there seems to be nothing flowing beneath.

records.title: Jugular vein
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Jugular vein

Robert Cushman on rare Marlowe

The Glasgow Citizens' company, off-form in their recent work, bounce back characteristically with The Massacre at Paris, Christopher Marlowe's brusque celebration of the slaughter of St Bartholomew's Eve, 1572.

The play, likely Marlowe's last, has come down to us in mangled form, and was probably no paragon even when intact. Speeding through the adjacent reigns of three French kings, it devotes only its first half to its ostensible subject. Catholic thugs murder Protestant ninnies in a succession of brief, heartless scenes, masterminded by the Duke of Guise, whom the Elizabethans took to be the very model of a modern Machiavellian.

The action then continues more diffusely, but in the same vein (half jocular, half jugular); Guise continues to knock off all who have offended him until King Henry III knocks him off. A surviving brother then has the king killed, by a friar; Henry dies, denouncing the Papacy and paying devout respects to the Queen of England.

Philip Prowse's production seizes on these last compliments, and on the probability that the play as we have it is a text cut for touring purposes, to bring on Queen Bess herself, silently smiling from a balcony while the piece is performed for her by a touring troupe of limited resources. The Citizens' can be very scholarly when it suits them. I had heard that they were performing the play with a cast of four, which, for a play with 28 named characters, seemed perverse. In fact they have added three supers, but one of these is permanently occupied as Elizabeth.

They still play a full text, with much frantic and amusing quick-changing, helped of course by the fact that few people in this play stay around very long; it has the briskest death-rate in English drama. The production manages to place the play as a piece of Tudor propaganda while still entering fully into its spirit. Marlowe plainly regarded murder with schoolboy relish. Reprehensible it may be, but the play tells you more about the springs of atrocity than any more tasteful piece.

Acting in Glasgow seems to be looking up. Of the four principals, Steven Dartnell is rather stiff but John Breck neatly differentiates a decadent king who sniggers from one who merely shakes, and Jill Spurrier honks imposingly as all the women and several of the men, the latter including a bespectacled massacre victim who stammers out an eloquent summary of Protestant theology before being despatched. Robert Gwilym, one of the Citizens' recurring pale young men, is chilling and capable in the guise of Guise.

It remains a weakness of this company that they cannot cope coherently with long speeches, prose or verse, but Mr Prowse's set is of the expected richness: carpeted stairs sweeping down past the proscenium to be met by a series of black-draped plinths topped with candles. No other theatre in Britain would have the cheek to do this play so well.

* * *

Marlowe's glancingly sardonic dismissals of religion are considerably more effective than the more solemn pummellings administered by Nick Darke in Joint Stock's Say Your Prayers (Riverside Studios). Here the particular target is St Paul, seen converting a Roman slave with a weakness for the sound of his own voice (i.e., a born preacher) and incidentally disabusing him of the absurd belief that his girl-friend might be worthy of serious consideration.

Paul's other adversary is an atheistic girl artist in love with a frog; the frog comments on the action while sitting, like the one Danny Kaye used to sing about, on a lilypad. Paul thus stands convicted not only of sexism, but (the ugliest coinage yet in the progressive lexicon) speciesism.

Mr Darke doesn't go in for jargon and his debate might gather some rhetorical force if he didn't keep interrupting it, either with rock-numbers or with flashes to the present. Here we behold an American pop evangelist, enlisting God on the side of law and order, and a beleaguered English priest glumly awaiting a congregation of four, while--since he is plainly, in worldly terms, on the losing side--confusing the argument. We start thinking of other recent activities of the church: in El Salvador, for example--that might confuse it even more. As it is, Mr Darke's play appears as blinkered and arid as its target. It is in the main limply performed, though Philip Donaghy does a good fanatic's turn as Paul and Richard Howard is together as the object of his attentions.

* * *

Nikolai Erdman's The Suicide (Aldwych) is not the near-masterpiece it seemed two years ago at the Other Place. There is a lack of sustained brio in the blow-up of Ron Daniels's production, and a fuzziness in Peter Tegel's translation. But greatness is achieved in the last half-hour when Roger Rees as Podsekalnikov, driven to contemplate if not actually to take desperate measures by his failure either to find a job or learn the tuba, delivers his glorious tirade defying all ideologies and proclaiming the last human right: the right to say that life is hard.

There is now a beautiful physical as well as vocal fluency in Mr Rees's performance; watch him, in one arc of movement, bring a pistol heroically to his head and end up quietly depositing it in a packing-case. There is a similar command of instant gear-change in Susan Tracy's performance of his wife, uncertain whether or not she is his widow.

There is, too, a fair amount of amusement still in the Jonsonian crew of predators, each hoping to benefit (morally, of course) from the suicide's suicide. Sharpest among them are Edward Petherbridge, Ian McNiece and (one to watch) Nicholas Gecks. Some other performances are below RSC standard; at least I trust they are.

* * *

Suburban Strains (Roundhouse) is Alan Ayckbourn's musical. His lyrics cover the intended ground, though sometimes out of breath, and they rhyme when they mean to rhyme (a relief after some of those in Say Your Prayers), but they lack shine. Paul Todd's music seldom soars, and its most memorable phrase recalls one from Evita. (The idea of pastiche Andrew Lloyd Webber is a disturbing threat to the accustomed order of things.) But there is a quintet number 'What Do They Expect' that lifts the whole show.

The schoolmistress-heroine is glimpsed simultaneously at two stages of her life entertaining two different men, one of whom will become her lover. Meanwhile her estranged husband is seen with an old flame who may possibly be re-lit. All are asking the same eternal titular question. And it is clear that the presence of music, never mind its handling, has done something for Mr Ayckbourn; it has taken his chill off.

It hasn't made him sentimental (if you except a rather glib ending), but it has let his characters speak out, becoming surprisingly likeable in the process, and it has given a new glow to his durable furnishings.

* * *

In Hobson's Choice (Lyric, Hammersmith) Arthur Lowe, sounding very much like Les Dawson, is an unexpectedly gentle patriarch: often funny but his slow-burn timing infects the rest of the production. Ronald Pickup acts Willie Mossop impeccably, but since he is obviously nobody's worm there is not much surprise in his turning. Julia McKenzie is a commanding Maggie and the play is virtually indestructible.

records.title: Tom among the thieves
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Tom among the thieves

THEATRE

Robert Cushman on a Victorian thriller and a new play by Howard Barker

Tom Taylor, the Victorian playwright who edited Punch and wrote The Ticket-of-Leave Man (Cottesloe), seems to have been an optimistic soul.

The play revolves around a young Lancastrian who comes to London, falls among thieves, and is unjustly arrested for passing a forged banknote. He goes to jail for three years and emerges, not in the least embittered, indeed positively ennobled. 'This place,' he says in a letter to his sweetheart, 'has made a man of me.'

Besides this implausibility, the others that necessarily arise in this vintage thriller (the play is that, rather than a melodrama) are of small account and are anyway -- especially in this production -- greatly enjoyable. The tribulations of our hero Bob Brierly are, except on a personal level, difficult to take seriously; he was innocent anyway, though inclined to carelessness and champagne, and his difficulties in finding work when released early, for good behaviour, on a 'ticket of leave,' are put down neither to his own inadequacies nor to those of society; they are solely due to the machinations of the two crooks who first ruined him and want to keep him in their power.

Opposing them is a plainclothes detective called Hawkshaw, who has a private feud going with the more daring of the wrong'uns, Jem Dalton, known as The Tiger. Goodie and baddie alike are masters of disguise, capable of sitting out an entire first act on either side of a restaurant garden without recognising each other. The play provides us with six locales, abundantly peopled. I don't suppose Taylor had any particular intention of putting Victorian society on stage; he just happened to be writing for a theatre that, as a matter of course, employed a large number of actors.

We have few such establishments ourselves, and are the happier to see a large-scale production when we can get it. The director, Piers Haggard, manoeuvres the swells and day-trippers of Act One and the navvies drinking at the dockside pub (same proprietor, down in the world) in Act Four with delightful adroitness. Taylor gives them fruity lines to speak, even if some of the fruit is preserved. Dickens apparently selected him to dramatise A Tale of Two Cities, perhaps making him a gift of something he would otherwise have borrowed. In this play we have a character called St Evremond, nee Traddles; and a landlady who talks like Sairey Gamp gone respectable. What he didn't get from Dickens was moral complexity: any sense that the law might ever be wrong or respectability a mask.

As a television director, Mr Haggard has demonstrated an immaculate sense of style and rhythm: I'm thinking not just of Pennies from Heaven, but of a production years ago of Gershwin's Tip-Toes, kept masterfully on the edge of absurdity. He brings off the same trick here. There is a musical trio in attendance; and their comments -- sad, baleful or romantic -- provide a necessary comic distance. Often they play behind speeches which are, however, delivered with perfect seriousness: a wonderful counterpoint.

Paul Copley's performance as Bob, in its successive shows of weakness and strength, has a depth I would not have thought the play capable of supporting; simple from moment to moment, complex in effect, it is the equal of Roger Rees's Nicholas Nickleby. Michael Elphick as Hawkshaw (with his extraordinary ideas of secrecy) and Jack Shepherd as Dalton are allowed more latitude; but if their swagger is playful it is never ludicrous.

Mr Haggard has a stunning cast: Rebecca Saire as heroine, Harry Landis as second villain, Pat Heywood as loquacious granny, Keita Jayne as infant prodigal, and Tim Wylton as comic lovers (and minor theatricals, which seems to have been a Victorian rule), Anthony Langdon as publican, all in key. Robin Don's set, which frames the play without patronising it, supports the finest succession of stage pictures currently available in the metropolis.

* * *

Howard Barker's No End of Blame (Oxford Playhouse) is also, in several senses, a play of notable pictures. It begins on a World War I battlefield where a Hungarian soldier, Grigor, confronts a naked, terrified woman. He is drawing her. His friend Bela comes on and, being of a more practical temperament, tries to rape her; though, not being as practical as all that, he takes all his own clothes off first. This leads to the two men being arrested.

Bela is a cartoonist by vocation and after the war we find him and Grigor at art-school in Budapest. Bela tires of conventional standards and goes off to Moscow. It is a revolutionary thaw-period, but eventually he finds himself in trouble for producing unhelpfully critical work, and is most ungently rebuked by a committee of politicians and bureaucrats. (The contrasting scenes are well-handled and probably, as far as they go, just.)

After the war this, as it might be, Vicky is retired from, as it might be, the Evening Standard and replaced by, as it might be, Jak, who promises more laughs. Bela attempts suicide and is last seen in a wheelchair in a mental hospital. Next to him sits Grigor, who has periodically reappeared, and who proves disconcertingly capable of working magic. Bela, at first beyond caring, ends calling for a pencil.

I suspect that Mr Barker would not much approve of this effortfully resonant ending if it turned up (as it very well might) in a Peter Shaffer play. His works are difficult to summarise because they proceed by incidents. As far as I can judge, Bela is a permanent rebel with a disabling strain of weakness. (He tries in the first scene to shoot an officer, but can't go through with it.) 'I believe the cartoon to be the lowest -- and most important -- form of art,' he says for, I assume, his author.

He refuses to worship either high art or any political creed. He is caught between two credos. One is 'cartoons are not about me, they're about us, I don't like me'; the other, 'I can only draw what I see.' He is bad at relationships; but here I falter, because Mr Barker isn't good at them either. It is difficult to make much of Grigor or of the girl who accompanies the two of them. Paul Freeman plays him well, but leaves little mark. He is making, after all, the same statement in a succession of circumstances. I fancy that Mr Barker's roles are not actually very rewarding to actors: what is there to do with them once you have got your tongue round the ornate sentences? Most of the performers here get their chance to play the icy orator. One of the Russians talks of 'stretching our little fingers out to try and catch the swinging boot of history'; who knows whether this is parody? Bela's cartoons have been drawn by Gerald Scarfe and they are fierce.

Thomas Middleton's view of humanity was hardly rosier than Mr Barker's, but he seems to have agonised less over it; in his comedies, anyway. The greatest of them, A Chaste Maid in Cheapside, presents a Jacobean London divided into cuckolds, lechers, whores and, nastiest of all, Puritans; with a couple of true lovers tossed in to make a plot.

The Cherub company, in their production at Theatre Space, come near to stylising the play out of existence. They seem intelligent and, by and large, talented; but they are too keen to let us know that the play's society is corrupt. It is also fun: a fact that in the second act gets inescapably through to the Cherubs, to the great benefit of them, us and the play. This week No End of Blame is playing at the Arts Centre, Warwick University; A Chaste Maid in Cheapside at the Upstream Theatre Club, Short Street, SE1.

records.title: Acting your age
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
THEATRE

Acting your age

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Turgenev at the National

ACCORDING to their creators Iago was 28 and Hedda Gabler 29. To these little-known dramatic facts -- unscrupulously concealed by generations of middle-aged actors and their admirers -- may be added a third: Ivan Turgenev swears that Natalya Petrovna, protagonist of A Month in the Country (Olivier), was exactly the same age as Miss Gabler.

Thus she is played by Francesca Annis in Peter Gill's new production and the effect is most instructive. Natalya, the wife of a rich Russian landowner, lives in perfect comfort; not only is her husband devoted to her, though inclined to neglect her for the management of his estate, but she has a resident platonic lover to be alternately teased and cultivated. She then falls in love with her son's tutor, a youth of 21.

Or at least she thinks she does. Maybe she fools herself and this is how Miss Annis seems to be playing her. What happens is that Natalya sees the tutor playing at kites with her 17-year-old ward, and feels jealous. (Miss Annis tellingly signals the onset of emotion by gazing fixedly at the spot where the young couple have lately stood.) They make her feel her age, and she complains to her standby, Rakitin, about what fogies the two of them are becoming.

The joke of course is that she is still presentably young; from these fabricated fears springs a fabricated passion, one she believes she owes it to herself to feel. Jealous of her ward Vera, she plots to have her married off to a local buffoon; and, by one of the play's numberless ironies, though she gives up on the plan, it still goes through. Exit Vera; exit Rakitin whose own passion has been exposed in the light generated by the new one; exit young Belyaev, scared and flattered by the emotions he has stirred and which he does not reciprocate; exit the indispensable match-making doctor, in tandem with the household governess. Natalya is left alone with her husband, which may not be the worst thing that could happen to her, though at curtain-fall this is understandably not how she sees it.

So we have a labyrinthine comedy of self-deception, meticulously plotted by Mr Gill, whose gift for clarifying emotional intricacies is almost unmatched among British directors. Our rewards are a good deal of hard-headed laughter and a silvery high-comic display, almost in the French tradition, from Miss Annis. Turgenev ceases to look like a flawed test-run for Chekhov, and comes on instead like a late Marivaux.

That at least is one way of looking at it. If Natalya, in however compromised a fashion, really does love Belyaev then Miss Annis, except for a penultimate tearful sequence in which she abandons vocal arabesques, is giving an intolerably artificial performance, all trembles and vibrato. (And it must be said for that view that three and a half hours is a long time to watch an imaginary passion.)

Otherwise the virtues and vices of Mr Gill's staging are pretty clear-cut. He holds the attention firmly through a play in which six duologues can seem to be doing the work of three; plainly his actors have been encouraged to think (rehearsals must have been fascinating, they should sell tickets) and they excel at sustaining and varying tensions while addressing each other from across huge expanses of stage.

His greatest weakness is that he undercasts: not so much in terms of talent as of temperament. Michael Gough's doctor is a charming sketch, rather than a full-blown portrait of shady opportunism. Vera (Caroline Langrishe) and Belyaev (Ewan Stewart) begin pleasantly but become stolid under pressure. I liked Nigel Terry's unforced self-contempt as Rakitin, and thought Robert Swann superb as the patient puzzled spouse. The translation is by Isaiah Berlin, and I can't think of a word to say for or against it (in any language) -- which is probably to its credit.

None of these performances actually distort the pattern.

* * *

The effect of seeing John Kani and Winston Ntshona in Waiting for Godot (Old Vic) is considerably more complicated. The curtain goes up on two black actors in a conceivably South African wasteland, and one thinks, well why not? They are confronted by the bullying Pozzo, played white, and the expected resonances are heard, though their effect is soon dissipated.

When Pozzo returns blind, to be alternately tormented and patronised, the situation becomes altogether more intriguing; as it does when our heroes vent their spleen on the helpless poor white, Lucky. And no Estragon can ever have compared in poignancy or point with Mr Ntshona when it comes to the line about being beaten up by the same gang as usual. Colour helps at moments, can be ignored at others; and incidentally is most useful in lending new dimensions of pomposity and fear to Bill Flynn's Pozzo.

It is the actual acting of Messrs Kani and Ntshona that disappoints; they have immense presence but little range. Mr Kani can work wonders -- of ingratiation or scorn or both combined -- with his gaping smile but can do little without it; at least he seldom tries. He has a marvellous commonsensical unanswerable inflection for the reiterated title line, but more often the actors' speech rhythms deaden those of the text. Jokes get lost and so, as a logical result, does the full impact of the play's despair: a despair that I take to be unanswerable since it takes full and sympathetic note of the ways in which we spend our time, and pronounces them all irrelevant in the face of darkness. We do things, it says, to give ourselves the impression we exist.

The first British critic to pounce on that line, incidentally, was Kenneth Tynan, whose 1955 Observer notice said everything important about the play. I mention this because it is now generally assumed (for example by Penelope Gilliatt speaking at Tynan's memorial service) that Beckett was one of Tynan's blind-spots. On the contrary: Tynan (unlike his rival Harold Hobson who has never stopped patting himself on the back for it) may have little instinctive sympathy with Beckett, but that made his criticism all the more rigorous -- far more than it was with Brecht whom he thought he liked.

* * *

Bernard Krichefski's A Perfect Retreat (Bush, closing tonight) takes two common themes -- a right-wing takeover of the English Government and lack of communication within a middle-class family -- and combines them to effect. Father, mother, son and daughter each have a strategy for resisting the cataclysm: what is more they all love each other but there is no way that love will involve trust. By the end of the evening -- especially at the end of the evening, with the shadows lengthening over the alfresco dinner table -- Mr Krichefski, though in excessively clipped dialogue, has said something.

records.title: Comic cuts
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas
records.body:
Comic cuts

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

I HAVE to go down on my knees, and maybe my hands as well.

When Rowan Atkinson first appeared in a show called Beyond a Joke I jumped on him, giving him credit for timing and an intimidating appearance, but not much else. He seemed to be doing more than he or the audience could cope with. A more limited sight of him in the Amnesty International show changed my mind, television of course assisted the process, and after seeing Rowan Atkinson in Revue (Globe) my capitulation is complete.

Mr Atkinson has at least two funny voices: one high, pinched and unaggressively demented, the other languid and incipiently sadistic. Neither, I feel fairly sure, is his own. This is one of the strangest things about him; after an evening in his company you emerge not knowing what he really sounds like, or indeed without much personal sense of him at all. He comes at you as a set of gifts.

He's a cult, but he never trades on it. He works. His stage-hand, failing to save a show when the star goes sick, is marvellously surreal, a one-man collage of earnestly mouthed routines. This of course is done in his dim persona. The smart one is most famously deployed in his sour schoolmaster, a derivative routine that continues to crease me up.

It reaches logical fulfilment in his Devil, obviously bored with the job and a little revolted by it, extending apologetic welcomes to Christians (`I'm afraid the Jews were right'), atheists (`you must be feeling a bunch of right Charlies') and Americans (God sends special regrets to the Mormons who, he realises, put in a lot of work). Mr Atkinson also gives accurate impersonations of the different kinds of Shakespearian messenger and finally dazzles as a newsreader for the deaf, supplying graphic physical commentary on everything including the House of Commons (actually commentary isn't the point of bestiality), Margaret Thatcher (a shake of the hand, a knee to the groin) and Willie Whitelaw (each component part of the name spelt out). If there is a funnier act around than this last one I would like it brought to me. Now.

* * *

Stories about prostitutes used to be defended in court on the grounds of their redeeming sociological value. The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas (Drury Lane) is brimming with sociological value though not much of it relates to whoredom. Based on a true story (I mean it was printed in Playboy), this musical tells of what seems a spectacularly inoffensive sportin' house closed down by a coalition of local interests, i.e. a combination of prurience and cowardice.

A television crusader reveals to an amazingly startled public that `Texas has a whorehouse in it' and then, proud of his scoop, hounds the politicians into acting on it, even raiding the joint on Thanksgiving when it's given over to the entertainment of a winning college football team, for whom a local Senator is standing treat. He declares that he was planted there by Communists, and from then there can be no turning back. The case goes to the buck-passing Governor, characterised in a diverting song-and-dance called `The Sidestep.' The sheriff, hating himself and his superiors, is forced to foreclose on his old friend and possible flame, the brothel-keeper Miss Mona.

One of the fascinations of the piece is its eye for hypocrisy. There is no great public outcry, and certainly the Press aren't fooled. But it's in too many people's interests to pretend otherwise, and television is unstoppable. The show provides a sharp, entertaining look at the tangles of power (there's a mayor in there too somewhere) and a winning, convincing picture--not that I've ever been to Texas--of a small township with the coffee shop as its second favourite rendezvous.

Credulity only stops short at the whorehouse itself, known as the Chicken Ranch and run by Miss Mona as a home from home with never a thought of exploitation. She is salty (`I'll be quick to hand you a sandwich and a road-map' is her form of dismissal) and compassionate (`some pimp beat up on you?' she asks a damaged new recruit). All right, accept all that; then you are faced with the show's periodic excursions into raunchiness. The footballers' lustful chant has point as satire, but it's prolonged to the point of grossness (and incidentally, given standard chorus-boy casting, is none too credible). That element overpowered the show in New York, where I hated it (this seems to be recantation week) and it sops goodwill here.

Nobody is going to give this show marks for neatness; the initial theme--the adventures of two new girls--is quickly dropped, and songs are arbitrarily inserted. A waitress's lament, a black maid's exultation, do nothing for the story, though something for atmosphere and celebration respectively. (The two singers--Sheila Brand and Miquel Brown--are excellent). Most of Carol Hall's score is attractive; country works much better in the theatre than rock, and is artfully blended with Broadway bittersweet in the girls' goodbye number, Hard Candy Christmas.

The direction by Peter Masterson and Tommy Tune is smooth. Of the two imported leads Henderson Forsythe is a fine spitting sheriff and Carlin Glynn--sitting doing her accounts in a wicker wheelchair wearing off-the-shoulder red and spectacles--a stunning Mona. Against all augury the show seems right for Drury Lane; it should be--and I mean this as commendation--really great for the coach-parties.

* * *

Richard II (Young Vic) is a puzzle. The stage is largely occupied by a hole, around which the actors gingerly progress. There seem to be steps leading down from it, so maybe some allusion is meant to the ladder of power; but it is hardly worth crippling the production for, and besides there is an upper level (largely unused) to make the point as well.

The hole seems to be in Russia in revolutionary year, a strange place for a play that keeps breaking into patriotic bits about England. A strange time too; it may account for Richard's feeling of divine mission, but not for Bolingbroke's desire to succeed him as king rather than party chairman. Perhaps the idea of Richard as the last Tsar was inspired by the Christian name of the actor, Nickolas Grace. (The surname may have been influential too.) A fearsomely intelligent player, Mr Grace gives full, if lightweight, measure to Richard's early frivolity and late maturity, but does little to fuse them. Stuart Wilson adds another to the line of strong quiet Bolingbrokes, and the uncles--Clifford Rose and Robert Eddison--are out in strength.
