records.title: Taking a look at tribal customs
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Taking a look at tribal customs

ROBERT CUSHMAN on plays by Mike Leigh, Brian Friel, Nigel Gearing and Arthur Miller.

IN ALL Mike Leigh's improvised plays he gets his characters socialising: formally as in Abigail's Party, or in the dismal drinking sessions of Ecstasy and Babies Grow Old.

Now we have Goose-Pimples (Hampstead), which begins with a dinner-party, progresses to the entertaining of a rich Arab by a girl croupier, and then proceeds to bring the two strands together, in a long second act during which hardly a dry breath is drawn by anyone.

It is obviously useful to Mr Leigh that wine loosens tongues. It can also--and in his plays usually does--loosen behaviour, and it gives scope for the satiric observation of the tribal customs. This is what Goose-Pimples is at. Vernon, in whose flat the play is set, has the effrontery to be a car salesman; as if that weren't bad enough, he takes obvious pride in the possession of a music-centre and in the obsessively neat serving of a meal that begins with melon and would go on to hotter things if only the supermarket didn't let him down.

His guests are Irving, in the same trade, and Irving's plump and heavy-braceleted wife Frankie, with whom Vernon is having an affair. Jackie the croupier is his lodger, and very respectable; however, her Arab, who knows only two or three words of English, thinks she is a call-girl and dutifully peels off wads of fivers when she offers him a drink from behind Vernon's very professional-looking bar.

This is a very funny moment, and the misunderstandings proliferate. In time, of course, the game of teasing the foreign national becomes ugly and we wonder apprehensively how much violence Mr Leigh and his team have in store for us.

Underneath it all we have a study in morality, or at least in mores. The Arab assumes he can buy sex, and spends much time closing doors, so that he may be alone with Jackie. But the two Englishmen are just as predatory, and far less generous; Irving never stops feeling up Jackie, while Vernon treats Frankie abominably and is making a subtle play for Jackie as well.

In fact what is being delivered is another one in the eye for social-climbing British hypocrisy. Improvisation is supposed to lead actors deeper into their characters; but here they seem to have passed judgement on them before the start of rehearsals. This is a far sprightlier piece than Ecstasy, but the blend of humour and compassion seems to have escaped Mr Leigh's work since Babies Grow Old six years ago.

Even while silently protesting, I laughed a lot. The standard of performance is extremely high. Jim Broadbent's Vernon is a continuous ooze, like toothpaste over rotten teeth, set off by Paul Jesson's clotted, contorted Irving, surviving on bogus confidence. Marion Bailey's Jackie sports an amazing accent (which involves offering callers a drink called `whisk-oy') seldom heard outside Mike Leigh plays, but is entertaining. Jill Baker finds desperation in Frankie as well as hard-faced greed, and keeps both within a comic convention. As for Antony Sher's Arab, words should fail me as they do him. His dialogue is limited to `okay,' a vocal shrug of uncomprehending resignation constantly repeated with infinite variation, and assorted slurs. Through all this he conveys lust, pain and finally dignity. There is no better acting in London.

* * *

Depths cannot save a play if its surface is boring; nobody is going to bother to look. The surface of Brian Friel's Faith Healer (Royal Court) is forbidding: four monologues, delivered in order by Patrick Magee, Helen Mirren, Stephen Lewis, and Mr Magee again. Mr Magee plays the title role, Mr Lewis his manager, and Miss Mirren his wife--or, as Mr Magee would have it, mistress; they are always contradicting each other, the point, I think, being less the fallibility of memory than the constant need to protect the ego.

The faith healer, endlessly touring the Scottish and Welsh hinterlands in a succession of one-night stands may, in his corrosive self-doubt and inhuman selfishness, stand for all performers, maybe for all artists. That at least is how his manager talks about him. But his trade is too specialised to function persuasively on that level, and I suspect that if rolled out into an ordinary play, with action and dialogue and suchlike adornments, Mr Friel's story would not seem wonderfully interesting.

The acting is good. Mr Lewis's gaping cockney gets some laughs, and Miss Mirren has a remarkable moment in which she remembers her father, a judge, and her face sheds years. Reference to the text confirms that Mr Friel has furnished them all with graceful sentences to speak, but also that he has chosen a dull method of telling us not much.

* * *

Not as dull though as Nigel Gearing's Snap (New End), which takes us through the life-story of Eadweard Muybridge, nineteenth-century photographer operating in San Francisco, who by his own account invented the moving picture. We see him at work with a trio of nude models. The male seduces one of the females, who happens to be Mrs Muybridge. Muybridge shoots his rival; at the murder trial his wife delivers a tearful speech, claiming that her husband has ushered in a new era in voyeurism, and prophesying a long new degradation for woman as sex-object.

Muybridge, from the look of things, knows all about photography, nothing about people. The look of things here is jumpy and joky, short scenes heavily strobed and linked by parody piano music. On this level Roland Rees's production is quite slick, but it does nothing to pump blood into the piece. Oliver Ford-Davies has some authority as Muybridge, and Colette Hiller is a treat to look at, in or out of clothes.

* * *

The performances in the National Theatre production of The Crucible (now at the Comedy) have grown in authority--notably Dave Hill's as the slimy Reverend Parris--but the improvement only points up the misconceptions in Bill Bryden's production. To praise a director for cutting the melodrama out of The Crucible is like congratulating him for leaving the farce out of Feydeau. Arthur Miller's account of the Salem witch-hunt is not melodramatic in its presentation of good and evil (he subsequently wished that it were), but in its shape and tempo; it builds to a thrillingly organised trial scene in which life-and-death debate gives way to fraudulent hysteria, and then to genuine hysteria as all pretence of judicial reason is destroyed.

Since hysteria is the play's historical climate, the method is perfectly valid, maybe inevitable. Mr Bryden gives us a play for, rather than about, Puritans; very slow, very level, very downbeat. In domestic conflict with his wife (Lynn Farleigh, strangely ineffective) Mark McManus as the accused farmer John Proctor displays a terrific battered stoicism, but in open court his vocal resources give out on him; he sweats blood for--as always--diminishing returns. The last act--Proctor in prison, torn between capitulation and intransigence--fades away, but then it always does; here Mr Miller's method does betray him and he is left with nothing to say, with postures but no characters.

The photograph illustrating last week's review of The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas showed Fred Evans as The Governor, not Henderson Forsythe as the Sheriff. Apologies to both actors.

records.title: National censorship
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
National censorship

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Birmingham.

It would be nice to know how the GLC proposes to distribute the money it has withheld from the National Theatre. It will go, it says, to help prop up other artistic enterprises. That sounds virtuous; the National is hardly the only organisation in the city that needs money. All we want now are the details. What we have to be going on with is a remarkably spiteful piece of retrospective censorship.

The National is, quite confessedly, being penalised for having staged The Romans in Britain. Not, though, on the grounds that it is a bad play; maybe the GLC thinks it is, but it hasn't said so. The Romans received unexpected canonisation from Bernard Levin last week in The Times; Mr Levin exaggerates as usual, but his heart is in the right place.

Anyway not even the GLC could claim that The Romans is a worse play than the National's other new ones, Thee and Me and Line 'Em -- if only because there being no buggery featured or reported in either of those, the councillors probably never got round to seeing them. All the same they may have contributed; I suspect that, lurking in County Hall, as elsewhere, is a belief that it is about time these young (or, more accurately, youngish) playwrights were slapped down a bit. Howard Brenton provided the longed-for provocation; he may even, somewhere inside himself, have intended to.

Over the years there has been good, bad and indifferent work done on the South Bank, with the bad occasioning no squawking from the paymasters. I rather wish that funding bodies would make decisions based on standard of work (as the Arts Council has begun to do) and would make their judgments public (as the Arts Council has failed to do). But they should be consistent about it, and not confuse criticism with sanctimony. And they should have some common sense, maybe even some self-respect; after all, if you believe a playwright is using shock tactics, why give him the satisfaction of showing you are shocked?

Feminists have claimed that there would have been no outcry had the play showed a woman, rather than a man, being raped. They are right, but for the wrong reasons: what is proved is not our low opinion of women, but our unease at any graphic depiction of homosexuality. This may not, though, be the case in Birmingham, where a scene of mass sodomy in The Triumph of Death (Rep Studio) has so far produced little public reaction.

Here admittedly there is no question of rape; all parties are positively eager. The scene is a religious orgy, at which some medieval woodlanders offer themselves to their god, who seems to be Pan. They are then dispersed, and mostly killed, by the forces of the Church.

It is never too clear in David Rudkin's play what is going on or why, but I had the impression that the author was on the side of the pagans. They seem to be descended from the survivors of the Children's Crusade, which ghastly event occupies the play's first section. We have some gloating from an all-purpose Papal figure, with humanity -- represented by the rest of the company -- grovelling in the folds of his voluminous garment. A couple of clerks give theological proof that it's all right to kill Saracens.

Stephen, leader of the children, is discovered seated happily on the lavatory, and is summoned first by Jesus ('yes, it's me'), then by a seductive blonde lady, who is probably Death. Christ later mutates into Pan; Death hangs around, collecting victims, working in cahoots with what somebody Shavianly calls 'the good Cross-tian folk.' One of the survivors of the forest massacre is a girl called Jehan; she is brought before the Inquisition, found guilty and pregnant, brought to bed and burned. She seems more like Joan of Arc, unauthorised version, every second.

Flash forward to Martin Luther, who proclaims himself the child of Joan and the religious sadist Gilles de Rais. One of Jehan's lovers was indeed called Giles (he was last seen turning into some kind of werewolf) and there has also been talk of a Bluebeard. Luther of course is constipated; the progress of Christianity seems to have entailed a narrowing of the spirit and a clogging of the bowel. Only this isn't really Luther, but a present-day female mental case. Her keeper -- Death again -- pronounces a heavily ironic valediction: 'Heaven, hell, all that antique delirium, now, we've come down to earth, we've got it right.'

Mr Rudkin's thesis is not ludicrous, and is passionately felt; you can tell that from the trouble he's been to, and puts us to. Ours at least is not justified; the play's structure is bewildering and much of the language an archaic swamp. I doubt if any writer has achieved a first-rate play by abandoning the language of his own time; and though Mr Rudkin brings off the occasional arresting phrase or incident his method here effectively precludes communication -- not only between stage and audience, but between actor and actor. The players in Peter Farago's production just about get through the text.

* * *

The Golden Age (Greenwich), by A. R. Gurney Jr, goes in for a different kind of archaism. Its plot is confessedly based on The Aspern Papers, which makes it a kind of structural pun. For in this case the scholar who comes seeking details and documentation of the literary past has as his quarry an old lady who, if she didn't know James, knew all his cultural heirs. She was a famous hostess in the New York of the Twenties, may have had an affair with Scott Fitzgerald and may possess a manuscript containing Fitzgerald's only sexually explicit piece of writing.

This is the prize in pursuit of which our sleuth seduces the chatelaine's grand-daughter, though one of Mr Gurney's twists is that both ladies are thoroughly in favour of this arrangement. Constance Cummings does not, especially in a fright of a white wig, look like a piece of history; she is at her best when the script allows her to come down to earth, recalling the servants who were exploited for her comfort, or, up to date, rebuking her young interviewer for not liking M*A*S*H. (She, having lived through the Golden Age, has no need to despise the present, and can salute the persistence of wit; he is an earnest snob.)

Angela Thorne is really fine as the heiress, calculating the odds on repression. Bernard Culshaw has designed a thoroughly convincing brownstone. Mr Gurney's writing is graceful, sometimes witty, but ultimately bland. He has, respectably enough, borrowed melodramatic devices from other writers, but he has not re-charged them.

* * *

In Twisted Cues and Elliptical Balls (Arts), John Judd, with much audience participation, does a skilled and ebullient music-hall turn based on the lives and songs of Gilbert and Sullivan. He also throws in some acting; gruff and conventional as Gilbert, he is a touching and vulnerable Sullivan. There seems no particular reason to stop him.

records.title: Surrendering to Laughter
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Surrendering to Laughter

Robert Cushman on plays by Noel Coward, Joe Orton and Feydeau.

In the heyday of the West End Noel Coward first nights were, one gathers, like no others. Or rather they were like all the others only more so.

It was a moot point, especially when Coward was appearing in one of his own creations, whether there was more glamour at large on the stage or in the stalls. Even now a Coward revival brings out the black ties and long dresses like nothing else. For one evening, progress -- if that's what you want to call it -- can be held at bay. If the play misfires the effect can be grisly, but if it works you surrender to the dream. And Present Laughter (Vaudeville) is the dream incarnate.

It concerns, you will remember, a highly successful actor called Garry Essendine, king of the London stage immediately before the war. His is a world where a star is sure of a long run, unless he makes a really criminal error in choice of vehicle, and where all crises can be resolved over lunch at the Ivy.

The play is a long and leisurely affair that hardly bothers to introduce a plot until the second of its three acts. The first is devoted to showing us Garry at home, which generally means Garry under siege. Women throw themselves into his bed; a manically earnest young playwright arrives to upbraid and remains to worship.

Telephones ring, appointments are made and tours arranged at a giddy pace. Garry regards himself as a martyr to his friends and business associates, but in fact his life is ruthlessly arranged to suit his own convenience. He is the Man Who Came to Dinner caught at home; and if the play has less vigour than a Kaufman-and-Hart crazy comedy, it compensates with a finer sensibility.

Then the story begins. We are told -- though, reprehensibly, not shown -- that Garry's circle is a small oasis of tolerant, civilised values. Enter, to throw herself disruptively at Garry, Joanna, who is the wife of his producer and the mistress of his backer. Or maybe the other way round; I can never get those two fellows sorted out. It is one merit of Alan Strachan's production that they here appear more like men and less like sticks than in either of the two previous versions I have seen.

His is also the only production in which the play improves as it goes on. Instead of declining from witty discursive autobiography to desultory comedy of incident it ascends into rampaging farce. This goes with the casting -- in a strict sense, the miscasting -- of Donald Sinden as Garry. Coward, though apparently very generous, was an intimidating figure; Mr Sinden is approachable. Coward was glacial and Mr Sinden is teddy-bearish. Coward was feline; with Mr Sinden the play's homosexual dimension disappears.

Garry has a soul full of doubts, but mere events don't really ruffle him. Mr Sinden, as a farceur, has no time to worry about his soul, but events can destroy his day, if not his life. It is a joy to see him sinking under their weight until finally, with superbly-timed effort, he dislodges them; and to hear some of Coward's funniest lines surviving an entirely alien, though equally skilled, delivery.

An uneven supporting cast is topped by Gwen Watford, as Garry's aide constantly on the verge of tears -- of joy, misery or amazement. There are two lovely studies in idolatry from Belinda Lang and Julian Fellowes (whose scarved and corduroyed enthusiasm is beautifully in period) and a brisk valet from Colin Spaull.

* * *

Third time lucky again. Unlike the original and the Royal Court revival, Kenneth Williams's production of Entertaining Mr Sloane (Lyric, Hammersmith) entertained me, thanks chiefly, to Dave King, who has the easiest stage manner imaginable and whose gear-changes, arising out of such deceptive relaxation, are transfixing.

This performance, balancing respectability and lubricity on a knife-edge and with every crooked epigram taking the hearer by surprise, is classic Orton. This puts it ahead of the play itself, which, though it takes acute glancing blows at attitudes towards death, sex and legality, lacks the wider reference and frantic activity of Loot or What the Butler Saw.

The chintzy oppressiveness of the setting is part of the satire, but to spend an evening looking at so much pink is fatiguing; the more accurate the design (and Saul Radomsky's is excellent), the greater the trial. And Orton pushes his effects very hard; most of the first act is devoted to the same joke: primness equals nymphomania.

So Sloane the leather-boy is seduced by his landlady while she piles on (most heavy-handedly in Barbara Windsor's performance) the protestations of innocence. All the same, this early, minor Orton still has a shape, a style, and an identity; few other plays of the Sixties would prove so coherent in revival.

* * *

The new Hammersmith director, Peter James, leaves his previous perch, the Sheffield Crucible, with Blow Hot, Blow Cold, the joint work of Feydeau and someone called Hannequin, whose name for it was The Ribadier System. M. Ribadier's system is to hypnotise his wife so he can go out and be unfaithful. And that really is all.

Compared with the accustomed Feydeau, this piece is short on characters, on intrigue, on doors. What it has is social significance: Feydeau fans (myself included) have always proclaimed him a scourge of the bourgeoisie; well, here he is, scourging them. M. Ribadier, discovered, shrinks from the thought of a duel, and he and the man he has cuckolded come instead to a mutually advantageous arrangement concerning the wine trade.

Meanwhile the somnolent Mme Ribadier is unavailingly pursued by a long-time admirer back from Batavia. Two sides of the Sheffield triangle -- Bryan Pringle as hypnotist and Ronnie Stevens as hopeful hypotenuse -- are admirable; the third, Joanna Dunham, is more decorative than adroit, though, as aggrieved party, much of the fun should rest with her.

* * *

The best two numbers in the revue Up in the Eighties (King's Head) begin the second half: One is a song about actors (a natural opener displaced), the other a sketch about box-office staff. Add, perhaps, Maggie-vieta, which makes good sport of Mrs Thatcher, but rather better of Andrew Lloyd Webber. In fact this show's inbred style is only good for satirising the theatre.

The spoken material is awful, taking indifferent ideas and beating them to death. The cast are bright, especially Amanda Barrie, who has the rare gift of being funny and sexy at the same time.

records.title: Having a ball with Bleasdale
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Having a ball with Bleasdale

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on an ingenious new comedy, a stand-up comic and Scottish Molière.

It happened at the beginning of the century and it's happening again. Northern comedy is providing us with the best and the most entertaining images of the way we live now. At one extreme, Alan Ayckbourn; at the other, Hull Truck. And somewhere in between, penetrating the capital with increasing frequency, the Liverpool crowd.

After the sexual and surgical frolics of Funny Peculiar, it was a cinch somebody would write a comedy about vasectomy. After Flying Blind, a tragic farce about Ulster, it was on the cards that a playwright would take a further step and write in similar style about the possibility of nuclear war. The surprise is that both these possible plays have been written in one: Alan Bleasdale's Having a Ball, due at the Lyric, Hammersmith, in May, scheduled for broadcasting as part of Radio Theatre '81 (barring intervention by the censorious gremlins who have bedevilled this project so far), and available right now at the Coliseum, Oldham.

The Coliseum is a theatre that has found an audience and saved itself from extinction by putting on new plays, rather as the Glasgow Citizens' has done by finding an individual style for putting on old ones. The presumption in both cases is that people are being offered an experience unobtainable anywhere else.

Any audience, faced with a comedy on vasectomy, might well feel that it could stay home and write all the jokes itself. One of Mr Bleasdale's achievements is that he manages to avoid the obvious right the way through: up to the final curtain, in fact, when he slips in an expected pun as a sort of festive farewell.

He does devote a fair amount of time to expected fears. His play is set in a Greater Manchester private clinic, with three male candidates in its waiting-room. One is attending for the third or fourth time this week, having fled at the last moment every day so far. His name is Lenny and he goes through life in a state best described as perky panic. He boasts 'such a flair for words that I've recently been described as that clever twat who thinks he knows everything.'

Some playwrights would let him get away with it, too; Mr Bleasdale makes him a figure of slapstick, and by doing so makes us respect him. He delivers his most eloquent speech in a state of terror, with no clothes on, overheard by a drunken lady called Doreen, whose appearance causes him considerable embarrassment, much compounded when she asks him to make love to her.

Lenny and Doreen are united in terror. Both have enemies. Lenny's is the tough smoothie who bullied him at school and who is now awaiting the same operation. Doreen's is her husband, the third patient, who happens to be a county councillor and the focus for her own horror of the bomb -- the same horror that has decided Lenny to have no more children. Both Lenny and Doreen can be irritating people, and Mr Bleasdale is fair enough to let us see that -- even to show us Doreen in a wife-battering scene, where it's her husband, alternating violence and remorse, who is truly his own victim.

Meanwhile the surgeon, a woman, is having troubles with her nurse, a man (and in this reproduction a dead ringer, vocally and physically, for Russell Harty, though this provides only incidental amusement). One of the clinic's specialities is abortion, which he is conscientiously against, and she is conscientiously for. The play is building up a series of arguments on -- to put it frigidly -- the prevention of life, while creating involving characters and building up a fine farcical structure. That is quite a lot.

It builds to a steaming climax, involving official plans for post-catastrophe survival. These plans are both frightening and hilarious. Mr Bleasdale goes for fright, which he achieves, but at the price of unbalancing the play. He has to slide to a conclusion which is that, where possible, life goes on. I wasn't sure what weight he wanted us to attach to this and I wasn't sure that he was sure. Kenneth Alan Taylor's Oldham production is something to catch or to envy; David Ross's Lenny, rabbity and rabbiting, is a hero for our time.

* * *

One of his sprucer spiritual cousins was in London last week, prior to returning to Lancashire, where his gigs this week include the NUS conference in Blackpool: Ernie Dalton of the North West Spanner company, in a routine called I A Mongrel. I caught him at the Hemingford Arms in Islington; appropriate enough since he's actually a Londoner, in the Jim Dale mould.

He does too much shouting into the mike, but he tells good jokes, though unfortunately he suffers from the delusion that there are certain hate-figures whose names are good for a laugh in themselves: as the Ayatollah for American comics, so Thatcher for him. He's a bit more subtle on Heath, but he's best, naturally, when attacking his own side, whether N.W. Spanner itself ('We'd tell the people, "Socialism that way." They'd say, "y'what?"') or his old man who used to talk about the long march to victory or the iron heel of capitalism. ('Politics was all feet to him.')

* * *

There's a new company in Scotland: the Scottish Theatre Company, masterminded by Ewan Hooper who founded Greenwich (the theatre, I mean). They aim to put leading Scottish actors either into new native plays or classics that can plausibly be given a Scots slant, and to tour the big theatres with them.

Their first offering is Let Wives Tak Tent, adapted by Robert Kemp from Moliere's School for Wives. I saw it at the magnificent Theatre Royal, Glasgow. This week it plays the King's, Edinburgh. It sets the play in fact in Edinburgh, behind one of those grey stone facades that look like fortresses, with embrasures for windows; a fearsome place for a girl to be locked up and one which lends considerable point to Moliere's comedy of incipient marital tyranny.

I greatly enjoyed what I could understand (almost the first word sounded to me like 'polygateeries') and found both shape and bite in a work which had previously seemed to me strictly a one-joker. In another sense this production does boast one joker: Rikki Fulton with a full mastery of avaricious double-takes, and considerable grotesque poignancy when he realises himself to be a victim of love. A good week for comics.

records.title: Malfi and Merchant
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: I'm Getting My Act Together and Taking It On the Road
records.body:
Malfi and Merchant

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Paris.

A COUPLE of supporting roles are played with less definition than before. The acoustics at the Roundhouse will never be as good as those at the Royal Exchange. These things apart, on its journey from Manchester to London, Adrian Noble's production of The Duchess of Malfi has done nothing but improve.

It seems to owe little to currently approved trends, since it is neither puritanically simple nor outrageously ornate. Lucid and decorative it is, in a style that I imagine Guthrie or the young Peter Brook might have approved. Sound and light are used with an emphasis that can only be described--with considerable gratitude--as old-fashioned.

As the revenge-plot goes into gear the three villains--Ferdinand, Bosola, the Cardinal--are each seen bathed in a separate spot, apart but complementary. Earlier on Duke, Duchess and Cardinal have frozen under waxen beams, while Antonio, normally lit, delivers his appraisal of their characters. Mr Noble's production cannot merely move easily from one style to another, it can accommodate two simultaneously; which is what Webster's text itself does.

There is a nice discrimination in darkness: a black-out for the imprisoned Duchess's reception of her husband's severed hand, but full visibility for the final massacre, whose confusions pass without a single titter.

If there is a Royal Exchange style, it is rooted in the enclosing use of sound. Here the effects, duly haunting, are supplemented by George Fenton's music, which comes in, cruelly but not sadistically, on every climax. The arena stage, meanwhile, lays the play, its inhabitants and its society, open before us. It is traversed in the first, courtly, half by a royal strip of carpet leading to the ducal throne; after the interval the throne is replaced by a prison chair, almost an instrument of torture; and the carpet is blood-stained.

Images crowd the memory: the Cardinal tied to his bed with silken ropes while his mistress humps him amid clouds of incense; the Duchess's courtiers surrounding her in a tight, sycophantic circle while the honest villain Bosola stands contemptuously outside; the madmen brought for the Duchess's torment in a cage on wheels, which falls open with a hideous clank.

Or there is the embrace bestowed by Mike Gwilym's Ferdinand on his sister, the Duchess, and with which he all but strangles her; his performance is now brilliantly uncompromising in its madness, and is perfectly set off by the suavity of Julian Curry's Cardinal. Peter Postlethwaite carves a real person out of the upright Antonio.

Bob Hoskins brings Bosola earthily to life before your eyes, but his voice is still not supple enough for all the shades the script requires of it. (The mechanical muffling of his bellman's epitaph--'of what is't fools make such vain keeping'--is the only gaffe in the production.)

Helen Mirren starts out a trifle cool, especially when choosing a husband; she is better at giving orders than at giving herself. But she rises to the prison sequences. Her actual execution--with the strangling of her maid as its electric coda--is superbly done.

The production's final achievement is that it duplicates the precarious balancing of Webster's forces, admitting a fascination in cruelty, but never wallowing in it. It makes most modern drama look childish. In its technique and its taste this production is something of a prodigy; I would put money on Mr Noble turning out the best classical director to appear since Trevor Nunn.

* * *

Next to him I would rank Mike Alfreds of Shared Experience; though his Merchant of Venice (Collegiate) is disappointing. (I saw it, though, at a dress rehearsal, when there were obviously few of us to share the experience anyway.) The production is staged in commedia half-masks, with Shylock a hunched Pantaloon. All the characters are seen in a harsh comic light and none of them emerges very creditably.

Maybe it was the masks that activated this approach, but they impede the play it has developed. The play has obviously been considered with great care, the actors driven to explore character and relationships. Portia delivers 'the quality of mercy' with unusual force, right at Shylock, so one wants to see how he reacts to it: not just in his stance and voice, but in his face. The full, direct acting that was always this company's strength has been thrown away and -- despite many passing subtleties in the production -- nothing has replaced it.

There is, of course, another argument for the masks; they are a method of getting through the play with eight actors. So, Philip Osment combines a stonily self-regarding Antonio with a deftly improvising Launcelot Gobbo. Most of these actors are musicians as well, but they are generally below the standard of Mr Alfreds's previous ensembles and try to colour the verse by delivering it in italics with exclamation marks at the end.

* * *

I'm Getting My Act Together and Taking It On the Road (Apollo) is a feminist primer disguised as a musical. The disguise is a thin one; what we get is a nightclub act with comments. Diane Langton plays an American singer whom we see rehearsing her new routine. Rightly tiring of the characterless ballads that have apparently made her famous, she intends to replace them with affirmative musical statements that turn out to be equally nondescript, but which have a surprisingly incendiary effect on Ben Cross, who plays her manager.

He thinks they will upset the audience, though heaven knows why; they sound indistinguishable from the self-pitying epics that have been pouring out of the radio for the last decade. The punters might of course complain that they have heard it all before, and that there is no point in listening again to complaints about a woman's role being predetermined from the cradle unless there is some individuality in the expression.

But this isn't what the manager has in mind. In fact it turns out that what he has in mind is his own marriage: a blackmailing baby-doll, a relationship whose falsity is exposed by Miss Langton's new image. Well, maybe it is; it's hard to say, since we never get a look at it. The contest is rigged.

There is this eternal thing in drama called conflict and, without wanting to lay down any iron-clad rules, I would hazard that the best way of expressing it in a musical is to let the protagonists attack each other with songs. Here Miss Langton sings, Mr Cross doesn't.

Actually the Gretchen Cryer-Nancy Ford songs aren't that terrible, but they leave no mark; as in most sort-of-rock musicals, they begin with a splash and then just jump on the spot for several minutes.

* * *

Balconville (Old Vic) takes us to Canada, and it takes Canada to the 'here is life, look at it' stage of drama. The scene is a Montreal tenement inhabited by two English families and a French one; the area is characterised by rickety housing, mutual suspicion between the races and 40 per cent unemployment.

The author, David Fennario, injects a lot of observation, a respectable amount of humour and a minimum of pathos. Soap-opera it isn't, since it lacks both sentimentality and contrived suspense; drama it isn't quite, at least not at this oceanic distance. One offers thanks for information received rather than for enlightenment.

The acting, by Montreal's Centaur Company, is a credit to whoever wants to claim it, though only one player--a crackling rose called Susan Wright--transcends type.

* * *

I have too little space to do justice to The Cherry Orchard, staged by Peter Brook at his unchanging but protean Bouffes-du-Nord in Paris. Here the peeling walls of the theatre do duty for those of the Ranevsky estate; the upper levels spring into life during the packing and clearing of the last act; every cranny is being searched.

By the end you feel you know the house if not the orchard, and its selling--though no ideological line is pushed--hurts. The final sounds of axe-strokes and twanging string are of Royal Exchange standard; and this production too excels in the atmospheric use of carpets. The third act, the party, is not just a series of dances, but one long dance.

Natasha Parry plays Lioubov and Joseph Blatchley Trofimov, but the actors are predominantly French; Firs, indeed, looks like a Parisian maitre d'hotel, a splendid apparition, though jarring a little with his more xenophobic utterances. Best of a round and rounded dozen is Catherine Frot's maid Douniacha, wide-eyed and vulnerable to everything, from the return of the family to the lecherous assaults of the valet. The acting reaffirms that Mr Brook's virtues are thoroughly traditional.
production_title: I'm Getting My Act Together and Taking It On the Road

records.title: The Seagull flies to Ireland
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The Seagull flies to Ireland

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Chekhov and Moliere revivals, a musical and two new plays in Bristol.

WHEN I first went to the Royal Court, in the Sixties, the fabled great days were already over and the decline, so volubly lamented by John Osborne, had already set in. Nostalgic self-pity was the prevailing mood, taking the stage in a long succession of plays by Mr Osborne or his contemporaries just occasionally broken by something more urgent: as when William Gaskill or Peter Gill took it into his head to direct a Restoration comedy.

For their twenty-fifth anniversary production the Court have chosen The Seagull: possibly a wry admission on the part of the incumbent director, Max Stafford-Clark, that this theatre's greatest strength (as well as, often, its financial salvation) has lain in its classic revivals. Mr Stafford-Clark has attempted to salve his theatre's conscience, or save its face, by commissioning a new version from Thomas Kilroy that re-sites the play in Ireland, but it is recognisably the old Chekhov that he is offering us in -- to make matters worse -- the best production of The Seagull that I have seen.

Mr Kilroy's argument is that Chekhov's rural Russia -- with its fecklessly absentee landowners, resentfully resident estate managers, and peasantry still confused by liberation -- is closely paralleled by the Irish countryside of the late nineteenth century. An historian might be able to demolish that, but it's good enough for the theatre.

Mr Kilroy throws specific political references around -- to Parnell or the Land League -- where Chekhov himself would be more circumspect; and the playwriting inspiration of Konstantin -- one of the few characters able to hang on to his original name in this version -- has changed considerably. Where once he looked outwards, to an international style stigmatised by his mother as 'decadent' or 'terribly modern,' he now turns to his own national legends. This time his mama -- the famous actress Isobel Desmond -- responds with 'Good Lord, it's one of those Celtic things,' and in so doing brings down the house.

It's a laugh of recognition, and the evening is full of them. I suppose they could be cheapening, but they aren't. The effect -- as with doing Shakespeare in modern dress -- is not to supply any blanket new interpretation; but is rather to sharpen individual characters and incidents. It prevents vagueness in the acting, and that is a terrific blessing.

So a minor character like the schoolmaster Medvedenko (I will assume from now on that you don't want to be confused by the new labels) becomes, in Tony Rohr's performance, more interesting than ever before; the details of his poverty, and of his long trek home when denied a horse by his father-in-law, are immediately comprehensible.

For us Russia is Russia; it's all a long way away, and we don't see why the characters should worry so much which bit of it they are in. But for a London actress to be cooped up, far away even from Dublin -- Arkadina's neurosis becomes, if not sympathetic, then certainly recognisable. Freed from any compulsion to act the charming chatelaine, Anna Massey is able to give full weight to the lady's cat-and-mouse games with her son, to her patronage of everyone about her, and to her fearful abasement before her lover.

Alan Rickman's Trigorin is similarly uncompromising; he faces the world in general, and women in particular, with a sickly defensive smile. It's a hedge against emotion but it also works -- literally -- like a charm. The analysis of his writer's disease is wonderfully lucid; Nina would have to be not only star-struck, but a bit deaf, to fall for him. This, in Harriet Walter's performance, she most believably is; she wags a lecturing finger at him when she speaks of being 'a great artist.' She lives up to her principles, sacrificing her life to his art; 'my life is yours -- take it if you wish' marks a strange junction of the two ideas. And at the end she cries real, jagged, disfiguring tears: like a person.

Anton Lesser's Konstantin is a tough misfit, instead of the usual foredoomed romantic; and there are fine choric performances from Stuart Burge and T. P. McKenna. Quite possibly Messrs Kilroy and Stafford-Clark believe that the play is about its social context; it isn't, but in establishing that context they have enabled Chekhov and the actors to reveal, more powerfully than ever before, what and whom it is about.

* * *

Moliere's Don Juan (Cottesloe), now, is more of an abstract piece, though it presents its ideas through a primal double-act. In Mr Gill's production this is masterfully handled, with Nigel Terry's Juan rattling airily through his libertine's creed, while Ron Pember as Sganarelle tries to put the case of conventional morality and progressively discredits it. (He also amusingly garbles his master's arguments for the benefit of strangers.) Both actors superbly serve, and are served by, John Fowles's translation, which is much given to hilarious undercutting of its own elegance.

So far, so marvellous. The supporting performances are unremarkable (unless you count one that is remarkably wooden) and I wasn't much taken by the silent, sullen chorus of possibly damned souls who throng the back of the stage; though I admit they turn out useful in the end: acting as mobile scenery for Juan's visit to the commander's tomb, and finally assisting in his descent to Hell.

Why does he go? The favoured current answer is that Moliere approves of his rebellion but damns him for his last respectable sin of hypocrisy. The trouble is that his hypocrisy is so plainly a joke, which we share. Moliere's people, however powerful, are flat. If he wanted to show us a new facet, he didn't dig; he simply turned the page. This is a very un-English way of doing things and Mr Gill deserves much credit for leaving the play, in his scrupulous and efficient production, as glitteringly opaque as he found it.

* * *

The Bristol Old Vic has been running a play-writing competition. The winner was Ian Sinclair with a Dostoevsky trilogy, now on view in the New Vic studio. I saw Part Two, The Governess, which tells, in bookish but moderately holding dialogue, of a Humbert Humbertish sort of guy who is a sight more interesting if you keep telling yourself that one day he's going to turn out some pretty great novels.

Meanwhile, and reasonably, the main stage is held by a runner-up, Brian Jeffries's Beside the Sea, which shows, on adjacent sections of beach, the families of an accountant and a garage owner, suspicious of each other and of their offspring. I kept wanting someone to do or say something independent of their author's scheme but even that turns out to be part of the effect. One longs for a rapprochement, and appreciates the author's craft in making the most sympathetic character responsible for its ultimate impossibility.

Under Anthony Cornish's direction the play is splendidly acted: Bill Wallis and Barbara Young v. Peter Copley and June Barrie -- a rattling game of doubles.

records.title: In black and white
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: The Knight of the Burning Pestle
records.body:
In black and white

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the National's 'Measure for Measure.'

MICHAEL RUDMAN'S production of Measure for Measure (Lyttelton) has enormous carnival vitality. It reminds us that Shakespeare's plays are constructed like variety bills, each incident designed to be bashed over to the audience with maximum intensity.

There were more individual rounds of applause on the first night of this production than I have ever heard in the classical theatre. Some of this, I imagine, had to do with the nature of the occasion; Mr Rudman has re-set the play on an imaginary Caribbean island, and cast it for the most part with West Indians. The actors' friends were in, and they reacted with volatile partisanship. It was after all an historic production; black actors have never been so abundantly employed on a central stage.

By Mr Rudman's lights the audience counted almost as an extension of the play; in a programme note (a welcome return to an old tradition whereby the director generously furnishes the critics with rope for use at his own execution) he writes that Measure is a public play, whose major characters live or die by the reactions of the crowd. Lucio's jokes, for example, are cracked for the delectation of an enthusiastic bunch of low-lifes, equally ready to lynch him when he falls foul of the Duke.

I think Mr Rudman is essentially right, but he does run into problems. Shakespeare in this play often mentions the people, but when he gets down to presenting them he seems only interested in what, even by Elizabethan standards, must have been an unrepresentative sub-section. Life is centred first on the brothel, all the characters being either inmates or customers, and then, after the vice-laws have bitten, in the prison. So Mr Rudman's basic set, right down to the last scene, has to be the red-light district.

It seems odd that the Duke should choose this area for his ceremonial re-entry; odder that none of the bourgeoisie should be on hand to welcome him; and oddest that he should be crammed, together with his henchmen Angelo and Escalus, on to a balcony at the side of the stage. A battery of microphones does something for their official image, but the stage-picture is lopsided and the action slips away.

Two major characters are white: Leslie Sands's magnificently worldly Escalus (who seems, confusingly, to be in on the Duke's masquerade) and Antony Brown's Provost, a good chap but hidebound. They presumably are the relics of some former regime. Now the island is in the hands of Stefan Kalipha's playboy Duke, who goes into priestly disguise because ... here I have to stop since Mr Kalipha's rather nervous performance offers no solution to this, the play's central problem.

Yvette Harris's Isabella states emotions without exploring or elaborating them. Both these actors have trouble with the verse: Mr Kalipha tries to bury it, Miss Harris lets it bury her. Only Norman Beaton is on easy terms with it; his Angelo is an uncompromising Puritan--a cleric, in fact--who deliberately retreats behind his desk and into officialdom when Isabella begins to get to him. An actor who once managed, quite superbly, to play Ariel as a civil servant, obviously has no trouble with Angelo; he is complete master of old words and new modes. Maybe his best moment is his icy retreat when the comic relief arrives; under the leadership of Oscar James's Pompey, which has real swagger, they pose an unaccustomed threat.

Bertice Reading plays Mistress Overdone, temporarily reprieved from jail so that, disguised as a night-club pianist, she may sing 'Take, O take those lips away.' That song of course is in the text; not so the number that Peter Straker's Lucio, promoted to super-pimp, sings about the beneficent effect of sexual prohibition on the flesh-market. He performs it wonderfully, polishing it off with a stunning falsetto, and Tammy Eytle's lyric beats the hell out of every new musical in London. But it puts us in another convention, and we spend the rest of the evening waiting frustratedly for it to be followed up. In sum Mr Rudman makes mistakes, but he makes them in the right spirit: joyous not reductive.

* * *

By contrast the gags in The Merchant of Venice (Old Vic) are aimless, means of somehow getting through the play, or up and down the steps of an archaic set, which makes the Queen of the Adriatic look as if she's being held up by scaffolding. Timothy West, redirecting a former production, is his own best actor and such subtleties as exist--apart from the engaging portrayal of Salerio and Solanio as a right pair of Job's comforters--are to be found in his performance; Shylock's realisation in the midst of mourning for Jessica that Antonio is now in his power is a sharp corner negotiated with a quiet businessman's relish that carries through into the trial. Stephen Jenn is a golden boy Bassanio who actually makes you listen to his casket speech, but Prunella Scales's Portia really needs a script by Congreve.

* * *

In Beaumont's The Knight of the Burning Pestle (Aldwych) an Elizabethan grocer and his wife invade the performance of a romantic comedy and demand a part in it for their apprentice. They remain on stage, treating the characters in the drama as real while egging their boy, who is quixotically infatuated with stories of knight-errantry, on to greater deeds. Michael Bogdanov's production puts the intruders into modern dress, thereby adding another convention to a play in which there are already about two-and-a-half operative at any given moment.

The couple's naivety becomes unlikely, and their dialogue, partly rewritten, an uneasy compromise between two centuries. But there is a tremendous swing to the show, with an uproarious multiple duel, a barbering operation that makes Sweeney Todd look humanitarian and a Morris-dance of surreal extravagance. Timothy Spall makes a prodigious hero; Margaret Courtenay and Timothy Knightley do the city proud, and John Woodvine sings a lot, which can't be bad.

* * *

The Accrington Pals (Warehouse) of Peter Whelan's play are a Lancashire regiment who marched off to be annihilated in the First World War, but the title also refers to the women they left behind who draw ever closer together in the face of deprivation: social, sexual and--in the sense that they are denied accurate news from the front--intellectual. One (sensitively played by Janet Dale) refuses to make common cause with the others; this, I think, was meant to be the fulcrum of the play, but it is late in developing and doesn't mean much when it does.

The writing is sympathetic but slack (there is a ghost-scene which is as puzzling as those in Mr Whelan's Captain Swing and a lot less powerful) and there is some greyish acting. Bill Alexander's supposedly three-sided production is something of a sham; I got irritated by the constant trundling round of a single set-unit, since its face was pretty well invisible from my flank anyway, and the performances were all delivered firmly out front.

Mr Whelan's basic situation was anticipated 50 years ago in Coward's Cavalcade; so was much else, including the whole of Oh What a Lovely War. The scene in which a bereaved mother forces herself to celebrate on victory night is as powerful a wordless episode as any playwright has contrived. (She's upper-class, of course, but as misinformed about events as any of Mr Whelan's workers.) For all that, Cavalcade isn't much of a play; the pageantry gets in the way of the people who are paper-thin, mere sounding-boards for offstage disasters. (We don't lose anyone we know in the Boer War, but the Titanic and 1914-18 make up for it.)

What everybody knows about Cavalcade is that it ends with a patriotic toast and a despairing song, Twentieth Century Blues; in that order. David Horlock's revival (the first ever) at the Redgrave, Farnham, reverses the sequence, but if he's trying to soothe us, he doesn't succeed. The song is electrifying, sung by Christina Matthews in a voice to match her gleaming white dress; the toast is tame. So the impact is confused; it could even, who knows, be Brechtian. Mr Horlock has staged the play with magisterial efficiency, and the crowd scenes--with local amateurs swelling the numbers to 300--are like nothing you have ever seen.

records.title: No laughter in Court
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
No laughter in Court

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

AT THE ROYAL COURT:
25 Years of the English Stage Company
edited by Richard Findlater
Amber Lane Press £12.95

IN an age when theatrical history is forgotten as soon as made, this book is immensely welcome. Described as a "celebration," it divides the Royal Court's history from 1956 to 1980 into seven sections. Each begins with a brusque survey, by Richard Findlater, of the plays produced, and the writers, actors, directors and designers responsible. Three or four of these then offer their reminiscences.

There are 23 contributors, counting Mr Findlater himself and Samuel Beckett who, mindful of his reputation, has sent a two-sentence greeting telegram. Then there are appendices; most crucially and creditably there is a list of all plays presented at the Court, upstairs and down, weekdays and Sundays, complete with casts: the kind of vital material that is becoming increasingly hard to find in print.

Vying in importance are a glorious series of photographs, apparently chosen by one of the Court's major directors, Bill Gaskill. Some are creamy with nostalgia: the 1950s (that check shirt worn alternately by Jimmy and Alison in Look Back in Anger, all those ties sported by the prickliest rebels) seem incredibly distant. But the most evocative shot of all is of the empty stage stretching unexpectedly deep as seen from the dress circle. John Osborne's accompanying claim "I think you can do anything on that kind of stage" seems impossible to dispute.

It is the theatre itself that provokes loyalties. Nobody has heard of the ESC; everyone has heard of the Court. To abandon it for larger or more "democratic" premises elsewhere would, as is intimated at the end of the book, be criminal madness. Nowhere else could such creative eccentricity be expected to thrive.

Outsiders -- critics especially -- will be relieved to find that their own love-hate (or at any rate admiration-mistrust) for the set-up is fully shared by those within. Among the most engaging contributors are Jack Shepherd recalling "baffling" acting classes and baffled playwrights ("no one wants a drink with a playwright who has just learned something") and Christopher Hampton on the fate of his play The Philanthropist ("disgracefully successful, so much so that I've always felt I left under something of a cloud").

Mr Hampton also writes amusingly of the Court's attitude ("savagery and contempt") towards the work of other theatres. Tolerant himself, he was "shocked." He's not alone. Court directors, like anybody, have the right to hate or walk out of any shows they please to, but dismissal of everybody else's work may not be the best way of enlivening your own. Over the years I haven't had many laughs in Sloane Square, and I grew weary in this book of the adjective "serious": a questionable theatrical virtue anyway, and here used mainly as a synonym for "our (or, in extreme cases, my) work." The Court is not the only theatre that seeks to present writers' work as well as possible (most places try) and a monochrome production style is not always the best means to that end.

Critics, often berated by the Court for not taking it at its own valuation, may note that they have frequently been more enthusiastic about the plays than have the Courtiers themselves: from The Entertainer on, it seems that no play has been mounted without a fearful internal struggle.

The founding figure of George Devine emerges as in Irving Wardle's fine biography, as movingly impressive: a practical genius. There seems general agreement that after his death the place went into decline; you can hear, beneath the usually benevolent tone of this book, the older and younger generations blaming each other. Once again Mr Hampton has the most balanced comment: "it is no longer ... the only outlet for serious new work, and if the offspring are as healthy or even occasionally healthier than the parent, that is not necessarily to the Court's discredit."

I think myself that there has been an upswing since 1977, marked by the appointment of Stuart Burge, a director from outside the Court tradition but with something of Devine's breadth of background. His successor Max Stafford-Clark has promised a "totally traditional" programme of "idealism tempered by compromise." That's more than a good joke.

records.title: The laughing Shylock
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: The Knight of the Burning Pestle
records.body:
The laughing Shylock

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Stratford and London.

I HAVE never seen a funnier Shylock than the one offered by David Suchet in John Barton's new Stratford production of The Merchant of Venice; or one more moving.

Obviously the two things go together, but getting the balance right is the problem that bedevils every production of this play. I happen to have seen three in the past four weeks. Shared Experience's Jew was a masked cringer in a convention that seems right for the play in theory, but breaks down in practice; the character undeniably expands as the play progresses, but this version refused to grow with it. Timothy West at the Old Vic was strong on pride, vindictiveness and professional concern: a well-rounded portrait in fact, but with no context to fit into.

Mr Barton is probably better on context -- comic context anyway -- than any other Shakespearean director. Ian McKellen once said of him approvingly that despite his reputation he wasn't an academic, he was a great vulgar showman; and he is also an insistent realist. More and more he has been setting plays in recognisable, if anachronistic, societies, with all rules observed; and more and more he probes for human details, asking obvious but generally neglected questions.

No other director has spotlit Portia's realisation that, with two suitors down, the leaden casket must be the one. Sinead Cusack's Portia indeed is understandably fixated on her father's trio of oversized fortune cookies; when we first meet her she is staring at them with fascinated loathing. She only learns to laugh when Bassanio gets them off her back.

Mr Suchet, by contrast, laughs from the start. Laughter -- mocking himself and everybody else -- is Shylock's line of defence. The amount that Mr Suchet conveys through the one word 'well' -- repeated at the end of each of his first three lines -- is extraordinary. 'You,' he says to Antonio and Bassanio, 'are coming to me': the ludicrousness of the situation gets to them as well. It embarrasses Bassanio, as it is meant to, but Tom Wilkinson's Antonio (who seems the most manic of depressives) can see the joke, especially the really hilarious bit about the pound of flesh.

There is of course another level of fun -- revenge-comedy -- that Shylock shares only with the audience. Mr Suchet's skill in drawing out and differentiating these strands is dazzling; but it does involve him in a continuous use of jovial falsetto and I began to wonder if he had anything else in store.

The aftermath of Jessica's elopement proves that he has. On 'to bait fish withal,' though it's still a savage joke, he strikes a table with his stick, and with a force that nearly jerked me out of my seat. The ensuing scene with Raymond Westwell's Tubal (all unctuous, sadistic concern) is a masterpiece of cat-and-mouse, with Shylock sometimes playing both roles himself; 'to curse never fell upon our nation' is undercut by a self-pitying 'I never felt it till now,' whose absurdity the speaker half-recognises as he speaks it.

Probably only a Jewish actor would take such risks in this role; Mr Suchet has no need to stand on his dignity, knowing that the play will take care of that for him. And it may be that only a Jewish actor -- an honest, uncompromising one -- can make sense of the play now. As written, The Merchant probably is thoughtlessly anti-Semitic; what redeems it, even makes it useful, is its insight into the effects of persecution.

* * *

The key line is not 'Hath not a Jew eyes,' but 'since I am a dog beware my fangs.' This is the passion that carries Mr Suchet through the trial scene, and on to disaster, by way of Portia's spurned appeal for charity: the moment at which the play's lines satisfyingly cross. She grows as he dwindles.

For all its charm and intelligence, Miss Cusack's Portia comes over as a directed performance, where Mr Suchet's is autonomous and unpredictable, and quite different in its sophistication from Patrick Stewart's greasy usurer in Mr Barton's very similar Other Place production. Terry Wood is physically and vocally a magnanimous Morocco, and Lorenzo -- not the most rewarding role in the play -- is given an intriguing gentleman-sportsman air by Michael Siberry.

Mr Barton goes in too much for the everybody-joining-in-the-joke joke, better handled at the Vic, where Jessica's chiming in with Shylock on his 'fast bind, fast find' proverb told us something about their relationship. Aided by Christopher Morley's twin set (gondola-poles for Venice, branches for Belmont), Mr Barton otherwise furnishes a musical, autumnal production, whose mercantile tone is set by constant recourse to brandy and cigars.

That makes it the fourth transported classic in succession. Like the Irish Seagull and the Caribbean Measure for Measure, it seems motivated by a mischievous desire to see what the play will look like in a new suit of clothes. The Knight of the Burning Pestle (reviewed too briefly last week), with a punk apprentice, is more concerned to make the play comprehensible to a modern audience. This, which appears the more respectable reason, is actually the more disreputable. Michael Bogdanov is being condescending both to his actors and his audience if he despairs of making the play funny as written.

And there are other problems. When Beaumont made his Jacobean Citizen's Wife claim that she'd never seen a play before, it was credible, and she had some excuse for mixing up life and drama. Margaret Courtenay's matron at the Aldwych has obviously spent a lifetime watching soap-opera on TV. She knows the score. Mr Bogdanov has had perforce to keep the play-within-a-play in doublet and hose; why should the Citizen's Wife now treat Mistress Merrythought as her neighbour when they are obviously separated by centuries? And isn't it rather a drag for Timothy Spall as Rafe to have to throw new grunts into old pentameters?

To overcome all these doubts, and still come up with a monstrously enjoyable show, Mr Bogdanov and troupe have to work very hard. Sometimes their endless inventiveness seems endless, but mostly it is extraordinarily apposite. There is a pedantic streak in Mr Bogdanov that compels him to find an equivalent for everything of the original he has jettisoned. Beaumont satirised his own theatre; so does he.

I doubt if there is any company as confident in its own identity and its audience's to spoof itself as successfully as the RSC does here. It produces a very warm feeling. The production shares the repertoire with the revived Nicholas Nickleby (all seats sold, eat your hearts out), so the Aldwych will probably find themselves faced with yet another housing problem.

* * *

The La Claca company from Catalonia apparently felt, after their successful collaboration with Joan Miro on Mori el Merma, that they were in danger of losing their own identity, becoming Miro images. On the basis of their Antologia (Riverside Studios), their fears were justified, but to act on them ill-advised. The performers (only two this time) are at their best when they re-envelop themselves in Miro's creations for an extract from their greatest hit. In their other work, earlier and later in date, they function mainly as puppeteers, and both their bite and their charm are smothered in whimsy.

I can't quite read my notes, but I think the best line in the feminist revue Female Trouble (Arts) was 'female trouble -- you can give it or receive it -- it's better to give.' Unfortunately the rest of Bryony Lavery's script fails to match it, either in wit or in spirit. These performers too are better at satirising themselves than anyone else. They make good jokes about women; when it comes to men, they simply state grievances. The music is variable, the performance level -- Anne-Marie Davies, Caroline Noh, Lou Wakefield -- very high, and the set, mostly composed of cutout zebras, mysteriously attractive.
