records.title: Clearing Ostrovsky's good name
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Clearing Ostrovsky's good name

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Russia's first and most prolific professional.'

IT HAS been written: 'No great European playwright -- not even Calderon, Corneille, Racine, Marivaux, Musset, Goldoni, Goethe, Schiller, Hauptmann or Schnitzler -- is more unrecognised in this country than Alexander Ostrovsky.'

That sentence, a choice piece of neglected Tynan, appeared in the programme for 'The Storm' which was the National Theatre's attempt in 1966 to do Ostrovsky -- and which actually, as far as the English theatre is concerned, did for him. It also did for neglected foreign classics generally, few of the other names on Tynan's whimsically accusatory list having reached the National since. The RSC meanwhile has sheered off from every one of them, maybe on the grounds that none of them is Russian. But Ostrovsky of course is; in fact he is the national playwright, Russia's first and most prolific professional. Chekhov, who came along two decades later, was just a doctor who dabbled.

Ostrovsky mainly wrote comedies; 'The Storm' was one of the few exceptions. Last week the RSC cleared his good name by presenting The Forest at the Other Place.

'The Forest' raises the number of plays about actors in their current repertory to three. (Four; I forgot 'Hamlet.') A couple of provincial strollers, down on their luck, meet up. One, looking like a broken-down Scottish Highlander, is Richard Pasco, unexpectedly but rewardingly cast as a low comedian sunk even lower. ('I became a prompter.') 'Were you good, sir?' he asks his companion: ill-advisedly since his companion, looking like a melancholy gypsy, is Alan Howard, mocking himself with a serene, drawling arrogance, a flashing eye, and a perfection of timing that makes his similar role in 'Wild Oats' look like the merest trial run.

Actors don't change much; at least Ostrovsky seems to have written a large number of RSC in-jokes. 'I've got an easier temperament than you,' says Mr Pasco, settling into his role as Sancho to Mr Howard's Don. Earlier they have shared a grumble about 'university people shovelling themselves on to the stage.' This scene is a self-contained delight, but at the end of it they decide to make contact with the rest of the play, which takes place on the estate of Mr Howard's aunt.

She is a rich skinflint, a Madame Ranevsky happy to sell every tree in the wood if she can get a good price for it. Barbara Leigh-Hunt gives her a classic performance, merging lust and cupidity; allowing a favoured suitor to peer briefly into her cash box as if she were giving him a quick flash. She is meanwhile making life hell for her niece, driven by her condition (in love, no dowry) to throw herself in the river, but fished out by Mr Howard who sees in her suicidal passion promise of the leading lady he has been looking for. Not surprisingly, since Janine Duvitski, sensible but odd, balances her emotions beautifully.

This is Mr Howard's cue to confront, with histrionic but heartfelt generosity, the entire menage of the rich, which includes Raymond Westwell, booming on two sticks. (One reason, I realise, why I like Mr Westwell so much is that he sounds like the great radio barons of my childhood: Felix Felton or Norman Shelley.) Between his two scenes in this show, he nips down the road to give his definitive Tubal at the big house. An award is in order.

Mr Howard confounds them all with subversive sentiments that turn out to be quotations from Schiller, passed by the censor. Ostrovsky's own comment comes in the reactions of the gentry who admire his pluck but refuse to drink with him, but he enforces his own kind of class distinction; Mr Howard may be noble, but Mr Pasco stays cunning.

It is a long and surprising play; and though Adrian Noble knows how to marshal its forces at any given moment, he allows the length to show and some of the surprises to surprise him. But it's an occasion, especially perhaps for Mr Howard. Acting for the first time in a studio space he confirms that he is, when not trumpeting, the kindliest of actors and suggests himself as ideal casting for Bottom the Weaver; he really can roar you as gently as any sucking dove.

* * *

According to Warehouse director Howard Davies the newest playwrights are beginning to move back towards closely observed personal relations. His last three presentations bear him out, and I wish I liked them more. Hanif Kureishi's Outskirts is a particular disappointment since the relations are actually so well stated: unemployed South Londoner to former friend, now a teacher; unemployed to psychologically battered mother; most elusive of all, friend to mother.

It adds up to an engulfing landscape of despair, with no facile emotions or solutions, and reflected in the setting; an upturned chair represents a wasteland, right way up it signifies a room, and there's not too much to choose. But we are transported in time as well as in space, from past friendship to present estrangement, and the information provided is too fragile to support the structure.

It all hones in on one past act of racial violence, committed not by the present sullen Fascist supporter but by the liberal teacher. It makes you think, as they say; but it doesn't gain from restatement; I felt an unregenerate wish to see the characters abandoned and the social issues explored. I also tired of the bloodlessly artificial dialogue ('a mechanic I'll be, a trade I'll have') that was the previous generation's worst legacy. There is a supple performance by David Bambur, a more gangling one by Tony Guilfoyle; Marjorie Yates is in danger of being typed below her worth as the actress you send for when you want someone to look ill.

* * *

Two echoes of the music-hall. In Gone with Hardy (Tricycle) an Australian playwright, David Allen, tells how Stan Laurel, not the innocent he seemed, climbed to success over the discarded talents of two colleagues, a Scots comic and an Aussie chanteuse. This is a story of stifling ordinariness, not much enlivened -- in fact desperately protracted -- by having its every stage acted out as a vaudeville routine. Mercifully the three performers -- Sylvester McCoy, Jimmy Logan and Toni Palmer -- excel.

As do Roy Hudd and Billy Dainty, thoroughly charming comics who in Just a Verse and Chorus (Greenwich) play Weston and Lee, authors of together or apart 'I'm 'Enery the Eighth,' 'With 'Er 'Ead Tucked Underneath 'Er Arm,' 'Goodbye-ee,' 'Paddy McGinty's Goat,' 'Knees Up Mother Brown' -- in fact just about every song you ever associated with the halls except the gritty, realistic Marie Lloyd specials.

There are some goodies in the Weston-Lee catalogue; some outrageous rhymes, but many are just repetitions of jokes that weren't too funny the first time. And don't ask which of them wrote the music; with those tunes it doesn't matter. When a song called 'You Give Me Ideas' turns up, with an atrocious lyric but some suggestion of melodic shape and harmonic movement, there turn out to have been others involved. The show is well presented with both songs and information pointedly dispensed. Mr Hudd's rendition of 'Brown Boots' (the boys' best) is very touching, but popular songs rank with news magazines ('Now' is not the 'Time' for all good men) among the things in which Britain lags behind America.

records.title: The cat's whiskers
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The cat's whiskers

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Andrew Lloyd Webber's new musical.

HERE is a hot flash. A musical called Cats, based on 'Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats' by T. S. Eliot, with music by Andrew Lloyd Webber, opened last week at the New London. That is the end of the mews.

You enter the auditorium to confront what promise to be the worst sightlines in town. The set is on view, but consists of a vast rubbish tip, piled high with debris, including most of a car. It looks very impressive, but it leaves little space for actors. There's hardly room to swing a cat.

However, when the lights go down, the rubbish revolves (as do the first half-dozen rows of the audience), the cluttered foreground becomes evocative background and the stage reveals itself as a marvellous arena for dancers. Already pairs of green eyes have flashed intriguingly and invitingly out at us; now the cast takes over in a prologue announced in the programme as 'Jellicle songs for Jellicle cats.'

Eliot may have thought of Jellicles as a special kind of cat ("roly-poly" and "of moderate size," he said, generalising rather), but in this production they seem to stand for all cats. Anyway they are a permanent ensemble, and the other practical pussies emerge from their ranks.

The Jellicles, as choreographed by Gillian Lynne, begin with an energetic but fairly routine routine, but rise at the end of the first half to a driving ecstatic ballet that must be the most exciting number ever seen in a British musical.

Mr Webber reveals very unsuspected powers as a rhythm composer--and more crucially, I suspect, as a rhythm orchestrator. Sometimes the ginger is applied indiscriminately; the motherly Old Gumbie is surely nobody's hepcat. But we get a firework display by Paul Nicholas as the maverick Rum Tug Tugger (clad in leather trimmed with leopard fur); a spoof hoof for John Thornton and Bonnie Langford ("Mungojerrie and Rumpleteazer were a very peculiar couple of cats" has always struck me as a perfect jazz line); a long zesty narrative number for Ken Wells as Old Skimbleshanks the railway cat; a jumping, swaying vehicle from which Wayne Sleep can amaze us as Mr Mistoffelees the conjurer; and, crowning all, a bounding jazz-dance in which Sharon Lee-Hill and Geraldine Gardner (the cat I would most like to take home, a flaming tawny) pay their respects to Macavity the mystery cat and Miss Lynne hers to Bob Fosse.

There are besides a soothing, wondering serenade for Brian Blessed as Old Deuteronomy and a music-hall soliloquy to Stephen Tate as Gus, the run-down theatre cat.

I'm not sure where Trevor Nunn's responsibility as director branches off from Miss Lynne's; but it seems reasonable to credit him with the show's technical excellence (David Hersey's lighting, Abe Jacob's sound, both superb), with its overall likeableness (you may look round, as I did, to find Mr Sleep crouching by your side and staring, which may give you paws), and for the smooth, amusing transitions from one number to the next.

But these don't make a shape. As a dance musical 'Cats' knocks spots off Mr Fosse's 'Dancin',' but it can't match 'West Side Story' or 'Chorus Line,' because though it tries to be more than a series of charming vignettes, it doesn't really go anywhere. Intermittent shuddering cries of 'Macavity' don't do much for suspense; nor does the temporary disappearance of Mr Blessed. (When the chorus suddenly intones 'we have to find' old Deuteronomy' it's a pathetic moment in the wrong sense; and very English.)

Then there is Grizabella the Glamour Cat (Elaine Paige), who hangs out 'near the grimy road of Tottenham Court,' emerging to sing a ballad whose gummy lyrics are matched to soupily derivative music. She is redeemed through something called 'the Jellicle choice' and ascends to, I suppose, heaven: 'Up up up to the Heaviside Layer, up up passed the Russell Hotel.' (The lines are constantly repeated, not to their benefit.)

It is all very nebulous, though the giant tyre on which the ascent is accomplished, and the huge ramp lowered from the sky to meet it, are reasons in themselves for seeing the show. This brings us to the closing number--all the cats join in--in which Eliot's sprightly envoy, 'the Addressing of Cats,' is given a surprisingly pompous setting. 'Cats' isn't perfect. Don't miss it.

* * *

Does the GLC realise that there are now two theatrical cat-houses in Drury Lane?

Brian Friel has found a beautiful binding conceit for his play Translations (Hampstead). We are in an Irish village in the 1830s, where Gaelic, Latin and Greek are spoken, but not English. English troops arrive to rationalise the country's topography; in other words to change the Irish place-names to equivalent English ones.

The play's dialogue is all in English, but half of it is assumed to be in Irish. So we have characters onstage speaking the same tongue, but failing to understand one another and constantly requesting interpretations; exploited by Mr Friel for effects comic, catching (in a cross-cultural love scene) and finally chilling. An officer disappears, and his superior threatens wholesale evictions in reprisal: he reads out the new names of the selected villages, while the old ones are relayed to his audience. This is a magnificent piece of dramatic shorthand that says chapters about Anglo Irish history.

Mr Friel presents two brothers: one a lame, grumbling nationalist played, in as strong and biting a performance as he has given, by Stephen Rea; the other is the sophisticated collaborator whose confusions are richly explored by Tony Doyle. Their drunken, eloquent father keeps a hedge-school, itself the most fascinating dramatic locale since Trevor Griffiths's college for comics; Ian Bannen, absent from the London stage for 20 years, has glittering authority, but not always the ease to convey it.

The director, another long absentee, is Donald McWhinnie; his fine cast includes Sebastian Shaw (derelict with total fluency in the classroom).

records.title: The mad and the military
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The mad and the military

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a musical and a new play in Scotland.

PHILIPPE DE BROCA's version of 'King of Hearts' is a cult film, about a soldier who on the last day of World War One walks into a French village to find that everybody has fled except the inmates of the local asylum. He gets to love them because they have no interest in killing people, which makes a change from the circles in which he has recently been moving.

I have now seen the stage musical version. A Broadway flop a few years ago, it has been given its British premiere at the Lyceum, which is Edinburgh's rep. Enterprising of them to try a new musical, but this one is a horror.

You can guess from contemplating that story-line the kind of writers who are going to want to put songs into it and what kind of songs they are going to put. When our doughboy hits town, the first person he meets is a cute mute. The other merry villagers are glimpsed playing games in white nightshirts as in nursery 'The Marat-Sade.' They also sing, rhyming 'scandalous' with 'abandoned us,' twice. Later they have a number called 'Deja vu'; the lyricist (Jacob Brackman) keeps flourishing his title-phrase, as if pleased with himself for being able to speak foreign.

The loveable lunatics start their own brothel, and the hero finds himself in love with a very young virgin whore. The madam warns him against being 'nice' (one moment more and she would be using really filthy words like 'bourgeois'). The crowd choose him as their king and he decides to stay with his subjects, there being apparently only two kinds of people--the mad and the military.

Why do men who have made a pile in the pop market feel entitled to hit us with the virtues of nonconformity? The tone, predictably, is sententious and sentimental. The music (Peter Link) has its pretty passages, but lacks cohesion; with no style of its own--let alone any sense of period--it wanders from one more or less modern mode to another.

The recurrent sound is a woeful compromise between soft rock and 1950s ballad; what the music press calls something like contemporary-adult-crossover-(mind-the-traffic)-middle-of-the-road: simplest perhaps to think of it as hyphenated music. It has no contours, and it's killing the musical theatre. It accounts for the worst bits of 'Evita,' 'Annie,' 'Cats' and 'A Chorus Line' and for nearly all of 'They're Playing Our Song' and 'I'm Getting My Act Together.' Those shows have, bar the last, enough going for them for us to turn a deaf ear; they are sophisticated, but 'King of Hearts,' as exposed at Edinburgh, is the thing itself, unaccommodated pap. The production has a resourceful lead singer in Martin Smith and a first-rate mime in John Moreno.

* * *

Up the road at the King's I saw the new Scottish Theatre Company in Civilians (this week they play Glasgow). Bill Bryden's play, self-directed, shows us Greenock during the war. It is excellently acted in the best Scots manner (hot and strong, with the laugh lines indecently well timed), predictably evocative, frequently funny (my favourite line was about somebody 'saving up to vote Tory'). But it is also aimless, so that its very virtues start to tell against it: both the jokes and the nostalgia come too easy.

Situations and characters are thin and foreseeable: a soldier's wife, first faithless, then pregnant, then bereaved; her air-raid warden dad (Fulton Mackay) a tartar with a heart o' gold. At the end it becomes another play about the lost electoral hopes of 1945. That--from a playwright who has kept his characters boozing, scrounging and amateur operaticising for three hours--is shamelessness worthy of O'Casey.

records.title: Back to Arden's Dance
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Back to Arden's Dance

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and at the Toronto Theatre Festival.

MY GENERATION was trained to consider Serjeant Musgrave's Dance a masterpiece done to death at its premiere in 1959 by philistine clodhoppers.

The truth, as revealed in the Cottesloe revival, is slightly less colourful, but only slightly. Colour, as John Arden knew very well, is one of his play's strengths: red uniforms on a black-and-white coalfield. The contrast works superbly on Peter Hartwell's set with its gleaming curtains and cyclorama, dotted with bare, significant props as specified by the author. Indeed John Burgess's lucid production is a paragon of fidelity; even to the point of rashness.

According to prescription, Annie, the village barmaid, drops her tray with a banshee yell. If she seems merely like a waitress suddenly taken queer, that's the author's fault. So is the fact that she and her employer both speak in folk-ballads; part of a playwright's theory rather than of a play. Mr Burgess's colliers don't get drunk enough, but he organises action sparely and well, especially the final dance of vested interest that displaces Sar'nt Musgrave's own.

He comes to Yorkshire from colonial service, sickened by reprisals exacted in a ratio of five to one, and determined by the end to exact the same from the sheltered guilty folks back home. Whether he has it in mind all through is an open question; his author doesn't seem to have decided whether he's decided and this confusion is the play's main flaw.

Musgrave's boasted logic derives from military life and the Old Testament; there is indestructible logic in John Thaw's performance, building a thoroughly convincing avenging angel out of a thoroughly convincing NCO.

Weaving his pattern of pacifism, revenge, love, industrial strife, Mr Arden never drops a stitch; every line has function and flavour. 'This town's wintered up,' says the Mayor; the compression makes the fancy writing of today seem more indefensible than ever. The closing note of fatalistic optimism (characters doomed, cause not) is beautifully judged. In an excellent cast Peter Sproule, Patrick Drury, Ron Pember, Philip Jackson, Leonard Fenton, Michael Gough and David Troughton are standouts.

* * *

The trio in Harold Pinter's The Caretaker (Lyttelton) are now West Indian. They have no particular problem with the rhythms, but they get little fun out of the play and only a prefabricated idea of tension. 'This ain't my bag,' says Norman Beaton's downtrodden tramp, and he never spoke a truer metaphor. It's a trudge of an evening.

* * *

Britannicus (Lyric Studio, Hammersmith) is more of a funeral march. Christopher Fettes's production catches Racine's sense of omnipresent trap, but little else. A pedestrian translation gives the actors little excuse for emotional flights, but they attempt them anyway, shouting above the odds approved for so small a space. In quieter moments Jonathan Kent's Nero pouts; Siobhan McKenna's Agrippina booms; she comes on first in red, down to her stockings and shoes, then in a dress of, I thought, green-tinted silver paper. Britannicus, shortly before being murdered, has been given a dance expressing misplaced confidence immediately preceding a line expressing misplaced confidence. Isn't irony a wonderful thing?

The play is given a police-state set, for no good reason; not all 'tyrannies are alike.' Compare Ben Jonson's Roman tragedy Sejanus, which is crawling with spies and informers and, if not crying out for revival, is emitting the odd insistent murmur.

* * *

Theatre in Canada was born, according to official reports, in 1953 with the founding of the Shakespeare Festival at Stratford, Ontario, which now occupies the position of a National Theatre: that is to say something to be regarded by various factions at various times as an object of pride, complacency, embarrassment or contempt. But it has served as the model for a string of civically-financed repertory theatres across the country--all calling incidentally on the services of the same small corps of leading actors.

There is also a lucrative touring network and, especially in Toronto, a proliferating small theatre movement, with some similarities to the London fringe, but rather more to off-Broadway. It has a commercial as well as a subsidised sector, and some producers work both sides of the street.

Such is the backdrop for Toronto's first theatre festival: an attempt to show off Canadian theatre in an international context, perhaps even to force a golden age. Four days were occupied by a business conference tailored to Toronto's mixed economy (there is more money there, public and private, and more enthusiasm than in almost any other theatrical capital).

The Habima Theatre came from Israel and Ekkehard Schall from East Berlin. There was a bunch from Britain. There were gratifying reactions to Hull Truck (down atypically to one actor, the frightening Alan Williams with his 'Cockroach' trilogy) and most especially for Shared Experience: the inspired story-telling of their 'Arabian Night' (the erotic one) was greeted as a revelation of what theatre is actually for. Those of us who have been saying precisely that about them for the past five years can--and indeed did--feel smug.

Mabou Mines, currently the most idolised experimental group in Manhattan, presented 'Dead End Kids,' a baleful look at nuclear power: an atypical subject for them, and indeed for the whole New York underground, which has scarcely touched politics since the Sixties. With facts, figures, choreography and special effects precisely marshalled, it was harsh, electric, and insistently un-benevolent.

And there were of course Canadian shows: about 50, covering the established groups and others who seemed to have sprung up for the occasion. There was, perhaps, rather more ferment than achievement. The biggest native hit was the local equivalent of 'Anyone for Denis?', 'Maggie and Pierre,' whose author, Linda Griffiths, appeared as both Trudeau and as a linking journalist called George: sometimes she held conversations with one of her selves, a confusing idea, since she played all three characters Jewish (and Barbra Streisand sing-song Jewish at that). With the possible exception of the Quebecois Michel Tremblay, there are no world-class Canadian playwrights, but there are a clutch of promisings.

George Walker, whose 'Zastrozzi' was seen at the King's Head a few Christmases ago, specialises in mannered spoofs and his 'Theatre of the Film Noir,' adapted from the French and taking off from post-war Bogart, might have been a delight had the cast had any idea how to play it. The group responsible, Factory Lab, are said to have fallen into a rut. ('For every play,' said an ex-employee, 'we have to hire Nazi uniforms.')

The most intriguing piece I saw was semi-professional, and questions of acting standards hardly arose. The idea was all. It was called 'Tamara' and it took place in a house. Not a set representing a house: a real mansion, through which the audience could wander at will, confident of finding a scene in progress in any room. These scenes added up to a play, set in Fascist Italy (a black-shirted guard saw us on to the premises) and concerning the life, loves and household jealousies of Gabriele D'Annunzio. The dialogue sounded commonplace, though the organisational feat was considerable; the furnishings, perfectly detailed, were what mattered and more fascinating than any stately home because we knew they were a stage set. The kitchen was a particular triumph, and in the interval we gathered there to consume almond cream gateau that for some of us marked the artistic peak of the festival.

records.title: Just two
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Hank Williams -- The Show He Never Gave
records.body:
Just two

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE SAMUEL FRENCH drama catalogue has traditionally offered help to amateur casting-committees by publishing succinct estimates of a script's manpower requirements: as it might be, 'The Two Gentlemen of Verona' (12m, 3f, 1dg, supers), or 'The Caretaker' (3m, no doubling), or perhaps in some future edition David Rudkin's seven-hour study of incest and colic in ancient Cardiff, 'The Misconceived' (63 indeterminate).

Playwrights have recently taken to supplying these necessary statistics in their titles. Americans have been especially informative. A recent musical began its life off-off-Broadway as 'Four Jews in a Room Bitching,' though when success and transfer struck, it opted for the blander 'March of the Falsettos.' ('So we know their range and their rhythm, but how many do you need?')

The trendsetter here has been 'A Coupla White Chicks Sitting Around Talking,' which could qualify as a generic title. It would do for several recent plays, and certainly for Mayo Simon's These Men (Bush), whose name is downright mendacious. The only characters are Shelly and Cloris. Shelly, in her late thirties and self-conscious about it, lives in the Los Angeles suburb of Laurel Canyon, theoretically with an endless succession of easily disposable boy-friends; that means that in practice she lives alone. Cloris, younger, shyer and prone to calling her psychiatrist at unsocial hours, comes to stay, in flight from her own lover, whom Shelly shoos from the door with a shotgun (though he never, for reasons connected with symmetry and economics, comes remotely within range).

Cloris is prim and house-proud and keen that her boeuf bourguignonne be appreciated, while Shelly is a raunchy slob who will take TV-dinners from the freezer and eat them unthawed. Much of their conversation is devoted to strategies either for getting men or doing without them. So we have a female version of 'The Odd Couple,' with the important addition of sexual explicitness. (This is purely verbal, and has its limits; Shelly, who narrates, refuses to tell us whether they become lovers; that's none of our business. At the time I thought she was copping out; in retrospect I think she has a right.)

What happens is unsurprising. Shelly gives Cloris advice on picking up men, though it's obvious that her own promiscuity leaves her just as desolate as her room-mate's celibacy; Cloris gets involved with one of Shelly's stable; the girls decide to settle for each other; eventually habit drives Shelly to destroy the menage. But the predictability does no harm; it provides a cast-iron frame for the exceptional warmth and buoyancy of the writing. If the plot reinforces Shelly's contention that 'all women are whores,' the texture of the writing denies it. (I'm not sure that the jokes, delightful in context, will bear extraction.) The play has been impeccably directed by Sarah Pia Anderson in a pine-timbered set by Sue Plummer so apt that it took me half the play to register it. Nicky Croydon is both amusingly and touchingly tense as Cloris, while as Shelly, Stephanie Fayerman hits exactly the right tone, an odd blend of strident and confidential, for the part, the space and the play.

What she actually gets is the amused naturalism I think of as Louisville style. It shone through a quartet of short plays the Louisville Actors Theatre brought to the Toronto Festival: most notably 'Chocolate Cake,' another female duet, this time for a pair of maritally frustrated compulsive munchers, whose feminism is more explicit than that of 'These Men,' but whose unforced funniness compound the evidence for a modest revival in American drama.

* * *

Toronto has remained on my mind with the arrival in London of two small Canadian musicals, each a vehicle for a single magnetic performer. Both display the naivete which can be a strength of Canadian theatre (it leads to shows getting on, in great numbers), but which can hamper its appeal outside. Billy Bishop Goes to War (Comedy) is about a World War One air-ace with an unrivalled record as a hit-man; its opening lyrics -- 'we were off to fight the Hun/And it looked like lots of fun/somehow it never seemed like war at all' -- are simply but hauntingly set and suggest irony. But it never materialises; ambiguities are bypassed, the evolution of a hero-killer unexamined.

The real preoccupation is with the alternate petting and patronising of a colonial figurehead by the British aristocracy; Eric Peterson, playing everybody, does a capital job on them. An actor of great delicacy, he takes full advantage of the show's strategy, which resembles that of the high command: put Bishop up there and let him get on with it. One of his transformations -- a smoky chanteuse -- he brings off simply and brilliantly by an arch undulation of his shoulders.

Supporting him as author, composer, director, narrator and pianist (he likely plays piano better than any other living playwright) is John Gray. The great Canadian musical will probably precede the great British one, and Mr Gray might conceivably write it, if he stays off intractable subjects and monotonous presentations. A previous show, 'Eighteen Wheels,' was about long-distance truckers; though it was full of exhausting monologues, it also included a pungent lament on 'hauling chicken-guts in the hot August sun,' which included the sobering reminder that 'someone has to haul the parts that ain't so finger-lickin' good.'

An immortal moment in 'The Blues Brothers' (a film not bursting with immortal moments) had a barmaid explaining that her establishment featured 'both kinds of music -- Country and Western.' The implicit monotony is hardly avoided in Hank Williams -- The Show He Never Gave, which comes to the Criterion from Vancouver via Liverpool and Islington, though Williams's lyrics (not his music) were cuts above the standard whining of the genre.

Maynard Collins's script intersperses the songs with biographical material dispensed by Carl Chase in a cracked twang more unnerving than Williams's song. But he adds to it an extraordinary haunted presence; when he says that playing one-nighters 'is as close as you can get to hell on earth,' you believe him. The sound he makes at moments of high emotion is extraordinary: between a belch and a croak.

* * *

Miriam Karlin's suggestion that the Old Vic be turned into a multi-racial theatre is the best idea anybody has had for that theatre since the National left: it should make the Arts Council think again about its determination to take on no new clients. Meanwhile Ed Berman's examination of that body, Show Trial (Tricycle), suffered from the compulsion to question, explain and entertain all at the same time. Mr Berman himself makes a ferocious DA (appearing as a witness, I felt in definite need of Perry Mason), but a straight inquiry format might have accomplished more.
production_title: Hank Williams -- The Show He Never Gave

records.title: Hero of the Big Top
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Charles Charming's Challenges on His Pathway to the Throne
records.body:
Hero of the Big Top

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

TEN minutes from the final curtain the stage of Barnum (Palladium) erupts with movement and colour. Clowns clown, jugglers juggle, high-wires are walked, trapezes swung from and batons twirled, stick-puppet wild animals appear in shadow-play upstage. In the centre struts Michael Crawford, resplendently uniformed, while cast and band exhort him fortissimo to 'Join the Circus.'

It should be exhilarating. It is, a bit. But there is something curiously redundant about it. Before this climactic sequence, we have watched Barnum as an entrepreneur of midgets, white whales, centenarian and bearded women, and voluptuous Swedish nightingales.

The difference between his kind of raree-show and the circus proper is bound to seem academic, especially as the circus is this production's chosen metaphor throughout. The company is made up of singing dancing acrobats, the set is a heavily strung big top, a ringmaster announces each crisis in the hero's life; leaving his wife for a brief fling with Jenny Lind, Barnum approaches her by tight-rope, singing. So the show's climax proudly leads us to exactly where we've been all evening.

The general pattern is that Barnum finds a new attraction, and then a number outlines the attraction's attractions. Michael Stewart's lyrics accordingly boil down to a series of nimble but static tongue-twisters. The Jenny Lind romance turns out to be a false trail, and the only conflict is between Barnum and his wife who wants him to be respectable. She temporarily succeeds when he goes into politics, to the accompaniment of a pounding blues called 'Black and White' with a stage design to match.

Eventually he revolts and the stage goes garish again; we are meant to rejoice but I found myself lamenting the departure of the most stylish visuals of the evening. The theme is fully stated in an oppressive ballad called 'The Colours of My Life'; this however is the only blemish on Cy Coleman's score which again demonstrates his ability to spark new and quirky life out of old forms. One song, 'I Like Your Style,' may be the first ever jazz-jig. A succession of cheer-up songs threatens to turn the show into a hip 'Hello Dolly' but Mr Coleman usually contrives some way to throw them jauntily off-centre. But here too the show's scheme proves self-defeating; the sophistication written into the tunes is largely erased by having them orchestrated for a deafening circus band.

Mr Crawford won the standingest ovation I have ever witnessed, a tribute to his energy and intrepidity. (William C. Witter, the ringmaster, spends the whole evening nonchalantly shinning up and down ropes without gaining so much as a hand-clap but then he isn't the star.) But Mr Crawford has not managed to transform his personality; his Barnum is curiously harmless. Jim Dale on Broadway gave the part more swagger but he was still unable to warm it up. For the truth is that beneath all the energy and inventiveness there is a very large hole.

* * *

I responded far less to Alan Bleasdale's Having a Ball at the Lyric, Hammersmith, than when it was premiered a few months ago in Oldham. Three explanations suggest themselves: (a) London critics relax their standards out of town; (b) the Oldham production was better; (c) I boobed. There is probably truth in all three, but I'll stick with (b), though I have to qualify it immediately. Technically, in the matters of sight-gags and visual finesse, Alan Dossor's London direction is much superior. It loses on human values, and most importantly on the most important.

The play concerns three men who come to a private clinic to be vasectomised. They are a council official, a one-time school bully, and his former victim, who is just beginning to get clever. This last was played by David Ross at Oldham as a fine example of the turning Northern worm. Mr Ross is still in the cast, but in the small role of a male nurse (which he plays very well). Meanwhile Philip Donaghy, most recently seen as Jesus and St Paul, tries without much success to change his uncompromising spots. But the play depends inordinately on getting us on his side.

For what has decided him to have no more children is the threat of nuclear war. If we can't swallow this theme when he introduces it we are really going to gag when it becomes blatant; as it does when the councillor, under sedation, starts babbling of privileged shelters and martial law. Other aspects of the play--which at Oldham seemed a rough but bracing life-and-death farce--start falling away, notably the conflict between the nurse and the (female) surgeon over the ethics of abortion. At Oldham this was at least resolved; at Hammersmith it is just forgotten (or was there a literal loss of memory on the first night?) disconcerting the audience so that the McGillian last line was received with puzzlement instead of uproar. There are still plenty of laughs, but they don't build.

* * *

Waiting for Godot is given immortal embodiment at the Roundhouse by Max Wall and Trevor Peacock. Mr Wall's Vladimir is the more dapper of the two; he does sport a bow-tie even if it's pinned somewhere far down his lapel, and his tones of high-strung indignation, resonant with sour memories of former glories and recent miseries, suit the text uncannily. Mr Peacock meanwhile is as grumpy as grubby, with the bedrock humour that comes of enforced tolerance, twinkling only when he gets the chance literally to put the boot in.

The funnier the play gets, the more disturbing; these two clowns don't have to manufacture laughs; they make a human relationship out of a professional bond. Wolfe Morris throws away much of Pozzo through huffing and puffing, though when he allows himself some legato he comes through. Gary Waldhorn's careful delivery of Lucky's tirade is the best I have heard.

* * *

Observer readers may have noticed that Clive James has written a new long poem called Charles Charming's Challenges on His Pathway to the Throne and that he is reading it, with assistance, at the Apollo. He's queering his own pitch; for though a brilliant off-the-cuffer he goes to pieces when confronted by a script, and his method of pulling himself together is to come down heavily on all the words like a Movietone newsreader with a grievance. He thus spoils many of the best jokes in a text that rarely falls below a decent level of funniness and sometimes--as in a sustained fantasia on Gordonstoun--gets well above it.

For the opposition Russell Davies blows horns of steadily increasing magnitude and impersonates on a very wide front (Pamela Stephenson, doing the ladies, has less scope and less tact until she springs her Lady Di in a coda) but his most important contribution is to establish Charles himself as shy, well-meaning and thoroughly sweet, thus giving the evening a dramatic centre: one that it needs since the media-figures brought into the princely presence for the purpose of instant lampoon are pretty indiscriminately assembled. The author's views on royalty were unwittingly summarised by another accomplished coupleteer as:

Always keep ahold of nurse
For fear of finding something worse.
production_title: Charles Charming's Challenges on His Pathway to the Throne

records.title: The war of the worlds
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The war of the worlds

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

TWO days after I had seen The Worlds (New Half Moon) I met a man who told me that Edward Bond had based his play on Timon of Athens. I wished (this is beginning to sound like one of Mr Bond's own parables) that he hadn't spoken. The Timon connection had struck me while I watched the play but I wanted it to be a surprise.

Mr Bond's Timon figure is an industrialist named Trench who is kidnapped by terrorists and who discovers when released that his subordinates have taken advantage of his absence to vote him out of office. Like Timon he invites them to a farewell party in order to insult them, and then disappears from society (although, like Tony Hancock when he became a hermit in one of his radio half-hours, he is careful to choose a wilderness within reach of the shops). In exile he re-encounters his former captors who now have a new prisoner and, in a bored disinterested way, offers them sanctuary. As he says, unlike his supposed friends, "those people told the truth: they said they were my enemies."

Like Shakespeare, Mr Bond runs into trouble finding things for his solitary misanthrope to do and fitting him with a credible opposition, but he does tell a better story than Shakespeare. The play has the customary Bondian virtues of speed, clarity and economy.

All the same Trench's gratified bitterness, as he sees violence conquering on all sides, threatens to take over the play. He manages somehow to welcome the chaos while despising its activators; and he has an important dramatic advantage which the author may not have calculated. He is always alone. He may behave smugly to his colleagues while still in power but they are characterised as creeps who deserve it.

When threatened by the terrorists he stands his ground, and his scorn for his supporters ("One advantage of being chucked out of my organisation is that I don't have to put up with your inane toadying") is completely captivating. One naturally sympathises with a man under the gun; a threatened human life always counts for more than whatever cause is menacing it. In addition, Ian McDiarmid's performance as Trench, one of his best essays in the grotesque-sardonic, dwarfs the rest of a competent cast. Theatre is an undemocratic form, responsive to star power.

To redress the balance Mr McDiarmid doubles as Trench's most articulate opponent (it's unfortunate that the two can never meet) who closes the play by declaring that "we're all terrorists... we live by terror." Mr Bond is at his best in attacking the hypocrisy that condemns one kind of violence while ignoring or justifying another, though he fails to acknowledge that that is a characteristic of the Left as much as of the Right. There are two scenes of confusion in which everybody shouts at once: one takes place among the capitalists, one among the guerrillas. Maybe we are meant to equate them.

The terrorists are acting in support - unsolicited as far as we can tell - of a strike. Second time round, the terrorists get the wrong man: a chauffeur, instead of his employer. He lies on the floor, tied hand and foot and bundled in white, for most of the second act. He is obviously meant to be a powerful image; Trench uses him as a cue for speeches about the human animal.

But he turns the play false; if this mistake were made in real life, the different parties would hardly be able to move fast enough to disentangle themselves. But here the jailers go on holding him (keeping him trussed up apparently for the author's visual convenience); the strikers make no concessions; the bosses do, but only because they realise it will improve their public image.

Mr Bond misses the deeper irony which is that they would probably act out of quite genuine humane feeling, which certainly would bump up the profits and leave things essentially unchanged. Every now and then Mr Bond slides in explicit lectures which, since they are brief and well written, the audience take like lambs; but which neither support nor are supported by the action of the play. You believe them or not, according to the ideas you have brought into the theatre with you; and the author seems to have written them in the same spirit.

However, they are not the whole play; and if Mr Bond sometimes seems to walk into complexities he wishes weren't there, such misadventures are a bonus for the rest of us. The play takes its title from the observation - acknowledged by both sides, though with different emphasis - that there are two worlds, everyday civilised discourse and the brute moneyed reality beneath; and there is power in the collision.

Trench by the way does act in the end: murderously. It occurred to me that his nihilism was meant to reflect that of Mr Bond's bete noire Samuel Beckett. Actually it is impossible to imagine a Beckett character killing anyone, even himself; in his world, talk is sufficient purgation. The wounds Mr Beckett contemplates seem to be his own rather than, as in Mr Bond's case, other people's; which sounds selfish in theory but in dramatic practice isn't.

* * *

However, I don't think Texts (Riverside Studios), derived from Texts For Nothing and How It Is, counts as dramatic practice. The legendary American director Joseph Chaikin is sole performer; fitted out with some Chaplinesque props he proves an accomplished mime, shifting from haunch to haunch in sympathy with the Beckett rhythm of instant self-contradiction, and a sensitive speaker. But he is also disconcertingly ethereal; to make Beckett's non-theatrical texts work on stage you need, I suspect, to go full-tilt for paradox and gallows humour. Probably you need to be Irish.

* * *

In Herbert Achternbusch's Ella (ICA) a man tells his mother's life story - one of poverty, humiliation and confinement - while she slumps in a chair, a zombie intent on watching television which she turns up louder when he collapses. That probably sounds a potent juxtaposition; at moments it is, especially since Bill Paterson, yet another virtuoso actor, gives yet another virtuoso performance, while Janet Henfrey is a picture of pathos.

But wait: Mr Paterson is not merely telling us about her, he is impersonating her; at least he is speaking in the first person and wearing a frock. In addition he is addressing us from behind wire-netting; the set is a chicken-run, infested by real birds. They are too, with their lofty squawks and scrambled feet. Mr Paterson, in many a throwaway, directs our attention to them as well as to his own situation as a Scots actor enacting a play set in Bavaria (not an area any current German playwright recommends). It is, in every sense, a lot to get through.

* * *

Unexpectedly I got more out of The Rocking Chair (at the Fountains Abbey pub in Praed Street), a first play with characters by no means as fascinating as their author, Gregory Day, thinks they are but still building up to an interesting two-edged study of selfishness. It is paired with Adaptations by Elaine May which has all the marks of a Sixties satire on the American Way of Life; some of them are amusing marks.

records.title: A fine life, a velvet life
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Tap Dance on a Telephone Wire
records.body:
A fine life, a velvet life

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Dekker's 'The Shoemakers' Holiday' at the National.

JOHN DEXTER'S production of Dekker's The Shoemakers' Holiday (Olivier) comes along 17 years after his revival of that other cordwaining classic, 'Hobson's Choice.' In a properly programmed world the National would be running the two in repertoire under such an appropriate generic title as 'A Load of Old Cobblers.'

Between the Elizabethan London of 'The Shoemakers' Holiday' and the Victorian Manchester of 'Hobson's Choice' the trade obviously shrunk. Henry Hobson had a staff of two, who were bullied, underpaid and kept chained up in the cellar. His ancestor, Simon Eyre, runs a happy and populous street-level shop, full of incipient trade union spirit. When Eyre, finding himself in an upwardly mobile situation, moves on up, his foreman takes over and the business expands, apparently giving employment to half the National Theatre company.

Hobson had three daughters to bully; Eyre only has a wife, but what he lacks in familial scope he makes up for in creativity. 'Midriff,' he calls her, and 'Dame Clapperdudgeon.' But they love each other; and are fairly benevolent towards everyone else.

The National's publicity describes the play as a 'romantic and bitter comedy,' the implication being that they wouldn't dream of wasting our time on comedy that wasn't bitter. Well, there are undertones. One of Eyre's journeymen is pressed to the French wars and returns minus a leg. Anyone considering turning 'The Shoemakers' Holiday' into a musical should note that here is a gift to lyricist and choreographer alike: a character who hobbles as he cobbles.

His homecoming coincides with Eyre's appointment as sheriff of London; the scene is masterfully orchestrated by Mr Dexter (Dekker having provided him with a wonderful score) and the crucial moment has the audience catching its breath. One of the subtleties is the guilty reaction of another journeyman who happens to be a nobleman, AWOL for amatory reasons and further disguised as a Dutchman. This is one of the few roles in world drama to combine the functions of juvenile lead and dialect comic.

At the end, after much banqueting and reconciliation, war closes in again; but the production makes surprisingly little of it. We are now in an unalterably happy mood, greatly fostered by the appearance of David Yelland as a King (unnamed but palpably Henry V), amiably bored with the royal routine and going through it at double speed.

Nor is a class-warfare theme easy to activate, since what the play exudes is class-content. 'By the Lord of Ludgate,' says Simon, now Mayor Eyre, 'it's a stirring life, a fine life, a velvet life.' Citizens are happy to be citizens, nobles like being nobles and shoemakers are almost insufferably chuffed about spending their lives making shoes. We don't meet any beggars.

There is some rancour when lines are crossed--when a grocer's daughter marries an earl's nephew or a gentleman tries to abduct a seamstress--but it is soon dispersed. All know their place; and Mr Dexter does a first-rate informative job of keeping them there.

Eyre himself is unexpectedly downbeat; the role is played by Alfred Lynch, a good actor of terrier temperament but lightweight. Whether casting determined interpretation or vice versa I wouldn't know, but though Mr Lynch is bemused, benevolent, prudent or shifty as required, his voice, a piping twang, deprives Eyre's rumbustious invective--and hence the play--of flavour and swing.

Prominent supporting members of the Lynchmob are John Normington, sober and shop-stewardly; Peter Lovstrom, hopping mad; and, pre-eminently, Brenda Bruce, who as Mistress, later Lady, Eyre (all right, the Eyress) copes wittily with hooped gowns of increasingly fearsome dimensions.

In the world outside too many roles go for too little. Exceptions are Selina Cadell, as ever; Nicholas Selby, a heavy father with a prodigy of a forked grey beard, (who scores the wittiest of the play's myriad double-entendres by remaining apparently oblivious of it; and Michael Beint, in the microscopic role of a swag-bellied Hollander. Julia Trevelyan Oman's three-panelled set handsomely summons the spirit of London, which the evening finally celebrates. You can have fun just collecting the place-names.

* * *

At the Theatre Upstairs a company magically entitled That's Not It presents a piece of feminine performance art, and manages to get the best of two frequently oppressive worlds.

The show is called Room and it takes off from Virginia Woolf's demand for one of her own. A writing wife, looking like a skivvy, asks for space, spiritual and especially physical, in which to live, evoking the social and domestic hindrances, invoking predecessors from Mrs Woolf back to Mrs Behn.

Natasha Morgan functions as writer-deviser, as soft-spoken doe-eyed leading actress and, most importantly, as director, in which role she makes excellent use of simultaneous action and of simple clutter. One moment in which sheaves of paper--presumably written by women--rise from the ground to the vertical where they proceed to hang accusingly, is inspiration.

* * *

Last Sunday the Oklahoma! cast gave a lively account of Minnie's Boys, a 10-year-old American show about the early days of the Marx Brothers. Confused as to whether it's really about star-struck Mom (pre-empted by 'Gypsy') or her brood (post--I suppose--empted by 'A Night in the Ukraine,') it nevertheless boasts some numbers which outclass anything more recent that's currently on view: music, Larry Grossman; lyrics, Hal Hackady.

Most recent of the recents is Wonderland, staged on a scale unprecedented at the King's Head and niftily choreographed by Tudor Davies. However, it too is confused with plot-lines going off into nowhere. It concerns Hollywood, chiefly during World War II; and it implicitly arraigns the movies for dealing in stereotypes. For issues the show itself has a Jew who pretends to be a Gentile and, for comic-pathetic effect, a vice versa. Quite apart from not being averse to a bit of tinsel itself, it cannot bring its own characters to life: The lummox who makes good by accident, the temperamental German director. (What, twice in a lifetime?) The cast are good, Dave Brown's music musicianly, William Fairchild's lyrics often the prisoners of their rhyme-schemes.

You couldn't say that about Donna Franceschild's song-words for Tap Dance on a Telephone Wire, but if I go on about their sloppiness you'll think I'm developing a nervous tic. At half-time they drove me out of the theatre, more in anger than in sorrow. A pity, since visually this is by far the best show yet at the Tricycle; Mary Moore's black-and-white set brilliantly evokes a Los Angeles telephone exchange, where none of the all-female workers is happy.

Again the cast are good; Susan Glanville, as the supervisor, offers a model of what I believe is Brechtian acting, meticulously separating nice person from nasty role. There are day-in-the-life scenes which are interesting, and gloom scenes which are gloomy. It's a trunk-call away from Judy Holliday and... Bells are Ringing; the brutal truth behind those switchboard messages of goodwill. Have a nice week.

records.title: Fresh air
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Fresh air

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Stratford and London

GEORGE FARQUHAR'S The Twin Rivals, (Other Place, Stratford) is widely regarded as a turning-point in English comedy.

Its place in the story depends on its morality, a new commodity in the theatre at the time of its premiere in 1702, introduced, according to Farquhar's own whimsical preface, in response to the clean-up campaign of Jeremy Collier, the Mary Whitehouse of his day.

Farquhar's subsequent comedies commended themselves to Victorian critics for having country settings, letting breaths of fresh air into the fetid confines of Restoration comedy, that kind of thing. The London locale of 'The Twin Rivals' is of the fetidest, but the sages excused this and commended Farquhar for his plotting: pitting a good brother against a bad, he leaves us in no doubt which is which and ensures that the good comes out on top. Bravo.

All this of course was a long time ago. For us, Farquhar's morality merely heralds the descent of comedy into sentimentality. But to herald a descent is not necessarily to exemplify it, and 'The Twin Rivals' seems the product of a brief but fortunate moment. We only feel cheated when a particularly reptilian villain, specialising in rape and rapier, turns Christian gentleman and repents.

Fortunately he is only a minor monster, and the major one makes no such blunders. This is Benjamin Wouldbe, who suffers socially and financially from being both a younger brother (by about half an hour) and a hunchback. When his father dies, he manages to grab the estate by the quaint expedient of forcing a forged will between the old gentleman's teeth. Mike Gwilym plays very artfully with our sympathies throughout the evening.

More surprising, perhaps, is the solid success of Miles Anderson as his respectable sibling, who wears spectacles with an air that guarantees virtue, and who loses them at the height of the most riotous stage duel (arranged by Malcolm Ranson) I have ever seen. Miriam Karlin is strong and entertaining as a bawd and procuress (helping them, so to speak, both in and out) and there are performances by Paul Shelley and Harriet Walter that fastidiously avoid period cliche.

The fleet direction is by John Caird, hitherto a rather shadowy figure (I never knew you, Caird), but now apparently his own man. He is much helped by his designer, Ultz, whose white fantastic costumes (the characters tend to resemble birds--of prey, passage or paradise--while Mr Gwilym in triumph takes to wearing frocks) reinforce the point that one man's puritanism is another's decadence; and by his author. Marvellously funny, an actor's delight.

* * *

Stratford's main theatre offers an enjoyable but skeletal version of The Winter's Tale. Patrick Stewart's Leontes flashes a terrifying smile. There is a cruel humour even in his worst rages. In repentance this becomes a moving performance and it is always a formidably accomplished one, but in Ronald Eyre's production Leontes never seems dangerous to anyone except himself. A crying baby is an excellent human touch that helps to place Leontes's jealousy and to link the play's two worlds.

There is a similar reality in Sheila Hancock's Paulina, who begins carefully comic, patronising everybody, and goes on to thrilling defiance and magical resignation. Other welcome arrivals are Gemma Jones as Hermione and, as old lord and chorus, the infallible Robert Eddison. The Bohemian scenes are jollied up by Stephen Oliver's pastiche Victorian tunes, vivaciously delivered by Geoffrey Hutchings, whose Autolycus arrives to shear the shepherds looking like John Wellington Wells (dealer in magic and spells) and behaving like a hopeful auditionee for 'Barnum.'

* * *

The RSC is obviously the right company to stage a play called Thirteenth Night (Warehouse), though Howard Brenton's title turns out to be kidding. His real model is 'Macbeth,' with a rabble-rousing touch of 'Julius Caesar.' A socialist politician dreams of himself as an initially high-minded dictator, ascending to power by murdering his Prime Minister, egged on by a fanatical girl-friend and three black-clad female activists who live in a multi-storey car-park. Later he progresses to murdering his colleagues or, when they are unavailable, their families.

Sometimes, as when the protagonist hysterically contemplates his axeman's hands, Mr Brenton invests his pastiche with considerable power. But the game palls; we find ourselves anticipating the parallels, and when Banquo's ghost turns out to be the visiting ambassador from Chad ('why aren't you black?' asks the haunted one), it becomes a bit of a joke. The dream and 'Macbeth' devices should in theory reinforce each other; in fact they cancel each other out. And, echoes apart, the progress of tyranny is predictable.

Most of us have already had this nightmare; Mr Brenton, having it--at least as far as his plays are concerned--for the first time, overrates its freshness--though sometimes, as when a character discovers and proclaims the idea of evil, you can hear a dramatist's mind moving. Michael Pennington strikes attitudes sonorously and energetically; Domini Blythe makes him a chilling mate; and he has an excellent posse of victims, including Derek Godfrey, Paul Webster and--a juvenile lead unrecognisable in glasses and slicked-down hair--John Bowe.

* * *

However portentous it becomes, Mr Brenton's play survives on narrative energy, a virtue he shares with Edward Bond and--surprisingly--John Galsworthy. The Skin Game (on tour at the Ashcroft, Croydon) is full of bloodless Edwardian slang. Set in 1920, it must have seemed quaint even then; not for nothing is its first gentleman nicknamed Dodo. The no-gloves fight he wages against an intrusive entrepreneur has lost its urgency; all this careful marshalling of issues is now self-defeating. The gentry are obvious snobs; and the arriviste plainly our man--Anthony Quayle, bruised and thrusting, gives the only live performance of the evening. But still I wanted to know what happened next, even while suspecting that I would be disappointed when it did.

* * *

During the interval of The Misanthrope (Roundhouse) the pundits were disputing the merits of Richard Wilbur's coupleted translation. I thought them snappy--the couplets not the pundits. But really one couldn't judge, since the cast murdered the metre and hid the rhymes. Nicholas Amer as the maitre d' is an exception, but his duties are confined to announcing people.

Second best is Tom Courtenay, whose bleating Alceste charts a careful but rapid decline from honest protestant to cry-baby clown. I missed the depths of enraged masochism that Alec McCowen discovered in the role, but maybe he was importing those English complexities into a glass-smooth French classic. (Why doesn't somebody revive 'The Plain Dealer,' stolen--and complicated--by Wycherley from this play?) Other performances vary from dull to deplorable.

* * *

One Woman Plays--four of them--by Dario Fo and his wife Franca Rame (Cottesloe) are very entertaining, considering they are all monologues of female complaint. Yvonne Bryceland, delivering them, displays unexpected comic flair. But her conception of comedy unfortunately pushes her towards silliness, which is already inherent in the script.

In the main segment she plays a woman locked in her flat by her husband with a crippled brother-in-law, a baby, a heavy breather and a peeping Tom. She refuses to let her lover release her; preferring to wreak vengeance for her confinement with a shotgun on all but the baby. This last omission is rectified in the last playlet, in which Miss Bryceland plays Medea.

records.body:
Comedy in the round

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

CONVERSATIONS WITH AYCKBOURN
by Ian Watson
Macdonald £8.95

THIS BOOK is an extended interview sustained, according to the acknowledgments, by 'several memorable meals.' Ian Watson points out that Alan Ayckbourn is the only major playwright in this country not to have been accorded a critical monograph, but seems to feel little inclination to fill that gap himself. The reason, he suggests, is that Ayckbourn is 'temperamentally incapable of standing still long enough for critics to pigeon-hole him' but, to the limited extent that that is true, it also applies to plenty of other writers.

The real difficulty Ayckbourn presents to critics is that his plays are so unquotable; he gives you less on the page than any other notable dramatist. I can recall numberless hilarious moments from 'Bedroom Farce,' but if I started transcribing them you wouldn't believe me. Everything depends on inflection and on situation. Credit to the managements who have seen the plays' potential; although of course to a great extent Mr Ayckbourn is his own management, trying out his own plays at the Stephen Joseph Theatre-in-the-Round, to whose direction he annually devotes the 50 weeks he doesn't spend knocking off a new comedy.

Critics have not, I think, really been blind to what he is doing. He has been writing drawing-room comedies which acknowledge -- without getting hysterically assertive about it -- that times have changed. To a great extent one praises his plays in negatives: he does not foist wisecracks on characters who would never utter them; he does not draw back from confrontations; he does not steer his characters towards artificially happy endings; he does not give them prettier homes than they could afford; he does not tell lies. All this is true both of his 'light' and 'dark' plays (it is a little disconcerting to find that he makes this distinction himself -- I thought it was just a reviewers' game).

All the same he does give us trouble; we recognise his achievement but are unsure how important it is. 'Absurd Person Singular' and 'The Norman Conquests' both made me laugh a lot, but I found their sombre elements both over-calculated and over-rated. 'Bedroom Farce' captivated me, and repeated viewings increased my respect for it. It keeps the audience amused for two hours, making them aware as the lights fade of the cost of the action in battered lives: something comedy writers always say they want to achieve but rarely do. It may well turn out the classic English play of the 1970s.

Since then I have been generally on Ayckbourn's side (a position made easier by the loutishness of most attacks on him); but I have to say 'generally' because the sheer volume of his work is making it difficult to judge his plays individually. This does not mean that he would write better if he wrote less, but that the plays are beginning to assume the aspect of a continuous tapestry.

Seeing his plays in situ at Scarborough has helped. Some of the best passages of this book deal with the establishment of this theatre by Stephen Joseph, the quirky English prophet of theatre-in-the-round, and Ayckbourn's inheritance of it. He characterises it, quite rightly, as a community theatre, dedicated to new writing and ensemble acting, and it's a pleasing irony that these aims should have been achieved in a milieu execrated by those who usually profess them. ('I'm on a crusade to try to persuade people that theatre can be funny; but one must start doing that; some bugger from the Left comes in and tells them it's instructive and drives them all out again.')

If Ayckbourn never wrote a word he would still be vitally important as a theatre director -- though it's his writing that enables his theatre to function. He has, incidentally, an unrivalled theatrical grounding as actor, technician and everything else; and he turns out, unsurprisingly, to be an unpretentious, wary, illuminating and entertaining talker. There are unexpected appearances (he has lovely tales to tell of Phil Silvers, the great neurotic comic who starred in 'How the Other Half Loves' on Broadway) and equally surprising absences; Eric Thompson, who directed most of his commercial successes in London, is never mentioned. A book of interviews is usually a disgrace; this one is worth all the critical examinations that haven't been written and most of those that inevitably will be.

Addendum, characteristic and revealing, from 'The Norman Conquests' -- 'I think other people's marriages are invariably a source of amazement. . . . I have found quite often it's the people you look at and say, well they won't last long, who cling on grimly till death. Maybe they're so aware of public opinion, they're determined to prove it wrong.' I found that at random. So he is quotable.
