records.title: Classroom memories
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Classroom memories

ROBERT CUSHMAN on plays by Colin Welland and Arnold Wesker.

TO judge from his programme-note Colin Welland thinks of his play Roll On Four O'Clock (Lyric, Hammersmith) as some kind of nostalgic polemic. The play is set in a northern secondary modern school some 13 years ago. Mr Welland taught in one himself, and he writes bitterly of the social divisiveness they both reflected and encouraged.

That's in the programme; in the play there are a few lines about the dead-end jobs awaiting the boys when they leave, but most of what we see - sub-military discipline, casual brutality, equally casual kindness - is common to British education at any level. I doubt if the comprehensives have changed it much. I went to a grammar school just down the road from this theatre, and much of the play struck, amusingly or uncomfortably, close to home.

The amusement outweighs the discomfort. There is a continuing thread of plot about the persecution of a possibly homosexual boy both by his contemporaries and by some of the staff, but it is not very deeply investigated and some of the characters' attitudes are inconsistent.

There seem to be only 10 people on the staff; small for a school but big for a play, and hard to keep track of if we don't have a camera to do our focusing for us. (The play was written for television.) There is a new young art-teacher. (Mr Welland taught art.) Maybe we are meant to view the action through his eyes; the end of the play suggests that, but nothing else does. His antagonists are dragged even more unceremoniously into the limelight.

Mr Welland sees the atmosphere in the staff-room as similar to that in the playground; the keynote of both is boisterous resignation. The kids are deprived of choice, and the masters mostly suspect they have made the wrong one. From this Mr Welland as author furnishes group-scenes of vivacity if not finesse, which are then brought triumphantly to life by Mr Welland as director.

The evening's highlight has Clive Swift, as senior art master, striding the floor with eyes rapturously closed, exhorting his class to get with the rhythm of clay-moulding, a rhythm that finally resolves itself into a stirring rendition of 'Dry Bones.' A companion piece has Glyn Owen's headmaster addressing us - the audience - at weekly assembly. These two players, along with Windsor Davies (woodwork), establish a pervasive air of beleaguered decency.

* * *

In Caritas (Cottesloe) Arnold Wesker takes the story of a young religious devotee, who walled herself up as an anchoress in Surrey in 1329, and moves it to Norfolk, for the dialect, and 1381, for the Peasants' Revolt. Christine Carpenter's retreat is seen as one way of grappling with a changing world; that of her former fiance, who dies with Wat Tyler, as another.

One sympathises with the Bishop of Norwich, faced with both problems at once, but seeing no special need to relate to them; and is less grateful than he must have been that all the exciting bits happen off stage.

For the first half of the play Christine is invisible behind her wall; a local crone drops by to regale her with stories of other self-imposed martyrdoms. On the other side of the stage her family doggedly grumble.

All this covers the ground; nothing in it defies belief, but nothing compels it either. Then the stage, or a section of it, revolves; and we are with Christine, who is having second thoughts. Her historical counterpart physically broke out and was put back in again, but Mr Wesker is not condescending to anything so vulgarly dramatic. His heroine stays where she is, going madder, which at least provides Patti Love with a superb opportunity to do what she does best, i.e. to be uncanny and to suggest that what the author does best is personal trauma.

Her huddled figure against the wall of her cell is as haunting as her speech, which is a desperate crash-course in Christian masochism. (Mr Wesker is of course Jewish; and his play, the dramatic equivalent of a fast, opened on Yom Kippur.) Frederick Treves as the Bishop begins suavely, but when he has to go to pieces he goes to pieces without, seemingly, much guidance from his director, John Madden. There is a Cottesloe tradition (broken only by 'American Buffalo' and 'Has Washington Legs') of doing small, lugubrious new plays. Caritas fits snugly into it.

There are, though I hate to admit it, worse things than nostalgia. The Mitford Girls (Globe) is bursting with calculated high spirits, not one of which managed to raise mine. It is the nadir of the compilation show. The only facts that seem to have struck Caryl Brahms and Ned Sherrin about the Mitford sisters are that they were upper-class, which rather argued for a fusillade of supposedly endearing West End snob jokes, and that they lived through the Twenties and Thirties, which makes them good for musical nostalgia.

Nostalgia in this context means that good old songs are performed not because they're good, but because they're old -- or because their titles are, in the authors' fevered imaginations, dramatically relevant. Thank You for the Memory, a very specific American lyric about a broken marriage, really has little to do with English nursery reminiscence.

There are also new songs; the authors' view of their characters' range of interests may be gathered from the fact that three numbers called 'Why Do People Fall in Love', 'Why Fall for Love' and 'I'll Fall in Love' are done virtually back to back and are remorselessly reprised. If you want to stage an inter-war songfest then do it, but why tie it to the Mitfords whose interests, apart from Nancy's surprising toughness as writer, lies in their bizarre political commitments, here treated as if they couldn't possibly have been serious. (Imagine a show that makes you feel sorry on behalf of Unity Mitford.)

The presumption is relentlessly coy; the girls quote at us all evening, but never do more than giggle with each other. They also play all the other female parts, which is confusing. Patricia Hodge gives a good performance, not two. There is some genetic tic to the look of things, but that somehow makes it worse.

One of the plundered classics, Cole Porter's Let's Do It, also turns up in Moliere's The Learned Ladies, as staged in Richard Wilbur's translation at (and indeed by) Pentameters, above the Three Horseshoes pub in Hampstead, by a new lot calling themselves the High Command Theatre Company.

This and other melodic interpolations, plus the removal of the play to the country-house Twenties, suggests that Moliere's bluestockings are to be reduced to Mitford status, and that the director thinks that their play too is about love. But it comes through as sex, which never did a comedy any harm, and a bright, intelligent cast bring all the characters to life.

The play comes over as better - certainly, with stronger situations and more pertinent satire - than either The Misanthrope or Tartuffe. Moliere, staged without solemnity and without camp, can make an audience freely and continually laugh; a last performance tonight.

records.title: A soaring Seagull
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
A soaring Seagull

by Robert Cushman

I did not expect to see a better production of anything this year than Max Stafford-Clark's Irish version of The Seagull. I certainly did not expect to see a better production of the same play. But here (at the Almeida, Islington) it is, directed by Mike Alfreds for Shared Experience and winning by a beak.

Both the grouping and the individual performances are three-dimensional. When the spectators at Konstantin's play begin chattering and interrupting we almost become accomplices in their rudeness; the break-up of the performance carries enormous force, and is a major foretaste of Konstantin's self-destructiveness.

The opening duologue sets an unsparing tone for the production. For a few seconds it seems over-emphatic; then it delivers the truth. We are beginning to learn that Chekhov can take tough handling; the marginal character of Medvyedenko (here played by Peter Wight) gets funnier and more wretched with each production. Masha's famous reply to him, 'I'm in mourning for my life,' is followed here by the unspoken words, 'you fool.' It doesn't stop the schoolmaster from whining on about Konstantin and Nina being in love, and uniting in the creation of 'one artistic image.'

Maggie Wells makes a meal of Masha's snuff-taking, and of her melodramatic confessions of love (delivered always to a third person, sympathetic but unsympathising). At every point the production homes in on the characters' small sillinesses and larger evasions. I think of Shamrayev (Matthew Scurfield) sashaying on with a riding-crop to play the part of brutal overseer; Sorin (David Blake Kelly) reflecting that to be 'a small literary figure would be nice' and wincing in memory of his own futile career when it is suggested that Konstantin should follow him into the Civil Service; the doctor (Philip Voss is the best and pearliest Dorn since George Devine) elegantly sidestepping emotional commitment; and his whimperingly adoring Polina (a funny and revelatory performance by Sandra Voe) snatching from his hand the roses presented to him by her daughter.

Philip Osment's Konstantin is a bearded, unruly mother's boy, who in the third act returns to the womb almost before your eyes. But there is enough fire and anger in him to make Nina's love seem at least a possibility, and a wonderful moment towards the end when she falls crying into his arms. As Nina, Lorna Heilbron passes from enchanted (and enchanting) impressionable girlhood to bitter maturity; she slides into 'I am a seagull' with dauntless conviction. Jonathan Hackett's Trigorin is properly deglamourised; his trousers are held up with string and he gravitates naturally to the outskirts of any group; but he lacks authority and his long speeches sag.

Gillian Barge wittily sizes up Arkadina's indulgences, but she overdoes them. She has great moments though: ploughing through a salad while supposedly worrying about her son, and at the end when she is plainly aware of the meaning of that pistol-shot. She eagerly accepts Dorn's reassurances, and the action is then prolonged a little; we see the doctor striding off to attend to the corpse, while the others settle back into their game of bingo.

If the rest of the production had not done so, this sequence -- extending the play without falsifying it -- would establish Mr Alfreds as one of our three or four best directors; add to it the huge audacious pause that follows the end of Konstantin's play when everyone waits for somebody else to say something.

* * *

Chekhov is briefly invoked in Michael Abbensetts's In The Mood (Hampstead), when a black actor tells about playing Uncle Van in a musical about three sisters who want to leave Atlanta to live in New York and in which one character wears black because... (For some reason nobody is threatening to chop down their cotton plantation.) Mr Abbensetts may also have been mindful of Chekhov's admonition that if you show a revolver in Act One, you must fire it before the end; he threatens, but there are no gunshots. In fact, little momentous happens.

In a cast of five, three men and a woman are West Indian; the fifth (played with appropriate washed-out attractiveness by Marty Cruickshank) is an actual or potential girl-friend for all the male trio, who represent different experiences and viewpoints among British blacks. One is a well-to-do plumber, another his WWII buddy hooked on reminiscent patriotism. The third is younger and angrier, but a chronic wastrel.

The play is decently entertaining, but everything about it seems obvious. The title refers to Glenn Miller; the fact that nostalgia is under attack doesn't make the shorthand any easier to accept. Stefan Kalipha is funny if disorganised, and Norman Beaton's contained irony makes him the favourite black actor of white spectators, this one included.

* * *

A few rungs down the same naturalist ladder is Ellen Dryden's Harvest (Ambassadors), in which a London refugee miserably returns to her provincial family. Just down the streets from the theatre a plaque commemorates the Wesley brothers; they are less vividly present inside. The play begins with a Methodist funeral service; for the ending see the title, probably also referring to what the characters have got out of their religion, which dramatically seems to be not much, despite a hovering minister.

Again the expected conflicts are gone through; the most potentially interesting -- involving the breakdown of a mature student on a degree course -- is frittered away by being filtered through to us only through the nominal protagonist, the victim's sister. Lynn Farleigh plays her with the tart, bloodless cadences of Glenda Jackson. (The play comes from the same stable as Miss Jackson's hit 'Rose.') Supporting acting is sharp; especially Constance Chapman as the eldest relative and Sylvestra Le Touzel as the youngest. Donald Gee is touching as the mazed brother.

* * *

Finally a late and early Shaw. The early is Arms and the Man (Lyric), given an attractive, good-natured production by Jonathan Lynn. Bulgaria here becomes Ruritania, and some of the cast too obviously relish the joke. Anna Nygh as the supposedly sensible maid looks constantly about to burst, red lips and hand on hips, into Ivor Novello; and though Peter Egan looks the ideal hussar as Sergius, his striving voice betrays his disbelief; his descents into bathos mean little because he's there already.

The evening's main success is the developing romance of Raina and Bluntschli; there is chemistry from the start between Alice Krige, who commands both the heroine's faces, and Richard Briers, who may not be the image of a professional soldier, but whose timing and delivery are impeccable. There are well-grounded elders from Richard Pearson, Pat Heywood and Anthony Pedley; pretty sets from Alan Tagg; and infallible patterning of theme, plot and dialogue from the author.

records.title: Molière's dying fall
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Molière's dying fall

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

The National Theatre is putting 'Le Malade Imaginaire' -- translated for once under the obvious and sensible title of The Hypochondriac -- as possibly Molière's greatest comedy and his last. Molière disposed of the second matter by dying four days into the original run. As for the first idea, I never heard it before -- but whoever believes it ought to be locked up.

Dying is the greatest thing Molière did in this play: that he, a noted hypochondriac, should have collapsed while actually appearing as one, is the finest of all sick jokes. It is not an effect readily available to a modern revival, though in his Olivier production Michael Bogdanov has gone some way towards finding an equivalent. But for most of its length the play is cut to formula: a pair of young lovers helped by a maidservant to foil the heroine's foolish father, who wishes her to marry some unsuitable suitor in line with his own obsession: a religious zealot or a fashionable poet or, in this case, a doctor. Between times the old man executes comic cadenzas in accordance with his particular humour.

At one point Argan, our imaginary invalid, feigns death in order to test his family's loyalty. 'Are you sure,' he asks before assuming the supine position, 'that this isn't dangerous?' For Molière, writing and then speaking that line while actually dying, it must have carried an irrecoverable charge. The rest of us have to be content with the basic joke of a thoroughly healthy man indulging himself with fantasied illness, and it is this joke that Daniel Massey plays, on all the stops of his flexible vocal pipe, balancing cures against enemas (his favourite vice) and both against cost. (Molière seems to have carried some of The Miser over into this play) or somersaulting over his sickbed to beat his younger daughter; the only dark moment in the play.

Around him Mr Bogdanov builds a presentation, not only of the play, but of its tradition, its author and its historical moment. The original is interspersed with commedia dell'arte sequences; Mr Bogdanov offers a whole festival and a troupe, who at one point -- in deference to Molière's repeated use of this plot and this subject -- perform a potted version of one of his earlier medical farces. At the end Argan himself becomes a doctor in a musical ceremony, which here culminates in an apparition of death: meaningless if you don't know the circumstances of the play's first production, but chilling if you do.

He also shows -- aided by Polly James's small northern maid, Emily Morgan's delightfully doubled daughters, Clive Arrindell's resourceful swain, and Anna Carteret's sweetly smothering stepma -- how much life Molière could still extract from the old stereotypes; indeed how at this stage he could do it without apparently trying.

A chorus of quacks with syringes rampant lend appropriate support; and the medical satire is delivered loud and clear, which seems to me all you could reasonably ask of it. (Sometimes it's too loud; Michael Bryant makes the regulation rational brother unexpectedly raucous.) The sum, in a rather pedestrian translation by Alan Drury, is solidly amusing rather than elating, but I doubt if a really great production of this play is possible. And I don't want Mr Massey to die to prove me wrong.

* * *

Doctors have always taken a hammering in French comedy. In Feydeau they are usually lechers; his Fitting for Ladies (Orange Tree, Richmond) shows us a fashionable physician who, to evade his wife and his mother-in-law and his ex-mistress, is forced to pretend a sudden conversion to the dressmaking trade. Hence the title: though in this production the play proves far more fitting for gentlemen; the actors are economically funny, while the actresses fuss about. This is a pocket-sized version of an economic play, reassembling all the loved familiar elements. I prefer my Feydeau full-blown; on the other hand it might be pleasant to see a commedia troupe whip through it in five minutes.

* * *

Two regional sidelights on the new depression. In Nick Darke's The Catch (Theatre Upstairs) an ageing fisherman, hit by the loss of his territorial waters to all the frog fisher-folk, turns first to junk-selling, then -- at the instigation of a disliked unthrifty son-in-law -- to cocaine smuggling. But he can't stand the pace. Neither, at first, could I; Cornish leisureliness began to turn my thoughts in other directions. Eventually though I smelt some fragrant dialogue, the beginnings of a story, and a fruitful Steptoe-ish relationship. Later Mr Darke turns some effective screws. There is a proddingly comic performance by Mike Grady, and a masterful one by Tom Watson.

From Liverpool Playhouse comes Blood on the Dole (Tricycle), a first play by Jim Morris, set in a Job Centre. At least the production is; the play roams all over town, and the orange poles and furnishings become constricting. That of course is the point; but it would have come across anyway. We are with four school-leavers. The girls take secretarial courses, and end up working in a supermarket. The boys can find no jobs, and try to set up their own, with invariably farcical results. Finally one settles for the army and is killed in Ireland; his friend is left to mourn him in a scene over-written but (by Andrew Schofield) powerfully played. The play probably cohered better in its home studio than in the narrow open spaces of the Tricycle; if it seems desultory now, then so, perforce, are the characters' lives.

* * *

The Aldwych is running a Ralph Koltai season; to the towering barracks and foundry of his Love-Girl and the Innocent and the thrusting platform of his Hamlet are now added the flat walls (less menacing than at Stratford) of his Romeo and Juliet. This will probably go down as the revival without a balcony; the lovers wander together in the garden, which is a pleasant shock while it lasts, but ultimately destructive to the careful escalation of their four-scene romance: from public meeting to impeded rendezvous to chaperoned marriage to bed. They are alone and untrammelled only once.

Judy Buxton is a pallid Juliet but Anton Lesser's feverish Romeo is now in control of the text, which is more than can be said for most of his contemporaries. However, Trevor Baxter and Barbara Kinghorn as the mismatched elder Capulets graphically illustrate why Juliet should have left home; so, in her warmer way, does Brenda Bruce's Nurse, making the girl's bed so as not to face her when telling her to marry Paris.

records.title: Strangulating the vowels
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Strangulating the vowels

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Decadence,' 'Into Europe,' 'Hosanna' and 'Angels of War.'

SOME readers have complained that I was too violent in declaring that anyone thinking The Hypochondriac Moliere's greatest play should be locked up. I'm sorry. I ought of course to have said that anyone thinking The Hypochondriac Moliere's best play should see a doctor.

Television viewers will know that the upper classes have been getting a good deal recently. Some incidental criticisms -- implicit or overt -- of their manners or habits by Evelyn Waugh, Trevor Griffiths, and whoever writes The Borgias -- but not enough to dislodge the traditional dramatic picture of them as people who say witty things while leading active and fascinating sex lives in attractive surroundings.

I was sure that Steven Berkoff -- as author, star and director of Decadence (Arts) -- would not fall into this trap. Nor has he. When his characters are working-class, as in East, Mr Berkoff will occasionally lend them his own self-pity, but that is as far as he usually goes with affection. There are two proles in Decadence and they are credited with all the grace and delicacy of Arthur Mullard.

Mr Berkoff and Linda Marlowe, who appear briefly in these roles, also play the more important, and only other, roles in the piece: a toff and his mistress. "Decadence," says Mr Berkoff in a programme note, "is a study of the ruling classes or upper classes, so called by virtue of strangulated vowel tones rather than any real achievement." Both the syntax and the logic of that sentence are hard to follow, but the emotional import is clear enough.

In order to function in the theatre Mr Berkoff needs a hate-object, so he has invented one. He has taken Bertie Wooster in full soup-and-fish, endowed him with genitals and a mouthful of dirty words and treated him as if he were (a) real and (b) a social menace. All the fellow actually does is talk a lot, screw his girl-friend, go to the theatre, and then proceed to a restaurant where he gets horribly sick, thereby hurting no-one but himself.

Mr Griffiths's TV play Country was far shrewder when it showed the brewery nobs adapting to progress by investing heavily in fizzy beer, even if it meant turning a revolutionary analysis into a commercial for CAMRA.

(A parenthesis on Griffiths before going back to Berkoff. He has said, "my plays are never about the battle between socialism and capitalism, I take that as being decisively won by socialism." But that can leave him with surprisingly little to write about. Linking the brewing Carlion dynasty to the Corleones of The Godfather didn't work. In the first place The Godfather is too recent a work to have acquired mythic associations. In the second, Francis Coppola's film had brilliantly likened the Mafia to "legitimate" business families, so there seemed little point now in likening a legitimate business family to the Mafia. The play, in Richard Eyre's direction, was still very watchable; and the same team's Cherry Orchard the previous week was excellent, though not as different from other excellent Cherry Orchards as they seemed to think.)

Decadence shows Mr Berkoff as a performer at his best. The strangulated vowels are funny, the timing is fine; the body twists itself as ever into remarkable contortions, and the teeth are the most expressive in London. Miss Marlowe, playing with and up to him, makes no mistakes. But it shows Mr Berkoff as a writer at his worst, dishing out excruciating rhyming couplets. ("We mustn't be late/you mustn't dip your spoon into the cup of hate"; "you are no further, no, in the exploit/than when I first discovered my painful plight.") Mr Berkoff regularly claims to be taking us beyond static/literary/bourgeois/West End theatre, but here we have a show that is totally hung up on its own text, and whose visuals amount to two fashionably dressed people on a sofa. This is the first time Mr Berkoff has been boring.

* * *

More overwrought overwriting in Ron Hutchinson's Into Europe (Lyric Studio). Here too there is verse, delivered as inter-scene commentary, in the manner of David Edgar's Destiny. Mr Edgar was writing about Fascism. Mr Hutchinson has the smaller subject of football, and the disparity grates still further in the dialogue, whose style is toughness-in-aspic.

The leading character is a groin-kicking, press-bribing manager who is losing his touch and whose directors want to get him out. Mr Hutchinson is a talented writer (The Irish Play was a lot more than its title), but this time I suspect he has come up with something unactable. Some of the cast patter delicately through the text as if expecting it to give way beneath them; others, including such good people as Philip Jackson and Stephanie Fayerman, go at it bull-headed. They topple over, but they may have the right instincts. In the play's best speech the departing hero proclaims, "the con is everything -- making sure they never get your number." The bravado spirit ("please God don't let it be this week I get found out") may or may not be right for football, but nothing else can keep you going in the theatre.

* * *

There have been first nights at both Half Moons. At the New, Michel Tremblay's Hosanna, allowing us to see an early, limited work by a playwright who has already moved on. This is his diploma duet piece: some enjoyable bitching between a gay couple in Montreal followed by the obligatory sad soliloquy for one of them, in this case a transvestite who went to a party dressed as Elizabeth Taylor and ran into stiff and humiliating competition. Jim Hooper plays him shrilly, bravely and effectively. His bulky biker lover is played by Ian Gelder, who manages to sound really French-Canadian in spots.

The Old Half Moon offers shelter to Mrs Worthington's Daughters, who patrol the country exhuming plays written by women. This one, Angels of War, written in 1935 by Muriel Box, concerns female ambulance drivers in France in 1918. They go heartily to seed, swearing and smoking, sneaking out of the dorm and standing by each other under fire. But real emotion often breaks through, and there is a pacifist ending that now seems positively mordant.

The main problems are that, like many well-made plays of its period, it devotes too much time to a single small incident, and that you can practically see the dialogue coming off the pages of the Samuel French Acting Edition. A couple of performances are strictly Amateur Dramatic, but there is sturdy work from Jill Stanford, aristocratic and shell-shocked, and from Cordelia Ditton bringing a tart touch of the fringe, both Celtic and theatrical.

records.title: Hot for certainties
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Hot for certainties

ROBERT CUSHMAN

ARTHUR MILLER'S All My Sons (Wyndham's) is a fit play for 1981, a year distinguished in theatre by revivals and by the re-emergence in strength of middle-aged playwrights.

Miller himself was only 31 at its premiere in 1947 but to us it seems like tradition incarnate: an American family drama with global overtones played out on a Middle West back porch. ('The porch,' as Tynan once said, 'is obligatory.') Joe Keller made money in the war as a manufacturer of airplane parts. He shipped out one consignment of defective cylinder heads, and 21 pilots died flying the planes. Joe's partner, a weakling, went to jail, but he himself got off. Now his worshipping son discovers Joe's guilt; another son was lost in the war; Joe is forced to realise that the dead pilots were 'all my sons.' Exit, to put a bullet in his head.

The play, as everyone has said, is modelled on Ibsen. Ibsenite is the narrative method: a continual reclaiming of the past. Imperfectly Ibsenite, too, is the symbolism of a fallen apple-tree, which serves only to clutter the stage while adding a few lines of portentous dialogue. The avenging son Chris is straight from Ibsen but an Ibsen drained of irony; a carping neighbour arraigns him as an 'idealist' but that idealism passes uncriticised by the author himself.

The play is hot for certainties. Miller convinces us because he convinced himself, both of his technique (we may gag at such devices as the fatal long-withheld letter and wonder about the characterisation of the woman who has concealed it but we still recognise Miller as one of the few great storytellers in modern drama) and of his meaning. He spells that meaning out--'there's a universe of people outside and you're responsible to it'--without diminishing it. Sometimes, his words are awkward, but they carry a self-generating conviction.

And there is something else: something that runs almost counter to the play's declared grain, and in doing so enriches it. Joe's main defence when cornered is that he was acting for the good of his family. Family, declares the play through Chris, is not a man's only responsibility, but it turns out to be the play's main concern. Chris destroys his father out of filial disappointment; he had loved and honoured him too much. (This theme, like much else in the play, was to be more fully and subtly treated in Death of a Salesman.)

In fact there are two families involved. Chris's fiancee is the daughter of Joe's partner; her brother arrives on the scene to smash the engagement, convinced that his old man has been victimised. But he is almost charmed out of his enmity by the massed hospitality of the Kellers, above all by Joe's wife Kate, whom the stage directions refer to throughout as Mother.

In Michael Blakemore's production this whole movement (more Chekhov than Ibsen) is subtly, dynamically handled with Richard Durden, an ominous young actor, first steely, then melting, then snapping tight again. His sister (an even-trickier role, composed of moods but not much character) is given firm definition by Jill Baker, last seen in Goose Pimples, being equally good and entirely different. Garrick Hagon as Chris bears the brunt of the play's gaunt self-righteousness; by refusing to soften it, by accepting its ungainliness, and by making it part of his character and even of his stance, he turns a dramatic fault into a virtue.

Colin Blakely's Joe may be physically smaller than Mr Miller imagined; part of his armour is a continually expressed pained pity for his colleague, 'a little man'; Joe has tried to re-create himself; he trades on joviality and kindliness which Mr Blakely shows to be almost real. The density of Joe's characterisation is the play's other great strength. He believes simultaneously that his crime never happened and that it was justified. Mr Blakely, maybe the most honest actor we have, is ideally equipped both to root out dishonesty and to make us all feel our kinship with it; and when his disintegration sets in it rolls relentlessly.

And there is Mother, even more adept than her husband at shutting out unpleasant truths; without her, in fact, he couldn't do it. In some respects Rosemary Harris is wrong for the role but her wrongness is pretty wonderful. Instead of bovine devotion she offers a strained intelligence breaking under a continuous (and self-contradictory) system of lying. If cover-up is the great American theme here is one of its pristine manifestations, making the play a companion-piece to Long Day's Journey Into Night. Vocally this performance is superbly fastidious; physically it is full, graceful and economic, creating its own white light. Miss Harris is Britain's great lost actress; there should be legislation to stop her returning to America at the end of the run.

Some of the neighbours overplay the bonhomie commonly thought inseparable from American backyards; otherwise there are no flaws. Hayden Griffin's set is colour-co-ordinated; the green of the trees reflected in the handsome house they frame.

* * *

Hanif Kureishi's Borderline (Royal Court) is the best young play of the year. It confirms the impression that Asian writers are taking over from the Irish as the creative rescuers of the English language. Offering a small panorama of immigrant and second-generation life in London, he is angry, despairing, compassionate, witty and charming. His people sound (as they did not in his last play Outskirts) spontaneous and authentic. Radical activists and frightened nostalgic parents are both accorded care and attention.

The production (by Max Stafford-Clark, for Joint Stock) is not always as considerate as the writing: patronage creeps in, and petulance, and that strange over-emphasis (between a whine and a hammer) which actors under 30 now promiscuously bestow on neutral, inoffensive lines. But the staging is visually sure, and there are two or three very good performances. Two British actors, David Beames and Deborah Findlay, have great sad authority as an old Pakistani couple and of the Asian players a total newcomer, Nizwar Karanj, is a nervous delight in the role of a total newcomer.

* * *

In Favourite Nights (Lyric, Hammersmith) Stephen Poliakoff ups his range of urban squalor to include soulless hotels and gambling casinos; also, as a sort of antechamber to the above, language schools for visiting businessmen, the teachers apparently doubling as hostesses. Once again he lets the decay seep through; he remains very good at tone. But he is presently hopeless on narrative; we spend the first half of the evening wondering who and what the play is really about and the second feeling cheated at having found out.

It seems that the Jewish father and the young girl and the Austrian gent (Peter Postlethwaite perfect) were not, despite the great length of their roles, important in themselves but only foils to their daughter-sister-teacher who is also a compulsive gambler and a symptom, presumably, of her self-destructive society. Susan Tracy gives her an appropriate sullen glitter, Gwyneth Strong supports her brightly, and a croupier is played by Marion Bailey, last seen in Goose Pimples, being equally good and entirely the same.

Peter James seems to lose his director's grip with this author; not only does the dialogue meander but the scene-changes are interminable. This, of all plays, might benefit from a revolving stage; baize tables and slot machines rotating towards and away from us might perk things up, and even be meaningful.

records.title: Betrayed by nerves
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Betrayed by nerves

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London, Glasgow and Liverpool

MY EARS may have deceived me, but almost my first impression at Tuesday's premiere of Richard II (Aldwych) was of Alan Howard in the title role addressing his uncle Gaunt as 'old John of York, time-honoured Lancaster,' a dynastic confusion that if spotted in time might have prevented the Wars of the Roses.

As the evening progressed Mr Howard did other weird things to the text; sometimes, after a misplaced word or omitted line, you could see him worrying about whether the speech would still make sense or whether the audience would notice. (It didn't, and neither of course did they).

These temporary aberrations jibed uncannily with what seems to be Mr Howard's abiding view of Richard: a man who regards kingship as a license to say and do outrageous, even meaningless things, and get applauded for them, but is cripplingly uncertain as to whether he can carry it off. This Richard insults Gaunt on his death-bed as if he were doing a turn, then turns to Bushy, Bagot and company apparently asking 'Didn't I do well?'

The nervousness betrays him. Before he has said a word, true or false, we see him in this production trying on his crown with an expression of fascinated distaste; plainly he is not getting job-satisfaction but he also sees no prospects in alternative employment. Then he turns to confront an impassive row of courtiers. (Gaunt is actually sitting down; you have to be really time-honoured to get away with that).

The ensuing scene, the quarrel between Bolingbroke and Mowbray, is brilliantly handled. Richard is almost in control, unleashing contempt on both contestants from behind a mask of royal raillery. David Suchet's Bolingbroke is playing his own version of the same game, unwearyingly polite to his king while plainly hating him.

The development in counterpoint of these two performances is the great strength of Terry Hands's production. Bolingbroke's ambition dawns as Richard banishes him: 'such is the breath of kings.' When Richard is virtually his prisoner he sends an ultimatum beginning grandiloquently with his own name: 'Henry Bolingbroke . . .'--here Mr Suchet breaks off for a moment, bemused and excited. (Hark at me, I'm talking royal). He has found himself; but so for an ironic moment has Richard, in the 'hollow crown' speech which casts a silence over the house of a different quality from the respectful hush which otherwise prevails. You understand why Richard is so angry at being diverted from his sweet road to despair: for him it has been the true meaning of kingship. All that remains is to teach it to Bolingbroke, which he does in the deposition scene, loading him with regalia, teasing him on to the throne.

The legacy is felt through the remainder of Mr Suchet's performance; the atrocious couplets of his last scene ('thy pains, Fitzwater, shall not be forgot/right noble is thy spirit, well I wot') are delivered as if in a daze, which is doubtless how they were written. But though Bolingbroke can reasonably be played to the end as a political case-study, Richard, like it or lump it, is a tragic hero; and his deeper triumph 'in being nothing' is one that this production has no room for.

It is otherwise distinguished by the friezes of Farrah's set, a lament for the passing of the Middle Ages, and by variously effective stabs at comedy. The best are in Tony Church's York, though even he is too knowingly conversational at times; more open to question are the gardeners' sending-up of the Queen, and Northumberland's rattling-off of the names of his co-conspirators, perhaps in settlement of a dressing-room bet. At such moments I wonder whether current Shakespeare is much improvement on, say, the Old Vic of 1959, which was where and when I first saw this play. Mind you, the Old Vic in 1959 was pretty good.

* * *

Dryden wrote a comedy called Marriage a la Mode which is half realistic sex-play in the customary Restoration prose vein, and half high romance in verse. The Glasgow Citizens' Theatre has inspected the text, kept the prose and discarded the verse, replacing it with a condensed version of Dryden's Antony and Cleopatra tragedy All for Love.

We are supposedly present at a Restoration rehearsal of this, done with toy-theatre attitudes through which real emotion occasionally, and with disconcerting effectiveness, breaks. Between scenes the actors step down and--as in the film of The French Lieutenant's Woman--conduct their own intrigues, in the words bequeathed them by Dryden's comedy. These words turn out to be extraordinarily good; if Restoration comedy is a meditation on marriage, then this is its high-point, exceeded only by Congreve in elegance of phrasing but with far more immediate impact. Wires are crossed between two gallants, the wife of one and the mistress of another. Their animadversions on the merits and disappointments of sex before, during and outside of wedlock, convulsed the audience with the laughter of recognition.

The ladies are given performances of sharp, controlled extravagance by Julia Blalock and Sian Thomas, with Rupert Frazer as a casually sardonic raisonneur. In the imposed theatrical setting an innocent quotation from Macbeth has, elaborately and hilariously, to be exorcised. This is one of the best Citizens' productions I have seen, though, and, mysteriously, the first to be directed by the theatre's chief, Giles Havergal.

* * *

From the old firm at Glasgow to the new one at Liverpool where the Playhouse has been taken over by a quadrumvirate of playwrights, most prominent among them Chris ('Sweeney Todd') Bond. He has co-director credit, with Pip Broughton, on A Tale of Two Cities adapted, it says, by the company. This, not to shirk the obvious comparison, is a far more hurried work, both in playing and rehearsal time, than the RSC's Nicholas Nickleby, and has less of a theatrical identity.

Some scenes are picture-book illustrations but others come alive: the storming of the Bastille with the whole cast on scaling-ladders urged on by Gillian Hanna's Madame Defarge; the same actress periodically crossing the stage with bits of Dr Manette's narrative (an inspired linking device); anything involving Chris Darwen as Jerry Cruncher; and, inevitably and infallibly, Sydney Carton (Alan David) taking the Only Way. (The audience are sent out to the strains of Frank Sinatra singing My Way, which suggests that Mr Bond is being cheeky, or just irresponsible.)

I suspect that the play started out with more serious thoughts about the French Revolution than were eventually realised but then so did Dickens. There is an invigorating medley of theatrical conventions employed as the need arises; and splendid life-giving sets by Voytek, sometimes (as in the trial scenes) reinforcing the cartooned action with Hogarthian malevolence, at others, as in an extended recap of the Doctor's tale, framing it with perfect artifice.

* * *

An even less manageable novel is far more neatly done in Richard Crane's version of The Brothers Karamazov which inaugurates a new policy of fringe transfers at the Fortune. The cruciform set is impressive now that it's fully visible, and Will Knightley's, who has taken over Ivan, adds a new dimension by looking like Stephen Boxer who plays Alyosha.

Seamus Finnegan is a playwright worth encouraging, though in Soldiers (York and Albany, Camden Town) his kaleidoscopic method of presenting Belfast is beginning to come apart on him. Stark scenes for British squaddies or IRA men are betrayed by a stereotyped presentation of 'the media' (i.e. television) and a suggestive but excessively laconic view of the Church. Good acting by Sam Dale and Derek Thompson.

records.title: Nunn's 'All's Well
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Nunn's 'All's Well'

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Stratford and London.

FOR Trevor Nunn's production of All's Well That Ends Well (Stratford), John Gunter has designed a set unflurriedly versatile and full of quiet, stately magic. Composed of glass and wrought-iron, it strongly suggests Marylebone Station; and the play has been given an Edwardian treatment, in which trains are never far off.

We begin with our hero and heroine, Bertram and Helena, dancing in silhouette: I suppose, a hesitation waltz. The lights go up and we are in the conservatory of the Countess of Rossillion, Bertram's mother. He is off to the French court and is already chafing impatiently by the door; Helena--his mother's ward, a physician's daughter--he hardly notices. A trio of maids wave the young master a tearful goodbye. (They are fixtures; and are deliciously ushered off the stage in the last scene when the stream of revelations become altogether too domestic for domestics.)

A sweep of curtains takes us to court which is Ruritanian and also given to dancing; having cured the king of a fistula, Helena chooses herself a promised husband in a game of Musical Suitors. When Bertram, her unwilling selection, flies from her to the Florentine wars, he comes to a landscape of smokey bivouacs and louche cafes. Recruits arrive in a city whose communications--symbolised by a battered rail-sign marked 'Firenze'--are clearly taking the strain. There seems, by the way, to be a direct line to Rossillion. The Countess seems actually to live by the track; rising smoke without lends the scene a Chekhovian enchantment, but must have been terrible for property values.

Visually this is Mr Nunn's most sophisticated production to date; it has the outward semblance of a masterpiece. Its innards are moving in that direction, but still have some way to go; last week several performances seemed muffled.

At the end Helena and Bertram are dancing again, still with a question-mark in their step. But the last scene had lacked authority; an attempt to build up Helena's return to the level of Hermione's resurrection in The Winter's Tale worked only superficially, since the audience never believes that Helena is dead.

Mike Gwilym offers an unsparingly puppyish Bertram, matched by a Helena from Harriet Walter of unswerving quiet practicality. Miss Walter is very good at heartbreak; the finest moment is her offer, realising that Bertram does not love her, to forgo the marriage. Only the King pushes it through. Helena's imperative becomes not to get a man, but to get his love. This she achieves by the traditional trick of substituting herself in another girl's bed. But the bed-trick is not just a plot mechanism; it's sexually acute. 'Lust doth play with what it loathes for that which is away.' Thinking Helena to be Diana, Bertram loves her; to each his own fantasy.

The play is full of such sharp corners. Its nicest characters are its oldest; they all lament the passing of better days, so constantly that what might be passing nostalgia builds up to a meditation on the cruelty of time. Peggy Ashcroft gives a lovely performance of the Countess, radiating generosity from the sidelines, but unable actually to do anything. She suspects that her son keeps bad company; this Bertram has a Jeeves, the braggart soldier Parolles, eventually subjected to an unmasking more brutal than Malvolio's, and funnier.

Bertram's rejection of him is, in this production, very like Hal's of Falstaff. But, unlike Falstaff, Parolles survives; his ensuing scenes of calculated self-abasement are like nothing else in Shakespeare, and Stephen Moore, only moderately hilarious as the peacocking Parolles, is terrific in his downfall. He parallels Helena; since both have a way to make, both depend on the same benefactor, both make things happen. This, though, is not Miss Walter's forte; hence, in part, the lag at the end.

The show is still full of marvellous detail: the conspirators' interplay in the baiting of Parolles; the silky inflections of Robert Eddison's Lafeu; Guy Woolfenden's unfailingly seductive piano music; Julia Swift's Mariana, camp follower turned broken blossom; Geoffrey Hutchings's hunchbacked clown, shuffling off the stage as the last waltz begins. Once I would have ended by looking forward to its arrival at the Aldwych. Now, remembering the play's doubts about progress, I cross my fingers for the Barbican.

* * *

At Stratford's Other Place there is a revival of Bulwer Lytton's 1840ish Money. Half of this is devoted to the old routine in which a masochistic hero tries to find reasons for not marrying the girl who is obviously right for him. Paul Shelley makes this infuriating paragon as palatable as possible, while Juliet Stevenson infuses the waiting-and-suffering bit with amazing appeal. The money of the title is his, though he begins poor but honest; then, to the consternation of his rich and selfish relatives, comes the Reading of the Will.

The Will is actually the best speech in the play, and Andrew Jarvis as the officiating lawyer does it justice. The rest is standard satire on greedy nobs, written with an anonymous kind of energy. It compares badly, not only with Dickens (see this, all who thought Nicholas Nickleby was of its nature undramatic), but with the genuine misanthropy of Gilbert's Engaged, nervously mounted by the National a few years back. A mostly good cast bare their fangs as required; George Raistrick is amusing as the hero's best friend, a congenial miseryguts, trapped into marriage by Miriam Karlin's merry widow.

* * *

Auden and Christopher Isherwood, now, really meant it when they attacked modern life in toto in The Dog Beneath the Skin (Half Moon). Their targets included monarchism, Fascism, American capitalism, journalists, women, the Boys Brigade, cheap entertainment, and right-wing country vicars who upbraided people for enjoying cheap entertainment. They tell a picaresque story in an expressionist style that is usually fun to watch but unsatisfying. A cartoon view of Nazism may have been useful for rousing consciences in 1936; now we need facts and explanations.

The choruses are said to represent Auden at his best, but what works here is the doggerel beneath the skin, as when hero and hound arrive at an hotel to be greeted with a litany of proffered services. More powerful than any verbal image is a visual one; a sculpted head on a bed, representing a temporary and rapacious beloved.

* * *

Steven Davis's The Last Elephant (Bush) will probably not be revived in 45 years' time, though an accumulation of funny lines and incidents helpfully distract attention from a thin vein of domestic anthropology. Good work from Alan Rickman as an absent-minded scientist (few other words will do), Jennifer Hilary as his unsatisfied wife (shades of Jumpers) and Michael Feast as a Red Indian who turns up on the South Coast because, it neatly turns out, someone gave him the address.

records.title: In love with books
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
In love with books

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

There were, for a rarity, two plays last week which produced in their audiences a palpable feeling of enjoyment. Usually the most you hope for is numbed respect.

84 Charing Cross Road (Ambassadors) consists almost entirely of letters. On one side of the stage is the New York apartment of Helene Hanff, aspiring playwright and TV scriptwriter; at the other Marks and Co., a second-hand bookshop located at the address in the title. In 1949 Miss Hanff saw an ad by the firm in an American paper, and wrote to it requesting volumes of Hazlitt, Stevenson and Leigh Hunt. The firm -- represented by a gentleman signing himself FPD -- was able to supply her with two out of three; and thus began a twenty-year correspondence.

FPD soon stands revealed as Frank Doel, chief buyer; within three years he and Helene are on first-name terms. She continues to demand books, and to dispatch forthright opinions on them when received. ("This is not Pepys's Diary, this is some busybody editor's miserable collection of excerpts from Pepys's Diary, may he rot in hell.")

For payment she always sends straight dollar bills. She also, during the years of rationing, sends Christmas food-parcels, thereby gaining a small shopful of devoted pen-friends, one of whom sends her in return a recipe for Yorkshire pudding, a dish later described by the recipient as "a high, curved, smooth, empty waffle."

Inevitably they beg her to come to London. So -- to great theatrical advantage -- a suspense element creeps in. Will she make it? If not, why not? The implication, never spoken, is that she is a born solitary. What is budding between her on one side, London, the shop and Frank Doel on the other, is a love affair, and she needs to keep them at ocean's length.

David Swift charmingly depicts the ageing, mellowing process in Frank; but the dynamo, the show has to be Helene, self-projected in the letters as a feisty, generous, irascible, Anglo-cum-bibliophile autodidact. Rosemary Leach's performance breathes New York; her presence conjures up the public library, the neighbourhood delicatessen and long, brisk walks in Central Park.

James Roose-Evans's production falters only in an abrupt ending and in some unfortunate bursts of music. Miss Hanff appeared alongside her impersonator (whom she looks, and may well sound, nothing like) at the first night curtain-call, which choked us all up a bit, but it is a warmly tearful evening even without that: a rearguard fanfare for London and literacy, and the most likeable West End offering in years.

* * *

Equally relished, though otherwise quite different, is Trafford Tanzi (Lyric Studio, Hammersmith). Here the audience have a chance to express themselves; since they are deemed to be spectators at a wrestling match, some of the heckles were as good as Clare Luckham's dialogue, and the shouts of encouragement in the final bout were blood-curdling.

In this match Tanzi, a lady wrestler, takes on her husband, Dean Rebel, a man wrestler. We have already watched her entire early life rendered as a series of wrestling matches; with her mother, alternately domineering and sentimental, with her father, alternately sentimental and domineering, with her prettier girl-friend, with the school psychiatrist, with Dean who finds her sorrowfully working in a chippie and produces a hanky from his fly by way of comfort. Nobody understands her, and her request for a career lands her flat on the canvas. But she learns.

Miss Luckham is hardly making new points, but she writes with edge, music-hall brio. Her metaphor, in Chris Bond's production, is irresistible and the cast, led by Noreen Kershaw, fair dazzling. Whether Tanzi's ability to floor her old man in the ring actually proves anything is another matter.

* * *

The main Lyric stage is taken by a Cambridge Theatre Company production of The Soldier's Fortune, a lesser-known Restoration comedy. Its heroes are discarded soldiers, infused with more than regulation bitterness by their creator, Thomas Otway, who was one himself. Its pimp, Sir Jolly Jumble, is the most fully-developed specimen of his kind: in love with his work and an inveterate toucher-up of both sexes. Its two heroines show an independence of mind in tormenting their men (in or out of wedlock) that goes beyond roguish giggles, and its cuckold, Sir Davy Dunce, is a real menace.

Sheila Hancock's production is stranded between two styles. Inclining more to realism than prettiness, it yet uses some of the old conventions. Where once maids and gallants stood around looking decorative, now drabs and ruffians loaf on corners looking downtrodden. But they still look planted; and Robin Archer's closed-in sets forbid us to imagine a society for ourselves. Individual performances impose themselves as the play proceeds, and the complex last scene is excellently handled. Hugh Paddick effortlessly dominates the proceedings as Sir Jolly, emerging from unfelt beds where his more timorous author only specified "a delight in keyholes." Brian Murphy is a less endearing Sir Davy than once was Arthur Lowe (in a production that also featured Miss Hancock as a Lady Dunce of Vanessa Redgrave radiance), but his resentful brutality may well be closer to the script.

Richard III (Aldwych) is another of Alan Howard's player-kings, able to assume any role except that of the clean-limbed. He succeeds, with Richard Pasco's Clarence, by making him partner in a double-act; at other times his dissimulations are so blatant you wonder he takes anybody in.

Neither Mr Howard's performance nor Terry Hands's production run out of energy or, much, out of invention, but the play is left stranded before its close. Half the laughs earned by Joe Melia's second Murderer are inspired, half regretted. Sinead Cusack as Lady Anne in Richard III is herself: it is a relief to find, in Derek Godfrey as Buckingham, an actor who can get his laughs on and with the text.

That text is not sacred, but the changes Mr Hands has made, here and in Richard II, seem to me impoverishments. Permit me to go into detail. In Richard II the Queen's proposal that Richard be sent overseas with her is greeted by Northumberland with the hint that there were some love but little policy. At the Aldwych, Richard appropriates the last three words. This tells us that he has a bitingly realistic sense of political humour, but we know that already from the deposition scene; we are deprived of Northumberland's only avowal of his own nature, one he never dared to make while Richard was still nominally king.

In Richard III, Tyrrel, who has just announced the murder of the Princes in the Tower, is dispatched with an invitation to return and tell the tale in full. Here he is followed off by two of Richard's cronies, who are obviously going to kill him. We trade this new insight into Richard the lip-licking sadist for the platitude of the dictator who lets nobody out of his employ alive. Before Bosworth, Richard is brought a threatening note, which in Mr Hands's production is changed to merely insulting, one aimed at his henchmen. The actor loses the chance to show the king faltering and recovering his nerve; the audience discovers that he runs an unpopular administration, which with half his country in arms against him can hardly be news.

With subtlety so suspected, it is hardly surprising that the production's excitement runs down. The Hands-Howard collaboration (black-avised designs by Farrah) has been long and often rewarding; but they bring out the overkill in each other. This year they have done their best work apart.

records.title: Masked tragedy
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Masked tragedy

Robert Cushman on Peter Hall's production of The Oresteia

The National Theatre is advertising The Oresteia (Olivier) as the world's earliest dramatic masterpiece. Appropriately, performances begin at five in the afternoon.

Even before that, the first actor is in place, peering at us through a chink high in the set. He seems to have a beak, but of course, like everyone else in the production, he is merely wearing a mask. When we embark on Agamemnon, the first play of Aeschylus's trilogy, he proves to be the Watchman sent by Clytemnestra to look out for her husband's return from Troy. He has a North-country accent, and is amusingly disgruntled. There is no patronising or desperate attempt to prove that Aeschylus can be fun; but we feel, for once, let in to a Greek tragedy. There are telling, and agreeable, see-saw rhythms:

Wish it were over, this waiting, this watching,
twelve weary months, night in and night out.

Score one up to Tony Harrison's translation.

The good impression persists during the long first chorus, the tale of Troy and the fatal sacrifice of Iphigenia delivered here by a dozen elders. (The choruses of the subsequent two plays are the same size). Voices are still mainly northern, and the alliteration now reveals a sharp dramatic edge: 'Batter, batter the doom-drum, but believe there'll be better' certainly makes more sense and better sound than 'sing sorrow, sorrow but good win out in the end' in the approved modern version, Richmond Lattimore's.

There are danger-signs in this chorus, though, and they intensify when Clytemnestra comes on. I wouldn't blame the actor for this, even were I allowed to tell you who he is. (Sixteen players in this all-male cast divide choral and individual speaking roles between them, with no specific credits provided. This apparently makes the actors feel good. It also furnishes critics and other regulars with a harmless guessing-game). Both watchman and chorus have displayed a taste for hard-edged and newly-minted compound nouns. The chorus now fling a few of them at their queen.

It's right that we honour the wife of our clanchief
when the manlord himself's
not here on the thronestone

A feud in Mr Harrison's diction is a 'bloodgrudge,' a divine command a 'godgoad,' a human destiny a 'lifelot,' and brace yourselves, death by drowning will land you in a 'wavegrave.' That last cuteness, though, is atypical. Once again Mr Harrison has done a virtuoso translation job: lucid, resourceful, a pleasure to read. Only it doesn't work; or, if you prefer, it doesn't play.

It hems the drama in, hammers it to death with monosyllables. (Even in combination, that's how they strike the ear.) It exudes a gnarled and forbidding primitivism which excludes the audience. Peter Hall's production reminds us that heroic Argos (or indeed Aeschylean Athens) was by our standards less a thriving city-state than a small tribal encampment. I half-liked Jocelyn Herbert's set: that is I approved of the wall done in strips of reinforced tinfoil, but not of the steps approaching it, which look as if they are filling in until the real ones arrive. I expected, I suppose, something more spectacular; the Olivier, we are told, derives from Epidaurus, where the views are magnificent. With grandeur gone, homeliness might at least involve us with the characters, but the masks prevent that. Mr Harrison's literary reference-point is Anglo-Saxon, but his six-foot line, however syncopated, reminded me of something more recent, encountered on this very stage: the verses of Mendoza, alias the Devil, in Man and Superman:

O wert thou, Louisa, the wife of Mendoza:
Mendoza's Louisa, Louisa Mendoza

They sent Jack Tanner to sleep.

The Oresteia can be a lulling experience, too, stretching a single moment for pages, then jack-knifing major events and heartlessly banishing vital characters who have served their immediate purpose. Something has to anchor us to it: if not aural or visual splendour, then psychological realism. (All drama aspires towards realism unless it has already got there, in which case it needs to be nudged back towards ritual.) I tried hard to feel moved or horrified when wife killed husband or son mother, but nothing came. There was some quickening in the second play Choephori, when Orestes and Electra were reunited and plotted murder, but not enough. The production had created no framework to which I could relate these events. Some vexing problems of choral speaking had been intelligently tackled, but only by the extreme (and self-defeating) method of virtually banishing unison delivery.

Then a surprise. The last play, The Eumenides, had been in my experience the most boring. (Oh yes, pace last week's Sunday Times, the plays have been done before in London in the past 2,000 years. In 1961 at the Old Vic I saw something that certainly said it was The Oresteia and which I have no reason to think was lying.) The case of Orestes's matricide is referred to the first-ever Athenian jury, who find for him and against the avenging Furies, thereby founding Athenian justice and Athenian Democracy.

As the actors drop their pebbles into the urns (or votepots), they seem for almost the first time to be playing real actions. We are caught up, and at the end respond gladly to the gentle command, 'stand while the Kind Ones pass,' as the now beneficent Furies exit through the auditorium. It is a stirring moment; but I cannot say that it truly places the drama in the audience's laps or that it gathers up all that has gone before. Many of the production's techniques, though, pay off here. Harrison Birtwistle's music crowns the most helpful and sophisticated score ever composed for the tongs and the bones. The masks have been good throughout, especially the pop-eyed ones for the foreigners, Aegisthus and Cassandra (whose caged entrance is an event), and the white creation, oriental and feminine, for Orestes (an unusually graceful performance, incidentally). Those for the Furies make very convincing emblems of female malevolence as, crowning the evening's drag-show aspect, do the actors behind them.

Does that brand me as a he-critic? Much as I longed throughout for an actor to enter barefaced, or to say 'king' instead of 'clanchief,' I yearned more to hear 'god' or 'goddess' instead of the 'he-god' and 'she-god' imprinted on our skulls to keep us aware of the play's roots in a patriarchal society; hence, though I can't follow the argument, the all-male cast. Certainly there was a gulp in the house when Athena pronounced the father the important parent, the mother a mere seed-bed; certainly Clytemnestra resents the unfaithful husband who also happens to have killed her daughter. But these things do not seem to have been felt by Aeschylus as issues, and Hall is too scrupulous a director to force them. So they merely, and awkwardly, hang around. The production's great failure is that in five hours it seldom lets us know why we are there.

* * *

What other attractions lie here in my playtray? Steafel Solo (at the King's Head through Christmas) is a richly-written and performed one-woman show; Sheila Steafel even succeeds in satirising other comics while being funny herself. A production of The Dresser, at least as good as the London one, has been going the regional rounds, coming this week in Nottingham; Joss Ackland is a touching Sir and Kenneth Haigh an unlikely but inspired choice for his acolyte. At the Beck Theatre, Hayes (this week in Croydon), I saw Mike Harding's Fur Coat and No Knickers, but forbear to speak of it. Stand, while this Kind One passes.

records.title: Paula's dark past
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Paula's dark past

Robert Cushman in London and Nottingham

Pinero's The Second Mrs Tanqueray (Lyttelton) is the archetypal drama of the woman with a past. Aubrey Tanqueray, a late Victorian clubman, takes as his wife a notoriously unchaste young woman named Paula. His acquaintances cut him; most grievously, Ellean, the convent-bred daughter of his first wife, dislikes his second and a respectable neighbour whisks her off to Paris to spare her any evil influence.

Then Ellean falls in love. Her father is pleased and perplexed. 'I thought you took after your poor mother a little,' he says on her return, 'but there's a look on your face that I never saw on hers.' That moment, the most explicitly sexual in the play, comes late in the action and throws it into sharp relief. It paves the way for a rapprochement between Ellean and Paula, and it tells us all we need to know about Aubrey's first marriage.

I don't think it is prurient to want to know more than Pinero is prepared or able to tell about his second. It is quite easy to guess: to build up a mental picture of Aubrey as a long-repressed man bowled over by his first real experience of sex. But he sees himself as the noble rescuer of a fallen woman, and the text gives him little opportunity to play anything else.

The play's catastrophe comes when Ellean's romance turns out to be an old lover of Paula's. She tells on him. She has been blamed for this, most recently by the critic of The Guardian, who points out that all she had to do was shut up and that by making trouble she disqualifies herself as a tragic heroine. Well, if Hamlet had decided that he didn't believe in ghosts, or if Oedipus had taken his wife's advice and stopped investigating the past, they too might have lived happily ever after.

They became tragic by insisting on the truth, thereby collaborating in their own destruction. Paula also tells the truth, partly under the influence of the Rosmersholm Complex which forces abnormally high codes of behaviour on girls who enter ancestral homes. (Pinero used the same motif comically, and therefore more felicitously, in Trelawny of the Wells.) Pinero has planted additional clues to Paula's behaviour. She says that she has felt furiously jealous twice in her life. Once is when she loses Ellean to Paris. She keeps mum about the other time, but it must have been when she lost the man who now reappears as her prospective son-in-law. Her two jealousies converge, and it's no wonder she snaps. You may perhaps blame Pinero for hedging his bets: nobility or revenge?

The suicide that ends the play (I haven't spoiled it for you, honest) is suspect. The drama has not burned hot enough to justify it. But don't accuse Pinero of propitiating Victorian morality; he is arraigning it for demanding such a sacrifice. A few minutes before, he has stirred and surprised us by letting Aubrey say all the things that have been staring him and his cronies in the face about the double standard.

All the same the play is infected with Victorian pieties. It is taken for granted that the pure Ellean will instinctively abhor her tainted stepmother; and however much we may be counselled against throwing stones, there is no suggestion that Paula's experiences could be a source of anything but shame. There is no hypocrisy in the piece, but there is myopia; and certainly Paula herself is not seen clearly. She is less a character than an alternating vehicle for anger and remorse: doubtless a great role for a barnstorming actress, but Felicity Kendal is hardly that. Faced with a major row, she resorts to sustained shouting that starts you worrying about the effect on her throat. Momentary outbursts she handles with stabbing effectiveness. Leigh Lawson, looking 10 years too young to be the father of his daughter or the contemporary of his friends, hardly saves Aubrey from dullness.

Harold Innocent rejoices in the mother-hen confidant role, but few of the other actors are at ease with the style (which is the plummy side of rich) and some are downright wooden. Michael Rudman's production is otherwise efficient, especially when evoking the imprisonments of convention, though Carl Toms's sets take this theme a bit far, surrounding the Tanqueray homestead with pitchy darkness while the text speaks of morning sunshine.

* * *

Lady in the Dark (Nottingham Playhouse) is a fairly famous musical, 1941 vintage, never before done in Britain, and confining its songs to a series of dream sequences. The dreamer is a New York fashion magazine editor suffering from depressions. With the help of a shrink she realises that she has always been nervous about her looks and has compensated in ruthless devotion to her job. She also learns to choose between the three men in her life; it is hinted that she will eventually devote herself to one of them, and give up unwomanly pursuits like work.

In Crispin Thomas's production the show plods; everything has to be framed within the analyst's office, which in Hugh Durrant's design is a white nightmare on its own account. Moss Hart's script alternates between awed sessions on the couch and in the office, lengthy banter that requires a cast of Eve Ardens, of both sexes. As for the songs: Ira Gershwin was, of all the major lyricists, the freest with heavy trick-rhymes; this score shows him sometimes charming, frequently elephantine. Kurt Weill wrote the music which, like much of his American work, is skilled but bloodless. There are some guts in the final circus dream, which includes the celebrated 'Saga of Jenny,' who would make up her mind ('At seventeen to Vassar it was quite a blow/That in twenty-seven languages she couldn't say no'); and the gentle 'My Ship' is deservedly a classic. Celeste Holm is too subdued for the saga, but she sings beautifully about her ship. She also finds wit and warmth in the dialogue, but she often looks marooned.

* * *

The School for Scandal (Greenwich) is weak on satire, strong on individual character. If there has to be a discrepancy this is the right one, since Sheridan himself plainly lost interest in his ostensible subject after the first two acts. The Teazles are here takingly played by Paul Brooke and Nina Thomas, marked out for special sympathy by being dressed in black and white, to match Bernard Culshaw's delicate and delectable sets; drawn rather than painted.

* * *

The People Show Cabaret (Royal Court) has, in Mark Long, the anti-compere of one's dreams: smooth, sinister and insulting. His stories are the ultimate in shaggy-doggedness. The bill he presents reminded me of a cherished Bob Hope throwaway about a musician who got wounded in a Spike Jones recording session; here a running gag about a frustrated tribute to Glenn Miller is reinforced by some fearsome knockabout, most of it executed by Emil Wolk, a small man with an impressive line in forward rolls. He can also, like the rest of the line-up (three horns and a piano), really play. I don't find him very funny, so the show wore me down.

records.title: Good company
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Still Crazy After All These Years
records.body:
Good company

Robert Cushman on Hull Truck and the RSC's pantomime.

I do not of course believe in decades, but I am prepared to suspend my disbelief in considering Mike Bradwell's 10 years as director of Hull Truck. He has largely devoted himself to showing us the flotsam of the Sixties surviving through the Seventies, succumbing to prosperity and disillusion. It has been an enjoyable trip, but now, a year into the Eighties, Mr Bradwell may be right to quit. He is leaving the company; Still Crazy After All These Years (Bush) is his valedictory.

The fans -- I speak as one -- will rush to see it; and so they should. They should in fact rush faster than I did; I arrived late, and could not be admitted until after the interval. Mr Bradwell, though, seemed quite agreeable to having me judge the show on its second half; and even provided me with a fast and entertaining rundown of the story thus far. (He is, as those who saw such early Truck shows as Oh What may recall, quite a performer.) I didn't feel that I had missed much plot.

What I saw was a four-sided conversation. There was a producer of TV rock shows and his wife, both of the above-mentioned generation. Then there were their juniors and house-guests: a French textile student with whom the producer has slept, and a new musician, hyping what he calls the new music by means of spiel and video-cassette. He arouses the enthusiasm of the young lady, a success and/or novelty worshipper currently en route to an Alternative Miss World shindig, and the mistrust of his elders. Somewhere, they seem to feel, rock sold out.

Scenes like these in Hull Truck shows inspire in me a malevolent delight that may be in excess of the company's intentions. My problem is that though I too am of the right age, I have never, from 1955 till now, felt any emotional allegiance to rock music. When confronted by a fight between two rock factions I can take no sides; I merely enjoy the discomfiture of both. I suppose I might concede that the electric guitar is a nobler noise than the synthesiser... no, I wouldn't. My sympathies are actually with the new boy; his music is terrible, but he never claims to be in it for anything but the money. That is what rock has always been about; and after the stultifying niceties of the previous generation it is a relief to hear it admitted.

The bile flows freely, and entertainingly. Thirzie Robinson, as the wife with reason to despise everyone else in the cast, conveys her disdain with witty rearrangements of haunches and eyebrows; Jonathan Kydd as the young prodigy displays a confident gaucherie that again confirms the power of improvised drama to evoke paradoxes and modes of speech no playwright could contemplate. The show presumes too much on previous acquaintance to rank with Hull Truck's best work, but as an entertainment, or whatever, it may well be forgiven that. Where Mr Bradwell goes next I don't know, and neither I believe does he; but he has behind him 10 years of the richest, sharpest and funniest work in the British theatre.

* * *

Hull Truck has attracted audience loyalty despite there being very few actors one instinctively associates with the group. (Rachel Bell and Alan David are the only ones who come to my mind.) The RSC has got itself a supporters' club audience by stressing permanence, and its pantomime, The Swan Down Gloves, which ended its run at the Aldwych last night, traded quite shamelessly on the punters' loyalty to company stalwarts. These included the house-playwright, impersonated with entrancing bashfulness by Michael Fitzgerald. Some more familiar players blossomed remarkably; Judy Buxton has never done anything as good as her Principal Boy, nor has Jonathan Hyde ever been so superbly stylish as here, playing a down-at-heel Puss-in-Boots.

Terry Wood, a vast actor noted for playing wrestlers, was positively the best Dame I have ever seen; and though I might have found the silently wandering Dragon just as touching if I hadn't known that Alan Howard was hanging in his scales, I wouldn't like to take the chance. Darker forces included David Suchet as an accident-prone Demon King, and Billie Brown as a treacherous baroness for whom I can identify no traditional model.

Mr Brown also wrote the show; as an Antipodean, he must view the English panto routine with bemused awe. That anyway is what emerged here; on an invented story concerning some magic gauntlets manufactured by the Bard's glover bruvver he hung just about every pantomimic ornament. He managed to celebrate and satirise the tradition at the same time; this admittedly is what often happens these days in official pantos (songsheets are seldom lowered without implicit or ribald apologies), but the fact that it was the RSC doing it undoubtedly added edge, as well as charm.

A lot of solemn guff is talked about company feeling; the main purpose of companies, as most RSC shows imply and this one proved, is to make audiences feel happy. This is not much different from the cosy feeling bred in seaside reps, nor should it be. It is something that the RSC, partly due to skill in public relations, has always been good at (in the Sixties anyone criticising David Warner risked lynching by schoolgirls); and it is something that Peter Hall, its original architect, has been either unwilling or unable to repeat on the South Bank. You go to the National's Christmas show Hiawatha for the staging and especially the set; the actors are all right, but they could be anybody. No accident perhaps that in their diplomatic show, The Oresteia, they have neither names nor faces.

Maybe the size of the complex imposes anonymity; things were not thus at the Old Vic. Maybe the Barbican will exert a similar influence. But I really believe that the RSC's secret weapon, the reason why it seems constantly to renew itself, is its patron, even though, with a couple of brilliant exceptions, it has not done too well by him this year. He deserved his starring role in The Swan Down Gloves. What other dramatist would stand being sent up for the best part of four hours?
