records.title: Speeding up the daisy-chain
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Speeding up the daisy-chain

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the RSC's production of Schnitzler's 'La Ronde'.

I HAVE a vested interest in La Ronde (Aldwych), one that originated some 17 years ago. I was at Cambridge, and involved in undergraduate drama.

The vogue word, then as now, was 'workshop'; and though none of us knew quite what it meant any more than anyone does today, there was a general feeling that Schnitzler's play, being a series of duologues, must have some relevance to it. Here were 10 discrete scenes that could be taken away, intensively rehearsed, improvised around and brought back for the judgment of one's peers.

I was given responsibility for three scenes. One of them, between a Husband and a Wife, took place entirely in bed, so that is where it was rehearsed; I still remember the surprise on the faces of fellow-students when they looked in to borrow the milk. I also remember being impressed by the sly humour of this scene, which consists chiefly of the man sermonising at a supposed innocent who in fact has already been unfaithful to him; by the sleek brutality of the subsequent restaurant episode, in which the Husband seduces a Viennese prototype of alluring helplessness referred to by most translators as The Sweet Girl; and by the vain regrets of Schnitzler's last duet, in which a faintly ridiculous Count awakens in a Prostitute's room and tells himself how beautiful it would have been if he had done nothing but kiss her eyes. (I don't know what became of the Prostitute or the Sweet Girl -- typical male negligence, I admit -- but I can tell you that the Husband and the Count both grew up to wear masks in the National Theatre production of 'The Oresteia'.)

I remember that the dialogue revealed great depth and resilience, warranting any amount of digging. And I remember that the text I used (an American anthology) bore on its fly-leaf the name of John Barton, now director and co-translator of the play for the RSC. To adapt Stanley Kowalski, Mr Barton and me have had this date from the beginning. A long time anyway.

However, one of the lessons of Schnitzler's piece is that long-awaited encounters are apt to issue in anti-climax. I was entertained by Mr Barton's production, but also disappointed. There is some difficulty in appealing to the author's intentions, since one of them -- formed long before riots and court cases fed him up with the whole business -- was that 'La Ronde' should not be staged. Being written in dialogue form by a dramatic genius it is playable, but it seems actually to have been meant as a literary exercise, a confessional joke for a small circle. One stage direction calls for a pause of 'a couple of minutes'. Clearly any director is going to have to speed that up. But Mr Barton speeds up the whole scene, which is one of leisurely summery seduction, and indeed the whole play.

When Trevor Nunn directed 'Once in a Lifetime', he called in Gillian Lynne to choreograph the scene-changes, thus eliminating gaps in the action. The device worked, since it provided a smoother ride for what was always intended to be a fast machine. Mr Barton, too, has summoned Miss Lynne; the play is built like a daisy-chain and she shows us the survivor of each encounter hurrying on to the next through a suitable cross-section of old Vienna. The character changes clothes while the sets prettily and efficiently change themselves. Continuity is preserved. Fatal.

If 'La Ronde' is a good play, it is so in a different fashion from any other good play. (For one thing it disposes of Tynan's over-quoted dictum about the necessity of a protagonist being brought to a state of desperation; there is no protagonist and nobody despairs.) Discontinuity is its point; no character on his or her second appearance makes any reference to the first. The theatrical effect lies in the surprise of discovering each in a fresh situation; and that surprise is destroyed if we have seen them dance their way there. Miss Lynne's work anyway is far below her best; a set of hesitation waltzes makes no call on her particular dynamism.

There are no gaps within the scenes either. Each includes copulation, represented in the text by a row of asterisks; we get to see thrashing bodies (generally under sheets) and to hear grunts and squeals. Here too speed is of the essence; clearly the Hapsburg Viennese did not believe in foreplay and had enviably rapid powers of recovery. Here we can call Schnitzler to witness; when he assisted on the first production he was all in favour of discretion. Would it seem unbearably square just to lower the lights and raise them again?

The alternative, on this showing, is forced and irrelevant comedy. So the sexual act looks funny from outside; it wasn't meant to be spectator sport. Here it imposes a farcical style on the true comedy of the surrounding dialogue, which is based on the lies people tell to their partners and themselves when sex is approaching or has just gone.

Not all the actors succumb. The restaurant scene (all Austrian plays should have one, and most do) proves as good as I had thought it, with Judy Buxton provocatively vulnerable and Tony Church swinishly complacent. Mr Church also shines in the marital chamber, lecturing Susan Fleetwood. Going another step farther back, Miss Fleetwood has fun as the wife getting herself bedded by an over-eager Young Gentleman (who winds up, after one false start, congratulating himself over at last having an affair with a respectable woman), but she misses a few layers of well-bred self-deception; she plays like one of those Restoration comedy ladies who cry 'rape' in a delighted whisper.

At the other end of the play John Nettles so stresses the Count's silliness that he has trouble in gaining our serious attention at the close; he just makes it. The prize couple, no question, are Richard Pasco and Barbara Leigh-Hunt as Poet and Actress, both monsters of egoism, professional as much as sexual; if, as full-blown caricatures, they step outside the play's boundaries, they do so in the script as well, standing as they do for the author and his warmest flame. And at this point we can do with the change.

The Prostitute begins and ends the play, making if you will the point that sex-without-love might as well be sex-for-money. No, I don't believe that either. And since the productions in London and Manchester have occasioned much male critical breast-beating (of male critical breasts) it had better be stated that, statistically, Schnitzler's ladies are almost -- not quite -- as predatory as his gentlemen, that the post-coital scenes do not consist entirely of male sneers and female tears, and that, to claim otherwise is the grossest sentimentality.

* * *

Playing the Game (King's Head) comes from Theatre Clwyd, and you will guess that the game is rugby. The first scene, sexier than any in La Ronde, shows the captain in bed with the chairman's wife. When she shows up on club premises, though, he goes off her; the male bond does its work. Later a stripper turns up, to tell the committee -- whom she has just met -- an implausible number of home-truths. The upshot -- that rugger clubs breed fear and hatred of women -- is probably true, but is hardly news.

The author, Jeffrey Thomas, has trouble getting his characters on and off; but his dialogue flows and he is recognisably a playwright. The acting is mostly too blatant for the space.

records.title: A company report
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
A company report

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN muses on the RSC and the National.

A few weeks ago I rhapsodised unconscionably about Shakespeare as the guiding light and salvation of the company that bears his name. I had artistic standards on my mind, but it frequently occurs to me, when musing as critics do in idle moments with a column to fill on the respective qualities of the RSC and the National Theatre, that the Stratford bunch also derives from their favourite son considerable administrative advantages.

The Stratford season gets longer every time and now stretches beyond 31 December into the following year, but it has so far avoided bumping into the one in front. It's possible to talk about a Stratford season, a finite one, with the same actors present throughout. They then proceed to the Aldwych (it is still just possible to write that in the present tense) and play another finite season. They know in short who they are and for how long; and so, more importantly, do we. Both parties can take a breath occasionally.

Compare the National, with its three auditoria open all the year round, staffed by actors on a contract system that doubtless makes sense to the organisation but baffles everyone outside. The result is that, despite long service from various individual players, the National has never, since arriving on the South Bank, had a recognisable company.

I attach no magical connotations to the word 'company': to me it means simply something that can be supported like a football team. It is no guarantee of good work; the National, with its ad hoc methods, may even have had the edge this past year. But what is missing is the promise in a good production that another one will follow.

Even when continuity exists, it is dissipated. Last year Peter Gill arrived with his own group who appeared in three shows; those actors then departed, and it is as if they had never been. Among the press of plays in three theatres, they hardly registered; anyway, they were at best one small company among several. The RSC at any given moment is two companies, one in Stratford and one in London, but the distances are great enough for them to get away with it. With three stages under the same roof the National's lack of unanimity is very visible.

I gather that the National's plan for the coming year is to have individual groups under individual directors, but for each to work in all three theatres; that seems a step in the right direction. Certainly on paper the National's list of associate directors is extraordinary: Hall, Gill, Rudman, Bogdanov, Eyre, Pinter, Schlesinger, Bryden, Morahan, Wood. What is interesting is that every one of them (with the possible exception of Bill Bryden) was a known metropolitan quantity before arriving there.

If you inspect the RSC's roster you find that apart from the guru figure of Peter Brook everyone on it--from Trevor Nunn to Adrian Noble--was virtually unknown before arriving in Stratford. Probably they all fight like hellhounds. They have had the same grounding and it shows. And if the RSC seems almost neurotically reluctant to hire star actors from outside, the National seems to find it difficult to hire anyone else.

Both are inevitably bemused by star writers; the RSC last year gave an inert Solzhenitsyn, and the National a feeble Sam Shepard. The latter though may be part of a constructive reappraisal of American drama; having rehabilitated Arthur Miller, they proceed to dispose of exalted claims for Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? and to lay the Shepard myth, I should think, forever. If I had to choose one National production from last year it would be the generally snubbed Ticket-of-Leave Man; with the RSC I would be tempted by All's Well That Ends Well, which lived up to its name in finally raising the tone of the Stratford main house, but would give the nod to almost anything at the Other Place.

Despite this miniature theatre's high standards (here if anywhere is the proof that other playwrights can be Shakespeare's beneficiaries) I think it represents a threat, or perhaps a capitulation. Nobody puts on a play in a small theatre if he thinks he can get an audience for it in a large one. The prestige of the Warehouse and the Other Place, like the studios in the big reps, is a tacit admission of a shrinking public. Occasionally a production comes along that would only work in a small space; like the Nunn Macbeth, which proved it the hard way by dying briefly in the big one. It is economics, not aesthetics, that keep the others from transferring.

I believe in large theatres and large audiences, the more heterogeneous the better. Community theatre--whether for bankers or factory workers--is another admission of defeat. I have never understood the scornful phrase, 'consumer theatre.' It seems to me the only honest approach: here is the show, come and get it. Whoever you are. That is why the West End--a place nobody lives in, but everybody visits--is worth preserving, and why the RSC's departure from it will be a sad blow.

There is a new community theatre in Deptford, or rather a new version of an old one. The Albany Empire, burned down and (by the Arts Council) turned down, nevertheless got itself rebuilt on a different site at a cost of £3 million. I know this because the performers in the initial show, All Who Sail In Her, keep mentioning it. They seem as far as I could follow some turgid dialogue turgidly delivered to feel guilty about the money and half-inclined to give it back, instead of (as they presumably did in real life) saying thank you and getting on with the job.

This is a breakthrough in theatrical self-pity, and a more inbred entertainment than anything the most highly-subsidised theatre would dare contemplate. The actors talk about the show they should be giving instead of giving it; I fled at half time. I had a few regrets; I like cafe theatre and this space--a cross between the King's Head and the Talk Of The Town--is very pleasant; Keith Allen is an extremely bright comic; and Debby Bishop makes her songs sound good, though she still confuses acting with belligerence.

Behind the Lines (Tricycle) is a poetry double act by Roger McGough and Brian Patten. Mr McGough is in the Spike Milligan holy fool tradition: for love and against the bomb. As a performer he has turned unassumingness into a style; Mr Patten, at a preview, had not.

records.title: Man of Method
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Man of Method

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Lee Strasberg, founder of the Actors' Studio, who died last week.

IF EVER there was an eminence grise of the theatre, it was Lee Strasberg: The public saw very little of his work directly, but he is credited as the major influence on two generations of American actors, and through them on two generations of American playwriting. American movies would be almost unrecognisable without his pupils and proteges. And it was in a movie -- 'The Godfather, Part Two' -- that he himself made his greatest popular impact, at the age of 73.

His career was comparatively simple. He was born in Poland in 1901; he was eight when his parents settled in America. He became an actor in 1925, becoming known for his work with the Theatre Guild, the foremost 'prestige' management in New York. Among his contemporaries there were two other theatrical gurus, Harold Clurman and Sanford Meisner.

The late Twenties saw the first major surge of American playwriting, most of it naturalistic, even journalistic. Sidney Kingsley's hospital drama, 'Men in White,' won a Pulitzer Prize, and Strasberg was in it. He became at first obsessed with finding a new American acting style to match the new drama.

In 1929 the Group Theatre came into existence, nurturing the talents of writer Clifford Odets, producer Cheryl Crawford and directors Clurman, Robert Lewis and Elia Kazan. Strasberg emerged as chief theorist, promoting an Americanised version -- now unfortunately but inescapably known as the Method -- of the Russian gospel of Konstantin Stanislavsky.

One crucial difference in circumstances was that Stanislavsky had a classical tradition to work from, and Strasberg hadn't. In the Thirties American drama meant exclusively contemporary drama, and America, first shaken by the Depression, then stirred by the New Deal, had little use for external disciplines. This at least seems to have been Strasberg's problem, conscious or not; the charge against him has always been that he emphasised the internal mechanics of acting, while neglecting visible and audible technique. He was not a showman, as Stanislavsky unquestionably was (Chekhov used to complain about it) and as both Kazan and Lewis became. Clurman's book 'The Fervent Years' provides evidence of how unharmonious the Group Theatre could be.

Nevertheless, between Strasberg and Kazan at any rate a fruitful partnership emerged. The Group collapsed during the war, but Strasberg went on to found the Actors' Studio (as a sort of post-graduate gymnasium), while Kazan became Broadway's leading dramatic director, developing the actors Strasberg trained. We forget now that for the 15 years after the war America led world theatre. Kazan had the early work of Arthur Miller and Tennessee Williams to direct, and Strasberg's actors to play them; if some other plays lacked fantasy and invention, the gap was supplied by the musicals; two men -- Kazan and Jerome Robbins -- effectively divided the territory between them.

Then, around 1960, it all fell apart. It was a legacy of the Thirties anyway, with the tensions of the old Left kept bitterly alive by the challenge of McCarthyism. When Odets, Williams and Miller slackened, there was no one to replace them; their contemporaries and successors offered only routine naturalism, psychologically intense but narrow -- the only kind of play, it was frequently said, that Studio actors knew how to act. There has -- despite Albee, despite Mamet, despite Shepard, despite McClure -- been no general revival. Besides, everyone had gone to Hollywood, Kazan leading such actors as Marlon Brando, James Dean, Rod Steiger and Paul Newman.

Those who thought Method acting mere behaviourism -- and it's certainly the opposite of character acting as practised by an Olivier -- thought this only logical. But, from Barrymore onwards, the best American actors, of whatever school, have always defected to the movies; the logic of stardom, emotional as well as economic, propels them. It may be significant that Strasberg's most publicised pupil was that greatest of non-actresses, Marilyn Monroe (who could hardly make a move on set without guidance from Strasberg's wife Paula), but of his other proteges nobody ever accused Julie Harris of being untheatrical, and those who saw Brando on stage in 'Truckline Cafe' and 'A Streetcar Named Desire' found him mesmeric.

That the Method failed when it faced up to the classics is undeniable. Kazan burned himself on a Jacobean tragedy and never tried again; Strasberg, having finally turned the Actors' Studio into a company, came up with a humiliating 'Three Sisters' (with Sandy Dennis, George C. Scott and Kim Stanley in the cast). He failed as a director. But teachers are as important for what they are and what they inspire as what they do, and his continued influence down to Al Pacino and Robert de Niro speaks for itself. At the very least he got actors, in Britain as well as America, thinking more intensely (if often talking too intensely) about acting. And when he came to play the senior mobster in 'Godfather II' his effortlessly towering performance proved that he could not only deliver the goods; he was the goods.

records.title: A spy is born
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
A spy is born

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Julian Mitchell's 'Another Country.'

THE evening begins with an offstage boys' choir singing that great religious and patriotic hit I Vow to Thee, My Country, first verse only. The second only comes round at the end of the show: "and there's another country I've heard of long ago." I had always imagined that other country to be Heaven, but at the Queen's, where a performance of Julian Mitchell's play called Another Country is sandwiched between the two choruses, another interpretation suggests itself. By Mr Mitchell's sardonic lights, that country, envisaged by his two central characters, could be Russia.

Our heroes are senior public schoolboys in the early 1930s. One of them, Judd, is the school's lone Marxist, or, the time being what it is, Stalinist, in a constant state of articulate fury over the system in general and the rules that stop him reading Das Kapital under the bedclothes in particular. The other, Guy Bennett, is a more complicated kind of rebel; in a milieu where casual homosexuality is the norm he makes the mistake of falling in love. His indiscretions land him a public flogging and (more woundingly) permanent exile from the school's privileged upper echelon. Recognising school to be a microcosm of the establishment world outside, he looks for a way of fighting back: covertly, since he doesn't want to lose any more perks. His eye falls on Judd's copy of Marx. A spy is born.

Mr Mitchell has written an acute, sympathetic and continuously entertaining play, one whose abundant joke-lines always remain in character. Its ultimate effect, though, depends on outside evidence. If I had not been alerted by the programme and the pre-publicity, I could easily have sat through the piece unaware that Guy Bennett was meant to be Guy Burgess.

If you can identify the Bennett connection then you concentrate on him and get a coherent evening, rising to an abrupt but satisfying point. Mr Mitchell, though, wants you to be interested in other characters as well; and here both he and Stuart Burge's production, on a creaky revolve with variable acting, are less successful. It takes some time to sort out the personnel, and the conscientious torments of the retiring house-captain never come into focus.

What does emerge is a properly ambiguous picture of a society thoroughly rotten (in both the literal and popular usages) and yet cosily attractive. Mr Mitchell offers us all the trappings of school fiction: the petty politics, the sport, the tormented fags (in the scholastic sense) who will be bullies themselves in time, the study teas. This, all too recognisably, is England; there is, unless you take desperate measures, no other country.

Guy's pale rebellion (born 30 years later he would be writing plays for subsidised theatres) is admirably caught by Rupert Everett, soft-voiced and hard-shelled; he is first glimpsed curled on the window-ledge of the house library (shockingly short on books by the way) searching through binoculars for likely beloveds, his tie loose and his braces hanging down from his waist, a perfect self-created artefact. Kenneth Branagh brings great flair to Judd's decent doomed doggedness.

* * *

Underneath the Arches (Prince of Wales) by contrast is nostalgia plain and unequivocal. Here is the Flanagan and Allen story, narrated with aplomb by Christopher Timothy as Chesney Allen, straight man and sole surviving member of the Crazy Gang: a point Mr Allen proves on certain nights by turning up at the end of Act One to supplant his impersonator and join Roy Hudd's Bud in renditions of Hometown and Underneath the Arches itself. He also proves, what Mr Timothy had already led us to suspect, that his flat honeyed vocal tones, though they sound a pushover, are actually inimitable.

Mr Hudd perfectly hits off Bud Flanagan's sweet, slightly Americanised croon; his anguished solo performance of Music Maestro Please is the evening's highlight. His oval countenance, though, is nothing like Flanagan's circular one, and for most of the show he settles for playing Roy Hudd. The other Crazy Gangsters are indistinguishable, except of course for Monsewer Eddie Gray in top hat, red nose and drooping handlebars. His card-trick routine is the one piece of Crazy Gang material that stands up as Max Miller's or Lenny Bruce's do away from their original performers.

The one-line crossovers are still fun but the sketches are a yawn. They are used here to tell the story and succeed in devaluing it; Flanagan's wartime sufferings under the sergeant whose name he adopted in revenge are obliterated by a tired parade routine. The songs are another matter, the best of them being highly insinuating; Strolling is wisely saved for the end, though surprisingly little is made of it.

The programme warns that numbers are not performed in chronological order; all the same it is numbing to find Franklin D. Roosevelt Jones greeting Bud's arrival in New York in 1910 ("Oh just play something American") and the title song divorced from any reference to the depression. Much is, perhaps intentionally, awful; Tiller Girl routines are faithfully re-created in all their high-kicking vacuity. An item called Just For Laughs is reprised three times, whenever it is felt that some explanation of the heroes' motivation or appeal might be in order.

Roger Redfarn directed; Patrick Garland, Brian Glanville and Mr Hudd wrote or at least collated; I should like to know the provenance of Bud's comment on Val Parnell: "So old that when he goes out with a girl he has to take a younger man and a set of jump-leads." For all its faults the show, unlike its American equivalent Sugar Babies, has a heart.

records.title: Doing the Dolls proud
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Doing the Dolls proud

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

IT IS about time the National Theatre got round to staging the real classics; and having finally taken the plunge with Guys and Dolls (Olivier) they have surfaced with a production that for sheer brazen pleasure is unequalled in London. They have done the show proud; but then it has done the same for them.

The show has the primary mark of a post-war musical: a story that the authors obviously believe is worth telling, and to which all other elements of the show are subservient; on this level it is the tightest job of its time.

What sets apart Abe Burrows's book and Frank Loesser's score is a total lack of solemnity; in spirit and setting the show returns us to the raffish, unbuttoned New York musicals of the Thirties. It is the closest Broadway has ever come to getting the best of both worlds.

Damon Runyon mythologised the seediness of Times Square and district in his prose, just as Cole Porter and Lorenz Hart did in their lyrics. It is indeed amazing that nobody thought earlier of turning one of his stories into a musical. But there is a little difficulty here. This Runyon is a joy to read, and there are some other scribes who take a delight in imitating his style as soon as they are asked or maybe sooner. He is a great guy for euphemisms; he will always speak of a Broadway character being cooled off, as among his acquaintances it is considered exceptionally gross to use such a word as murder. But when he sells his stories to the movies the flow of the narrative is much hindered by his loquacity and the pictures are generally stinkers; and while Damon is content to take the money, it causes his friends no little grief.

But this Abe Burrows is a smart guy, and though he allows himself one paragraph of strict Runyonese (rather screwed up in the National production), he generally sticks to quick-fire gag-writing. He offers his own equivalent of Runyon's affected innocence; when Nathan Detroit satirically announces that he will hold his floating crap-game in Radio City Music Hall, Benny Southstreet faithfully inquires, 'how you gonna fix the ushers?'

The show is besides beautifully, indeed classically structured, with the crap-shooters looking forward to their game, the Save-a-Soul missionaries to a make-or-break prayer meeting, and the fate of both gatherings hingeing on the bet made by gambler Sky Masterson to take mission sergeant Sarah Brown on a date to Havana.

Meanwhile Loesser's lyrics preserve spirit and style. You know you are home when in the opening 'Fugue for Tinhorns' Nicely-Nicely Johnson sings of his favoured racehorse, 'I tell you Paul Revere--now this is no bum steer--It's from a handicapper that's real sincere.' The triple rhyme gratifies the ear; the juxtaposition of the slang 'bum steer' with the orotund 'sincere' is in the best traditions of both Runyon and Broadway. For the comic short story and the theatre lyric live under the same threat: one false word and both are dead.

Obviously the National production offers the attraction of straight actors essaying song-and-dance. But this only becomes blatant in a tap routine occupying a limbo between closing number and curtain-call. Otherwise we are constantly aware that these are British actors; but that is a bonus. Cast and audience conspire together to animate a myth with which both are familiar, but to which neither is native.

And Richard Eyre's direction has the subsidised theatrical virtue of respect for the text. There are no crass modernisations; it is not only the comic dialogue that is cherished here; the first encounter between Sky and Sarah yields real tension.

Julie Covington sings beautifully as Sarah, but could afford to be, literally, more out-front; Ian Charleson delivers a gutsy 'Luck Be a Lady,' but does not justify the awe in which Sky is held by his fellow high-rollers. Bob Hoskins's Nathan is superbly vulnerable, notably when hoisted shoulder-high by a couple of dancing admirers. It is a shame he is starved of songs. (Actors who sing as badly as Sam Levene, the original Nathan, are hard to come by.) He is the evening's linchpin; its star is Julia McKenzie as Adelaide, 'the well-known fiancee,' a paragon of put-upon poise; her delivery of the glorious Lament ('a person could develop a cold') sets the show unshakably on its feet. Hers are the funniest numbers, and the most touching.

There is great support, especially from John Normington's avuncular soul-saver. Bill Paterson's Harry the Horse has the weirdest accent I have ever heard, but he also has a sinister jack-knifed walk like Eagle Eye Fleagle in 'Li'l Abner.' This brings me to David Toguri's choreography which, after an overly studied opening montage, gets steadily better, progressing through the Havana and crap-game ballets to a staging of 'Sit Down, You're Rockin' the Boat' that, to judge from the photographs, improves on the original; and in which David Healy's Nicely-Nicely justifies his encores.

John Gunter has designed a wonderful surround of shop-fronts, neon ads, scrapered sky-line and--my special delight--a real solid subway entrance. Two final thoughts. A crucial difference between Runyon's hoods and those of the show is that you always believe the former capable of real mayhem, but never the latter. This was only Loesser's second theatre score, but how strongly even a conventional ballad like 'I've Never Been in Love Before' takes the stage. There are 16 songs in the score and, dramatically at least, 16 hits.

* * *

Eric Bentley once wrote that as a piece of art 'Guys and Dolls' far surpasses Broadway's efforts to be artistic, and Lillian Hellman's The Little Foxes is at the Victoria Palace to prove the point. It seems unfair, since Miss Hellman made a far better showing in front of the Un-American Activities Committee than Mr Burrows, but her melodrama of Deep Southern greed is now very dead indeed, and this production--in the dying-fall manner deemed appropriate by Americans to a native classic--embalms it.

But such criticism is probably irrelevant. The audience come to see a star; not to see her act but just to see her. Elizabeth Taylor's performance hardly carries into the auditorium.

Ambrose Hammer--a critic who loves to heave the old harpoon into actors--might carry on from there. I merely say that the first night, for which many citizens in penguin suits shell out £25-notes each and which has the gendarmes out with barricades, is as grisly as an undertaker's picnic and may be grislier.

records.title: Party and passion
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Party and passion

ROBERT CUSHMAN on plays by Sartre and Steve Gooch.

SARTRE'S The Assassin (Greenwich) is about as good as a play can be while remaining strictly unbelievable. It is the piece written just after the war that the British theatre used to know as 'Crime Passionnel,' but whose French title was 'Les Mains sales'; 'Dirty Hands' has never been thought to be much of a come-on for home audiences.

Anyway, the assassin who gets his hands dirty through what may have been a crime of passion is Hugo, a new-born Communist of middle-class origin whom the party sends to liquidate Hoederer, who is supposed to be one of their most prominent own, but is suspected, with good reason, of compromising with the enemy. (The class enemy, stupid.) We are in an unnamed small central European country, of the kind so useful to parabolically-minded playwrights, and the war is on. The themes of collaboration, betrayal and violence are those which were rattling around France at the time and for years afterwards. It now seems a shame that Sartre did not set the play firmly in his own backyard.

He does, on the other hand, make distance work for him. The most impressive aspect of the play is the remorselessness with which Sartre dissects his own party. As often happens with left-wing playwrights, the most sympathetic figure on stage belongs to the opposition: no mere bourgeois (how could you think such a thing?), but the ancien regime incarnate: a prince indeed, written (and played here by Stephen MacDonald) as affably imperturbable.

This of course is mischievous devil's advocacy of the kind any playwright might permit himself. The pain comes when Hugo, having accomplished his mission, emerges from prison to find that his comrades have now adopted the principles of Hoederer, whose fault, it is now revealed, was merely that of being ahead of his time, out of step with history. (In other words, directives from Russia have changed their tune.) Hugo the idealist is stranded, bitterly and forever.

All that is likely. What strains credulity is that the young and totally untried Hugo should be trusted with such a mission in the first place; that having been introduced into Hoederer's home as his secretary, he should take his wife along with him; and that he should reveal to her the full details of what he plans to do. She is a teasing, unawakened girl who calls him 'my little honey-bee.' She persuades him to ask Hoederer to defend himself intellectually; and this Hoederer does, producing a highly convincing defence of his heretical opportunism. Hugo is not convinced, but he still surrenders to hero-worship, as does his wife to downright love. Hugo discovers her in Hoederer's arms and, finally, he shoots. Just which of them he was jealous of remains an open question.

You can see why Sartre, meshing personal and political passions, needed the characters of Hugo's wife and of the doctrinaire girl at HQ, who loves him, but he hardly animated them; nor did he do much better with Hugo himself. A playwright of ideas can bring characters to life, but only if they express not so much his own beliefs as his own temperament. In Sartre's case the tougher the better. A coldly intellectual production--such as we fondly imagine to be typical of the French--might make all viewpoints equal; Frank Hauser's direction, unremarkably human, reinforces the biases. James Simmons flails as Hugo, promising more than he currently delivers.

The play perks up when a pair of bodyguards appear, one (Richard Cubison) sullen, the other (Michael Melia) engagingly flip; and erupts when Edward Woodward comes on as Hoederer. He has the practical confidence of a successful trade unionist, the lilt in his voice under control but dominating the stage. The arguments between Hoederer and his murderer--pragmatist against intransigent, worker against theorist--are strongly, even excitingly done, but we already know all the arguments. It is a sad augury for political drama that not even Sartre can surprise us.

* * *

Acknowledged or not, he is the father of the British playwrights who arrived in the late Sixties and early Seventies and who have specialised in polemical melodrama. Of them all Steve Gooch has remained the truest to his roots; that is to say he has continued to write chiefly for fringe or touring groups. One of these--Solent People's Theatre Company, operating out of Southampton--has arrived above the Crown and Castle pub at Dalston Junction with Mr Gooch's Fast One.

A disillusioned adventurer (written cockney, but played scouse) turns up with his barmaid girl-friend in another unnamed country--South American this time, time and the theatre having moved on--and commences running guns to whoever wants them. He can't really tell the difference and neither--since Mr Gooch's dialogue and characterisation here lag rather far behind his action--could I. It is a good thing I don't demand uplift from my drama; there seemed to me nothing to choose on the evidence offered between military oppressors, moderate opposition and revolutionaries. But Mark Donford-May's production achieves one signal triumph; its sub-tropical characters neither look nor sound ridiculous.

records.title: End of an era
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
End of an era

ROBERT CUSHMAN looks back over the 21 years the RSC has spent at the Aldwych. In May the London company reopens at its new home, the Barbican.

AFTER 21 years the Royal Shakespeare Company, Barbican-bound, has vacated the Aldwych Theatre. The Aldwych has been taken over by a commercial management, which will begin its reign by presenting the RSC in 'Good.' Good.

I suppose it's traditional to leave home on your twenty-first birthday. It is anyway an irresistible cue for a retrospective. But first, a digression. A series of books is about to be launched by Cambridge University Press: its title, 'Directors in Perspective.' The first two volumes deal with Ingmar Bergman and Peter Stein; future subjects are Roger Blin; Peter Brook, Joseph Chaikin, Jerzy Grotowski and--representing the deceased--Appia, Brecht, Craig, Reinhardt and Stanislavsky. There is something numbingly predictable about that list: not so much who is on as who is off it.

When the series was announced last year, I was prepared to lay odds that the editors were not commissioning monographs on, say, Trevor Nunn or Michael Blakemore or even--despite his unexampled output here and abroad--Tyrone Guthrie. It would be wrong to say that Guthrie never theorised--he evangelised constantly for the open stage--but academics always thought him frivolous and he would probably have agreed with them.

In the American theatre one hardly expects serious attention to be paid to the men who have really done the work--to Jerome Robbins, Elia Kazan or Hal Prince. Who in France cares any more about Jean Vilar, whose Theatre National Populaire was in its day the beau ideal of a subsidised rep? I am not knocking the chosen few. The dead ones are important as influences (and in the case of Craig, whose actual directing career was negligible, as nothing else) and I have seen brilliant work from all but one of the living. But I do get the impression that they have qualified on their ideas, especially when written down, rather than on their practice; Brook once wrote a wonderful article called 'Don't Be Bamboozled by Theories,' which should be required reading for everyone concerned, not excepting its author.

The RSC has frequently been praised, or damned, as a director's theatre, but it seems that by international standards it has still a long way to go; whether one wants it to is another question. Assembling my memories, I find myself aware of directors but not usually to the detriment of either actors or plays. This pleases but surprises me.

First, let us classify the product. Aldwych shows have divided into those born in London and those imported from Stratford; and over the 21 years the second category has become increasingly dominant. Peter Hall's first stated plan was to stiffen a repertory of classics and new plays with the occasional proven Shakespeare. From his first Stratford season in 1960 he chose for London his own production of 'Twelfth Night,' whose acting, as seen from the upper circle by this jaundiced 17-year-old, had faded to almost nothing.

A few months later it was supplemented by a far livelier 'Taming of the Shrew'; Kate was Vanessa Redgrave, already glorious for her Stratford Rosalind, which soon and duly came to London. Her performance is legendary, and the production should be; this 'As You Like It' was the only play directed for the RSC by Michael Elliott, a loss for both parties. It was more benevolent in tone than was to prove typical of the company, but it heralded an era of microscopic scrutiny of the text, which, here at least, was never portentous; the opposition of court and county was illuminated, but not heavily underlined, as sometimes happened in later years.

These were all decorative productions, the legacy of a previous regime at Stratford. Sterner and bitterer times were heralded by Peter Hall's sandpit 'Troilus and Cressida,' a miracle of balance and Hall's best Shakespeare production ever; relieved by Clifford Williams's 'Comedy of Errors,' hilarious but simple; and definitively embodied by Peter Brook's unforgiving 'King Lear,' with its leather costumes and visible thunder-sheets, with Paul Scofield's growling Lear and, in Irene Worth, a Goneril who managed to make 'pluck out his eyes' sound sympathetic.

The authority with which Brook imposed his vision made us wish, in retrospect, that he had tackled the whole play: roughly, he cut the redemptive bits. The production is now--and I say this without prejudice to the excitement with which I watched it at the time--intellectually discredited. So, for other reasons, is the crowning achievement of those early years, the 'Wars of the Roses' cycle. It no longer seems as permissible as it did then for John Barton to rewrite even junior Shakespeare; you can tell the difference, and the endeavour reeks of a desire to make Shakespeare say what you think a twentieth-century audience wants him to say, thereby selling both sides short.

This production--the power game in three instalments--set a fashion; from now on barons were to be mistrusted on sight. (When they actually proved traitors, the surprise was gone.) All this, though true, is very unfair. The Hall-Barton production was more than a concept; there was immediate life in every minute of its 11-hour progress. Peggy Ashcroft went through it all in the same role, girl to crone. I have never cheered anyone louder.

Actors were being taught subtlety of speech, though this did not always equal subtlety of characterisation; often in fact it was reductive; cf. Barton's 'Troilus,' overheated; over-rated. Brook lit the next beacon with 'A Midsummer Night's Dream,' which saw in the Seventies. Everybody loved it-or-hated it; everybody but me. I thought it looked lovely and was fun, especially the juggling, but those who claimed that it redefined the play can never have read or seen it. The lovers are always played young and comic, the clowns are usually funnier and therefore richer; and, apart from a fine Titania and Puck, the acting was nothing special.

I found it far less enlightening and invigorating than Barton's bitter-sweet productions of 'All's Well that Ends Well' and 'Twelfth Night,' both crammed with high comic performances, the former an explosion, the latter a miracle of sustained tone. Both were radical improvements on their Stratford selves; this came to be expected of the RSC, a tough break for other managements who have to get it right first time.

In general energy was slackening; productions were becoming cerebral and the cerebrations were producing odd results. Nunn's Roman cycle, brought wholesale to London, revealed a painful lack of personality in supporting ranks; Nicol Williamson's anguished Coriolanus showed everyone up.

Revival came in two stages. Terry Hands, whose earlier productions had been carnivals of overwrought flamenco acting, simmered down for a rousing series of English Henries (though his later Richards showed him slipping back into his old ways); Nunn recruited a largely new and breezy company that restored our faith in ensemble.

His 'Macbeth' with Williamson had been the RSC at its worst, straining painfully after new insights; his 'Macbeth' with Ian McKellen and Judi Dench was the RSC at its best, the insights coming unstrained and at a rate of one a line. We were seeing far more Shakespeare at the Aldwych than we used to: Stratford seasons transplanted whole. Partly, we were told, this was for reasons of company morale; it must also have had to do with there being a guaranteed audience for Shakespeare.

It has meant, though, that new plays have been fewer than ever, mostly siphoned off to the Warehouse. Once the Aldwych virtually had Pinter as a house playwright, but when Hall went National, he went too. They persevered with David Mercer; and were rewarded, in 'After Haggerty,' with one good play out of four. There was Stoppard's 'Travesties,' and there have been a couple by Peter Nichols, both fine, though neither had much to do with the RSC as a company. The Aldwych was never a playwright's theatre, though the taste in modern drama paralleled attitudes to Shakespeare.

First it was dressy: Giraudoux, Anouilh, John Whiting; then they discovered Beckett and Pinter. The RSC has fully exercised its prerogative of not being the National Theatre, committed to a broad-based repertoire. It started out with 'The Duchess of Malfi,' but has done few Jacobeans since, though Nunn's 'Revenger's Tragedy' and 'Alchemist,' both Stratford transplants, were triumphs. The company's addiction to things Russian has become a joke, but a good-natured one; there has been at least one Gorki, too many, but Russian realism, in novel and drama, is the nearest thing there is to Shakespearean inclusiveness, so it fits.

Only Dickens competes; and there is no doubt that the glory of 'Nicholas Nickleby' could only have been encompassed by a Shakespearean company. It connects too with the appetite for showbiz demonstrated in 'Once in a Lifetime' and the musical 'Comedy of Errors,' and with the good theatrical equation of quality and quantity as in 'The Greeks.' Company attitudes seem to me fundamentally sounder than at any time since the heady early Sixties.

I should have mentioned many more actors; Ian Richardson who was there at the start and put in 13 years becoming supremely accomplished, Tony Church who seems never to act on anyone else's stage and Patrick Stewart ditto, Holm, Howard, Pasco, Sinden, Suzman.... But we have lost two superb actors who never played with either major company, though doubtless they were asked; Alan Badel--who in his generation ranked with Burton and Scofield--and Harry H. Corbett. Both died prematurely; both, maybe, had the careers they wanted. But both leave in their wake a feeling of waste.

records.title: Soliloquies in Louisville
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: They're Coming To Make It Brighter
records.body:
Soliloquies in Louisville

ROBERT CUSHMAN reports from America on a festival of new plays.

THERE are currently two plays on Broadway, and a third one off, that were first staged in the annual New Play Festival at the Actors' Theatre of Louisville, Kentucky. That makes Louisville the main provider of material for intelligent middle-brow drama in New York and subsequently the rest of the country.

I doubt whether this year's bash, which culminated last weekend in a monster weekend of plays attended by producers, scouts and critics from America, Europe and even China, will yield much to enrich the world repertoire; you could hardly call the work experimental, except perhaps in the sheer scale of the organisation and in the proliferation of plays lasting one act or less. Lunchtime theatre is a British phenomenon unknown in the States, but here were pieces ready made for it, available with every meal. In three days I saw 27 plays.

That may be an unfair count; since 18 of them were short monologues, combined to make three separate entertainments. There is no question at Louisville of the soliloquy being a dead convention; the Actors' Theatre may be doing more than television to kill the art of conversation; and when the third programme arrived most auditors were sighing for a good old extravagant two-hander.

Not that the Louisville solos were ill-written; they provided basic proof that the average American playwright writes tangier sentences than his British equivalent. They offered well-seized opportunities to a strong bunch of actors, who were however playing to an audience of professional egotists, prepared to tolerate monologues only when delivered by themselves.

The fashion apparently grew from the work of a mysteriously reclusive resident playwright named Jane Martin. Nobody knew, or anyway was letting on, quite who Miss Martin is (or, as some sceptics would have it, are), but I side with those who hold that she must be an actress. Of the 11 numbers she contributed, comprising a programme called Talking With, one depicted a leading lady, in her dressing-room pondering her audience ("how can they live in a town without one decent Chinese restaurant?"), another a desperate auditioner, and both of these wit triumphed over whimsy; in too many of the others it lost out. Miss Martin's overall title suggested to me a rule, not infallible, for one-person plays. They are more effective when the speaker is talking with an actual unseen someone than with himself or herself. Solitary musing too often turns to self-pity. Even the touring actress at one point told us, "I am not an entertainment." Tough, maybe.

An actor called Robert Schenkkan wrote and performed a chilling, deadpan, mock-lecture about post-holocaust survival. This was almost the only play in the festival you could accuse of having political content; monologues in general are turned inexorably inwards like most American drama, only more so. A writer in New York's Village Voice recently arraigned British playwrights from Peter Shaffer on the right to Trevor Griffiths and Howard Barker on the left for tidying up experience. I know what he means, but the American alternative seems, as they might put it in Kentucky, right sloppy.

A couple of years ago Louisville plays afforded the visitor some insight into different levels of American society: from the alienated working class Mid-West to the alienated affluent of California. This year we have been taken, as if by Greyhound time-machine, to witness charity and suspicion in Minnesota 1915, cosiness and compassion in Arkansas 1951, and madness and mayhem in Nebraska now; but the settings, and even the dates, seemed immaterial; all that mattered was what Tennessee Williams once called "personal lyricism," sweet or sour.

This year's likeliest candidate for Broadway (everybody who writes about the festival ends up sounding like a stringer for Variety, weighing up commercial chances) was Oldtimers Game, a baseball comedy that lapsed into sentimentality, but had an attractively jaunty air to it. It belongs to the salty, bustling American genre epitomised for all time by The Front Page, and represented at Louisville two years ago by a piece called They're Coming To Make It Brighter. The author of that one, Kent Broadhurst, this time moved down in scale, but up in quality, with The Eye of the Beholder, a witty, logic-chopping, role-reversing playlet about two artists and their model. It was the best play of the festival.

The big guns, though, were two adaptations of novels, both familiar to us as John Ford movies. The Informer gradually recovered from an impenetrable start, the fruit of obscure plotting and dubious accents, without ever persuading us that another play about Dublin in the Troubles is what the theatre needs now. It had a fine production by the theatre's director, Jon Jory; a wizard with large casts. His touch was much missed in The Grapes of Wrath; Steinbeck's story still grips shamelessly, at least when disasters start mounting up, but the stifling nobility of his persecuted migrants was in no way mitigated by presentation and acting that made these Oklahoma workers look like the Beverly Hillbillies.

This, though, was an exceptional lapse. Acting standards were very high, with individual players recurring rapidly and gratifyingly throughout the weekend. Susan Kingsley, who moved from a funny old geriatric to a graphically frightened young wife, is a major actress, scarcely less good than Anne Pitoniak, who presented a formidable number of crabby old ladies without ever getting her wires crossed.
production_title: They're Coming To Make It Brighter

records.title: Variations on a theme
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Variations on a theme

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Song and Dance' and 'Boogie.'

IN New York a week ago I was told by a producer that he could slam Victor Borge into a Broadway house for three weeks, make a profit and enliven the season to boot. He seemed depressed about it; no reflection on Mr Borge, but this was not quite what he thought of as theatre.

The West End scene is currently brighter; all the same, one can feel managers casting feverishly about for stop-gaps. The only gloomy thing about Song and Dance is that it springs from the financial necessity that nothing by Andrew Lloyd Webber should go unstaged. Mr Webber has left lying around a recorded song-cycle and a set of variations on a theme by Paganini. So into the Palace they go.

Mr Webber does his own orchestrations which are even brighter than those for 'Cats.' He is especially generous with solo lines, which the musicians, under the skilled direction of Harry Rabinowitz (God, I never expected to see Mr Rabinowitz; I always thought he lived in a radio) fairly lap up; his music certainly has dramatic punch, but it always sounds like pastiche, never quite authentic. It is also, for all its jazz and rock rhythms and its operatic upholstering, curiously dry.

Actually he has never been freer than in the avowedly imitative 'Variations,' where the music combines with the dancing of Wayne Sleep and his acrobatic cohorts to tilt us out of our seats. Anthony Van Laast's choreography is fiery and funny, its execution still more so. Those of us who don't normally get to see much ballet were exhilarated; and relieved to find our enthusiasm shared by the buffs.

At least I think those were buffs, cheering every time someone described a circle very fast; they out-shouted even the musical fans and made the legit audience seem pallid indeed. Suppose we were to erupt every time Judi Dench smiled or Alan Howard hit a high note? (Though actually, at the last matinee of 'The Forest' at the Aldwych, the house accorded Mr Howard and Richard Pasco some furious bravoes; my wife commented--and I can't argue with her--that it's enough for actors to over-act without the spectators doing it as well.)

The song half, 'Tell Me on a Sunday,' is the story of an English girl whose heart is successively broken by a California movie-man, a young New Yorker and a married New Yorker; in between times, she writes to mum in Muswell Hill. For linking passages Mr Webber writes buttressed recitative for which his lyricist, Don Black, is hard-pressed to find not so much the right words as the right syllables; the stresses are continually misplaced.

Both partners are happier in the set numbers: a bouncy satiric piece about Los Angeles life-styles called 'Capped Teeth and Caesar Salad,' an ingenious threnody to man number one ('Sheldon Bloom'), more sardonically reprised for number three ('Married Man'); the words here are full of assimilated detail. The title-song, a touching plea to be let down gently, rightly suggests that Sunday in New York (no wonder there are so many songs about it) is unique, unlike the place any other day or the day any other place.

Marti Webb sings full and well and gives the piece theatrical weight. The flaw is that nothing happens to her in New York (and what's she doing there? For a living, I mean) that could not equally well have happened in London, while the homesickness theme is underplayed, so the local colour comes to seem meretricious. It is well sprayed on, though, in the blow-up decor. John Caird's production fills the stage with three mobile platforms: one for Miss Webb, one for the conductor, and one for the band. It all looks very perilous. Speaking of which, the Paganini theme is also the theme of 'The South Bank Show'; next time I switch on I hope to see Melvyn Bragg turning cartwheels.

* * *

The Mayfair programme says Boogie! on the cover, 'Boogie Woogie Bubble 'n' Squeak' on the title-page; and I share its confusion. Three energetic South Africans (Leonie Hofmeyer, Sarah McNair, Michele Maxwell) take us through the pop decades as the Andrews Sisters, the McGuire Sisters (the McGuire Sisters?), the Beverley Sisters; and then, deserting showbiz sisterhood for committed Sisterhood, as the Shangri-Las (all leathery as in Leader of the Pack), the Supremes (three to a dress) and the Pointer siblings. (They satirise the 1940s from a pacifist standpoint; Pistol Packin' Mama is backed by a picture of a mushroom-cloud ('Lay that pistol down, babe') and 'Rum and Coca-Cola' by starving Caribbeans. Well, fair enough. They satirise the 1950s from a feminist viewpoint; but masochistic ballads like 'Little Things Mean a Lot' and 'Mister Wonderful' were always laughable anyway. They then run out of things to say; they just want to get into that gear and sing those songs.

One of them sang consistently flat, and their impersonations are approximate. Their Beverleys sound as the Andrewses might have done if each of them had been christened Julie; and I never knew that Diana Ross had a Fenella Fielding lisp.

* * *

Four days earlier I had encountered another lampoon of the Supremes, having gained entrance to the one new Broadway hit, Dream Girls, boosted by raves in both the New York and London Times. Friends, more temperately, had told me I would find it entertaining but empty. They were wrong. Au fond 'Dream Girls' is serious. Its subject is the commercialisation of black music from Motown to disco; and it attempts an unusual density of treatment by reflecting this through half a dozen leading characters. These include a successful female trio called the Dreams, one of whom is cast out and spends a disproportionate amount of the action thereafter bewailing her disappointment in an extremely powerful blues voice.

Meanwhile the Dreams themselves remain shadowy, as do the other principals. The show roars sharply along for half an hour, establishing a milieu; then it loses its nerve and settles for the characters' love-lives. The score, supposedly parodic, offers several varieties of nothing; and the show, despite Michael Bennett's staging, sinks into boredom.

Not that Mr Bennett is short on coups; he can do much with the mere whisk of a curtain, and his basic set--an arrangement of lighting-towers and gantries, ceaselessly mobile--is a technical wonder. There are also two or three exciting dances; but on the whole Mr Bennett choreographs sets rather than people. I owe this phrase to John Heilpern's Times article; he and I differ radically as to whether it is a good thing.

records.title: Nine O'Clock laughter
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Not in Front of the Audience
Give Me Sunshine, Give Me Smiles
records.body:
Nine O'Clock laughter

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Not in Front of the Audience' at Drury Lane.

FEARFULLY we await the stage version of 'Over the Top.' Meanwhile the Not the Nine O'Clock News collection have gone flesh-and-blood with Not in Front of the Audience at Drury Lane. (Do they despise the theatre? Their television title was impeccably truthful; its stage equivalent is a flat lie.)

With 'Not' (etc.) Oxbridge comedy reverts to type, or at least to 'Beyond the Fringe.' Both shows ridicule public figures, not through any strong conviction, but just because they are there. (The public figures, I mean, not the performers, though it works with them as well.) The Fringies knew that the mere mention of C. P. Snow was funny; and 'Not' (and so on) knows the same about the Duke of Kent.

'That Was the Week That Was,' for all its opportunism, was more serious; its very presence on television, then the most cocooned of media, made it so. It had axes to grind, and it helped to topple a government. It used up its anger fast and became indistinguishable from its pale imitators.

The Monty Python team, the next innovators, reacted by forswearing explicit topicality, relying on imagination, whimsy and the breaking of taboos--which, politics and sex having already been commandeered, meant violence and death. Oh yes, and advertising. They consumed the territory, leaving 'OTT' to flail raucously and helplessly around and the atrociously smug 'Whoops Apocalypse' to rant dementedly as if the end of the world were such a self-evidently groovy subject that it made comic skills irrelevant.

Fitting in just ahead of this last crevasse are the crew of 'Not' (u.s.w.), purveyors of shock to the unshockable. When the TV series appeared at the Lane, they interleaved a re-run of favourite material; a cosy laugh-along. The new numbers have worked harder and, though they incorporate some recycled numbers, theirs is a real show. But they too are cosy. They scream at us, but their screams really go over our heads; we join them in mocking faceless, nameless conventionalists situated somewhere outside the theatre.

Compare Barry Humphries, the previous attraction, now prostrating himself on the road; when he picks on his audience, getting ladies on stage to cut up salads and barbecue steaks, he makes us quiver--partly because we could be next, partly because we recognise the ritual of instant stardom. It is the game-show phone-in routine taken to its extreme with Edna Everage, the housewife who got away, as both its exemplar and its celebrant.

The 'Not' quartet often imitate punk-rock groups; they enjoy the aggression, but they enjoy the send-up more. They don't, as the more fanciful Pythons did, mean business--or not often; they do say the last word on 'The Romans in Britain' by solemnly lowering respectable trousers and bending over. (What has the law to say to simulated simulated rape?)

They inhabit the same shrugging, showbiz-by-proxy world as the rest of us, presenting a papal visit as a massively sponsored production involving dance-routines and a blank pontifical performance of Mike Yarwood jokes. They issue cod fire-warnings over the PA system and offer Freddie Laker as the hero of an 'Evita' musical. They also realise the contribution of brand-names to the great old British tradition of the absurd; any word or object becomes surreal if you stay at it hard enough.

Rowan Atkinson as something from space outlines the differences between his civilisation and ours: "We have no death, no gravity; we have a different shaped gear-stick in our Mini Metro." This was my favourite number, though Mr Atkinson's great strength can seem out of place in a team-show; I remember whole TV episodes going by without finding much for him to do. Pamela Stephenson's mimetic and musical accomplishments still don't quite come together, but Griff Rhys-Jones keeps improving.

The most useful participant, though--as link-man, actor and co-director--is Mel Smith; Smith the slob and Rhys-Jones the juve-lead sometimes exchange roles, breaking down still further the ancient distinction between clown and straight-man. In modern comedy, as in modern life, everyone does both. In modern comedy, as in modern life, jokers write their own jokes; I am always mildly disappointed to find this lot, like so many politicians, relying wholly on other people's.

* * *

Some barriers remain impregnable. Michael Frayn's much-advertised failure to find a resolution for the hilarious backstage drama Noises Off (Savoy) suggests that he has barked his shins on one of them. The leading character--anyway the star-role--is a director, but the piece concerns dress-rehearsal, and performance, the period at which the director begins to disappear. Bringing him back on becomes increasingly difficult; rewriting the last minutes has not solved the problem.

This should bother future historians more than present audiences; once again, as in 'Donkeys' Years,' Mr Frayn moves easily from verbal comedy to physical farce; only this time he has been critically blessed, instead of cursed, for the transition. We learn slowly, but we learn. That both modes are firmly rooted in reality may be judged from the impeccable performances of Michael Blakemore's cast; their commitment extends not merely to the play-within-the-play (a sex farce that Mr Frayn must get round to completing some day), but to the programme-within-the-programme: each supplies a biography of his own character whose glosses on long periods of failure and unemployment could only be so feelingly parodied by adepts.

* * *

Not even C. P. Taylor's untimely death can obscure the fact that his characters habitually talked too much. In Give Me Sunshine, Give Me Smiles (Shaw) they assail the ears of a tolerant Geordie whom they finally drive to distraction. His own chats to the audience had much the same effect on me; when action threatens, he stops it in its tracks. Some lines are funny, most seem truthful, but the total is (a) too much and (b) not enough.

The visiting Tyne Wear Company perform efficiently; Rosalind Bailey is sharply alluring; Tim Healy is comfy as the recipient of everyone else's sexual recollection. Sometimes he remembers these memories, creating flashbacks within flashbacks. He commences the evening by making tea--high and Northern--for his womenfolk; a breakthrough for something or other. He attracts wholehearted sympathy when, in his greatest need, a whole parade of public telephones die on him.

The best 'La Ronde' yet is offered by Shared Experience at the Drill Hall. In Mike Alfreds's production even the costume-changes are stylish; as, with two actors dividing 10 roles, they had better be. Jonathan Hackett transfers amazingly well from unfeeling Soldier to primly adventurous Young Gentleman, though the older characters give him more trouble; Pam Ferris makes a commandingly seductive Actress, a trembling and perpetually virginal Housemaid, but her Sweet Girl comes across as a distinctly Tart Girl.

Though generally excelling the RSC's version in wit and honesty, they fall surprisingly short of it in the brutal restaurant scene: Comedy having been on my mind this week, let me recall that in 'The Tempest,' and especially in 'The Soldier's Fortune,' Arthur Lowe, who died last week, gave two of the funniest classical performances I have ever seen.

records.title: Bewitching Much Ado
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Bewitching Much Ado

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Stratford and London.

THE STAGE for Much Ado About Nothing (Stratford) is literally divided by a wall of perspex. There is a door cut in it, through which you may glimpse a couple of chairs. The effect is so dazzling that I thought at first I was seeing them in a mirror. The director, Terry Hands, does his own lighting, bathing the set in gold, then sepia, then gold again. The final fade-out leaves Beatrice and Benedick dancing and bantering in creamy-white, like the primal Fred and Ginger.

One of the best Astaire-Rogers pictures, 'Swing Time,' was originally to be called 'Never Gonna Dance'; the central conceit was the length of time it took to get the predestined pair into each other's arms. That is also the pattern of this production; the story of two wallflowers lured into the sun. (A red orb actually flames above them at the close.) The Messina they inhabit is one in which everybody else dances at the slightest provocation. Even old Leonato essays a few delighted steps when hearing of Don Pedro's victory. The minor villain Borachio, talking of 'what a deformed thief this fashion is,' suits action to words.

Thereby he clues us in to the more dangerous qualities of the play's surface: merriment. Claudio (Robert O'Mahoney) is the very essence of fashion, ready to woo Hero, reject her and regain her with equal sincerity and equal shallowness. There is a disturbing tinge of melancholy to Don Pedro's role and a quality which return Derek Godfrey to his best form: at the end, celibate and alone, he is as much an outcast as Jaques or Malvolio. Or as his own bastard brother, elegantly portrayed by John Carlisle; there is a real family likeness here, with both black-clad siblings taking a delight in plotting.

In this atmosphere it is not surprising that Derek Jacobi and Sinead Cusack should present Benedick and Beatrice as vessels of mutual detestation rather than affectionate raillery. The theory is fine, but the result is initially little fun. Mr Jacobi fares the better of the two; an experienced comedian, he can use his expertise to set off his rancour. The scene of his gulling is enlivened by a running gag concerning the boy who, sent to bring him a book, keeps returning with it at inopportune moments. (Mr Hands may be the first director ever to have found a rationale for this character.)

The protagonists have to wait for their flowering until the church scene, where--glowingly fitted out, like the whole company, in white glad rags--they find love as a reaction to their shared distaste for the world around them. There is a violent tension to this scene, sustained in Benedick's confrontation of his former friends, whose callousness is for once allowed full rein.

Terry Woods's Dogberry is similarly shown to be a bully as well as--or rather than--a clown; and there are charming glimpses of a laid-back pipe-smoker among the Watch. The last scene is a brilliant medley of moods, with the stars prolonging their brinkmanship to the end. This is not the funniest or most touching 'Much Ado' I have seen, but it is among the most intelligent; while in its trappings, Ralph Koltai's sets, Alexander Reid's cavalier costumes, Nigel Hess's music--it is in a bewitching class of its own.

* * *

Now for austerity. The Prince of Homburg might be the title for a play about the deputy drama critic of The Times, who has a dashing line in headgear. There is little dashing about the show at the Cottesloe. To suggest what is missing from it, let me quote the first stage direction of Kleist's text (James Kirkup's translation): 'Fehrbellin, a garden, in the old French style. In the background, a castle with a balustraded slope leading down from it. It is night. Early summer . . .' We then read of the Prince 'lying on a garden seat', 'half-sleeping under an oak-tree', plaiting himself a wreath. Other characters 'steal quietly out of the castle and look down upon the Prince from the balustrade.'

A modern production does not have to reproduce all those details, but it had better find suitable magical equivalents. John Burgess's production contrives an impressive grouping of spectators, but reduces setting to a bench and a nondescript backcloth.

Stripped of its dream elements, and of any sense of its Prussian nationalism being either challenged or confirmed, the play becomes a slow, bewildering melodrama about a military hero who leads an unauthorised cavalry charge like Sergius in Arms and the Man, but unlike him is subjected to imprisonment, sentence of death, and eventual pardon at the whim of an inscrutable Elector. We are given no reason to care; characters merely line up and say the words--in the case of Patrick Drury's Prince, with very little expression.

You might claim this to be a plain-text production, but how can that be true when Kleist's madness is missing? Whether it can ever be released in performance is another question. On the strength of this version and the one that opened the Royal Exchange (better-acted but visually a mess), I am inclined to doubt it. But I would be delighted to be proved wrong. Whatever the play is, it is not an earnest pre-Brechtian military chronicle. At one moment when we hear of the prince seeing his own grave--some power is released.

* * *

The best thing about Rents (Lyric Studio, Hammersmith) is that since writing it Michael Wilcox has gone on to other plays. It was first staged at the Edinburgh Traverse, and if I had seen it there I would probably have roared at the local jokes; even here, some of them still tickle. They are attached to the story of two part-time male prostitutes; one is otherwise engaged as a drama student, the other as a shop assistant. Into their joint orbit comes a college lecturer; just outside prowls a crazy queer-basher.

As a pattern of jealousy and violence emerges, we begin to realise that very little is happening that could not occur in heterosexual relationships; that we are in fact watching a thoroughly conventional play, chopped up in contemporary fashion into innumerable short scenes (plus monologues) which steer the play towards nothing but tedium. In Chris Parr's production, multiple playing-areas are handled with--for this director--amazing clumsiness.

* * *

There is more bottom-drawer reclamation in Stephen Lowe's Funny Pictures (Gate at the Latchmere), two one-act plays staged years ago by Alan Drury. The first brings Donald McGill postcard characters to life; to point the transition from old vulgarity to new porn: a bright and pertinent idea, but not, on this showing, capable of much development. The second goes back further for its nostalgia: to wartime Britain, where we meet a provincial cinema manager, his senior usherette, an aspiring junior and a GI.

Age attempts to get off with youth, with predictably disillusioning consequences. Mr Lowe seems steeped in the period, and though his elongated treatment invites tedium, his writing is mostly (not always) shrewd and sympathetic enough to avert it. The acting quartet is the same for both plays; but happier in the second, where Janet Dale has a good line in acerbic suffering.

records.title: Just Camp
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Just Camp

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

ROBERT DAVID MACDONALD'S Summit Conference (Lyric) is a Glasgow Citizens' play and production, fitted out with a couple of West End stars. Glenda Jackson appears as Eva Braun and Georgina Hale as Mussolini's mistress, Clara Petacci, in an antechamber done up in battleship grey and looking like a lofty mausoleum.

This set was designed by Philip Prowse, Glasgow's resident genius, who also directed; and one of its fascinations is the amount of massive detail it crams in while remaining spacious. Even the sofa is monumental, while the red-swastika cushions that adorn it are the embodiments of Nazi chic. The scene is Berlin, the date 1941: offstage, with the war going against them, Hitler and Mussolini are conferring.

Their ladies take tea, cakes and liquor, and then begin to squabble. They slide into the identities of their masters and exchange rancorous generalities about the character and the war-record of their respective nations. One of the stunning insights that emerges--at some length--from their debate is that Hitler used the Jews as a scapegoat. This seems to be the subject Mr Macdonald is working towards; in the second act the girls turn on an attendant soldier and tauntingly pretend first that he is a girl prostitute, second that he is a Jew. There is a flash of light and he steps out of character to tell us that death-camps are horrible.

George Steiner once remarked how sinister it was that "camp" had become a vogue word for a flippant semi-style. I thought at the time that he was being both over-obsessive and over-ingenious, but Mr Macdonald has unwittingly proved him right. His play is camp in its details (Eva and Clara turn out to be movie-buffs) and in its general effect; it is a humourless joke. You might respect a dramatist who tried to put Hitler and Mussolini directly on stage; however painfully he failed; to do it at this remove is merely to add a layer of titillation.

You never believe in these characters. Possibly you are not meant to and the ideas are the thing. But Mr Macdonald says nothing new, and says it aridly. The pedagogical tone is relieved--no; it's reinforced--by the occasional Lady Bracknellism (Eva to Clara: "I advise you to find a persecutable minority by Christmas at the latest."). As for the performances: Miss Hale survives through a prima-donna accent and a tottering high-heeled gait; Miss Jackson, having established Eva's commonplaceness, has nowhere to go. As a fan of the Citizens, I have to admit that this production is a fair example of their style. This is how their shows look, this is how Mr Macdonald writes. It's also how he translates; but when he can spill himself over a great and usually inaccessible script, the staged results--though with some of the same self-admiring flavour--are very different.

At one point Eva-Hitler says: "I've done more for the Jewish consciousness than anyone since Arthur Balfour." This, to give Mr Macdonald his due, is something one can just imagine Hitler saying. It is utterly different from the "defence" advanced in Mr Steiner's Portage to San Cristobal, whose whole point was to confront us with subtleties and horrible historical ironies out of the Fuhrer's mental range. Steiner challenged himself to keep his sense of the Holocaust as something uniquely horrible; and he succeeded. It was a necessary and honourable book for him to write, and the dramatised version--while adding nothing--preserved the essentials.

* * *

C. P. Taylor's Good (now at the Aldwych) is a believable, and theatrically ingenious, picture of a man stumbling into genocide, and is the one Taylor play that justifies its author's loquacity; its hero has to keep talking to stop from thinking. Both these works have absurdly been accused of trying to whitewash Nazism. Orwell once wrote that an atrocity is worse than an atrocity story; it actually happens. These words imply a grim test. Steiner and Taylor survive it. Summit Conference collapses giggling.

* * *

Nigel Williams's W.C.P.C. (Half Moon) is a farce about police, corruption and cover-ups, with a sideline in Gay Liberation. The two themes don't quite cohere, and in the finale, enjoyable in itself, the second gets clean away from the first. It is a strange play: that keeps threatening to collapse and then recovering. After the first five minutes you wonder if Mr Williams can have anything left to say after establishing that all coppers are bent, except for one necessary innocent who happens to be a bigot. He hasn't; but he keeps inventing, and even throws in a few really funny lines, though more would be welcome.

Oh yes, the title. The play treats of a subdivision of the Vice Squad detailed to haunt public lavatories in order to arrest men engaging in homosexual activities, but also indulging itself in said activities on a large scale. These are not the circumstances in which you would expect to find Robert Stephens giving one of the best performances of his life, but there it is, and there he is.

He seems newly jowly, playing a police commander who combines a voracious sexual appetite with a public-school sense of propriety. He functions as both tempter and tempted, a combination that allows Mr Stephens a double ration of double-takes, all executed with consummate authority. He has always been good at bewilderment; now he has weight as well. Pam Brighton's production is very racy.

* * *

Beth Henley's The Miss Firecracker Contest (Bush) is, though never staged there, very Louisville Festival: that is, it takes a loving look at a stretch of the American hinterland which it has peopled with eccentrics. A mild word that. Miss Henley actually runs to screwballs, loonies and--let us not mince words--nutcases. But then her territory is Mississippi, and her style is southern Gothic.

In the small town of Brookhaven the event of the year is a beauty contest.
