The belle of them all, of course, is Blanche DuBois, the heroine of Streetcar, who comes to her sister's New Orleans apartment, echoing to the sounds of jazz from the streets, weakly but valiantly upholding the flag of art, reeling from marriage to a homosexual, toying with the men who come her way until Stanley, her brother-in-law, ups and rapes her.

When Streetcar was revived in London in 1974, it seemed as full of quotations as Hamlet: "It's Della Robbia blue," "Sometimes there's God so quickly," "I have always depended on the kindness of strangers" -- the last a wonderfully moving plea as Blanche surrenders herself to the men from the mental hospital. Williams had a feeling for degradation which at this time was wholly compassionate. It may be that Streetcar drained him of what he had to say; though he arranged it more ambitiously, or at least more allegorically, in Camino Real, a flawed fantasy that preaches idealism while revelling in the gutter: a Spanish-American gutter (Williams was always a Hispanophile) that must be an irresistible lure to directors.

Streetcar was first presented in London in 1949 by a non-profit company exempt from entertainment tax; there was much fuss about the taxpayer's money being used (or at least rebated) for immoral purposes. Ludicrous as that now seems, Williams's later plays began to look like parodies of the sex-obsessed dramas he had been accused of writing.

Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, powerful in its day, now reeks of Southern Gothic and also of a homosexual writer's self-conscious attempts to grapple dramatically with heterosexual themes. These became increasingly strident, just as the titles -- Orpheus Descending, Sweet Bird of Youth, The Seven Descents of Myrtle -- became increasingly flowery. A sort of sadism crept in, the cruelty being piled on in direct ratio to the helplessness of the victims. It got more than Jacobean; there was cannibalism in Suddenly Last Summer, a poet dismembered by dogs in Orpheus.

Williams had always had talents for melodrama and farce; some of his later work became unconsciously farcical as the melodrama jumped out of control. But there were still surprising spurts of genuine humour. The Night of the Iguana was a notably benign work, and Vieux Carre, his last to be seen in London, revisited the scene of Streetcar in rambling autumnal mood.

In person Williams was an unpredictable but enthusiastic laugher; I once sat in front of him when he almost brought a performance at the Royal Court (of someone else's play) to a roaring standstill. He was also a fully paid-up paranoid. Kenneth Tynan has left an affectionate portrait of Williams preparing to meet Ernest Hemingway ("they tell me that Mr Hemingway usually kicks people like me in the crotch") and William Goldman wrote of him passing from the particular ("the reviewers don't like me") to the general ("I was not a well-liked kid"). Working, he said, was his escape, and he never let up.

The RSC wanted to do Sweet Bird last year, but say they were gazumped by Elizabeth Taylor. Either way we should see it soon. It was once dismissed as over-heated but our harsh climate is surprisingly favourable to hot-house art. We could be in for a Williams renaissance.

records.title: Living in the dark
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Living in the dark

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Glasgow

THERE are two plays going on in Crystal Clear (Wyndhams), which in a short show is remarkable and - since they don't get in one another's way - very good value. One is an informative account of the experience of blindness. Of all the afflictions recently examined on the stage, this is probably the one most suited to exploration in the theatre; the one most easily related to what the audience itself experiences.

There are three characters: Thomasina, who is blind; Jane, who can see; and Richard, a diabetic who loses his sight in the course of the action. The most electric moment comes after a scene between Thomasina and Richard; he is now blind, so obviously the light is off. Enter Jane, who switches it on. The audience, who have also grown accustomed to the gloom but still find it frustrating, blink.

Earlier we have watched a one-eyed Richard, trying to seduce Thomasina, bring her back to his flat and show her round. That may be an odd choice of phrase, in the circumstances, but it's how he behaves; he even hides the underwear that, being a born slob, he has left lying about. "What are your first impressions?" he asks. "It feels," she says, "very spacious."

The piece was evolved by its three actors, under the direction of Phil Young. They have uncovered extraordinarily fruitful territory; the opportunities for heartrending comedy are almost limitless. With remarkable tact they pass on to other ground. Richard and Jane are at the fag-end of a relationship. She wants commitment from him: failing that, confrontation. He will do anything - including, it seems, go blind - to avoid confrontation. What Richard wants is to be dependent, on his own terms: a neurosis which, allied here to great joky charm, lifts the play partially clear of the current rut of disability drama.

Does that sound grudging? The play is thoroughly honest but obstinately small, and the two qualities are interdependent. A row, here, is just a row; so baldly that Jane (Diana Barrett), meant to be caring but tactless, comes out bloody-minded. Anthony Allen's Richard is finely balanced between the attractive and the unforgiveable, and Philomena McDonagh gives Thomasina an aspect of serenity that the play finally shatters.

The shattering, though, is where the production falls shortest: when the two blind lovers lose their defences, we get two actors shouting at each other. But the piece pulls itself together, ending, with universally applicable bleakness, as a picture of love trying to shut out the dark. Images like that seem impossible to avoid. The play vibrates with them. Jane says to Richard, "I'm fed up with a relationship where we never see each other." Intentionally or not, it rings.

* * *

I don't know why Michael Wilcox wrote Lent (Lyric Studio, Hammersmith), but I'm glad he did. He tells of a boy being 13 in 1956; as Mr Wilcox was himself, and as I was. Greedily I lapped up the references: Journey into Space, the Goons, The Cruel Sea (cadet edition), the Jennings books, Ainsworth's antiquated Old St Paul's borrowed from the school library and cherished for its horrific bits. Only the local cinema bothered me, showing The Crimson Pirate and Captain Horatio Hornblower; but maybe they were revivals, shrewdly programmed for school holidays.

Our orphaned hero spends these holidays at school; he has to, since his grandmother owns it, or at least holds it in trust for him. This is one of a series of puns supporting the temporal title. The boy starts by "borrowing" a starting pistol. "Don't be foolish, Paul," says his headmaster, temporarily misleading us as to the kind of play we're getting into, "hand over the gun."

The headmaster is a narrow man, but he is also a disappointed one, and Dennis Edwards makes him comprehensible and almost sympathetic: ditto Jean Anderson as his peremptory wife, who lets murder stories go to her head. Grandma, whom they simultaneously fear and despise, gives Patience Collier her best, and best taken, opportunity for years: dignified and probably wise. An assistant master, Paul's confidant, is given an enchantingly easygoing performance by Wensley Pithey: beset, like all the adults, by a long consciousness of failure, but transmuting it into autumnal avuncularity.

The play, indeed, has some of the shock-effect of 84 Charing Cross Road; everybody in it is decent. This even applies to Paul, played without embarrassment (high praise for a grown-up) by Jonathan Kent. I can't see that it is about anything more than the delayed consequences of having been born in 1943. I think that's a superb subject, but I'm biased.

* * *

The Custom of the Country (Citizens', Glasgow) written in 1619 by Fletcher and Massinger, is the most improbable play I have ever seen. The custom is a droit du seigneur; to escape it, two heroes and a heroine rush off to Lisbon, where they are separated, and meet with many strange and sexy adventures.

One fellow becomes the prey of a rich nymphomaniac; his ruttish brother is employed as a stud in a brothel for ladies. Both get exhausted. There are also duels and potions. After five acts have elapsed the play stops.

This kind of purely narrative, purely titillating drama stopped being written when the theatre ceased to be a mass medium. It passed, of course, to the cinema; accordingly Robert David Macdonald, directing, and Michael Levine, designing, have set it in Hollywood, or at least have peopled it with movie archetypes. After an outrageously drab prologue we pass to a land full of pink furniture, lit by studio lamps.

Guiomar (Jill Spurrier), a predatory matron, is Gloria Swanson in Sunset Boulevard; Duarte (Rupert Farley), her braggart son, is Mickey Mouse, complete with tail; Zabulon (Ron Donachie), the sinister Jew, is Sydney Greenstreet; and Hippolyta (Fidelis Morgan) sounds like Mae West, but looks like Jean Harlow; whichever, her entrance, acknowledging applause and clutching an Oscar, had me laughing very loud. The melodrama can be played full out, and the occasional genuine emotion can quite unexpectedly register.

The less lovable side of the Citizens' is also on show. Heavy cuts become, by the end, cavalier and confusing; and whatever became of the funniest line, a ruffian's declaration that he is always available for a murder, but he's out of practice at beating? More serious is a pervasive misogyny that delights in leaving all the women frustrated, and plays the plight of the knackered gigolo (Lorcan Cranitch) not for laughs against him, but for horror of the predatory female sex. Still, where else?

* * *

Clare Davidson's production of Miss Julie (Duke of York's) is much the most lucid I have seen, particularly in its marking off of the social and sexual components in the confrontation of lady and servant. Stephen Rea as Jean lets us see every calculation, every spasm of lust, every pang of fear. Cheryl Campbell, tresses flaming, is audacious to a fault, sounding as if she has wound herself up in the wings, and doesn't dare let go. Occasionally she touches ground and is great, but she is in danger of acting herself into a corner.

records.title: Half-cock Heartbreak
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Half-cock Heartbreak

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Shaw at the Haymarket.

IT would be nice if the classical programme at the Haymarket had managed to include one play that had not previously been done by the National Theatre. The management might have done themselves a service as well as us; unfortunate comparisons were bound to be made, never more than in the new production of Heartbreak House, which, with Captain Shotover at its helm and his nautical house as its setting, seems fair to describe as the flagship of the season.

John Schlesinger directed this play, to great admiration, in the National's last days at the Old Vic; and I feel, after all this time, like apologising to him. I stated then that, given a good enough cast (and this play always attracts stars), no director could go wrong with Heartbreak House; the luminaries, all having their moments, would automatically arrange themselves into an ensemble governed by the English sense of fair play, and Shaw's text, self-orchestrating, would do the rest. John Dexter's production is here to confute me. It is cast to the nines and it is no disaster, but it falls continually short.

His actors rarely connect with one another, and the play disperses into a series of random conversations, which themselves sometimes become collections of random remarks. I now see that for the whole thing to come together, and to make patterns in the mind, some kind of confidence trick has to be worked.

Shaw gives the hint by insisting on a thick and rambling setting, and by beginning romantic comedy; Jocelyn Herbert's ascetic design kills its atmosphere almost at first glance, besides denying the actors effective entrances. It improves in the second act when curtains are drawn, and even more in the third when the action moves outside, but by then the damage has been done.

It is compounded by Rex Harrison's performance as Shotover. He has some perfectly timed deflationary throwaways, and he rises to the prophetic moments, but in the middle ground of the role he offers only mildly eccentric geniality. There is no iron in him; and we disbelieve not only the captain's seafaring past, but his despairing present. Shotover talks of "the horror of an old man drinking," but we feel no horror here. It should represent Shaw's terror of his own decay; if that is absent, the play becomes very complacent.

Of course it is an attack on the governing and intellectual classes of the First World War, but that assault is less comprehensive than is often supposed, and unless the author is personally involved, it is of little interest. Anyone can satirise other people.

On the first night Mr Harrison was uncertain of his lines (he destroyed Shotover's first good joke and his last great cry) and slow on his cues; and the second fault was even more alarming than the first. It defused the tension of the air-raid, otherwise the best of the production, with Doris Hare's nurse turned to a harpy exulting over the dead.

En route there are other lightweight performances: note Rosemary Harris's Ariadne, professional but subdued, and Frank Middlemass's capitalist Mangan, pleasant enough, but too unassuming to be worth bringing down. Paul Curran, another actor afflicted with uncertainty, nevertheless brings great quizzical force to the gentle Mazzini; Simon Ward is a public schoolboy spoiled for life as Randall the rotter; Mel Martin, though too old for the virginal role, goes a fine disillusioned progress as Ellie.

The flamboyant Hector is done by Paxton Whitehead, an actor to whom extravagance comes natural; only his Act Two invocation, "fall and cease," is underdone. On which note, it is ingenious to have the personnel singing the blues for the incantation that ends the previous act, but the effect is to make the words sound as much like doggerel as they look.

There remains, thankfully, Diana Rigg's Hesione, which combines gypsyish beauty, moon-faced comic attack and an honest, unembarrassed audience rapport. Miss Rigg is a rarity - an apparently unselfish personality performer. But Shaw needs - and used almost automatically to get - star performances thoroughly fused. The recent National Major Barbara gave us the fusion without the stars; this offers the reverse. Neither is enough.

* * *

La Fianza Satisfecha is the play, conjecturally by Lope de Vega, which John Osborne once adapted as A Bond Honoured. As The Outrageous Saint, it now arrives at the Grove, Hammersmith, unadapted but not quite unashamed. In some ways the Stage Fright company's approach is more perverse than Mr Osborne's. He found a play he could not stomach and rewrote it, chiefly by denying repentance to the central character.

This is Leonido, a Sicilian blade who rapes his sister, blinds his father and is probably not above ringing the church bell when everybody is trying to sleep. Like Satan, Cain, Don Juan and Faust (there is, incidentally, a play called Don Juan and Faust by the German romantic Grabbe, and I want to see it), he gets a divine comeuppance, and ends crucified and repentant.

Mr Osborne kept the crucifixion, but not the development, which was odd; Gub Neal's production keeps both, but signals its disbelief in them, which is odder, especially since the play plainly has the courage of its convictions and communicates them powerfully. I see the problem, but I cannot officially approve of the solution, nor in any capacity of the musical interludes, even if it is fun to hear a Moorish maiden sing country-and-western.

However, staging and performance are far above the level we addicts usually endure when seeking neglected texts in neglected venues. John Lyne Pirkis acts Leonido as a baffled biker; the others, including several women playing men and playing them well, portray his opponents as deserving everything they get. His conventionally conventional servant is changed to a sceptical harlequin (or columbine), but what else would you expect? Some day - not necessarily tomorrow, since there are other Spanish plays to be attended to - I want to see this work done straight.

* * *

The Soho Poly last week harboured two plays advertised as about radio, and full of static. The first, Nature of Communication, was sketchy; the second, World Service, protracted. They're off now anyway.

records.title: Florentine intrigues
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Florentine intrigues

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Oxford.

I GRUMBLED recently about the National Theatre's weakness for small-cast plays, but the British premiere of Lorenzaccio (Olivier) does a lot to balance the books. I counted 45 actors' names in the programme, and most of them are doubling. It is a gladsome spectacle and surprisingly easy to keep track of.

Alfred de Musset wrote this Renaissance extravaganza in 1832, and its prodigality has two traceable causes: (a) he and his compatriots had just found out about Shakespeare, and felt liberated; (b) precociously disillusioned with the theatre at the age of 23, Musset gave no thought to practicalities. His text has as many scenes as this production has players.

Lorenzaccio is a denigratory nickname bestowed on Lorenzo de Medici, young cousin of the equally young Duke of Florence. Tyrannicide is his mission in life, and he becomes the ruler's confidant and procurer, so as to get within sword's reach of him.

He gives Florence the chance to become a republic again, a chance Florence - through a combination of clerical intrigue, military intimidation and popular apathy - fails to take. In this, we are assured, Musset saw the reflection of his own society, the bourgeois monarchy of Louis Philippe.

He stakes everything on his protagonist, and wins. Lorenzo has been described as a modern Hamlet, but in fact he is never in doubt about whether to murder. He more resembles Hamlet's Jacobean successors, the cankered sensualists, critical appraisers of their own degradation.

Lining up a female relative for the ducal bed, he more or less re-enacts 'The Revenger's Tragedy.' He feels himself unworthy of his destiny because he has been corrupted, not by his revenge, but by its preparation. He has been the duke's accomplice, so, except as a kind of suicide, his deed is ethically meaningless. It turns out to be politically meaningless as well.

It is a fragile, skin-deep world we are presented with, alive to sensation, but to little else. Its hero, embodying it, gives unity to a sprawling canvas.

It is, in the best sense, a lightweight play, and one informed by a lazy whimsicality very much of its period. In the original - not, unfortunately, in John Fowles's adaptation - we hear of Lorenzo 'spitting into a well to make circles in the water: my greatest pleasure.' That may be camouflage, but it also sums up the play and the character.

One of Lorenzo's pranks is striking off the heads of statues; and one he seems to have decapitated - unknown to art historians - is Michelangelo's 'David.' At any rate, there it is when we enter the Olivier, its head on the ground, but still dominating John Gunter's set, and there it remains. I suppose it is possible that the National imported the original from Florence and dropped it, but it seems more likely that we are being offered a metaphor.

The statue sprouts scaffolding, and a stonemason - who appropriates the citizenry's most defiant lines - spends the evening on it, trying to put Humpty Dumpty together again. He never does succeed.

The stage is patrolled - Florence being a fief of the German empire - by guttural soldiers with gutterish manners. These devices are heavy-going but effective, and this is true of Michael Bogdanov's production in general. It has no special imagination, and the abrupt endings to the brief scenes often leave it with egg on its face; actors stomp off or stay to move the furniture. But it has plenty of guts and energy, and these are the immediate requirements.

Later productions may add in subtlety, but they are not likely to improve on the bloodbath Mr Bogdanov offers at the climax. His casting in the higher reaches is, shall we say, unsurprising: Michael Bryant as wronged honest man and grieved father, Basil Henson as smooth cardinal. Lower down there is a lot of backslapping, more verbal than physical; Mr Fowles's version may not be virtuoso prose, but it deserves finer tuning than it gets here. Frances Viner pummels her way through the moral qualms of the duke's mistress, and she is one of the better ones.

The duke himself is more a condition than a person and Clive Arrindell leaves him that way. Everything rests on Greg Hicks as Lorenzo and he, if lacking in mischief, gives a very clear picture of a disgusted spirit. The play makes sense, grips attention, and smells of immortality.

* * *

Second billing in Marilyn! (Adelphi) goes to a character called the Era, who sings at the close: 'Write your books and write your plays and try to capture her in your songs/I'm the one to whom the girl belongs.' This, preceded by a brilliantly engineered montage of Monroe clips, decisively trumps the show itself: they say one cannot capture Marilyn Monroe on the stage, and we believe them.

To do it, they upstage their own star, Stephanie Lawrence, which is unfair. She acts well, dances splendidly, sings superbly: the last without the self-congratulatory air generally assumed by British musical starlets when they hold a high note. She cannot capture the original's sexuality, but it is a condition of the myth on which the show trades that nobody could.

As an actress Miss Lawrence is at her best before the fall, growing up in an orphanage, marrying teenage, switching off the radio which is only announcing something about Pearl Harbour. As Tom Stoppard might have phrased it, she wasn't Marilyn then; the script is happier with Norma Jean. Once in Hollywood it accelerates through the familiar biography, leaving by default the impression that Marilyn consciously created her own image. If she was that much in control, why did she go to pieces?

Meanwhile one ticks off the echoes, some of them probably accidental: 'West Side Story,' bopping at the prom; 'Annie,' an orphanage and two dogs; 'Sweeney Todd,' a crazy mother; 'Fiddler on the Roof,' a Jewish wedding, courtesy of Arthur Miller; above all 'Evita': distant but omnipresent narrator, media heroine and the experience of being told nothing you did not already know.

Also the form, pop eclecticism with the bits joined together to make a kind of opera. As such, it is a smoother job than 'Evita'; the music may not be distinguished, and the lyrics less than, but they do link up persuasively, sped on their way by Larry Fuller's very tidy staging, which incorporates a couple of fine ensemble numbers, including a dance by adoring males gazing at the famous nude calendar: the one time the show makes a real musical-comedy statement. Bill Byers's orchestrations resound with nervous energy, though the music may be what they are nervous about.

* * *

The Oedipus Plays (Oxford Playhouse) should really be called the Creon plays; he is the one character common to 'Oedipus the King,' 'Oedipus at Colonus' and 'Antigone,' the Sophoclean trio (not trilogy) here combined by Stephen Spender. Arthur Cox plays him as a pot-bellied politician who never dared hope for kingship and is over-assertive when he gets it. Having made his fatal mistakes, he exits moaning 'blind, blind,' thus linking up of course with Oedipus, who puts out his own eyes (and starts the proceedings by announcing that he has come 'to see'), and Tiresias, the sightless prophet.

If this strikes you as facile, I would not argue with you. All three plays are done as bold political melodrama, the last right, the first tight but bafflingly cheapened, and the middle one incomprehensible. Richard Durden as Oedipus maintains his actor's dignity whatever may have been done to his character; Moira Redmond is a smooth and powerful Jocasta; and the choruses seem out of place.

* * *

Vanbrugh's The Provoked Wife (Warehouse) is the best of the three ATC productions I have seen: a sane, bitter view of sex, marriage and divorce. Lady Fancyfull, a spoiled beauty, is serenely played as a frump, but Christine Braddell's Lady Brute is a treasure, an actress more provoking (never mind provoked) drawing her clothes on than many are taking them off.

records.title: Bits of Bradshaw
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Bits of Bradshaw

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Howard Barker's new play at the Royal Court.

There is a current form of play that proceeds by seizing a small historical moment, and imagining around it. An example is Howard Barker's Victory (Royal Court), which begins with the exhumation of John Bradshaw.

Bradshaw was president of the judges who condemned Charles I to death; at the restoration of Charles II he was one of those whose corpse was dug up, gibbeted and exhibited. Bradshaw's wife, or widow, is the central character of this play. Described in text and programme simply as Bradshaw--either for feminist reasons or because Mr Barker did not want to remind us of the Mrs Bradshaw who featured so prominently in early soap-powder commercials--she goes through the play searching for the remains of her severed spouse.

By the end she has assembled all the bits, including the head: a collectors' piece, since the current monarch has been using it as a mascot. Bradshaw's quest thus serves dramatically as a means of bringing disparate characters together. This is Mr Barker's shapeliest play; his penultimate scene is as comprehensive a reunion as could be found outside a Shakespearean epiphany or a pantomime finale: less cheerful though.

Apart from Bradshaw and the monarch (Sellar and Yeatman laid it down that Charles II, being merry, was less a King than a Monarch, and Mr Barker's Charles likes it that way) those present include the founder of the Bank of England, a semi-discarded royal mistress, a court poet, a cashiered Cavalier bully who has spent the play in lubricious pursuit of Bradshaw, the atheistic Puritan who has accompanied her on her flight, and her long-lost son, a medic now specialising lucratively in venereology. They make up a ripe slice of post-revolutionary old England: a state-of-the-nation play in wigs.

Victory is Bondishly subtitled Choices in Reaction. Main title and sub are both, of course, loaded with puns. There is the royalist victory, which leads to acts of revenge on dead bodies and a reign of terror against the living carried out by pox-ridden old soldiers. There is Bradshaw's victory in coming through this landscape with herself, if not her husband, in one piece. There is her reaction to her situation, which is to keep her head down and her pockets, where possible, full; and there is that of her male companion, who blunders outspokenly into martyrdom, but happens to be consumed by guilt at having revealed the dead leveller's grave in the first place.

Bradshaw thinks this man is a fool, and she is probably right. Her own course is not heroic, but it is not despicable either, and any blame can be attached to the times rather than to her. Some of her actions may be reactionary; as are certainly those of the king, trying to hang on to his prerogative, and of the new financiers, trying to limit it. Reactionary of course meaning right-wing; by what romantic-semantic convention do we accept that the left never reacts to anything?

A primal banking conference is cartooned in Mr Barker's best brand of deadly knockabout, and he is very good on sex: from Charles's compulsive fumblings to Bradshaw's enforced composure after rape to her assailant's disappointment: 'I come off so miserable. I think love would be to come off and be happy.' That is the best moment in the play. On the other hand Charles's melancholia is over-extended, and his courtiers are grotesques assembled so that the author can tell us at length how grotesque they are.

The movement from one set piece to another tends to be clotted. But the dialogue can be off-handedly funny and is modern without obvious anachronism. Continual expletives do a lot to link the two periods, though I had an old-maidish sympathy with the odd character who wished they would stop from time to time. Bradshaw, in this Joint Stock production, provides a superb role for Julie Covington, who excels in commonsense and bewilderment, the last reserved for people--the majority--who do not see the world as clearly as she does. Also notable are Eleanor David as two strumpets and a maid, David Lyon and Kenny Ireland. Nearly everyone in fact.

Clegg, Mr Barker's poet, says that he has written a tragedy and been promised production 'for what a promise is worth, not a lot in the theatre.' That little in-joke gets us to Michael Rudman's Short List (Hampstead), which is about the deliberations of a committee judging a playwriting award apparently modelled on that given annually in memory of George Devine. At least, the Harry whom this one commemorates, and whom the characters obsessively remember, was a producer much given to encouraging new talent.

His heirs are a shifty but engaging bunch: rather frightening emblems of the radical impulse gone prosperous, and furious at the idea of rebellion going on without them, and clutching a young writer yearly to their collective breast as a prophylactic. A young male playwright who turns up and insults them (they interview candidates as well as reading their plays, which seems a daft idea) is obviously one of their sort; a shy, resentful female playwright is obviously not. Morally, if in no other way, she has the last laugh.

I got a great deal of pleasure merely out of trying to identify the characters. Three I was certain of; and even if I am wrong, it's too late now, I've had my fun. Mr Rudman's prowess at keeping a stageful of characters verbally active and alive should not be underestimated, even if at times he coasts on bitching. He did not direct the play; Mike Ockrent did, with a wonderful cast.

He has Ian McKellen, fur-coated and duffel-bagged as an international director of carefully cultivated feyness; Bernard Hill nearly stealing the show as an acidic exhibitionist; Philip Voss as a cheery old academic, patient except when he loses his temper; Glyn Owen as a professional northern minimalist ('I challenge you to read my play as quickly as I wrote it'), who jerks laughter every time he brusquely breaks a sullen silence; Maxine Audley as Harry's gracious female relict and spiritual executrix; Susan Engel up from the country; Michael J. Jackson about whom I can think of nothing to say, which is not his fault; and Barbara Flynn who takes the whole thing down in shorthand. Towards its close the play says something about success. And it is no more incestuous than Mr Barker's play. It merely comes from a different family.

Romantic Comedy (Apollo) by Bernard Slade also looks inward. Fearing himself to be old fashioned, Mr Slade shows us two playwrights who have a similar problem and probably write the same sort of play. Note the tiny defiance of the title. The collaborators are Pauline Collins, odd accent but fine presence, as an innocent, and Tom Conti, whose croaky presence as a sophisticate makes the thing look more than ever like They're Playing Our Song, retitled They're Doing Our Play. I cannot lie: I wanted to see if they would end up together, and I laughed sometimes. But the humour, like everything else, is thinly derivative.

Last week, reviewing The Provoked Wife, I invented an actress called Christine Braddell. She is Valerie Braddell: I portmanteaued her with Christine Bishop, who is also in it. Both, in excuse, are charmers.

records.title: Caesar in double focus
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Caesar in double focus

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN
on Shakespeare and Saroyan at Stratford.

Ron Daniels's production of Julius Caesar, which opened the new Stratford season last week, has great immediacy. Much of its attraction is visual. Farrah's designs for the battle scenes of the second half -- a muddy place for men to die in -- are dark without being dispiriting. Ann Curtis has invented a high Roman fashion, and a becoming one; she has put all the men into red jerkins, signifying empire and blood. When the conspirators pay their nocturnal call on the insomniac Brutus, he stands white-gowned against their scarlet, ironically Christ-like; which is rather how they see him, and how he sees himself.

The most public scenes we watch in double focus: in actuality, and on a giant telescreen. I could live without this, but it does allow us to contrast the boom of rhetoric with the nervous tics of the boomers. It is particularly appropriate with the opaque character of Caesar, dominantly played by Joseph O'Conor, obviously able, possibly megalomaniac, certainly miffed when allowed to refuse the crown. He has bought himself a young wife (Lesley Duff, very comely), whom he lectures affectionately on fear of death.

The justification for killing him is canvassed in the programme by selected politicians. Harold Wilson says no, and seems shocked anyone asked the question. Michael Foot says yes, by all means, and adds romantically that Shakespeare meant Cassius to be the hero; Emrys James does actually play him Welsh (well, he would), but not at all romantic. Neil Kinnock says no, are you kidding, by that bunch; and the production seems to be on Mr Kinnock's side.

Mr O'Conor has his foibles, but he is nicer than Mr James, who plays Cassius, well, for envy rather than misguided patriotism; it is he, not Brutus, who strikes the last blow, and he seems to enjoy it. What is endearing about him is the weariness that overtakes him; he is dog-tired in the quarrel scene, while Brutus still has the energy for righteous indignation.

A bearded looker, used to adulation, Peter McEnery worries his way conscientiously through Brutus's self-questionings, coming infallibly up with the wrong answers. Lecturing the crowd, his hand pedantically cupping his chin, he is in his element, though he would never admit it.

This is a more sympathetic Brutus than John Wood's celebrated expose of a liberal ('liberal' being one of those words, like 'middle-class' and 'English,' used scornfully by critics and playwrights to whom they all apply) and therefore more appropriate to the play, one of whose donnees is that people, not all of them self-seekers, like Brutus.

At the end he goes throaty, tired either by life or by the verse. The latter is a constant problem. Antony these days is always under-cast. It should be possible to find a youngish actor who can handle rhetoric; and he doesn't have to be that young. He is Brutus's and Cassius's contemporary, not Octavius's. David Schofield, shock-headed, does not look like an experienced reveller, but at least he lets us appreciate Antony's strategy. He brings Caesar's widow along as Exhibit A, getting the mob to weep before they even hear the will.

John Dicks, an actor I have much admired with Shared Experience, seems lost in this company, and is the only unfunny Casca I have known. But the conspirators are generally well differentiated. Metellus Cimber, who keeps suggesting safety precautions, is played very nervous; the actor, Paul Mooney, seems to have a gift for this sort of thing, since he subsequently gives us a nervously assertive Young Cato.

There are also some welcome old stagers: Gemma Jones a fine Portia who shows us the wound in her thigh (very nasty); Oliver Ford-Davies who doubles in the programme as helpful Roman historian, and as the Soothsayer, with the prescribed voice 'shriller than all the music'; Griffith Jones, who has made a corner in prophets. His scene with Portia is a collector's item.

* * *

Lorenz Hart asked, 'Will Saroyan ever write a great play?' He won't now, he's dead; and he didn't then, but The Time Of Your Life (Other Place, Stratford) is the nearest he came. Another lyricist, E. Y. Harburg, said that 'in fact he's damned annoyin', Saroyan.' He was roguishly saluting a fellow spirit; Harburg was professedly radical, Saroyan professedly apolitical, but they both wrote whimsically satiric celebrations of America.

In this play a pinball fanatic beats the machine and is rewarded by a pop-up American flag. The system may be rotten; the country is great. The hero and governing spirit is Joe, who claims to have grown rich, like all rich men, on the backs of the poor; but neither he nor his creator seem very worried by it. He makes everything come right, and the one unpleasant character is disposed of. If you accuse the play of sentimentality, it would admit the accusation, proudly.

It is set in a bar. That is the secret. We enjoy watching the actors enjoy playing an uncross section of drifters and dreamers; the last important, since the play is a sweet, upbeat equivalent of The Iceman Cometh. Both plays were written, obviously independently, in 1939; and there are parallelisms between nearly all the characters.

Daniel Massey gives a fluent, governing performance as Joe; John Thaw is rock-solid behind his bar; Zoe Wanamaker, mobile-featured, introduces suffering as the San Francisco whore Joe turns into a lady; Paul Greenwood spins like a top as her lover and Joe's gofer; Henry Goodman clowns and dances as a performer the play claims to be great and terrible at the same time.

The one heavy is too light, but the miniature roles of two posh intruders are perfectly done by Christopher Neame and Caroline Harris. The amount of good acting going on in this confined space is nearly immoral. Howard Davies directed, in a more than real set by Bob Crowley.

records.title: Every inch, a King
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Every inch, a King

ROBERT CUSHMAN,
our theatre critic,
writes about Olivier's
Lear on television.

Laurence Olivier as King Lear (Channel 4, last Sunday) made me cry. I did not expect this. In theory, Lear is the most moving play ever written, but recent stage productions, trying to be tough, have paid more attention to terror than to pity. So, in my memory, has Olivier, about whom I, like many people under 40, have had something of a block. Unlike Gielgud and Richardson, he has always needed to impersonate. The necessity apparently wrecked his stage Lear of 1946.

Well, he was a young man then. His position now, a heroic theatre actor confined to films and television, parallels Lear's after his abdication. A mischievous awareness of this informed his whole performance. The division of the kingdom was an impressive charade; he took delight in appearing a little plaintive, less the magnificent monarch than we or his court had expected. The protestations of his elder daughters fed his humour hugely; when Cordelia refused to play, he took it at first as another stage in the game. 'Nothing will come of nothing' was -- as surely it must be -- a joke.

Sometimes he was too arch, employing the clipped, mincing tones that have been part of his armoury, I suppose, since Richard III. Some lines came out equipped with three separate cesuras; and some, including his first, just came out wrong. (The errors don't matter; the attendant unease does.) And yet once the crown was laid down, and there was no more profit to Lear in playing the dodderer, the bewilderment at his false position was very powerful.

He seemed on more intimate terms with this drama than with any other in which I have seen him. Unusually you can feel him quizzically testing a text, to see if it will bear his weight. This one he seemed confident in. 'Let me not be mad' brought him up short and terrified, with no forcing of the point; he could creep up on the curse to Goneril, as if he too was surprised by it. (She was devastated).

The storm scenes suffered, as such always do on television, from sheer lack of volume, though Olivier avoided the usual attempted solution of tense muttering. It was the scene on Dover cliffs with the blind Gloucester that woke him to magnificence. His mind almost visibly wandered, but each cruel paradox it seized on ('Handy-Dandy, which is the justice, which is the thief') was brilliantly lucid. He would begin small ('Behold, yon simp'ring dame') and would never rant at a climax, but by the time he reached it ('There's damnation'), you, like Gloucester, were seeing with his eyes.

And he was every inch a king; Leo McKern as Gloucester shuffled towards him with the duty that a very fine actor pays to a great one. Their duet was, literally, breathtaking. The weeping began in the reconciliation with Cordelia, gently played from beneath a Blakean expanse of white flowing hair. As for the last scene over Cordelia's corpse, 'How, how, how, how' was in the great line of Olivier cries; 'Pray you, undo this button' was as moving, as unexpected, as we have always been told it should be. It was the promised end.

I cannot hold Olivier solely accountable for my tears. Chief accessory was Anna Calder-Marshall, who, as Cordelia, made us see the reconciliation through her streaming eyes. (She was beautifully supported by Paul Curran as the Doctor; so tiny a role can seldom have been so feelingly played.) Casting Miss Calder-Marshall, an actress who seems to believe in goodness and is capable of embodying it, was an earnest of Michael Elliott's intentions as director. Most productions are self-conscious about Cordelia, or try to play her as an arrogant chip off the old block.

Witness, too, Mr Elliott's emphasis on Edmund's last-minute (and quite unavailing) repentance, and his treatment of the servant who protests at the blinding of Gloucester. This heartening intervention cannot be cut, since it is vital to the plot, but most directors obviously wish it wasn't there, and hurry it into oblivion. Mr Elliott lingered over the man's challenge to his master Cornwall, and over his own death at the hands of Regan: we watched her slowly walk up to him and stab him in the back.

The production was far from perfect. It was nearly sabotaged by obtrusive and old-fashioned music (a distant echo of the Walton scores for Olivier's films) telling us what was meant to be sinister and what was meant to be sad. But even this turned out to have a negative virtue; when Shakespeare's own music arrived -- I don't mean the poetry, I mean the accompaniment he calls for in Cordelia's tent -- it sounded positively healing. (It is, textually, what the doctor ordered.)

Again, setting the opening in the middle of Stonehenge seemed to throw us back to the days of Donald Wolfit; it was odd of Lear to give his kingdom away in so uncomfortable a place. But when we returned there for the last scene, we did feel -- again as demanded -- that the wheel had come full circle. In the quieter of the intervening scenes there was a rewarding and appropriate stress on the natural world, vegetable and animal; Lear rode a horse and, in his madness, skinned a rabbit. It provided a basis for the production's final ascent into symbolism -- a long fight between Edgar in white and Edmund in black -- which the vigorous performances of David Threlfall and Robert Lindsay kept from appearing merely misty.

Indeed the star cast justified their employment. If they were there in tribute to Olivier, the feeling showed, most of all, in Colin Blakely's Kent, the only one I have seen to suggest that the disguised ex-nobleman does not much enjoy standing around in the mud being insulted, and one of the few to justify his promotion to chorus at the end: his 'break heart, I prithee break' had the force of the whole play behind it. The Fool (John Hurt) made less impact than usual -- there seemed a determined effort not to let him steal the show -- but Geoffrey Bateman's Oswald was oily insolence personified.

There was both union and contrast in the neurotic villainy of Dorothy Tutin's Goneril and the bold amorality of Diana Rigg's Regan, as too in their husbands: Jeremy Kemp's Cornwall, goaded to compete with his wife in brutality, and Robert Lang an Albany who went from ineffectual -- padding through the opening scene as if he feared he had come to the wrong ancient monument -- to regal, with a gladdening moment when he recognised in Edgar the true avenger.

I asked myself when I had last been made so potently aware of the metaphysical in Shakespeare, and thought back to the eight lovers responding to the trumpet call of Hymen at the end of Mr Elliott's As You Like It: the Vanessa Redgrave one. That, beautifully recaptured on television, was originally a stage production; and by so much more complete.

Though there were occasional pieces of technical virtuosity this time -- the interpolated arrest of Gloucester and the camera's approach to the outhouse through a hole in the roof -- TV can never be a wholly satisfying medium for Shakespeare. But it can sometimes point a way for stage production: An Age of Kings did it 20 years ago, and Mr Elliott's direction did it here. It made recent theatre endeavours -- including some I have applauded myself -- seem cynical, stupid, whiz-kidding.

records.title: National Bath-night
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
National Bath-night

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on The Rivals, two Shakespeare productions and a musical.

The stage of the Olivier is now wholly occupied by John Gunter's cityscapes. Surpassing his Florence (Lorenzaccio) and almost equalling his New York (Guys and Dolls) is his Bath. Even today the town looks like a set for The Rivals; Mr Gunter has reproduced it so faithfully, but so imaginatively, that to enter the theatre is to feel as though you have just got off the train from Paddington.

Black and white crescents turn into black and white drawing-rooms and coffee houses, incidentally marking out a semi-circular acting area that is spacious but comfortable. Robert Bryan's lighting takes us meticulously through the single day of the play's action, and lays on a particularly ravishing sunset. Peter Wood directs with his usual accumulation of wit, clarity and showmanship; also with the modicum of restructuring and rewriting he usually affords to old comedies. There are double-entendres that cannot be found in the standard editions.

Some of the jokes have been spruced up, Mrs Malaprop being allowed ('ah, Sir Anthony, men are all Bavarians') a final malapropism. If ever a performance deserved to go out with a bang, it is Geraldine McEwan's as a precieuse a little unsure of her own pretensions. Suspicion is one of this actress's natural modes; eyelids flapping, body turned three-quarters towards an opponent in a posture of aggressive defence, she constantly sniffs the possibility of mockery. Somebody, somewhere, is putting something over; and if it is nobody else, it must be herself.

Each of her verbal coinages is delivered with faultless bravado (the number of laughs extracted by author and actress from what is essentially the same joke is amazing), but each is surrounded by an apparatus of doubt. Am I going to get this right? Is that what I meant? Didn't I do well? Miss McEwan finds a whole subtext in a verbal tic.

Nothing could better her delicious confusion--eyes modestly sealed, then opened amorously wide--when finally confronted by her supposed lover. 'Oh,' she breathes, 'he will perforate my mystery.' Sheridan did not write that line, not exactly, but somewhere he must be wishing he did.

On with Miss McEwan comes Michael Hordern as Sir Anthony Absolute. Where she radiates apprehension, he radiates old-gentlemanly lust, inspired mainly by a passing maidservant's backside. He develops this theme when describing, over his breakfast boiled egg, the charms of his son's intended, climaxing in a lecherous gulp, timed with sublime unexpectedness.

On the first night Mr Hordern--I beg his pardon and send my felicitations, Sir Michael--lacked some of the gusto for the baronet's rages, but every detail of his tyranny was endearingly in place. Other attractions include Niall Buggy, who as Sir Lucius O'Trigger scores with every line he utters, and Tim Curry, whose Bob Acres is a cavalcade of bashfulness.

And then the lovers. Jack Absolute is a juvenile lead with a sense of humour and with the responsibility of knitting the play together; Patrick Ryecart discharges both obligations. As Lydia, Anne Louise Lambert languishes wittily. Edward Petherbridge plays Faulkland as a Scotch man of sentiment, mocking the character's masochism while establishing it as a dark fact in the play. Fiona Shaw's Julia, overripe but genuine, supplies just the right balance. I suppose nothing is definitive, but I cannot see this production being improved upon. It ends with a bewitching show of Chinese lanterns.

* * *

A Midsummer Night's Dream, transferred from the Cottesloe to the Lyttelton, ends well too; in the last scene Bill Bryden's production moulds a folk-play of all moods and all periods, the mortal and fairy worlds thoroughly interpenetrating. The mechanics' play is far funnier than before, Derek Newark's Bottom having slipped the leash with no loss of dignity. Robert Stephens's Oberon is more arrogant, less mellifluous, than Paul Scofield's; Susan Fleetwood is a superb Titania, whose impact on the seasons is thoroughly believable.

* * *

There is some careless verse speaking on the way through; though less than in the RSC's Antony and Cleopatra (Pit), which has some small-part playing of school-play standard. Adrian Noble's production has surprisingly little spark; characters stand on a featureless upper level gazing determinedly into space. There is intelligent detail, though: an intimate, sycophantic atmosphere to the Egyptian court, and a final implicit clash between the ruthless Caesar and compassionate Dolabella; maybe what Mrs Malaprop meant by an allegory on the banks of the Nile.

Michael Gambon as Antony truly looks like an imperial relic, and he rises to every large moment: of fury, generosity, abandon. But he cannot avoid monotony in the long trudge through defeat. Helen Mirren's Cleopatra excels in emotional quick changes, most notably at the end; in a full-scale production this might be a great performance.

Bob Peck's Enobarbus is satisfaction guaranteed, though no great departure for him; there is interesting minor work from Penelope Beaumont, Ken Bones and Albie Woodington. Set against this a self-consciously sinister treatment of the Clown who brings Cleopatra death in aspic.

* * *

Let's have a quiz. In what musical is the hero, unemployed and with a pregnant wife to support, persuaded to assist in an armed robbery whose discovery proves his downfall? Who said Carousel? These days that plot belongs to Blood Brothers (Lyric), and it follows on a lot of other melodrama. A Liverpool working-class matriarch gives birth to twins and is persuaded to give one of them up to the barren middle-class lady whose house she cleans. Despite all endeavour, the two boys meet and grow up friends, but are sundered by fate and/or economics.

As an omnipresent narrator puts it, in speech that takes English dramatic verse back to before the days of Gorboduc, 'Do we blame superstition for what came to pass/could it be what we, the English, have come to know as class.' Willy Russell's music starts out ominously well, as do his lyrics if you're not fussy about rhyme, but both run out of steam very quickly.

The only reasons for having the songs are that they lubricate a sprawling action, and that they provide a pretext for getting Barbara Dickson back on stage. She acts the natural mother with great sympathy, though she has little to do but suffer; her opposite number is a monster who finally provokes catastrophe by an action so motiveless that Mr Russell has to keep it off stage. There remains his domestic prose, which still has the stuff; and which enables some good acting to get done. George Costigan and Andrew C. Wadsworth as the boys are finely contrasted studies in gaucherie; though the time spent on the lore and language of school children, engaging in itself, throws the structure even further out of whack.

records.title: The Rumpscuttle
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The Rumpscuttle

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN
on two RSC productions

Two rowdy Elizabethan ladies are appearing in tandem at the Barbican, in productions by Barry Kyle.

The Roaring Girl is Moll Cutpurse, who actually lived. She was an adventuress and permanent tomboy ("a Tomrig or Rumpscuttle" -- Anon., 1659), who went through the stews of London living with men on their own terms and beating them: frequently up. She ran with the criminal classes and seems historically to have been one of them. But, since everyone loves a lively lass (at least from a distance), she became a popular favourite and was eventually mythologised upon the stage.

Her play is the joint work of Middleton, arch-realist of his period, and Dekker, the arch-sentimentalist; and the joins show. Dekker obviously lost his heart to Moll, and cannot bring himself to say a word against her. His roaring girl probably bears about the same relation to the original as Lionel Bart's Fagin to Dickens's.

The play is remarkably coy about what Moll actually does for a living; the plot keeps her fully occupied bringing true lovers together, rescuing improvident gallants from the claw of the law, and thwarting heavy fathers who want to have her locked up. Also smoking, of which she was a great pioneer, and, in a sidestep from her main business, violently disabusing a whey-faced gentleman who thinks he can have her: an especially heartening scene.

She is the comic spirit personified -- a transvestite blend of Falstaff and Cupid -- but playing a personification presents difficulties, and Helen Mirren's performance is almost submerged in the general rough-and-tumble. Either Miss Mirren should be more rumbustious or the production less.

She only comes into her own near the end in a bout of thieves' slang: a scene that reads impossible, but acts very well. She then has to translate what has been said for the benefit of some noble tourists, and her blushes are both pretty in themselves and a sudden revelation of character.

A virginal, maybe sexless, heroine is matched against a eunuchoid villain. Her would-be seducer spends most of his time in another, Middletonian, compartment of the play, blackmailing city wives for strictly financial favours. Meanwhile other, more orthodox, blades are trying to get shopkeepers' wives into bed, and their husbands are getting jealous.

It is a familiar routine, but Middleton was very good at it; the play keeps sprouting beguiling details. It is easy to get lost, but best to enjoy each as it comes. None of the performances leaps immediately into your lap, but by the end of the evening you have met a surprising number of people. Praise one, praise all; so let us consider that done and pass on to The Taming of the Shrew.

* * *

This is tricky. Shakespeare keeps as many plots going as Middleton and Dekker, but he is far clearer about them. Mr Kyle puts this to the test by adopting at least three separate styles of direction. The Induction is a bit of Merrie England, with extensive roistering, fully-equipped huntsmen led by a polished elderly Lord (Raymond Bowers) and strolling players singing carols.

Christopher Sly's somnambulistic state is carefully stressed (this is the RSC and they know that dreams equal themes) and from time to time he wanders into the play proper, with oddly haunting effect. For the production has now gone way beyond him. The Players prove to be prophetic souls, whose Elizabethanism does not prevent them dressing young lover Lucentio in Edwardian boater and blazer. They are also learned, and make Gremio the pantaloon into a figure of Roman comedy.

It would not be true to say that anything goes; Mr Kyle has the last scene in view, in which the professed romantics prove uxorious fools, and here his conceptions of Hortensio as clod and Lucentio as outright ninny come in very useful. That may console you as you watch these characters being built effortlessly up. The accredited low comics are actually played straight, by Pete Postlethwaite and David Shaw-Parker, and they are far funnier for it.

Most productions play Petruchio and Katherina as in love anyway; only Michael Bogdanov has treated the taming as outright sadism. I think myself that from the moment when Petruchio, at their first meeting, calls his lady "the prettiest Kate in Christendom," the romantics have an open-and-shut case; "Kate" seems to have been the most affectionate word in Shakespeare's vocabulary.

Mr Kyle tries to have it both ways. Alun Armstrong's Petruchio is, in intention, both lout and lover, making the benevolent break when, having denied her new clothes, he lectures Katherina affectionately on the virtues of "honest, plain habiliments." This is to place a lot of weight on one speech, and Mr Armstrong has not yet the vocal command to bring it off.

Sinead Cusack, though, has it to spare; and, after having lapped stick with tremendous intrepidity (falling successively into a pool of water and the front row of the stalls), she delivers her recantation with a transfixing suppleness and wit. Elsewhere in the RSC things have sunk so far that the actors cannot even fit syllables to metre. (Gallant and choleric are specific abominations.)

The playwright wins through. I share Mr Kyle's enthusiasm for the Jacobeans (with whom he has an excellent record), but, frankly, the worst of Shakespeare (The Two Gentlemen of Verona, right?) stands a better chance on stage than the best of his contemporaries: not through genius, but through competence.

* * *

Some of the magic has flown in the transfer of Mr Cinders from King's Head to Fortune. We lose the sense of collusion with the performers, the dances are harshly exposed, and some alterations in Tony Craven's production seem perverse; where are the heads that once peered so engagingly through holes in the drop-curtain, getting the show off to an irresistible start? It now seems a long time, and a lot of songs about tennis and blue blood, before Denis Lawson comes on.

Once he does, he takes over; there is still enough of Pal Joey about him to lend a discontented edge to his male Cinders, an edge which increases his charm. He has resentments to work off; he has to distance himself from his oppressors by transforming domestic drudgery into a Dying Swan routine. These are the resources that entitle him to sing "Spread a Little Happiness" (the greatest of cheer-up songs, winsome not aggressive) with hard-won conviction. His South American explorer's song, "On the Amazon" (full of lethal polysyllables), is now diversified with a sand-dance and he exits insouciantly across a table.

His new girl is Christina Matthews, who acts pertly and sings sweetly, and unlike her predecessor does not have to look her father full in the face as he sings "She's My Lovely" at her, which is anyway an interpolation from another Vivian Ellis score. There was an international musical-comedy style in the Twenties, with its roots in Wodehousian upper-crust farce; English Mr Ellis shares composing credit with American Richard Myers, whose rhythms syncopate after Gershwin, and whose ballads modulate after Kern.

The show plods at times, and I would not like to explain the thought-processes of the villain. But much of it is really funny, and the final glass slipper variation is a delight.

* * *

White Gloves (Lyric Studio, Hammersmith) is a full-length combination spoof of Sherlock Holmes and The Cherry Orchard that has about 20 minutes life in it.

records.title: The rusty chain
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: You Can't Take It With You
records.body:
The rusty chain

ROBERT CUSHMAN
on new plays in
London and (below)
New York.

THAT STEELY and humorous Irish actor T. P. McKenna spends a lot of time in The Communication Cord (Hampstead) tethered like a cow. He plays a modern doctor and senator with a sentimental liking for the antique; and he finds himself in an old Irish cottage.

One of its features is a chain with which the peasantry once used to secure the beasts who were their most precious possessions; imagining an ancient domestic scene, Mr McKenna assumes the milking position, and cannot get out of it. The clasp has rusted. Moral: sentimentality about the past merely ties you down. Or in this case up.

The senator's presence in the cottage, and indeed in Brian Friel's play, has to do with his daughter Susan. A young man called Tim Gallagher, an untenured university lecturer, wants to please her by impressing him, and to that end borrows the cottage for an hour from a barrister friend called Jack. But this, as you may have gathered, is a farce, and so everything goes wrong.

Unwanted visitors turn up; compromising bits of Tim's past raise their pretty little heads and display their pretty little underwear. The house itself is unhelpful ('Did you ever have a sense that a place hates you?' asks Tim rhetorically), what with fireplaces that breathe smoke, beams that give way and lamps that refuse to stay lit. The entire cast are frequently reduced to groping around the stage, like the characters in Black Comedy.

The resemblances to Peter Shaffer's piece are, overall, pretty startling. There is the central situation of boy, girl, and father. There is the chum from whom things are borrowed, and the old girlfriend who arouses the new one's jealousy, while obviously wanting our hero back. There is an intrusive old woman. There are even people imitating Germans and Germans imitating people.

Mr Friel's dialogue is of course his own, and much of it is extremely funny, especially when delivered by Mr McKenna or by Martin Cochrane's Kraut, both of whom end up believing that 'Gallagher' is a synonym for 'mad.' Unfortunately, in Nancy Meckler's production, it isn't.

Stephen Rea, who plays Tim, seems too capable and even stolid to be the hero-victim of a farce; indeed he looks more assured than Brian Protheroe, who plays worldly Jack. With the balance wrong, the two of them make heavy weather of the exposition; and though the comedy does come to a satisfying boil, it lacks foundation. It also fades too long before the end.

Underlying everything is an impatience with the exploitation of Irish myth, which is seen as very rickety. This is fine when implicit, but it does not provide the climax that was obviously hoped. Another theme, announced in the title, is even less helpful. Tim is seven years into a Ph.D on linguistics; his thesis has to do with the fragility of discourse, the ease with which life can destroy the shared assumptions on which comprehension depends. This of course is what farce is about, what it depends on; but a running philosophic commentary does not increase the fun.

West, in this vein, is only east from another angle; and Steven Berkoff's West (Warehouse) is certainly his 'East' revisited. Once again disaffected London youth prowls the streets and the dance-halls, only this time in packs. Gang-warfare is the theme, the upshot a single fight between Mike, our star, and his arch-foe, the Hoxton Fiend.

This, or the preparation for it, is all the plot there is, and it is unconscionably protracted. I am as tired of writing complaints about Mr Berkoff's joky-Shakespearean manner (or, in this case, manor) as he is of reading them. At least there are no couplets this time; the real frustration of the verse is that Mr Berkoff can write terrific prose, as here in Mike's account of a day in the life, with special reference to travelling to work on the tube.

This is later reiterated in group-mime, but the observation is quite strong enough to go round twice. Also, though nobody would call Mr Berkoff a feminist, he writes extremely well for women; Stella Tanner as Mike's mum, Susan Kyd as his girl, are both given sequences of reminiscence, complaint and--in Miss Kyd's case--erotic fancy, which they take with gratitude as obvious as deserved. I believed in them as in very few female characters from male writers.

The machismo is monotonous by comparison, and Mike's underlying self-pity allowed to break all bounds at the end. Mr Berkoff does not appear himself (though there is a Berkoff-clone among the lads), but there is brilliance in his staging, especially in the close-drawn quartet that tours the playing-area in a cross between a march and a lurch, heads well down and forward, belching rhythmic obscenities. It says more than the speeches.

Incidentally the Warehouse may well have to close. A small, central and (since the RSC left) comfortable space, ideal for new work, it deserves rescue at least as much as Riverside or the Roundhouse.

Nick Darke, author of The Body (Pit), has been quoted as believing that all writers should be writing about the bomb. The corollary of that is believing you can plant a bomb in any old play and achieve significance. 'The Body' may not have been written like that, but that is how it plays.

World War Three will probably start for farcical reasons, but not, I think, because of the combination in one Cornish village of an American marine dropped, dead of boredom, a male and female yokel possessive about his corpse, a farmer brainwashed into replacing him on a missile base, a rector who dresses as a Chinaman without his parishioners noticing, and a marine lieutenant who goes apes when he runs into sartorial competition at the local hop.

There is no comic logic to any of these details; they are willed into existence so that all the English characters may be corralled in the second act by the Americans who have access to doomsday. There is some excitement here (well squeezed in Nick Hamm's production), but it is not difficult to achieve suspense by training a gun on the audience and dicing with the end of the world, especially if you have actors like these.

Christopher Benjamin, Clive Wood, Jenny Agutter, David Shaw-Parker, Derek Godfrey, John Bowe and Pete Postlethwaite are among those contributing to the familiar RSC claustrophobia effect: infinite riches in a little room, furnished by 'Dr Strangelove,' 'Man is Man,' 'Cold Comfort Farm' and didactic fringe musicals.

Nigel Williams's The Adventures of Jasper Ridley (Half Moon) is about youth unemployment and is appropriately hopeless. Mr Williams's sentiments--rage and (unless he's kidding) respect for gentleness--are unimpeachable, and his attitudes to official philanthropy interestingly ambivalent. But he tells an aimless, picaresque story in a string of dilapidated sketches; any hope of a sharp cartoon effect is dashed in Pam Brighton's production for Hull Truck (yes, Hull Truck, read it and weep), which is fuzzy and underpowered. There are some glints of acting, especially from Billy MacColl; the riot scenes, involving local kids, deserve to be done over by Mr Berkoff.

* * *

A Briton salutes NY

A NEW YORK season that in January was being pronounced the worst in living memory had, when I returned only four months later, brightened unrecognisably up.

There are two new plays on Broadway better than almost any in the West End. Neil Simon's Brighton Beach Memoirs has been generally and justly pronounced his best play. The beach is the Brooklyn district, in which Mr Simon grew up, and the piece, set in 1937, is in some measure autobiographical. How completely does not matter; the central character, a vociferously pubescent Jewish boy called Eugene, would engage us even if we had never heard of the author.

He comes from an overcrowded home. The first act shows this menage facing minor crises and surviving; the second shows them facing major ones, and again surviving. At the end they are all, including those who threatened or attempted to leave, gathered round the table, awaiting the incursion of more relatives, miraculously escaped from Nazi Europe. This finale could be taken as deceptively bitter; and I have heard it persuasively described as such. But I have to admit that it plays soft. It does not, however, vitiate the truthfulness of the characterisation, or the extreme dexterity of the craftsmanship.

The play tells three or four stories, and goes all over the house, and the smoothness with which the scenes interlock is very satisfying. It is also, of course, funny; and for once the wisecracks are unforced and unembarrassing. They all belong to Eugene, who tells the story as if writing a book while it happens. This, we are persuaded, is how a precocious gagman would think, write, talk. The role is brilliantly squeaked by a 21-year-old actor, Matthew Broderick.

Marsha Norman's 'Night, Mother' is also a family play, though the visible family is here confined to old mother and middle-aged daughter. The former is looked after by the latter, an epileptic divorcee with a disturbed delinquent son: with, in her own persuasive view, nothing to live for. She begins the play by telling her mother she is going to kill herself, and in the end she does so.

The bleak implacability of this is a greater achievement than anything in the Simon play, but the whole is less satisfying. I always gag on delayed revelations between long-time intimates. Kathy Bates gives a marvellous account of a lumpy, determined woman who has set deliberate limits to her consciousness.

'Night, Mother' was the only Broadway show I saw not set, or revived from, between the wars. 'You Can't Take It With You,' Kaufman and Hart's celebration of a family who opt out of the rat-race (and apparently have the money to do it) has been lovingly revived under the direction of Ellis Rabb. His starry cast -- Jason Robards mellow and crackling as Grandpa, Colleen Dewhurst enjoying herself as a Russian princess now working in a pancake house -- have thoroughly ensembled themselves; charm, humour and even romance ebb and flow unimpeded.

The National Theatre is to mount You Can't Take It With You in the summer, and had better, as is said in another Kaufman and Hart play, look to its laurels.

The latest hot musical (I meant to type 'hit,' but let it stand) is On Your Toes, which in 1936 brought ballet to Broadway in the shape of George Balanchine's 'Slaughter on Tenth Avenue.' Better still is the title-number, a song described to me by a New York singer as 'the meaning of jaunty' and turned by current choreographer Donald Saddler into an uplifting extended encounter between jazz dancing and classical: first contest, then union.

It makes the show seem briefly like an ancestral concept musical: song and dance not merely the medium, but the subject and certainly the message. Unfortunately there is also a plot; not only wearing in itself, it fails to frame the songs, so a prime Rodgers and Hart score (their best, I think) goes by without anybody noticing.

The original librettist-director George Abbott directed again (at 95), but he has some lack-lustre principals, notably excepting the ballerina Natalia Makarova, who has as much fun as Miss Dewhurst while going in the opposite cultural direction.

A more elaborate musical resurrection is My One and Only, which started out as a revival of the 1927 Gershwin show Funny Face, but has arrived, after a troubled passage out-of-town, as a new show with Gershwin songs from all over. When I saw it in preview I felt that visually nothing more needed to be done; on geometric -- indeed formalist -- sets, Tommy Tune has devised a spectacle that has all the inventiveness of his hit show Nine without the pretention.

The immensely tall Mr Tune is also a revelation as a performer: a proven dancer with a strong voice and personality. Twiggy, his co-star, disappointed me; but then she has not been given much to act. The abiding problem was the story, or at least the lack of something to make us care about it.

At the other extreme of Gershwin, there was Porgy and Bess, staged almost complete in Radio City Music Hall: my chance to catch up with two ancient monuments at once; since Porgy has not been staged in London for 30 years, it must be the most neglected of modern theatrical masterpieces. Catfish Row looked well on the vast stage--the show is the study of a milieu and we may as well see as much of it as possible -- but the unimaginably cavernous auditorium created severe sonic problems.

But the production was able, and the music -- the sheer, dramatic weight of it -- won through. There is a doggedness in this score that amounts to inspiration, then to greatness, and finally--when the crippled Porgy sets out on his crazy journey to New York in a goat-drawn cart--to myth.

Robert Cushman
