records.body:
The paper tiger

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Giraudoux at the National Theatre.

JEAN GIRAUDOUX'S The Trojan War Will Not Take Place (Lyttelton) is a title that gives fair warning. It invokes and inverts Greek mythology, it is darkly frivolous, and it hints at eternally important themes. It signifies, as does the play itself, a schoolboy's view of what constitutes great drama.

That is not a sneer; it is a confession. A schoolboy is what I was when I first read it, and a masterpiece is what I thought. That, admittedly, was in 1950, when it was already a 20-year-old play; Christopher Fry's translation, still in use, was billed in the melodramatic fashion of the time as 'Tiger at the Gates.'

The tiger signifies the threat of war creeping up on Troy since the abduction of Helen. It also signifies Hector the Trojan hero, anxious to prevent the next war. He finds the Trojan women on his side, the old men, besotted with Helen and glory, against him.

But he battles on to return Helen, even getting the theoretic co-operation of the lady herself and the Greek envoy Ulysses, though both are sceptical that destiny can be cheated. It wants a war, and Helen is its instrument. But so may Hector be. The violence in him is the indirect cause of the calamity. It is very nearly, as he comes within an ace of killing the Grecian Ajax who is insulting his wife, the direct cause.

This is less a pacifist play (its credentials in that line, coming to you direct from the age of appeasement, are pretty disreputable) than a fatalist one. It exudes the kind of fashionable pessimism that is never out of fashion, since the eternal cussedness of human history gives it every chance of being the truth.

At the end Hector says simply, 'The war will happen'; that moment, which shoulders the weights of past struggle and legendary future carnage, is immense. So is its sequel; the symbolic Gates of War swing open to reveal Helen kissing young Troilus. Sex, like warfare, cheapens itself even as it prevails.

I am beginning to convince myself all over again. So, to backtrack: the play's style is very dated. What once we called 'civilised' we now, disdainfully, call 'clever.' This is not to say that it could not be rescued; the scenes in which old civilians, the ones not at risk, plan their propaganda war, should still strike a topical chill through their jokiness.

Actually, most of the play is jokey. If the jokes don't work, nothing will. The Lyttelton version, directed by Harold Pinter, goes disastrously for grandeur. Eileen Diss's set is a scramble of white steps, which draw the eye up to a nondescript blue cyclorama; finding no rest there, it climbs further and meets the stage lights: I have never spent so much time looking at lanterns. (The Gates of War are more impressive, though reminiscent of the old lift-doors at Selfridges.)

Nobody would dream today of inflicting such Pearl and Dean designs on a real Greek tragedy, or on Racine or 'Troilus and Cressida,' but because Giraudoux is comparatively modern he gets the treatment. It cripples the actors; try acting conversationally while strutting up and down stairs in a short tunic. Martin Jarvis is trapped between heroic poses and a hopeful smile. He does the stinging Oration to the Dead as well, but he never manages to look the living in the face: no contact, no pulse, no play.

The same generalised Greekness afflicts David Rintoul's Paris and, to a degree, Barry Foster's Ulysses, though with him we do move to a higher level. (So, self-consciously, does the play; the arrival of Ulysses is a signal that we are to stop giggling and pay attention. Here Giraudoux unveils his metaphysics, and they have shrivelled over the years.)

The play's sinister lightness is best captured by Nicola Pagett as Helen; her seduction of Troilus (Julian Firth) is the production's high spot. Annette Crosbie's Hecuba is a highly skilled dispenser of acid drops.

* * *

The play still survives better than John Osborne's 20-year-old A Patriot For Me (Chichester), which tells us that a homosexual military officer in the diplomatic service, in this case Austrian, could be blackmailed into spying for a foreign power, in this case Russia. Whatever next. The play is competently written on the 'King of Hearts' principle: begin at the beginning, go on until you reach the end, and then stop. It takes a long time.

A drag ball is famously thrown in, though it tells us nothing about the protagonist; we are merely directed to look at it and think, gosh. People will tell you that the play presents a picture of pre-1914 Austrian society, but all they really mean is that it has a large cast, many in uniform. They are seen to best advantage slowly revolving at the curtain-call.

Otherwise the visual problems are scarcely solved in Ronald Eyre's production, which uses drab projections for decor. The total effect is very literary, giving a new meaning to the term closet-drama; Mr Osborne's most vilified works ('A Sense of Detachment' or 'Watch It Come Down') have more life in them than this. Alan Bates, in icy control, is worth seeing; George Murcell is flavourful as the bluff, brutal Russian, a role he has played in many plays, including the original production of this one.

* * *

'Why,' I have found myself humming this week, 'must the show go on?' Coward's brilliantly dyspeptic attack on showbiz sentiment turns up, as the acme of chutzpah, in Noel and Gertie (King's Head); the title, again, tells all. 'Is it quite fair/To ask us to share/Your dreary private life'; the assumption here is that we hunger for every crumb of the joint private and public life of Coward and Gertrude Lawrence, though both seem to have been meagre.

They did two shows together, and were friends for a long time. As Sheridan Morley bizarrely puts it in his narration, 'physically they were in constant contact even though 5,000 miles away.' Whatever magic Miss Lawrence may have possessed is absent from Joanna Lumley's frankly insipid performance, but Simon Cadell is an excellent non-imitative Coward.

Among other things he sings a first-rate 'Mrs Worthington,' which makes it doubly absurd that most of the vocalising should be entrusted to a couple of cut-glass singers. Whoever said that Coward and Lawrence had voices? The dramatic excerpts are growing over-familiar, though Private Lives itself refuses to turn dreary; topping and tailing the evening with it gives shape, and a piercing sense of evanescence.

I have grown sickly weary of the perspex sets for Much Ado About Nothing (Barbican); they dehydrate the action. But Terry Hands's production has otherwise gained in shapeliness; Sinead Cusack's Beatrice is a serious, wounded creature from the start, whereas Derek Jacobi's Benedick has visibly to grow up in the church scene where he circles her praying figure.

Remarkably catchy music (Shakespeare's greatest hits?) is supplied by Nigel Hess. His more solemn setting of 'Sigh no more, ladies' deserves to be more than a hit: a standard.

Ghostly sonatas

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

SOMETHING, to put it gently, has been missing from the Peter Ustinov plays seen in London in recent years; Beethoven's Tenth (Vaudeville) strongly suggests that it was Mr Ustinov himself. As writer he has furnished an amiable little play, which as actor he proceeds to turn into a major comic event.

The text is a mix of Amadeus and Blithe Spirit. A contemporary London music critic (and failed composer) lives in unease with his wife who is a former singer, at odds with his son who has already written his own fifth symphony, and in open warfare with the au pair, an Austrian girl named Irmgard. She worships Beethoven, who happens to be the critic's special subject.

At the height of an argument, Irmgard, screwing her face up, wishes that Beethoven might actually appear before them, and what you imagine would happen happens. Everyone takes this manifestation calmly; a doctor fits the great man with a hearing aid. He has never, of course, heard his own complete works, so the critic sits him down to listen to them on disc.

Beethoven is very impressed by the shelves of review copies ('You mean critics get presents these days -- as well as bribes') and by his host's industry ('Articles appear week after week and will be collected in one large volume.') He is delighted to have aural proof of his own genius, though he thinks the Ninth far too long; it sends him to sleep, and is still playing when he wakes up.

He also knocks at the door like fate at the start of the Fifth, and refers to Liszt as 'that Hungarian boy with warts.' The play is full of jokes like these, shamelessly flattering the audience's shallow cultural sensibilities: the kind by which I am almost invariably slain. (I suspect that Tom Stoppard was bitten at an impressionable age by Mr Ustinov.)

Mr Ustinov moves slowly around in a cloud of dust, occasionally going into nervous spasms which leave his head and hands vibrating long after your ordinary limb would have called it a day; his uniqueness is to be simultaneously febrile and lethargic. He is cunningly matched here against the trim, barbed urbanity of Robin Bailey, an actor still coming into his kingdom. (As he says, accurately and with superlative timing, 'You are a great man and I am merely rather important.')

In Robert Chetwyn's refreshing production, enviably if unrealistically set by Kenneth Mellor, the rest of the household is well acted by Clare Higgins, Reece Dinsdale and Dilys Laye, though they have little to play. When Ludwig (so he is billed in the programme) sorts out their lives for them, it hardly matters, since their lives seem of so little account.

Nor is there anything fresh in his view of modern London; the writing gets tired in the second act and drops right off in a solemn reconstruction of the composer's own past. You do not go to the play for what Mr Ustinov has to say, but for the way in which he and Mr Bailey say it.

I now want to see our author in a revival of his greatest hit, The Love of Four Colonels. I am vulnerable of course; I grew up hanging on his every word as relayed on radio or television. (By the way, and while being nostalgic, I should like to clarify last week's gremlined copy; I first read Tiger at the Gates, as it then was, in the 1950s, not in 1950; I am not that old, nor, since the translation did not appear till 1955, that clever.)

Tom Lehrer wrote a song about the super-special just plain folks, all sluts and maniacs, in his home town; and another ('be it ever so decadent') about the South. Beth Henley's Crimes of the Heart (Bush) is like a simultaneous animation of the two of them.

In Hazlehurst, Mississippi, 'five years after Hurricane Camille,' live three sisters: Lenny, who ain't never had a man on account of feelin' self-conscious 'bout her shrunken ovary; Meg, who went to the big city to make it as a singer and couldn't; and beautiful Babe who has just shot her husband after prolonged unpleasantness.

She says 'he started hating me cos I couldn't laugh at his jokes' (a key line) and eventually she took up with a well-endowed coloured boy; 'Why, Babe,' says one of her sisters, interested rather than aghast, 'I didn't even know you were a liberal.'

Miss Henley obviously cares about her characters, but finds them, and the gothic world they inhabit, very funny. But she is satirising a literary convention rather than a real one. Her wide-eyed view of disaster recalls Joe Orton, but unlike him she is not attacking a social structure: she is merely sending herself up as she goes along. This has a tart, appealing, but unsatisfying effect.

Two of the players in Simon Stokes's production seem out of place, but Robert Glenister as Babe's defence lawyer is shyly effective, and I have few complaints about the sisterhood. Wendy Morgan has intermittent trouble with Babe's outrageousness, but Amanda Redman makes a swashbuckling Meg, and Brenda Blethyn as Lenny gives a wonderful display of mixed-emotion close-up acting.

Liza Minnelli (Apollo Victoria) begins her act singing, offstage, a neglected Yip Harburg lyric, 'There's a Great Day Coming Manana.' My heart was warmed, but it cooled as she entered and the song continued: she seemed to have rewritten its quizzical sentiments in the interests of upbeat. And so it went; though what with an atrocious sound system, a skilled but overblown orchestra, and a lack of any vocal colouring between smoke and fire, it was not always easy to tell what she was singing.

It works for some people. The audience screamed loudest when the word 'CABARET' appeared in neon; take a bow, Mr Electrician. The Guardian proclaimed her one of those 'like Billy Holiday (sic, and again sic) and Edith Piaf,' who can transform rubbishy material into music and poetry. Actually most of her material is first-rate; and she transforms it into gibberish.

Not always: I respect anyone who can even remember the words of the 'Trolley Song' (they're mainly sound-effects) and when she quietens down and gives herself the chance to be funny or sad, she proves she can still be a fine singing actress: as she was on her first records and in Pookie and Cabaret.

Her writer, Fred Ebb, who has staged the show with some economy and style, has supplied a routine about her getting the Oscar for the latter film, after losing out to Maggie Smith when nominated for the former. I sympathised; it should have gone to Jane Fonda.

At the Cocteau, temporarily beached from a schools tour, there is an inventive workshop Macbeth, on which I hope to enlarge sometime; but I want now to memorialise a neglected death. Pat Smythe is not a theatre name, though he did once appear in a play at the Open Space; he was, though, one of this country's finest jazz pianists, a tolerant and sympathetic accompanist (as I have some cause to know) and a soloist at whom I have seen American virtuosi stand and marvel.

records.title: One for Mrs Worthington
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
One for Mrs Worthington

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Bugsy Malone'

THE self-willed senescence of the West End is frighteningly demonstrated by Bugsy Malone (Her Majesty's), which is a whole evening of freak-show. It is based on the Alan Parker film of 1976, a gangster musical with a cast of children. I can make no direct comparisons, since I stayed away from the movie; having no desire to see two of my favourite genres purged of sex and violence in the interests of cuteness.

The show is what I feared of the movie. It is actually billed as 'Bugsy Malone On Stage'; managements now are banking on the special thrill offered by letting you see again something you have already caught on a screen. There is a lot of this thinking around, and in the short term it may be commercially sound. In the long term it is suicidal.

The added gimmick of staging is, of course, subsidiary to the one carried over from the film. We have, again, a cast of kids: British kids, aged 10 to 14, playing American adults. They have plenty of enthusiasm, and some skill (especially in dancing), but hardly any discernible acting talent.

The show has a lot of dialogue: supposedly smart lines delivered by performers who can neither speak nor time them. The timing of lines is what gives a play tension, continuity and -- ultimately -- sense; and you never properly value it until you are deprived. I felt pauperised at Bugsy Malone, sapped of the ability even to follow the story.

It seemed a pointless one anyway. Bugsy Malone is a well-meaning slob who hangs around New York, being in love with a hopeful ingenue who wants to go to Hollywood and has a dream-sequence to prove it. He also befriends a budding prizefighter, but this theme, laboriously set up, then just disappears; it is merely an excuse for an energetic number in a gym.

There are two gang leaders, Fat Sam and Dandy Dan. We are meant to be on Sam's side, or at least Bugsy is, but there really seems nothing to choose between them. They fight with guns that spray custard-pies. This is very confusing: are the victims dead or not? If not, what kind of gangster-story is this?

The rationale is, of course, that it would be intolerable to see children actually shooting or actually shot; which seems a good reason for not casting them as gangsters. There is nothing satiric about this patisserie warfare; it is pure bowdlerisation. Elsewhere old jokes are used -- the hoods who repeat every word their boss says, for example -- which in an adult context could only make us groan or maybe rub our eyes. But children are trusted to make them funny by sheer ineptitude.

It could persuasively be claimed that this show exploits children, but it is more to the point that it exploits audiences. (It also, by omission, exploits adult actors. Is Equity pleased?) It is not even true to its own lousy convention: the kids do all the dancing and talking, but the singing is entrusted to half-a-dozen off-stage adults. The children, miming to their large ill-fitting voices, are reduced to marionettes.

The other grown-ups have worked rather well. Paul Williams has composed a competent bunch of songs. Michael Dolenz, surmounting what must have been fearful logistical problems, has directed spectacularly. Gillian Gregory has put her pubescent chorus line through some high-class low-down routines. (The one boy who makes an impression, Scott Sherrin, does it through hoofing.) Ralph Koltai's set is a three-decker wonder that should be kept in storage against the advent of a real show. Also working hard was a first-night audience of Mrs Worthingtons, augmented by some rejected but still hopeful little Worthingtons. They raised the roof.

* * *

Angelo Beolco was a sixteenth-century Italian actor and playwright credited with building bridges between the popular and academic theatre of his time. He was nicknamed 'Il Ruzzante,' meaning, apparently, the joker. Four of his jokes have been assembled by Shared Experience at the Lyric, Hammersmith, under the heading of The Comedy Without Title, which is what Beolco himself called the first and longest of them.

In it a Paduan peasant, Zilio, falls in love. He spends the first part of the play shyly confessing to his friends, and hearing their counsel. He then, with as much instructed bravado as he can muster, proposes; and is scornfully rejected. Only the intervention of his friend Nale wins him the girl; and the two men come to blows when Zilio realises that a menage a trois is in prospect.

He kills Nale; and we then -- for the first time -- meet the widow. She bewails her husband's prowess in the fields and in bed, swears she will never take another, and a couple of minutes later succumbs to an old admirer on the grounds that in this life we must take what we can get.

If the first, bucolic, part of the play moves slowly, this conclusion is farcically fast, the effect of the juxtaposition is to deliver us from time, to leave us with the sensation that we are merely watching the truth. It does not feel distorted, even if we know it must be. The humour -- and much of the seriousness -- is obsessively scatological; but this is offset by Mike Alfreds's production, by playing of remarkable fullness and delicacy.

'What won't you do when you're in love?' is the despairing question which runs through the shorter pieces that follow the interval. In the only one to have any previous track-record in English (under the title Ruzzante Returns from the Wars) a soldier is battered by his wife's new protector and tries to fantasise his defeat away.

In the next, a young man tries to rescue his beloved from a stock pantaloon, who disconcertingly turns out to have human feelings. These are beautifully expressed by Mr Voss, who also dominates the last play, in which hunger bites, deepest and imagination cruelest. The evening could be funnier (it lacks natural stand-up comics), but Beolco's 'gay and gentle' reputation is amply vindicated.

* * *

Another touring group, Cliffhanger, has touched down in this theatre's studio with They Came From Somewhere Else, which burlesques a science-fiction story that nobody shows signs of believing in the first place. This is the second unfunny spoof in succession at the Lyric Studio, which should make it popular with those people who like a theatre to have a recognisable policy.

records.title: Light blue backdrop
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Footlights!: A Hundred Years of Cambridge Comedy
records.body:
Light blue backdrop

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

FOOTLIGHTS! by Robert Hewison
Methuen £8.95

IT must have been early in the 1950s that I heard a radio programme called The Cambridge Footlights Take the Mike: a spoof of all other radio programmes presented apparently by a bunch of undergraduates. It was delicious. I doubt if I knew at the time what a real footlight was, let alone a human one; but the fact that Cambridge University could not only win the Boat Race every year but make me laugh as well clinched my scholastic ambitions. I think I was in primary school at the time.

Robert Hewison makes no mention of Take the Mike but there is not much else he leaves out. (I knew he had been thorough when I found my own name in an appendix since my own eventual membership was fairly passive.) His history is subtitled A Hundred Years of Cambridge Comedy, the Footlights having mounted their first production in 1883. It was a burlesque called Bombastes Furioso, and yielded a published song-hit, The Cambridge Boating Song ('Bow, your back's out ever so far,/What a very consummated muff you are'). Boaters have remained part of the Footlights' image ever since, in the eyes of the world if not in those of its members, causing considerable embarrassment in recurring periods of austerity or social consciousness. Social snobbery was actually replaced in the 1950s by performing snobbery; audition procedures were fearful. But now, it seems, they have to tout for members.

Footlights themselves are a long outmoded form of illumination; and revue -- which the club did not adopt as its format until 1921, but to which it has stayed faithful ever since -- has generally been declared extinct as well. It survives only at universities, and pre-eminently at Cambridge. Mr Hewison (a broadminded Oxonian) concludes that 'the concentration of intelligence in one of the country's leading universities guarantees that a fresh supply of potential talent is available every year'; and he might have added that fledgeling writing talent is better employed on short sketches than on long plays. Funniness is something that burns out early in many people; what is often stigmatised as 'undergraduate humour' is frequently the funniest there is. It comes from people sharply aware of absurdity, and able either to attack or exploit it. If it can stay fresh at the post-graduate stage ('Beyond the Fringe,' 'Monty Python,' 'Not the Nine O'Clock News') it is priceless.

Mr Hewison reveals that the first real star Footlight, from 1910 to 1913, was Jack Hulbert, 'the model of the "Cambridge actor" long before the type was recognised.' If he was a theatrical all-rounder, his successors have been revue specialists: Peter Cook, Jonathan Miller (a Footlights star but, incredibly, never a member), John Cleese, Eric Idle, Griff Rhys-Jones.

Satire, it seems, has never really existed in the Footlights; the prevailing moods have been whimsy and craziness. (The funniest quoted material is by Cook and Cleese.) Music has been in and out. In the 1950s Michael Frayn wrote sentimental songs with misgivings; in the Sixties Cleese, having been penalised for his own inability to sing or dance, stamped them out.

The book traces the Footlights' social as well as cultural history. Its succession of clubrooms, with lunches and late licences, made it the centre of theatrical Cambridge, especially when the introduction of Associate Membership in the 1960s opened it to those with no personal revue ambitions. How the whole apparatus survived redevelopment and homelessness is a wonder. It has, apparently, suffered. But it is unlikely to die.
production_title: Footlights!: A Hundred Years of Cambridge Comedy

records.title: Waspish celebration
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Waspish celebration

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Nancy.

IN the first scene of The Dining Room (Greenwich) a house is apparently changing hands. In the second scene, equally apparently, a house or its contents are being divided up by a separating couple. It is probably not the same house, though it is definitely the same set: scenically and socially.

Locationwise, we are in the room promised by the title. In class terms we are American upper, and rich. We have, invariably, servants. We are in a play by A. R. Gurney Jr, celebrated for celebrating the WASP and for doing it, on the whole, waspishly.

For what happens in the third scene, or the fourth, or any of those that follow I cannot precisely vouch. The final tally is well into double figures, and a fellow gets confused. There is no story line to cling to, and no continuing or even recurring characters. Half a dozen actors play a kaleidoscopic assemblage of parents, children and domestics.

The dining-room symbolises the house, the house the family, and the family a social attitude. The dining-room is cherished, especially by the more authoritarian figures, as a sanctum and a retreat. "Nowadays," says a grandfather, "people eat in living-rooms and kitchens," and he deprecates these people, though he recognises their inevitability. He appears late in the play and late also in the chronology--not necessarily the same thing.

An earlier patriarch is more inflexible. He disapproves of progressive education, of any American involvement in foreign affairs, of any grammatical sloppiness ("Dad, can I read the funnies?" "Certainly you may."), and of the New Deal. These dining rooms are cold beds of isolationism. One diner took shredded wheat with him on his only trip to Europe, and returned when he had eaten it all.

What happens? Younger generations shock their elders, exchanging spouses, uttering slang (the room is described as "viciously nice") and even profanity ("it sucks out loud . . . it bites the big one"), and planning slide-shows on the "vanishing culture" they inherit. Elders shock their youngers by being caught with lovers. Fathers with hernias face fist-fights to defend the honour of homosexual uncles. Staff are flattered or berated. Drinks are drunk and meals of course eaten, though not by those who have cooked them.

Mr Gurney is shuffling and recycling the conventions of drawing-room drama, and he brings to his task, as you will have noted, an exceedingly sharp ear and tongue. Some of his cliche situations, though, take their revenge, refusing to keep the elegant distance he has prescribed for them.

Alan Strachan has directed with precision, aided by fine lighting from Mick Hughes. His cast comprises four former stalwarts of Alan Ayckbourn's Scarborough company, one real American, and Polly James. They all slide up and down the age-scale very proficiently, though a lack of Yankee boldness sometimes results, paradoxically, in near-caricature. The teak and the archways of Bernard Culshaw's set are a grand environment.

* * *

"We think it is important for you to see both productions," say the RSC in their new leaflet, referring to The Roaring Girl and The Taming of the Shrew. They have gone to the trouble of juxtaposing these two plays; the least we can do is show up. The same schoolmasterly tone is implicit in their plan to have their production of King Lear (Barbican) cross-pollinate with Edward Bond's Lear in the Pit.

Actually Adrian Noble's production now seems less Bondish, more generous, than it did at Stratford. True, the crucial protesting servant at Gloucester's blinding who claims to have served Cornwall ever since he himself was a child sounds as if he still is a child, but I'm sure this is accident rather than debasing design. I had expected this production to suffer from my intervening exposure to the Olivier television version, but it is in fact as thrilling as before, and richer.

Michael Gambon's Lear has, so to speak, grown into his age; and he takes the first half of the play superbly. His capriciousness is massive, more so because of this actor's native reasonableness. He never sounds saner than when he curses Goneril or prays not to go mad; gradually his sanity becomes alarming; it cloaks gigantic self-deception. He goes mad logically; of course Poor Tom was ruined by his daughters. The mock-trial remains wonderfully serious, its crowning paradox, Lear's earnest "Is there any cause in Nature that makes these hard hearts," uttered as he stabs the Fool.

That irony aside, this, the production's most famous invention, is perplexing. People say it is symbolic, but of what? Why should Lear, who is learning to think, kill his conscience? It makes, of course, a spectacular end to a spectacular performance, though I doubt if Antony Sher's pyrotechnics actually reveal more than Michael Williams's quieter music-hall veteran in the last Stratford version. If the play dwindles in its second half, it is not through the Fool's absence, but through Lear's. There is no special vision at Dover, and no surprise at the reconciliation; it is just Mr Gambon being gentle, as usual. But he is moving at the end.

In Shakespeare, intelligence backed by experience equals authority: practice has made Malcolm Storry's Kent perfect, and Sara Kestelman's Goneril, gradually extinguishing conscience, very near.

The Scottish 7:84 production of Men Should Weep, which I admired at last year's Edinburgh Festival, is now at the Theatre Royal, Stratford East.

The peripatetic Theatre of the Nations should come to rest next year at Nancy: an architecturally gracious French town currently holding its own sixteenth drama festival, directed by Mira Trailovic, who presides over the similar jamboree in Belgrade. Fitting, then, that the most distinguished production I saw should have been Yugoslav: Requiem for Boris Davidovich, a blend of poor and epic theatre.

The audience sit in the middle of the floor; the action unfolds in tableaux around the four walls. The life, death (under Stalin) and, especially, times of a Russian revolutionary are depicted in every available style: narrative, choric, choreographic--and in, we were promised, 10 alternating languages. English seemed, to my defective ears, to come round less often than was fair, but it did have the last words; they were sung to the surprising tune of She's Leaving Home--Goodbye U.S.S.R.

Elsewhere jadedness could be scented. From Cologne came a solemn Misanthrope, impressive at any given moment by virtue of its slow pace and its set, a huge and perilous flight of stairs; I don't suppose German directors actually want to maim their actors.

There was a Chilean play at which respect--since these were actors playing peasants and probably playing them well--faded into uncomprehending boredom. It is no accident that festivals like Nancy flourished in the heyday of the American alternative groups, whose appeal was largely non-verbal.

Some performers seem to exist wholly for the festival circuit; at home they are prophets, without honour, or honoured without profits. I had never heard of the British representative, Johnny Melville, but his one-man show, Members Only, was packed out; perhaps because word had spread that it was funny. Mr Melville proved to be Scots and an accomplished mime: too winsome, like most mimes, but engaging, especially in the merciful failure of his benevolent fantasy to deal with its advertised subjects of protest unemployment and punkdom.

The festival utilised 14 venues: from municipal opera house, for establishment types, to bare rooms for those who yearn for the days when fringe was fringe and only walking counted, for seating or heating. A scarce-converted tobacco factory housed three of these penitentiaries; it seemed a tacit acknowledgment that some theatricalia should carry a health-warning.

records.title: Falklands tragedy
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: The Man with the Flower in His Mouth
records.body:
Falklands tragedy

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

A YEAR ago today Lieutenant David Tinker, RN, was killed in action on HMS Glamorgan. He was 25. His letters home, to his family and his fiancée, were collected by his father, Hugh Tinker, and published under the title A Message from the Falklands. Selections from them form the first half of Falkland Sound/Voces de Malvinas, the new show at the Theatre Upstairs.

Two actors appear before the window in the theatre's back wall, which gives on to real summer greenery abetted by the contents of cunningly placed flowerpots. It makes a highly affecting image of the England for which David Tinker officially died, and of the part of it from which he actually came. Paul Jesson's schoolmasterly Hugh is almost part of the scenery: all quiet and sensible moderation. David, fresh and enthusiastic, goes from public school to a naval career, with a spell at Birmingham University.

It is of course moving to hear of the hopes and affections of a young man we know to be under sentence of death. It is made almost unbearable by the gradual revelation that he had no belief in the cause for which he was fighting.

His first reaction to the prospect of "wog-bashing" in the Falklands is that it sounds "very exciting," but experience of combat cures him of that. Yes, the ideal of defending the islanders is fine, but he finds the diplomacy inconsistent, the tactics inept, and the politics cynically exploitative. "They shouldn't," he says ruefully, "send naval ratings to university to read History". Perhaps he was lucky to have been spared the general election.

It is fair, I suppose, to point out that David Tinker's disillusion was not widely shared in the Falklands task force, and certainly life can rarely have handed the Royal Court audience so congenial a hero: not one of us, but agreeing with us. There is great dignity, though, in Max Stafford-Clark's production, and Julian Wadham's David is achingly believable.

The sequel consists of five intercut monologues, derived from interviews conducted with people connected with the campaign, but not part of it: Falklands dependants, perhaps. Though the war hangs over everything they say, they offer little actual comment on it; Lieutenant Tinker has given all we are to get in the way of protest, though a reporter with the fleet (Mr Jesson again) does offer a few caustic bemused comments on terminal imperialism.

He also tells us of a book he has "seriously toyed with" (sic), depicting "scenes at the margin of the news," the kind that get "squeezed out" of the usual reports. This speech was not incorporated until the last preview: odd, since it is the key to the piece.

Marion Bailey plays a British teacher who spent 20 unhappily married years in the islands; she vividly sketches the stifling culture of the expatriate establishment, and her own political awakening. It has no bearing on the ethics of the war but it is fascinating.

A South American actress, Stella Maris, plays an Argentine girl living in Britain and amazed at our passivity. An Anglo-Argentine businessman gives Mr Wadham a chance to show he can play oily as well as wide-eyed, but he is the sketchiest presence.

The fullest is Lesley Manville as the CND wife of a task-force sailor: clearly a mésalliance, though we notice that she may marry again, this time a soldier. As much an anomaly in her world as David Tinker in his, she counterbalances him by recalling the xenophobic callousness of her ex-husband and his mates: the sleeping beast that Mrs Thatcher awoke. She is a very recognisable person.

I daresay that a dramatist could have drawn all this material towards a central point: made it centripetal instead of centrifugal. I dare say, but I do not really believe, and I am anyway far from sure that it would be an improvement. Much more than an improvised play like Crystal Clear, this compilation calls in question the necessity of the playwright (though a good one, Louise Page, edited the text).

A television documentary might offer us the same material, but it would be less compelling, since it would deny us the pleasures of impersonation: bold in outline, delicate in shading. I hate making exaggerated claims, and I am sure you never believe them, so let me merely say that this timely and informative entertainment is one of the least boring things in London.

* * *

Willy Russell's Rita, asked in the course of her education to suggest a solution to the problems of staging Peer Gynt, said, "Do it on the radio." It seems a logical way of dealing with all that violent, extravagant action, all those shifting scenes and supernatural personages, but it also seems a cheat. The best thing to do with the unstageable is to stage it, if only for the perversity of the thing; what Dr Johnson should really have said is that a dog walking on its hind legs is excellent showbusiness. (I'm not so sure about a woman preaching.)

The next best, or next worst, thing to radio is a studio theatre such as the Pit, where Ron Daniels solves most of the problems by pretending they do not exist. The opening Norwegian episodes become scenes of Irish peasant life. The African travels are done before a screen bearing sketchy projections of Peer's ship, Memnon's statue and the Sphinx. The last wanderings at death's door are played sternly, in a suggestion of fog.

It is all very efficient, but much of the life of the text has drained out. For all its symbolic complications, the play is a decoration of a fairly simple point about self-realisation; the decorations need to be fun in themselves. Though every scene is played here, many--notably the fight with the Great Boyg--pass by without making any point. It seems rather a short evening; and that is not a compliment.

David Rudkin's curt translation is perfectly good in its own right, but just as it took the couplets of Richard Wilbur and Tony Harrison to bring Molière alive for us, so it will be necessary for somebody to put this mutant folk-satire back into rhyme for its joy to be released in English.

As far as anybody can be miscast as Peer Gynt, Derek Jacobi is. He has some very fine moments--such as his first and last meetings with Solveig--but they are all emotional. As a comedian he is, essentially, knowing: not really at home as the country boy, and too much at home as the rich sophisticate. He looks dashing in his Valentino prophet's robes; Peer should look ridiculous. (The great British Peers--Ralph Richardson, Peter Ustinov, Leo McKern--have all been ungainly: in a plump comic tradition of which the current inheritor is Simon Callow.)

There are some good performances on the circumference: Katy Behean's Solveig, Brenda Peters's Aase (earthy, but underpowered), Sinead Cusack brilliant as the one-night (and one-scene) stand called Ingrid, Josette Simon fine as Anitra and finer still as an amorous herd-girl, Nigel Hawthorne as two messengers of death, one sober and one fantastical.

Speaking of which, two powerful intimations of mortality--Ghelderode's Escorial and Pirandello's The Man with the Flower in His Mouth--are at the Upstream; Tim Woodward is admirable in both, especially the downbeat second.
production_title: The Man with the Flower in His Mouth

records.title: Sir Ralph in Naples
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Portrait of the Artist as a Young Dog
records.body:
Sir Ralph in Naples

THE cherished National Theatre production of Saturday Sunday Monday is still the image most of us have of the plays of Eduardo de Filippo. It was set in a Neapolitan kitchen and it was to a great extent a celebration of food. People in it may have suffered but, emphatically, none of them went hungry. However that play dates from the comparatively equable 1950s. Inner Voices (Lyttelton), the National's new de Filippo, was written soon after the war; and it depicts a Naples with its stomach emptied by occupation and defeat, and its morale depleted by years of Fascism.

It begins all right. In the kitchen of the Cimmaruta family macaroni is being cooked, for breakfast. An amusing neighbour drops in and amusingly wolfs it. There are family tensions, but of course there would be. A spinster aunt is possessive, Father is jealous of Mother, who supports the family by telling fortunes, in suspiciously long private sessions. Their son is a disrespectful lout. We have been here before.

There enters Don Alberto, brother of the guzzling neighbour and his partner in a junk-shop. He seems agreeably whimsical; since he is played by Ralph Richardson, overpoweringly so. He trades jollities about moving the Cimmarutas' furniture around and letting them drop in to move his. (He has, as we discover when the scene shifts, mountains of it.) Suddenly the mood changes. Police swarm on to the stage. Alberto accuses the family of murder. He cannot, however, provide any evidence. Perplexed, he says that he may have dreamed the whole matter.

Naples, we learn from the programme, was full at this time of frivolous accusations. But Alberto's dreams are portent. De Filippo, though mercifully lacking his master's mannerisms, was a disciple of Pirandello; and the Cimmarutas reveal themselves as six characters (and a seventh who has died) who have found an author. They fall in with Alberto's scenario.

In a classic succession of scenes (that is, predictable but thoroughly entertaining) each says in accusation against another. Later they are to combine, to sinister effect, but before that Alberto is to find treachery as frightening on his own doorstep. The play keeps its balance by making him a victim as well as a seer. He is the sanest character in the play, but he gets his facts wrong.

Richardson, of course, is perfect casting. No actor, for a start, can get more out of the vital word 'dream'; none can so delicately kick himself for foolishness that may be wisdom after all; and none can pass so effortlessly from a world of his own to the crispest of everyday comic timing, as demanded by N. F. Simpson's neat translation. He has an old uncle, who, despising of the world, communicates only by spitting and setting off fireworks. (The stage looks wonderful in the green glow of his last Roman candle.) Sir Ralph understands him perfectly, and interprets with the ease of C3PO responding to R2D2.

Mike Ockrent's production radiates authoritatively outwards from its star. There are major performances from Michael Bryant, deceptively harmless, and Robert Stephens, self-tormenting and self-abasing; good work, too, from Marjorie Yates, Glenn Williams and Stephen Hattersley.

Raimonda Gaetani, de Filippo's own designer, supplies a monumental store of bric-a-brac. The author wrote the play, like Alan Ayckbourn, for his own company, and he knocked it off with Ayckbournian speed; the two, despite obvious differences in temperament, have much in common.

'I come no more to make you laugh,' says Richard Griffiths, speaking the prologue to Henry VIII (Stratford), and his subsequent performance in the title role is a triumphant -- though, one hopes, temporary -- repudiation of his clowning past. His Henry is a serious young man working his passage from dependence to despotism. (Benevolent, says the play.)

At first overshadowed by Wolsey and by his queen, but intent on learning, he is erotically aroused by Anne Bullen (as most of the cast remember to pronounce her) and discovers his own strength in wrecking the divorce-court when the cardinals fail to deliver. From there it is an easy step to humiliating Wolsey; and his further progress is only checked by his encounter with Cranmer. 'Poor man, he weeps,' says the King, impressed, not accustomed to emotion in courtiers.

This performance, developed from hints in a distinguished text, is the main prop of Howard Davies's production; though how Mr Davies works out that it shows the transition from absolute to constitutional monarchy beats me. Henry finishes a lot more powerful than he starts. True, he has a council; but he can cow them with an entrance.

Mr Davies's production is the most thoroughgoing Brechtianisation of Shakespeare I have seen (and therefore rather old-fashioned). Ilona Sekacz's music ('How play the musicians?' 'Weill-ly, my lord') underlines or, more frequently, sends woodwindily up. Hayden Griffin's sets, toytown fragments hanging from rails, have belief suspended alongside them. Such patriotic irritants as the coronation procession are disposed of with playful minimal pageantry. Question: if all the ironies assumed by Mr Davies were really present in the text, would he have to labour so hard to bring them to our attention?

The answer is plainly no; but the treatment is generally lively enough to inspire interest if not conviction. Besides, Mr Davies might plead (though I doubt that he would) divided intentions on the part of his authors. This may be the first production to give programme credit to Shakespeare's presumed collaborator, John Fletcher.

An earlier director, Margaret Webster, wrote for example that the character of Buckingham is 'full of salt in his first scene (Shakespeare) and of sugar in his second (Fletcher),' and maybe the production is backing the Bard against his apprentice in accentuating the struggles and parodying the pathos. (David Schofield, previously obeying orders, goes to Buckingham's death with a self-satisfied smirk.)

Katherine never gets off her high horse, and it is fascinating to see how unbendingly regal Gemma Jones can make her. Such apparently harmless supporting acts Sands and the Old Lady (here, less endearingly, a middle-aged lady) are sternly placed at the service of comic purpose, both of them. On the other hand the porter and his men (Roger Hume and Paul Mooney tremulous) are allowed more extensive and affectionate treatment than the christening they precede.

John Thaw's Wolsey, being a prelate persecuted by nobles, lets loose for his lamentations; and John Thaw's authority in the role, like Mr Griffiths's flexibility, returns to front rank the interpretation to the more important matter of technique. They have it; the others are mostly known to be talented but listening to the play, as too often at Stratford these years, is like hearing an opera done entirely by tenors: short-winded ones at that.

I am afraid I still find the script of Woza Albert! (Criterion) flimsy and predictable. But since its parable of Christ returned to South Africa gives plenty of opportunity for acridly humorous depiction of life in the land of the passbook that may not matter. Certainly the performances of Mbongeni Ngema and Percy Mtwa remain dazzling. Their combination of economy, involvement and virtuosity may make them the only performers on the contemporary stage with the right to be called naturalists.

Portrait of the Artist as a Young Dog (King's Head) is a winsome, twitchy and subject to constant infection from an arch piano accompaniment, but Roger Hume's Dylan, who looks like a sulky puzzled Rowan Atkinson, is as young and sexy as D. Thomas said he was.

Compellingly played by the American actress Linda Hunt (a daring and wholly successful piece of casting), Billy is a most engaging creation, and at times powerfully eloquent in a somewhat woody style. But he is forced to bear an impossible dramatic burden. Eventually he reacts to public events in so dramatically unspecific a fashion that we first distrust his intelligence, then cease to believe in him as a character.

records.title: Unexplosive bomb
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: A New Way to Pay Old Debts
records.body:
Unexplosive bomb

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Stratford.

JOSEPH PAPP founded the New York Shakespeare Festival, which gives it away for free in Central Park, and he runs the Public Theatre, which comprises a multitude of auditoria in which have originated many hits.

His exchange plan with the Royal Court (new plays to cross the Atlantic with their original casts) could have beneficent repercussions; and its first round is certainly a tribute to his business acumen. We sent him Top Girls, and he brings us Buried Inside Extra. He got a good deal.

There is something undigested about Thomas Babe's title. It sounds like an amalgam of three others, and was probably meant to. But the play itself is a similar confusion, and this must be a mistake. Part of it is hard-boiled newspaper drama, with the traditional snap. Part is personal relations: the city editor has long been involved with a lady journalist for whom a younger reporter now makes an inconclusive play. An ancient employee of uncertain function turns out to be her father, giving great scope for recrimination and also--since he has a radical past--for Arthur Millerish reminiscence.

Overhanging all this, there is apocalypse: not only is the paper about to fold, but somebody has planted a bomb in the building. An atom bomb. Mr Babe's real theme is probably that lives are carried heedlessly on, whatever the threat. It sounds good as a subject, but it has a way of defeating itself dramatically.

Mr Papp is here his own director, and a lax one. Both the text and the actors are indulged in the belief that they are being terribly smart. The cast chew the lines as if they were scenery. Dixie Carter, a doubly southern name with accent to match, acts like the wisecracking sufferer was going out of style, and almost makes one wish she were. Hal Holbrook, playing a man who has squandered his talent, abuses his own.

Vincent Gardenia and William Converse-Roberts are old and young respectively. Sandy Dennis appears as the editor's drugged and cheated wife, her face funereally wreathed in smiles; she even has nervous teeth. She speaks in a numb monotone that gave me a headache, but that also has an edge of truth. For her one scene Mr Babe has stopped fancying around; we are shown one person's life and fantasies and through them a relationship. After she leaves, everyone goes back to striking attitudes.

* * *

Father and daughter feeding one another's fantasies, that good old American theme of the family lie, can also be found in the late O'Neill play, A Moon for the Misbegotten, revived at Riverside Studios. Ian Bannen resumes the role he played 25 years ago in Long Day's Journey Into Night of James Tyrone, alias the author's elder brother, now drinking and whoring more than ever, struck by an everlasting guilt over his behaviour after his mother's death.

Those of us who are not relatives may feel that O'Neill rattles his skeletons at excessive length, but the heart of the play is with Tyrone's tenant farmer, Phil Hogan, whose scheming blarney shows O'Neill to be a surprisingly good comedian, and his daughter Josie. Their common aim, pursued for widely differing motives, is to get Josie into Tyrone's bed.

O'Neill saw life as composed of two slabs labelled reality and illusion. His characters see themselves and each other with unnatural clarity (not necessarily accuracy) and they keep harping on what they see. Josie, a virgin and in her own words "a lump," pretends to be the lay of the land. Her father believes her; Tyrone, nursing his own dream of big-breasted maternal purity, does not.

We get a tragi-comedy of humours; to each his or her own idee fixe, leading to banal missing on a Chekhovian scale. Add a dash of Irish fatalism (Phil's sons leave home as regularly if not as irreversibly as Synge's riders to the sea) and overlay everything with the remembered melancholy, beyond sorrow, that O'Neill discovered in the great last act of Long Day's Journey.

David Leveaux's production is journeyman work, but it keeps the mood alive; one can think of it, per the title, as a romantic comedy for lost souls. The droop in Frances de la Tour's voice makes her sound very fey when she raises it, but for most of the time she is a creaking and commanding Josie, and she gets good enough support from Ian Bannen and Alan Devlin.

* * *

Massinger's A New Way to Pay Old Debts (Other Place, Stratford) was for centuries the most popular Jacobean play outside Shakespeare. This was partly due to its tidy construction and partly to its high moral tone; virtue is unambiguously triumphant and there is not even much bawdry. But beyond this the character of Sir Giles Overreach, land-grabber and extortioner, was reckoned a great star role, one to make women faint in the gallery.

It is difficult now to see why. Sir Giles is not frightening because he never looks like winning. The play's decent characters get together early, and they are continually a jump ahead of him. Emrys James does what he can to restore the balance, a fine figure of a businessman radiating contempt for the goody-goodies and ne'er-do-wells who make up the supporting cast. "Why?" you keep him expecting to snarl, "must I be surrounded by fools?"

Mr James is technically in complete control, but the only victory he is allowed is the offstage intimidation of a refractory cook. Adrian Noble's production relies heavily on such venerable gags as the loud crash in the wings and the interrupted conspiracy, but usually turns them to account.

He has given the action an anti-morality tinge; characters strut in black and white against a surround of grey, decaying furnishings: you feel that, historically, the victory of the Lord Lovells and Lady Alworths over encroaching capitalism will be short-lived. Miles Anderson plays the spendthrift Wellborn in the most picturesque tatters; thrown out of an inn and laden with luggage, he looks like Lucky in Waiting for Godot.

The other outstanding performance, at the opposite emblematic extreme, comes from Anthony O'Donnell, amazingly furred and feathered as a crooked lawyer. (Which, in the drama of the time, is a tautology.) Colin Sell has composed a very amusing score. It remains a high pleasure to see RSC actors, between grappling with the big one up the road, relaxing in the coterie plays of his successors; easy professionals who wrote verse because it was expected of them, but were in essence good prose technicians. We may yet get round to the pre-Restoration comedies of Shirley and Brome.

The modern actor most at home in the period died last week. I cannot actually imagine a theatre without Derek Godfrey; he joined the Old Vic, making a victorious and prophetic debut as the Renaissance villain in Cymbeline, at the exact moment I commenced my education there. His speciality shifted from villainy to witty innocence; if he had a fault, it was an excess of good taste, but if this could be breached (as for example in Marston's The Malcontent) the gleeful demon was let loose. Earlier this year he was at the top of his form, suave, urbane and mellifluous--in Much Ado About Nothing at the Barbican. Personally and professionally, he will be greatly missed.
production_title: A New Way to Pay Old Debts

records.title: Singin' on the stage
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: The Love of Don Perlimplin and Belisa in the Garden
records.body:
Singin' on the stage

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a 'new' musical at the Palladium

Tommy Steele: A lack of iron and irony.

I FIRST heard Tommy Steele on the subject of Singin' in the Rain in an interview. He quoted the Gene Kelly line, "Dignity, dignity, always with dignity." That, he said, was his own motto as a performer. What he did not mention was that in the film we hear those words from Mr Kelly while watching him get a custard pie in the face.

That interview was a long time ago, and somebody has obviously explained the joke to Mr Steele in the meantime. At the Palladium, in the stage version which he has directed and in which he plays the Kelly role, he delivers the line with a hearty appreciation of its absurdity. He is actually over-emphatic about it; and that goes for much of the production.

Singin' in the Rain is the best film musical ever made, but it is far from the biggest. There is not a full chorus number in it until the Broadway Ballet near the end. True, a dancing girl emerges from a cake to be joined by other dancing girls in a quick shimmy, but neither the dance nor the cake are made a meal of. They are thrown away. But it is difficult to throw a dance number away on a stage, and practically impossible at the Palladium. Harold Fielding, the producer, would probably have anyone who tried it arrested.

The best things are the simplest: a buck-and-wing by Mr Steele and Roy Castle to the tune of Moses Supposes, and Mr Steele's wooing of Danielle Carson with You Are My Lucky Star, a relaxed routine on a smoke-draped stage. The first is funny and athletic, the second funny and romantic.

The original Singin' in the Rain is one of the few musical comedies to deserve both halves of the name. Devised by producer-lyricist Arthur Freed as a tribute to his own song catalogue, it was transformed by its writers, directors and performers into a unity. Mischief infects the love-story of silent-movie star Don Lockwood and ingenue Kathy Selden; music supports the satire on the birth of talkies.

The scene in which the dumb, scheming female star Lina Lamont grapples with a microphone concealed under foliage ("I can't make love to a bush") is as hilarious in the theatre as in the cinema: a tribute to screen writers Betty Comden and Adolph Green, whose giddy dialogue is retained word for word, just as the interpolated clips of Lockwood and Lamont's last silent and first talkie have been reshot frame for frame, and the celebrated choreography of the title-song and the Good Morning trio is duplicated step for step.

Nothing that money and basic competence can do to reproduce the images of film on a stage is lacking. Minor roles have been cast and costumed by Identikit. Sarah Payne's Lina is a very funny replica of Jean Hagen's performance (which was even funnier) in the movie. Where changes have been made, one feels that they were a last resort; who knows how long Messrs Steele and Castle wrestled in rehearsal with American accents before it was decided to allow them the line, "We were kids together in England." (Actually the idea of alien Britishers amid the Hollywood corn works well.) Mr Castle brings off, live before our very eyes, every pratfall, every crash, every somersault of a routine that must have cost Donald O'Connor dozens of takes. It's wonderful. So why isn't it wonderful?

Mainly, because it's too slow. And so are the fade-outs, and the timing of the dialogue, and the story. The tempo of the film is stoked up by the play. And this brings us up against the undodgeable, unanswerable question: Why bother? Why try to reproduce--not reinterpret--a masterpiece that is already permanently there, smiling?

Of course, something in us wants to applaud a good imitation; one is awed at the thought of Mr Steele getting very wet, six nights a week, and being squirted by a fire hydrant at the right remembered moment. But even at this level it has to fail: the pulse of the number depends on camera angles as well as choreography.

Gene Kelly's numbers are great because they are an expression of Gene Kelly. Troupe though he is, Mr Steele is not Mr Kelly: not as a dancer, not as an actor. Mr Kelly grinned a lot, but Mr Steele grins all the time. He deprives the entertainment of its iron and its irony. My heart was lifted only once: at the curtain-call, when the principals came on arm-in-arm, singing the title-song: just like in the movie.

One of the things whose origin is delightfully spoofed in Singin' in the Rain is the dubbed singing voice, a filmic practice that has recently begun to plague the theatre: vide that other transplant, Bugsy Malone, and now Y, the long cursed spectacular that has finally opened at the Piccadilly, now transformed into a rather taking dinner-theatre, complete with performing waiters.

This means that you can avenge yourself on the man who poured champagne all over you by watching him look uncomfortable in a rouged, smirking chorus-line. The food is better than expected, and the show itself is not quite the prophesied disaster. The costumes are great and the corps execute a terrific charleston (charlestons tend to be terrific), preceded by something they call the Black Bottom; London's intended answer to the Crazy Horse has not got its accents sorted out.

A modest decadence is the apparent aim (men cracking whips at women, that sort of thing), but it is often scuppered by inadequate performers, numbers that fail to be sexy because they have no climax, and a structure that is arbitrary even by floor-show standards. "I've got some news for you," says the head-waiter, in English unfortunately. "We're going to Venice"; and suddenly we are into an eighteenth-century soft-porn number.

One of the Venetian ladies creates a sensation by opening her mouth in song, and the men act shocked. Well they might, for out of it is coming the voice of Barbra Streisand. This is not a joke, understand; we are meant to be impressed. Just occasionally a lady brandishes a microphone, and may be assumed to be doing her own chirping.

The star turns are Suzy Casabianca, a semi-stripper, who can dance, and Arturo Brachetti. He can dance too; he can be his own partner in a tango, since he nonchalantly combines the skills of illusionist and female impersonator; so nonchalantly that he is in danger of disappearing even when that is not the point of the trick.

* * *

Ghelderode's Escorial is not a play you expect to encounter twice in a lifetime, but I caught it (at the Grove, Hammersmith) for the second time this month. It blends King Lear with Macbeth: a monarch, hearing that the queen, my lord, is dying, goes into a role-reversal act with his jester. It provokes portentous playing.

It is coupled, in Michael Batz's production, with Lorca's bliss, officially The Love of Don Perlimplin and Belisa in the Garden, a light-footed and compassionate study of infatuated cuckoldry, a comic theme brought with superb delicacy to tragedy. The staging is the kind that assumes a play to be automatically the richer for having its actors' faces covered in white paint and all its lines whispered, intoned or sneered. Mr Batz plays leads in both pieces; his Don Perlimplin is passable, but his fool counts as gross directorial self-indulgence.

There is a more effective use of stylisation in Tennessee Williams's Suddenly Last Summer (New End); eerie, insistent music and white-net curtains hung with trailing plants set the tone, and for this piece--the Williams that moves from frozen daiquiris to cannibalism--the tone is right.

records.title: Pleasant warmpth
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Pleasant warmpth

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a musical--and an opera.

I ALWAYS approach Fiddler on the Roof (revived at the Apollo Victoria) with apprehension: something you may put down to a phenomenon known as Jewish anti-Semitism.

Knowing the territory from the inside, I dread being smothered in sentiment; and nothing looks more sentimental in prospect than a Broadway musical whose theme-song is called Tradition, whose setting is a Jewish village in Tsarist Russia, whose chief character is an orthodox patriarch with the endearing habit of chatting up the Deity, and whose narrative runs to three love-stories, one of them culminating in an onstage wedding.

I should have learned by now. Fiddler is an immensely powerful show. Its climax, as must be generally known, is the eviction of the villagers from their home of Anatevka. Many, including our hero, Tevye the dairyman, set off for America. Among the things created by their descendants was the American musical, of which Fiddler on the Roof is one of the culminating achievements. In a sense the show is its own happy ending. It obviously had to be written sometime; that it was written and staged so well is a blessing.

I can think of only three and a half things to hold against the show. (1) In accordance with Broadway and Hollywood tradition, the word Jew is hardly mentioned; I am not sure whose susceptibilities this is meant to protect. (2) The Russian authorities are amazingly gentlemanly, and their idea of a pogrom is to knock over a couple of tables; the average family regularly inflicts more damage on itself. (3) Some tiresome gossip scenes pad out the second act.

My half complaint concerns the divided nature of Jerry Bock's score. The Hebraic part is fine and stirring; the rest is conventional 1960s Broadway. The matchmaker song is really a jazz waltz, and what would Anatevka know of jazz or indeed of waltzes? But it is a delightful example of a delightful form, so who's counting.

Joseph Stein's book is a remarkable piece of craftsmanship. The affairs of Tevye's three marriageable daughters are cunningly overlapped, with the larger drama kept looming behind them. Take for example the wedding song, Sunrise Sunset. It crystallises the present moment; it enables the parents to recall the past; and it sets the next couple dreaming of their own future.

It also presents a piece of ritual that will survive, but whose significance is about to be altered by both history and geography. A young radical is brought on to criticise his elders' stoic acceptance of their fate; he is obviously right, but the authors are not out to attack their grandparents. They are concerned to record and to admire. They present history; something the musical--a broad form--can do without embarrassment.

I once saw a film cartoon about a singer whose manager despaired of his lack of emotion; "What you need," he kept crying, "is warmpth." Fiddler obviously has plenty of warmpth, but it is not stifling; Tevye never forgives the daughter who has married out. The show's most memorable image is of his rejection of her, a slowed version of his characteristic movement: arms upstretched and bent, belly forward, legs astride, everything swaying, tradition.

Topol has, over the years, grown right into the role; he makes every gag and every monologue a part of the man. The rest of the cast are ordinary, and Maria Charles as the matchmaker embodies one's worst fears of the show as a whole.

In many ways the revival is tacky; in the giant pavilion of rip-off that is the Apollo Victoria, Boris Aronson's Chagallian sets look panto-mime. But Jerome Robbins's choreography retains its glory: this is not obviously a dance-musical, but scene after scene explodes into motion. And the bottle-dance--four men waddling at a wedding--is a wonder of the modern stage.

* * *

I have had a musical week. I went to Mozart's Idomeneo as a treat (my first time at Glyndebourne), but I can justify it as a means of keeping tabs on Trevor Nunn, making his debut as an opera director. Maybe I am projecting my own reaction on to him, but I felt him becoming increasingly excited by the story (more perhaps than he had expected to be), increasingly delighted with the problems of telling it.

Faced with a line-up of self-sacrificing Ancient Greeks, expressing themselves in monologue and duologue, he found a Racinian severity and--in Philip Langridge and Carol Vaness--Racinian passion. This figure has little in common with his recent theatre work, which has tended towards overflow, but it recalls his studio Macbeth in its use of simple techniques to gain terrifying effects.

The sea-monster is represented by a huge black shadow, encroaching from the front stalls. It sweeps over the huddled crowd on stage, to be succeeded by a black and menacing white light. Drama directors are often accused of sacrificing musical values, but I have never listened to a score more intently. I have certainly never been so held by recitative. The Japaneserie of this production has been over-stressed; many of its scenic motifs are authentically Cretan.

* * *

Stiff upper-lippery returns with The Winslow Boy (Lyric, Hammersmith), Rattigan's meticulously well-made play about the cadet accused of theft and expelled from a naval academy out of which he seems to be well out. It still grips, less from its plot-mechanics than from its determination to be fair, to subject even professions of decency to decent scrutiny.

The Winslow boy's close examination by the eminent barrister plays less well when you know the upshot, but Ian Hogg is ferociously lionised, the least silky of silks. Buried in it all is the portrait of a marriage; Barbara Jefford is beautifully unobtrusive at the start, beautifully obtrusive as both her doubts and her excitement increase. Winslow pere, who sacrifices many of his family prospects to his quest for justice, might be a spikier personage than Alan MacNaughtan presents, but what he does he does finely.

The play, I think, comes down on his side, but it is to its credit that it never stops worrying. All that worries me is that it has--as John Whiting said of one of his own plays--no private parts: none of the torments of The Browning Version, and after. Michael Rudman directs it; maybe it takes an American to make this so emphatically a play for England.

Arnold Wesker has never lacked warmpth. His Annie Wobbler (Birmingham Rep Studio) is, in a modest way, loaded with it. It is a sequence of three monologues for ladies who share the author's initials. The fullest and, after a disconcerting start, the subtlest, is for a lady novelist who knows she should have opinions, but is not sure what they are.

Nichola McAuliffe, a young actress with a robust talent for self-satire (and also, though it is not used here, a robust singing voice), plays all roles; she starts with competent senile impersonation, goes on to a notable appearance in black undies, and a ginger wig, and ends stark and stunning as the scribe.

I may return next week to Undrowned (Prince of Wales), which shows mayhem on the District Line. If you're planning to be murdered on a train, better take the Orient Express and go out in style.

records.title: Sin of fawnication
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Sin of fawnication

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

DIRECTORS may talk about approaching classic plays as if they had just received them in the mail, but audiences, who are more important, know different and -- of course -- better. We approach old and new plays in totally distinct frames of mind.

Most attempts to put a classic into modern dress, or otherwise make it relevant, are jokes -- conscious or otherwise -- at the expense of the play. I am not against this; I am all in favour of jokes. But a joke has to be shared, and those of us who have never seen the play before are in no position. The desire of any audience, meeting an old play for the first time, is to get a good look at it. Once we know the territory, we can all enjoy defacing it.

This is of course the preamble to a consideration of two revivals. The good news first: at the Cottesloe John Marston's The Fawn is given, probably for the first time since its premiere in 1606. Marston's critical stock, low for centuries, has risen dramatically; damned by the Victorians as a malodorous cynic, he has been accepted by moderns as a satirist, a sexual obsessive, in fact one of us.

But The Fawn was Marston's last comedy, and it is remarkably good-tempered. It has a lovely artificial structure. The elderly Duke of Ferrara seeks marriage with the daughter of the Duke of Urbino, and sends his comely but unromantic young son as ambassador. He himself follows disguised, and is soon devoting himself to forwarding his son's match instead of his own. He also observes the sinister follies of Urbino's courtiers, and encourages them. This makes him very popular. They call him Faunus, because he fawns.

This is a great English comedy, in the line of Love's Labour's Lost. The court fool proclaims 'a figure called in art Ironia,' and irony is the whole technique of the play, almost its subject. Marston grasped that there is nothing as funny as self-satisfaction, especially when coupled -- as it logically must be -- with self-deception. Faunus watches the characters blowing bubbles, and he hardly has to prick them; they explode of themselves. Most of their offences are against women; in the end, they are all found guilty by a Court of Cupid, and consigned to a Ship of Fools. Urbino's Duke himself proves the biggest fool of all, complacency steering his daughter into marriage with the wrong man; an old device but a perennially good one.

Giles Block's production gets the play exactly right. We watch it, as it must have been written, with a constant smile that erupts into frequent chuckles and occasional belly-laughs. Poppy Mitchell contributes a fine and soothing courtyard: a paved floor with matching wall, a green-leaved tree begirt with cushions, a blue sky alight with stars and fireworks. (In a just world The Trojan War Will Not Take Place would have been done in this theatre, on this kind of set and with this kind of wit.) The ensemble work is the best at the National in moons; the actors seem to enjoy the play, and they make the dialogue dance.

Bernard Lloyd, playing the Fawn with acerbic joviality, sets the tone. He is seconded by Peter Needham's bitter fool, and countered by Basil Henson's ducal one: a delightful study in sententiousness. His second is an ostentatiously silent flatterer who in Roger Gartland's performance looks a bit drunk as well.

The most spectacular of the gulls is James Hayes as a pathologically jealous nobleman; he has a great scene hanging from the wall by his fingers, agog to observe his wife's infidelities. Karl Johnson, who woos all available women, and Edward de Souza, who claims to bed them, make a good duo, one piping, the other booming. Jessica Turner heads a posse of hurt and sensible ladies; as the princess Dulcimel, Miranda Foster is the most delicious thing to arrive on a London stage this year.

* * *

Now then. John Gay's Polly (Cambridge Theatre Company on tour, seen by me at Oxford Playhouse) is a sequel to The Beggar's Opera. It has more plot than its predecessor which, in view of Gay's talents and limitations, is no good thing. The epigrams remain ('tis only for poor people to be brave and desperate, who cannot afford to live') but they have turned mechanical. Polly Peachum is now a sentimentally virtuous heroine, still in pursuit of her Macheath who has turned pirate, following on transportation to the Caribbean.

The Caribbean. That gives the fatal cue for updating. The songs are buried beneath a calypso-and-reggae beat; the story is turned into an anti-colonial tract. Where The Fawn lets us observe a timeless pattern of human conduct, Polly belabours us with liberal sentiments we all share anyway.

I don't know if Polly is a viable piece, but she is stillborn here. The prevailing note of the performances is aggressive slovenliness; Martin Connor, in drag as a handbag-swinging Mrs Ducat, is the only actor to combine attack and precision. Gay's funny prologue ('Musick might tame and civilise wild beasts, but 'tis evident it never yet could tame and civilise musicians') is replaced by a representation of his funeral, supervised by a bored and venal priest. Doubtless there was corruption among the eighteenth century clergy, but I don't see what call we have to be so smug about it. David Pownall did the rewrites.

* * *

Joseph George Caruso, an American, did the rewrites for Pinero's The Magistrate which he has re-titled Little Lies (Wyndham's). He has cut some characters, changed a male hotelier to a French bawd (substituted, that is, a cliche for a cipher) and added a thin thread of judicial corruption. You can see why he bothered -- it's money for old rope -- but the management's motives are more obscure: what they save in actors' salaries they must cough up in royalties. Every so often I heard a racy line I thought might be new, but it always turned out to be echt Pinero.

Mr Caruso has weakened Pinero's ending by way of giving greater prominence to the magistrate's wife, she who lops five years off her child's age in order to conceal her own. This is ill-advised since Connie Booth in the role is as out of place as nuts in the drawing-room.

John Mills, as the beak lured into dissipation by his strangely pubescent stepson, is a sweet and agile old party, without much dignity to lose. Tony Tanner's production seems to think the late Victorian period funny in itself, and the solemn love-play of Malcolm Sinclair and Angela Scoular is some vindication. The unsinkable original provides some fun.

To come back to timeliness: if Wednesday's vote had gone differently there would, I guarantee, have been a queue for the rights of Brendan Behan's anti-hanging classic The Quare Fellow. Now is the time for somebody (Bill Bryden at the Cottesloe would be ideal) to demonstrate his integrity and do it anyway.

records.title: But what comes after?
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
But what comes after?

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

SNOO WILSON writes great entrances. His new comedy Loving Reno (Bush) begins with Philip Donaghy walking in through the double doors of what the programme tells us is a private airport lounge in Florida. Mr Donaghy looks dazzling, being dressed for polo; he is also moustachioed and oily all over, especially on the crown of his head. He is a Latin American stage magician. Tony Reno is his name.

The play lines him up with his wife and the mother of his children: two different ladies. These children, now grown, are twins, both girls. Reno has exploited them: used them as assistants in his act, and also used them sexually. One of them hates him for it; the other loves him and wants to marry him. She's retarded.

All the women in the play seem to have suffered from paternal abuse. Reno is macho, indeed machissimo; for him, male genes carry the power and the glory, especially the power. The play is a cool blast against patriarchy, and it makes its points with satisfying neatness.

Having made them, though, it has little left to do but talk. Mr Wilson may bring his character on in a storm, but he becalms them once they have arrived. There is a plot -- involving an undercover agent hired by Reno's wife to shadow and expose him -- but it cuts little mustard. Anyone remembering the ceaseless activity -- verbal, physical and intellectual -- of Mr Wilson's The Glad Hand (my favourite play of the past 10 years) is likely to be disappointed. He is almost the wittiest playwright we have, and this play is a good listen, but there is something closed-off about it. It is presumably the product of Mr Wilson's recent year in America, but I suspect he would have written it much the same if he had never been.

If unforced arrogance makes a star, Mr Donaghy (who is also very funny) should now be one; certainly it makes a Reno. He must have had a daunting time in rehearsal, being directed by Mr Wilson who wrote the role and Simon Callow who could well have played it. Judy Elrington gives an on-off performance as the soberer sister but Cassie Stuart tucks into the kewpie-doll nympho (of whom it is said that she must have cost a fortune in broken-down hotel doors). Anna Raitt and Tony Guilfoyle are worth their weight.

* * *

Mr Wilson was one of the first fringe playwrights, class of '68, and he sometimes seems likely to be among the last, his contemporaries having mostly moved on to larger stages and his juniors having hardly made it to any stages at all. This means he has spent 15 years as a member of an endangered species. Fringe theoreticians were prophesying the death of the playwright when he started, and they are at it again. Their temple is the ICA, now specialising in works that claim to yoke the creativity of the stage performer to that of the visual artist. Which, you must admit, sounds absolutely fine.
