The trouble is how it looks, or at least how it looks after the first 10 minutes which is as long as most of us are prepared to spend gazing at a set. The art then has to reside in the actors, who are liable to swan about making elliptical passes at the incomprehensible, occasionally surfacing with a meaning that seems, literally, too banal for words. They may look pretty doing it but it hardly makes an evening.

Rococo, brought to the ICA by the Rational Theatre Company, meets us verbalists more than half-way; it is full of chat. It also suggests that performance art (a term I have been trying, lucklessly, to fend off) is developing its own cliches; we get a surround of mirrors, and a white-clad actress who stands dimly surveying (accusing?) us before the lights go up. She then meets a flock of old-style stage aristocrats who draw her into their world where they proceed to bemuse, humiliate and seduce her; her experience is a bit like that of Lewis Carroll's Alice, and a lot like those of the real, virtuous heroines of Jean Anouilh. Her tormentors fancy themselves, and their dialogue sounds like a poor pastiche of Restoration comedy, delivered by actors who don't know how. The Glasgow Citizens' Theatre do this kind of thing all the time, often throwing in a good text as well. At times the show justifies its pretensions and makes a witty visual statement, as when a pinky lady haunts a white gentleman into taking all his clothes off.

A lady called Sandy Powell (can you hear her, mother?) is the designer; Jim Whiting, guest artist, created a couple of ingenious mechanical contraptions. You can get good trick effects at the Palladium too. A handout says that the show 'supposes a society in a state of advance future shock,' but I wouldn't have guessed. Rococo and the Wilson play are really in the same bind: what do you do after you have astonished the audience? The prophets are of course right in saying that most written drama is deadly, but the playwright still has the best chance of following through. We want shock, and then logic, and then more shock.

* * *

Jukebox (Astoria) is a rapid-fire, one-chorus-and-off, pop-music retrospective. It starts with cavemen, the theme from 2001, and a voice telling us that rock music started long ago, in a galaxy far, far away. This is not true, even if it ought to be; meanwhile, the unabashed plagiarism gives the theatre the air of one of those outlying cinemas that mysteriously survive through endless programming of what used to be cult movies.

A jukebox duly materialises; emanating from it is the sound of Teresa Brewer singing 'Music, Music, Music.' She is brutally silenced. This may not mean much to you, it may even be aesthetically just, but that 1950 song was the first pop record I ever knew, and I resented it. I resented some of what followed even more. Behind the performers there are projections. An all-purpose 1960s protest-song is backed by a blown-up photograph of a real, agonised Vietnamese child. But it's all right, because the child disappears in time for the next number which is 'Oh Happy Day.'

Not all of the show is that offensive, but it is all that mindless. This is not always a fault; it suits the bubble idiocies of vintage rock'n'roll and it cannot do much harm to the machine-gloomy, sex-on-the-percussionness of the 1970s, though when the earnestness starts selling it needs resenting. As for contemporary British pop, do they come much more American perhaps than Boy George? This sounds like bitching, but does the choreographer, if I may abuse the old quip, is possibly better than it looks.

* * *

For an antidote there is Bertha Reading. Every inch a Lady (King's Head), the inches extending out rather than up. (She does a brisk balletic interlude as Sugar Plum Fairy who seems to have overdosed on the sugar.) Miss Reading is where critics go to enjoy themselves, a jazz-queen who can be blowsily hilarious or rollingly emotive. She should know better; though, then, to sing Shirley Bassey dirges, especially Send in the Clowns. Her accompanist is Jules Rubens, a venerable imp who looks like a bit of old Soho and can swing with his left hand while knocking out saloon-bar basses with his right.

* * *

The world which has been waiting for two whole weeks to know what I really thought of Michael Sloan's thriller Underground (Prince of Wales), may now unbate its breath; it's tough to admit but I agreed with everybody else, especially about the unlikelihood of supposed strangers conversing in the Tube, especially when the first line is 'Why have we stopped?' Then there is a tramp who forces his demented conversation on everybody but waits for gaps in the dialogue to do it, just like a character in a play.

All one can do to the cast of TV favourites, led by Raymond Burr, is commiserate with them on their woodenness. One might perhaps get angry with Peter Wynarde; he can still put on a turn of speed impressive enough for us to wonder just what he thinks he has been doing with his career.

records.title: Errors of comedy
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Errors of comedy

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

WHEN he was very young, Kenneth Tynan laid down that no really first-rate director could be at home with broad comedy. He was wrong, of course, but I find his opinion of some comfort when considering Adrian Noble's Stratford production of The Comedy of Errors. Mr Noble is a director of proven brilliance, but his first major attempt at drama designed to provoke laughter is catastrophic.

There are some touches that are truly Noble. One is the lost, questing arrival in Ephesus of the visiting Antipholus and Dromio. Coming through a door in the white wall of Ultz's set, they appear dazed, almost blind. This of course is not a funny moment, nor meant to be. When the farce begins -- when master and man are mistaken for their respective twins -- Mr Noble works diligently at it. He must have done no end of research into traditional comic routines. Some of it showed in his production of King Lear with Antony Sher's clown-compendium performance as the Fool. The one thing that performance was not was amusing; nor did it need to be. But The Comedy of Errors does need, and this production is all technique and no humour. It keeps stepping on its own laughs. Blows and pratfalls, of which there are many, are accompanied by tympani-rolls in the orchestra. The pulling of a Dromio's nose provokes ruder noises in the pit. Pedantry, the RSC's recurring vice, here takes a new form. This, the production seems to be saying, is clowning; aren't you impressed?

Design and music run the show. Nigel Hess draws for his tunes, pleasingly enough, on Scott Joplin, Vincent Youmans and the Keystone Kops. In the scene of Pinch the conjuror he takes over (or the play throws in the sponge) and we get a number. Pinch is painted yellow, and the text does indeed say that he has a saffron face. But it makes no mention of the Dromios having red noses, or of the Antipholi being blue. They look like Atlantines (who, old Eagle readers will remember, were the good Venusians oppressed by the green Treens). Farce works by putting recognisable people in extreme situations. I don't recognise anyone with a blue face. I even jib at a heroine (Jane Booker) whose hair has been tied up like an ice-cream cone, however stylish.

The performances display some skill and, in the case of Paul Greenwood, who plays a scene hanging upside-down from a window, intrepidity. Peter McEnery is brisk, Henry Goodman earthy, Richard O'Callaghan nicely woeful and Zoe Wanamaker, trimly volcanic, nearly creates a character. Joseph O'Conor and Timothy Kightley are solid elders. There are some graceful notes: the final reconciliation, and an earlier rapprochement between master and servant when the former has beaten the latter and, penitent, gives him a cuddle.

There is also some atrocious verse-speaking, especially from the Duke. While they wait to mature into comedy directors (and it is not just Mr Noble's problem -- John Caird with The Twin Rivals is about the only young director in or out of the RSC to have displayed any sustained lightness of touch), Stratford chiefs could practise counting the number of beats in iambic pentameter. They used to know how.

* * *

Shakespeare festivals seem doomed to be erratic. The Canadian one at Stratford, Ontario, is still, after a period of upheaval, trying to find itself. It remains the best Shakespeare stage in the world: a beautifully proportioned timbered platform edged and surmounted by steps but with plenty of flat space around a simple central facade. It is timeless; but it lends itself with dangerous ease to archaic production. Men-at-arms may line its perimeter in stolid ranks, or a play be reduced to a series of entrances down right and exits up left.

Two of the three plays I saw this year succumbed. Macbeth had some good notions about witches but sank around a featureless performance by Nicholas Pennell. Another Briton, Richard Cottrell, directed a more efficient but equally uninspired Richard II, distinguished only by the performance of one of our great lost actors, Brian Bedford. Most Richards play for irony, but Mr Bedford's was the completest tease I have seen. Having sent the whole of England up rotten, he turned on himself; "for God's sake let us sit upon the ground" was a self-conscious bright idea. How much was Richard having fun, and how much the actor, was difficult to say but the role yielded a surprising amount to the approach. A flash of royal lightning, though, was needed to round it out.

This Stratford is not only, or even primarily, a haven for expatriates. It was left to the theatre's director, John Hirsch, European-born but Canadian-nurtured, to redeem matters with an admirable As You Like It. This not only filled the stage but animated it. There was a strong contrast between court and forest: the first a finely detailed sadistic tyranny, the second near to paradise. Probably too near: everyone looked well insulated, and some of the play's sting was drawn.

But there was delight in the playing; led by Roberta Maxwell (an unusually intent Rosalind, considerably less than common tall), actors who had been dullards in the other plays shone with spirit and intelligence, acting on and through the lines in a manner the current RSC rarely achieves. They revealed that a Canadian school of Shakespeare might, after all, exist; and that it would not be all that different from a good English school.

Back to Warwickshire, and how. The Dillen (old Midland, apparently, for runt) takes the National Theatre promenade style a step further: indeed, a whole route-march. It starts in the Other Place and finishes there; but for three hours in between it takes itself and us on a tour of the district. The company is swollen by a hundred local amateurs who pick peas in a field, run races, punt or fish on the Avon (and, in one case, get thrown into it) and, as night falls, form exhilarating torchlight processions.

The play itself, adapted by Ron Hutchinson from a book by Angela Hewins about the long hard life of her grandfather, runs thin. Barry Kyle's production, aiming to forge a link between theatre and town, does so more through his method than his subject. Actually, though most of the story is set in and around Stratford, the local fields are most effectively used to represent the trenches of the First World War. The Somme can never have been this green, but to see men disappearing in the long grass, never to return, is an extraordinary experience. Mr Kyle reveals something already known to the Greeks and to the druidical fringe group Welfare State: we have completely misjudged the nature of drama in the open air. We think of it as pastoral. Actually it is -- or should be -- epic.

* * *

Cowardice (Ambassadors), by Sean Mathias, is about a brother and sister -- he a would-be playwright, she an actress -- obsessed with Noel Coward and Gertrude Lawrence. Why with them rather than with any other stars is never explored; nor is much else. A couple of songs accurately mimic the odd shapelessness of Coward's own: the words pulling the music, the rhymes pulling the words. Ian McKellen is monotonously little-boy-lost; Janet Suzman, allowed to range more freely, does so with vigour.

records.title: Kings and drag queens
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Kings and drag queens

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and New York.

WHEN critics write the regulation essay on what they did in the hols, they offer glowing accounts of companies encountered abroad of extraordinary vision, audacity, intellect and good manners. Sometimes they are taken up on this. So comes the Teatro Colletivo di Parma to the Riverside Studios in a season of very free Shakespeare. The Parma company offered a joky Macbeth set in a film-studio, the protagonists as narcissists; the highlight was the apparition of Banquo, like the head of John the Baptist on a platter. Some of the action was impenetrable, but most was imaginative and good-humoured. Their Henry IV (ends tonight) is more substantial. The audience sits on three sides, a privileged few at café tables, which the actors--eight of them--sometimes share. All the world's a tavern.

That is very much the angle. The court scenes are raced through. A man who comes on wearing a crown and a carpet must be the king. Presumably he is saying, `so shaken as we are, so wan with care.' He certainly looks careworn. Bad news is brought to him by maimed messengers crawling like biblical serpents.

Confusion descends for those without Italian (and, I gather, for those with it as well.) We become aware of motorbikes racing excitingly round the stage. That roaring fat man with his trousers down must be Falstaff. Certainly he has the presence for it. Watching him later, beaming in his braces, calling himself `Johnny,' we know him to be--what shall I say?--the real Marconi. That mounted tearaway has to be Prince Hal.

The roistering scenes are lovingly, riotously done, Falstaff's hearers almost choking on their spaghetti as they encourage him in his lies. Romantic pop songs back the revels; Falstaff gets rejected with Peachum's cynical song from `The Threepenny Opera.' All is as exciting and immediate as the travellers told. And it's a play; not just an essay on one.

But we don't have to feel inferior. Shakespeare in English and Shakespeare in foreign are different animals. Nobody cares if a translation is mucked about with. A British production seeking this degree of license would either have to play against the text to a degree fatiguing to both actors and audience, or paraphrase, which is an abomination. There are those rhythms, prose or verse, and we are stuck with them. They can take their revenge in strange ways.

* * *

Howard Davies's RSC production of Macbeth (Barbican) is as sober as the Italian is high-spirited, but it has a similarly disapproving view of its hero. Bob Peck's Macbeth is a soldier, and to be a soldier here is to be a thug. Those in the opening scene go on fighting long after the battle's lost . . . and won. (I learned that pause from this production's witches.) Mr Peck, dour and determined, implicitly denies Macbeth any scruples and the play any real development. The production puritanically denies him a visible ghost. A gibber at, but he hardly seems capable of imagining one for himself.

Despite the discrepancy between what he shows and what his lines say, Mr Peck speaks the verse superbly; he explores it, inhabits it, makes sense of it, never loses its shape. Vocally and physically, he has the power to occupy space. So do many of the others: David Waller, Pete Postlethwaite, Malcolm Storry make us feel Duncan's complacence, Banquo's suspicion, Macduff's grief, as fresh things.

There is an overpowering devil-porter (Geoffrey Freshwater), who dismisses comedy with a leer and a caper; and, in Sara Kestelman, a Lady Macbeth whose command is instant and whose crack-up is harrowing. There are also two percussionists who, playing Nigel Hess's score, seem to have usurped the witches' place as governors of the action. Chris Dyer's skeletal set is surly but shapely. If Mr Davies can bring himself to like his characters, he will be a fine Shakespeare director.

* * *

Terry Hands's production of another Elizabethan murder story, the anonymous Arden of Faversham (Pit), is admirable stuff, funny, gripping, persuasive. Everyone in it seems capable of mayhem, even Christopher Benjamin's Arden the victim, solid in a sombrero.

Jenny Agutter is a white-hot adulteress, though the love-scenes falter. John Bowe and David Bradley as the cut-throats (six tries all botched: a disgrace to an efficient Tudor profession) develop their brokers' men from `The Swan-Down Gloves.' A superb invention has their offstage voices circling the terrified servant Michael (Mark Rylance), who emerges as the most fully drawn character in the piece.

* * *

What did I do on my holidays? I failed to see La Cage aux Folles, which promises to be the most successful American musical in years. It opened at the Palace, New York's Palladium, tonight. I could not get into its try-out run in Boston, because there was not a seat to be had through press-agents or even authors. When booking opened in New York, there were queues round the block, and--a remarkable sign of confidence--the cast album was recorded two weeks before the first night. I went to the session, to get a sneak hearing of some of the songs, and to meet the director and composer.

When I arrived, a song called `A Little More Mascara' was in progress: a big celebratory number in which the singers, while descending a staircase, tells of how terrible everything feels until the make-up has been applied and the world can be faced again. A probable show-stopper, it bears the unmistakable composer's autograph of Jerry Herman, who also wrote those perennial matron-vehicles `Hello Dolly' and `Mame.' The only difference here is that the star is male; the character is a drag-queen. It represents a certain kind of musical number coming out.

Arthur Laurents, the director, says that he pulled `every trick in the book' on this number. A slight, outspoken man with his own successes as playwright and musical librettist, he speaks of the show, with its two middle-aged homosexual heroes, as `a real love story, which most musicals only pretend to be' and says that he liked the film, but did not admire it. He thought it condescending and sometimes camp: defining camp as `getting easy laughs from screaming queens,' and claiming to have eliminated it from the show.

I doubt, even so, if the show will prove radical enough for militant gays. Even if it only reflects an already changing climate (Laurents admits: `we are not doing anything devastatingly new') that is a kind of health.

I wonder how it will cope with the French provincial atmosphere of its original, and how music will affect its tight and traditional farce structure. (It was a play before it was a movie.) But I like the source material, and the people concerned, and I wish them well.

I did see a revival of Mame, with Angela Lansbury in her original role; it is machine-made, but she gives it strength and wit. At the opposite extreme of musical resurrection there was The Cradle Will Rock, a social-protest expressionist musical of the Thirties. (Stand-out song: `Joe Worker Gets Gypped.') It is a museum-piece that gets up out of its case and lives: New Half Moon, this is for you.

My holiday discovery I almost blush to reveal. Years after everyone else, I learned to love Sam Shepard. He has traditionally been praised for his presentation of American archetypes. Fool for Love--a mysterious comedy set in the seediest of last-chance motels and featuring violence, memory, jealousy, incest and more violence--shows that he actually works outwards from passion. The play is as self-contained and as unashamed as a vintage Pinter.

A couple of words for the lyricist Ira Gershwin, who died last week: they are `sly' and `charming.'

records.title: Kraus the Grouse
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Kraus the Grouse

ROBERT CUSHMAN on official and Fringe productions.

AS far as the theatre is concerned, the Edinburgh Festival's theme of `Vienna 1900' has so far meant a brace of plays in which the glories of the Austro-Hungarian Empire have crumbled before our eyes. The stages have shimmered with old gilt; and also of course with old guilt.

In the Assembly Hall, the Glasgow Citizens' Company have, with typical generosity, been offering The Last Days of Mankind. This piece has defied even their unflappability; their version, weighing in at four hours, is a mere sliver of an 800-page original. That original, a chronicle of the First World War, was written more or less contemporaneously, and published complete in 1922.

Its author, Karl Kraus, was an Austrian journalist who hated journalism. The main purpose of his play was to expose the lies and distortions of the patriotic papers, along with the fatuities of the politicians and soldiers they served. Much of the play consists of direct quotation, many of the characters are animated topical cartoons. I apologise if I sound as if these are things I have known all my life. Like all the other reviewers, I learnt them only last week from the Festival brochure.

That same brochure says of the piece, `It has half of Europe as its stage.' That sounds exciting, doesn't it? It also sounds tricky, and the solution adopted by Robert David Macdonald (who as usual directs his own translation) is to set all the scenes where Kraus set some of his: in a restaurant. My recurring impression of Austrian drama as being just one long meal is given spectacular confirmation.

Of course the characters do not just eat and drink; they also read the news, and they discuss it. From time to time the scene is transported, gentles, to the battlefield, with no change of decor. The transitions are seamless: so smooth that it took me some time to realise what was going on. Admittedly, I had a bad seat.

It is impressive. What else would you expect of a four-hour epic from a company to whom flamboyant gesture, satirically honed, is second nature? But it is not, despite an abundance of picturesque sex and violence, very enjoyable. Kraus, though obviously a pungent pamphleteer, had no observable gift for story or character; and the production concept sacrifices whatever interest might have accrued from constant changes of locale or personnel.

The people are identified as `a Patriot and Optimist' or `a Reader of Newspapers.' The only one allowed a name is a figure representing the author himself, called in the cast-list Kraus the Grouse, and played by Giles Havergal, who--since he is kept sitting throughout--it is tempting to re-christen Giles the Piles.

He observes the follies and cruelties of humanity and comments on them. He is always right. The play goes on (and on and on and on) making the same point. It is a good point, and Kraus makes a better fist of symbolising and lampooning 1914-18 military lunacy than did O'Casey in The Silver Tassie, though he falls far short of Joan Littlewood in Oh What a Lovely War. But it does not amount to drama.

At the end--and after more loud bangs than I have ever heard before in a theatre, some of them dislodging unnameable substances from the rafters of the Assembly Hall--the world is destroyed, i.e., the restaurant closes forever. God, who apparently resides on Mars, declares himself unwilling to go on picking up the tab--at least he, coming over a celestial Tannoy, is audible; most of the cast are defeated by the hall's notorious acoustics.

* * *

Also living in Vienna in 1900, and dying there by his own hand in 1903, was Otto Weininger, an apparently brilliant Jew who hated Judaism. He was 23 when he killed himself. Hitler approved of him. The Soul of a Jew (a less grandiose title than The Last Days of Mankind, but not much) is his story, dramatised by an Israeli playwright, Yehoshua Sobol.

One of the Jewish things that Weininger hated was nascent Zionism, and Mr Sobol has understandably given this great prominence. The play raised a storm in Israel. But it distracts from what should be the play's main theme. Otto's self-hatred is a common neurosis carried to fascinating--and historically ominous--extremes. But neuroses are difficult subjects.

The temptation is to cut the protagonist's psyche into neat gobbets and then distribute them about the stage: one supporting character for each influence. Mr Sobol does this, and throws in some other jaded devices. The play is a flashback just before suicide; Otto encounters his father in a brothel; he also--since he is anti-woman as well as anti-semitic--has a feared but fascinating female Double.

I may have been soured by the very poor English translation circulated in Edinburgh; the Haifa Municipal Theatre, playing in Hebrew on a mirrored stage in the Assembly Rooms, give the play more theatrical life than I had expected. Doron Tavory's Otto is a mixed-up kid in the best tousled tradition; Leora Rivlin as his mother is chicken-plucking good, this being what she does while simultaneously soothing and upbraiding her boy in the play's best scene.

* * *

The Fringe grows ever more unruly. I read in the Festival Times that my colleagues, dismayed by the impossibility of reviewing it all, are saying that it should be put a stop to (how?) and transplanted somewhere else. This is rubbish: since (a) drama does not exist to keep critics at work, and (b) the point of the Fringe is its accessibility; over 37 years people have learned where Edinburgh is, and when it has its festival.

One of its charms is that it breaks down barriers. Far from home, critics can afford to fraternise with performers. This can be embarrassing. I seemed to have a friend in every show I have seen. My chief problem--as I am performing on the fringe myself--is a musical, written and composed by Colin Sell, who also happens to be my accompanist.

By the time we meet tomorrow afternoon for our final performance together he will have learnt that, though I liked many of the songs in his Iron Harvest--they sound like a concert-party scored by Noel Coward--and thought it well performed, I found his post-Falklands message heavy, and his use of recitative excessive. I must speak to him about his habit of rhyming `fruit juice' with `root loose' and `Bracknell' with `shrapnel'.

Iron Harvest lives in the same segment of the Assembly Rooms as Andy Armitage's Oil Strikes Back, yet another one-act play about depressed youth doing dead-end work, decently but quite unexceptionally written. Set in Manchester in 1968, it does at least enable Phil Daniels and Tilly Vosburgh, talented players habitually cast as London punks, to extend themselves backwards in time and northwards in accent.

There are even two better performances--by Stephen Boxer and Sarah-Heliane Elliott--in Muzzle, at Buster Brown's, but the play, by Stuart Delves, who has won Fringe firsts--belongs to an even deader genre: whimsical-spiritual. I do believe it could only happen in Edinburgh.

records.title: The book made flesh
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The book made flesh

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on two stage adaptations of Dostoyevsky.

BRITONS never, never shall be Slavs; so at least the legend goes. We have no reason to be ashamed of our record with Chekhov, but Dostoyevsky put on the stage--as, despite all impossibilities, he constantly is--is another thing.

His characters are on a constant switchback between self-assurance and self-abasement. `Prince,' they will say to someone to whom they have just been introduced, `I am unworthy to touch the hem of your garment, and by the way will you lend me 20 kopecks?' You can play them from the outside and make them grotesques, but that is no answer. Getting inside them, though, must be like boarding an express train between stations.

In Crime and Punishment (Lyric, Hammersmith), directed by Yuri Lyubimov of the Moscow Taganka Theatre, with a British cast, everyone gets on and hardly anyone falls off. This is high-grade ensemble work extracted from an ad hoc company: a distinguished team who would be well worth keeping together.

The production is continuously, even monotonously, exciting; Dostoyevsky may actually be too theatrical for the theatre. Lyubimov has apparently re-created the design, the lighting, the music and sound effects of his Moscow production. They are all hallucinatory; and I suspect that he imposed a performing style by exposing his actors to them. How many ways are there of acting in a maelstrom? These are not, however, generalised performances; and though fast they are not rushed. The amount of detailed intelligence applied to the dialogue would be impressive in any circumstance; in a production directed through an interpreter it is extraordinary.

Lyubimov's adaptation is less radical than has been suggested. I may be corrected by those who have read the novel more recently than I have, but as far as I can see he jumps in at Raskolnikov's murder of the two old women and carries steadily on from there. True, he proceeds in short, abrupt scenes, and he cross-cuts from one group of characters to another, but so does the book.

Our own brand of self-abasement has been at work in the reviews; the subterranean message has been that this is really all much different from, and far superior to, `Nicholas Nickleby.' Well it isn't; in fact--since I would back Roger Rees as a hero and John Woodvine as a grand and complex villain against anyone on the Lyric stage--it isn't as good.

It is still fine. It is dominated by doors that have an acrobatic life of their own, turning somersaults to confound the characters who lurk behind them; by dreamlike processionals; and by a harsh, aggressive use of lights; Michael Pennington as Raskolnikov begins the evening by shining one of them at us. This is all thrilling, but it feels--not at all to its discredit--a bit old-fashioned. It is what an Eastern European production of a certain avant-garde stripe is supposed to look like. (It is also, from what I have read, the kind of thing that Peter Brook was doing in London in the 1940s.)

It is not, though, just technique for its own sake. It is at the service of an interpretation--a condemnation of the theorist who puts himself above morality. Nothing here bites harder than Mr Pennington's final gloomy citation, out of character, of a schoolgirl who thought Raskolnikov perfectly admirable.

His performance before that is technique for its own sake. No, that's not fair; it is a skilled and conscientious approach to a fiendish acting problem, one that avoids any suggestion of the inverted holy fool. But it involves him in more shouting than should be required of any actor; and in bypassing the compassion that should make Raskolnikov a criminal worth contemplating.

Indeed when you start to break them down individually, several of the performances disappoint. Among other fine actors Bill Stewart is jerky, Peter Kelly invisible. Gary Waldhorn finds a sourly jocular way of putting over Svidrigailov, the hero's distorted reflection; Paola Dionisotti has a fine mad scene; and Bill Paterson as the inspector--traditionally the most playable role--is a quirky mixture of ministering and avenging angel. He has brought his Schweyk walk with him; when he says `forgive me for moving about like this,' he brings a section of the house down.

Sonia, traditionally the least playable role--the prostitute as redemptress--is splendidly done by Veronica Roberts, who never gives an inch to mawkishness. Best of all, aggressively dejected in a single scene at the beginning, is Christopher Guinee as the doomed drunk Marmeladov (did someone say that he was `In a jam' or was I hallucinating?); he is a page of the book made flesh.

* * *

Nastasya Filippovna (Riverside), Andrzej Wajda's adaptation of Dostoyevsky's The Idiot, also begins with a murder: the one at the end of the story. When we are permitted to enter the room, Nastasya's two lovers are already locked in converse. Jan Nowicki is the killer Rogozhin, ceaselessly padding the floor; Jerzy Radziwilowicz is the saintly Myshkin, white-suited and apparently contained before falling into terminal catatonia.

These Polish actors convince you that there are areas of the soul into which none of our players could penetrate. But a caveat: not knowing Polish, I have no means of measuring their intensity against what they are actually supposed to be saying; the acid test we automatically apply on home ground. To me it sounds terrific, but it could be the merest rant.

* * *

Back at the Lyric Studio (aspiring critics are advised to rent a villa in Hammersmith) is Shelter, a double bill of black-and-white studies by Caryl Phillips. In the first, stylishly written and (by Jules Wright) authoritatively directed, an eighteenth-century English lady is shipwrecked along with a Negro, whom she calls `ape.' As well as ape we get essence; this is a political morality play.

The second bit takes us to a London pub in 1958; it deals more prosaically with miscegenation and is less interesting, perhaps because plays set in pubs are far easier to come by than plays set on desert islands. Rudolph Walker, the man in both plays, is very relaxed; the women are Kathryn Pogson, an exceptionally alert actress whose refusal to be type-cast as a waif is one of the few hopeful things to happen in the 1980s.

* * *

David Gooderson's The Killing of Mr Toad (King's Head) is another play requiring literary knowledge. It deals with the married problems of Kenneth Grahame--which were serious without being desperate--and with the hopes of the Grahames for their young son who ended it all on a railway-line while still a student.

He apparently inspired Toad; and one fault of the play is that it makes him the centre of attention (as Toad's friends always had to) when the man we are really interested in is Grahame himself, seen timidly as Mole. Rat and Badger are family friends; and Mrs Grahame remembers the whole thing.

I wish Mr Gooderson had been more rigorous and more inventive with his Wind in the Willows framework and that he had eschewed parody songs; pointless since none of the characters is musical. But the first half is both well written and well edited; and Peter Watson gives it a clever and sensitive production. Deborah Norton is a vinegary raisonneuse, Robert Austin a veritable supermole and John Warner, Hugh Sullivan and Rupert Graves do the other honours honourably.

records.title: The mad professors
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The mad professors

Theatre

Robert Cushman on a new play by Howard Brenton.

PLAYWRIGHTS must get the horrors as they sit trying to devise a plot and characters to fit their chosen theme. A story can twist away from the point, apparently from the mere necessity of filling out an evening, and people be reduced to interchangeable ciphers, making it spin. The problem, rampant this year, is vividly illustrated in Howard Brenton's new one, The Genius (Royal Court).

Mr Brenton writes in a hard, plain style that turns out to be full of ambiguities. Start with the title, which is probably a joke on sexual conditioning. We assume it to refer to Leo Lehrer, an American mathematician washed up at a university near Birmingham. Not Alabama: Warwickshire. But the genius could also be Gilly, an undergraduate who has unknowingly worked out an equation that has already driven Leo into appalled silence. It is apparently the key to the invention of a new bomb. How Mutually Assured Destruction could be made any madder is not explained (the question is, so to speak, academic), but we swallow it anyway.

Mr Brenton is said to have got the idea from translating Brecht's Life of Galileo for the National Theatre. The scene in which Leo opens Gilly's eyes to the consequences of her own brilliance parallels Galileo's seduction with science of the Little Monk. At one moment Leo quotes Einstein's famous declaration that, had he foreseen the results of relativity, he would have settled for watchmaking. "Didn't though, did he?" snaps Gilly, bringing the play up against a point that Brecht evaded.

He treated the scientific appetite as ungovernable until his last scene, when he primly suggested that a scientist ought to confine himself to humanely (i.e. politically) sanctioned areas: an intellectual and theatrical sell-out. Friedrich Dürrenmatt was more realistic in The Physicists, the best and toughest play yet written on the subject: "What has been thought cannot be unthought."

Gilly has her own paraphrase of that: "A thought is a thought. You can't not have it." Leo shouts her down, but he never really contradicts her, and neither does the play. So, there they are, possessed through their own literally undeniable talents of intolerable knowledge. What are they to do with it?

What they should probably do is shut up, but that would mean an early end to the play. So they stage a campus happening, to demonstrate the terrors (I apologise for the inadequacy of the word) of nuclear war. The play has, you see, a secondary theme: the idea of a university. Here is an allegedly humane institution, run by artsmen seeking a rapprochement with science: Leo is actually seen as a kind of artist. (Mr Brenton's chosen parallel is music.)

And, of course, since this is a Brentonian Play for England, the university betrays itself. It is financed by government, for government. It is crawling with spies, of both factions. It shops Leo; and his friend the Bursar (who is also his cuckold: there is a lot of plot) is given a very nasty time by the police. With the secret known to the West, Gilly drops it through the letter-box of the Russian Embassy as well. Having cheerfully maintained the balance of terror, the play proceeds to a peace demo. Well, all right, I sympathise; what else is there to do?

The trouble is that all this--the play's second half--depends on rapid changes of heart that are just not dramatised. There is a full bag of clichés available to carry the narrative. The wine-sipping, cancer-ridden vice-chancellor, squatting on his shooting-stick, is one of them. So are the liberal-ineffectual don, and the spouting student activist (though for him, it turns out, Mr Brenton has an alibi).

If Leo's rebirth has to be taken for granted, his earlier cynicism is extensively documented. He even gets to tumble a lady in the snow: a scene actually written with considerable panache and strikingly intersected with the discovery of Gilly's genius sums. "Equations in the snow" is the scene-heading; and that is the kind of image for which one prizes Mr Brenton. Belief may give out, but not attention.

The play has been excellently staged by Danny Boyle, in economical designs by Peter Hartwell largely composed of evocative, adaptable streamers. There are good performances by Hugh Fraser, Clive Swift and Paul McGann, though Trevor Eve has let Leo's aggression go to his head and Anna Nygh, beginning as the bored and sexy lady (God, aren't the middle classes rotten?) standard in this kind of play, is later defeated by a staggering number of changes of front.

* * *

I always thought that I preferred oblique oddball satire to head-on political statement; so imagine my confusion at liking Mr Brenton's play more than Hanif Kureishi's Birds of Paradise (Hampstead). Mr Kureishi is clearly working out for himself a valuable comic style, but there is little substance in this account of a South London family, upper-working class, bought out by a Pakistani student. (Echoes of The Cherry Orchard only become deafening in a last scene full of dust-sheets and suitcases.)

There are good satiric touches about England now, a timeless tea of lettuce, tomato and salad-cream, and the memorable inquiry "Do you think the taxpayer educated you just to enjoy films with sub-titles?" But the dialogue is rarefied to the point of other-worldliness, especially when delivered by Joe Melia, whose acting is too informal even to be conversational.

Jean Boht, an undervalued actress, functions as housewife and much-needed anchor. Howard Davies directs, on what must be the busiest set he has ever countenanced. (I am about to say something unfair and untrue: they don't design at Hampstead, they merely shift the furniture around.)

* * *

Back to the mad-scientist theme in, of course, The Tempest. This has good comedy from Christopher Benjamin and Ian Talbot, too little of anything else from Bob Peck as Caliban, and unusually lively court scenes, with especial credit to Jeffery Dench's cynical weakling of a Sebastian.

The main merit of Ron Daniels's production, though, is the frame it provides for Derek Jacobi. Flames fly up at the end of Prospero's renunciation speech, and very impressive they are, but they are only appropriate because they correspond to the sparks that have flown from Mr Jacobi. Giving up his magic costs him, but then so, earlier, has the exercise of it.

Mr Jacobi is now a superb verse-actor on four counts: tonal colour, lucidity, architecture, and characterisation. He builds a pleasing relationship with Alice Krige's Miranda (faint echoes of early Judi Dench), an angry and passionate one with his enemies; while with Mark Rylance's Ariel he forges a master-servant bond, funny at times, but woundingly painful when broken.

* * *

Medea (Riverside Studios) is a South African adaptation of a play by Grillparzer, Austrian, nineteenth-century. What can be discerned of the original is interesting, especially the detailed spitefulness with which Jason abandons Medea and she retaliates. Barney Simon's production, which must be aiming at simple stateliness, is however horribly dull, Yvonne Bryceland's Medea rarely more than competent, and the others rather less.

records.title: All-American boys
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
All-American boys

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

NOW listen. This is important, this is vital information, classified, and there is no second, I said will you listen, please, there is no second chance. Right. A lead is a guy who might just want to buy a piece of land in Florida, and a sit is when you sit down with the guy and you sell it to him, I mean you sell his ass off. And the board is the sales figures. It's a picture of how you sell. And you better be up on that board, I mean right up there. Because number one on the board, numero uno, gets a Cadillac; and number two gets a bunch of steak knives; and number three and number four get fired. Number five? What do you talk, number five? There is no number five. This is a small operation.

Now you better get all this, and get it good. Because, without it, you go to see David Mamet's Glengarry Glen Ross at the Cottesloe and you are nowhere. You walk into this theatre and you see a curtain for Christ's sake. And you think a curtain? In 1983? Where have they been? And what have they got to hide?

Only the best play in London. I will stop this. It was meant to be an approximation (only an approximation, because, hell, this is a family newspaper) of Mr Mamet's Chicago dialogue, and I can hardly hope to reproduce the intoxicating mixture of evasions, pleadings, browbeatings, stonewalling and spiel: the fantastic ear for emphasis and repetition and the interrupting of people who weren't actually saying anything. Nobody alive writes better American.

The curtains part on Hayden Griffin's munificent impression of a stiflingly plush Chinese restaurant, precise and atmospheric to the last table-top bottle of soy sauce. Banquettes and flowering lampshades are in a tasteful shade of blood-red. This is a tank for a breed of nervous piranha fish to swim or flounder in; politic, heavy, sanguinary men.

We meet them two by two. Levene, a pudgy ex-champ salesman, tries to bribe Williamson, the young office manager, to give him better leads. Moss, even pudgier and oily, discusses with Aaronow, who is shabby and rattled, the possibility of stealing the leads for their own use or for sale to a rival firm. (Aaronow is rash enough to use the word 'robbery': Moss looks at him like he never heard it before.) Finally we see Roma, the current high-flyer, courting a client with worthless tracts of real estate called things like Glengarry or Glen Ross. I know, I too went into the theatre expecting a contest between two rival brands of malt whisky.

Act Two takes us to the burgled office, grey but at least daylit. Mr Mamet, who in 'American Buffalo' had a character advise caution 'in case, God forbid, something inevitable should happen,' this time kicks off with the startling observation, 'People used to say that there are numbers of such magnitude that multiplying them by two made no difference.' A cop is around to grill the staff, provoking a hilarious mixture of fear and contempt. The result of the investigation is surprising.

Meanwhile we have watched Roma getting high on the job, Levene even higher on an unexpected triumph, and the four - who never quarrel among themselves - turning on Williamson, the despised desk person who has power over them all. 'American Buffalo,' three men in a junk-shop, was as closely wrought as 'The Caretaker'; this one is as smoothly incarnadined as 'The Birthday Party' or 'The Homecoming,' with the difference that we are told who the people are and what is at stake (and, strangely enough, that doesn't diminish the suspense one bit). Here at last, carving characters and conflicts out of language, is a play with real muscle: here, after all the pieces we have half-heartedly approved because they mentioned 'important' issues as if mentioning were the same as dealing with. 'Glengarry Glen Ross' mentions nothing, but in its depiction of a driven, conscienceless world it implies a great deal.

Bill Bryden's boys do good by it, though one sequence that should be an explosion of embarrassment is underdone and a very tricky downbeat ending merely tails off. I imagine too that American actors would find richer Jewish and Italian rhythms in the dialogue. Jack Shepherd, who plays Roma, always goes high-pitched when he goes Transatlantic, but he is highly watchable, as is James Grant's dour Aaronow.

Derek Newark's sweating glad-handedness is matched by Trevor Ray's fleshy impassivity: two fat studies. John Tams is an implacable detective, and Tony Haygarth's customer is amazing. He comes to the office to welsh on his deal because his wife has told him to; and he ends up apologising for not letting himself be cheated. He obviously feels that he has broken a masculine bond. In the fewest words author and actor tell us everything about the man's marriage, his fears and dreams, his vulnerability to sales-talk, and his wife's cooking.

* * *

More Americana. Sam Shepard's The Tooth of Crime is revived at the Bush with a black cast, and with many of the musical references, though not the music, changed to match. The play has not dated, but it hasn't improved any either; and though Charlie Hanson's production is less portentous than the Open Space one x years ago (I missed the intermediate versions), it grinds to a slow finish. Mr Shepard's work, as I learnt from seeing his own production of his latest and best, 'Fool for Love,' benefits from a light touch.

I take it we are all opposed to racial stereotypes: one we could lose is the notion that black English actors are better than white English actors at playing Americans. The only one here in easy command is Victor Romero Evans as Hoss, the bizarre amalgam of rock-star/ganglord/dragstrip racer whose musical/criminal/sporting - and add sexual - empire is won from him in a musical duel by the young pretender, Crow. Crow does, in Chris Tummings's performance, take intermittent wing but nobody else has much style, and this play is all style. I grant that nobody else could have written it, but the language is plastered over just two situations: Hoss waits for Crow, Hoss meets Crow. In 'Glengarry Glen Ross,' or come to that, in 'Guys and Dolls,' the argot serves the action; here it merely serves itself. I'd call it camp (at its lowest, in one performance); or another deadweight rock musical.

* * *

Having strutted off with 'You're a Good Man, Charlie Brown' Snoopy (Duchess) gets a 'Peanuts' musical under his own name. In Teddy Kempner's performance, which is white-sweatered and two-legged, he thoroughly deserves it. Keeping a properly ineffable distance from the surrounding humans except when he needs them, he is a fascinating hybrid of satirist and satirised, erupting into a top-hat-and-bone routine when elected head beagle but subsiding under the epitaph 'He isn't much of a dog but after all who is.' The cartoon is actually more pungent on the stage than on the page: Charlie Brown more mercilessly sat-upon, Lucy (who surely begat Miss Piggy) more implacably emasculating, Linus more convulsively neurotic. Only Woodstock is too cute for words; and indeed doesn't have any.

There is a very cunning blend of sting and honey in Hal Hackady's lyrics, which make the major uplift song into a showpiece, and showstopping, laundry-list number. The resourceful score, starting from ragtime and working forwards, is by Larry Grossman, who earned all our gratitude as musical consultant for the Muppets, and is one of a youngish Broadway generation (along with Craig Carnelia, David Shire, Robert Waldman, and others equally unknown) who persist in writing actual music for musicals. Best musical. Best play. Some week.

records.title: Back to the Fifties
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Back to the Fifties

Theatre

by Robert Cushman

Plays of the 1950s seem further from us at the moment than plays of the 1930s. Depression chic did a great deal for last year's revival of Clifford Odets's Rocket to the Moon. Cold war chic, however, has yet to happen; and without it Odets's later work, The Country Girl (Apollo), looks a little forlorn.

The director, Robin Lefevre, punctuates it with the moody sounds of Judy Garland and Mel Torme; and that helps a bit. This is a play about actors, and it starts on a bare audition stage; the fire escape and the step-ladder of John Byrne's design sum up a whole phase of American drama, from the Group Theatre to West Side Story; and that helps a bit more. The actors help a lot; and Odets puts up a respectable fight on his own account. There is lots of good detail but not much centre.

The Country Girl was first seen here in 1952 under the imposingly meaningless title of Winter Journey; its original name is another kind of problem. The country girl is the protective wife of Frank Elgin, an ex-star lured back on to the stage and off the bottle by a determined young director. It is a three-cornered personal drama with no social resonance. You may see in Frank the plight of Odets himself, the former committed playwright now sweating it out in Hollywood, sob sob; but this thesis is more help when writing a revue than when watching a play. The play catches our author at an awkward moment, between the passion of Golden Boy and the enjoyable self-pity of The Big Knife: plays which, not having seen them, I imagine to be more revivable.

The people talk in well-rounded, well-aimed phrases from which the salt of slang has disappeared, leaving only swagger. Odets has a craftily delayed revelation about the Elgins' marriage that works very well the first time you see the play. This, though, was my second; and I got frustrated at being denied a good, hard look at the relationships. If the wife is the centre of the play she is a curious one; Hannah Gordon's performance is strong on long-suffering nobility but the director takes her for a destructive shrew and all one can respond is, funny, you don't look shrewish. The battle for Frank's soul never really happens; the play subsists on wilfully engineered misunderstandings.

Martin Shaw is the boy genius metteur-en-scene if not to the life than at least to the accepted convention; and John Stride does very well as Frank. The accent sits so lightly on him that I actually started hoping for one of those transatlantic rewrites explaining that Frank had come to the States after a successful career at the Old Vic; but his silver-maned golden-toned performance is otherwise a fine blend of disgust, egomania and burgeoning professional excitement. Supports are okay; Michael Perceval as a stage manager has an actor's dream line, telling off a producer for being rude to his performers.

* * *

Cut and Thrust (Drill Hall), devised and directed by Robyn Archer, is a hybrid of cabaret, anthology and revue. Songs, poems and monologues are tidily grouped according to target: the Tories, the bourgeoisie, capitalism, liberalism, unemployment, racism, war (with special reference to the Falklands), imperialism, the bomb, men, the Tories.

Do you detect a certain predictability? Listening for two and a half hours to the strident proclamation of opinions with which I mostly agree, I began to wish that I didn't. Shared anger can keep you going for five minutes in the theatre; after that you need something else. In a play you would ask for conflict; in a revue you would settle for irony or at least a few good jokes. Most of the audience were getting too high on hate to notice, but Cut and Thrust (a misnomer for a show that is mostly bludgeon) has a very low laugh-count.

The pandering is shameless: whether to shared masochism ("middle class" treated as an automatic term of abuse by people to whom it applies on both sides of the curtain) or shared prejudice. A Mrs Thatcher impersonation is assumed to be funny in itself. This is sloppy as comedy, implicitly misogynous, and horribly simplistic; since it treats the Prime Minister as a cause rather than a symptom. They even seem to be blaming her for the advent of AIDS and herpes.

Complexity comes as an occasional blessing, notably in a piece written by Miss Archer herself about the impotence of the floating voter, and in a rendition of the Coward masterpiece There are bad times just around the corner, an apolitical song, going on reactionary, here turned effortlessly against itself. It's unkillably hilarious whatever you do to it. I got specialised joy out of raids on two neglected American musicals: How Now Dow Jones deals satire on Wall Street, which is senselessly and half-heartedly anglicised presumably on the assumption that the audience are incapable of making the connections for themselves; and from Jamaica there is an anti-atomic calypso with coruscating E. Y. Harburg lyrics and an electric arrangement by which Harold Arlen, the composer, might be surprised but not I think displeased. It is wonderfully sung, in Carmen Miranda gear, by Noni Hazlehurst, a small and perfectly controlled dynamo equally magnetic when up in song or down in soliloquy. There are reasons for seeing the show, and she is most of them.

* * *

I write this from Dublin, now halfway through its festival. I have seen only one play but there was a lot of it; Thomas Murphy's The Gigli Concert, at the Abbey, goes on for three and a half hours with only three characters which beats even O'Neill for gall.

It belongs to the Physician, cure thyself genre pioneered by Equus: a dynamatologist (you heard) claims to turn people into what they want to be, but of course cannot work the trick for himself. To him comes a burly soak who wants to sing like Gigli; he is magnificently played by Godfrey Quigley, whose rapt fantasies are so spellbinding that one feels cheated when they turn out to have been just a passing phase. His therapist, meanwhile, is played by Tom Hickey with a hop, skip and a jump and many of them; this gets wearing after three hours, or indeed after three minutes, but it is not his fault that the writer has failed to line the characters up properly.

Last week, raving over Glengarry Glen Ross, I inadvertently and inexplicably failed to mention Karl Johnson. He plays the kingpin role of the office manager, and his quiet implacability, gradually revealed, is one of the major attractions of the evening.

records.title: In Vienna and Venice
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
In Vienna and Venice

THEATRE

Robert Cushman in Stratford and London

I started in this column, 10 years ago, just in time to catch Laurence Olivier's last performances in the theatre. It is five years, though there has been no official farewell, since John Gielgud appeared on a London stage. Ralph Richardson remains to us. Peggy Ashcroft gets younger. These four dominate British acting and have done so, incredibly, for half a century. I have waited for a decade to announce the triumph of the next lot; but I am quitting at the end of the year and the transition is obviously not going to happen before then.

Not that I lack memories. I have watched Judi Dench become great on an unassumable blend of instinct and technique; listen to her when her tumbling words are chasing her feelings and you will get a definition of theatre. She can be voluble or implacable: as can Michael Gambon, a delicate shambles who could well be the next Sir Ralph.

I have looked into the eyes of Ian McKellen, glittering from the other side of the abyss. I have witnessed David Suchet raising direct and vigorous character-acting to a higher power. I have seen Julie Walters bouncing and enjoyed the impudence of Simon Callow. Jonathan Pryce has scared me, Bill Paterson convulsed me, and Julia McKenzie has done more with a song than I would have thought possible.

Entire Royal Shakespeare Companies and Shared Experiences have blown my mind. I have held my breath at Antony Sher and Cheryl Campbell, and will do so again when they stop treating every role as if it were an assault-course. There are dozens more. It is acting, not writing, that people discuss on the journey home.

All the same, talking about my g-g-generation, I have to admit. In Britain acting, at the last judgement, means classical acting. Our old lions were lucky because their elders (I generalise, but not wildly) were boulevardiers, offering no challenge. Their juniors go into films and television. It gets annually harder to assemble a decent company at Stratford. Adventurous casting merges into sheer wishful thinking. I forget when I last heard a Mark Antony who, when he announced that he was no orator as Brutus is, did not have me muttering "too right." (Not that the Brutuses have been so hot either.)

This year's Mark was David Schofield, a good actor with a hollow eye and voice, who last week at Stratford took on Angelo in Measure for Measure, and played him as a creepy but conscientious junior civil servant. This indeed is what Angelo is, as far as character goes, but he does have these racking speeches about being sexually tempted, and as long as they're there it seems a pity not to do anything with them.

A greater pity, since entering the lists with him, and going straight to the top of mine, is Juliet Stevenson as Isabella. A long, serious girl with a questioning voice and a melting face, Miss Stevenson discovers several things about Isabella, all to do with being young and sheltered. One is precociousness: she has hardly entered the judge's chamber before she is sitting at his desk. Another is conceit: when she first pleads for her brother's life there are spectators present and she plays to them. There is sanctimony: consigning Claudio to death, she gets him to kneel down and pray with her. And compensating for all these there is vulnerability: driving her first to cling to her chastity and then to surrender it to the Duke. She goes a journey from ice-maiden to romantic heroine: maybe the first such heroine this play has ever had.

A similar progress is hinted at in Daniel Massey's Duke, but only hinted. A critic once said that what you make of the play depends on what you make of the Duke, and that personally he didn't know what to make of him. Neither do I; and Mr Massey, though a pleasure to listen to, leaves the role and the piece opaque. Adrian Noble has placed his production in a Mozartian Vienna: a choice that does more for shape (the resolution is very satisfying) than for atmosphere; the darkling piece has little to do with the Enlightenment.

The best of Bob Crowley's sets is a savage diagonal of a prison wall. An omnipresent mirror is appropriate for the play's talk of glassy essences, and for the introversion of its central trio. The last scene though is fatally split between indoors and out. The funny scenes are fair, with a pinched Lucio counterbalanced by a fruity Barnardine and a massive Mistress Overdone. Paul Mooney, the season's most promising actor, makes a rough-edged but compelling Claudio.

* * *

Bill Alexander, who has been lagging behind the RSC's other directors, narrows the gap with Volpone at Stratford's Other Place. The Jew of Malta, spoke of "infinite riches in a little room" and that is what Jonson, a studio natural, provides. As Volpone and Mosca goad their predatory dupes before falling upon one another, the production has us relishing the construction and gleefully joining in the chase.

It gets off to the best of starts when compartments open in Alison Chitty's set to reveal the Fox's gold; rottingly lovely music (Guy Woolfenden, the RSC's senior composer, returns in glory) serenades it. Richard Griffiths as Volpone has new sonorous notes in his voice, though he finds them difficult to sustain; his natural unassumingness, though, is very skilfully channelled into casual contempt. The finest moment is when he and Mosca, momentarily detaching themselves from the action, lie on the bed watching, with some wonder, the rapacious merchant Corvino beating up his wife.

Miles Anderson is a very class-conscious parasite, John Cater an excellent dotard, while in the subplot of the English tourists is quite wonderful. Bruce Alexander, who has stood on the edge of distinction all year, crashes over as Sir Politic Would-be, diarist and projector, living in a world of his own and exacting tribute at the rate of a laugh a second.

Foils to his impossible benignity are an incredulous James Fleet and, as his importunate madam (for whom "lend me your dwarf" is a workaday request), Gemma Jones. Some staging is pedestrian and some speaking slipshod (pronouncing proper names in metre seems beyond the RSC at present), but the play floods the theatre with comic energy. It is, as Jonson intended, therapeutic.

Nigel Cooke, earnestly bespectacled, even makes something of the virtuous youth, though goodies were never Ben's strong point. He dispensed with them entirely in The Alchemist, an example encouragingly followed by Stephen Fagan's The Hard Shoulder (Albery), which is about a fledgling property developer whose schemes are threatened by a new motorway, and who resorts to arson and possible murder in order to protect his investment.

The inexorability of this would have delighted Jonson as would the teasing, powerful ending. Mr Fagan, by refusing to tell us what to think, soars above the flabbiness that usually passes for contemporary drama. The Hard Shoulder is the truest comedy in years, and very well performed. Stephen Moore is certainly one of my actors of the decade, even if he does repeat himself here. Peter Blythe and Philip Bird give impeccable support; other attractions are a set that flaps up and down like Tower Bridge, and a recession-hit teddy bear.

The Dublin Festival had a new play by Stewart Parker, Pratt's Fall, that may be better than a singularly wooden production made it seem. The Druid Company, who are touted as the new hope of the Irish theatre and act very well, revived a thirty-year-old play, M. J. Molloy's The Wood of the Whispering, that began with an old tramp saying "at all, at all" and went on from there. Plays do not come more Irish than this; at least I hope they don't.

records.title: Faust and furious
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Faust and furious

Theatre

by Robert Cushman

It took me a long time to appreciate Ralph Richardson. In my schooldays he struck me as blind and remote. From a knighted classicist I wanted passion and/or protean transformation: qualities I got, in various degrees, from Olivier, Wolfit, Guinness and Redgrave.

Then I heard him, on a record, reading Blake. This was one genius illuminating another, and it was the poet who lit up the actor, showed him to be great. When Richardson inquired, "little lamb, who made thee," he was at once childlike and inexorable. It was the voice, though it took me years to realise it, of the King Lear he never played, certainly the Lear of the madness and the reconciliation. Can you imagine what that performance would have been like? We would have cried on our way into the theatre. He, though, would not have cried.

I have one other fugitive memory, of his performance in Dr Zhivago, as Zhivago's father-in-law. Told of the murder of the Tsar, he exclaimed (I think), "Oh, that's a savage deed." Any other actor would have made that line sound stilted. He also made it sound inevitable. You got the impression -- a recurring one with him -- that he had written it himself.

On stage I remember a wholly unsentimental Shylock, in a duff West End production, and his emergence over the past 10 years -- at benefits, award-ceremonies and chat-shows -- as a consummate stand-up comedian. He had, we thought, to be putting us on; but the mask never dropped. Maybe it had stuck to the face.

The same dignified outrageousness characterised all his recent performances, without ever compromising them. He seemed to have a hotline to the numinous. As Old Ekdal in The Wild Duck, he lifted the play bodily onto another plane. When he appeared last year in a piece called The Understanding, I tried to get to grips with him. This was the best I could do:

"Sir Ralph is one of the wonders of the world, and also one of the great wonderers. While taking the impossible in his stride, he contemplates the everyday like one new-born . . . you want to hug him, but doubt that he would ever let you close enough."

I can only add that he radiated compassion without ever seeming to ask it for himself; that, playing the disturbed dreaming conscience of Inner Voices, he went out on a very high note; and that he must have died the best-loved of all actors.

* * *

He was also the best-loved of all motor-cyclists. A candidate for least-loved Orin, who figures in Little Shop of Horrors (Comedy). Orin is a leathered leader-of-the-pack, he's-a-rebel-and-he'll-never-ever-be-any-good figure from the rocking 1950s, who has channelled (not sublimated) his vicious instincts by becoming a dentist.

His long-suffering (I mean that) girlfriend, Audrey, is loved by a much gentler person called Seymour, but what can she do? As she sings, "I know Seymour's the greatest/But I'm dating a semi-sadist." I think we may forgive that dubious rhyme for the sake of others that chime perfectly, while pushing good jokes along. "When I start extracting those molars," sings Orin, Elvis-like, to the shing-a-linging trio of Crystal, Ronette and Chiffon, "you girls'll be screaming like holy rollers."

Orin meets a gruesome end, between the jaws of a highly carnivorous plant. Other characters fare no better, but it is worse for them because they are fully conscious when they go, while Orin has been happily asphyxiated in his own gas. (Better dead than fed.)

The plant has been innocently raised by Seymour in the Skid Row flower-shop where he lives and is exploited, and he names it, in his love-sickness, Audrey II. It grows -- there is more of it in each successive scene -- and develops a raucous soulful singing-voice (halfway between Ray Charles and Clarence Frogman Henry), makes promises and demands. Seymour, Faust-like, succumbs to its blandishments until he realises, too late, that it is too late. The plant wants the world.

Little Shop of Horrors is a witty, loving, detailed raid on an identifiable era. It so disdains anachronisms that there has to be a glossary in the programme. They could have got an easy laugh by substituting Macdonalds for Howard Johnson's, but, no, they preferred to have integrity.

Serious rock-musicals (no names, no imminent closures) are intolerable; the form is so unyielding, the style so overheated, that the emotions look ludicrous. Singing a rock-song on stage is inherently funny; and the only successful shows are the ones that trade on the fact -- that are celebratory like The Wiz or mockingly camp like this one, which makes The Rocky Horror Show look amateurish. (Actually The Rocky Horror Show made The Rocky Horror Show look amateurish, but that was the point.)

Taking off from a B-movie that was more like a Z-movie, Little Shop of Horrors piles one rubbishy idiom on another, and emerges with something valuable. The show is really frightening. Now in London, as last year in New York, Audrey II -- its voice, its puppetry, its failings and its yawning maw, not to mention its tendrils that finally engulf the stalls -- scared me right out of the theatre.

From New York with it comes Ellen Greene as Audrey (I), a walking blonde lisp who can slip into invisible quotation marks to deliver the prim rebuke, "Seymour, you're aythtewical," and right out of them again to give him a dainty little slap. A definite London bonus is James Wood's Seymour, complete nebbish; and Howard Ashman's direction is as adroit as his book and lyrics, which is to say very.

There is probably no point in saying this to a world that applauded the verbal and musical tone-deafness of Blood Brothers (sorry, it slipped out), but the wedding of Mr Ashman's words to Alan Menken's gleamingly exact song-parodies exemplifies what the musical theatre is for.

* * *

William Humble's Fly Away Home (Lyric Studio, Hammersmith) is a painstaking, and painsgiving, dissection of a breaking marriage. Hywel Bennett, very engaging, plays the man with a fatal yearning to stay one of the boys. Diana Quick is his wife: a subtle performance, since, though not allowed to show any amiable qualities, she leaves us in no doubt that she has them.

Occupying adjacent territory is Sarah Daniels's ferociously-named Masterpieces (Theatre Upstairs), which blames male brutalisation of women on pornography, though, since the play defines pornography as male brutalisation of women, the argument, as a famous philosopher once said, is circular and not worth much.

What the play actually shows is pornography leading a woman to violence against a man: she pushes him under a train. The actresses -- Kathryn Pogson, Patti Love and Shirley Dixon -- are far better before their consciousnesses have been raised than after, when they have to deliver all their lines through clenched teeth. Miss Love has an uproarious speech about contraception, and I spent one whole scene happily admiring Miss Pogson's legs. I mention this only to suggest what a very tricky arena the theatre is for the discussion of sexism. One of the occupational hazards of my job is falling in love four times a week.

John Guare is an American playwright who can be wildly funny about contemporary Manhattan. In Gardenia (Gate, Notting Hill) he is uncharacteristically sober, though still witty, about the Puritans of nineteenth-century New England. The themes are bedrock American -- idealism and violence -- but the trouble, as in all his plays, is that you stop believing in his characters as soon as they shut their angelic mouths. Still, Mr Guare writes like nobody else. Ce n'est pas magnifique mais c'est le Guare.

records.title: A matter of tyranny
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
A matter of tyranny

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a new play by David Edgar.

ONE SCENE in David Edgar's Maydays (Barbican) really takes off. An exiled Russian dissident, named Lermontov, is being feted in London by an organisation supposedly dedicated to Liberty: actually a right-wing front.

As he listens to the speeches in his honour, he realises that he is being used. When he says his own piece, he abandons his notes, and haltingly informs his hosts that they are the mirror-image of the tyranny from which he has escaped. They may not, he says, be jailers, but they look like the people who employ jailers.

The force of the writing is here matched by that of the acting. Bob Peck, the preternaturally honest actor, plays Mr Edgar's honest man and does so, abandoning his recent steamrolling tactics, with superb delicacy. You can see his confusion, his shock, his passion; and I have never known the plight of a man fumbling for words in a foreign language to be presented with less fuss or less trickery.

This scene comes near the end of a long play. We have seen Lermontov doing time in a camp, having first met him in 1956, a Russian officer allowing an Hungarian rebel to escape. That rebel, now a sleek professional empire, appears as one of his sponsors in London.

So does an American, who makes a stomach-turning speech appropriating Russian sufferings as an argument for cracking down on protest in the West; the more disquieting since some 10 years earlier, Vietnam time, we have heard this man making a sorrowful appraisal of his own radical past and his children's radical present.

Also on hand, and I am sorry this has taken so long, are two disillusioned British intellectuals. One, Jeremy Crowther, was a post-war socialist, turned sour by Hungary and bilious by student sit-ins a decade later. The other, Martin Glass, was a child of the Sixties who went through all the protests, the parties, the splinter-groups, and came out the other side. He is the central character.

The play, like Mr Edgar's Nicholas Nickleby adaptation, is composed of huge building-blocks, artfully arranged. There is rarely any confusion of time, place or character. The sections balance; they support and illuminate one another, with the broadest contrast drawn between political struggle in Russia and political struggle here. ('We are both defectors,' says Lermontov to Glass in a line that Mr Peck makes the weightiest of the evening.) And yet the play is a crushing disappointment; the bitterest in ages. Within those blocks, there is nothing going on.

In Mary Barnes, which I now think his best play, Mr Edgar inserted a portrait of a generation into an exciting human story. In Destiny he hit on a wonderful untried subject - British Fascism - and surprised us with the sympathetic rigour of his approach; you could feel his mind expanding as he wrote it.

Maydays, being about his own side, should catch him on the raw, but it all seems very distant. He has written a play about people changing their minds, and - except in that one fine banquet scene - failed to show us the changes happening. Crowther's disaffection is taken for granted; Glass is given a good speech repudiating his comrades (a memorable line about Communism destroying the feelings that made people Communists in the first place), but he has made up his mind before he comes on stage.

Besides, Mr Edgar lets these comrades off rather easily; he has some good laughs at their infighting and their intransigence, but he spares them the hard questions. (What do they think about the IRA? Or the Baader-Meinhofs?) And though he mocks their reliance on slogan and cliché, he often resorts to instant metaphor himself. A scene between Glass and his mother is especially flat.

Behind it all - not just the play, but the advance publicity - is a large misconception: that what the world needs now is ipso facto a monster play about politics, on a subsidised stage. And even that is a red herring because much of Maydays is not about politics at all, but merely about politicking.

Politicking is a legitimate human activity. So is stamp-collecting, but I think that if the philately lobby wanted to get a play on at the Barbican, we would demand either that it was hilariously funny or that it offered some really searing insights into the human condition.

The irony is that Mr Edgar knows all this. He knows that most of his characters are playing private games, and he attacks them for it. A phrase of Trotsky's runs through the play: 'human dust,' the people who have to be sacrificed for the revolution. Which apparently includes those it is supposed to liberate. But he never brings any of them on stage. That confrontation, honestly handled, might be dynamite.

* * *

Nicholas Wright's The Custom of the Country (Pit) takes the title and situation of a Jacobean rarity (one by Fletcher and Massinger, thoughtfully revived by the Glasgow Citizens' earlier this year). Setting the intrigue up is a laborious job, and the wit rarely fizzes enough to justify it, but in David Jones's production a couple of scenes work. The best - the pitiful plight of a stud in a brothel for ladies - is the truest to the original.

Sara Kestelman does some bravura bulldozing as a gold magnate, and Josette Simon takes magical advantage of the author's trite invention: an African girl who, when words fail her, expresses herself in hypnotic snatches of native dance.

* * *

I have little space for The Cherry Orchard (Haymarket), but that may be as well. Lindsay Anderson's production passes swiftly but limply from one bit of acting to another. The best is Bill Fraser's Pishchik; he got a laugh with his first line, and at the end a restive audience was palpably held when he made his embarrassed farewell to the family.

Another set-piece - Lopahin's drunk speech - is finely done by Frank Finlay; indeed he is the best I have seen in this role, especially in his silent establishment of his crippling love for Ranevskaya. Frank Grimes also does Trofimov's long speech well. Some of the lower orders are played very crude, but, confusingly, not all. Joan Plowright, with a constant sob in her throat, made Madame seem so sorry for herself that my own sympathy froze.

records.title: A question of treachery
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
A question of treachery

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a new play about the Kroger case.

HUGH WHITEMORE is best known as a television playwright and his Pack of Lies (Lyric) apparently originated as a television play. It bears some of the marks. Its action shifts back and forth between the kitchen and living-room of a suburban couple. They, their teenage daughter and their neighbours make up more than half the cast. It would be tempting to describe the environment, and the play itself, as cosy. It would also be terribly wrong.

Mr Whitemore takes us back to 1960, to the Portland spy case: the arrest of Gordon Lonsdale and his American aides, the Krogers. His central characters are the Jacksons, who live opposite the Krogers in Ruislip and — slightly to their own surprise — have been enthusiastically befriended by them.

Their house is commandeered by MI5 for use as an observation post. It is all very politely done; but the Jacksons are given no real choice in the matter, and before they know where they are, they are being reminded of the existence of the Official Secrets Act.

At first they are not told that their friends are the suspects; when they do know, the Krogers are about to be arrested, and they are faced with the fact that it is partly their responsibility. They are impaled on the old Forsterian dilemma — to betray one's friend or one's country — and Mr Whitemore is a lot less glib about the resolution than Forster was.

Amazingly, the play has been interpreted as a naive attack on British intelligence for using the same dirty tricks of which it accuses the Russians.
