Well, Mr Whitemore does make a few sallies against native officialdom, but his main concern is with a subtler kind of treachery: that indulged in, against their wills, by the Jacksons themselves. It isn't really their fault, but they suffer for it. (Oedipus had the same problem.) He is especially concerned with Mrs Jackson, since it is she who worries and protests and finally cracks.

Here, admittedly, Mr Whitemore has a great advantage. He has Judi Dench to play Mrs Jackson. Other actresses could probably establish cheerful, nervous suburban motherhood as efficiently as Miss Dench does, but I doubt if any could match her for anger and anguish. Her emotions seem to be coming up from her belly and they hang, immovably and disturbingly, in the air of the theatre.

Miss Dench seems an effusive actress, but she is quite ruthless at paring-down. Mr Whitemore gives each of his characters a monologue: a dubious device, but hers is a good one, about her mother-in-law who lived in terror of authority, so that it rode right over her. She plays it not for pity, but for determination (it won't happen to her) and entrapment (it already has). And she has an unforgettable moment at the end of the first act when she learns the worst; she has been painting, and her body slumps over the easel. It is the profile of shock, beautifully held in Clifford Williams's excellent production.

Michael Williams, drilling furrows in his brow and holes in his pockets, makes a fine worried partner, and Eva Griffith is a highly credible schoolgirl. Richard Vernon is the essence of Whitehall, and Barbara Leigh-Hunt is the female Kroger, dangerous even when ingratiating. (Her American accent impressed me until it transpired that she was meant to be Canadian. Then she turns out to be American impersonating Canadian. But Larry Hoodekoff, who plays her husband, really is Canadian. It makes the head spin.)

Last week I castigated David Edgar's Maydays for not bringing on stage the 'human dust' — the politically discounted classes — to which it frequently alludes. Mr Whitemore does bring them on, and he shows the chariot wheels passing over them and then forgetting. Mr Jackson acquiesces, and Mrs Jackson gets no thanks, but they keep some dignity.

The dialogue is somewhat grey. This is not the best play in London, but it is the most moving. And it does what we are always being told popular theatre should do: takes a despised genre — in this case soap-opera — and reactivates it.

* * *

It has of course a lot of fashionable strikes against it. Not only is its author from television, and its characters lower middle-class, but it has opened in the West End. So, the following night, did Charles Dyer's Lovers Dancing, a much more adventurous choice; you have to be adventurous to put on so bizarrely unworkable a play. It comes with heavy acting insurance. Paul Eddington, Colin Blakely, Georgina Hale, Jane Carr. I kept repeating their names to ward off the evil spirits. Paul and Colin and Georgina and Jane. Like Bob and Carol and Ted and Alice.

They play two married couples who, like the aforesaid, once attempted an orgy. From it a child was born, its paternity uncertain. So all four meet every year on its birthday, for the sake of fairness, though Mr Blakely and Miss Hale have done far better out of life, on the surface, than the other two. (The living-quarters Carl Toms has designed for them look baronial.) They reminisce, mainly about sexual failure.

Mr Dyer can turn a phrase, numbing though they become, and Mr Eddington can time almost anything. Miss Hale has so many mannerisms that the actress, never mind the character, almost vanishes, but she can plead self-defence, and she exits with a tirade that brought her some justified applause.

* * *

Compared with this, Hay Fever (Queen's) exudes the pleasant glow of mediocrity. If we are really experiencing a West End revival, as these successive openings indicate, I would like all concerned to take their courage in their hands and try to get through a whole year without doing a single Coward play. It looks too much like trading on past glories, especially since his four revivable comedies must come round in far too rapid rotation.

Penelope Keith as Judith Bliss makes a bossy star rather than a feathery one, but she shares Mr Eddington's ability to make almost any line funny; he does it by keeping us waiting, she by casually unfamiliar emphasis: on, for example, the line about sex and shrimps-nets, not previously one of my favourites. Her supports range from the anonymous to the insupportable, except in the two smallest roles, Abigail McKern being a neatly intimidated flapper and Elizabeth Bradley a dresser-turned-housekeeper who pads about in a ferocious world of her own.

* * *

When I first read Vanbrugh's The Relapse (Lyric, Hammersmith), I thought it was full of misprints. There was Lord Foppington, saying 'praud' instead of proud, and addressing his brother Tom as 'Tam.' When I grew up and became sophisticated, I realised that these were the basis of a full-length portrait of a fop, and a gift to the right actor.

This Simon Callow obviously is (the only disappointment with his performance is that we have seen so much of it already in Edward Bond's Restoration) and he erects a whole Byzantine structure of mispronunciation; on this occasion he is the architect, Vanbrugh a mere bricklayer. He is, as a colleague has noted, much the most likeable character on the stage, partly because he has pace. William Gaskill directs with expected taste and intelligence, but of the others only Nicky Henson really knows how to drive the dialogue.

records.title: Good Wood
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Sister Mary Ignatius Explains It All For You
records.body:
Good Wood

AFTER all her hard work, Victoria Wood deserves an evening to herself, and she gets it at the King's Head in a show that she self-deprecatingly entitles Lucky Bag.

Gone — on a tour of remote places like Scotland — is her conjuring husband the Great Soprendo; and though I miss him, and trust that she does too, her new show is a triumph for simple arithmetic. Two hours of Miss Wood turns out to be twice as funny as one.

Miss Wood comes before us in an ensemble of shocking blue and electric pink. Her hair is cheeringly flaxen, her figure reassuringly stocky. (She says unkinder things about it herself, but then she's a comedienne.) She alternates monologues with music in the manner of Michael Flanders, with whom — technically if not socially — she has much in common.

I doubt if any performer since Flanders and Swann has raised so much mirth from a programme of songs. Generally you expect a lyricist, however witty, to provoke smiles rather than guffaws. Miss Wood is cunning; by getting you laughing at her spoken material she loosens you up for the numbers. She makes you laugh till you cry with most of them, and then in one called 'Love Song,' supposed to be sung by an old man to his just-dead wife ('Made your breakfast this morning like any old day/then I remembered and I threw it away'), she makes you cry outright.

There's a point. Miss Wood is known for her dismissive attitude towards the opposite sex. Her most celebrated song is called 'I've Had It Up To Here With Men' ('Perhaps I should phrase that again'), but she can empathise marvellously with old men and small boys. 'Music and Movement,' about a male mixed infant suffering a 1959 schools broadcast, remains the most endearing selection in her repertoire.

A new non-musical item is a speech delivered at a schoolboy debating society in favour of the wearing of school uniforms. She does it in an eager self-righteous squeak, hurrying nervously past non-existent jokes ('but to be serious for a moment or two') and leaping suddenly forward ('but there is another point of view to this vexed question') from statements that have never been made. This is a brilliant piece of writing, and of acting.

Indeed Miss Wood's new prowess as a stand-up comic is the great feature of the show. She comes out of northern music-hall as refined by television (well, she lives in Morecambe and she's wise) and she injects into it not only detailed observation — nobody else has summed up the experience of a nightmare InterCity journey as sitting opposite a man making a model of the Forth Bridge out of used lager cans — but human feeling.

A lot of it concerns sexual exploitation, but she links it to other things. Her most powerful song, 'Don't Do It,' is a warning against marital waste. It deals, though, in individual cases, not generalities.

That is her strength throughout. It makes her, as well as a fount of genuinely good advice, the acutest social critic now working in the theatre; that, and the fact that she doesn't try to impress us with anger. She mocks a plastic world, but she does not rage at it; she even recognises that it is, in certain lights, fun. She is the poet of Tesco's, 'Crossroads,' and the launderette down the street with one functioning tumble-dryer.

I don't really mean that. Songwriters are not poets. A couplet about letters from dull girl-friends, 'Those of whom you are not fond/Relentlessly wield the Basildon Bond,' probably looks nothing on paper. Set to music, the rhyme reinforcing the reference, it is a killer. Miss Wood is no great composer or piano-player, but her tunes support her words, which is what they are there for. I want to write about nearly everything she does.

* * *

As a designer, Ultz has set his stamp on a number of fantastical comedy productions, notably the RSC's Twin Rivals and Comedy of Errors. Pericles (Stratford East), however, is the Ultimate, since he has directed it as well. He does it as a gentle, mocking cartoon that can turn serious, indeed moving. Reverend even.

It may be camp, but it is not camped-up; and it is dead right for the play we have, of which two-fifths is not only un-Shakespearean, but plain terrible. The dialogue, anyway; the story is fascinating.

Gower, the narrator, talks in dire couplets, here charmingly transformed into half-song half-speech by the composer Martin Duncan. Designers and musicians have been threatening to take over Shakespearean production for some time now; here they do it, with encouraging results.

There is much doubling, done according to rank. Brian Protheroe shuffles a whole pack of kings, to excellently various effect. Only one man in his time plays a single part; this is of course Gerard Murphy in the title-role. He still clenches up, physically and vocally, at moments of stress, but he finds more development in the role than any actor I have seen.

The play unfolds around a set of outsize cupboards. In the physician scenes one of them opens to reveal a staggering array of drugs and surgical instruments; in the brothel it is a bare cell, with an off-white wall smudged with red, and a shelf on which crouches the terrified but obstinately virtuous Marina, played with radiant goodwill by Felicity Dean. When it comes out of the closet, the production is liable to reveal such wonders as an endless green net, hauled ashore from the wings by a trio of fishermen.

* * *

Snoo Wilson can make me laugh more heartily and unexpectedly than almost any other playwright, and he does so again in The Grass Widow (Royal Court), which is a sort of transplanted Volpone. The title-figure who, following a recent death, owns a marijuana farm, is besieged by creditors, lovers, seekers of shelter.

Bizarre and exciting things happen, though Mr Wilson seems to be laying them on in deference to his own reputation. I stayed with the play, but did not feel it had altogether rewarded my loyalty. A strong cast: Alan Rickman, Ron Cook, Leslee Udwin and (apparently playing Linda Lovelace) Tracey Ullman.

* * *

At the Ambassadors, a double-bill by the American Christopher Durang. ('Durang Durang,' we said wittily in the interval.) The Actor's Nightmare is proverbially to find yourself in a play you have not rehearsed; it falls flat here because making it a dream enables Mr Durang to change the rules at will, and because the production and Christopher Timothy's performance are stolid.

Sister Mary Ignatius Explains It All For You is a monologue for an exceptionally bigoted teaching nun, followed by a confrontation with some of the pupils whose lives she has warped. Excellent black comedy, it suffers from anglicisation (national, not sectarian) and from the fact that Maria Aitken's well-pointed performance is half the requisite weight and age. Both she and Mr Timothy are actually at their best as supports in each other's plays.

The show is presented by the Theatre of Comedy, an imposing collection of talented players, many of whom were visible on the first night, though only in the audience. At the Cottesloe, mainly for schools, there is a workshop Antigone that begins promisingly tight and taut, but finishes up fast and featureless.
production_title: Sister Mary Ignatius Explains It All For You

records.title: Ed's good deed
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Ed's good deed

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN decides he hates musicals.

Spacious and resplendent, the redone Old Vic is once again an exciting place to visit. Ed Mirvish has done a good deed, giving the place not only a new coat of paint, but a new sense of purpose.

His first subscription season kicks off with Blondel, which is fun if nothing else. Its hero is the medieval minstrel who notoriously hung around outside every prison window in Europe, humming and strumming, before finally locating his incarcerated monarch Richard Coeur-de-Lion.

In this version he unhistorically, or at least unlegendarily, arranges his master's escape, though since he is but a singing fool he needs help. He gets it from his determined girlfriend; she may be a serf (though an uncommonly well-dressed one), but she is never the weaker vassal. Also of assistance is an assassin; hired by Prince John to kill the king, he would prefer to murder the minstrel (he knows his own limitations), but he actually and accidentally bumps off Richard's gaoler, the proto-Nazi Archduke of Austria.

Blondel ("he was overdue to write a million-selling rondel") is presented as an aspiring pop-star whose previous near-misses include Groats from Heaven and Send in the Jesters and who travels with a trio of back-up vocalists called the Blondettes. Doesn't that tell you all you need to know? Welcome to 1189 and all that.

Narrative links are chanted by a quartet of monks; these are played by Cantabile, who sound like the King's Singers, only -- since their plainsong McGonagall is meant to sound funny -- a lot less irritating. They explain that the Lion Heart's subjects would never have thought of him as Richard I, since they were ignorant of any future royal Dicks.

Tim Rice's lyrics take him back to Joseph and the Amazing Technicolour Dreamcoat, a good place for him to go. His jokes do not always sit comfortably on the music, but they are mostly good and they keep coming. Stephen Oliver's tunes have less theatrical size than Andrew Lloyd Webber's, but more wit and taste; and the main love-duet, The Least of My Troubles, is charming. It does not manage to make the love-interest interesting; and though Paul Nicholas does heavy duty as Blondel, the evening runs out on him.

It is probably impossible to be funny to music for a whole evening; and, like all the Rice and/or Webber shows, this one eschews dialogue almost entirely. If the most successful performances come from David Burt as John and Chris Langham as his hit-and-miss man, this is partly due to the allure of villainy, but also because they are occasionally allowed to talk.

Peter James's production makes the most of all opportunities, including those provided by Tim Goodchild's sets, which divide and conquer like richly coloured amoebae. The Falklands are momentarily a factor when our heroine derides the Third Crusade as "a war in some far-off place no one has ever heard of." (Jerusalem?) Blondel, outside the prison, does not sing "Open the door, Richard."

Blondel was by far the best of the week's three tuners. Many of its weaknesses -- a dull central romance, undeveloped characters, a tendency to wander musically into the middle of the road -- are shared by Dear Anyone (Cambridge), where they are far more damaging, since this show takes itself very seriously. Its heroine is the agony-aunt on a New York daily. She seems to reply to her correspondents directly rather than in print, but this odd practice at least brings together (through a mix-up in envelopes) a shy Manhattan cabby and a New England illiterate.

Their story is told in the best number of the evening; they are then dropped. So, for the most part, is the show's ostensible subject; we proceed to the familiar story of the career-woman, and the conflict between her work and her love-life. We are told nothing substantial about either, so the show keeps wrong-footing itself.

Don Black's lyrics are competent and consonant, but lack any individual spark. Geoff Stephens's music is mostly hollow, especially when it attempts to be dramatic. Jack Rosenthal wrote the book, which, coming from so able a workman, is a disgrace. However, since he had to fit his script around existing songs (this is one of those started-as-an-album projects), it may not be his fault that the story caves in. The uncertainty of focus was there from the start, and he has thrown in some good one-liners.

An abiding puzzle is why an all-British team set their tale in America. Have they doubts about its universality? Or are they merely trying to make us, and themselves, feel hip? Imitation Americana is all over the theatre at the moment; it is a trend to which I have probably contributed myself, but that doesn't mean I have to approve of it.

As a vehicle for Jane Lapotaire (authentically tender-tough) it halts. Better to have brought over Woman of the Year, a more efficiently mechanical show with the same plot. Or revived Bells are Ringing, which also has a scatty interfering heroine. Other influences, conscious or otherwise: Chicago, for one whole song; On the Town, for one whole dialogue routine. Not to mention Guys and Dolls; Stubby Kaye, the first man to sing "Sit Down You're Rockin' the Boat," obliges here with another gospel rouser, only this one doesn't rouse. Was it in his contract, or just last-minute desperation?

Mr Kaye, who is wasted, plays a mailman who gets to be features editor. I thought this was going to turn to a practical joke, but it's for real. (The other way round, I might believe it.) Ralph Koltai's three-decker set is equally cut off from journalistic reality; it also eats up most of the playing-area, confining choreography to a few automaton formations on the front strip of the stage. I liked Arlene Allan best, as Birdbrain of Boston. David Taylor's direction is diffuse.

* * *

The Duenna (Young Vic) is a ballad-opera by Sheridan to which Lance Mulcahy has affixed not only new music but additional dialogue and extra lyrics. You do not need a crib to identify these; whenever a clinch is imminent, Mr Mulcahy has one lover sing to another "Each time I wonder where you are/I turn round and there you are." This happens five times; no wonder we are gladdened.

Sheila Steafel looks deeply uncomfortable in the title-role, Trevor Peacock is a reliable heavy father; but the only performer to emerge with real credit is Amanda Redman, a very handsome heroine. Sheridan's comic Jew, who was not very offensive, has been changed into a comic Australian, who is. The setting is Seville, so Frank Dunlop's production has a lot of heel-clicking. I think I hate musicals.

* * *

Marivaux's masterpiece False Admissions has been brought to the Lyric Studio, Hammersmith, by Shared Experience. In this comedy every character is simultaneously gripped by sexual and economic passions, and in his determination to make all clear Mike Alfreds offers an over-disciplined but fascinating production. Another Marivaux is added this week, so we shall speak more of this.

records.title: Masterly Marivaux
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Masterly Marivaux

THEATRE
by ROBERT CUSHMAN

MARIVAUX, who wrote comedies in Paris in the first half of the eighteenth century, has a fair claim to be the classic playwright most unfairly neglected by the British theatre. Very few of his plays have ever been published in English; though I remember stumbling some 15 years ago on a clumsy translation of his 'Fausses confidences' and deciding, in its despite, that this was a masterpiece.

I have waited ever since for official confirmation, now finally supplied by Shared Experience at the Lyric Studio, Hammersmith. The play has been translated by Timberlake Wertenbaker under the title False Admissions; and is performed in repertoire with another Marivaux, here rendered as Successful Strategies. They come, in Mike Alfreds's productions, as a pair.

Paul Dart -- responsible for sets, costumes and lighting -- has supplied each with a unified colour-scheme. Successful Strategies is decked out in a dazzling array of whites and creams; False Admissions rings more changes on the colour black than might have been thought possible.

Both are plays of amatory intrigue, with several characters in common. Each cast, for example, includes an Arlequin, wearing the traditional suit of lozenges, bleached up in one play, mired down in the other. He comes, in False Admissions, disconcertingly close to the Watteau idea of a broken-hearted zany. I suspect that Marivaux meant Arlequin's comedy to be rather broader (he is a pushy, discontented domestic) than Mr Alfreds has allowed for. But these possible distortions are forgivable in productions that give each play so strong an identity.

'Amatory intrigue' may be a phrase that slips too easily off the typewriter. These are plays about lovers lying, without ever -- which is where Marivaux gets his peculiar tang -- ceasing to be in love. In False Admissions, Dorante, who is poor, gets a job as steward with his adored Araminte. On his behalf Dubois, his former servant, wages psychological warfare; he tells Araminte that Dorante is crazy about her, and waits to see propinquity, vanity and his master's personal charms do their inevitable work.

All good fun: the pain comes in with Marton, Araminte's paid companion, who is led to believe Dorante loves her and who gradually finds out her mistake. Maggie Wells does some memorable silent suffering in this role, while Holly Wilson is decorous and alluring as Araminte.

A scene between them reminded me of the two women quarrelling over the young tutor in A Month in the Country, or at least of how that was done in Peter Gill's National Theatre production, which placed Turgenev firmly if unexpectedly in the Marivaux tradition. Instead of a matchmaking doctor, we have here a matchmaking solicitor: a good enough fellow in Philip Voss's performance, but a thoroughly practical one who cannot see what business people have marrying for anything other than money. Araminte's mother would agree with him, except that she thinks in terms of rank rather than cash.

Apart from the chessboard manoeuvrings, the fascination lies in the degree to which emotional and monetary desires can coincide. The clarity and the subdued intensity of the acting matches that of the decor, though there are times when the banked-up feelings threaten to outgrow the studio.

If False Admissions sometimes becomes oppressive, Successful Strategies makes amends. Here everything sparkles, not least Miss Wertenbaker's text. This time we have a Comtesse who loves another Dorante, but jilts him in favour of a conceited Chevalier. Dorante makes common cause with the Chevalier's old flame; and their subterfuge carries them almost to the marriage-altar.

The same comedy is played out among their servants; Mr Voss's complacency as the Chevalier is matched by James Smith, superbly supercilious as his valet; while Sam Dale makes an aggrieved Arlequin, fearing forcible separation from his fiancee. Miss Wilson is again the cynosure; serene before, she is here manipulative and flirtatious without ever becoming dislikeable. Her caprice -- her greed, if you like -- and the jealousy she both suffers and inspires are, after all, thoroughly human.

These complex comedies make one wonder whether we have not been misdirecting our energies; we have persevered with Moliere, to be rewarded by powerful sermons on the inadvisability of being a miser, a hypochondriac or a possessive husband: sermons that have left us thinking yes indeed and what else is new.

The depth and ambiguity in Marivaux is far closer to our own tradition, even if the style takes some decoding. This task has been masterfully performed by Mr Alfreds, to whom a final bouquet: for his consistent adventurousness and for the relish with which he has shared his experiences with his excellent actors and they theirs with us.

* * *

Bob Fosse's Dancin' (Drury Lane) begins with a proclamation about how musicals have been destroyed by their sappy and portentous books. I have some sympathy with that position; I certainly think it a welcome confession from the creator of Pippin and Chicago. This show promises amends; no speech, just movement and music. Of course it breaks its own rule even by announcing it; and it goes on doing so.

It is a choreographic revue that feels compelled to explain everything. Mr Fosse is not for the most part at his best (the best of Sweet Charity or How to Succeed) and his American company is less than top-notch; all right in their dancin', but not in their singin' or their talkin'. Just one number burns up the stage: a homage to swing in which the performers are shot across the stage in groups of three (Mr Fosse's favourite formation) before combining for a marathon jitterbug.

The music is the Benny Goodman war-horse Sing, Sing, Sing, and it helps a lot. The insinuating I Want to Be a Dancing Man (by Warren and Mercer) similarly supports a mass tribute to Fred Astaire; you might think that the Fosse tension was at odds with the Astaire cool, but there is an area of nonchalance, the hat tipped rakishly over the brow, at which the extremes meet.

* * *

Michael Abbensetts's Outlaw (Arts) takes us nostalgically back to Rachmanism and the beginnings of Black Power. Another thing it takes is a long time; I was reminded of a favourite Goon Show in which, every two minutes, Peter Sellers would intone, 'this is where the story really starts.' That it never did was fun then, but not now.

Robert Gillespie's production does nothing to sharpen matters, either in staging or editing, but there are lively performances from Raul Newney as a would-be wide-boy turned politician and Joy Richardson in a witty double of his girl and his mother. Jacqueline Pearce, who once did the nude scene in Otherwise Engaged, has come on a lot since.

records.title: The girl from Iowa
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The girl from Iowa

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Jean Seberg.'

AT the very least Jean Seberg makes an interesting bridge in the National Theatre's repertoire between Tales from Hollywood and Saint Joan. For those of us with a romantic streak it was pleasing to discover that the rumoured disaster at the Olivier was no such thing. It has in fact some striking merits.

Peter Hall has delivered a polished, logical production. John Bury's designs get us from Iowa to Hollywood to Paris through exquisite use of back projection. Barring a couple of lapses, Marvin Hamlisch's score is the best he has written for the theatre. (It is an indication of Broadway's decline in quality and quantity that we should already be talking of Mr Hamlisch, who has written only three shows, as if he were an old master.)

Two other New York professionals, orchestrator Bill Byers and vocal arranger Buster Davis, give the music the best possible chance. The Olivier is a marvellous theatre in which to see and hear a musical, and this is in many ways a slicker, sleeker presentation than Guys and Dolls.

It is nothing like as enjoyable; and that is not just because it has a serious subject. It traces Miss Seberg's career from small-town drugstore-counter girlhood, through her disastrous film debut as Joan and her subsequent success riding the nouvelle vague, to espousal of the Black Panthers, persecution by the FBI, and suicide.

That is a lot of ground to cover; music speeds us along, rather too fast. It also imposes some conventions of its own. Hopful Minds audition for Otto Preminger by singing a bit of text. This is bizarre; Saint Joan was not a musical. It also signals desperation: almost inevitable in a musical show about a non-musical performer.

Jean Seberg has to go looking for hooks on which to hang its song-and-dance. Some are all too obvious: the Panthers get a juiced-up number to which they caper belligerently while chanting Black Revolution. Some are crazily far-fetched: at one point Jean puts on view the body of her dead child, in order to prove that it was not black. A suitable song for such a moment is hard to envisage, but what we get is a homogenised lament about loneliness, shorn--like the egregious "What I Did For Love" in A Chorus Line--of any reference to the dramatic situation. When Mr Hamlisch's pop instincts come out, there's no holding them; I wish there were still a Tin Pan Alley so I might call him Hamlisch, Prince of Denmark Street.

Somewhere between these extremes comes a wisecracking female duet for two of Jean's Hollywood enemies. It is much in the manner of Bosom Buddies, from Mame, and is presumably trying to transcend it. But it ends, for lack of wit, not using the musical genre, but being used by it. Julian Barry's book has similar problems. It is one device after another.

Jean at the point of death watches and comments on the mistakes made by her younger self. Within this framework is another: Jean as Joan, on set and on trial, with J. Edgar Hoover doubling as Inquisitor. Gamely Mr Barry touches all the bases--puritan upbringing, father-fixation, early social conscience, black boyfriend, dreams of stardom--without exploring them.

In a musical that may be the job of the songs, but it places on Christopher Adler's lyrics a responsibility they cannot sustain. They are, on the whole, painless, but they never dig and they never glisten; they merely paraphrase the obvious. All we discover about the heroine is that she was a victim; and victims are not interesting.

Our pair of Jeans are an appealing Kelly Hunter and a stylishly ravaged Elizabeth Counsell. There is solid work from Joss Ackland (spending yet another evening getting sung at) as Romain Gary, and from Michael Bryant as Hoover. He doesn't sing, but Jean-Luc Godard does. So does Otto Preminger, a fabulous-monster role fully relished by John Savident.

At the end these distinguished British players relax into their native accents to deliver an epilogue. It is a dignified moment, and it takes some of the curse from the experience of being lectured, by a British company, on the failure of the American dream.

* * *

Our luck is holding with the Spanish Golden Age; Calderon's Life's a Dream works finely in Stratford's Other Place, staged by John Barton in an enclosure that looks like a corrida. (My stock reaction to Spanish sets.) Adrian Mitchell's translation swings, taking in enormous narratives and short jokes.

This is an amazing play, a tragedy in which only the clown dies. The tiresome platitude adumbrated in the title is brought to life through ceaseless twisting narrative energy; how lucky is a theatre that believes in romance. A Polish prince, kept confined since birth, is allowed a testing day as king and blows it by turning Caliguloid. Persuaded that it never really happened, he achieves maturity. In counterpoint, an enthusiastically wronged maiden learns to snap out of her own dream of revenge.

These roles are enterprisingly played by Miles Anderson and Barbara Kellermann, though Mr Anderson is too spryly earthbound to realise the play's full scope, and bright-eyed Miss Kellermann occasionally flags. They have fine support from Anthony O'Donnell, Charles Kay, and David Waller, who has now attained a state of grace that enables him to play wisdom.

The play, by some extra-continental coincidence, wakes echoes of half-a-dozen Shakespeares. On the first night a steed made a notable appearance underneath Mr Anderson, but cannot, it seems, be afforded in future. Obviously Equine Equity drives a hard bargain, but here is an opportunity for anyone wishing to put money on a horse.

* * *

Songs in Wedlock/Deadlock (King's Head) weakens an already ailing fabric. This is a concatenation, by Fidelis Morgan, of three eighteenth-century comedies, one called--the third time this year--The Custom of the Country. It plays as a collection of roistering Restoration jokes about marriage, camped up into a Caribbean musical. There are imaginative touches, though, in Miss Morgan's direction, and witty performances from Paola Dionisotti, Sian Thomas and Celia Imrie. All these ladies are former Glasgow Citizens. Their presence is missed back at the ranch, where a tragedy of similar vintage, Southerne's Oroonoko, suffers from lack of acting. It does not of course lack design; it is set in a West Indian slave-port, which Philip Prowse has envisaged as a ghostly shanty-town.

records.title: Adultery, adulteration
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Adultery, adulteration

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

DENNIS POTTER'S Sufficient Carbohydrate (Hampstead), his first theatrical original, starts, as so many other plays seem in memory to have done, with Dinsdale Landen being witty and hung-over. It is early morning; he is holidaying in a Greek villa. 'The sun is not up yet, so why,' he inquires of another character, 'are you?' Asked 'Is there any juice left?' he replies with a rueful sense of double-entendre. His virility is in question: a necessary condition, the play suggests, of being English. Now where have you heard that before?

Actually we are not in for yet another attack on an undefended home team; rather we are attending the xenophobic school of which John Osborne is the headmaster. Jack, Mr Landen's character, has many weaknesses, but just wait till you meet Eddie. Eddie is American, and both men are high up in a food-manufacturing business, a transatlantic conglomerate that has bought up Jack's smaller concern, while being obliged to keep him on the strength.

They are having this trip, along with their respective wives, on the firm. 'Have you ever wondered,' asks Eddie as the dialogue moves, a little ponderously, from atmospheres to exposition, 'why Greenace should pay for this jaunt?' The reason is that Greenace, as exemplified by Eddie, are heavily into additives and strange vegetable mutations, while Jack is a traditional whole-food man who is to be made to see the error of his ways. Also, Eddie is getting off with Jack's wife: adulteration on the one hand and adultery on the other.

A fifth sunbather is involved: Eddie's teenage boy by his first marriage, gazing with idealistic disgust at the antics of his elders while harbouring a secret passion for his young stepmother. He is a dead ringer for the student son in Smiles of a Summer Night (whom I of course think of as the student son in A Little Night Music). He scores fairly highly in the test that Mr Potter has devised for all the characters to take at the end of the play.

Jack, though smashed in more ways than one, can see a ship, a 'black freighter' -- a mystic sign of hope and continuity on the horizon. Those who can see it with him are saved. (Eddie of course is damned.) This seemed to me an image laboriously manufactured to prove a point that Mr Potter had had in mind before ever creating his characters. The development of the action is not altogether predictable -- Mr Landen has a mid-play outburst of violence that is a surprise at the time and a puzzle afterwards -- but you feel that the people have been programmed, even if only the author knows the code.

My problem was that I was less interested in the characters' souls than in their sex-lives, and more interested in their business problems than in either, while Mr Potter's priorities appeared to be the exact reverse. And though he probably tries to be fair, he really does seem to regard Americans as slimy things that have crawled out from under stones.

I found myself wondering if the food-juggling was a metaphor for what Hollywood had done to Pennies from Heaven; then remembered that Hollywood had actually improved it, and that Mr Potter himself had written the screenplay. Anyway, Eddie is a boor who can't tell Keats from Shakespeare; and is patronised passim.

Jack, a glamorous blend of sinner and seer, gets all the witty remarks, together with a crucial sermon which says that what people really like to eat is other people. He is also allowed to be the audience's point of reference while the other characters pose behind a glass partition. The narrative excuse is that they are taking refuge from the heat, but the dramatic effect is to make them look like insects.

Nancy Meckler's crisp production, perhaps wisely, makes no attempt to suggest the temperature of which the characters keep complaining. She may have erred, though, in casting Mr Landen. He does a spectacularly effective job, but he has now played so many despairing zanies and mid-life madcaps that we find ourselves thinking of Jack just as the Dinsdale Landen role: a disservice both to the play and to the actor who can (vide On the Razzle and Uncle Vanya) do other things.

Nicky Henson as Eddie has to work hard at the age, the insensitivity and the accent. Jill Baker and Jennifer Hilary do creditably with the underwritten ladies, while Rupert Graves glowers and suffers quite admirably as Youth, insufferable one moment, unanswerable the next. There are some really funny lines. Boring the play is not, but it is sanctimonious as heaven.

* * *

At Theatro Technis, Mornington Crescent, a musical version of Aristophanes's The Frogs closes tonight. Aristophanes was never a great one for keeping his eye on the object and the famous frogs' chorus ('brek-ek-ek-ek ko-ax ko-ax,' and if you believe that's what frogs do, even in Greece, you'll believe anything) is gleefully mined for its irrelevance to the main plot, which has to do with Dionysus travelling to Hades in order to bring back a dead playwright: an extreme example of practical criticism.

The candidates are a languid senior common-room Aeschylus and a redbrick Euripides. A comic slave is played by David Shaughnessy with a winning surliness, which he combines with a singing voice far too good for a frog; he should be ideal when they get round to The Birds.

* * *

Currently weighing down my desk are two volumes of financial scrutiny of the Royal Shakespeare Company, commissioned by the Minister for the Arts. It is an intimidatingly thorough document, full of interesting details of people's salaries and even running to a certain amount of dramatic criticism, some of it indulgently enthusiastic, some quite terrifyingly rigorous. There are productions that have got clean past me and my colleagues but which these accounting gentlemen take firmly to task.

Conclusions are that the RSC cannot continue on its present subsidy, that its only means of doing so would be to abandon the Barbican, and that this would be disastrous. Well, the report doesn't actually use the word 'disastrous,' but it does say that 'without a London base the Stratford theatre would lose its "national" company status.' In other words the report confirms what the rest of the world, or those of us enthusiastic about the theatre, or me and my mates, have always known.

The two stages in Stratford, the two in London, the season in Newcastle, the small-scale provincial tour, are all necessary and interdependent. They enable the good work done in a season of Shakespeare to reproduce and extend itself; without which opportunity, it could rapidly cease to be good. Besides, scale has its own attractions. Small may still be beautiful, but big is exciting; medium is tedium.

records.title: In Acton --and India
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
In Acton
--and India

THEATRE
by ROBERT CUSHMAN

BRIAN THOMPSON last appeared on a London theatre programme as author of a National West End comedy called Tishoo. He now has a play at the Bush called Turning Over, and it is a beauty. The play is exotically set in India and Acton. Not that the Acton shown here is the Acton I remember, rather it is the new featureless could-be-anywhere Acton as colonised by the BBC.

In a Shepherd's Bush theatre, Mr Thompson's play must almost count as community drama. Half the stage represents a cutting-room, where editor, director and writer in that order of importance are toiling over a documentary that was shot on the other half, back to which we constantly flash. It is part of a misbegotten series entitled I Could Be Happy Here. The writer, a children's author new to television, decided that he could be happy in India. So they took him there.

Happiness, rather than India, is what the play is about. It is, as the bumper-stickers have always proclaimed, different things to different people. It is also, as the bumper-stickers forgot, unattainable, especially if you go looking for it. This is not a revolutionary idea, but ideas are less important in plays than the way in which they are fleshed out, and here Mr Thompson scores highly.

He distributes his theme right across his cast. The chippy editor in Acton, the lugubrious sound-man in India, mainly want to get their respective jobs done; they stand a chance. The director is pushier; he wants a finished film and a divorce and the opportunity to look down on the writer, who was brighter at school than he was.

The writer is the most muddled of all, increasingly conscious of his presumption in projecting his own dreams onto a society of which he knows nothing, and grabbing frantically at an illusory permanence with an expatriate married lady on the basis of -- if I counted rightly -- a two-night stand. Mr Thompson also throws in a P.A. girl, rushed out from England at short notice, and projecting her dreams on to a middle-aged Indian tour-guide with problems of his own.

The casual way in which Mr Thompson brings this young lady into the centre of a picture to which she had seemed peripheral, is quite masterly. Indeed all the parts are worth acting, and all in David Hayman's production are well played; especial mention for Gary Waldhorn's puzzled ache ("I have no influence; I write for children"), Charles Dance's sparky spikiness, and Geraldine James's placid radiance.

Mr Thompson stands with Stephen Fagan (The Hard Shoulder) among a new breed of acute social comedians, the heirs of Alan Ayckbourn and Peter Nichols. And though he has Scarborough training, it is Mr Nichols (who is earth to Mr Ayckbourn's air) that he more resembles. He also has television training, and much of his play's appeal comes from the hilarious accuracy of its ear for jargon and its eye for the boredom and indignity of filming. Note how those at home are always accurate when speculating on what may have happened sexually on location. And why has nobody thought before of acting out the way that sight and sound get distorted when a film is run backwards.

* * *

As it happens, they have thought of it again in Abbacadabra (Lyric, Hammersmith) which, in conception at least, is a super-pantomime, corralling characters from four or five different fairy-tales and turning them loose in a staged video-game, with three modern children to show them the works. The title, which you had better look at again, is occasioned by the musical interruptions: hits by Abba fitted out with new lyrics, which, since they don't belong, are even worse than the old. This is music that rots the teeth and stops the action, what there is of it.

The show's central conceit, pleasant and accurate, is that kids are far more at home with technology than are grown-ups, but they cope here so easily as to deprive David Wood's script of danger and finally of interest. Nor, apart from the odd mechanical wonder, is any supplied by Peter James's production; he seems to have used up his current stock of energy on his ace direction of Blondel.

The stage is occupied by actors given too little to do and non-actors given too much, though in the latter category B. A. Robertson comes through as an engaging Beast (as in Beauty and). Dexter Fletcher is a masterful schoolboy wizard and Elaine Paige as the wicked fairy tries hard, but fruitlessly, to send up her own Eva Peron. But she is unexpectedly convincing as a frumpy teacher in prologue and epilogue.

The mixture of myths, though, is a tempting economy offer, pre-empting both the West End's Aladdin and the National's Cinderella (Lyttelton), on whose first night a child in the audience stopped the show by shouting, as Buttons improvised a ball-dress for Cinders, "she hasn't got a belt." This was the best line of the evening, though it was closely followed by those which Tony Haygarth, a charmingly bashful Buttons, had to invent to save the situation.

Anyway, some contact with the target-audience was obviously achieved. (Of course you may doubt whether National Theatre children are real children. Give them another year and they'll be on the mailing-list.) To this particular Scrooge, however, the evening seemed supine. The script is "adapted by Bill Bryden, Trevor Ray and the company" from what sounded to me, with my limited experience of panto at the Players', like a remarkably sub-standard Victorian original.

The couplets, which are almost constant, are not gorgeously awful, but just execrably limp. They imprison the actors; you can feel Derek Newark, Robert Stephens, Jack Shepherd and the others pining to get out and be funny, but to no avail. The only escapers are Janet Dibley in one song as the heroine, and two guys who emerge from within the pantomime horse to perform a highly professional whitewash routine.

Susan Fleetwood's Prince, William Dudley's backcloths, and the transformation scene (with real ponies) are all worth gazing at; but the total experience makes you feel nostalgic for the commercial product. I may of course regret having said that before the week is out.

* * *

The School for Scandal (Duke of York's) was, at its final preview, in a semi-comatose state, certainly as far as the scandalous college itself was concerned. Things improved when the plot veered towards domesticity, with Nicola Pagett a Lady Teazle of great comedic skill, if hardly a country girl, and Donald Sinden a Sir Peter who made all his humorous and emotional points, even if he did deposit them too firmly in the audience's laps.

There is too a ripely fruity Sir Oliver from Michael Denison, a Joseph from Clive Francis of amusingly stylised primness, and in Julia Josephs a Maria who bounds on as if to announce that she knows this is a thankless part but is not going to be defeated by it, and, as it turns out, isn't. John Barton's actual staging, on Christopher Morley's silver-gilt sets, is often admirable; the screen scene, for once, almost lives up to its reputation.

records.title: Capturing the whale
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Capturing the whale

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN
In Manchester and London.

By all accounts including his own Michael Elliott has for years been as intent on bringing Moby Dick to the stage as was Captain Ahab on bringing him to the slaughter. A director can convince an audience with complex machinery or seduce it by extreme simplicity. Mr Elliott, at the Manchester Royal Exchange, does both.

He makes super-subtle use of his theatre's unrivalled acoustics, and his towering arena is ideal for evoking first a port, then a ship, finally the sea itself. Laurie Dennett's setting, as one would have expected, fills the stage with rigging. Also as expected, the cast, in the cause of atmosphere, spend a lot of time and energy heaving at capstans while singing shanties.

And yet, when the hunt is on and the boats are out, we easily accept a new convention whereby groups of actors sit straining at invisible oars, before being tumbled into invisible waves. Finally, by a magnificently simple trick that it would be heartless to reveal, the naked stage becomes simultaneously the ocean and (Tynan's phrase when reviewing Orson Welles's adaptation) the supremely unstageable whale, unstageable no longer. For a moment, Mr Elliott captures him.

The whalers prove unexpectedly harder quarry. Mr Elliott keeps faith with the language Melville gave them, that flaming amalgam of Victorian badinage and Jacobean oratory. Ahab's 'I'd strike the sun if it insulted me' is one perfect iambic among many. His last harpooner's rhapsody ('What ho, Tashtego, let me hear thy hammer') is shirked, but we do get the second mate's request, when on the verge of becoming whalemeat, for one red cherry ere he dies: one of those lines that passes in a mere book, but shrivels when exposed in a theatre.

I usually think of Moby Dick as a novel I never finished, but under pressure my memory reveals that I did indeed get to the end, though only by skipping large portions of the middle. What stays with me is the beginning, and I recall in Ishmael's narrative a humour, and even wit, that is missing here; Mr Elliott would hardly have cast so truculent an actor as Nigel Terry had he wished to preserve them. Something of them survives in Terence Wilton's Queequeg; and there are worthy performances from John Cording, earnest as Starbuck, and Tim Healy, jovial as Stubb.

No other individuals come through, but maybe none needs to. Everything must depend on Ahab: a natural dramatic subject (the classic avenger), but conceived in a totally undramatic fashion. He cannot be acted, he can only be embodied; and whom would you cast? Brian Cox approaches him with devout intelligence, but he seems even saner than Gregory Peck. His eyes grow wild and his hair matted, but his voice refuses to follow suit. He seems a strict but amiable man with a sound Presbyterian upbringing and, it has to be admitted, an unaccountable thing about whales: not enough, you feel, to keep him from yielding to Starbuck's entreaties and sailing right back to Nantucket.

Failing to draw us into Ahab's obsession, the production cannot involve us with what it might actually mean. (Mr Elliott does some regrettable circling in his programme note: the whale must be meaningful because the novel is so great, and the novel must be great because the whale is so meaningful.) But if we are not caught up in the captain's quest, we are enthralled by the director's; by quiet things like the swaying of the crew even when the seas are calm, and by overwhelming ones like the vision of St Elmo's fire, which strikes black magic from the lighting grid.

* * *

Bernard Slade, the Broadway playwright who through taste or economic instinct specialises in two-handers, presents us in Special Occasions (Ambassadors) with the passage through the years of a divorced couple. Always each other's best friends and confidants, they remain so, whatever the breaks: an easy situation to swallow, but a difficult one to develop.

By the end of the second act Mr Slade's dramaturgy has degenerated into a prolonged tease over whether our hero and heroine are going finally to remarry. (The slob in you hopes they will, the pedant prays they won't; choose your weakness.) Some of the earlier writing connects with real pain, though the fatal flaws -- she drinks and he writes -- are never very believable.

Somebody has transferred the characters from there to here: a decision that involves them in uttering such typically English remarks as 'You resent the hell out of me' and in claiming to have got drunk on the flight from London to Manchester. (Try even getting a drink.) Jan Waters does handsomely, though John Alderton is hamstrung by the author's refusal to acknowledge what a bastard the fellow is. Mr Slade also directs, on somebody's misconception of a unit set.

* * *

Peter Pan (Barbican) impressively consolidates last year's uneven promise. With everyone sure of the special effects, events in the lagoon and on the pirate-ship are twice as lucid as before. Katy Behean, as Wendy, unemphatically brings out all the facets of the child-mother; and Mark Rylance, with his vigorously piping voice, gets both the boy Peter and the spirit Pan.

Edward Petherbridge is a winsomely confidential narrator, and though Stephen Moore hardly tries to make Hook frightening, he does make him very entertaining. There has been a definite rise in the quality of pirate and lost boy, and the wildlife remains endearing, especially the crocodile, the only character in world drama of whom it is reasonable to inquire what makes him tick. (Cap'n Ahab's life would have been transformed if Moby Dick had swallowed a clock.)

* * *

The revival of Oliver! (Aldwych) is glorified by the return of Ron Moody to the role of Fagin: capering in his juvenile thieves' kitchen with his tattered cloak outstretched in all directions, like an inspired animated cartoon of the Pied Piper of Hamelin. Sean Kenny's copious set, wonderfully lit in blues and ambers, shows its age with dignity.

Some of Lionel Bart's lyrics may be slipshod (not all) and some of his music cheap (again not all), but his fairy-tale version of Dickens's horror-story has its own integrity; like My Fair Lady, it corresponds to a romantic image which, however perversely, we have all carried away from the original.

* * *

Hello Dolly (Prince of Wales), by contrast, merely trims and decorates its source. Its historical importance is that it institutionalised the idea of the Broadway leading lady, forever descending staircases. Carol Channing, when she finally climbed down in London, was playing like a drag-queen; to cast Danny La Rue seems the logical next step. Unfortunately Mr La Rue's talents are not musical; to play Dolly you do not have to sing exactly, but you have to move the earth with your voice. Here we are asked to get our kicks from a parade of frocks.

The only performer I felt like applauding was Lionel Jeffries, a beleaguered walrus. 'Hello Dolly' depends on its original staging; in David Toguri's new choreography respectable shops are invaded by dancers who plainly have no business there. Several of Jerry Herman's tunes still appeal. When a musical is described as having a one-song score, the description is always false and the song that is meant will be far from the best. That is infallible wisdom. Goodbye.

records.title: The world over
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The world over

ROBERT CUSHMAN

SALESMAN IN BEIJING
by Arthur Miller
Methuen £9.95

IT should by rights be eerie to carry a 35-year-old success around with you as if it were a case of samples. Arthur Miller hit his stride early with "Death of a Salesman." It remains his masterpiece, and he shows no signs of bitterness or embarrassment towards it. He not only loves it, he admires it: passionately but, it seems, objectively. He knows what it means, why it moves people, and every detail of how it works. He seems to be its ideal director.

Last year he directed it. In China. This book is the diary of his rehearsals at the People's Theatre of Beijing. Michael Rudman, who directed the most recent revivals in London and New York (the latter with Dustin Hoffman as a scrawnily brilliant Willy Loman), says that the main problem with the play is to keep the actors from playing their own families, since we've all been through similar rows and regrets, rather than the people Miller has drawn. The fact that we can all identify with it has always guaranteed the play a kind of success. Taking it to China -- where salesmen and Western drama are equally unknown -- was testing that guarantee to the limit.

It survived. "The audience," Miller notes at the end, "laugh in just about the same places as we do in the West, and I have seen many of them weeping for Willy." He found unexpected areas of recognition among the actors. Trying to explain Willy Loman's trick of ignoring obvious disasters, he is told "we're always doing that -- finding some hope where there really isn't any. It's our whole history." Apparently it's "as Chinese as hell." "I had always thought it Jewish. Obviously it's merely human." With Willy's overriding passion -- his love and ambition for his sons -- the Chinese had no trouble; they call it wanting their sons to be dragons.

The book is not especially surprising about China outside the theatre; rueful complaints about service and plumbing alternate with humane anger over the Cultural Revolution. What counts is Miller's remarks on the play. Like Willy, he lives partly in flashback, recalling Elia Kazan, Lee J. Cobb and the original production: the solving of problems that in China have to be faced all over again. Pondering the play for himself so that he can explain it to the cast he comes up with a definitive diagnosis:

"Willy is a lot of things but he is not particularly Good; it may even be that his faults and failings dominate him altogether. But at the same time the play obviously presents him sympathetically . . .

"Willy is indeed a social product while his autonomy as a person remains intact, and this can drive the dialecticians crazy."

It drives them crazy here too; academic critics, incensed that a play should succeed on Broadway and be taken seriously, have never ceased pointing out the protagonist's faults as if they somehow disposed of the play. (Try that line of reasoning on "Macbeth.") Actually it is purely a critic's problem; it has never bothered actors or audiences. A play that can make people laugh and cry for 35 years -- or one year, come to that -- is obviously a good one, though it may have to hit a century before it can be judged great.

It stands a chance; Willy's fate is shaped by the society he grew up in, but is in no way limited to it. In another culture he would have found another way of screwing up his life, and he would still have told himself that he was doing it for his boys. Miller always knew that; the Chinese confirmed it for him. "Death of a Salesman" may have kept him young.

records.title: Burton's Farewell
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Burton's Farewell

The last interview Richard Burton gave was to ROBERT CUSHMAN. He said: 'I can't keep away from the stage. I can't stop scratching the pimple.'

I met Richard Burton, three weeks before his death, at Shepperton Studios. He was filming an American TV series called Ellis Island. It was about immigrants in New York at the beginning of the century, so naturally it was being shot over here. The hook for the interview was the fact that his daughter Kate was co-starring with him; her role in fact was larger than his.

I went in trepidation, half-expecting to meet a wreck. I knew that drinking had once nearly killed him, and that a neck operation was said to have immobilised him. At all events it had put paid to his much-vaunted ambition of playing King Lear. (He said: 'I couldn't carry on Cordelia at the end.') In fact, the man I met was alert, relaxed and apparently unshadowed, his eyes and voice -- his prime acting assets, both hypnotic -- in fine working order. Kate Burton confirmed that, in recent years, she had never seen him look better.

There was, all the same, a tiredness about him: spiritual rather than physical. Shepperton had supplied him with a caravan ('comparatively glamorous -- at least we can have a fry-up') though it compared unfavourably to the 'super-glamorous' dressing-rooms he had known when stars were stars and film studios made films. Sitting hunched on a couch he pointed out of the window behind him at a housing estate where once, apparently, there had been a lawn.

'That's where we danced the pavane in Anne of the Thousand Days. Worst dancers I've ever seen. Brook was one of them, weren't you, Brook?' Brook Williams, son of Emlyn, smiled agreement, having graduated from acting to being a one-man Burton entourage, responsible for handling connections to the outside world. Next to Burton, and saying little, sat his fourth and last wife, Sally, English and young.

He spoke of the film career to which he had devoted most of his life as enjoyable but frustrating. 'You accept a part in good faith. The script seems all right. Then six or seven people re-adapt it and ruin it.' However, since he claimed to have seen only seven of his own pictures, he may not be their most reliable critic. He had made, he said, some 70 films, and done about 60 plays. The reference books suggest that he exaggerated on both counts, but his claim to be a workaholic was clearly justified. But -- more obviously even than most actors -- he was drifting where the work took him.

In Ellis Island he played an unscrupulous US senator. Watching a rehearsal did not convince me that it would rank among his greatest roles, but he went through it with grizzled cheerfulness. Kate said that acting was not the all-important thing in her life, and that this was a balanced attitude -- 'working very hard but not taking it too seriously' -- that she had inherited from her father. It may well be true of her. I was not sure about him. The man I met seemed kind, good-humoured, and a little desperate.

The self-destructive Celt is a stock figure in British mythology. Usually he is Irish, but two men, Burton and Dylan Thomas, have staked a solid -- or if you prefer, a liquid -- claim for the Welsh. Both were in part weighed down by the expectations placed upon them. Burton grew up as a figurehead for his family, his community, then his country, and eventually his profession.

He always retained a passion for the written word: the 'absolute passion' (his words) of someone who had once had to fight to master it. Home, in his last years, was officially either Switzerland or Haiti, but really it was 'where the books are,' which mostly meant a converted barn near Geneva. Here he had, among other things, all thousand volumes of the original Everyman's Library.

Perhaps because English was officially his second tongue (he still spoke Welsh every time he went home) he was audibly enraptured of it. His most enduring performance may well be his radio narration of Thomas's Under Milk Wood, with its imperious sense of wonder, its delight at what another Welshman had done with the language, and its whimsical pride in the village whose 'lazy, lecherous day' he was describing. His bookishness never hampered his performing.

The young Burton had the voice of a Gielgud, the virility of an Olivier, and an 'aura' (a favourite word of the time) all his own. His Stratford season in 1951 crystallised it.

Burton himself said to me, 'I'm not as at home in film as on the stage. I can't keep away from the stage. I can't stop scratching the pimple.' He started outlining plans for next year, which he said was still 'relatively free so far.' He talked of doing two plays in repertoire, one Shakespearean and one modern, and doing them on both sides of the Atlantic. He said that as a classical actor he was luckier than most, able to come to the plays absolutely fresh, 'rather than being pushed into the mannerisms that come with the sort of workload you get at the National Theatre or the RSC.'

This sounded to me like rationalisation on a large scale, and I did not feel much confidence that his theatre plans would actually materialise. Nor was I very sure that I wanted them to materialise. When an actor returns after a long absence, the expectant audience are on trial as much as he is; it's difficult to make an honest response. We have seen it with all the men who have, wholly or partially, followed the Burton trail, all the dynamos: Albert Finney, Peter O'Toole, Richard Harris, Nicol Williamson, Anthony Hopkins (something of a Burton clone), maybe Jonathan Pryce. The only heroic actors who have followed the Scofield line and stuck to the stage are Ian McKellen and Alan Howard.

Burton's most recent, and most notorious, stage venture was Private Lives, which he and Miss Taylor, professionally reunited after two divorces, played all over America. It broke, as he said, box-office records everywhere; although he admitted in the same breath that most of the audience were there for the wrong, voyeuristic, reasons. (You've read about the Burtons fighting; now see it on stage.)

But he also claimed to have discovered a comic finesse he didn't know he had. While Elizabeth, he said, 'is a natural clown.' He brought her name up, warmly, casually, and early in the conversation, knowing perhaps that I would have to if he didn't.

Another subject he brought up early was money. He was 'amazed at the money being so good in TV' but that 'truly didn't influence me at all.' In the same vein, he's never had any 'ego problems or bothers about billing; it's only agents who care . . . once I hit the jackpot as 'twere (a favourite phrase) no one ever had billing over me except Elizabeth.'

This can only have been amiable doublethink; he simultaneously wanted the money and prestige (and indeed the Dick-and-Liz notoriety) and felt he should despise them. But, given his early struggles, that was inevitable.

This kind of dichotomy ran through his life. The rolling sonority of his television Churchill, simultaneously weary and indomitable, was a perfect match for the massive folds of Churchill's rhetoric. But once it was shot he felt he owed it to himself to write an article in the New York Times attacking Churchill as a mad, sadistic warmonger.

I saw him a few years ago on Broadway playing the psychiatrist in Equus. He seemed to be sleep-walking through it. He only roused himself at the end, for a long speech riddled with self-disgust; there the actor and the orator in him caught fire, and it was thrilling. And from his films it is the guilty, tormented, disillusioned moments that one remembers best.

His drunken, eloquent (and tempestuously married) academic failure in Who's Afraid Of Virginia Woolf? must have tapped a large part of him. Few actors can have made the decline-of-civilisation aspect of the script so convincing; it must be one of the best bespectacled performances in movies.

Best of all perhaps was his double agent, used and abused by both sides, in The Spy Who Came In From the Cold; it is impossible to forget the ravaged deliberation with which, at the end, he exposed the rules of realpolitik to his idealistic girlfriend. (She was Claire Bloom, the actress -- with one obvious exception -- whose career has most frequently intersected with his; from their joint West End debut in The Lady's Not For Burning, right down to Ellis Island.)

And we have still, most of us, to see the nine-hour Wagner in which, by his own account, he 'never stops talking' -- and the new 1984 in which he plays the interrogator O'Brien. In the novel Orwell emphasises his intellect and his weariness; it should be ideal Burton material.

In The Sandpiper, the most fondly remembered abomination of the Burton-Taylor period, he played a lust-tormented priest. It was oddly appropriate; there has been an element of the defrocked saint in most of his best work. At Stratford a fellow actor described him as 'bringing his own cathedral on with him.' That is apt and impressive, and also a tribute to the transforming powers of art and of ambition. For Burton himself, of course, was strictly chapel.

records.title: Cry God for Harold
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Theatre in Britain: A Personal View
records.body:
Cry God for Harold

ROBERT CUSHMAN on theatre books

HAROLD HOBSON still writes an elegant, teasing prose unmatched by any practising theatre critic. He can be roguishly apt. In Theatre in Britain: A Personal View (Phaidon £19.50), his new survey of the theatre since 1920, he observes that many social plays seem to have been written not out of liking for the human race, but out of a curious detestation of everyone who does not agree with them. 'Right, as we used to say, on.'

Hobson piles on the paradox, which can be provocative but also provoking. Faced with such bland, unremitting irony you begin to wonder if he actually means any of it. His gift to criticism is the principle of the still, small voice. Where others single out ringing lines and thunderous effects he dwells on quiet, hidden moments; murmured declarations of marital love are favourites. He is quite justified in picking these out, but whether he should cite them so remorselessly is another matter.

Taking his cue from Matthew Arnold's theory of poetic touchstones (itself a suspect monument to High Seriousness) he trots out the same instances again and again across the years; the focus has shifted from whatever value they may once have possessed to his own tenacity in remembering them. Here he recalls yet again the impression made on him in 1947 by five words spoken by a walk-on in a production of The White Devil: 'The message is "aren't I sensitive?"' and, latterly since the actor turned out to be Patrick Macnee, 'aren't I a good talent-spotter?' Hobson is an artist in self-congratulation; after their deaths he wrote startlingly uncharitable pieces about George Devine and Richard Burton saying what second-rate men they were and how they always made a point of asking for his advice.

One longs, in the face of Hobson's boast, to blow a few gaffs. To point out that, whatever he and Ken Tynan may have done for its fortunes in London, Waiting for Godot came here (as Tynan admitted) with a ready-made Continental reputation; and that Hobson's deservedly famous championing of The Birthday Party was done from a position of advantage. Alone among critics, he had already seen a Pinter play: The Room at the NUS festival. He knew what to look for.

He is not prepared to allow other crusaders much credit; he lets us know that he had to fight for Beckett and Pinter, while Brecht entered unopposed. This is rubbish; Brecht received a lot of flak -- some of it from Sir Harold -- and still does. These writers, along with Osborne, founded (he says) the modern drama: something he used to approve of but now has doubts about. The argument here gets curious but it seems that the progressive drama has been irredeemably tainted since Auden fled the country in 1938. Since Auden was barely a playwright at all, it is difficult to believe that anyone in the theatre cared much about his defection then or now. But it gives Sir Harold the chance to compare the overtly highbrows with the brave Entertainers who kept the wartime theatres open (presumably because people were actually going to see them).

The intellectuals, he says, despise entertainment and this has caused a 'ruinous rift in our theatre.' My own observation is that the intellectuals are dazzled by entertainment; witness their compulsion to turn everything into a musical. They pilloried Rattigan -- though not as pertinently as Sir Harold suggests -- not because he was entertaining, but because he was an unfashionable kind of serious.

Actually, it is not so much laughter that Sir Harold misses in recent drama, as religion. It sometimes seems that he will give a rave to any play that contains a Biblical quotation, though he does not always salute joy and compassion when they are set before him -- there is no mention here of Jumpers or Nicholas Nickleby. Another oddity is that he seems to think Bob Peck and Jonathan Pryce are the same actor. The danger for the Christian critic (a category into which Sir Harold fits somewhere between G. Wilson Knight and Malcolm Muggeridge) is that, being on the side of the angels, it makes him very cavalier to those below. Which explains why Sir Harold can be the most patronising, and on occasion the cruellest, of modern theatre critics.

From theatrical management, two autobiographies. In Empty Seats (Hamish Hamilton £9.50), Michael White, who progressed from novel-writing in a lighthouse to being our second most prominent independent producer, infectiously conveys the dandyish enthusiasm that he brought to A Chorus Line, The Rocky Horror Show, Joe Orton, Edna Everage, and an aborted disaster called I.T. Sometimes radical and usually chic, he has done more than anyone to keep alive the spirit of Carnaby Street; when he writes, as he often does, of 'a key Sixties figure' he means it as a compliment.

Kitty Black writes of the days when Tennents, under Binkie Beaumont, ruled the West End. That would be worth exploring in depth; but her Upper Circle (Methuen £10.95), occasionally evocative, is more often pointlessly anecdotal. Black and White presumably know more about their own lives than I do; but both books seemed to me full of mistakes. Some of them are grammatical (whatever happened to publishers' editors?) though both can give points to Michael Coveney, a full-time writer, whose Theatre Royal (Quartet £12.95), an otherwise conscientious history of the Theatre Royal, Stratford East, dangles enough participles to cause a hernia.

records.title: Yip, hip hooray
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Yip, hip hooray

Robert Cushman on the joys of an American lyricist

THE THING I have always loved most about the classic American lyricists is their mixture of casualness and formality -- a national characteristic, in writing and in conversation, that they carry to delicious extremes. "Anything goes," said Cole Porter, and he meant it as far as diction and subject matter were concerned.

But when it came to form, he and his peers were fanatical. Their rhymes were exact, even when outrageous; their scansion ensured that the stress always fell on the right conversational word. Anyone bred on them is likely to find most pop lyrics (and a lot of current British theatre lyrics) physically painful.

As a wartime baby, glued to the radio in the late forties and early fifties, I caught the bug young. When rock came along I found myself out of step with my generation. Bill Haley, the Beatles, Bob Dylan left me successively unmoved. I was now hooked on the theatre as well as on song, and I learned that Broadway (and, to a lesser extent, Hollywood) had originated most of my favourites; their verbal and melodic strengths were born of dramatic discipline.

I was learning to distinguish Kern's music from Gershwin's, and to tell the wordsmiths apart. I noted that Porter was a hothouse wit who needed exoticism to stir him into passion, and that Ira Gershwin was sly and easy-going, and that Lorenz Hart displayed a mixture of smartness and vulnerability ("the self-deception that believes the lie/I wish I were in love again") worth striving for as an ideal -- except that it was fatal to look as if you were striving.

I loved the way that Johnny Mercer, the only country boy in a predominantly urban Jewish profession and one of the few with strong links to jazz, came on as a mixture of hayseed and hipster. And when it came to getting high on words -- ransacking them, re-arranging them, up-ending them, and sometimes inventing them -- I learned to revere E. Y. (known universally as Yip) Harburg.

Harburg wrote at least two of the iconic songs of our century. Buddy Can You Spare a Dime and Over the Rainbow -- and they have more in common than you might think. Both are songs about hope deferred: one stark and accusing, the other brave and wistful. One stems obviously from the Depression, the other, less obviously, from the New Deal. When I came to consider doing a stage show about Harburg that would be a mixture of anthology and biography, I considered calling it Brother Can You Spare a Rainbow. I was persuaded that Look to the Rainbow would be catchier.

Look to the Rainbow is actually a song from his most successful show, Finian's Rainbow. The persistence of rainbows (and of moons and zippers) in Harburg's lyrics must, to an extent, be automatic writing. But much of it is conscious, and serious. There was no rainbow in The Wizard of Oz until his song put it there.

Harburg actually lived his lyrics -- he was a romantic who found fantasy an outlet for his wordplay and a vehicle for his satire. The son of turn-of-the-century immigrants, he enacted the classic American progress from ghetto to penthouse, felt guilty about it, became a prominent Hollywood radical, and fell inevitably foul of McCarthyism after the war.

Before that, in collaboration with some of the best composers -- Jerome Kern, Harold Arlen, Burton Lane, Vernon Duke -- he had run the popular-song gamut from yearning (April in Paris) to torchy (Happiness is a Thing Called Joe), and from brash (It's Only a Paper Moon) to hilarious. He wrote naturally for Durante, Bert Lahr, and Groucho Marx, for whom he created the immortal Tattooed Lady, Lydia ("that encyclopaedia"). His most characteristic song was written for a leprechaun; "When I'm not near the girl I love, I love the girl I'm near," proceeds from that opening gambit to half a dozen closely-woven conceits that tell an everyday story of helpless promiscuity.

Yip died in 1981, leaving a mound of first-person material, and it seemed more and more logical to have him tell his own story in his own voice. I screwed up my courage to ask the ideal actor, Jack Gilford, Broadway veteran, comedian and musical star, a friend of Yip's with the same background, many of the same experiences (including the blacklist), and something of the same puckish personality. To my delight he accepted, and had to face the unaccustomed rigours of a London fringe theatre before moving into the West End.

I hate to see these songs classified as "nostalgia." I could no more be nostalgic about Harburg or Porter than about Beethoven, and I hope that their current revival is a matter of musical appreciation, not of fashion. The musical director, and most of the cast of Look to the Rainbow are ten or more years younger than I am, but they are more at home with the idiom than most of my contemporaries. I may have been a freak in my own generation, but I feel vindicated by the next.

Look to the Rainbow is playing at the Apollo Theatre, Shaftesbury Avenue.

records.title: Goodbye Columbus
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Goodbye Columbus

Robert Cushman goes to the Ritz to meet a new master of the classic show tune, Michael Feinstein

"IF YOU'RE interested in show music you don't have much outlet in Columbus, Ohio," said Michael Feinstein, over tea in his suite at the Ritz.

This boy from Columbus is the latest in the line of propagandists for the classic show tune to play late-night cabaret in the Ritz dining-room. He wears a tuxedo, plays piano, and sings Porter, Coward and (his speciality) Gershwin. He is not a leathery survivor of the golden-age 1930s. He is 29, and has been a full-time entertainer for only four years. Before that he was an archivist; in a way he still is.

He will be at the Ritz until August 29 after a record-breaking season at the Algonquin Hotel in New York, a trail previously blazed by Julie Wilson and Steve Ross. They share a repertoire, and a standardised sartorial elegance, but their styles are different. Feinstein does not have Julie Wilson's ashen theatrical intensity or the Grande-dame slyness of the late Mabel Mercer or the fizz and drive of Bobby Short. He does share with Ross an appealing boyishness of voice and manner. Ross is the eternal Princeton man, a vocal Scott Fitzgerald. Feinstein suggests more the bright scholarship kid from the Bronx. He has yet to find his own style. In the meantime his strengths are enthusiasm, musicianship and knowledge.
