Father sang as an amateur with local bands; mother had been a tap-dancer. When he was five they bought a piano. "I started playing it by ear -- to everyone's amazement. I played Do Re Mi from The Sound of Music. My mother said, 'When did your father teach you that?'; I said I'd taught myself, and got sent to my room for lying."

His contemporaries of course were listening to rock, and he grew up "a lonely, isolated child" which only pushed him further into show music. By the time he was 10 he knew who George Gershwin was, and what he'd written; the rest of the pantheon followed. He had to know who had written what, and for which musical. He still collects this information, and details it in performance. This sets him apart from most singers, who don't know anything.

He began his opening show at the Ritz with a statement of purpose: a song called Wanna Sing A Show Tune. I thought this self-conscious -- I'd rather he'd just gone ahead and done it -- but there is something to be said for a lyric that rhymes "stylish" with "Kurt Weillish." But then he was on to a totally forgotten antiquity called China (America's congratulations to the old country on becoming a democracy) that was captivating, and made me wish he would do more comedy songs.

His set was heavy on ballads, some of them throbbed too much, but on one, Oscar Levant's Blame It On My Youth, he was truly touching, finding the vulnerability the cabaret medium needs. There was a medley from Of Thee I Sing, full of verve, and a lot of other Gershwin, including famous songs with unfamiliar lines. I never knew before that "'S Wonderful" contained the couplet, "Say, what's all this dizziness/I thought that I came here on bus-i-ness," or that How Long Has This Been Going On climaxed with the declaration, "Heads may roll but bless my soul." In both cases I was delighted.

Feinstein has access to this classified information because he spent his early twenties working for Ira Gershwin, George's lyricist and elder brother, at his home in Hollywood. First he was engaged to catalogue Ira's record collection; then, as his employer realised the scope of his knowledge of the Gershwin oeuvre, he became his full-time archivist, friend and "the son he never had."

And of course through the Gershwins he encountered other musical greats. ("I always seemed to meet them a few days before they died.") He also met Liza Minnelli, a Gershwin god-daughter and his second great patron. She threw parties for him, opened doors. On his first night at the Ritz she sent him a gargantuan first-night bouquet that now dominates his room.

Ira Gershwin, Feinstein says, "had an endearing, whimsical quality." Like his songs? "Exactly." It's that innocently sophisticated delight in the choice of words that Feinstein communicates in his singing of Gershwin songs.

He's chosen his moment well. Next year is the fiftieth anniversary of George's death, and already the record albums are pouring out. Porgy and Bess is thrilling Glyndebourne audiences with the forbidden aroma of show music. Feinstein himself is planning a book setting down Gershwin anecdotes hitherto unpublished. Goodbye Columbus; hello world.

records.title: Demon drive
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Demon drive

The star of Ziegfeld has the right training for his challenging part. Robert Cushman weighs him up

FOR ME, Len Cariou will always be a homicidal maniac. That is not a personal aspersion. It means I am haunted by his New York performance as Sweeney Todd in the Stephen Sondheim musical. Sondheim's demon barber is a man much wronged for whom revenge is the force that drives him to slit his customers' throats. Cariou's feeling on approaching the role was "Thank God I've done Lear."

He is about the only actor whose career alternates between leads in Broadway musicals and major classical roles, usually at repertory theatres in America or in his native Canada. Florenz Ziegfeld, the role that brings him to London for the first time, is not exactly in the King Lear or even the Sweeney Todd class. All the same, it is quite a weight to carry.

To begin with, the musical Ziegfeld has cost about £4 million to put on at the Palladium, and to be the centrepiece of something so expensive is a responsibility.

Cariou, in the role of Broadway's legendary impresario, is on stage almost throughout. The show purports to be Ziegfeld's autobiography, his story as he would have told it had it been one of his own shows, festooned with showgirls and sequins.

Of course nobody's life really resembles a spectacular revue, and in the end reality catches up with him. In Cariou's words, "He's told, 'OK, you've done all right, you've more or less stuck to the truth, but that's enough.' He's interwoven so intricately with the show, it's like reading your own obituary."

Ziegfeld was obsessive, getting through money and mistresses as relentlessly as Sweeney got through throats. It's the girls rather than the gelt that the show focuses on. We see Flo with two wives, two floozies and a secretary: a representative sample.

Along the way Cariou gets to sing a lot of standard songs: from A Pretty Girl Is Like a Melody, which historically has very strong Ziegfeld connections, to I'm Always Chasing Rainbows, which has no Ziegfeld connections whatsoever.

Singing is where it all began for Cariou: "I was born a singer. My mother was a singer. The Irish side of my family were all musically involved."

He started in the musical theatre but quickly went legitimate, somewhat aided by geography. He grew up in Winnipeg, where, in the late 1950s, a brilliant Hungarian-born director, John Hirsch, was starting Canada's first major regional playhouse -- the Manitoba Theatre Centre. Hirsch let him play his first Shakespeares, Petruchio and Caliban, but also advised him, "Don't ever give up musicals."

In the early Sixties Cariou did three seasons at Stratford, Ontario, but found himself "pretty low on the totem-pole", unlikely to get the leads he coveted. Stratford's then director, Michael Langham, whom Cariou now rates "far and away the best Shakespearean director alive", told him: "There's no way you can play Prince Hal."

But Stratford also had an operatic arm and Cariou was able to spend a pleasant season ("the first time in my career I had the leisure to play golf") appearing in Mahagonny.

From there followed an invitation to cross the border to act at the Guthrie Theatre in Minneapolis; he played Orestes in The Oresteia for Tyrone Guthrie himself. Since 1966 his career has been US-based.

He was at Stratford, Connecticut playing Henry V when the call came to audition for the musical Applause, a vehicle for Lauren Bacall. He had a conventional leading-man role and displayed not only personality but one of the most pleasant voices on Broadway. He left after 13 months to return to rep. "Betty Bacall couldn't understand it. She said, 'Why are you leaving this job?' "

Hal Prince, after seeing Applause, told Cariou: "You're the best leading man I've ever seen." That was in 1969. In 1973 Prince got round to honouring that opinion and cast him in the male lead in Sondheim's A Little Night Music. From that followed Sweeney Todd. "Hal told me it was written with me in mind. I don't know if Stephen would agree."

Whatever the case, Cariou sang and acted it with a fierce lucidity that allowed the passion and fury and sour wit of the score to shine as if through clear glass. I thought it was a great tragic performance.

He has since returned to Stratford, Ontario as a star, playing a Coriolanus stronger on blunt anger than patrician pride. He also directed his old home theatre in Winnipeg for a season, but found his energies diverted from administration into a couple of whacking leading roles.

He wants to go on directing occasionally, but running theatres for the time being is out. "I'm an acting animal."

Ziegfeld opens at the London Palladium tonight.

records.title: Night of passion
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Night of passion

Robert Cushman reports from Ontario on the Shakespearefest

THE BEST Canadian theatre, rather to my surprise, happens in small venues and is off-the-wall comic. But prestige and expectation still reside, as they must, in the two classical festivals: the flagship Shakespearefest at Stratford, Ontario, and the more gemütlich affair at Niagara-on-the-Lake, where the patron saint is Bernard Shaw.

Stratford's current director is John Neville, the Old Vic's golden juvenile of the 1950s and a buccaneering director of regional theatres -- first in England, then in Canada -- for the last two decades. This is his penultimate season.

Official secrecy surrounds the choice of his successor, but most local money is on the return of Robin Phillips, who ran the place dynamically if unevenly for most of the seventies.

Whether or not Phillips returns, Neville's regime has had an inescapable feeling of interregnum.

He has restored the theatre's financial fortunes and recaptured some of its departed talents. One of them is Phillips himself, who has been running a training battalion, known as the Young Company. This is housed in the Third Stage, smallest of Stratford's trio of theatres.

Its inaugural production this year is Twelfth Night, staged with the emphasis on romantic self-deception -- but treated sympathetically rather than satirically for once. True, Orsino (Kevin Gulahi) begins the play on a masseur's table but this may suggest virility as well as languor, and he balances these qualities beautifully.

Olivia is a similarly full-blooded conception; at the height of her passion for Viola/Cesario, this lady lies down and offers herself to him/her. This is startling, but we do need to be reminded that there is actual sex behind this play's formality.

The contrast is accentuated by Phillips's choice of an 18th century setting: a mixture of the mellow and the sedate, with Malvolio played as a majordomo imported from Japan. Oriental impassivity unfortunately spills over into uninflected dullness. There is, though, a sardonically vigorous Toby Belch and a very funny duel scene: an episode scorned by a recent generation of puritan directors.

It is heartening that a director who might have overdosed on Shakespearian comedies still has things to say about them.

This Twelfth Night is ahead of recent RSC attempts but behind Cheek by Jowl's.

* * *

The two plays with which Tyrone Guthrie inaugurated the theatre in 1953 have been revived this year, in unluckily tame productions.

Richard III is a stolidly archaeological affair, incongruously framing a super-cool Crookback by the current white hope, a slim and dapper actor called Colm Feore. He has too little weight, the production too much.

It keeps tumbling into hearty conventionality, ending with the victorious faction shouting, uncanonically: "Long live Richmond, King of England" -- a solecism on any number of levels.

All's Well That Ends Well, directed by Peter Moss on the proscenium Avon stage, is given (as in Guthrie's and Trevor Nunn's productions) an American Civil War setting, though it was not until Confederate uniforms started swaggering through the Tuscan wars that I got the reference. The stepped classical facade that dominated the stage was meant to be the Tara of Scarlett O'Hara; I had taken it for the British Museum. I had also taken Helena (Lucy Peacock) for a Charlotte Brontë governess.

Bertram's apparent seduction of Diana was played in her bedroom: fine -- we appreciated the psychological reality that underpins the Elizabethan bed-trick.

But the scene was prolonged so that we saw Helena creep in to take Diana's place. Fatal: theatrical convention cannot bear that much reality (and besides, it's supposed to take place in pitch darkness).

There was a time -- Guthrie's time -- when fluidity was the watchword of Shakespearian production. These days we pause to change scene as frequently as did the Victorians. The Stratford first-night audience is very occasion-conscious and it loves to applaud. So it clapped at the end of each scene.

That, when the show is going less than wonderfully, can begin to seem ghoulish. Fortunately, the remaining Shakespeare opening gave cause for applause.

* * *

Richard Monette, a noted Canadian actor, made an auspicious directing debut on the festival stage with The Taming of the Shrew. He peopled the stage with irresistible bravura, pitching his tent in the Italy of the 1950s. This was evoked with a mixture of Zeffirelli carnival, Bogdanov brutalism, and the kind of ice-cream extravagance that I recall from Frank Dunlop's production of Scapino: a super-jape under Martini parasols. Some comment on machismo is plainly intended but the main business is pleasure.

It doesn't quite fit, however, with the director's unusually lyrical view of the two central characters. Colm Feore's Petruchio, though a dab hand at beating up servants, is an introspective sex-warrior genuinely uncertain of the best way to tame a shrew, and in love to boot. Goldie Semple's Kate does a brisk about-turn half-way through the play, so as to match him in warmth; earlier on, however, she has been a strident virago. Hints in the text that Kate's home-life fully justified her tantrums are inflated literally beyond beliefs. Bianca, the spoiled and subtly exploitative younger sister, is here a vulgar dumb blonde who would not fool the most credulous parent or suitor. But the show does buzz.

* * *

Stratford's non-Shakespeare repertory has always seemed pretty arbitrary. This year they celebrate the T. S. Eliot centenary with Murder In The Cathedral, given an appropriately elocutionary production by David William. Everything is lucid. Nicholas Pennell's Becket fights a good and even gripping fight with his Tempters; the four disinterested knights are engaging as they discuss how much against the grain it goes to kill an archbishop. This is a Brechtian scene before the fact; the murderers attempt to implicate us in their crime and we are supposed to consider their arguments and reject them.

Actually, the play's spiritual snobbery -- its unqualified endorsement of its hero's martyrdom -- becomes so oppressive that we're likely to defy the author, do the knights' bidding, and endorse their verdict of "suicide while of unsound mind".

In the early stages the production tries unwisely to individualise the Women of Canterbury, which is not convincing, over the hieratic rhythms, which are.

But they come together at the end and so, consequently, does the play.

Murder is doing brilliantly at the box-office so, predictably, is My Fair Lady. Stratford's big money-maker last year was Cabaret; in Canada as in Britain classical companies turn avidly to musicals. This one, with the orchestra sounding as if it were being piped in from the next province, is an actors' show. Nobody can quite make the songs work -- make them, that is, the dramatic forces of the evening.

records.title: Top hat, white tie and tails
records.author: Robert Cushman
productions: Jazz Singing: America's Great Voices from Bessie Smith to Bebop and Beyond
records.body:
Top hat, white tie and tails

Robert Cushman

JAZZ SINGING
America's Great Voices from Bessie Smith to Bebop and Beyond
by Will Friedwald
Quartet £22.50

ONE of my favourite neglected vocalists, an intelligent lady named Barbara Lea, once wrote that she believed in jazz and in singing but not necessarily in jazz singing. She counts as a jazz singer none the less. Her work is ignored in Will Friedwald's book -- one of the few things I have against it -- but he takes a wide view of the territory.

He includes Fred Astaire. In 1952 Astaire, with Oscar Peterson as his accompanist, recorded a three-LP set of his signature songs: the most delightful vocal album I know. I was waiting in suspense to see whether Friedwald would include him, and on page 364 he came through with a passage that left me, as any good description of Astaire should, smiling. 'Astaire doesn't try to scat . . . or "sing like a horn" or any of the other things that hack reviewers think "jazz singers" are supposed to do.' He 'sensitively interpret[s] great songs through a dancer's sense of rhythmic style'.

Except that they didn't get their sense of rhythm from being dancers, the same holds good for most of the other figures in this chronicle. Innumerable lyricists have named Astaire as their favourite mouthpiece, and at the outset Friedwald notes that far from being note-bending for its own sake, vocal jazz 'operates as a key to lyric interpretation'. Manipulating the beat entails balancing the words, which calls for words and melodies worth interpreting. Here again Astaire provides a key.

The jazz-singer's repertoire, like the art itself, expands as you look at it, but in practice it has drawn most heavily on the songs that Gershwin, Berlin and their peers furnished for Broadway, Hollywood, and Tin Pan Alley. In one of the century's happier coincidences, jazz and musical theatre grew up together with the technology needed to preserve them and to inspire new practitioners.

Pursue these lines of repertoire and interpretation to their logical conclusion and you arrive at Frank Sinatra. Arriving after Bing Crosby, Louis Armstrong and others, Sinatra can hardly be judged America's first great singer, but Friedwald makes a convincing case for him as the first to be great on purpose. And if he isn't a jazz singer, then so much the worse for jazz.

Perhaps anticipating some purist grunts, Friedwald sometimes falls back on a parallel category that he calls 'adult pop', figureheaded by Sinatra and Peggy Lee, and best represented now -- in my judgement -- by Rosemary Clooney, who has found an easy route, comparable to Billie Holiday's, except that where Holiday's was bruised, hers is bruised-and-healed. It is rare to find Lee and Clooney taken with the seriousness they deserve, and unprecedented to find it accorded the male post-Sinatras, generally dismissed as faded showbiz. Friedwald, by distinguishing among them, rehabilitates them. At last I can take my Bobby Darin and Sammy Davis records out of hiding.

His technique is to start with an aphorism -- 'Billie Holiday's art is the kind that takes you deeper inside yourself and ultimately out again; Ella Fitzgerald's is the kind that takes you outside yourself and ultimately in again' -- and then dig in to what his favourites do and how they do it. He hangs this on a lively narrative thread that runs from Al Jolson, at whom he declines to scoff, to Bobby McFerrin who abandons conventional song but exhilarates anyway. He does all this with an authority unpardonable in one who turned 30 last year. But his youth may be an advantage. So much of this happened before he was born that he surveys an even field. It makes his dismissal of rock'n'roll particularly invigorating.

He has his deaf spots, principally comic or cerebral singers: Blossom Dearie scanted, the wonderfully brainy Jeri Southern buried in a list of 'cool singers', Pearl Bailey ignored though her clowning depended on her jazz-derived sense of time. And to dismiss Judy Garland as 'the stuff of anti-swing' is evasive; this 'square at the fair' interpreted pop songs better than most of the hip.

I wish too that some of the book were better written and much of it better edited. He sneaks his boldest assertion into a parenthesis; Bing Crosby 'gave American music the wherewithal at last to compete with (and, in my ears at least, surpass) opera and the European art-song tradition.' I agree. I would not make an equivalent claim for instrumental jazz, much as I love it. Jazz that disdains singing doesn't know its own strength.
production_title: Jazz Singing: America's Great Voices from Bessie Smith to Bebop and Beyond

records.title: The Lord of the Rings
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The Lord of the Rings

Theatre

Princess of Wales, Toronto

The parade of images in Matthew Warchus's production of The Lord of the Rings is ceaseless and astonishing. The Black Riders are truly terrifying, especially the first one who appears out of nowhere as a spectral compound of man and horse. The senior Orcs travel on great curved snowshoes; other ranks push themselves into battle on sinister crutches. The Ents, on stilts and held up by wires, do a superb job of looking like trees. The stage itself is a spectacle, constantly moving up, down and around, splitting apart and coming together again. It even takes a bow at the end and nobody could begrudge it.

This show, reputedly the most expensive yet staged, has spent its millions wisely. Practically too, as devices work strictly to serve the story. Rob Howell's set, superlatively lit by Paul Pyant, is an arrangement of branches that makes an environmental statement as well as a narrative one; and unlike the film it includes the last episode, in which hobbits chase the polluters from the Shire.

The obvious problem remains: how, in one three-and-a-half-hour show, do you adapt a book that barely fitted into three long films? Warchus and his co-adaptor Shaun McKenna have done it cleverly, cutting out great patches of plot and sensitively binding the remains together. This show is intelligent, but it isn't satisfying. The sheer proliferating bulk of JRR Tolkien's trilogy is a major part of its attraction. Reduced, however cunningly, it loses weight and even urgency.

Most of the score, by AR Rahman and the Finnish group Varttina, is serviceable, underlining rather than advancing or creating the plot.

The British actors James Loye and Peter Howe play Frodo and Sam admirably. Most of the rest are Canadian. Gollum is superbly played by Michael Therriault, who a few years ago was a fine Ariel; now he's a Caliban, malevolent and tormented. Evan Buliung's Strider, glamorous even in tatters, is that rare commodity, a genuine hero. The others make less of a mark or have less of a chance.

In this show the human element fights hard and sometimes wins, but the mechanical element, which is after all a human invention, is wonderful. Robert Cushman

records.title: Lower Fifth
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Not unexpectedly Terence Rattigan's The Browning Version, 28 years old, stands up very well in revival at the King's Head. It has, it must be confessed, a fair amount to stand up to; Rattigan's dialogue may be understated, but his play is made up of confrontations and these need more space than the huddled stage of a pub theatre can afford.

The rhythm of Stewart Trotter's production is not firm enough to compensate; or at least it was not on the first nervous night. This was characterised by a succession of timorous exits and entrances, as the actors manoeuvred between a small door and a large folding screen. This object was prescribed by the author and his executants on this occasion may well have cursed him for it.

It is characteristic of Rattigan, though, that having ordered the screen, and made one of his characters remark on its kindness to eavesdroppers, he makes very little use of it. This is not carelessness; it is sophistication. Rattigan finds space, within the confines of a long one-act play, not merely to tell his story, but to comment on his own means of telling it: on what he doesn't use as well as what he does. The title, you may remember, refers to a translation of the Agamemnon, a story, as Rattigan's schoolmaster hero remarks, of a murderous wife and cuckolded husband.

This is precisely the situation of his own marriage, though it is spiritual rather than physical assassination that his partner has in view. About to depart from a school where he has been at worst loathed and at best taken for granted, Andrew Crocker-Harris, known as "The Crock" and worse, finds the courage to insist that, for once, he will not be passed over. He, and not a more popular master, will make the closing speech at the end-of-term assembly. It may be an anti-climax but, as he says, an anti-climax can be effective.

The elegance of this closing line is rather spoiled in Mr Trotter's production by a thunderous delivery from Nigel Stock; we are given no chance to judge the effectiveness of anti-climax because what we are offered is a climax, perhaps to make up for the excitement we have been denied in earlier scenes where the text provides for it. Mrs Crocker-Harris's most venomous action is to cast doubt on the sincerity of the boy who has presented her husband with a copy of the Browning version as a farewell present; it should chill the blood, but it passes by quite casually here.

Perhaps it is the fault of the play, or more precisely of my previous acquaintance with it. Rattigan's method of progressive revelation is particularly subject to the law of diminishing returns; people may keep their power to surprise, but not incidents. And apart from the Crock, the characters here are thin. The boy Taplow (a tenacious name in school fiction, as will be recognised by students of Professor Jimmy Edwards) veers quite arbitrarily from scorn to affection, and though Rattigan is careful to make his protagonist fair to his wife, he cannot manage to be quite that generous himself while she is on the stage. The result is that though The Browning Version compels attention (it is quite remorselessly watchable), it does not always reward it.

Mr Stock as the Crock is pretty good, but not really right. He is pudgy and crumpled not only in soul but in body, and so gives his author's game away from the start. He is not merely soft-centred (as the writing finally proves him to be), but soft-coated; when he is identified as the Himmler of the Lower Fifth, it seems odd and amusing rather than sad and inevitable. The rest of the acting is undistinguished, or the best of it is; Barbara Jefford is an actress I am always glad to see, but I feel she would be more at home as the Clytemnestra whom the play invokes than as the small-time harpy it actually provides.

The play, being less than great, suffers at the moment from its concerti with a style and a milieu we have grown unused to taking seriously, but (to answer the obvious question) I would be puzzled to name a current play that would revive as well in another 30 years.

* * *

Played with it is Carol's Christmas by Frank Marcus, an afterpiece on the first night, but a curtain-raiser thenceforward. Future audiences will thus be spared a bathos which threw a harshly ironic light on Crocker-Harris's last line. Mr Marcus is the only writer known to me who still takes waif-heroines seriously. This one is a prostitute who receives a visit from Santa Claus.

records.title: Oh no you don't!
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The new policy at the Phoenix--short runs, movie stars and season tickets--is inaugurated with I DO! I DO!, a two-handed musical about marriage that should do a lot for divorce.

At curtain-rise Rock Hudson takes Juliet Prowse. Over the rest of the evening they age 50 years. (The audience come out feeling pretty old, too.) They mature at different rates. Mr Hudson, sensing perhaps that grey hair becomes him, makes straight for middle age and stays there a good long time. Miss Prowse, on the other hand, remains pert and youthful until the very last moment: a moment at which both performers advance to the footlights, sit down, get out their paint-boxes, and mercilessly line their faces. Having thus earned their pensions, they totter (all old people totter; it's a rule) out of the house which they have inhabited for the duration.

But where do they go? This is the first time that we have been led to believe there is any world outside. When we think about it, we realise there must be, and we also realise that in 50 years it must have changed somewhat. We are never even told which 50 years are in question; the only clues are that Mr Hudson wears a funny old nightcap on his wedding night (until Miss Prowse giggles him out of it) and that about 10 years later, or so I would guess, they can apparently manage to keep a houseful of domestics (unseen of course) on what Mr Hudson makes from successful novels that sell 3,000 copies.

But, confusingly enough, the dialogue throughout reeks of the fifties--or at least of that decade's omnipresent TV comedies of domesticity. Stolid Mr Hudson, dizzy Miss Prowse: the eternal couple. And nothing happens to them, even inside the house. Once or twice, there are hints that they may be falling out of love, but a single song is enough to restore them to bliss. The tagline is something about marriage being difficult but worthwhile. It doesn't square with the facts of the show, which are that marriage is too easy to be worth the attention of mature people. If you're going in for it, say the authors, be like Miss Prowse: don't grow up.

Little good that his big number is followed almost immediately by Miss Prowse's one opportunity to stretch her own nimble legs, providing the only moments that approach excitement. Her voice, though, is a squawk. The score dates from 1966, and if I had heard no worse since I would count myself lucky. I found the first half of the show supportable, the second (where inertia really runs riot) not.

* * *

Neither, I am afraid, is there more joy in Cakewalk (Hampstead), an even smaller musical though with a larger cast. There are five performers, all pleasing; Dinah Stabb projects a schoolteacherish primness which makes her outbursts of song agreeably surprising, Gaye Brown, on the other hand, is a red-hot lady for whom song is a natural condition; she might be an English Elaine Stritch, and her Theatre Workshop experience has made her adept at distancing herself from ramshackle surroundings.

This is a valuable gift for a performer in Cakewalk since it has virtually no structure. It does have a setting and some kind of ambience; we are on a Hollywood island inhabited by hard drinkers and tempestuous ladies. It suggests Rain remade as a vehicle for Humphrey Bogart and Carmen Miranda. It was suggested to me afterwards that the idea was to parody nostalgia, but that is something that cannot be done. You indulge nostalgia or you let it alone. This show is an indulger. The music is variable but even the good numbers are sapped of effect by the script, which is limp to nonexistent. A show composed simply of good-humoured songs ought, in theory, to work; but in practice it is always dejecting. We need to be given some reason for being there.

* * *

Funny Peculiar (Mermaid) by Mike Stott is the newest of the sex-manual comedies. Like The Bed Before Yesterday and such, it not only preaches liberation but practises it. A good laugh is always liberating, and this piece has more of them than any other play in London. To be sure, they are mostly concentrated in the second act; the journey to the interval is tedious, redeemed only by a few bright lines. Mr Stott, a charitable dramatist, expends too much time on a couple of characters whom neither he nor his actors can make interesting. But his hero, Trevor (Richard Beckinsale), shows signs of life from the start; he is a small-town grocer who is understandably perturbed when the local vicar, suspected of homosexuality, hangs himself from his own bell-rope, but who cannot quite communicate the promptings of his permissive conscience to his wife. He wants to experiment, and she cannot bring herself to like the idea.

The play becomes enjoyably farcical when Trevor is seduced by a voluptuous customer and has to hop naked out of the window to escape her husband; touching when his wife (Julie Walters) finds out and tries painfully to define the limits of her own tolerance; and downright uproarious when Trevor relieves his frustrations by a prolonged bun-fight with a proud confectioner (Peter Postlethwaite). This scene is brilliantly directed by Alan Dossor.

Mr Stott has not quite worked out to what extent Trevor is to be taken as the comic victim of his own principles, or indeed whether he is fooling himself about their integrity. Having met with a slight accident, he spends the last scene encased in plaster, which is not a good position from which to communicate moral niceties; and the final resolution is, both ethically and theatrically, a bit glib. However this closing scene is also the occasion of a hilarious device for whose invention Mr Stott may be forgiven almost anything.

* * *

Henry V (Aldwych) lacks the invigorating back-to-the-wall quality which distinguished its first night at Stratford: an occasion on which the RSC fought free against odds as heavy as those at Agincourt. Farrah's sets now seem nothing special; they depended a lot on space, with which the Aldwych is far less generous. But individual performances are firmer, and the play interestingly emerges as having little to do with war. That aspect is covered at second-hand, through the excellent offices of Emrys James's friendly Chorus. But the main burden lies on the tension in Alan Howard's Henry, not between man and warrior, but simply between man and king. He yearns, not quite wholeheartedly, to be the one; performs--arduously but not without satisfaction--the duties of the other. This lends a peculiar excitement both to the ceremony speech and the encounters with Dan Maden's Williams, who is again unaffected. The other actors move through Terry Hands's production with a confidence that does both parties credit.

records.title: Sir John in splendour
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The Royal Shakespeare Company, journeying between Warwickshire and London, seldom remains in a state of equilibrium. Of the RSC histories now on view at the Aldwych, two--Henry V and Henry IV Part II--now seem less exciting than they did last year at Stratford, but the remaining instalment, Henry IV Part I, has improved enormously.

First and foremost, Brewster Mason no longer has laryngitis, so the play no longer lacks an effective Falstaff. Effective is actually a mean word to describe Mr Mason in this role, which represents the summit of his career. He laid the groundwork years ago when he portrayed the Falstaff of The Merry Wives of Windsor as a stately victim, majestic even in defeat. He is much the same character now, never a buffoon but certainly the funniest Falstaff I have seen. He is the first in my experience whose words are as rotund as his belly; he lets them slip in his own good time but effortlessly.

This is a quality that has always distinguished him in a pretty earnest company and it is true that when you consider his past performances there is nothing startlingly original about this one. Mr Mason has always been a massive gentlemanly actor with a weighty presence and a rolling voice; all he apparently does as Falstaff is to magnify these attributes to their fullest and richest.

The only variable with Mr Mason is his worldliness: the precise balance he strikes between geniality and cynicism. If there is to be any criticism of his Falstaff it may be that he is too sunny throughout. Even when he parades his infirmities ("how subject we old men are to this vice of lying") we do not believe in their reality; he is too disarming. It is a little difficult to see in what way he can possibly be misleading Hal; and though this may be all right for Part I--which may be regarded as a self-contained play with a happy ending--it weakens Part II.

I still feel that in this play Falstaff should be sourer, less confident of his future; but he does now have a splendidly rattled moment at the end of the tavern scene, thrusting the recalcitrant Prince into the arms of Doll Tearsheet. "His grace says that which his flesh and blood rebels against" and Falstaff's only hope lies in encouraging the rebellion and destroying the grace.

In order to keep the outcome an open question Terry Hands, the director, has been forced into some shuffling. One problem of presenting the two plays together is that Hal's reconciliation with his father seems so complete at the end of Part I as to make their further estrangement in Part II incomprehensible. So the two of them have artificially to be kept at loggerheads: Emrys James presents a crafty, paranoid usurper with the gift of alienating everyone; he legitimately enrages Stuart Wilson's Hotspur (an attractive performance, but lightweight) and has much the same effect on his son. It is a little surprising that he commands the loyalty of his courtiers, not all of whom are creeps.

There are lines which can be held to justify Mr James's interpretation, but he has to do a suspicious amount of heavy acting to get by with the others. His death seems to go on for ever; and Alan Howard as Hal has somehow mislaid the agonised assumption of royalty that was previously the summation of his performance. He remains patchily magnificent, with some moments of ringing command and others of beguiling ease. His early attitude to his companions ("I know you all") is neither indulgent nor Machiavellian: just studiously playful.

Later on, with his first battle behind him, he outlines with distinction a weary struggle between two kinds of distaste; homesick for the tavern when at court and for the court when in the tavern: happy nowhere. The habit of play-acting grows on him (his mimicry of his father is excellent) and once king he plays a fearful tyrant for the Lord Chief Justice before forgiving him. This is a faultless interpretation which only fits of manner prevent from turning into a faultless execution.

Mr Hands has laid the plays out beautifully, in stunningly economical sets by Farrah. In Part I he keeps the strands of action running in parallel by overlapping exits and entrances. At the beginning, Hal relaxes at one side of the stage while his father, miles away, denounces him on the other. At the close of Part II, while a couple of lords discuss the coming war with France, Falstaff remains silent with his back to us, reminding us of what we shall miss in Henry V. The Gloucestershire scenes are the finest comedy in English and I have never seen them so well done; Sydney Bromley's busy Shallow is balanced by Trevor Peacock's uproarious Silence ("I'm sorry, I'll read that again") (Mr Peacock is in glorious plumage this season with a fine sycophantic Poins and in Henry V an excellent Fluellen.) Both parts may, on occasion, be seen on the same day; but I think they will yield more if taken separately. They are lively enough to hold attention easily for three hours but, unlike the last Stratford history cycle, they lack the supreme excitement that keeps you in thrall for six.

* * *

Trevor Griffiths's Comedians, transferred to Wyndham's, remains the most vital play and production in London. Jimmy Jewel, the old master, grows and grows, though his longer speeches can still go slack; Kenneth Cranham, who now plays Gethin the rebel clown, is strong on rebellion but short on comedy. His predecessor, Jonathan Pryce, was a grotesque dandy and sharply aggressive; Mr Cranham is bluntly aggressive, doing ample justice to the play's arguments but not to its style.

* * *

At Greenwich Love's Old Sweet Song, written and directed by John Hale, is equally shapeless and horribly repetitive. A mother and daughter maim their menfolk, across two continents, pausing only to exchange self-pity. Finally someone tells them how horrible they are, which is a relief but only increases the imbalance. The evening's only pleasure is the sight of the theatre's founder-director, Ewan Hooper, acting on his own stage; first erect and military, then crumpled and civilian, managing both moods with consummate tact.

* * *

These transfers from the National and RSC dwarf the week's new offerings. At the Shaw there is a revival of J. P. Donleavy's The Ginger Man, set among American student-expatriates in Dublin in the fifties. The combination of lingoes makes it worth the hearing, but not necessarily worth the watching. It is a procession of incident (four characters, but the script is all dialogue) which could be unified only by an electric performance in the title-role. John Shrapnel, despite his arrestingly jagged voice, is placid. The play comes to life only when he charmingly seduces a three-quarters willing spinster whom Helen Ryan makes a fascinating mixture of primness and provocation. Hers is one of the best quiet performances in London.

records.title: The Other Hamlet
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
To get good notices it helps to be dead; when the Royal Shakespeare Company's studio Hamlet was first shown to the critics at Stratford's Other Place, its director, Buzz Goodbody, was already the late; and within a week she and the production were almost legend. This coincidence offered great cause for suspicion; so did the reiterated claim that this was "a Hamlet for our time," which usually means that the actor is not up to the role. The production has now transferred to the cellarage beneath the Roundhouse, and I made my way warily downstairs.

I was tired, apart from anything else, of director's Shakespeare; the current National Theatre production had found me willing to forgive much crudity for the sake of plainness, speed and an exhilarating central performance. I still think that for the moment that is the way to act Shakespeare in a large theatre; not to worry the text, but to let the text worry us. But a small room imposes different rules; it shows up any kind of sloppiness. The present version, for example, done in modern costume, closes with a military take-over by a sinister Fortinbras who has come to Denmark dressed for Vietnam. Offstage the boots of his soldiers mechanically crunch. We end in fact with a rampaging cliche: which I mention at the start in order to dispose of it quickly, since it is the only blemish on what, to my surprise, I found a fascinating evening.

This is a conversational "Hamlet" which discovers meaning from moment to moment without (as tends to happen at the Aldwych, even in a superior product like the "Henries") vaingloriously brandishing it in our faces. It exhibits, not merely intelligence, but common sense. White screens slide apart for entrances and make a superbly penetrable arras. The stage, at one end of the room, puts out arms along its sides: ledges which also serve for approaches and retreats as does the centre aisle which divides the audience. We are in the middle of the action; though this is a point of strategic rather than interpretative interest. George Baker's Claudius does tend to address us, in the quietly ingratiating tones of a modern royal, as if we were his privy council, but this must be because there are no actors to spare for that function onstage. There is no consistent effort to involve the audience as participants or accomplices; Ben Kingsley's Hamlet makes far less use of us in soliloquy than does Albert Finney at the Old Vic.

Mr Baker presents a Claudius outwardly bland, really troubled by Ophelia's madness, more than willing to stop at one murder. His avowal of enmity to Hamlet ("like the hectic in my blood he rages") is a frantic admission, long pent-up. Gertrude is immature and Ophelia a baby; but age triumphs. Griffith Jones, whose Ghost haunts the play as well as the castle, and Andre Van Gyseghem, a silky Polonius, are notably more impressive here than in the histories. Mr Van Gyseghem is particularly fine when briefing Reynaldo, whom Charles Dance makes a respectfully supercilious diplomatic cadet; for once this scene fulfils its text-book function of indicating a climate of suspicion and intrigue, one which duly infects the whole play.

The colouring stops short at the central character, who here, as always, seems unaware of what kind of story he is caught up in. Ben Kingsley, compact and swarthy, looks like an unco-operative defendant at a show trial, but except when matching wits with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern (who are excellently differentiated, R being the brain and G the heavy) shows little interest in politics on any scale. If the Finney Hamlet is questioning, his is quizzical; he is continually catching himself out in histrionic gestures and shamefacedly withdrawing. This is a Hamlet who thinks he knows about acting; his advice to the Players (as an amateur suddenly granted the right to instruct professionals he should appeal to all critics) is delightful in its rapt assurance, but no less warming is the respectfully dismissive response of Bob Peck's tragedian-in-chief.

Earlier his subdued treatment of the Hecuba speech has taught Hamlet a valuable lesson which, Mr Kingsley suggests, he is willing but not quite able to learn. He cannot take the simple way out; faced with the golden opportunity to kill Claudius he hurls himself against the nearest wall, desperately arguing himself ("that would be scanned") out of an easy solution. When, a moment later, he stabs Polonius the discovery that he has got the wrong man hardly seems to surprise him; we may suspect that he would have been slower on the draw had it been the right one. For once the Ghost seems right in referring to his purpose as "almost blunted." Mr Kingsley does his incisive best to sharpen it in the meeting with the Norwegian army; but he seems too intelligent to be taken in by so obviously thuggish a Fortinbras.

He suffers, like all Hamlets, from having the crucial shift in his character take place offstage, but he compensates better than most with "This is I, Hamlet the Dane" delivered not as rant but as quiet assertion. And the end, the duel becoming a fevered punch-up when he realises Laertes's treachery, is excellent. Mr Kingsley has been tagged as an unromantic Hamlet; I wouldn't know about that, but he must be the most sympathetic in years. Performance and production come, as always, separately wrapped but they do not clash; and each is generous.

* * *

Christopher Hampton's Treats (Royal Court) has one very funny delayed-action line and other instant but less satisfying laughs. It is also well-formed, its last scene a deftly graded echo of its first. But the action is very thin, plumped up by a kind of negative significance. The characters are insulated from events outside but occasionally rebuke themselves for it. This struck me as false; people who are not bothered are not bothered about not being bothered. Anyway, if their personal lives are all they and we have got, the dramatist ought to dig into them, and Mr Hampton supplies a regulation triangle which he keeps determinedly commonplace. Jane Asher, blanched as an almond, is a sour girl who shacks up alternately with James Bolam, a bastard, and Stephen Moore, a blunderer. Mr Moore's efforts to placate Miss Asher are amusing and a touch poignant, but this is ground that both author and actor have trodden before.

* * *

At the Palladium Shirley MacLaine is doing a first-class job of being irresistible, despite obstructions. Some of these are self-created; she actually tells us about her legend, which is the opposite of disarming. She goes on though to justify it; her voice, her legs, her smile are precision instruments. She makes tear-jerking material touching (she literally touches us with it in a way which, for better or worse, is only possible in the theatre) and tough stuff dazzling. Her music (of which the best, naturally, comes from "Sweet Charity") is by Cy Coleman, who cannot be matched for rhythm by any other popular composer in the world.

* * *

Beetles and Buckman (Mayfair), comedy doctors, are also rousing song-and-dancers, though not often enough. Beetles (who was ill and is now well, which is comforting) looks a touch macabre, so his function as the straighter man of the two is intriguing. They are very clever and I wish they would sing more.

records.title: Fond farewell
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
This week the critics, in advance for once of the public, are allowed into the new National Theatre. My column next Sunday will very likely be full of its wonders. But last Saturday we witnessed the National company's last performance at the Old Vic, its 12-year home; and an event less calculated to make anyone glad at the move to the South Bank it is difficult to imagine.

The performance was entitled Tribute To The Lady and it celebrated the eccentric and indomitable Lilian Baylis who in 1914, seeing attendances flagging at her Royal Victoria Coffee Music Hall, turned "in despair" to Shakespeare and who, by her death in 1937, had seen her Old Vic become the most important theatre in the country. Peggy Ashcroft played her rejoicingly; at the close, acknowledging that her boys and girls were about to depart to a posh new building costing thousands and thousands and thousands of pounds (she seemed to think them mad but forgivable), she promised that if new incumbents were not found for the old place she would come back and haunt us.

This injunction was delivered much in the style of Miss Baylis's own curtain speeches; or at least in what Dame Peggy fully convinced us to have been their style. She could pat her audiences' heads a bit; if they had been especially good; but on the whole flattery of the public was not her style. She was more likely to rebuke them, in a cascading voice, full of teeth: they had come short, or not come at all. Mondays were particularly shameful for poor attendance; and an entire production of King Lear seems to have perished from neglect. On such occasions the audience were addressed as "bounders"; and as they bent over in their stalls and tugged guiltily at their socks they had presumably to console themselves with the reflection that their task-mistress must have loved them, so to chastise them.

The real Miss Baylis, as was made clear by an actual recording, did not sound much like Dame Peggy; her voice had a double twang, part Cockney, part South African. Nor, I would guess, was she as endearingly aware of her own outrageousness as Dame Peggy seemed to be. But if not a historical facsimile, her attacking eccentric was a magnificent creation. This actress has not knocked me so completely out since The Wars of the Roses (not quite as long ago as it sounds); and never before has she made me laugh, though here she overflowed with comic energy. She seemed as grateful for its release as anyone; and it was this sense of liberation that pervaded the occasion.

Earlier Sir John Gielgud had given us a superb, indeed revelatory, account of Hamlet's "rogue and peasant slave" soliloquy, marking, with a precision I have never heard before, the transition from ungoverned emotion to disciplined thought: "About, my brain." Later Ralph Richardson wandered on to the stage and ambled around it for several heavenly minutes reminiscing. He then waylaid two unsuspecting fellow-actors who found themselves supporting him in the barge scene from Antony and Cleopatra. There should, of course, have been a third knight. The absence through illness of Laurence Olivier, whose career has been more closely linked with the Vic than that of any other actor, made the evening incomplete. He was to have read the narration; Albert Finney deputised with great good-humour.

A couple of nights later I passed the Vic in its newly darkened state; already it looks sad and peeling. This is the first time it has ever been closed with no company imminent to open it again. Anybody who has grown up in London, interested in theatre, must have received part of his education there. Mine began in 1951: Henry V, with Alec Clunes, directed by Glen Byam Shaw, and, if anyone asks you, definitive. I grieve and hope for the place as much as anyone: the fact that it has now had a perfect requiem is the more reason for not laying it to rest.

Miss Baylis's attitude to her plays, her players and her audiences--proprietorial, committed, and, except with money, generous--has yet to be improved on. But the Vic's glory resided in its doing work no one else would attempt; it was, for years, our best and only classical theatre. A reconstituted Old Vic on original lines would now be a poor relation of the National and the RSC. It has, when it re-opens, to find a new identity. I would rather see it permanently closed than second-rate.

* * *

In The Bells (Greenwich), Freddie Jones plays Irving's legendary role of Mathias, the guilty Burgomaster driven to despair and death by the ringing in his ears (sleigh-bells, church-bells, all sorts of bells). Mr Jones, a heap of crumbling flesh, brilliantly conveys the tell-tale gnawings of fear; only the final set-piece, a silent re-enactment of his crime, strains his resources and our attention.

As regards Eric Thompson's production I must tread carefully; I once directed a Victorian play at this theatre and was dashed to find comic business that I had lifted bodily from the stage directions derided as my own insensitive invention. The silent-picture music which Mr Thompson repeatedly employs, though it seems to me to undercut the reality of Mr Jones, is indeed specified in Leopold Lewis's text. Maybe melodramatic conventions wear out more quickly than comic; I can see no justification for the lurid green light that hits the stage for Mathias's briefest asides. At best these devices remind us that we are seeing a specimen of nineteenth-century drama; it might be more enjoyable merely to see a play about a conscience-stricken murderer. In fairness, Mr Thompson's staging of Mathias's fatal vision is impressive.

* * *

Sporting the best-heeled set ever seen at the Bush, Andy Smith's Winter Visitors has one penetrating lovers' row, and a great deal of overwrought domestic bickering. At the end the writer calls down vengeance on his characters for taking up everybody's time with their tedious and rather fanciful problems; it's difficult not to feel that he has himself to blame. The final scene brings on a gunman and with him some real suspense, not all caused by natural dread of a loud bang in a small theatre.

* * *

One of the Bush's biggest successes, Stephen Poliakoff's City Sugar, now makes a smaller bang in a larger theatre, the Comedy: strong on detail but short on punch and shapelessly directed. John Shrapnel's weary ambitious DJ has gone, and with him much of the lazy, grimy, three-in-the-morning feeling that previously distinguished the play. Adam Faith's performance has speed, but no grip.

records.title: First impressions
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The National Theatre's administrative staff moved into their new home on the South Bank some time before the actors. I have been haunting the place for a couple of months, researching a book and enjoying the view of the river: a glorious prospect from Somerset House to St Paul's. I was therefore inclined to regard the building as a marvellous office block which someone, reversing the usual practice, had to go and turn into a theatre.

Last week the opening repertory--Hamlet, John Gabriel Borkman, Plunder, Happy Days, Watch It Come Down--transported from the Old Vic, was unpacked for the critics. The process took four days, at the end of which I begin already to take the new National for granted. It is very rare for a critic to spend four successive days anywhere: quite enough to convince him that he has found a home.

It is not a building to lift the heart: the squat grey fly-towers which crown and dominate it put paid to that. But there is a reassuring sturdiness about it. I like concrete; I even like the South Bank. Unless I am actually in a hurry to get somewhere, I enjoy threading my way through the channelled mazes from one culture-dome to another. The theatre is separated from the rest of the complex by Waterloo Bridge, but it is enfolded by its own profusion of balconies. Since the building fronts the river you have, if you come by car, to drive right around it, which spoils the impact and makes you feel like a tradesman. Much better to take a bus or taxi, get off on the bridge and descend on its steps. Do not, however, go straight down to entrance-level; make a detour, along as many terraces as possible. They are wide and gratifying.

The foyer seems at the moment the architect's most decisive success. It has two drawbacks: the carpets are decidedly tacky and the ceilings are menacingly low, progressively so as you ascend the building. But the three storeys do interact; they are furnished with what are referred to in Macbeth as buttresses and coigns of vantage. Looking up you are always liable to see someone poised nursing a drink and playfully prepared to spill it over you. Denys Lasdun's professed aim of using the patrons themselves to furnish his open spaces looks like being brilliantly realised. The fact that last week the obliging bodies were largely those of my colleagues made the effect all the more comforting if not invariably decorative.

But, even denuded of life, the main foyer is far from being a bleak plain: it curves, oddly, beguilingly, and unpredictably, from box office to bar to bookstall to bar again. And you can get a drink without too much suffering, and having got it can consume it without being buffeted. You can even sit down, at tables which break the area without cluttering it. The bookstall sells newspapers, which is a good idea, and the usherettes continue to sell a mass-produced ice-cream, which isn't. If the National could do a deal with one of the more individual manufacturers they might make theatrical history. The programmes are those from the Old Vic, slightly blown up and almost purged of advertising.

Of the three auditoriums, only the Lyttelton is operational and that only just, as witness the lengthy scene-changes on Plunder and the roaring air-conditioning (particularly noticeable in the pauses of Happy Days, where it made its own contribution to Beckett's desolation). It is a strange animal: an orthodox, though phenomenally wide, proscenium stage matched to an auditorium that seems uneasy at being yoked to anything so conventional. The picture-frame stage is now old-fashioned. That does not invalidate it--many good plays have been written for it, and the National must produce them--but it demands a certain cosiness. Since the audience cannot enfold the stage, as in an open or studio theatre, the auditorium must caress the audience (as at the Old Vic or Wyndham's). There has to be some affection somewhere; Peter Hall, talking contemptuously on television of plush, gilt and cherubs, simply begged the question. The Lyttelton has, undeniably, the air of a large lecture-hall; the audience, spread out in long rows with never the relief of a centre aisle, are beleaguered by an imminent back wall. You feel splayed and crushed and the leg-room is none too generous.

Undeniably, everybody in the stalls is near the stage and nothing obviously mars the sight-lines, but the focus, if you are seated at the end of a front row, can be odd. There is not so much to look at in Happy Days that you want to view it extravagantly sideways-on. The crowded action of Plunder is even more resistant to such angling. The plays in general seemed dwarfed by the stage; the only exceptions were Hamlet and Borkman, both ironically major classics which belong, according to Mr Hall's plan, on the unfinished open stage of the Olivier. Ibsen's play, especially its last scene, attained mythic dimensions. For Hamlet I had the luck to be seated dead-centre: the lines of John Bury's set (dowdy at the Vic, magnificent here) were completed by those of the auditorium. The stage-floor was patterned like a target, and soliloquies were delivered with magnetic effect from the bull's-eye.

A seat in the circle frees you from claustrophobia, but removes you from the action. Such distance is unkind to actors (except acoustically--aurally, upstairs is even less peccable than downstairs) but generous to designers. The plays look mapped out; a full view of Hayden Griffin's majestic railway-station lent a new dimension to Watch It Come Down; it has to stand for something.

The plays themselves seemed, in last week's ambience, like so many demonstration-discs; and anyway no company can be at its best before an audience composed exclusively of freeloaders. Detailed criticism would be out of place, so I merely suggest:

(a) that Happy Days on a Monday afternoon was an ostentatiously bleak beginning; that one immured actress is a boring spectacle, however terrifying the insights (and they are intermittent in this play); and that I would rather have seen Peggy Ashcroft give her Lilian Baylis again, since here, with all the finesse in the world, she seemed a bit bland and lacking in individuality;

(b) that Dinsdale Landen now supplies Plunder with just what it needs (viz, a new self-perpetuating comic convention); his silly ass continually taking himself by surprise is miraculously delicate;

(c) that Albert Finney's Hamlet, sketchy at first, flowers in madness and never loses its hold; that Susan Fleetwood's Ophelia is heartbreaking; that Angela Lansbury (though still handicapped by an unyielding voice and a crown and costume fitted for Snow White's stepmother) now fully imposes her view of Gertrude as an amenable woman, lulled by queenship, whose illusions visibly fall from her in the closet scene; that most of the other performances are now at least respectable; and that this was the peak of the week.

(d) that nobody who hated Watch It Come Down the first time will be converted by a second look but that a sharp unspecified pain often breaks through the flaccid construction.

(e) that though I believed in the crazy present of Ralph Richardson's Borkman, and strongly in his apotheosis, I extended no credit to his banking past; that Dame Peggy is nastier and more precise than she was, Wendy Hiller even more horribly erect, and Philip Stone a definite acquisition, but that this seemed, in general, an off-night.

Anyway, I'm glad it's open.

records.title: Dame with a difference
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Very late last Tuesday night the Australian comedian Barry Humphries opened his one-man show at the Apollo. It was called Housewife-Superstar, after his most famous creation, Dame Edna Everage.

Edna, on this occasion, lived up to the title, and several new stars cropped up in her orbit. They were not played by Mr Humphries. As a matter of fact they had paid to get in. They were called Dave and Leo and Meredith and Judy.

Dave, seated in a side-box, was just someone for Edna to say hello to, to get the act started. Leo was actually a Leo, who responded, from a vulnerable spot in the front row, when Edna asked him what sign he was. But Edna, once she has made a friend, does not relinquish him, and he was Leo, by name, for the rest of the night and (since we didn't even get started till 11) well into the morning.

And then Judy. Edna is clean and proud of it. "The bathroom," she explained to Dave, who hadn't asked, "is an extra room we have in Australia; like your English woodshed." She then a bit inconsistently, quizzed Judy, who did not seem to be Australian, about her bathroom. "What colour are the tiles? The tiles, Judy!" Edna can get very excited, not to say snappish, when answers on her favourite topics are not as rapidly forthcoming as she would like. Nor will she tolerate bad manners. "What's the matter?" she demanded of us as we rocked. "Haven't you ever sat in a West End theatre at midnight and heard a lady describe her bathroom before?"

It seems that when Edna's daughter Velma lived in London she knew a Judy and Edna wondered if she could have been the same one. Judy, by now understandably bemused, said that she was. "A reply which, it seems, Edna is not used to receiving at this point, and which sent the act deliriously spinning. But she had her revenge: half an hour later, in quite another context, came a quick, venomous reference to a girl called Judy "posing as a friend of my daughter Velma." Edna's natural mode is syrupy and benign, but she is a viper when crossed.

She is a patroness to the manner born, though I dare say her damehood encouraged her enormously. She was, all things considered, very sweet to a gentleman in the stalls whom she suspected of being foreign (she knew that words would be wasted on him so she waved a scarf--"they love bright colours"--to keep him involved) and she could not have been kinder to another whom she tagged as a Senior Citizens (or, as the hour grew later and friendlier, simply Senior). What an escape, she mused, a night at the Apollo must represent for him: what a change from the Twilight Home--a world, like the one into which she had cast her own mother, "of rubber sheets."

Sometimes one forgot Edna and remembered Mr Humphries: wondered whether he always flies as high and fast as this, or whether he was inspired unrepeatably by the lateness of the hour and the firstness of the night. Subsequent performances begin at normal times, but I may return if only to discover what happens in the second half. For, Mr Humphries having held forth for a staggering 90 minutes, the interval arrived well past my bedtime, and so I went home determined--since I had already enjoyed myself far more than critics are entitled to--not to tempt Providence. The insurance paid off, since next night I laughed again.

* * *

13 Rue de L'Amour (Phoenix) is the best production of a Feydeau farce since the National's A Flea in Her Ear. In some ways it even surpasses that dazzler since it eschews camp (an indulgence that Flea could afford, but which has fatally attacked the Feydeau productions which have infested the posh reps ever since.) Peter Dews's direction has other things on its mind besides unnatural speed; indeed Glynis Johns, as a Parisian wife who takes to adultery because she quite justifiably suspects that her husband has taken to it first, is notably poised and reflective. Probably she is too much so--her performance lacks daemonism--but there is compensation in Louis Jourdan's lover, sourly wounded in his self-esteem, and above all in James Grout's four-square husband, a compulsive bluffer who ends by deceiving himself.

This final scene, also prettily taken by Miss Johns, does more to justify the now standard comparison of Feydeau to Moliere than any other I have seen. After a sequence of comedies (by Coward, Lonsdale, Ben Travers) that have nearly come off, it is comforting to recognise the cool, merciless touch of a real master. The technical details delight as always; but so do such incidental touches as Mr Jourdan's declaration that he keeps a poem on Miss Johns next his heart--after which he tugs it out of his pants pocket. Then there is Margaret Courtenay, in the best scene-stealing performance in London; quivering with delight whenever a man raises his voice to her, and two well-contrasted ditherers in David Stoll and John Baddeley.

* * *

The best week that the commercial theatre has had in ages was only partly sustained by Mardi Gras (Piccadilly). If colour, rhythm and vivacity could make a musical, this one would be fully made. It falls down on melody and on architecture. Melvyn Bragg's script is transparently in love with the New Orleans of jazz legend, but he has not been able to deliver a story of more than conventional melodrama.

There is plenty of performing talent (Lon Satton, Gaye Brown and Marsha Hunt are notable), but no real star. Nicky Henson is supposedly the hero, and the opening number reveals him to have a good growling jazz-voice, but he is kept idle for most of the evening. (And though he can do almost everything else, he cannot, it seems, radiate.) The score (Alan Blaikley and Ken Howard) is, like all English musicals, desperately weak on ballads; the stompers are not as good as the real thing, but when the beat is going you hardly notice; the programme lists seven orchestrators, which seems to show where the heart is. Dancing is better than average; Abd'Elkader Farrah's shiny set participates in the choreography, and his costumes help. But by the second act these elements are being employed indiscriminately to stop the rot of the plot, and the result is monotony.

* * *

Back in the land of the subsidised, Yemi Ajibade's Parcel Post is a domestic comedy (school of Quiet Wedding and Sailor Beware) that the Royal Court would not have dreamed of presenting (at least, I hope not) if the author and the characters were not African. The paternalism only begins to be justified 20 minutes from the end, and even then interest peters out.

At the University Theatre, Newcastle, David Rudkin's The Sons of Light is a massive allegory (three hours in a cut version) which sways between inflammatory inspiration and sci-fi banality. It needs to be done again; though, since its action is confused and its characterisation non-existent (except in the stage-directions which are brilliantly written), it will probably always fail. It need not, however, fail as abjectly as in Keith Hack's production which reinforces all that is worst in the writing. A character written as a schizophrenic hermaphrodite emerges as a routine mad girl. That the one sequence of clarity should be a prolonged account of death by torture is a comment certainly on the director, possibly on the author, and confessedly on the receptivity of us in the audience.

* * *

The Chairman (Globe), a comedy about the PR department of a large company, whose members demonstrate a similarly mystifying standard of behaviour, is mildly amusing and--given its theme of the corrupting force of a totalitarian organisation--one which might have raised a few ripples outside its little frogpond. Most of the performances do better than the script, especially Tony Britton's smooth, peacock-pleased David and Peter Blythe's waterfall torrent of breathy giggles and hyper-kinesis as Peter.

records.title: The pure in heart
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
This week's musical is quite the most feathery and unperturbed of shows. In the escapist musicals of the twenties and thirties, some disturbance--a couple of gangsters, say, or a team of fortune hunters--was generally admitted to menace the well-being of the virtuous. But Very Good Eddie belongs to an earlier age when it seems the pure in heart had things entirely to themselves. It was first staged in New York in 1915, though the programme at the Piccadilly dates the action as two years earlier. Even in its cradle, it seems, the show relied on period charm.

It may have taken 60 years to cross the Atlantic, but of late it has been a fast mover. Last July it was revived in Connecticut at a place called, prophetically, Goodspeed. A few months later, David Merrick had it on Broadway. A few months more, and we have it here. At least five other current New York shows--all of them, on the face of it, demanding importation more urgently than this one--are still struggling to get through Customs. But then, they are heavier laden.

Very Good Eddie fits into the current West End scene with twofold neatness; it is light and it is old. To take the age first: I suspect that the omnipresence of revivals in the West End owes less to audience nostalgia than to managerial neurosis. No sane impresario could doubt that there is still a profit to be made on new plays, but how to choose them? Anyone can make a mistake, and play-readers doubtless make more than most. It is obviously safer to unearth a proven success from the past, even if you forfeit not only the good opinion of the critics but any chance of the big money. Please note that even in the last couple of years no old play has run as long as the new ones of Alan Ayckbourn and Simon Gray. The only revival that looks like challenging their longevity is Murder at the Vicarage, whose popularity has nothing to do with its age. I doubt if its audiences notice anything old-fashioned about it; it is timelessly terrible.

Very Good Eddie moves on a higher plane, so its survival cannot be guaranteed. It is a work of composite authorship: one composer, one librettist, and nine lyricists, among whom Schuyler Greene may be credited with the hardest work, Elsie Janis with the neatest joke, and P. G. Wodehouse with the most famous name. Wodehouse turns out to have been an early rhymer of "life" with "care and strife," but otherwise his "Bungalow in Quogue" (pronounced Quog) is one of the best numbers celebrating innocence with a touch of aerated fantasy. His colleagues are generally content just to smile, but at least their scansion is irreproachable.

The music is early Jerome Kern: post "They Didn't Believe Me," but pre everything else. It has plenty of grace but--like much of Kern's work before his brilliant flowering in the thirties--it lacks spice. "Good Night Boat" has a suave lilt and "I've Got to Dance" prefigures the Kern who wrote for Fred Astaire. It's good to have neglected songs in circulation (the real justification for productions like this one usually is the original cast recording), but at a first hearing these tunes, blandly arranged, are disappointing. They sound, in truth, strangely English.

Some of them have been interpolated from other Kern shows of the period: a succession of entertainments which were praised, in a period of inhuman extravaganzas, for their modesty and wit. The modesty is now more in evidence than the wit, and it is well preserved in Bill Gile's production, which itself contrasts refreshingly with the overblown style in which other old musicals have been revived. The performers never patronise their material, but it is difficult for the audience to avoid doing so. One wonders how they coped in 1915; did they too find it deliciously simple-minded, did they take it for real or for granted?

Nothing dates faster than realism in musicals (consider South Pacific) and the proper objection to Guy Bolton's script is not its lack of credibility but its lack of energy; it is half-hearted farce. The verbal humour is, on a strict count, awful; but it is the kind of awfulness that a bright vaudevillian--John Blythe in this case--can make irresistible. Mr Blythe's professionalism puts you in touch with the ages.

There is a deal of charm around, but it rarely makes any dramatic point. In fact it does so twice in the final revelation that the title of the show actually means something, and in a dance-duet which Richard Freeman and Prue Clarke turn into an enchantingly fleet-footed demonstration of falling in love. They play (if you can bear to hear the plot at this stage) two short people apparently condemned to marry two tall people. This is taken to be a particularly alarming kind of miscegenation; I don't know that I agree. Miss Clarke apart, the women in the show are inferior to the men. (What can be done about the British chorine?) Robert Swann is engaging as a chap who was at Yale with all the other chaps and who sings two songs, one at each end of the show, and both saying exactly the same thing. Act One takes place on a boat and Act Two in a honeymoon hotel. There you have plot and atmosphere.

* * *

Patrick Hamilton's Gaslight has both, but atmosphere is the more important. The plot is a drawn-out anecdote; what counts is Hamilton's relish for the details of his Victorian setting: the murk, the orotund speech, and the studied cruelty, class and connubial. Most of this is scuppered in the Criterion revival. There are three major roles, all radically miscast. A man is attempting to drive his wife mad; she fears and worships him. Anton Rodgers offers bloated sulks for calculated murderous caprice. His victim is Nicola Pagett, unalterably balanced and self-reliant; in the horrible final scene, where the worm turns, she has no reversal to make, and merely displays an anxiety to get the play over as soon as possible. An avuncular policeman, who adjures her to look into his face for comfort, is played by the greasily menacing Peter Vaughan.

* * *

Sur Le Fil (Greenwood, London Bridge) is the first Arrabal play I have seen which amounts to more than a heap of self-regarding neuroses. Usually his directors indulge him; Jorge Lavelli keeps him on a tight lead and, miraculously, he ceases to whoop, or to whimper. His dramatic landscape takes on a sculptural reality--a ghost town, the end of the line--excellently realised in Max Bignens's set, and in the performances of Daniel Ivernel, Pierre Constant and Georges Chorafas. Poise is not a quality I expected to grant an Arrabal work, but here it is (M. Constant walking the tightrope of the title) in abundance.

records.title: Reviving a mixed Salad
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
THE PRESS looked a bit sheepish as it filed into Salad Days (Duke of York's). Most of it was weighed down with memories. The Evening Standard had reviewed the original production; had disliked it, and had been regarded - until enlightened opinion caught up with him - as a notorious curmudgeon for his pains.

The Observer also recalled that production, which he had seen when he was about 12. He had loved it then, but he had come to believe that 12 was the optimum age for a spectator of this show and that reaction had long set in. Still, nostalgia is a strange bloom and he was perhaps as likely to be re-enchanted as disgusted. On the whole, it was a test he would rather not face; particularly as it was likely to have no definite outcome and to leave him sitting, dispiritedly as usual, on the fence.

It is in fact from that fence that I now address you. Parts of Salad Days hold up well; others do not. The present production has some pleasing performances, but is not very good.

Salad Days, as you too may remember, is about a boy and girl, just down from three suspiciously idyllic years at what seems to be Cambridge, which they follow up with a very similar month in London. The time is the early fifties, when the sun shone and birds sang in the park and that sort of thing. It is in the park that Jane and Timothy spend their time: he avoiding work, she (a reluctant deb fractionally before her time) avoiding marriage.

The first problem is solved when they take temporary possession of a magic piano, so constituted that all who hear it break into frenzied dance-steps which involve the transfer of money from their pockets into an upturned hat, thereby providing Jane and Timothy with a living wage. The second is settled by having the couple marry in the hope that they will subsequently fall in love; which, as the show proceeds, they unobtrusively do. (With each other.)

So far, you may be surprised to hear, so good: the romance is pleasant and uncomplicated, the magic piano is an inoffensive and efficient piece of whimsy, and the romance uncomplicated and likeable. It is buoyed up by three ballads which, to make no great claim for them, are as beguiling as anything heard in a British musical since the war. Thus far we have a piece of juvenilia as well worth your attention as Very Good Eddie.

But Julian Slade, though we have to look at their subsequent careers for proof of this, was no Jerome Kern. He filled this score out with chorus numbers of jigging, undistinguished cheerfulness; one or two of them (any one or two, really) would be all right, but a batch of them clogs up the evening. Such charm as they have is anyway destroyed in this production by the emergence from the pit of a droning mechanical noise, attributable to what the programme calls a Keyboard.

Something similar happens to the script, which is padded out with a succession of unrevivable revue sketches. These are now mainly entrusted to Elizabeth Seal, who looks alarmed, and Sheila Steafel, who looks dismissive (a more effective strategy). The leads, Adam Bareham and Christina Matthews, are unobjectionable, except on some of her high notes, and if there were still a great future in playing debs' delights, Osmund Bullock, as perfectly poised as named, would surely have one.
