It is in fashion now, and identified with Sinatra, even though many other fine singers have performed it. When a Rod Stewart or a Michael Bublé records an album of standards, it's hard to say whether they are doing it because they want to be Sinatra and therefore sing those songs, or because they want to sing the songs and so cannot help but ape Sinatra.

They, like Rat Pack imitators and enthusiasts, can only sound superficial because they have, as actors say, no centre. They either show off or are dull; either way, they think it's about them. Sinatra didn't sing about himself, he sang from himself, and it's a distinction I'd stand by, though I think some of his more bellicose fans might have trouble telling the difference.

There are of course songs in which Sinatra sounds directly autobiographical - charmingly in "Nancy", unbearably in "My Way" - but they're a minority. And even "Nancy" is as concerned as much with itemising his daughter's qualities as with expressing her father's feelings. For the most part Sinatra is singing about common experience, or occasionally about a very particular other experience; we assume that he is drawing on similar experiences of his own but we have no proof and we don't need it. It's showbiz lore that his bruising relationship with Ava Gardner in the 1950s informs In the Wee Small Hours, his first great ballad album, but you don't have to have heard that to be moved by the music. There's no self-pity in his singing of "Glad to Be Unhappy" or "Last Night when We Were Young", just wry, searching, majestically structured readings of magnificent songs. Read up on Sinatra's actual behaviour at the time, and it's a lot less ennobling, a lot more self-indulgent. But one is in the past, the other is for ever.

This insight, this dramatic quality, grew with time. Sinatra's career falls into four periods, in each of which he was affiliated with a different record company. As boy-singer for the Tommy Dorsey orchestra on RCA, he sounds appealing but callow, additionally constrained both by the big-band format and by most of the songs. His contemporaries were struck by his apparent belief in his material (we, who are used to hearing him sing as though he means it, tend to take it for granted), and by the sheer tender beauty of the voice. That we can still hear, as we also can, in his pop-idol years with Columbia. The warmth on these is overwhelming; so is the vulnerability that makes his performance of "Someone to Watch Over Me" something like definitive.

These were the years of the string-laden, swoon-inducing Sinatra. He wasn't yet a swinger, to listen to in the musical sense. To listen to his impeccably cheerful version of the light-hearted "Five Minutes More", one of the biggest hits he ever had, is to be surprised by the chances for rhythmic variation that he passes up, missed opportunities that he was to repair when he re-recorded the song in the 1950s for Capitol.

The Capitol years were, by common consent, his finest. They offer the best of both worlds, the charm and the vocal bloom of the preceding period offset by a new rhythmic variation and a fierce intelligence. His technical and interpretative mastery are in perfect sync. He seems to revel in taking the measure of classic song after classic song. This, not coincidentally, was the age of the LP; singers who were more than cabaret cultists had the chance to explore the catalogue and, on occasion, to add to it. These were the years of his unsurpassably melancholy "One for My Baby" and his unsurpassably happy "You Make Me Feel so Young". The last stage began in the 1960s when he started his own company, Reprise, which he quickly sold but for which he continued to record. There was no immediate break in style but the voice became grittier and, if anything, more interesting.

It was a long period, which went to schizophrenic extremes. At its crassest there was "My Way", ill-written and bombastic, which unhappily still counts for many people as his identity-song. It gets, anachronistically, into all the Rat Pack tributes; my opinion of the Palladium show will rocket up if they have the guts to leave it out. It's not just that it's a terrible song; it's that its blatancy is a direct contradiction of everything that the true, subtle Sinatra is about.

But there were compensations. He took the measure of genuinely dramatic pieces like "Ol' Man River" and the "Soliloquy" from Carousel, songs he had sung in the 1940s when he neither the depth of voice nor of sensibility to do them justice. "Ol' Man River" is a triumph of imaginative empathy; he isn't black, it's decades since he's been downtrodden, but he gets inside the song and its bleak message ("tired of livin' and feared of dyin'") of universal suffering. He had maybe his finest hour recording a bossa nova album - a style he'd never sung before - with Antonio Carlos Jobim. He takes it over; or let it takes him over. On one track, "Dindi", you can actually hear him being humbled, amazed by the mysterious beauty of the song. This is a pop singer? He sounds like the wisest, most compassionate man you ever met.

As a person Sinatra was at his most appealing when acknowledging contradictions and obligations. ("I've been over-rewarded in my life and that's the truth." "An over-privileged adult ought to do something to help under-privileged children". "Whatever else has been said about me is unimportant; when I sing, I believe I'm honest".) Most of us are capable of both good and bad behaviour, but his position gave him more scope in both directions; my own guess is that, even outside music, he did more good in the world than harm. But it's the music that counts; 60 years of self-expression that mostly transcended self and still have the power to touch.

records.title: Casting a critical eye over a Miller's tale of the West End
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Jonathan Miller, announcing a brave new season of plays for his first year at the Old Vic, took the opportunity to inveigh against the rest of the British theatre. "Bureaucratised" was his word for the subsidised wing. The West End, where four plays closed only last week, was a wasteland, governed by the untutored whims of "Attila the tourist". Actually the situation is even bleaker than he describes. I am not at all sure, though, that any individual, even Attila, is to blame.

Nobody could accuse Dr Miller of pandering to the Philistines. Planners looking for untried classics to fill up their seasons, or even fans wondering what theatrical cadavers they would most like to see resurrected, are apt to throw up their hands and fall back on the same old Chekhovs, Ibsens, and Shaws. Dr Miller has come up with seven titles of which only one could possibly be called familiar. And that one, being The Tempest, hardly counts. Shakespeare is allowed to break everybody's rules.

For the rest, we have a musical, Candide, which I have seen in New York and Edinburgh, but never in London; and plays by Racine, Ostrovsky, Lenz, Chapman and N. F. Simpson, that I have never seen at all. And I've been around.

It's a cheering catalogue, made more so by Dr Miller's assertion that the season only needs to play to a modest sounding 60 per cent of capacity to break even. "There is," he said, "no way we can make ourselves millionaires out of this theatre." But then his backer, Ed Mirvish, already is a millionaire. He rescued the Royal Alexandra, which is Toronto's most beautiful theatre, and is doing the same for the Vic, which is ours. A few years ago he saved its body. Now he's working on its soul. Dr Miller's tribute to his "pragmatic philanthropy" is, if anything, an understatement.

Some of Miller's pronouncements are more questionable. To declare in advance that none of your productions will transfer to the West End sounds to me like giving hostages to misfortune. True, a West End management is not that likely to bid for Bussy d'Ambois - not, at least, without Michael Caine in the leading role - but it is possible to imagine the Shaftesbury Avenue boys knocking on the door at Waterloo Road and asking if Candide can come out to play. If they do, and if they ask very nicely, will Dr Miller really say no? And if so, why?

One reason may be that he needs something to fight against. He has to construct a demonology. I imagine that he sees bureaucracy and commercialism as aspects of the same phenomenon and would point to the National Theatre and RSC's string of West End transfers as proof. Some years ago Lindsay Anderson started a classical repertory company actually in the West End and used the occasion to proclaim the virtues of the commercial theatre (against which he had been inveighing all his working life) and to deplore the feather-bedding of the subsidised theatre (which he had always supported). Funny how your view of other people's work is governed by the conditions under which you yourself happen to be operating at the time. As it happens, Mr Anderson's company speedily found itself playing a straight run of a Ben Travers's farce, and then expired, thereby confirming everybody's worst fears about the West End. A question-mark hangs over the more recent attempt to buck the system of another distinguished director, John Dexter.

On the other hand... the success of The House of Bernarda Alba, a play of which few West End punters could previously have heard, has been hailed as a sign that a play of quite menacing seriousness can survive in the West End. And so it can, if it has rapturous notices and Glenda Jackson. Miss Jackson can sell almost anything. Television stars, the West End has been discovering, lack the magic, maybe because on their own turf each of them is only half a star. Peter Bowles doesn't sell without Penelope Keith, or George Cole without Dennis Waterman, or Mel Smith without Griff Rhys-Jones. Les Liaisons Dangereuses, the remaining class contender, has no stars but it does have rapturous notices, plus sex. It was also, for more than a year, an acclaimed play in a small theatre that nobody could get into. One of the subsidised theatre's attractions for a commercial producer, greater even than the money it saves him, is the expectation it creates.

That leaves the mega-musicals about which there is nothing to be said except that they run because people enjoy them. This may sometimes be perplexing, but it is not sinister. I cannot see that anybody's pleasure in Les Liaisons can reasonably be damaged by the existence round the corner of Les Miserables.

It all means, though, that there are few categories of shows with any chance of West End success. Dr Miller blames it on the tourists ("the Huns of modern Europe"), but this is unfair. Tourists can only patronise the shows that producers offer them and most producers would be far happier to play to a more reliable indigenous audience. The problem is that it does not exist, or at least not in sufficient numbers.

Does it matter? Probably not, except to those of us hoping in one way or another to make a living out of it. The average theatre-goer does not care much about "the state of the theatre". He only wants there to be a few shows on that theme which he would like to see, and it cannot matter much to him whether they are located in Islington, Chelsea or the Strand.

Or, of course, on the South Bank or in the Barbican. The National Theatre's repertory is, all of a sudden, as varied and as well performed as anyone could expect. The RSC is known to be in desperate financial trouble, but this does not seem to affect the monotonously high standards it achieves on its smaller stages. The big ones are more problematic, apparently resistant to any play that is not either a set text or a vehicle for Jeremy Irons. The directorate has been publicly flagellating itself for its choice of non-Shakespeare plays at the Barbican, but they actually looked perfectly reasonable on paper. A few years ago there would have been a decent audience for them. The awful truth may be that there is now almost nothing that a large audience really wants to see. I do not like to think about this very much. Neither, I imagine, do most people in the theatre. But it must give us all the odd, unguarded sleepless night.

So Jonathan Miller's instinct - to retire to a promontory in the Waterloo Road and fortify it - may be the correct one. He will be putting on minority plays for short runs on, presumably, modest budgets. That may be the best that anyone can do. Unless they want to get rich.

records.title: A whiff of anti-Semitism on the Rialto
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Shakespeare in Britain is like the weather. One does not complain about either, since both are inescapable. The Merchant of Venice is produced at least every other year, and nobody gets too exercised over Shylock as a figure of anti-Semitism.

If anybody does, there are two ready answers: Shakespeare was an Elizabethan and could hardly be expected to transcend the prejudices of his time; and the play is actually subversive, with Shylock its most sympathetic character. As a British Jew, product of two pragmatic cultures, I enjoy reconciling these two contradictory positions.

In Britain, Shakespeare is simply there. In North America he's often nowhere, so when he does appear he gets a reaction. Joe Papp, the impresario most responsible for keeping him on display in Manhattan, was recently informed in the correspondence columns of New York magazine that, having once produced The Merchant, he had forfeited his right to take any moral stand whatever on questions of racial prejudice.

American Jews are perhaps more sensitive, certainly more vocal, than British (also, of course, more numerous) and many of them, when they come across The Merchant, cannot believe their ears. Even the Canadian Shakespeare Festival at Stratford, Ontario, has fought shy of the play. In 37 years this British byword for theatrical popularity has surfaced there only five times. When the festival first attempted it, in 1955, the Canadian Jewish News denounced the play as "pure, unadulterated anti-Semitism" with "no place in modern society".

Since then Shakespeare has become enough of an institution in Canada for outrage to have modulated into polite concern. When the play was announced for this year's season, the Canadian Jewish Congress expressed the reasonable hope that visiting school parties would be confined to children old enough to understand the play and its implications, and that their teachers would tell them all about its historical context. (They certainly should; that's their job.)

For a modern audience the play's main stumbling block is Shylock's enforced conversion, as a condition of his pardon, to Christianity. This is a happy ending? Michael Langham, the director at the Canadian festival, then surprised everybody by announcing that he was going to cut it. He believed in the play's final harmony, the victory of mercy over justice, and he did not want it compromised by what a modern audience would take as an act of gratuitous cruelty.

This decision, undoubtedly well meant, pleased nobody. The Jewish community said it certainly was not being done at their instigation. Censorship is as live an issue in conservative Canada as it is in Britain, and teachers and libraries were aghast to see Stratford apparently censoring itself.

Newspaper editorials, calling for the sacking of just about the entire festival, defended the play's integrity as shrilly as if it had once been attacked. Real anti-Semites strutted out of the woodwork proclaiming, usually on the telephone, that Jews ought to be forcibly converted, or that it was too good for them, or both.

At the theatre, Brian Bedford, a brilliantly contained actor, delivered the speech "hath not a Jew eyes" with furious effect into the face of a small boy who had been taunting him a second earlier. I thought it a wonderful image of the persecuted turning on his tormentors, but a Jewish professor of English condemned it in a Montreal newspaper as a stereotype of the Jew as bogeyman. Both of us, I suppose, saw what we looked for. Art may have the power to change our opinions, but it is far likelier to confirm them, whatever they are.

No critic noticed, but it was not only Jewish sensibilities that were spared in this production; Portia's parting shot to the Prince of Morocco ("let all of his complexion choose me so") went as well. But the better Langham's production got - and it got very good indeed - the more one regretted its compromises. He was obviously capable of giving us the play in its full complexity.

I wondered what would happen if he went to the logical extreme and cut all references to Jewishness. You would be left with the comedy of a villainous usurer who lost his daughter and his ducats, and deserved to. Maybe that's all that Shakespeare, who probably never met a Jew, really intended. But one clings to the belief that he intended and what he wrote were two different things.

Peter Hall, interviewed about his London production with Dustin Hoffman, was quoted as saying that The Merchant is "the most pro-Semitic play ever written". I'd like to know how he works that one out.

The play's superficial assumptions are certainly anti-Semitic; the Jew is assumed to be a villain, and proves one. But it's also his villainy - his flesh-and-blood unwhining villainy, more interesting than any sanctity - that saves him and saves the play.

If it were deeply anti-Semitic then its vileness would, in some form or other, infect all its author's other works and we should expunge them from the centre of our culture. But if some remain they all must: including those, like The Merchant and The Taming of the Shrew and Henry V, that offend against fashion. A theatre explicitly devoted to Shakespeare - in Stratford, Canada or Stratford, England - has to keep showing us all the play in all their facets.

records.title: In the languages of star-crossed lovers
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
For the last 30 years, consciously or not, most productions of Romeo and Juliet have been competing with West Side Story. They may emphasise sex, like Franco Zeffirelli's Renaissance epics of lust and dust on stage and screen, or violence, as in Michael Bogdanov's spirited RSC attempt to pin the blame on Verona's capitalist system. Here is one Shakespeare play - about teenagers, for God's sake - that should be able to realise the fantasy of every populist director and hit the kids where they live.

If where they live is Canada, there are other possibilities. This is a riven country, maybe on the verge of splitting apart. So a homespun company called Shakespeare on the Saskatchewan has pitched tent - literally - at Harbourfront, which is where Toronto holds its annual international theatre festival, with a bilingual production. Anglophone Montagues spit their hatred, in the original text, at Francophone Capulets who retaliate in translation. When they want to get really nasty, either side is liable to adopt the other's speech. Appropriately, there are two directors: Saskatchewan's Gordon McCall and the Quebecois Robert Lepage, whose massive original creations are too dynamic to be called performance art, and who is one of the world's best directors.

Characters enter by car or, more commonly, truck. We are in a car-town, and the lovers meet at the Capulet barn dance. Some oddities cannot be overcome. The man reverently referred to as the Prince is more like the local cop. Gee, Officer Krupke, fancy meeting you here.

At first the concept seems to have got stuck in the traffic. It is impressive to see just how many vehicles can force themselves into a space, and exciting to watch them and their occupants bashing one another. The opening brawl is as mean as it should be ("Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?" is the first line in clear English). Juliet's balcony is the top of a pickup truck: no deterrent to Romeo who is on top of her - literally - before they have exchanged so much as a sigh. This is presumably meant to be fantasy, but the heavy-handed staging has no magic. The first half is brutalist Shakespeare at its most reductive. After the interval all is superbly changed. A tiresomely coarse Mercutio becomes witty just in time for death. The traffic thins; the lovers wheel a bed on for their farewell scene, with a rope attached. When they part, Juliet pays the rope out and Romeo crawls along it. Somehow we are convinced this horizontal flight is a vertical one. This means Lepage is in charge. Every moment seems right, and most of them reverberate. When Juliet takes the potion we share her fearful vision of the corpse-strewn family tomb; this time we are not confused, and we do believe.

Unlike most directors praised for command of imagery or the ability to create events, Lepage is sensitive to text and acting. From the start the two leads show unusual promise: Romeo sturdy rather than moonstruck and Juliet's accent enchanting enough to justify the language experiment on its own. They grow remarkably; and the other characters give them a belated but illuminating context. (A young, coldly frightened Lady Capulet explains a lot about her daughter). The last speech, done by the whole cast, with alternate lines in French and English, returns us impressively to the concept. But anyone can have a concept: Lepage has peopled his.

The importance of basics has been further demonstrated by Kenneth Branagh's Renaissance Theatre Company which wound up its six-month world tour in Toronto prior to a British tour leading to the Edinburgh Festival. Branagh's King Lear and A Midsummer Night's Dream are disfigured by a unit set that looks dingy under lights and too many performances of matching shabbiness. But they survive as fine pieces of story-telling. Richard Briers's Lear has unexpected authority, somewhat at the expense of his own actor's identity; but his madness has a lucidity and immediacy I have never known bettered. The Dream has lively lovers and brilliant mechanicals, among whom Branagh's Quince is a real original: a smug village intellectual, resentful of Briers's buoyant Bottom. Clearly, if you are going both to act and direct in the Dream, Quince is the role to choose. In Lear Branagh plays Edgar, another character who tries to control peoples' lives. It must work off all kinds of tensions.

records.title: National's continental drifter
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
AFTER Robert Lepage's show Polygraph, at the Almeida Theatre in 1989, Richard Eyre called it "the most exciting piece of theatre I have seen all year". Now Eyre has managed to lure Lepage to the National with Tectonic Plates (see review), an epic play about continental drift which also contains some very funny scenes set in restaurants.

Still in his early 30s, Lepage is one of two Canadians in the performing arts attracting worldwide attention; the other is the film director Denys Arcand (in whose Jesus of Montreal Lepage was an actor). Both are French-Canadians; both, that is, are part of a culture and society that seems in the process of cutting its links with the rest of Canada.

Quebec theatre attracted attention some years ago with the aggressive plays of Michael Tremblay (Lepage calls it "Tremblay's outburst"), and subsidy began to pour into the province's theatre, most of it going into lavish productions of Broadway-style musicals.

"We thought," says Lepage diplomatically, "that that was wrong." He looked towards other influences: "Dance theatre... visual theatre... it helped Francophone theatre to express itself without language."

In practice Lepage himself has never spurned language, on or off stage. (Some of the more intimate scenes that I saw in the Quebec Tectonic Plates might have been directed by Mike Leigh.) Lepage warily accepts the definition of his work as "performance art" - "though not," he qualifies, "in the Laurie Anderson sense" - but it has few of the more forbidding aspects of that genre. It welcomes the audience in.

Eyre wants Lepage to direct a play - "a European classic" - for the National. On the basis of what I have heard of Lepage's productions of Galileo and A Midsummer Night's Dream and what I have seen myself, it sounds a great idea. This year, working in conjunction with a Shakespeare troupe from Saskatoon, he directed a literally bi-lingual production of Romeo and Juliet set in a town - the Capulets spoke French and the Montagues English - that begged a few questions, but was both poignant and thrilling.

Two months ago he staged Durrenmatt's The Visit, exploiting the play's bizarre imagery to the limit. The two castrati, who are the playthings of the vengeful Old Lady, were discovered trussed up in a giant suitcase; the unemployed citizenry sat around the railway station glued to the kind of tiny TV monitors you see in airports; about as potent an image of depression, spiritual and economic, as could be imagined. The play's glib parable was sharpened but not distorted, its human action moving as well as frightening.

This was Lepage's first production at his new home base, the National Arts Centre in Ottawa, where he heads a Francophone drama unit. It seems a good place for him, since, apart from being Canada's capital, Ottawa is on the cusp of the country's two major cultures. It is a kind of no man's land, and ironically Lepage feels he may be more necessary there than in his native province.

"As Quebec gets more independent culturally, they don't need me." He begins to see himself more as a world citizen. Certainly he is in international demand. He ranks with the hottest: "Interviewers used to compare me with Peter Brook. Now they say I remind them of David Lynch."

He manages to be bold without pretension, playful without facetiousness. The movement of oceans and land masses in Tectonic Plates corresponds to "separation, meeting and drifting of people - or society or a culture."

It is evidence of his charm and authority that he can persuasively make a claim like that within moments of describing himself as "an actor, a group guy, a trouper: more a coach than a director". In fact, he is suspicious of conventionally scripted plays (and hopes gradually to wean his new Ottawa audience away from them) because, he says, they force him into the traditional theatrical hierarchy: below the author, above the cast.

It's all been said before: and nobody really believes that Lepage, even if he lets his actors write most of his experimental pieces themselves, really functions as no more than a catalyst. The Group ethic can be oversold. But whatever it is he does, it has rarely been done so winningly.

records.title: A kick out of Cole
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Today is Cole Porter's 100th birthday, and what a swell party this is. Porter knew all about swell parties, and his public image - he really was a legend in his own lifetime - was that he was always either giving or attending one. The legend survives, and so does the work. The celebratory CDs have been coming out, compilations of old performances, and collections of new ones. He has even, on one of the latter, acquired a new identity as a crusader against Aids.

This would have surprised him. Porter was never regarded in his lifetime as socially conscious. Society-conscious, yes: he was born rich, and married richer, to Linda Lee Thomas, a bruised divorcee who was content to provide gracious cover for her husband's voracious homosexuality. Song-writing made him a third fortune. He was not just rich and famous; he was famous for being rich. Though not a native New Yorker - he was a back-country boy from Peru, Indiana - he and his work came to typify smart Manhattan society. Icy-smart he often seemed, and so did his work, at least the verbal part of it. The music, though, could be tropically torrid: making for a highly personal mixture - half refrigerator, half hothouse - that had huge appeal. Porter, as an admiring contemporary remarked, made sophistication popular.

He still does. In fact, the composer-lyricist who in Kiss Me Kate advised us to Brush Up Our Shakespeare ("and they'll all kow-tow") has himself been undergoing a Bardic canonisation. Like Shakespeare, he attracts two types of devotee. There is the purist, represented by last year's EMI recording of "Anything Goes", which might have been sub-titled "Everything Stays". Every word and note of text, score and orchestration was recreated from the 1934 originals.

Then there are the modernists, the proponents of Porter our Contemporary. This has been going on since the Twenties when, after a long apprenticeship devoted largely to amusing himself and his friends in Paris and other backwaters, he arrived on Broadway (and subsequently in London) as the composer of scabrously romantic propositions like "Let's Do It" and lush philosophical inquiries like "What Is this Thing Called Love?"; and was acclaimed as the playboy of the West End world, the spirit of the age. Then came the Crash, and Porter couldn't have cared less. All through the Thirties he wrote successful stage musicals that were purely escapist. The only changes he noticed were of style, not substance:

In olden days a glimpse of stocking
Was looked on as something shocking
But now God knows
Anything goes.

For this he was not merely forgiven but feted, as if he had grasped some fundamental American truth.

In the staid Fifties, his raffishness was forgotten and his yearning love-songs enshrined in the respectable fabric of middle America. Frank Sinatra and Ella Fitzgerald recorded them superbly, for many definitively, but they worked from edited texts. To the vast pop-song public that never went to the theatre, Cole's bawdier comedy numbers were unknown. In 1965, the year after Porter died, an American revue that emphasised his naughtier songs ("Do you use the breast-stroke, dear" / Yes, I use the breast-stroke, dear / But in the morning, No!") claimed him as a liberated and liberating harbinger of the permissive society. That was pretty desperate opportunism; Cole, despite the splendour of his buttonholes, was nobody's flower-child.

This year, the charity record Red Hot and Blue - known as "The Cole Porter Aids Album" - inadvertently proved the point. The performers, all current pop acts, show what 35 years of rock have done to the ability to inflect a lyric. Or, apparently, to understand one. A rap reduction of "I've Got You Under My Skin" tells us repeatedly to "Use your mentality, wake up to reality", that being all that is left of the original lyric, apart from the medically suggestive title. To wake up to reality apparently means to use a condom. Porter would probably endorse that if he were alive. But it's not what his song says. In fact, it's the opposite. The lyric tells us that the singer is beyond using her mentality. The music agrees, even more insistently. So do Porter's other trademark love calls, a variant of the torch song that we might describe as a scorch song. "Night and Day", "Begin the Beguine" are about being too consumed by passion to want to take precautions. For a pop song to convey that amount of emotion without making itself ridiculous is very rare.

"Begin the Beguine" is actually about remembering that kind of passion rather than experiencing it, which is just as well, since its exotic throbbing would be pretty hard to take neat. It has an ironic thread running through it, a thread superbly sustained through an extra-long lyric. This is one of Porter's special strengths. His rivals could throw off brilliant one-liners, but Porter had a unique ability to construct in paragraphs.

He never tells us much about his love-objects. "You're The Top" is wonderful fun, but no beloved is actually like the Louvre Museum. What is really celebrated is the ingenuity, skill and effervescence of the admirer. Even an apparently tender ballad like "Easy to Love" ends up focusing on the gently woebegone suitor who sings it: without asking, however, for more than token sympathy. Others could admit to vulnerability and indulge in self-pity. Porter never stooped to either.

"Let's Do It" (1928) was his first classic and in some ways the archetypal Porter song. It is a biological catalogue whose arch subtitle "Let's Fall in Love" allows it to pass itself off as a ballad, risque, of course, but probably sincere. (It actually replaced a more direct and therefore less acceptable invitation, "Let's Misbehave".) The world accepts it as a celebration; the initiated note its jaunty and slightly chilling reductiveness:

Old sloths who hang down from twigs do it,
Though the effort is great,
Sweet guinea-pigs do it,
Buy a couple and wait.

As assured as he was, Porter was an outsider in his professional life. In the procession of lyricists and composers he was the only patrician, the only Yale man, practically the only Gentile. His competitors were mainly lower-middle-class Jewish boys with their ways to make. He ended up composing more minor-key laments than any of them. He wrote riper, more urgent boy-girl songs - sometimes exaggeratedly so - than the heterosexual lyricists.

The comic counterparts of his famous ballads are the countless speciality numbers, many introduced in the Thirties by Ethel Merman, in which every woman is a nymphomaniac and every man either a stud or a dud. He amused himself and his audiences with patter songs that catalogued the Manhattan party-givers and world-cruisers among whom his life was lived. The songs are as much celebration as satire. Porter reserved his bile, expressed with acidic restraint, for social unfortunates: for Miss Otis who allowed herself to stay down in Lovers Lane and was lynched by a vengeful mob; for Mrs Lowsborough-Goodby, too gauche to know how to organise a weekend.

In the quintessential Porter song, love is "a trip to the moon on gossamer wings" (breathtaking invention so precisely matched to its music that we take it for granted) to be dismissed with delicious panache as "just one of those things". We would all love to say goodbye like that. Unless there's a war on, in which case, Ev'ry Time We Say Goodbye, we would like a tug as romantic as the one depicted in 1944:

Why the gods above me
Who must be in the know
Think so little of me
They allow you to go.

At the famous climax, when the lyric talks of the strange change from major to minor which the music proceeds to enact, we react to the emotion rather than to the cleverness. We smile but we are also moved. The serenely beautiful music gives us little choice. It may be his best song.

His tastiest opening couplet is the one that begins "At Long Last Love":

Is it an earthquake or simply a shock?
Is it the good turtle soup or merely the mock?

Porter claimed to have written that song, in 1937, as he lay trapped beneath a horse which had thrown him and crushed both his legs. It inaugurated 20 years of agony, endured with stoic courage, and marked the beginnings of a slow artistic decline - arrested by the creation of Kiss Me Kate, possibly his masterpiece, certainly his greatest success. Porter would attend it with friends and murmur artlessly, "Good, isn't it?"

'Robert Cushman's Songbook,' exploring the American popular song, starts on Radio 2, Saturday 29 June at 2pm.

records.title: Five go up, down and round the bend
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
There is real grass on the stage of the Bush, and a real play on top of it. Catherine Johnson's Dead Sheep is about five variously troubled people who set out to climb a Brecon Beacon, represented on Geoff Rose's set by a large boulder that rises and falls with majestic ease according to whether the characters are huddled at its foot or perched on its peak. They do have their ups and downs.

This is hardly surprising. Three of them are ex-addicts. Middle-aged Eve was an alcoholic whose children were taken into care. Zoe and Holly were both junkies. All three are inmates of a rehab centre presided over by Philip, a nannyish religious fanatic who, like many evangelists, identifies God's will with his own. He has brought his flock on this adventure weekend as a treat. Jon, their hired guide, is ex-SAS. A self-made macho man, he could well be more disturbed than any of his charges.

All have their decent moments, but there is too much envy, frustration, resentment simmering inside each of them for the party to go by without disaster. The petty strains of five people in two tents are nearly enough to get the outing cancelled. The play chronicles them in hilarious detail and Mike Bradwell's production revels in it. Bradwell, who founded the Hull Truck company, has over the years perfected a farcical style that goes effortlessly into higher gears, and this play is ideal for him, becoming progressively bleak without ever losing its salty comic texture.

One subject he has always been good on is religion: both its pain and its absurdity. Philip, always ready with a prayer or with a fulsome word of rebuke or encouragement, is seen by the other characters as an embarrassment. Partly this is because he is a dwarf; both his enthusiasms and his malevolence seem out of scale. He embarrasses the audience too, but that doesn't mean that the author dismisses him. By the end he has lost one of his flock (see title) and is ranting uncontrollably, addressing his principal antagonist as Satan, desperately denying facts that he cannot face. But he has at least - strikingly so in Jon Key's performance - the dignity of his own fury.

What does him in is the women. Ex-pop singer Zoe (Kate Hardie) is supposedly his success, having forsaken dope, chosen Jesus and decided to set up as a carer in her own right. Holly (Katrin Cartlidge) is at the other extreme, practically catatonic. In her few lucid moments she sounds like the most intelligent person around and Jon (Gary Love) brings her right out of herself, by what you might call the traditional route: direct but, as it turns out, extremely dangerous. The other girls are both curious and furious, and Gwen Taylor's Eve - the most strikingly fake of a quintet of fine performances - especially takes fire. One moment she is raucously asking Holly how it felt since in her own case it's been so long; the next she is an avenging angel. She exemplifies the most imposing thing about the evening; its seamless mastery of tone. I have not seen Catherine Johnson's previous plays but on this evidence she is a treasurable talent.

Johnson creates stage-size characters, something notably lacking in The Manchurian Candidate. This may be because it is based on a novel, though one best known as a film. Here too the personnel go through all kinds of hoops, and though some have the excuse of having been brainwashed, others do not.

Richard Condon's original fable concerned a US marine sergeant in the Korean War, turned by communist manipulation into a killing machine and used, in a sublime game of double-bluff, as a weapon to advance the cause of McCarthyism. You want to destroy America, was the caustic message, what difference if you do it from the left or from the right? John Lahr's new version advances the story to 1996; the rabble-rousing senator now takes for his theme not the number of commies in the administration but the proportion of America owned by the Japanese. Lahr may be prescient; this could be the theme of US stump politics in elections to come. But the new wrinkle does not provide the frisson of the Cold War original which lampooned a very recognisable demagogue.

Lahr is an adept adaptor, with some nifty lines and a competent way of unfolding a complicated story. The production only shudders to an embarrassing halt when the cast sing a xenophobic anthem obviously intended to chill our blood and discourage anyone who might be considering voting Republican. But the more techniques the show uses, the harder work it all seems; and the occasional use of video only reminds us of how much more we would like to see in close-up. These people need to be brought close for us to believe in them or to be gripped by the story they serve. Gerard Murphy, even from the middle distance, has the right sickly grin for the homicidal hero; Sian Phillips is the monster's suitably monstrous mother; and Manning Redwood is a boyish senator to the podium born. Clive Carter, as the officer who drags the truth to light, looks craggily and appropriately like a junior George C Scott; and Connie Booth lends him a sympathetic ear, which is all that is asked of her. A fella needs a girl if he's in a novel or movie, but in a play, with time at a premium, he should be able to do without.

Tovarich is a 1930s success by Jacques Deval disturbed from its long slumber to provide a vehicle for Natalia Makarova. When it wakes up, which takes time, it allows her to exude a ravishing hauteur while twirling about in a maid's uniform and to fill the theatre with romantic longings for a White Russian past. She and her Grand Duke husband (Robert Powell) are forced into domestic service with the bourgeoisie through poverty and loyalty, and some of their encounters with their dazzling Parisien employers are very funny. The evening then starts leaning on sentiment and charm, but the two stars supply both.

Alan Ayckbourn's Scarborough Theatre has moved into its restaurant to accommodate the American Tom Dulack's Breaking Legs, which is set in one: a New England Italian establishment whose proprietor (Jeffrey Chiswick, all olive oil and unction) ropes in two business associates (Glyn Grain, a master of slow-burning comic menace, and Robert Austin, a credible hulk) as backers for a play written by a nervous but increasingly confident academic (Peter Bourke, priceless) who happens to be loved by his daughter (Susan Denaker, making energetically like Angelica Houston). Ayckbourn wonderfully orchestrates a stagefull of flawless cartoon performances. The production outshines the play which is a collection of mild gangster and showbiz jokes, though one speech does begin "I can only speak for myself but I know I speak for all of us." Now that's eloquence.

records.title: Lady of the deep gets stuck in the shallows
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Lady of the deep gets stuck in the shallows

THEATRE
ROBERT CUSHMAN

LET no one say that Ibsen's later plays are invariably dark and obscure. The Lady from the Sea has a happy ending that can be seen coming a nautical mile off. A minute into the show a painter, working on a picture of a mermaid, says that "the lady who lives here inspired me to paint it". Enter Ellida, the lady of the painting and of the title. She has been for a dip ("she swims every morning, whatever the weather") and surfaces in this production cropped and shiny in a green towel. She looks healthy but asked if she feels refreshed she replies: "I don't; I never do."

She is pining for the open sea beside which she grew up and which she associates with a sailor to whom she once plighted her troth and who then disappeared on suspicion of murder. Now he arrives to reclaim her from her husband, an amiable if incurably land-locked doctor who would be many women's ideal son-in-law. A dab hand at a diagnosis he picks up immediately on his wife's complaint that if she stays with him it will be "not of my own free will". He gives her her freedom - you half-expect him to write a prescription for it - and she exercises it by electing to stay with him. That is what the play has promised to show, that is what it does show, and there is not a note of irony to be heard.

Heidi Thomas's adaptation, from which I have been quoting, is brisk and generally colloquial and it enables director Jules Wright to deliver the play in what may be record time. There are no significant pauses, and few insignificant ones. The principal emotion transmitted is a terror of being thought pretentious.

In the last major British production, Vanessa Redgrave gave a visual and verbal resonance to Ellida's marine compulsion that transcended polemics. The one before that, also with Redgrave though in a different role, found its texture in the life of the household, this being one of the few Ibsen plays to have one. Ellida attracts men as ineluctably as a Chekhov chatelaine, and they sublimate their feelings by hovering around her two stepdaughters. The elder of these is courted by her ex-tutor who wants to take her away and show her the world, which is fine with her, but also wants to marry her, which isn't. She looks like repeating her stepmother's mistake with a far less sympathetic partner. Or maybe they'll be all right.

But in either case we have here two people at a crisis of their lives, and it passes belief that they would get through it at an even pace, in unvarying profile, without once taking a moment to sit and think. But that is how this production goes. People face one another and deliver their lines, as conversationally as possible. When passion seems unavoidable they stomp about a bit and switch to a tone of petulant self-pity.

Kathryn Pogson as Ellida has a still, troubled presence that persuades you something is going on beneath, but it never breaks surface. "I can't see him any more" - referring, at the height of her disarray, to the husband she cares for - is not a line that can plausibly be muttered. And with the central performance so battened-down, the others sink automatically lower; for a man in imminent danger of losing the wife he loves Hugh Fraser's doctor is amazingly unruffled. Alister Cameron as the local jack-of-all-trades is nice, but his is the smallest role. We learn that mature Ibsen played purely at dialogue level seems impossibly glib.

After The Lady from the Sea, The Boys from Syracuse. (Next week The Girl from Nantucket, The Man from U.N.C.L.E., and The Creature from the Black Lagoon.) This is the 1938 Broadway musical based, with considerable resource and fidelity, on The Comedy of Errors. The opening number, "I Had Twins", handles the cumbrous exposition a lot more adroitly than did Shakespeare. Otherwise Lorenz Hart's lyrical wit shines less in the obvious comedy songs than in the bitter-sweet spin he puts on the love ballads. In fact the best-known lines are the best: "falling in love with love is falling for make believe", "this can't be love because I feel so well" - the latter sung by the visiting Antipholus to (I think I've got this right) his brother's sister-in-law. Meanwhile the prodigal grace of Richard Rodgers' music extends to what, for any other composer, would be throw-away numbers; mark the tripping verse to "What Can You Do with a Man?"

Grace is what George Abbott's book rather lacks, but it keeps the jokes coming, and some of them are funny, and Judi Dench's good-natured production enjoys them all. It reaffirms that, barring the occasional Anything Goes, musicals of this vintage are more fun when done on a modest scale, and it plays wittily with its own pastoral setting.

The action revolves around a parkland bandstand, and James Merrifield's bold, gorgeous costumes make the ladies look like animated bell-tents. Accents are emphatically American, with Jenny Galloway's frustrated wench a Brooklynese triumph. Louise Gold, one of our best soubrettes, makes a valiant prima donna. Gillian Bevan sings beautifully. Musical direction is excellent.

As long as wars leave human debris Euripides' Women of Troy will be the world's most topical play: so pertinent as almost to defy revival. The women awaiting deportation and enslavement are eternal. The murder of the boy-child Astyanax, slaughtered for policy, is the greatest atrocity in world drama, a breach in nature. Millennia later, Edward Bond in The Woman presented it as the way of the world. By so much have we fallen.

The temptation to cheapen the play with facile parallels must be enormous, but Katie Mitchell's production never succumbs. Nothing is vague; every line means something, either as fierce lament or - where the gods or Helen are involved - bitter comedy. The style, which involves a lot of perfectly controlled chanting and dancing by a large ensemble, is extraordinarily strong.

I didn't like all the choices (Kathryn Hunter's crazy Cassandra, a Jewish-American rather than a Greek princess, I found especially hard to take) but the point is that they are choices, intelligently made and uncompromisingly carried through. Paola Dionisotti's flinty Hecuba is too young to suggest the mother of them all, Barbara Flynn's bereaved Andromache almost too selflessly stoical to be moving, but they are fine performances and great figureheads.

The Lady from the Sea, Riverside Studios (081-748 3354); The Boys from Syracuse, Open Air, Regent's Park (071-486-2431); Women of Troy, Gate (071-229 0706).

Irving Wardle is on holiday.

records.title: Sir John replays his greatest hits
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Sir John replays his greatest hits

SHAKESPEARE: HIT OR MISS?
by John Gielgud with John Miller
Sidgwick £17.50

JOHN GIELGUD and Shakespeare have not kept company much in recent years. Although a compulsive theatre-goer since the late 1950s, I have seen Gielgud in only three Shakespeare roles. Two of them, Wolsey and Julius Caesar, he was essaying for the first time and neither ranks among his greatest hits. The third was Prospero, which he had already played twice and which I saw him do twice more. He also had behind him multiple assaults on Lear and Hamlet, and was reckoned supreme in both parts - as he was in Richard II, Angelo, Benedick, Cassius and Leontes.

All of which suggests that Shakespeare is a young man's game. (Or, increasingly these days, a young woman's game: we breed far more Rosalinds than Hamlets.) Sir John, in this book of reminiscence, seems inclined to agree, constantly protesting how out of touch he must seem, how long ago his triumphs were, and how seldom he goes to the theatre.

Actually this most effortlessly modern of actors seems to have kept up with all the best things, from Peter Brook's Dream to Richard Briers's Malvolio, and he is discerningly enthusiastic about them. Even at his most apparently reactionary he talks sense, as when he doubts that young audiences are much beguiled by seeing the plays done out of period.

This is a light, anecdotal book, pleasing because you can hear the Gielgud voice in it but frustrating because he says so little about the characters he has played. He checks them all off, unchronologically, but almost the only specific comment he makes is that Richard II "has no humour". This is startling, given the actor's own comic genius, but it does reveal what the subsequent line of waspishly witty Richards have been reacting against. His editor/collaborator should have pressured him for more.

Far more instructive, and almost justifying the graceless title, is his constant emphasis on the theatre's fallibility: on the things that work one night and not another, and on the actor's quixotic insecurities ("I was afraid," he says of an early success, "of becoming a bit too pleased with myself"). He combines specific modesty with an overriding assurance of his own place in history. "Audiences," he says "often credit you with far more intelligence than you actually possess."

Critics, I am sure, will often take a hint from a performance and proceed to father on the actor their own fantasies about the play; several set-pieces of criticism are reproduced here. There are also some invaluable notes on Lear from Granville-Barker, who once directed Gielgud in the role, and whom he reveres as he does Brook. This book could use a director.

records.title: The Astaire way to heaven
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
The Astaire way to heaven

LIVES OF THE GREAT SONGS
THE WAY YOU LOOK TONIGHT

There are a million songs about falling in love, but few that capture the moment like the Kern-Fields classic. For the third in our weekly series, Robert Cushman tells its story

POPULAR songs freeze the moment. That is what they're best at. Some of the finest - the Gershwins' "How Long Has This Been Going On", or Rodgers and Hart's "I Didn't Know What Time It Was" - celebrate the moment of falling in love, and are bemused rather than euphoric. The joy is tempered with a wistful incredulity. How could this have taken so long to happen? How can it possibly last? My favourite song, "The Way You Look Tonight", music by Jerome Kern, lyric by Dorothy Fields, does all this and more. It evokes the moment of discovery, dramatises it, and - the last and most brilliant refinement - discusses it. It is, in the least pretentious way, about itself.

Like many songs of its era, it leads a double life. If you hear it as an independent pop song it seems to be about a first, rapturous meeting or - perhaps more likely - about the start of a date. Man greets woman, who is looking especially radiant, and compliments her. You can, within limits, construct your own scenario; and it helps if you have someone in your mind to attach it to. But it was written for a specific situation in a still-current film: Fred Astaire sings it to Ginger Rogers in their 1936 film Swing Time.

The extra-musical portions of Swing Time are, for me, the hardest to sit through of any in the Astaire-Rogers canon. This is largely because Astaire's usual comic foil, the heavyweight bumbler Edward Everett Horton, has been replaced by Victor Moore whose clowning is so gentle as to be practically invisible. Alas, the film's planned opening number was cut, so there is an interminable wait before any singing or dancing gets done. When it does, and for as long as it does, the film is a masterpiece. Song by song, it may have the best score of the series; certainly the numbers are the best integrated with one another and with the plot. In fact, the songs are the plot.

"The Way You Look Tonight" has a modest set-up. There isn't even any dancing. Fred sits at a piano while Ginger is showering in the next room. As he plays and sings she appears with her hair all suds and enchantedly drinks in the praise. It's absurd that this should be the way he is vowing to remember her: absurd and, of course, totally endearing. His singing is straightforward, with a hint of melancholy; the tone, in the fashion of the time, is surprisingly formal, though the phrasing isn't. The song, interestingly, jumps straight into sadness: "Someday when I'm awfully low / And the world is cold . . ." Having admitted the odds the song makes its first and most important statement with a slight but definite lift in the melody: "I will feel a glow / Just thinking of you / And the way you look tonight."

Then comes the masterstroke: "Oh, but you're lovely . . ." That "oh, but", deftly fitted by Fields to Kern's pick-up notes, forestalls any chance of the second eight bars being mere repetition. Disarmingly conversational, it also suggests uncertainty, inability to find words, a sense of how-could-you-be-so-lovely, and of "lovely", though conventional (and more or less patented by Kern's contemporary Irving Berlin), being the only possible word. The song then proceeds to specific compliment: "Your cheek so soft . . . your smile so warm . . . with each word your tenderness grows tearing my fears apart." The qualities praised are gentleness, wit and compassion; and the song exemplifies them even as it cites them. Kern's middle eight, trim but expansive, is remarkable even for him (by this point, it seems, an orchestra has crept into the room); and Fields's climactic bouquet - "that laugh that wrinkles your nose touches my foolish heart" - clinches both the romance and the reality. A person is being sung to, whether it's Ginger or another. And that "foolish heart" phrase has been plundered by other lyricists ever since.

The last section begins by repeating and savouring the word "lovely" - this time without the hesitation. The song and the singer have moved on to a new plane of confidence. "Never, never change / Keep that breathless charm / Won't you please arrange it . . ." Obviously she can't - nobody can - and in making the request the song acknowledges its impossibility. Nobody but Astaire could be so urbane and so diffident at the same time. But, of course, he and his writers have worked the trick anyway. As long as the song lives, so will the beauty it commemorates. Shakespeare and Keats had observed this phenomenon for their respective centuries. Kern and Fields have done it for ours.

As usual Astaire made a commercial recording of the song, done in suave dance-band fashion. It's more insistently rhythmic than the film version, more obviously sung, but also more acted. "Your cheek so soft" is gently emphasised; "Never, never change" is quietly pushed home; "breathless charm" has a tremble to it. Astaire's great singing years, though, were the Fifties when the voice was lighter, more intimate, and, if I may, de-theatricalised. His film vocals of this time were a marvel, and a three-LP set on which he reprised his classics with a jazz quartet led by Oscar Peterson must be the most charming vocal record ever made. He murmurs a lot here, moving at a conversational rubato through the opening section, caressing the first "tonight", then picking up a moderate tempo, kicking the beat with an amiable desperation on "There is no-thing for me but to love you". That "for me", by the way, is a hidden rhyme with the "warm" in the previous line; it keeps other lyricists goggling.

Though nearly everybody you would expect has recorded the song since, only Astaire has come close to owning it. Billie Holiday, who spent most of the Thirties singing inferior songs, never seemed to realise her luck when, as here, she got a great one. Her version is jaunty, no more. (Her records of the Fifties tell a different story, but this song is not part of it.) Like nearly everybody, including Astaire, she neglected the song's coda; a series of precisely notated hums that balance the stammers of the beginning. (Once we couldn't find the words; now we don't need them.) Most singers leave these sighs to their accompanists; a happy exception is Peggy Lee, who recorded the song with Benny Goodman in 1942. Cool and tingling, it's one of the few mementoes of her band-singing days that forecast greatness.

My two favourite instrumental versions date from the early Fifties, and both emphasise joy, not regret. A buoyantly rhapsodic interpretation by Coleman Hawkins (with Miles Davis in support) does especial justice to the coda. Sonny Rollins's work-out with Thelonious Monk ("The Way You Blow Tonight") is an amiable hurricane. Its vocal counterpart is Mel Tormé, paying tribute to Astaire in 1956, and sailing exhilaratingly through and around a fast West Coast arrangement. He starts with a coda: "Lovely . . . never, never change." There seems no chance that she will. There is no uncertainty in Tormé's version, no psychological progression; the drama comes from his exploration of Kern's harmonic possibilities and from the insouciant accuracy of everything he does. Dick Haymes, a magnificent balladeer, took the opposite tack. He starts sombre: "Awfully low . . . the world is cold." He is wonderstruck, and gets half way through the song before he can believe his good fortune. His final "I love you" is triumphant (it helps that he can hit the note so ringingly) but the possibility of loss still hovers.

Neither Ella Fitzgerald nor Frank Sinatra got to the song till the early Sixties: a little late, I think. Both used arrangements by Nelson Riddle. Ella's is a lullaby version: sweet, of course, but too slow to flow. And since she isn't a dramatic singer, the pauses don't mean anything. Sinatra merely crosses the song off his list: a swinging lovers' treatment, without the commitment. Neither he nor Ella explores the song as they could. They should have exchanged tempos. More recently and eccentrically Peter Skellern offers one of his passionately sedate, oddly touching Astaire homages; Kiri Te Kanawa, though less overbearing than often in this territory, glides through the song without leaving a mark.

The song itself glides. That is the mark of an Astaire number, even one that excludes dance. But I can imagine it being sung out of tempo all the way through: thoughtfully, musingly, ecstatically. With each word its tenderness grows; and the encounter might as easily be sexual as social. The voice I hear in my head is that of Rosemary Clooney, who today sings classic pop more warmly and expressively than anyone, and has never recorded this song - she might do it definitively.

Recently too, "The Way You Look Tonight" has gone back to the movies. It is a grace-note in Kenneth Branagh's film Peter's Friends - a quiet moment in the otherwise stormy reunion of half a dozen college friends. Hugh Laurie sits down at the piano and dreamily plunks it out; Imelda Staunton, the singer of the bunch, begins it sweetly; the others - Branagh, Alphonsia Emmanuel, Emma Thompson, Stephen Fry - drift over and join in. Whether the writers chose the song purposefully or whether anything equally "squishy" (their word) would have done as well, remains uncertain. But the song brings the friends together as almost nothing else does (the hangers-on they have brought remain pointedly outside the circle). It's a hedge against the world for them, the poignantly miserable, just as it was for Fred and Ginger, the poignantly happy. The song, concerned with preserving the present, began by projecting itself into a chilly future which it proceeds to redeem. It seems to have got it right.

Robert Cushman's series "Book, Music and Lyrics" returns to Radio 3 on Monday 26 July.

records.title: Side by side by Glynis Johns
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
Side by side by Glynis Johns

Sondheim wrote it; just about everybody has sung it. Robert Cushman, re-starting our series, tells its story

LIVES OF THE GREAT SONGS
SEND IN THE CLOWNS

VICTORIA WOOD once wrote a musical called Good Fun whose heroine, at a point of emotional catastrophe, sang out approximately as follows: "This isn't going to be a song about clowns; I hate bloody clowns." I know how she felt. However, the song to which she was implicitly referring isn't about clowns either.

The story goes that Harold Prince, directing A Little Night Music on Broadway, summoned Stephen Sondheim, author of the music and lyrics, to rehearsals to watch how Glynis Johns, the leading lady, was playing a particular scene. The show is based on Ingmar Bergman's Smiles of a Summer Night; Johns played an actress who tries to lure her ex-lover, a lawyer, away from his unresponsive young wife. He feels the tug but cannot break free. Johns was bringing such intensity to the scene that a song seemed called for, an expression of her pent-up feelings. And so, impromptu, a song was born: not Sondheim's best song, not even his best ballad (I prefer "Not a Day Goes By", a real heartbreaker from Merrily We Roll Along), but easily his best-known.

The tale has always puzzled me. "Send in the Clowns" is Johns's only song in the musical's second act, and her only solo anywhere. Weren't they intending to give her one? The show would certainly have been unsatisfying without; in a musical songs are how we get to know people, and she is the heroine. In the event, "Send in the Clowns" not only evened the balance; it centred the show.

I found this out in stages. Night Music opened in 1973; I first saw it the following year in Toronto: the road-company version with Jean Simmons playing Desiree, the actress. I admired its elegance and I liked the music, but I was unmoved. The next week in New York I was persuaded to see it again. To begin with, the show and I kept our accustomed distance from one another. But Glynis Johns's husky humanity warmed me from her first entrance, and when she got to the song she transformed the evening. Night Music is a parade of lovers, most of them poignantly or hilariously mismatched; the pattern was clear but not very involving. Johns's song - about the acceptance of heartbreak - not only brought her own situation to life; it illuminated the complications and resolutions that were to follow and - in some not quite explicable way - made sense of what had gone before. It was as if a frieze had come to life.

The entire Night Music score is composed in waltz time, though the lilt is often disguised. "Clowns" is a sober, cold-light-of-dawn variation on the theme. It begins with a chaste woodwind statement of the melody, taken up - still soberly - by the strings. Then the voice comes in: "Isn't it rich, are we a pair . . ." The lines are short, and they could conceivably be bitter, but the tone is maturely ironic: if there is any anger she's directing it at herself and saving it up for later. This man has been chasing her and now, when she's ready to give herself, he's unavailable: "Me here at last on the ground, You in mid-air . . ." The images are economically exact if you know the story, tantalising if you don't. Sondheim habitually deals in half-truths and unconscious self-betrayals, but here Desiree is singing exactly what she feels. The greatest irony is that her partner isn't listening.

Since she is an actress, her vocabulary is theatrical. "Send in the clowns" - the phrase that, with variations, ends every section of the main strain - is the traditional command when something goes embarrassingly wrong in a circus or vaudeville and the audience has to be distracted: a kind of desperate shrug. Towards the end Desiree ruefully recognises the image's reference to herself - "Don't bother, they're here" - but she isn't indulging in Pagliacci self-pity.

The song is divided into the pop song's traditional four sections, AABA; and one of the loveliest things about it is the ease with which the A section, the main strain, flows into the B. This bridge begins in very similar vein - same rhythm, same sawn-off lines - "Just when I'd stopped / Opening doors" - and then stretches itself, gets more open and voluble - "Finally knowing the one that I wanted was yours / Making my entrance again with my usual flair" - before returning to cryptic defeat - "Sure of my lines / No one is there". We are back in the mood and meter of the main melody, so the second transition is as tight and logical as the first. At the end, when her lover has gone, Desiree sings an extra A section: an instant reprise. The short phrases were written to accommodate Johns's limited voice, which also accounts for the song's truncated range. It's meant to be acted. But it's also meant to be sung, and it's notable that Johns sang nearly every note. The glory of Sondheim's lyrics is their conversational quality, but this point is lost when people start speaking them. After all, anyone can talk conversationally.

Matter-of-fact, gently sardonic, temperamental but vulnerable, Johns's performance - of the song and the role - remains definitive. How much so was revealed in London when Jean Simmons resumed the part, and was beautiful but bland. (Elizabeth Taylor in the film was blank.) However, by the time of the West End opening, Night Music was able to advertise itself as "the 'Send in the Clowns' musical". The song had become a hit.

This was odd. Plenty of good theatre songs, including Sondheim's own, have been ignored by the pop world; and, out of its context, this one is hard to understand. But paradoxically that may have helped it. The Seventies were the time of the singer-songwriter, when the favoured style was the sensitive-obscure. "Clowns" must have seemed to fit right in with Joni Mitchell; certainly it did in Judy Collins's best-selling and totally uninflected performance. Listeners could make of it what they wished; and I swear that most of them thought it was a Pagliacci song. So did some performers. I remember a Manhattan club singer furiously embellishing the lyric: "Where are the clowns? You promised me clowns." It didn't work.

Other singers were more thoughtful. Cleo Laine, one of the first to adopt it, appreciated the drama; she was actively sad, bristlingly ironic, sometimes coming close to milking pathos but stopping in time. Some tried to explain it. Bing Crosby provided an outline of the plot, adding that he was surprised more singers hadn't taken the song up. (Where had he been? It was inescapable.) Late Bing made any song a pleasure to hear, but his mellow style hardly suited this one.

Frank Sinatra was another story. Most unusually, he provided a spoken introduction on record as well as in person: an edited but acceptable version of the facts. "This is about a couple of adult people . . . it's a break-up." His voice is at its gravest and most gravelly, and so it is in the song itself. He starts with world-weariness - the opening is slightly dismissive - then opens up, emotionally and technically, with virtuoso extended vowels - "you in mid-a-a-air, one who can't mo-o-ove" - to activate the rhythm. The accompaniment is solo piano, and there are seconds of troubled silence. "Just when I'd stopped opening doors" is harsh and abrupt, "making my entrance again with my usual flair" speeds up lightly for self-mockery, "sure of my lines . . . - no one is there" gets one of those haunted pauses. It's one of his finest, most compassionate performances; the fastidious separation of consonants on "don't you love farce" is trademark Sinatra - though this time Glynis Johns got there before him - the insistent definition giving both performances a signal authority.

The song also brought out the best in Barbra Streisand, who tackles it on her The Broadway Album without a trace of histrionics and with an orchestration closely resembling the original. She claimed never to have understood the lyric, and Sondheim obliged with a second B section that spells everything out: "What a surprise! / Who could foresee / I'd come to feel about you / What you feel about me?" I doubt that it improves the song, but it gives it a more orthodox shape.

The song has undergone other kinds of expansion from singers who feel that the one Broadway standard of the last 20 years deserves the grand manner, or can be knocked about a bit, or both. From the first it was a fixture in New York supper clubs. Mabel Mercer, the Queen Mother of cabaret, was in her 70s when it came out, and she sang it on a rising arc of passionate regret. Her successive readings of the recurring title-phrase - beginning nonchalant, ending up fierce - epitomised her fastidious fanaticism about lyrics. (I once heard her get the pronouns in the opening lines the wrong way round. She stopped, briskly apologised, and started again.) She also insisted, more firmly than any other performer, on the song's identity as a waltz. Mel Tormé made it an explosive jazz waltz, with a Stan Kenton-ish big band and a roguish introduction to the effect that he hoped the composer never got to hear about it; the lyric comes out neutral, but an all-out sarcastic whiplash approach at this tempo might be very effective.

In 1977 the song went disco, courtesy of Grace Jones, with a calliope-carousel intro to show that nobody was afraid of the obvious. Jones sings the words clearly, but they could be any words; though "making my entrance again with my usual flair" is an idea she seems to relish. This is her Broadway medley; the song segues into "What I Did for Love" and thence into "Tomorrow" - with both of which she seems to have more empathy and in both of which the beat makes more sense.

Perhaps the furthest stretch from the song's original economy was Sarah Vaughan's use of it as a showpiece encore, doubling the number of octaves the author first thought of and making all the drama strictly technical; "she holds the word my," wrote the American jazz critic Gary Giddins, "longer than you can hold your breath and then plummets into career." Whatever she was losing, it wasn't her timing.

The song, or its title, has also long served as a headline for any story involving comedians; and I once appropriated it myself to deplore some lacklustre comedy in a Shakespeare production at Stratford. "Where are the clowns? There ought to be clowns. Well, maybe next year." Unfortunately, my editor lopped off the last phrase, and I've waited all these years to reinstate it. Capers like these, added to the song by just about everybody (Ella Fitzgerald may be the only one holding out), have made it over-familiar; but it keeps coming back to life. It did in the show. At the final curtain, happy ending secured, it surges up full-bodied in the strings to feed the starved romantic in all of us. It's just as well he went to that rehearsal.

records.title: Theatre's living-isms
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
HAROLD PINTER and Peter Brook have gone beyond being legends in their own lifetimes. They are myths.

There hardly seems to have been a time when Pinter was merely a successful playwright. One moment - 1958, actually - The Birthday Party, his first full-length play, was a three-performance flop savaged by nearly every critic. The next - well, almost the next, 1960 - his second full-length play, The Caretaker, was an instant classic, and incontestably The Play To See In London.

No subsequent British play has quite achieved that status, and no subsequent British playwright has been accorded the same cultural authority. We talk occasionally of something being Stoppardian or Ayckbournian, but never with the same confidence, the same certainty of being understood, as when we dub an action, a line, a moment - in life or art - Pinterish or Pinteresque. The man is a fact of English literature.

This can make meeting him in the flesh daunting. When he first spoke to me - I don't think I would have had the nerve to speak first to him - it was a little like being accosted by T. S. Eliot. There was this thing abroad, this body of work called Pinter, and you didn't expect to encounter it in a suit. You certainly didn't expect it to start quizzing you about your own work, which is what he did to me, asking me to clarify something I had said in a column the previous week. He really seemed to want to know. I felt elated.

When it comes to talking about his own work, Pinter has been famously unforthcoming. His own reticence has fused in the general imagination with the celebrated opacity of his plays; their refusal to supply what others would regard as essential information.

This was what most infuriated critics about The Birthday Party and, it seemed, what most impressed them about The Caretaker. The turnaround was lightning-fast; it was eased by a TV production of The Birthday Party that played up the sinister ballooning cross-talk of the dialogue to the point of gimmickry, but was totally riveting.

The concept of Pinterism was born, I suspect, in that production, which prepared a large audience for the subtler virtuosity of The Caretaker whose star role - the lying, scheming, pitiable tramp Davies - may be the last great character creation in British drama ("You were in the colonies, weren't you?" "I was over there, I was one of the first over there"). He takes on independent life through his author's mastery of language: his ability to take familiar speech rhythms and make them sing, to build up long tirades and crown them with catchphrases.

This mastery of tone remained when Pinter - perhaps reflecting his own material success - moved into glossier stage surroundings; the speeches of Spooner, the poetaster of No Man's Land, are quirky and elegant at once, and frostily witty. No other current playwright writes as well; he established his authority by insisting, almost to the point of perversity, that his plays speak for themselves and by giving them a triumphant voice to do it in.

Pinter, however the academics may celebrate or condemn him, is an exceptionally adroit nuts-and-bolts playwright, who works through comedy and suspense. Peter Brook, who ranks among theatre directors as the guru's guru, has a similar command of showbiz values. In his youth, he directed musicals, drawing-room comedies, and pictorial Shakespeares, and even the most ascetic or exotic of his more recent works are designed to have maximum impact as shows.

The Ik, his study of a starving and predatory African tribe, was as casually stark as he could make it. Ubu Roi, the foundation stone of the Theatre of the Absurd, was as anarchically funny as he could make it. Both displayed a very light touch. These latter-day Brook productions originated from his International Centre for Theatre Research, a multi-ethnic troupe based at the Theatre des Bouffes-du-Nord in Paris. There is a sense of Brook holding court, either in the theatre or the cafe opposite; he enjoys being a sage.

The Bouffes-du-Nord is an old suburban theatre with much of its interior torn out. It looks at once the essence of all theatres and the negation of one: the paradox is obviously intentional and very Brookish. He seems sometimes to want to get away from the idea of theatre altogether, and once took his actors on a tour of African villages, playing to people who had never seen anything approaching the European idea of drama.

The trip was much publicised, and widely attacked as a piece of fake primitivism. But Brook has never claimed that what he was doing was superior to playing to bourgeois audiences, in orchestra stalls, just that it was different and might shed some light on the irreducible essence that keeps audiences looking at actors in the first place.

Brook started the tradition of the brilliant post-war just-graduated director, a line over which he still presides. He still seems like a prodigy, having been the premier director in the British theatre probably since 1946 when, at 21, he directed a ravishing Love's Labour's Lost at Stratford.

His austere Measure for Measure and horror-comic Titus Andronicus were the leading Stratford productions of the Fifties; and, in the Sixties, he moved into the reconstituted Royal Shakespeare Company with a monumental King Lear - you could practically smell greatness on it - and with The Marat-Sade, a historical-philosophical piece which he staged like a musical.

In 1970, came the legendary Midsummer Night's Dream which Brook described as his return, after a spate of fearsome Vietnam-era productions, to the light.

It was also virtually his farewell to Britain. But, despite two decades of apparent exile, everybody thinks of him still as part of the British theatre. He never went away, just as Pinter, despite writing little more than playlets in the Eighties, was never seriously thought to have dried up. They still set the standard.

A revival of Pinter's The Birthday Party opens at The National Theatre on Thursday (071-928 2252). Peter Brook's The Man Who begins a national tour at the Contact Theatre, Manchester on Wednesday (061-242 2555).

records.title: Reaching for the king's crown
records.author: Robert Cushman
records.body:
GOODBYE, Renaissance Theatre Company. Or, at the very least, au revoir. The announcement of the company's closure stresses that there will be no more Renaissance films but says that the theatrical end of the operation will retain a nominal existence "in case we want to resurrect it". So there could be a renaissance of Renaissance. But I doubt if anyone is betting on it.

The obvious thought is that the company has been the victim of its own success. Or, more precisely, of Kenneth Branagh's success. The company's moving spirit is currently directing Robert De Niro in Frankenstein. When you are in demand for that grade of movie project, running a theatre company must be difficult to fit in. The wonder may be that he has managed to keep it going at all for seven years.
